164 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Gallbladder The gallbladder is easily imaged with ultrasound because it is fluid filled. The gallbladder is generally round to oval; however, it may be bilobed, particularly in cats, and this is generally of no clinical consequence (see Figure 8.4C). Several artifacts are common when scanning the gallbladder, due to its fluid‐filled nature, and the novice sonographer should become familiar with these artifacts in order to minimize misinterpreta- tions. These include acoustic enhancement, side‐lobe artifact, edge shadowing artifact, and mirror image artifact (when the gallbladder contacts the diaphragm– lung interface). Gallbladder Wall Evaluation of the gallbladder wall is generally easily accomplished due to the contact between the anechoic bile and the more echogenic gallbladder wall and sur - rounding hepatic parenchyma. The normal gallbladder wall appears as an echogenic (white) line surrounding the luminal contents (see Figure 8.4A–C). Diffuse gall- bladder wall thickening may occur with a wide range of conditions such as acute or chronic cholecystitis, hepatitis, canine anaphylaxis (Quantz et al. 2009), right‐sided heart failure, iatrogenic volume overload (Nelson et al. 2010), and hypoalbuminemia (Nyland et al. 2002) (see Chapters 7, 20, 26, and 36). Therefore, the finding must be interpreted in conjunction with additional ultrasound findings as well as clinical signs and biochemical alterations (Figure 8.11; see also Figures 7.11, 7.12, 18.22, and 39.6). Generally, gallbladder wall thickening is nonspe- cific for any of the above conditions and thickening is typically associated with wall edema with similar sonographic features despite the underlying patho- logic cause (see Figure 8.11 and Table 7.5). Most com- monly, the gallbladder wall appears diffusely hypoechoic with parallel hyperechoic lines on either side, referred to as a “double rim effect” or “halo effect” (Nyland et al. 2002; Quantz et al. 2009) (see Figures 7.11, 7.12, 18.22, and 39.6). This change needs to be distinguished from small‐volume fluid external to the gallbladder, where effusion within the gall- bladder fossa can mimic the double rim or halo effect. Focal and/or irregular thickening of the gallbladder wall is less common, and may be consistent with chronic cholecystitis or neoplastic change. A flaccid or undulating gallbladder wall may be consistent with wall rupture and warrants correlation to the index of suspicion for biliary peritonitis as well as clinical and biochemical assessment of the patient. Gallbladder Lumen Evaluation of the luminal gallbladder is typically straightforward due to the ease of scanning through a fluid acoustic window. • Biliary sediment or sludge is common in dogs and can be easily recognized (Figure 8.12). In general, the finding of gravity‐dependent, mobile material is an incidental finding but could be an indication of cholestasis. Gallbladder wall abnormalities should be correlated to clinical and/or clinico- pathological signs of hepatobiliary disease changes (Tsukagoshi et al. 2012). Luminal sedi- ment is usually hyperechoic (bright) and non- shadowing. When mineralized, the debris may cast a distal acoustic shadow (see Figure 8.12D). Biliary sludge is classified as gravity or nongrav- ity dependent and mobile or consolidated. Nongravity‐dependent material may further be classified as adherent or nonadherent to the gall- bladder wall. • Calcified material or choleliths can occasionally be observed within the biliary tract and may also be an incidental finding. These gallbladder stones will cause a distal acoustic shadow similar to a urolith (Figure 8.13; see also 8.12D). • Gallbladder mucoceles always have significant impli- cations and their presence should be confirmed by an experienced sonographer as surgery is often indicated. Gallbladder mucoceles have a distinct appearance and, in the mature form, have a stellate Pearl: In patients in which peritonitis is sus- pected (ruptured gallbladder, perforated bowel, low‐grade bleed), especially in dehydration, fluid resuscitation and reevaluation (serial exam within the next 2–4 hours) with AFAST and an abdominal fluid score often prove most helpful because once rehydrated, peritoneal effusion develops or progresses (higher abdominal fluid score) and sampling for fluid characterization becomes possible. Pearl: When suspicion is raised for intraluminal gallbladder contents, the gallbladder can be reex- amined at the end of the study to see if the possible intraluminal pathology has settled into gravity‐ dependent regions.

Such findings can be seen incidentally or in patients with clinical evidence of advanced hepatobiliary obstruction. The Global FAST approach is used as a screening test to rapidly discriminate between localized and dissem- inated disease, comorbidities, and complications. Global FAST offers a rapid assessment to survey for pleural and pericardial effusion and cardiac and pulmonary abnormalities, including lung nodules, with minimal restraint upon initial patient triage. Pearls and Pitfalls, The Final Say • Normal echogenicity rule of thumb. The spleen (S) is more echogenic (hyperechoic, brighter) than the liver (Li), which is the same or slightly more echo- genic (hyperechic, brighter) than the cortex of the kidney (CK). Remember this as S > Li ≥ CK or the mnemonic “SLiCK” for dogs. For the feline, hepatic echogenicity is often compared to the adjacent fal- ciform fat and the feline liver should be isoechoic to slightly hypoechoic to the falciform fat. • Benign conditions may appear ultrasonographically “malignant.” Hepatic echogenicity can be difficult to interpret and significant liver disease may still be present even with an unremarkable exam. Ultimately, tissue sampling is necessary for defini- tive diagnosis of hepatic parenchymal diseases. • Be familiar with the possible artifacts related to the liver and gallbladder. The fluid‐filled gall- bladder is subject to several artifacts including side‐lobe, edge shadowing, and far‐field acoustic enhancement. A mirror image artifact of the gall- bladder and liver may appear on the thoracic side of the diaphragm due to the air interface between the diaphragm and lung, and can be mistaken for diaphragmatic hernia, pleural and pericardial effusion. • The origin of a large midabdominal mass can some- times be difficult to determine when the mass con- tacts multiple origins. In this case, try repositioning the patient from dorsal to lateral recumbency. This will often separate the liver and spleen from one another and help determine the origin of the mass. • Always look into the thorax through the diaphrag- matic hepatic interface when evaluating liver to investigate the pleural and pericardial spaces, and the lung surface along the diaphragm. • An AFAST and assignment of an abdominal fluid score should be considered as routine for POCUS liver and gallbladder examinations and the Global FAST approach should be performed so as not to miss comorbidities including intraabdominal bleeding or peritonitis as well as intrathoracic conditions. The AFAST and its fluid scoring system should be used on initial patient evaluation and also to mon- itor for complications such as hemorrhage or peri- tonitis after interventional procedures including liver and gallbladder surgeries, percutaneous aspi- rates and biopsies, and laparoscopic procedures. The Global FAST approach is used for postinter - ventional intrathoracic complications including aspiration pneumonia (see Chapters 23 and 36). Quick Reference of Normals and Rules of Thumb • Liver assessment is subjective. Edges of the liver lobes should be sharply pointed. Rounded margins of liver lobes and hepatic extension (especially the left lobes) beyond the costal arch suggest enlarge- ment. Abdominal radiography is more reliable for the determination of hepatomegaly. • Target lesions. Single target lesions have a high pre- dictive value for malignancy. When multiple target lesions are seen, the positive predictive value of malignancy increases from 74% to 81% (Cuccovillo and Lamb 2002), and Global FAST is a rapid and quick assessment test for localized versus dissemi- nated disease by surveying the remainder of the abdomen (AFAST), the thorax (TFAST) including heart (TFAST), and lung (Vet BLUE). • Normal echogenicity rule of thumb. The spleen (S) is more echogenic (hyperechoic) than the liver (Li) which is the same or slightly more echogenic (brighter) than the cortex of the kidney (CK), remembered as S > Li ≥ CK or by the mnemonic “SLiCK.” For the feline, hepatic echogenicity is often compared to the adjacent falciform fat and the feline liver should be isoechoic to slightly hypoechoic to the falciform fat. • Gallbladder wall thickness is normally <1 mm in cats and <3 mm in dogs (Hittmair et al. 2001; Spaulding 1993; Quantz et al. 2009). • Gallbladder luminal content is generally homoge- neous anechoic bile although degrees of gall- bladder sludge may be considered as clinically irrelevant or may indicate cholestasis based on the patient’s clinical profile (Tsukagoshi et al. 2012). • Being fluid filled, the gallbladder is subject to sev- eral artifacts including side‐lobe, slice thickness, edge shadowing, and acoustic enhancement in the

171 POCUS: LIVER AND GALLBLADDER far‐field; and the liver and gallbladder, being adja- cent to the strong soft tissue–air interface between the diaphragm and the aerated lung, are subject to mirror image artifact. • In cats, tortuosity of the bile duct can be a normal variation; however, a bile duct greater than 4 mm (≥5 mm) is considered to be consistent with extra- hepatic biliary obstruction. • When you are unable to effectively visualize the gallbladder using ultrasound (likely due to miner - alized material or air), a good rule of thumb is to add radiography. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 173 Introduction The POCUS examination of the spleen is a valuable diagnostic tool for guiding clinical care and, with ade- quate care and awareness, can be effectively performed by a nonradiologist veterinarian. The POCUS spleen examination is not meant to replace a complete detailed abdominal ultrasound study by a veterinarian with advanced training (the veterinary radiologist or inter - nist) but rather serves as a screening test for obvious abnormalities. Ultrasonographic findings involving the spleen may be subjective and nonspecific, including splenic size and generalized changes in echogenicity. Additionally, the frequent close anatomical contact of the spleen and liver can make it difficult to differen- tiate the origin of a mass, particularly for a less experi- enced sonographer. As stated in Chapter 8, a concurrent AFAST exam- ination should be performed with any of the POCUS abdominal organ examinations to rule out intraab- dominal, retroperitoneal, pleural and pericardial effusions, and in the case of the POCUS spleen exam- ination, to rule out splenic hemorrhage. The AFAST not only detects free peritoneal fluid but also semi- quantitates its volume using its abdominal fluid scoring system and assigning an abdominal fluid score (see Chapter 6). The abdominal fluid score helps predict the degree of anticipated anemia in cases of hemoabdomen (Lisciandro 2011; Lisciandro et al. 2009). Global FAST is an even better approach to survey for pleural and pericardial effusion, cardiac and pulmonary abnormalities, and patient volume status. Moreover, Global FAST is used as a screening test to rapidly discriminate between local- ized versus disseminated disease, comorbidities, and complications, which may be especially helpful in hemoabdomen cases. What the POCUS Spleen Can Do • Identify focal or multifocal splenic masses or nodules. • Identify parenchymal changes by screening for changes in echogenicity associated with diffuse splenic diseases. • Identify splenic infarction and thrombosis. • Help the clinician to recognize splenic torsion. • These last three goals are inherently more difficult for the novice sonographer and abnormalities should prompt referral for a complete detailed abdominal ultrasound examination. What the POCUS Spleen Cannot Do • Differentiate benign from malignant splenic masses. The Global FAST approach is a rapid add‐ on assessment screening test for localized versus disseminated disease through surveying the abdomen (AFAST), the thorax (TFAST) including heart (TFAST), and lung (Vet BLUE) as well as for detecting other comorbidities. • Definitively diagnose diffuse and localized splenic conditions based on echogenicity. • Reliably determine splenic size (large or small) in dogs (more reliable for size in cats). Indications • Cranial organomegaly or pendulous abdomen. • Abdominal pain. • Abdominal trauma. • Hematological disorders such as anemia or thrombocytopenia. • Generalized lymphadenopathy. • Episodes of collapse, lethargy or vomiting. 174 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Objectives • Recognize splenic masses (single, multifocal). • Recognize regional and diffuse changes in splenic echogenicity. • Recognize splenic venous congestion, thrombosis, and infarction. • Recognize splenic torsion. Patient Positioning and Probe Selection A curvilinear (microconvex) probe is most frequently used to image the spleen, and the MHz is adjusted for the size of the animal. Smaller dogs and cats are gener- ally imaged using higher frequencies of 7.5–10 MHz (less penetration, better detail) and large dogs are gen- erally imaged using lower frequencies such as 5 MHz (deeper penetration, less detail). In small dogs and cats, a linear probe may also be used in order to maxi- mize image quality (due to the higher resolution) when greater penetration depth is not of concern. Patients are most commonly imaged in dorsal recumbency. In large dogs, however, the cranial aspect of the spleen is often located under the ribcage on the left side. Repositioning these patients into right lateral recumbency allows visualization of the cranial aspect or head of the spleen using a left intercostal approach (Hecht 2008). The authors recommend performing a Global FAST to screen for any intrathoracic problems including pleural and pericardial effusion, cardiac and pulmonary conditions, and abnormal volume status that may pose patient risk before moving the patient into dorsal recumbency. How to Perform the POCUS Spleen The patient is placed in dorsal recumbency, the abdomen is shaved, and acoustic coupling gel is applied for best visualization. Although image quality will be diminished, ample application of 70% isopropyl alcohol to haired skin can be utilized in an emergency situation. The spleen is located caudal to the stomach on the patient’s left side and can provide an acoustic window for the left kidney (see also Figures 6.18, 16.3, 16.4, 16.5). The spleen is identified by its hyperechoic (bright white) capsule and blood supply splitting its capsule, unlike the liver. Spleen position and size vary between patients and with the degree of gastric filling. The entire length of the spleen is generally not visual- ized in one acoustic window and so its entirety must be traced cranially to the head of the spleen and cau- dally to its tail. The position of the spleen may vary between patients. The head or cranial aspect of the spleen is generally located on the left side caudal to the last rib. In large dogs, it may be located under the ribcage and therefore, repositioning into right lateral recumbency with a left intercostal approach may be necessary. The spleen is then traced caudally toward its hilus where the splenic vein is imaged and seen branching in a “Y” configuration, referred to by some sonographers as the “whale tail” shaped like the tail fluke (Figure 9.1; see also Figures 39.8 and 39.9). Splenic arteries are usually not visualized (Hecht 2008). Evaluation of the spleen continues as the sonographer follows the spleen dis- tally along the left side of the abdomen to examine the caudal aspect of the spleen to its tail so that the entire organ has been examined. Remember that the spleen is anchored at the head by its short gastric vessels along the greater curvature of the stomach but has a relatively mobile tail. In some patients, the tail of the spleen may be located medial and to the right side of the patient instead of the left. Several sweeps along the length and width of the spleen may be necessary for a thorough interrogation, especially in animals with splenomegaly. Ultrasonographic Findings in a Normal Spleen When assessing the spleen, systematic evaluation should include the following four features: estimation of size (subjective), evaluation of changes in parenchymal echogenicity, interrogation for mass lesions and nodules, and assessment of splenic vasculature. Size and Shape The general contour of the spleen is tongue‐shaped and when viewed adjacent to the left kidney, it appears more triangular (than flat) in cross‐sectional views. Since the size of the spleen can vary in normal animals, estimation of size is generally subjective in dogs except in cases of marked splenomegaly. In cats, splenomegaly Pearl: Identify the spleen by its hyperechoic (bright white) capsule and blood supply splitting its capsule, unlike the liver.

175 POCUS: S PLEEN is almost always due to pathology and should prompt further evaluation. Spleen thickness greater than 10 mm or a folded spleen invariably indicates spleno - megaly in the feline species (Hecht 2008; Reese et al. 2013) (Figure 9.2; see also Figure 39.9). Benign spleno- megaly is uncommon in cats and if present, additional evaluation is warranted. Echogenicity The echogenicity of the splenic parenchyma should be evaluated for diffuse and focal changes. Normal splenic parenchyma is homogeneous in appearance with fine echotexture, and its thin hyperechoic (bright white) capsule may be apparent on long‐axis (sagittal) views. Spleen parenchyma is generally mildly to moderately hyperechoic (brighter) to normal liver parenchyma (Figure 9.3A,B), and significantly hyperechoic (brighter) to normal renal cortex (Hecht 2008) (see Figure 9.3C,D). Splenic Size Splenomegaly is usually a subjective assessment except in cases of severe enlargement. Ultrasonographic clues that help in discriminating between normal size and splenomegaly include the following. • Marked enlargement may result in the distal tip of the spleen folding back on itself (Figure 9.5,B) and therefore the distal tip or tail is visualized medial to the left kidney (see Figure 9.5C,D). In addition, the markedly enlarged spleen may extend caudally and come in contact with a small to medium‐sized urinary bladder (Figure 9.6). In cats, a folded spleen supports splenomegaly (Hecht 2008), as does a spleen thicker than 10 mm (Reese et al. 2013) (see Figure 9.9B). • Marked splenomegaly most commonly occurs with neoplasia (lymphosarcoma), other infiltrative processes (fungal infection), acute inflammation, or in some cases of immune‐mediated hemolytic anemia. Extramedullary hematopoiesis can cause marked splenomegaly. Marked spleno - megaly may also occur in animals with splenic torsion (see additional description below) (see Figure 9.15). When splenomegaly is confidently ascertained, corre - lation between size and echogencity can be clinically helpful as follows. • Mild to moderate splenomegaly with normal echogenicity and architecture is most commonly associated with sedation, extramedullary hema - topoiesis, antigenic stimulation (acute inflammatory and infectious diseases), and passive congestion (Figures 9.7 and 9.8A,B). However, diffuse infiltrative processes including lymphoma and mast cell tumor can also have normal echogenicity. • Splenomegaly with mild to moderate hypoechogenicity may be associated with nodular hyperplasia or extramedullary hematopoiesis, passive congestion, inflammation, infection (fungal, bacterial, rickett - sial), immune‐mediated diseases, and lymphosar - coma. Comparison with adjacent liver and the renal cortex can help when assessing echogenicity (Figure 9.9; see also Figure 9.8; see normal relative echogenicity in Figure 9.3). Figure 9.4. 178 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Splenic Mass Lesions Masses and Nodules The identification of nodules or mass lesions within the splenic parenchyma is the most basic of the four features of the POCUS spleen (size, echogenicity, nodules, vasculature). It is important to recognize, however, that ultrasound does not allow differentiation between benign and malignant processes, unless advanced contrast‐enhanced ultra - sound studies are performed (limited availability) that still may not prove helpful (Fife et al. 2004; Rossi et al. 2008). The sonographer should keep in mind that according to one study, benign splenic masses are more common than malignant splenic masses in dogs (Fife et al. 2004). • Nodular hyperplasia. Nodules associated with nod - ular hyperplasia or extramedullary hematopoiesis may be variable in echogenicity (hyperechoic, hypoechoic, isoechoic or mixed echogenicity) when compared to normal splenic parenchyma (Figure 9.10A,B). In addition, nodular hyperplasia may be associated with a mildly irregular splenic capsule without associated nodular lesions. This change is commonly seen in older dogs. Figure 9.5. Splenomegaly. 179 POCUS: S PLEEN • Myelolipoma. Myelolipomas are incidental findings in older dogs and are identified as discrete, strongly hyperechoic (bright) and frequently irregularly shaped nodules most often located near the hilus or associated with the parenchymal vessels. Less commonly, they are smooth in shape and buried within the splenic parenchyma. They are generally small in size but are occasionally quite large and can also be seen in cats. Myelolipomas are typically of no clinical consequence (incidental finding) (see Figure 9.10C,D). • Hematoma. Abdominal trauma may be associated with hematomas and splenic parenchymal injury (Figure 9.11). Hematomas (benign masses) may be variable in appearance but initially are generally anechoic to hypoechoic (darker) when compared to normal splenic parenchyma. As the blood within the hematoma forms a clot, the lesion may become more isoechoic or hyperechoic to normal parenchyma. As the clot retracts, the lesion may again become hypoechoic. Anechoic fluid may form around the clot and appear as a cyst‐like lesion. These factors may make hematomas diffi - cult to distinguish from other mass lesions, including neoplasia. • Abscess. Splenic abscesses are uncommon and usu- ally cannot be distinguished from other processes that produce nodular or mass lesions. The appear - ance may be variable with well‐defined or indis - tinct margins and variable echogenicity. Abscesses most commonly appear as hypoechoic lesions, which may have cystic components or mixed echo- genicity. A more conclusive finding for an abscess (in contrast to neoplastic processes) is the presence of gas (due to gas‐forming bacteria) within the lesion. This appears as focal areas of hyperecho - genicity with distal edge shadowing (see Chapter 3). Figure 9.6. Splenomegaly with spleen extending to urinary bladder. This severely enlarged spleen extends caudally to the fluid‐filled (anechoic) urinary bladder. Although it appears relatively normal regarding its echotexture and echogenicity, this dog had splenic lymphosarcoma diag - nosed by percutaneous needle biopsy. Compare to Figure 9.14 showing the ultrasonographic variability of splenic lympho- sarcoma (LSA). Figure 9.7 . Splenomegaly with normal echogenicity. Infectious diseases can cause splenomegaly with variable changes in echogenicity. Shown here is an image from a dog with ehrlichiosis. Pearl: In cases with nodular lesions, it may be diffi - cult to differentiate changes associated with nodular hyperplasia from other processes without further testing (cytology or histopathology). Pearl: Fine needle biopsy of hematomas generally yields nonspecific cytological results and therefore the absence of neoplastic cells on cytology does not rule out neoplasia. A more definitive diagnosis of hematoma is obtained by splenectomy and histo - pathological evaluation; however, even this may be complicated by a large hematoma associated with a smaller malignant mass, resulting in a possible misdiagnosis.

180 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Neoplasia Splenic neoplastic lesions can have a wide range of ultrasonographic changes. As emphasized above, it is not possible to distinguish between benign and malignant lesions based on ultrasonographic appear - ance alone. The most common types of splenic neo - plasia found in dogs are hemangiosarcoma and lymphosarcoma (Hecht 2008) but other primary and metastatic tumors are possible. • Hemangiosarcoma (HSA) generally appears as complex mass lesions with mixed echogenicity and cavitations that distort the splenic capsule (Figure 9.12). HSA of the spleen is often associ - ated with acute or chronic hemorrhage, and ani - mals with ruptured splenic masses causing hemoabdomen have a higher likelihood of malig - nancy (hemangiosarcoma) (Hammond and Pesillo‐Crosby 2008). One must keep in mind, though, that a sonographic target lesion is a nonspecific finding and a biopsy is required for diagnosis. When finding a splenic target lesion, look for other intraabdominal or intrathoracic masses using Global FAST, radiography (screening for lung nodules) or both. The identification of additional nodules provides further suspicion for malignancy and may also provide a more acces - sible scanning plane for percutaneous sampling. • Lymphosarcoma (LSA) has a variable appearance when associated with the spleen. LSA may appear as a focal mass lesion, multifocal mass lesions, or as diffuse parenchymal disease referred to as a “honeycomb,” “moth‐eaten” or “Swiss cheese” appearance (Figure 9.14) (Nyland et al. 2002). Mass lesions due to LSA are gener - ally hypoechoic with indistinct margins and may be singular or multifocal in nature. However, they can also be isoechoic or slightly hyperechoic to normal splenic parenchyma, and may or may not distort the splenic contour (see Figures 9.6 and 9.8A,B). Figure 9.12. Therefore, it is always important to base a diagnosis on other clinical findings as well as cyto- logical and histopathological evaluation. Echogenicity and Parenchymal Conditions Evaluation of diffuse parenchymal disease is subjective and can be difficult for the novice sonographer. Echogenicity of the spleen is assessed by comparing splenic parenchyma to the adjacent liver and left renal (kidney) cortex as described above. Changes in echo - genicity can be seen with extramedullary hematopoi - esis, passive congestion, nodular hyperplasia, inflammation, infection, neoplasia, and splenic torsion. • Extramedullary hematopoiesis . Generally associated with mildly reduced echogenicity (hypoechoic). • Passive splenic congestion. Generally associated with hypoechoic changes in acute phases but may be associated with hyperechoic changes in more chronic processes. Architecture is rarely disrupted. • Nodular hyperplasia. May be associated with either hypoechoic or hyperechoic changes which are relatively mild. The splenic capsule may be mildly irregular as described above. Nodular hyperplasia is a benign condition commonly seen in older dogs (see Figure 9.8C,D). • Inflammatory or infectious diseases (fungal, bacterial, rickettsial). Generally these conditions cause mild to moderate splenomegaly with diffuse hypoecho- genicity. With acute inflammation or infection, the changes are more pronounced with more prominent hypoechogenicity and a finely mottled appearance (see Figures 9.7 and 9.9A,B). • Neoplastic conditions . Lymphosarcoma, mast cell tumor, and other myeloproliferative diseases gen - erally produce an appearance of generalized coarse mottling referred to as a “honeycomb”, “moth‐eaten” or “Swiss cheese” appearance (Nyland et al. 2002) (compare Figure 9.14 to Figures 9.6 and 9.8A,B). It is important to remember that both lymphosarcoma and mast cell tumor can also be present with very mild diffuse changes and the spleen may even have a normal appearance. As a result, fine needle biopsies of the spleen may be indicated even in the absence of sonographic abnormalities. • Splenic torsion. Marked splenomegaly with a dif - fusely hypoechoic to anechoic lacy appearance (compared to the hyperechoic [brighter] lacy appear- ance seen with LSA of the parenchyma) is typical of Figure 9.14. Lymphosarcoma (LSA). The “Swiss cheese” or “moth‐eaten” appearance of the spleen is often caused by LSA. However, LSA has variable presentations including a diffuse homogeneous echogenicity change that is hyper‐ or hypoechoic. Moreover, splenic LSA may appear ultrasono - graphically unremarkable. Compare to Figure 9.6 showing the variability of splenic LSA and Figure 9.16 showing the lacy appearance of splenic torsion. Figure 9.13. Target lesion. Target lesions suggest metastatic neoplasia and should trigger a search for a primary tumor as well as other sites of metastasis, and the Global FAST approach serves as a rapid screening staging test. Pearl: Diagnosis of all presentations of lymphosar - coma may be made via percutaneous needle biopsy (Crabtree et al. 2010).

Routine Add‐on of AFAST and Its Abdominal Fluid Scoring System (or Global FAST) In the authors’ experience, it is extremely valuable to perform an AFAST examination with assignment of an abdominal fluid score in either lateral recumbency for the best approach. The positioning of small animals in dorsal recumbency for POCUS abdominal organ exam- inations can obscure small‐volume peritoneal effusion and underestimate the volume of effusion present because peritoneal effusion will flow into the less sono- graphically accessible diaphragmatic recesses. AFAST improves the diagnostic potential of ultrasound by detecting peritoneal effusion. The early detection of abdominal effusion is clinically important and helps direct additional diagnostic recommendations while avoiding morbidity, complications, and patient mortality in the event the effusion is missed. Global FAST offers a rapid assessment of the abdomen (AFAST) and to survey for pleural and pericardial effusion (TFAST),and cardiac and pulmonary abnormalities (TFAST and Vet BLUE), including lung nodules, with minimal restraint upon initial patient triage. Pearls and Pitfalls, The Final Say It is important for the nonradiologist veterinarian to respect the limitations of the POCUS spleen examina- tion because of the sonographic variability of many diffuse and nodular conditions. Fortunately, the spleen is amenable to minimally invasive cytological evalua- tion by percutaneous needle biopsy or aspirates when sonographic abnormalities are identified. Although hemorrhage is an uncommon complica- tion of percutaneous fine needle biopsy, the AFAST format with fluid scoring system (see Chapters 6 and 7) is an excellent tool for postsampling monitoring (four hours post procedure and as needed thereafter), and is more sensitive than traditional means such as packed cell volume (hematocrit) for occult hemor - rhage. Finally, a splenectomy with appropriate culture and histopathological testing may be required for definitive diagnosis and treatment plan, and the spleen may be surgically removed with little long‐term consequence in both dogs and cats. Global FAST is an especially helpful approach to rapidly survey for pleural and pericardial effusion, and cardiac and pulmonary abnormalities, and is used as a screening test to rapidly discriminate between localized and dis- seminated disease, comorbidities, and complications (see Chapters XX and XX). • Evaluation of splenomegaly is a subjective assessment in dogs unless splenic enlargement is severe. • Splenomegaly in cats is almost always due to pathology and warrants additional evaluation. • Nodular and mass lesions within the splenic parenchyma are common and usually easy to iden- tify. It is not possible to distinguish benign and malignant processes without cytology or histopathology. • Splenic hematoma and hemangiosarcoma cannot be differentiated on the basis of ultrasound alone, and may be concurrent. However, use of the Global FAST approach is helpful to rapidly screen for localized versus disseminated disease. • If the origin of an abdominal mass is difficult to determine, move the patient from dorsal to lateral recumbency. By doing so, the liver and spleen will often separate from one another, helping to better determine the origin of the mass. • Needle visualization by ultrasound facilitates fine needle percutaneous biopsy of the spleen. Nonspecific cytology results with fine needle biopsy do not rule out the possibility of a malig- nant lesion, and further diagnostics are required. However, the use of the Global FAST approach is helpful to rapidly screen for localized versus dis- seminated disease. • Mild diffuse changes in echogenicity are subjective and can be challenging for the novice sonographer. • Remember the mnemonic “SLiCK” regarding the echogenicity between the spleen (S), liver (Li), and cortex of the kidney (CK). The echogenicity of the spleen is greater (brighter) than the liver, which is slightly greater (brighter) or isoechoic (same as) than the cortex of the kidney. For the feline, hepatic echogenicity is often compared to the adjacent falciform fat and the feline liver should be isoechoic to slightly hypoechoic to the falciform fat. • Several benign processes cause mild to moderate diffuse changes in echogenicity including extra- medullary hematopoiesis, passive congestion, and antigenic stimulation. • Diffuse changes associated with lymphosarcoma or other myeloproliferative disorders can be vari- able in appearance and occasionally can be associ- ated with a normal or unremarkable splenic appearance. • Fine needle percutaneous biopsies are indicated in cases of moderate to severe splenomegaly or in ani- mals with diffuse changes in echogenicity. Quick Reference of Normals and Rules of Thumb • Spleen size is subjective. A spleen that extends to a small or medium‐sized urinary bladder is consid- ered enlarged. • A folded spleen in a cat is always as a general rule considered abnormal and indicates splenomegaly (Hecht 2008).

188 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER • Normal cat spleen thickness is <10 mm (Reese et al. 2013). • Benign nodular hyperplasia usually consists of nodules that are of homogeneous echotexture being either hypoechoic or hyperechoic. • Single target lesions have a high predictive value for malignancy. When multiple target lesions are seen, the positive predictive value of malignancy increases from 74% to 81% (Cuccovillo and Lamb 2002). • Normal echogenicity rule of thumb: the spleen (S) is more echogenic (hyperechoic) than the liver (Li) which is the same or slightly more echogenic (brighter) than the cortex of the kidney (CK), remembered as S > Li ≥ CK or by the mnemonic “SLiCK.” For the feline, hepatic echogenicity is often compared to the adjacent falciform fat and the feline liver should be isoechoic to slightly hypoechoic to the falciform fat. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 189 Introduction POCUS to evaluate the kidneys can provide valuable clinical information to the nonradiologist veterinarian to expedite diagnosis and treatment. The POCUS kidney examination may be especially beneficial in patients with an index of suspicion for acute kidney injury, kidney failure of undetermined cause and postrenal obstruction by screening for several easily recognizable ultrasonographic findings. The POCUS kidney cannot predict kidney function and, in most instances, does not provide information regarding response to therapy. Animals may have a normal ultra- sonographic examination with severe kidney dysfunction. Conversely, some animals may have an abnormal ultrasonographic examination with normal kidney function. The POCUS kidney does not replace a complete detailed abdominal ultrasound study per - formed by a veterinarian with advanced training (a veterinary radiologist or internist). As with all imaging modalities, ultrasound has inherent weaknesses and should be used in conjunction with, and not to the exclusion of, other diagnostic tests such as abdominal radiography and other renal imaging procedures (e.g., intravenous radiographic, enhanced computed tomography, or retrograde positive contrast pyelography), tissue and fluid sam- pling, microbial urine culture, sampling of peritoneal effusions, renal cortical fine needle aspiration or biopsy, or other renal function screening and confirma- tory tests. Finally, as with all POCUS abdomen‐related organ examinations, the concurrent use of an AFAST is rec- ommended for further patient assessment. The AFAST increases the likelihood of identifying effusive condi- tions (e.g., hemorrhage, ascites, uroperitoneum and uroretroperitoneum, or other forms of peritonitis), which plays an important role in guiding clinical care and decision making. Global FAST provides further assessment for pleural and pericardial effusion (TFAST), and cardiac (TFAST) and pulmonary abnor - malities (Vet BLUE), and can help differentiate bet- ween localized and obvious disseminated disease, while aiding in the diagnosis of comorbidities and complications (see Chapter 36). What POCUS Kidney Can Do • Recognize renal parenchymal abnormalities such as cysts, nodules, and masses. • Identify kidney stones (nephroliths). • Evaluate for pyelectasia and dilation of the proximal ureter. • Identify hydronephrosis. • Determine the presence of retroperitoneal fluid. • Help determine the presence of renal infarcts (espe- cially cats). • Measure kidney size and margination and evaluate for asymmetry. In addition, serial assessment may be beneficial in acute kidney injury. What POCUS Kidney Cannot Do • Differentiate benign versus malignant kidney masses. • Diagnose pyelonephritis. • Define the character of retroperitoneal fluid. • Provide reliable information regarding renal function and glomerular filtration; ultrasound also cannot determine potential response to therapy. • Definitively diagnose ethylene glycol toxicity or other causes of acute kidney failure. 190 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Indications • Hematuria. • Polyuria and polydipsia of undetermined cause. • Acute kidney failure of undetermined cause. • Discrepancies in comparative palpable or radio- graphic kidney size. • Uncharacterized, perceived back pain, peritoneal or retroperitoneal abnormalities of uncertain etiology. • Abdominal pain. Objectives • Recognize changes in echogenicity consistent with diffuse parenchymal disease. • Recognize focal parenchymal changes such as kidney cysts and masses. • Recognize kidney stones (nephroliths). • Recognize acute and chronic renal infarcts. • Recognize pyelectasia. • Recognize hydronephrosis/hydroureter. • Recognize retroperitoneal and perirenal (subcap- sular) fluid. • Determine the presence of renal agenesis. Patient Positioning and Probe Selection Imaging the kidneys is most frequently performed using a curvilinear (microconvex) probe of the highest possible frequency that allows adequate penetration. Higher frequency linear probes (7.5–10 MHz) provide less penetration but better detail and may be used in smaller dogs and cats. Conversely, a lower frequency probe (5 MHz) provides more penetration but less image detail, and is usually required in larger dogs. Depth should be adjusted to visualize the entire kidney in both the long‐axis and short‐axis views. Dogs and cats may be scanned in dorsal or right and left lateral recumbency. In most small animals, both kidneys can be adequately imaged in dorsal recum- bency. However, in large or deep‐chested dogs, it is often necessary to also image kidneys in lateral recum- bencies (right decubitus for the left kidney and left decubitus for visualization of the right kidney) due to their dorsal position within the retroperitoneal space. Left lateral recumbency and an intercostal or subcostal scanning acoustic window are particularly helpful for the right kidney because of its more cranial and some- times subcostal orientation. The left kidney, located caudal to the last rib and caudomedial to the spleen, is generally easy to image in dorsal recumbency in both dogs and cats regardless of patient size. A gas‐filled gastrointestinal tract (particularly the transverse or descending colon) can obscure complete renal visuali- zation because ultrasound does not transmit through air. Minor adjustments in patient positioning to redis- tribute intestinal gas can address this issue. Patient Preparation Image quality is improved by shaving the ventral abdomen for evaluation of the kidneys. If an inter - costal approach is used, additional clipping may be required, but clipping may be avoided for cosmetic reasons by parting the hair and applying alcohol to the skin in addition to acoustic coupling gel. How to Perform the POCUS Kidney When the patient is in dorsal recumbency, the left kidney is visualized caudal to the stomach and spleen within the left dorsolateral abdomen. The spleen is visualized in the near‐field and provides an acoustic window for visualization of the left kidney, which is deep to the spleen (Figure 10.1A,B; see also Figures 6.17, 6.18, and 39.13). The entire kidney can be seen on the ultrasound screen by adjusting the depth of field as needed. In some very large patients, the full sagittal length of the kidney may not be visualized regardless of depth. In these cases, fanning while scanning with rocking and sliding motions of the probe should help to fully evaluate all aspects of the organ. The kidney should be completely scanned from just beyond the serosal margins in both the long (longitudinal/sagittal) and short (transverse) axes (or image scanning planes). Scanning and fanning can be facilitated by obtaining the long‐axis (longitudinal/ sagittal/dorsal) view and then gently fanning the probe medially and laterally followed by reorientation of the probe 90° counterclockwise to the long axis. This motion leads to the short‐axis (transverse) view upon which continued slow fanning and scanning with the probe from the cranial to caudal pole can be performed. Pearl: The intestinal tract falls away from the nongravity‐dependent kidney when the patient is in lateral recumbency.

192 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER The right kidney is generally more difficult to find due to its location, especially in large or deep‐chested dogs. The right kidney is located more cranially than the left kidney and in dorsal recumbency is typically found tucked under the right costal arch, caudal to the liver, and sits in the renal fossa of the caudate liver lobe (see Figures 10.1C,D and 6.34) so that the cranial right renal cortex contacts hepatic parenchyma. The right kidney is also anatomically caudal to the pyloric outflow tract and adjacent to the duodenum. Remember that the kid- neys are located dorsally and it may be necessary to sweep to the right and caudally, following the caudal border of the costal arch to find the right kidney. In large and deep‐chested dogs, it may be necessary to angle the probe (its beam) cranial under the last rib, or to reposition the patient in left lateral recumbency for an intercostal approach. Left lateral recumbency gener- ally allows for better long‐axis (longitudinal/sagittal) views of the kidney through an intercostal space, rather than the angled appearance of the kidney when imaged from caudal to the costal margin in dorsal recumbency. Once the desired long‐axis (longitudinal/sagittal) image is obtained, the probe is gently fanned from medial to lateral to obtain images through all planes of the kidney. The probe is then rotated 90° counterclock- wise (turn to the left) for the short‐axis (transverse) view and moved from the cranial to caudal pole to allow for evaluation of the entire kidney. Ultrasonographic Findings in a Normal Kidney Four main organ features (anatomy, size, margin - ation, and symmetry) should be assessed when determining whether or not the kidneys are normal or have changes consistent with pathology. Furthermore, in normalcy, fluid is absent. No perire - nal (subcapsular) or retroperitoneal fluid should be evident in clinically normal patients. Basic normal renal ultrasonographical anatomy is shown in Figures 10.2 and 10.3. Kidney Anatomy The kidney is divided into three distinct regions that need to be assessed: the cortex, medulla, and renal pelvis. Cortex The cortex is the outermost region of the kidney and is hyperechoic (or brighter than) the inner medullary tissue. A distinct demarcation is noted between these two areas and is generally referred to as corticomedul- lary distinction. Corticomedullary distinction may be classified as normal or decreased by variable degrees (mild, moderate, severe). 194 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER (also called the renal contour) is also assessed and should be smooth with a thin echogenic renal capsule. Normal cortical tissue is isoechoic or slightly hypoechoic to normal liver tissue, although it may also be slightly hyperechoic to the liver in cats in the normal state due to increased renal tubular fatty deposition (see Figures 39.10 and 39.11) (Yeager and Anderson 1989) and in some dogs as a normal variation (see Figure 10.1C,D,E). Renal cortical tissue is hypoechoic to the echogenicity of normal splenic tissue (see Figure 10.1A,B). Apparent alteration in the normal echogenicity between adjacent organs generally indicates pathology in one or more of the organs being com- pared. However, echogenicity is affected by the type of probe, frequency, depth of evaluation, and gain settings. Therefore, the ability to perceive subtle dif- ferences in comparative echogenicity may require more operator experience or may sometimes not be possible (see Figure 10.3E). The astute sonographer must consider the concurrent conditions of organs (liver, spleen) to which the renal cortex is being com- pared in order to determine which, if any, are normal or abnormal. Medulla The medulla is hypoechoic or darker than normal renal cortical tissue and there is a clear demarcation between normal cortical and medullary tissue. The normal medullary margin has a circumferentially symmetrical appearance with radiating linear echo- genicities due to the presence of interlobar vessels (see Figures 10.1F and 10.3B,C) and pelvic diver - ticula (see Figure 10.3D) which are uniformly arranged (like the appearance of a tomato in cross‐ section) (see Figures 10.3A, 39.10, and 39.11). In addition, some animals may have a linear hyper - echoic (bright) medullary rim sign (incidental rim sign) that can be of normal variation and clinically irrelevant (d’Anjou 2008). Renal Pelvis The renal pelvis is more difficult to evaluate, especially in normal animals where it may not be readily visual- ized (see Figure 10.3A–D). The renal pelvis may be dis- tended and thus more apparent in animals receiving intravenous fluids or diuretic therapy. In these cases, the degree of distension is usually bilaterally symmet- rical and mild (but can be unilateral) (Pugh et al. 1994; Felkai and Voros Fenyes 1995) (see section on Pyelectasia later in this chapter, and Figure 10.11). The pelvis is frequently surrounded by fat, especially in felines, which is hyperechoic (bright) and is distin- guished from mineralized material by the absence of an acoustic shadow (see Figure 10.2D). The renal pelvis appears linear or “T”‐shaped in sagittal views and “V‐shaped” in transverse views. There is variability of normal pelvic measurements in both cats and dogs. Normal renal diameter in cats is typically 1.5–2 mm, with a maximum diameter of 2.8 mm, and in dogs is 2–3 mm, with a maximum diameter of 3.8 mm (d’Anjou et al. 2011) (see Figures 10.13A–D, 39.10, and 39.11). The normal ureter should not contain fluid and is difficult to image due to the small luminal diameter (typically 1–1.8 mm) (Neuwirth et al. 1993). Any degree of ureteral dilation typically indicates pathology (see Figure 10.13C). Kidney Size Kidney size should be evaluated through measurement of long‐axis views. Symmetry of size and architecture between the right and left kidney is equally important (Figure 10.4; see also Figures 39.10 and 39.11). • Cats. Normal kidney size in cats is generally considered to be 3.0–4.4 cm in length depending on the reference (Nickel et al. 1973; Walter et al. 1987). Pearl: Remember the “SLiCK” mnemonic regarding canine echogenicity: the spleen (S) is hyperechoic (brighter) to liver (Li) which is slightly more hyper- echoic (brighter) or isoechoic (same echogenicity) to the cortex of the kidney (CK). In the order of most echogenic to least echogenic, this spells “SLiCK.” For the feline, hepatic echogenicity is often com- pared to the adjacent falciform fat and the feline liver should be isoechoic to slightly hypoechoic to the falciform fat. Pearl: The normal renal medulla appears like a tomato in cross‐section. Medullary rim signs, while once thought to be clinically relevant, are found in both normal and abnormal kidneys and in many cases are clinically irrelevant. Pearl: The renal pelvis should be considered dilated (referred to as pyelectasia) if it measures ≥3 mm in cats and ≥4 mm in dogs. Pearl: Renal anatomy, including the cortex, medulla and pelvis, is one of the basic characteristics to assess when evaluating the kidney.

195 POCUS: K IDNEY • Dogs. Normal kidney size in dogs varies signifi - cantly with body weight, and normal size values for dog kidneys have not been established. Thus, renal size in dogs is a subjective assessment, and assessment of symmetry is more important. Asymmetry of size or architecture supports kidney pathology. Clinical Significance and Implications of Abnormal Kidney Findings The goal of the POCUS kidney is to identify abnormal- ities such as parenchymal disorders, kidney stones (nephroliths), renal infarcts, subcapsular renal fluid, margin irregularity, renal pelvic abnormalities such as pyelectasia and hydronephrosis, and perinephric or retroperitoneal fluid. Kidney Parenchymal Disorders Evaluation for kidney parenchymal disease should include the ability to detect the presence of diffuse abnormalities as well as focal abnormalities such as masses and cysts. Diffuse Parenchymal Disease Diffuse parenchymal disease may be more difficult to detect for a less experienced sonographer. Changes are evaluated by comparing renal cortical echogenicity to normal liver and splenic tissue. Recall the “SLiCK” mne- monic discussed previously for normal echogenicity: splenic parenchyma is brighter than liver parenchyma which is slightly brighter or the same echogenicity as the cortex of the kidney (see Figure 10.1A–E). In general, disorders that result in increased echo - genicity (cortical tissue that is hyperechoic or brighter than spleen and liver) include ethylene glycol toxicosis, pyelonephritis, other acute toxicities, glomerular dis - ease, interstitial nephritis, end‐stage kidney disease, infiltrative neoplasia (lymphosarcoma), amyloidosis, and hypercalcemic nephropathy (see Figure 10.4). The presence of a hyperechoic medullary rim sign in animals with hyperechoic cortical tissue (medullary rim sign) is nonspecific, but may increase the suspicion for hyper - calcemic nephropathy, ethylene glycol toxicosis, pyo - granulomatous inflammation due to feline infectious peritonitis, leptospirosis, and chronic interstitial nephritis (Adams et al. 1991; d’Anjou 2008) (Figure 10.5C). It must also be noted, however, that these changes (both hyper- echoic cortices and hyperechoic medullary rim signs) can be seen in normal cats and occasionally in normal dogs (see Figure 10.5C). Therefore, evaluation of a patient’s full clinical picture, further assessment by an experienced sonographer, and interventional diagnos- tics such as cortical aspirates or renal biopsy are often necessary to determine the significance of these changes. 196 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Focal Parenchymal Disorders Focal parenchymal conditions such as cysts and masses are easier to detect than diffuse abnormalities and are subdivided into mass lesions, renal cysts, and other fluid‐ filled pathology (e.g., abscess, granuloma, hematoma). Mass Lesions Mass lesions may occur in the renal cortex or medulla and frequently result in distortion of the renal contour. Figure 10.5. Hyperechoic kidneys and medullary rim sign. (A,B) Images from a middle‐aged dog with unexplained acute kidney injury that was minimally responsive to intravenous fluid diuresis and antibiotic therapy. The kidneys were asymmet- rical. Note the severely hyperechoic renal cortices. Differentials for these ultrasonographic changes include hypercalcemic nephropathy, pyogranulomatous inflammation due to feline infectious peritonitis (FIP), leptospirosis, amyloidosis, and chronic interstitial nephritis. It should be noted that in fact hyperechoic cortices may be a normal finding more commonly seen in cats (because of a higher renal tubular fat content) than dogs (FF, free fluid; LIV , liver; LK, left kidney; RK, right kidney). (C) The medullary rim sign may or may not represent true renal pathology and has been referred to as the halo sign through its obser- vation in dogs and cats with ethylene glycol (EG) toxicosis. However, its observation should be cautiously interpreted because there are other causes than EG and the sign may be seen in canine kidneys with normal renal function. Pearl: The halo sign and medullary rim sign are two different renal ultrasonographic findings. The halo sign is a hypoechic (dark) rim in between hyperechoic (bright) medullary and cortical regions and is best known as occurring with ethylene glycol toxicosis (Adams et al. 1989, 1991). The medullary rim sign is a hyperechoic line within the medulla parallel to the corticomedullary junction and is nonspecific (Biller et al. 1992).

It is not possible to differentiate benign from malignant processes based on sonographic appearance alone. For example, benign processes such as retroperitoneal hemorrhage and subsequent large blood clot, or fungal disease causing a granuloma, can mimic a mass lesion and be misinter- preted as a malignant process (Figure 10.7). 199 POCUS: K IDNEY Renal Cysts Renal cysts are easy to identify and may either be due to benign processes or associated with functional dis - ease. Characteristics of true cysts include the presence of thin walls with central anechoic fluid and distal acoustic enhancement artifact. Cysts may be solitary or multiple and involve one or both kidneys. Benign cysts are generally cortical although they may extend into the medulla, and may result in distortion of the renal contour but rarely disturb the corticomedullary architecture. They may be relatively large and the sig - nificance of cysts is determined not by size but by number (Figure 10.8A,B; see also Figure 16.18). In ani - mals with congenital polycystic kidney disease (as can occur in long‐haired cats and cairn terriers), the cysts are generally numerous and result in distortion of both the renal contour and the corticomedullary architecture (d’Anjou 2008) (see Figure 10.8C,D). 200 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Perinephric Pseudocysts Pseudocysts are accumulations of fluid under the renal capsule creating the appearance of a cyst (a pseudo- cyst). A kidney can be identified within the large volume of pseudocyst fluid, which is typically anechoic. As they are frequently associated with chronic renal disease, the kidney is often small and may have chronic degenerative changes (such as irreg- ular margination or cortical hyperechogenicity). Other Fluid‐filled Structures True cysts must also be differentiated from other path- ological processes such as abscess, hematoma or tumor. These disorders are more likely to be present if the cystic structure has a thick wall, echogenic contents, or the presence of internal septations (Figure 10.9). Aspiration of fluid may help to identify and charac- terize these disorders and should generally be per - formed by an experienced sonographer. Infiltrative Processes Infiltrative conditions such as renal lymphosarcoma or diffuse renal carcinoma result in changes in echo- genicity as well as distortion of the normal corticome- dullary architecture (enlarged irregular kidneys and loss of symmetry) (Figure 10.10A,B). Lymphosarcoma in cats is typically diffusely infiltrative and associated with increased cortical echogenicity. In dogs, lympho- sarcoma may be infiltrative but more commonly causes mass lesions (typically hypoechoic). These disorders are often accompanied by the presence of a rim of sub- capsular perinephric fluid as well as distortion of normal corticomedullary architecture (see Figure 10.10C,D). Kidney Stones Kidney stones (nephroliths) may be detected by POCUS kidney. Kidney stones or renal calculi have bright reflective surfaces and typically cause strong acoustic shadowing distal to the mineralized area (Figure 10.11A–D). Very small calculi may cast negligible acoustic shadows. The calculi may be non- obstructive or obstructive and assessment of the renal pelvis for dilation will help to determine significance. Renal calcification, also referred to as dystrophic mineralization, may involve the parenchymal tissue usually at the corticomedullary junction or the renal pelvis (see Figure 10.11E,F). Calcification of the cortico- medullary tissue must be differentiated from the normal hyperechoic tissue seen at the corticomedul- lary junction due to the presence of interlobar/arcuate vessels (see Figures 10.1F and 10.3B,C). These normal structures do not result in acoustic shadows. Calcification at the renal pelvis must be differentiated from the presence of renal pelvic fat (see Figure 10.2). More recently, a new artifact described using color Doppler, called the “twinkle artifact,” has been used to detect uroliths (renal, ureteral, and bladder) that are <5 mm in people (Gliga et al. 2017). See Chapter 11 for greater detail. Pyelectasia Pyelectasia is defined as renal pelvic dilation without other dilation of the collecting system. It should be characterized as unilateral or bilateral and its symmetry as symmetrical or asymmetrical in determining the sig- nificance of this finding (Figure 10.12; see also Figure 16.18). The normal renal pelvis is collapsed, typically measuring less than 2 mm. Normal renal pelvic dilation ranges in cats from 1.5 to 2 mm, with maximum height of 2.8 mm, and in dogs from 2 to 3 mm with a maximum height of 3.8 mm (d’Anjou et al. 2011). A general rule of thumb is to consider the renal pelvis abnormal if it mea- sures ≥3 mm cats and ≥4 mm dogs. Causes of pyelectasia include pyelonephritis, total or partial obstruction of urine flow, intravenous fluid therapy, diuretic therapy, a distended urinary bladder, acute kidney injury, and some congenital disorders (Pugh et al. 1994; Felkai and Voros Fenyes 1995; Cole et al. 2019) (Table 10.1). Pearl: Polycystic kidney disease is most common in domestic long‐haired cats and cairn terriers. Pearl: Kidney stones (renal calculi, nephroliths) are usually identified in B‐mode by the presence of strong acoustic shadowing distal to the mineralized area. This helps differentiate mineralization from normal hyperechoic findings due to interlobar/ arcuate vessels at the corticomedullary junction or fat in the renal pelvis. In other words, interlobar/ arcuate vessels and renal pelvic fat may be hyper - echoic (bright white) but generally do not cast a distal shadow. Pearl: Small nephroliths and renal mineralization may be more readily visible by abdominal radiography.

201 POCUS: K IDNEY Pyelonephritis cannot be determined on the basis of ultrasound alone but is more likely when associ - ated with clinical signs (polyuria/polydipsia, active urine sediment). Generally, pyelonephritis causes mild to moderate dilation of the renal pelvis, which is usually unilateral but may be bilateral with chronic infection. The dilation is usually asymmetrical and concurrent dilation of the proximal ureter (>1.8–2 mm) may also be seen (Neuwirth et al. 1993). The absence of pyelectasia does not rule out the presence of pyelo - nephritis, especially in acute disease, and the presence of pyelectasia does not confirm pyelonephritis. In contrast, diuresis (from either intravenous fluid therapy or diuretic therapy) often results in mild sym- metrical dilation of the renal pelvis and therefore the symmetrical form of pyelectasia seen in these patients is usually of lesser clinical concern. Kidney Infarcts Renal infarction generally results when the blood supply to part of the kidney is impaired. The appear - ance of renal infarcts can be variable and is based on Figure 10.13. Renal infarcts may be hypoechoic (dark) initially and gradually become more echogenic (brighter) over the course of 7–17 days when they generally appear as focal‐shaped, triangular hyperechoic (bright) regions within the cortex, followed by depression and shrinkage of the parenchyma due to fibrosis (Figure 10.14). Other causes of focal hyperechoic renal cortical lesions include calcification, papillary necrosis, and neoplasia. Infarcts typically have a wedge‐shaped appearance with the broad base of the wedge near the surface of the kidney and the point of the wedge extending toward the medulla. When chronic, the infarcted tissue may cause a flattening, distortion or indentation of the cortex along the surface of the kidney due to fibrosis. Infarcts do not produce a distal acoustic shadow as is expected with calcified lesions. An absence of perfu - sion may also be noted upon color flow Doppler interrogation of acute renal infarcts. Small amounts of perire - nal fluid may be seen with infection including feline infectious peritonitis (FIP) and leptospirosis, inflamma- tion, toxicities, coagulopathy and other causes of acute kidney injury (AKI) (Figure 10.15). Neoplasia such as renal lymphosarcoma may cause variable degrees of perirenal fluid, especially in the cat (see Figure 10.10C,D). Correlating the presence of perirenal fluid with the overall renal appearance may help determine the cause of the change. Fluid within the retroperitoneal space is external to the kidney capsule and separate from the peritoneal space. Retroperitoneal fluid may be secondary to urine leakage from a compromised or injured urinary tract, hemorrhage from a coagulopathy or traumatic injury, and abscessation (such as with migrating grass awns) (Nevins et al. 2015). In cases with accessible volumes of fluid, fine needle aspiration for fluid analysis, cytology, and culture may be accom- plished with ultrasound guidance. Routine Add‐on of AFAST and Its Abdominal Fluid Scoring System In the authors’ experience, it is invaluable to include an AFAST examination with an abdominal fluid score (AFS) to improve the diagnostic potential of the POCUS kidney. In the authors’ experience, the posi - tioning of small animal patients in dorsal recumbency for complete detailed abdominal ultrasound exams can preclude the discovery of small‐volume peritoneal effusions and at the same time underestimate volume. As a result, moving the patient into lateral recumbency (right or left, with right lateral generally preferred), waiting a few minutes for any free intraabdominal fluid to redistribute, and then performing AFAST with an AFS is now the authors’ standard protocol. The addition of AFAST and AFS adds little extra time, while improving diagnostic evaluation. Although no veterinary studies have compared the detection and volume estimation of abdominal effu - sions in dorsal versus lateral recumbency, AFAST per- formed in right lateral recumbency through experience has proven to better detect small‐volume intraabdomi- nal effusions and the AFS allows for objective assessment of volume over the terms trivial, mild, moderate, and severe. The early detection of abdominal effusion is clin- ically important as it helps direct additional diagnostics and decision making, while reducing morbidity and mortality when such effusions are missed. Lastly, the use of Global FAST helps rapidly differen- tiate localized from obvious disseminated disease, as well as screening for comorbidities and complications, by imaging the thorax for pleural and pericardial effu- sions (TFAST) and echo views (TFAST), and lung (Vet BLUE). Serial renal imaging can provide great value in monitoring the progression or regression of lesions, as was the case in this patient.

208 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Pearls and Pitfalls, The Final Say • Most patients can be imaged in dorsal recumbency for the POCUS kidney examination. However, in large and deep‐chested dogs, repositioning to lateral recumbency may be needed and is particularly beneficial when imaging the right kidney which may require an intercostal approach. • Changes in kidney parenchymal echogenicity may be identified by comparison to the adjacent organs. The renal cortex is normally isoechoic or slightly hypoechoic to normal liver and significantly hypoechoic to normal spleen. As a normal varia- tion, however, the renal cortex may be hyperechoic to liver in cats and some dogs. Remember the “SLiCK” mnemonic regarding canine echogenicity. For the feline, hepatic echogenicity is often com- pared to the adjacent falciform fat and the feline liver should be isoechoic to slightly hypoechoic to the falciform fat. • Subtle changes in echogenicity of the renal parenchyma are subjective. Changes may indicate pathology in either the kidney or the comparative organ (liver, spleen) and the patient’s clinical pic- ture must be considered to avoid interpretation errors. • In addition, the presence of normal anatomy, and the size and symmetry between the right and left kidneys should be used to evaluate for pathology. • A hyperechoic medullary rim sign may be seen with multiple pathological conditions including hypercalcemia, acute toxicities such as ethylene glycol, and infectious diseases such as feline infectious peritonitis (FIP) or leptospirosis. It is, however, a nonspecific finding that may also be seen in animals with normal renal function, and must be interpreted in association with additional clinical findings. • Mineralization within the kidney can occur due to calculi or dystrophic mineralization. Both will cre- ate a strongly echogenic near‐field margin and an acoustic shadow. This can be confused with hyper- echoic vascular walls at the corticomedullary junction caused by interlobar/arcuate vessels, and with fat around the renal pelvis. Neither of these confounders causes a distal acoustic shadow. • Mild symmetrical pyelectasia may occur with intravenous fluid administration or diuretic therapy and should not be misinterpreted as pyelonephritis. • The presence of pyelectasia or hydronephrosis should prompt further evaluation for a cause of partial (pyelectasia) or total (hydronephrosis) ure- teral obstruction. Additional evaluation by an experienced sonographer and perhaps additional imaging techniques (such as intravenous pyelogra- phy or computed tomography) are warranted. Quick Reference of Normals and Rules of Thumb • Normal kidney size for cats is generally considered to be 3.0–4.4 cm in length depending on the refer - ence (Nickel et al.1973; Walter et al. 1987). • Normal kidney size in dogs is variable and depends on the size of the dog so assessment is generally subjective. Therefore, assessment of symmetry and size between the two kidneys is particularly impor- tant in dogs. • Normal renal pelvis size (height in mm). Variability in both species. Cat 1.5–2 mm with maximum of 2.8 mm; dogs 2–3 mm with a maximum of 3.8 mm. As a general rule of thumb, consider abnormal if ≥3 mm cats and ≥4 mm dogs) (d’Anjou et al. 2011). Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 211 Introduction POCUS assessment of the urinary bladder is relatively easy to learn because, as with the gallbladder, fluid‐ filled structures are easily imaged with ultrasound. As a result, ultrasound examination is more sensitive than abdominal radiography for detecting abnormal- ities of the urinary bladder wall and evaluating for nonmineral dense luminal contents such as sediment, proteinaceous and cellular debris, and radiolucent calculi. The use of the POCUS urinary bladder examination optimizes patient care and clinical course with improved diagnosis and recognition of abnormalities otherwise undetected by traditional radiographic means. POCUS urinary bladder exami- nation does not replace a complete abdominal and urinary tract ultrasound study by a veterinarian with advanced training (radiologist or internist) and provides only a limited evaluation of the proximal urethra. A combination of ultrasonography and special contrast‐assisted radiographic studies may still be needed for a comprehensive evaluation of the urinary tract and adjacent structures. What the POCUS Urinary Bladder Can Do • Recognize abnormalities of the bladder wall such as cystitis, polyps, and tumors. • Recognize abnormalities of the urinary bladder lumen such as stones (calculi), sediment, and blood clots. • Take advantage of a newly described technique for the detection of small uroliths (<5 mm) using color flow Doppler and the “twinkle artifact.” What the POCUS Urinary Bladder Cannot Do • Cannot differentiate benign from malignant urinary bladder wall infiltration or mass lesions. • Cannot confirm urinary bladder infection (bacte- rial cystitis). • Cannot accurately diagnose bladder wall abnor - malities in a poorly filled urinary bladder. Indications • Hematuria, dysuria, stranguria, and signs of urinary tract infection. • History of previously confirmed urolithiasis. • Undifferentiated caudal abdominal pain or spinal pain. • Unexplained urinary retention and urinary bladder distension. Objectives • Identify urinary bladder wall (mural and extra- mural) abnormalities such as cystitis, polyps, and tumors. POCUS: Urinary Bladder Stephanie C. Lisciandro and Sarah Young CHAPTER ELEVEN Pearl: Be aware of ultrasound artifacts that may lead to a misdiagnosis. Gas in the colon and small intestine may be mistaken for a calculus or mineral- ized sediment, edge shadowing artifact may be mis- taken for a wall defect, and slice thickness and side‐lobe artifact may be misinterpreted as luminal sediment or a mass.

212 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER • Recognize urinary bladder luminal abnormalities such as urinary bladder stones (calculi), sediment, and blood clots. Patient Positioning and Probe Selection A 7.5–10 MHz curvilinear (microconvex) probe is ade- quate for evaluation of the urinary bladder in most patients. A 7.5–10 MHz linear probe provides increased image resolution (but less penetration) and can be use- ful for smaller dogs and cats, or when subtle changes of the urinary bladder wall are noted. A linear probe can be of particular benefit when evaluating the urinary bladder neck and proximal urethra for mural and luminal abnormalities. Moderate distension of the urinary bladder is ideal for complete evaluation of the bladder wall and lumen, and reduces the incidence of misdiagnoses due to artifact. If reevaluation within 5–8 hours does not lead to sufficient urinary bladder dis- tension, then a low dose of injectable furosemide or infusion of sterile saline into the bladder via catheteri- zation are strategies to consider in order to obtain optimal bladder distention. The patient is typically positioned in dorsal recum- bency but in reluctant patients, lateral recumbency may be used. Clipping the caudoventral abdominal hair and applying acoustic coupling gel will maximize image quality. If calculi or other intraluminal abnor - malities are suspected, then changing patient body position throughout the scan, for example from lateral to standing, can discriminate moveable from non- moveable abnormalities. Unless they are adherent to the urinary bladder wall, sediment, blood clots, and calculi will fall to the gravity‐dependent luminal sur - face, whereas artifacts and mural abnormalities will persist. The authors recommend performing a Global FAST to screen for any intrathoracic problems including pleural and pericardial effusion, cardiac and pulmonary conditions, and abnormal volume status that may pose patient risk before moving the patient into dorsal recumbency. How to do POCUS Urinary Bladder With the patient in dorsal recumbency, the caudal abdomen is scanned using a transabdominal approach. The entire urinary bladder should be visualized in both longitudinal and transverse planes. This can be achieved by fanning from just beyond the apex to the shadowing brim of the bony pelvis in the transverse plane, and from just beyond either side of the serosal margins of the urinary bladder in the sagittal plane. This is especially important when assessing for wall thickening or mass lesions since reverberation artifacts may alter the appearance of the bladder wall and may mimic abnormalities (Figure 11.1A). These artifacts can be minimized by examining from multiple scanning angles. If review of the POCUS urinary bladder is sub- mitted for specialty evaluation, submission of cine clips in both the transverse and sagittal planes is imperative for an accurate assessment. In addition, the proximal urethra should be assessed for dilation, normal wall thickness, and intraluminal abnormalities. The prostate should be subjectively assessed for size (expected to be approximately 1 cm in the neutered male dog), symmetry, pain upon interrogation and parenchymal abnormalities such as abnormalities of echogenicity and mural lesions (e.g., masses, polyps, and cysts), and intraluminal and intra- mural mineralization (see Chapter 13). The primary purposes of the POCUS urinary bladder examination are to evaluate for obvious abnormalities of the urinary bladder wall (diffuse thickening versus focal abnormalities) and for intraluminal abnormal- ities such as calculi, sediment, and blood clots. Ultrasonographic Findings in a Normal Urinary Bladder The normal urinary bladder wall consists of four layers: an outer serosal layer (hyperechoic), muscula- ris layer (hypoechoic), submucosa (hyperechoic), and inner mucosal layer (hypoechoic). These layers are not well delineated and the inner mucosal layer is rarely distinguishable from the urine unless inflamed and irregular. As a result, when the layers are visible, the wall typically has a three‐layered appearance, having two thin mildly hyperechoic (bright white) layers with a thin hypoechoic (dark) central layer (see Figure 11.1B). The thickness of the urinary bladder wall varies with bladder distension. In cats, reported normal wall Pearl: A urine‐filled bladder optimizes sonographic imaging of the bladder wall and lumen. When pos- sible, refrain from walking dogs and remove the litter box from cats several hours prior to their POCUS urinary bladder examination.

213 POCUS: U RINARY B LADDER thickness ranges from 1.3 to 1.7 mm (Finn‐Bodner 1995). In dogs, the reported normal range is from 1.4 mm in moderately distended bladders to 2.3 mm in minimally distended bladders (Geisse et al. 1997), with normal generally being less than 3 mm. Additionally, wall thickness increases with body size by up to 1 mm in heavier dogs (Geisse et al. 1997). Urine Normal urine is uniformly anechoic (black) in dogs; however, cats have more concentrated urine and may have lipid droplets which affect echogenicity (see Chapter 39). The presence of echogenic, amorphous material within the urinary bladder lumen may be consistent with crystalline, proteinaceous, lipid or cel - lular debris. Side‐lobe, slice thickness, and edge shad- owing artifacts should not be misinterpreted as luminal debris or mural lesions, and care should be taken to distinguish these artifacts from true lesions (see Figure 11.1; see also Chapter 3). Ureters Normal ureters are difficult to identify as they enter at the trigone. With experience, they may be identified as two small echogenic structures approximately 1–2 mm shaped as “equalsigns” on either side of the trigone, best seen in the transverse plane. The ureters should not be fluid filled; however, the ureteral papillae (ureterove- sicular junctions) are occasionally seen as paired small, isoechoic to slightly hyperechoic (white) bumps pro - truding into the lumen from the caudodorsal bladder wall, which is in the far‐field in dorsal recumbency and should not be mistaken for a bladder wall mass (Figure 11.2). Urine may at times be seen jetting into the urinary bladder from either ureter. This vesiculoureteral reflex typically appears as a faint jet of echogenic moving or swirling fluid, and is visible due to the slight difference in specific gravity between the urine from the kidney and the urine within the bladder. Color flow Doppler or power Doppler can also be used to visualize the urine jet and thus distinguish a ureteral papilla from other causes of focal wall thickening (see Figure 11.2B). Figure 11.1. 214 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Artifacts Associated with POCUS Urinary Bladder It is very important to be familiar with artifacts associ- ated with the fluid‐filled urinary bladder and the closely associated and potentially air‐ or fecal‐filled colon. Fluid‐related artifacts include side‐lobe, slice thickness, edge shadowing (refraction), and acoustic shadowing and enhancement (see Chapter 3). Air‐related artifacts or reverberation artifacts can cause false abnormalities of the bladder wall and lumen. Both fluid‐ and air‐ related artifacts can mimic pathology and combinations of the aforementioned may confound ultrasound inter- pretation of the urinary bladder (Figure 11.3; see also Figures 11.1B, 11.9, 11.10B, and Chapter 3). A recently described and practical artifact, referred to as the Figure 11.2. Normal ureteral papilla. (A) A linear probe ultrasound image showing the ureteral papilla. (B) Swirling or jetting of urine entering the urinary bladder lumen from the same ureteral papilla as in (A) is obvious using color flow Doppler. Note the red flow toward the transducer, and the normal urinary bladder wall (double line) in the near‐field along the ventrum of the patient positioned in dorsal recumbency. Figure 11.3.
