215 POCUS: URINARY BLADDER “twinkle artifact,” may allow detection of small uroliths (renal, ureteral, and bladder) that are <5 mm in people, a traditionally difficult size range to diagnose accurately with B‐mode (Gliga et al. 2017) (see section on Calculi below). In this study, the artifact was over 90% sensitive and specific and over 90% for positive and negative pre- dictive values. The twinkle artifact (also referred to as the color comet tail artifact) employs color flow Doppler evaluation of the region of interest to evaluate for a focus of alternating colors behind a reflective object (such as a calculus) (Gliga et al. 2017). Clinical Significance and Implications of Abnormal POCUS Urinary Bladder Findings The primary purpose of the POCUS urinary bladder is to detect obvious abnormalities of the wall and lumen. Abnormalities of the proximal urethra and prostate may also be identified and may be clinically relevant. Abnormalities of the Bladder Wall The urinary bladder wall should be assessed for dif- fuse and focal changes. Diffuse Changes Diffuse changes in the urinary bladder wall are most consistent with cystitis or other infiltrative or systemic disease processes, such as mural hemorrhage due to coagulopathy or rodenticide toxicity. Cystitis Cystitis is the most common cause of diffuse change and may result in diffuse changes in echogenicity, such as hypoechoic urinary bladder thickening, but can especially occur along the cranioventral and apical aspects of the bladder. Cystitis may also result in irreg- ularity of the luminal surface (Figure 11.4A,C). Polypoid cystitis is a chronic form of cystitis occasion- ally seen in dogs that results in multiple pedunculated masses projecting into the lumen (see Figure 11.6B–D). Emphysematous Cystitis This uncommon form of cystitis is most often seen in diabetic animals secondary to chronic bacterial infec- tion with mural extension and gas‐producing bacteria within the urinary bladder wall. It results in hyper - echoic foci of gas within the wall and subsequent mural reverberation (comet tail and ringdown) arti- facts (Figure 11.5). In some cases, the changes may be severe and can be confused with neoplasia. The appearance may be very confusing for the unsus- pecting sonographer as the gas‐associated artifacts from within the wall can be so severe that they obscure visualization of a normal urinary bladder altogether. The general rule of thumb during ultra- sound when you cannot acquire an acceptable image is to perform radiography. In the case of emphyse- matous cystitis, radiography should reveal a gas bubble within the lumen of the bladder consistent with air within the lumen. Focal Irregularities Focal irregularities in the urinary bladder wall are gen- erally easy to detect when the bladder is urine filled and appropriately distended. These focal changes most commonly are due to either benign polyps or neoplasia. Remember that the presence of the ureteral papillae protruding from the dorsal wall of the bladder at the trigone is normal and should not be confused with a mass lesion (see Figure 11.2). Benign Polyps Usually have a pedunculated appearance and are attached to the mucosa by a narrow stalk (Figure 11.6 B–D). However, it is not possible to distinguish between benign and malignant bladder tumors based on ultra- sonographic appearance alone. Neoplasia The most common neoplasia of the urinary bladder is transitional cell carcinoma (TCC). The appearance is variable but generally the tumor presents as an irregular, hyperechoic, broad‐based mural lesion (Figure 11.7). Other possible tumors of the urinary bladder wall include squamous cell carcinoma, leiomyosarcoma, lymphoma, and a variety of Pearl: When diffuse wall thickening is noted, a urinalysis and microbial urine culture should be per- formed to rule out bacterial cystitis. If clinical signs and diffuse sonographic changes persist following appropriate therapy, then traumatic catheterization, ultrasound‐guided fine needle aspiration or biopsies are indicated for definitive diagnosis.

Thrombi are typically mobile within the bladder and will organize and contract with time. Changing patient body position to assess for movement within the lumen and serial monitoring for changes in appearance may be helpful. Use of color flow Doppler can generally differentiate between neoplasia and thrombi based on the presence or absence of blood flow within the structure. Neoplasia will have blood flow and thrombi will not (neither will artifact). Thrombi may be iatrogenic and associated with a recent history of cystocentesis. Regardless of etiology, these should shrink and resolve with time, whereas neoplasia will typically progress over time (see Figure 11.11). In the dog, the most common location of TCC is near the trigone (Leveille et al. 1992) but they can occur in any region of the bladder wall or urethra, and can occasionally be seen extending into the urethra from the bladder lumen or into the bladder lumen from the urethra. TCC is more common in females. Obstruction of the ureters with secondary hydronephrosis may occur due to obstruction of the ureteral papillae by tumor. Therefore, assessment of the ureters and kid - neys is indicated, and easily performed for further evaluation of the urinary tract in patients with sus - pected TCC. In fact, the Global FAST approach allows for rapid same‐day staging for obvious hydronephro - sis, liver, and pulmonary metastasis as well as any cardiac complications (see Chapters 10 and XX). In cats, TCC is less common than in dogs and more often seen in older males. Feline TCC, how - ever, originates from any region of the bladder wall and the entire bladder should be thoroughly evaluated (Wilson et al. 2007). Sonographic characteristics of TCC bladder tumors include a broad base and an irregular luminal surface and they may contain foci of mineralization. Concurrent bladder sediment, calculi, and/or cystitis are common. More recently, TCC of the urinary bladder has been referred to as a urothelial carcinoma (Sommer et al. 2018; Lin et al. 2018). Cytology may be acquired via urinalysis, traumatic catheteri- zation or fine needle aspiration (risk of seeding tumor). 219 POCUS: URINARY BLADDER Percutaneous fine needle aspiration of bladder tumors should be pursued with caution. Although extremely rare, TCC has the potential to seed along the needle track, resulting in regional spread of the tumor (Nyland et al. 2002; Vignoli et al. 2007; Liffman and Courtman 2017). Ultrasound‐guided suction biopsy of the mass by urinary catheter may provide ample cells or tissue for diagnosis. Referral for a complete detailed abdominal ultrasound by an experienced sonographer is recommended if fine needle aspirates are to be pursued. Intraluminal Abnormalities Intraluminal abnormalities of the urinary bladder include calculi, blood clots (thrombi), and sediment. Calculi (Bladder Stones) Calculi (bladder stones) are discrete mobile objects with curvilinear hyperechoic (bright) surfaces within the lumen of the bladder. They are generally round in appearance but may be variable in shape and size, and may be clustered together. Calculi usually have a distal acoustic shadow but very small calculi (<1–2 mm) may not produce an appreciable shadow (Figure 11.8). However, in people, a new artifact, referred to as the “twinkle artifact,” has been used to detect uroliths (renal, ureteral, and bladder) that are <5 mm, a tradi- tionally difficult size range to accurately diagnose with B‐mode (Gliga et al. 2017). This twinkle artifact, cre- ated by intrinsic ultrasound machine noise seen with color flow Doppler, has been shown to be more sensitive for the detection of small stones (<5 mm) than acoustic shadowing. The twinkle artifact is most apparent when the reflecting surface of the urolith (renal, ureteral, or cystic) is irregular and the focal zone is placed below the reflecting surface of the suspect object. In summary, the twinkle artifact occurs when color flow Doppler is applied to the region (suspect stone) in question and red/blue turbulent or pulse‐like “twinkling” is seen behind the mineralization (Gliga et al. 2017). Interestingly, the twinkle artifact may be applied to other organs with suspected mineralization (Gliga et al. 2017). Size of the calculi is important to note and record as it may have clinical implications regarding therapy, particularly for evaluating the likelihood of a calculus safely passing through the urethra either spontane- ously or by voiding hydropropulsion. The following guidelines for voiding urohydropulsion (VUH) have been published (Defarges et al. 2013). • Female dogs (>2 kg) can typically void stones <3–4 mm. • Female cats may be able to void stones <3 mm. • Male dogs weighing 5–10 kg may be able to void stones <2–3 mm; male dogs >10 kg may be able to void stones <3 mm. • Male cats: voiding urohydropulsion is not recommended. The number of calculi is also important to assess, although cannot often be accurately established, par - ticularly when calculi are clustered together. Note also that calculi may be located within the urethra, and the proximal and prostatic urethra should be visualized for intraluminal calculi. Pearl: The ease of passing a 9 French urinary cath- eter correlates with the successful voiding of 3 mm stones. Pearl: The presence of echogenic urine is not specific for urinary tract infection or other pathology and a urinalysis (and urine culture) should be obtained to determine the significance of the ultrasonographic finding(s). Pitfall and Pearl: Gas, formed fecal matter in the colon, and associated artifacts (i.e., acoustic shadow) can mimic a urinary calculus when the bladder rests against the colon, and the bladder wall indents and curves to the contour of the fecal‐filled colon. While centering on the possible calculus, slide the transducer cranially. If the hyperechoic mass with the acoustic shadow can be followed cranial to the bladder, then it is not a calculus. Alternately, turn the transducer 90° and if the suspected item elongates into a tubular structure, then it is not a calculus (see Figure 11.3). Pearl: The “twinkle artifact” is a recently described effective technique (>90% sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values) to detect small calculi and mineralization of <5 mm in the urinary tract from the kidney to the urinary bladder through the use of color flow Doppler. The tech- nique may in fact be applied to any organ with sus- pect mineralization (Gliga et al. 2017). Pearl: Calculi can be assessed for mobility within the lumen by agitating the bladder (ballottement) with the transducer or by changing patient body position. Repositioning into a standing position is

They may be isoechoic, hyperechoic or hypoechoic to the urinary bladder wall, do not display distal acoustic shadowing and can often have mixed echogenicity with an indis - tinct layered appearance. Blood clots consist of irreg - ular focal echogenic structures within the urinary bladder lumen and are generally mobile but may occa- sionally be adhered to the urinary bladder mucosa. When mobile, the luminal location of the clot will vary with changes in patient body position. When adherent, they can sometimes be difficult to differentiate from a mural mass. Color flow or power Doppler interrogation can be useful in this case, as there is no blood flow within a clot, but flow should be visualized within a bladder tumor. Figure 11.8. Bladder stones. 221 POCUS: U RINARY B LADDER Sediment Sediment typically appears as gravity‐dependent hyperechoic particulate material within the bladder. It will produce an acoustic shadow when mineralized (i.e., crystals, sand, tiny calculi). Agitation of the bladder (ballottement) is recommended in all urinary bladder interrogations and may result in suspension and swirling of the sediment or the so‐called “snow globe” appearance. Repositioning the patient can also result in movement of the sediment to the gravity‐ dependent surface (see repositioning for cystic calculi above). A urinalysis should be performed to evaluate the significance and composition of sediment seen on ultrasound examination (Figures 11.9 and 11.10; see also Figure 11.8B). Routine Add‐on of AFAST and Its Abdominal Fluid Scoring System (or Global FAST) In the authors’ experience, it is invaluable to perform an AFAST examination with assignment of an abdominal fluid score in either lateral recumbency for the best approach. The positioning of small ani - mals in dorsal recumbency for POCUS abdominal organ examinations can obscure small‐volume peri - toneal effusion and underestimate the volume of effusion present because peritoneal effusion will flow into the less sonographically accessible dia - phragmatic recesses. AFAST improves the diagnostic potential of the ultrasound examination by detecting peritoneal effusion. The early detection of abdominal effusion is clinically important and helps direct addi - tional diagnostic recommendations while avoiding Figure 11.9. Urinary bladder sediment and artifact. 223 POCUS: URINARY BLADDER Pearls and Pitfalls, The Final Say • The urinary bladder is generally easy to evaluate for obvious intraluminal (e.g., calculi or blood clots) and mural (e.g., mass lesions) abnormalities. • Moderate distension of the urinary bladder is necessary for optimal assessment for urinary bladder wall thickness and the presence of focal wall abnormalities. An empty urinary bladder can often be misinterpreted as having a thickened urinary bladder wall. • When evaluating for diffuse changes, cystitis gen- erally results in hypoechoic thickening, most often along the cranioventral or apical aspect of the urinary bladder. • Severe or polypoid cystitis is not distinguishable from diffuse mural urinary bladder neoplasia. If ultrasonographic changes persist or worsen dur - ing/following medical therapy for cystitis, tissue sampling should be pursued. However, the add‐on of a Global FAST rapidly screens for localized versus disseminated disease and should be used the same day for staging the patient. • Ureteral papillae occasionally may be seen on the dorsal surface of the bladder wall near the trigone and should not be confused with a urinary bladder wall abnormality. • The contents of the colon can cause shadowing artifacts that may be mistaken for calculi or sedi- ment and moving the patient to a standing position will help discriminate artifact from true abnormal- ities. Unless adhered, uroliths and sediment will fall to the gravity‐dependent location (artifact will not) and pressure impingement from the colon along the ventral urinary bladder surface will be relieved. • The ultrasonographic interrogation of the urinary bladder is susceptible to many artifacts, which may lead to misinterpretation. Therefore, it is impera- tive to be familiar with these artifacts and how to mitigate them as with interrogating the urinary bladder from multiple vantage points or changing patient position in order to provide an accurate assessment of the findings and paying attention to gravity‐dependent regions where sediment, cal- culi, and blood clots would settle. • Blood clots (thrombi) may be variable in echo- genicity and may be difficult to distinguish from bladder wall masses, especially if they are adhered to the wall. Use color flow Doppler to help differ - entiate them as neoplasia generally has positive (blood) flow and blood clots and artifacts do not. • Additional diagnostic techniques may be needed following the POCUS urinary bladder examination to further define disorders of the lower urinary tract. This may include referral for a complete detailed abdominal ultrasound by an experienced sonographer and/or additional perineal radiog- raphy in the male patient for urethral evaluation, special radiographic studies or computed tomo- graphic imaging of the entire urinary tract, which are especially helpful in further assessing the kid- neys, ureters, urethra, and pelvic inlet. Quick Reference of Normals and Rules of Thumb • The thickness of the urinary bladder wall varies depending on the degree of distension. • Normal range for urinary bladder wall thickness is cats 1.3–1.7 mm (Finn‐Bodner 1995). • Normal ranges for urinary bladder wall thickness in dogs are from 1.4 mm in moderately distended bladders to 2.3 mm in minimally distended blad- ders (Geisse et al. 1997). However, wall thickness in dogs has been reported to increase with body size, with heavier dogs having increased thickness by up to 1 mm or a maximum normal thickness of ≤3 mm (Geisse et al. 1997). • The urinary bladder, being fluid filled, is subject to several artifacts including side‐lobe, edge shadow- ing, and acoustic enhancement in the far‐field. • Voiding urohydropulsion guidelines are as follows. ◦ Female dogs (>2 kg) can typically void stones <3–4 mm. ◦ Female cats may be able to void stones <3 mm. ◦ Male dogs weighing 5–10 kg may be able to void stones <2–3 mm; male dogs >10 kg may be able to void stones <3 mm. ◦ Male cats: VUH is not recommended. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 225 Introduction Typically, a point‐of‐care ultrasound (POCUS) examina- tion is not extensive, thorough or complete. Rather, it provides a limited examination designed to answer brief and important clinical questions in an organ system or for a symptom involving multiple organ sys- tems (Mateer et al. 1994). In the emergency setting, it can provide early diagnostic information that can guide treatment of the critical patient. This is especially true in situations where delaying ultrasonographic evaluation until a specialist is available, or positioning the patient for complete ultrasonographic evaluation or radiog- raphy, might lead to further patient compromise. Some gastrointestinal (GI)‐related conditions that have been evaluated with emergency ultrasound in people include intussusception, small bowel obstruc- tion, pyloric stenosis, appendicitis, gastric ulcers, per - forated hollow viscus, gallbladder rupture, septic peritonitis, acute mesenteric ischemia, and acute pan- creatitis (Rozycki 2001; Dean et al. 2002; Unluer et al. 2010; Testa et al. 2010; Jang et al. 2011). Using the AFAST examination technique to evaluate for the presence of peritoneal fluid has been validated in dogs (Boysen et al. 2004; Lisciandro et al. 2009) and whether or not peritonitis exists is an important clinical question to answer. However, a more detailed approach to scanning of the gastrointestinal tract (GIT) and pancreatic pathologies requires considerably more expertise and training, which may limit the use of POCUS GIT and pancreas by some emergency clini- cians. It must be stressed that POCUS GIT and pan- creas should not replace abdominal radiographs, complete detailed abdominal ultrasound or computed tomography (CT) examination for a more compre- hensive peritoneal cavity evaluation. Furthermore, in people the correlation obtained between emergency physician POCUS and a gold standard pathology confirmation varies by operator experience and the extent and type of training received for the above‐ mentioned GI conditions (Raymond‐Dufresne and Ghanayem 2012; Hasani et al. 2015). This emphasizes the potential advantages and limitations of POCUS GIT and pancreas emergency examination in the acute GI setting. However, abnormal ultrasonographic findings (a positive result) can be extremely valuable in providing a diagnosis and guiding initial case management. A negative emergency POCUS GIT and pancreas exami- nation is not uncommon and does not necessarily rule out disease (false negative) indicating the need for further diagnostic testing, serial POCUS GIT and pan- creas plus AFAST, or follow‐up with an imaging spe- cialist. In other words, POCUS GIT and pancreas should be considered a rule‐in test for organ pathology. On the other hand, AFAST for intraabdominal fluid detection, evidence for peritonitis, is both a rule‐in (highly specific) and rule‐out (highly sensitive) test for the nonradiologist sonographer (Boysen et al. 2004). For the sonographer who is not confident in assigning the GIT or pancreas with a pathological sonographic diagnosis in acute abdomen cases, AFAST remains a very good screening test for peritonitis, a POCUS GIT and pancreas‐related consideration that warrants a prompt diagnosis. No studies exist evaluating the efficiency, accuracy, sensitivity or specificity of equivalent POCUS emergency GI ultrasound when performed by POCUS: Gastrointestinal Tract and Pancreas Søren R. 226 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER veterinary emergency clinicians compared to a boarded radiologist or internal medicine specialist. However, evidence suggests that the diagnostic accuracy of detecting small intestinal mechanical obstruction in dogs using ultrasound is lower when performed by a novice sonographer compared to a boarded radiologist and that the learning curve is steeper for ultrasono- graphic GI assessment than for many other emergency POCUS techniques (Sharma et al. 2011). Currently, there are no standardized guidelines or recommenda- tions in the veterinary literature for performing POCUS emergency GI examinations. The accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity of our POCUS GIT and pancreas exami- nation have not been evaluated. We propose that POCUS GIT and pancreas be adapted and/or tailored to the critical patient and that, in many cases, it will provide valuable diagnostic information to better direct resuscitation, screen post resuscitation, and better keep patients alive for gold standard testing and treatment. The specific application of POCUS emergency examinations of the GIT depends on patient status, history, physical examination findings, clinical suspi- cion, and operator experience. Whether or not POCUS emergency examination for suspected GIT and pancreatic disease is warranted should be dictated by the availability of an experienced sonographer or radi- ologist and the assessment of preliminary diagnostic tests and dependent on the clinical questions to be answered by the attending veterinarian. In summary, when negative, POCUS GIT and pan- creas should not be considered a definitive test in the assessment of patients with suspected acute GI condi- tions. Instead, the application should be used as an initial screening, ancillary test to supplement the his- tory, physical examination findings, and other prelimi- nary diagnostic screening tests given its potential ability to direct initial therapy and guide appropriate diag- nostic testing, especially when other imaging modalities might be detrimental to the patient’s critical status, such as in those patients with profound anemia or compli- cating respiratory distress. When combined with AFAST, life‐threatening peritonitis can be ruled in or out, and a Global FAST approach can screen for thoracic (TFAST), cardiac (TFAST), and pulmonary comorbidi- ties (Vet BLUE) (see Chapters 7, 18, 23, and 36). What POCUS Gastrointestinal T ract and Pancreas Can Do • Provide a preliminary evaluation of patients with GI signs or evidence of acute abdomen in an effort to answer a specific question when complete abdominal ultrasonography is not available. • Rapidly assess the unstable patient with GI signs in an effort to rule in (or out) significant diffuse peri- toneal effusion. • Complement radiographic findings in cases with GI signs. • Support the clinical suspicion of moderate GI and pancreatic pathology for further testing to obtain a definitive diagnosis (i.e., ultrasound‐guided fine needle tissue sampling). • Detect the presence of peritonitis through the add‐ on of AFAST in initial and serial evaluations, and be complemented by Global FAST for further assessment of the thorax, heart, lung, and volume status. What POCUS Gastrointestinal T ract and Pancreas Cannot Do • Cannot replace a complete abdominal ultrasound examination or abdominal radiographs. • Cannot rule out focal or specific causes of GI pathology (particularly pancreatitis) when results are negative. Indications Two key factors to consider for POCUS GIT and pan- creas examinations are what the emergency clinician suspects is the underlying cause for presentation, and the urgency of finding an answer to the question asked. The stable patient may benefit more from a complete abdominal ultrasound exam whereas the unstable patient presenting “after hours” with signs of acute abdomen/GI signs is considered the ideal candidate for the POCUS GIT and pancreas examination. The indications and type of POCUS GIT and pan- creas examination vary and depend on the operator’s level of experience and training, presenting complaint, preliminary minimum database bloodwork results, physical examination findings, and suspected underlying condition of the patient. The indications for POCUS GIT and pancreas (plus AFAST) examination in the veterinary patient with acute GI signs include the clinical suspicion of pancre- atitis, screening for peritoneal effusion that might sug- gest perforated intestines, septic or biliary peritonitis, right‐sided cardiac failure, hemo‐ or uroabdomen or an underlying neoplastic process. The peritoneal space, stomach, and small and large bowel are readily evalu- ated for supportive evidence of GI perforation such as effusion shadowing GI foreign bodies, bowel intussus- ception, intestinal obstruction, and evidence of ileus.

227 POCUS: GASTROINTESTINAL TRACT AND P ANCREAS Although not the ideal screening test for pneumoperi- toneum, peritoneal gas may also be detected. Examples of scenarios where an emergency clinician has a specific question that could potentially be answered by POCUS GIT and pancreas examination include the following. • In a patients with an acute abdomen, vomiting and unexplained hypotension, it is reasonable to ask if the patient has peritoneal effusion, which could be indicative of GI perforation and septic peritonitis. In these patients, an emergent AFAST examination may be performed to evaluate for effusion and aid in ultrasound‐guided abdominocentesis to screen for cytological evidence of sepsis. • In patients with acute abdominal pain and vomit- ing that are negative for peritoneal effusion, the emergency clinician may ask if the patient has localized or indirect evidence supportive of GI perforation or if a shadowing intestinal foreign body is present. POCUS GIT and pancreas exami- nation of the intestines may then be perfomed and may lead to the discovery of an ultrasonographi- cally detectable foreign body or raise the index of suspicion of intestinal obstruction. Indirect evi- dence of obstruction, such as a severely dilated jejunum with luminal dilation measuring greater than 1.5 cm, may highlight the need for a more extensive and complete ultrasonographic evalua- tion, abdominal radiographs, upper GI series or exploratory surgery (Sharma et al. 2011). The his- tory, physical examination, and other ancillary tests should be correlated with, and supportive of, the findings. • If the emergency clinician is experienced with ultrasonographic evaluation of the pancreas and the patient is hypotensive with a history suggestive of pancreatitis (such as exposure to a high‐fat meal followed by vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain), then a POCUS GIT and pancreas examina- tion may be performed to evaluate for ultrasono- graphic evidence of pancreatitis. If criteria for acute pancreatitis are present (e.g., hyperechoic or hyperattenuating mesentery with parenchymal pancreatic hypoechogenicity and elicitable pain in response to probe pressure during pancreatic eval- uation), the emergency clinician can then institute preliminary supportive measures while consid- ering further diagnostic and therapeutic options. • In patients that have undergone GI surgery and are deteriorating, the clinician may ask if dehiscence, septic peritonitis or postoperative ileus is present and may elect to perform an AFAST examination which would aid in ultrasound‐guided abdomino- centesis if peritoneal effusion is present. • In the postoperative patient that is vomiting, anorexic or painful, it is reasonable to ask if the patient has functional ileus and perform a POCUS emergency GIT examination to assess GI motility. Although perioperative gas may obscure ultraso- nographic peritoneal evaluation, if postoperative functional ileus is present, the clinician should search for and try to correct the underlying cause while considering specific therapies directed at addressing ileus. These are only a few examples of specific POCUS GIT and pancreas examination applications designed to answer a specific question. Although many factors dic- tate the clinical value of an AFAST study (the experi- ence of the operator, patient’s presenting complaint, and physical examination findings), there are many other clinical situations in which a patient can benefit from POCUS GIT and pancreas examination. Objectives • To identify the location, size, and shape of normal and abnormal peritoneal structures. • To identify pathology warranting specific or emergent treatment, optimizing early diagnosis and outcome of intraperitoneal disease, particu- larly in the unstable patient. Patient Positioning and Probe Selection Peritoneal Effusion See Chapters 6 and 7 for information on patient posi- tioning to look for the presence of peritoneal effusion. Gastrointestinal Evaluation Depending on the comfort level of the patient and preference of the sonographer, the POCUS emergency examination of the intestines may be performed in dorsal, left or right lateral recumbency. The overall status of the patient, with a particular focus on the cardiovascular and respiratory systems, should be determined to ensure patients are stable before placing them in dorsal recumbency. If there is any doubt regarding clinical status, the patient should have thoracic POCUS, such as TFAST and Vet BLUE,

228 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER performed to screen for intrathoracic problems including pleural and pericardial effusion, cardiac and pulmonary conditions, and abnormal volume status that may pose patient risk before moving the patient into dorsal recumbency (see Chapters 18, 23, and 36). • Left lateral recumbency helps with visualization of the pylorus and duodenum while right lateral recumbency allows for evaluation of the fundus (Penninck 2008a). • Repositioning the patient may redistribute intestinal gas and fluid allowing for specific regional evaluation. • Ultrasound probes with a frequency of at least 7.5 MHz are recommended for bowel evaluation (Penninck 2008a; Garcia et al. 2011). Pancreas Pancreatic scanning is frequently performed in dorsal recumbency although left and right lateral recumbency may also be used (Nyland et al. 2002; Penninck 2008b). • For pancreatic evaluation, a 5–7.5 MHz or higher transducer is preferred as higher frequencies improve visualization of the pancreas (Nyland et al. 2002). • Avoid examining the pancreas under high output or gain settings as the increased reflectivity of the pancreatic region prevents visualization of abnor - malities and leads to both false‐negative and false‐ positive results (Nyland et al. 2002; Hecht and Henry 2007). Scanning Technique Intestinal T ract The detection of GI lesions may be challenging given the difficulty of consistently evaluating the entire intestinal tract. Many factors, including normal or abnormal gas accumulation in the GI tract and oper - ator skill, influence the success of identifying GI lesions. A consistent and systematic technique will minimize false‐negative results. We propose the following POCUS GIT with the probe in the longitudinal plane. • One common technique involves starting in the region of the pylorus/stomach on the right side of the patient just caudal to the ribs and fanning the probe from the right to the left of the patient, paying specific attention to the stomach (located caudal to the xiphoid and liver) on the first pass. • Slide the probe 1–2 cm caudally and fan toward the far left side of the patient. Then fan back across the abdomen from left to right while paying specific attention to the bowel loops. • Repeated fanning of the probe across the abdomen in this fashion with a zig‐zag (or grid‐like) pattern while moving caudally will aid evaluation. If stable enough, the patient may be repositioned in various recumbencies for redistribution of fluid and gas, while repeating the evaluation (Figure 12.1). • The intestines are orientated in many directions. The above described approach results in the evalu- ation of many sections of small intestine in mul- tiple planes (sagittal, transverse, and various oblique planes), which depends on the probe‐to‐ intestinal tract orientation. • Once completed, if no irregularities are seen, the pylorus and descending duodenum can be evalu- ated in greater detail by returning the probe to the right side of the patient, just caudal to the ribcage (or, depending on patient conformation, some- times between the last ribs). The body of the stomach may first be located and traced to the pylorus, and then the descending duodenum. • This is a good time to get a general and subjective impression of overall gastric and small bowel motility (see section on Ileus below). • If a specific area of pain, mass or foreign object is palpated on initial physical examination, specific attention should be paid to the area in longitudinal and transverse planes. • Abnormal findings in close proximity to the area of suspicion might include intestinal wall structure layering abnormalities, abnormal intestinal peri- stalsis, focal loculations of peritoneal fluid, seg- mental focal dilations of small bowel, plicated bowel, target‐like lesions or hyperattenuating/ hyperechoic fat or mesentery. • Suspicious areas of intestine should be followed both orad and aborad to allow a more detailed assessment of these areas. • If structures within the GI lumen are visible, they should be carefully examined for a hyperechoic reflective interface and the presence of acoustic shadowing. Pancreas There are several scanning techniques that may be used to identify the pancreas, but a preferred tech- nique for POCUS emergency evaluation has not been

229 POCUS: G ASTROINTESTINAL T RACT AND P ANCREAS formally described for veterinarians. One of the more commonly used techniques in dogs involves an initial search for the right lobe of the pancreas as the right lobe is more easily imaged than the body and left lobe. Furthermore, the right lobe is more frequently affected by acute pancreatitis in the dog (Nyland et al. 2002; Hecht and Henry 2007; Penninck 2008b) whereas a higher prevelance is seen within the left pancreatic limb in cats with combined chronic pancreatic and gastrointestinal disease (De Cock et al. 2007). We propose the following POCUS pancreas. • The ultrasound probe is placed over the right kidney in transverse orientation. • After identifying the right kidney, the probe is slowly fanned laterally and medially until the descending duodenum is identified in transverse orientation. • The probe is then oriented in the sagittal plane, demonstrating that the duodenum may be evaluated along its length medial to the right abdominal body wall. • The pancreas is triangular shaped, and iso‐ to slightly hypoechoic (darker than) to surround - ing mesenteric fat. It has an echogenic capsule and is found dorsomedial to the duodenum, directly ventral to the right kidney (Hecht and Henry 2007). • The pancreaticoduodenal vessels and pancreatic duct may be seen as round anechoic structures within the pancreas (compare Figures 12.2 and 12.3). Color flow Doppler evaluation, if available, provides differentiation between the structures (see Figure 12.3A,B). • The portal vein may be seen and can be a useful landmark. It lies left and dorsal‐left to the pancreas and is best evaluated from a right dorsal intercostal approach (Brinkman‐Furguson and Biller 2009). • In very large or deep‐chested dogs, it may be easier to evaluated the right limb of the pancreas 1 2 3 6 7 5 8 4 Figure 12.1. Scanning the gastrointestinal tract. The pancreatic body is located between the right and left lobes of the pancreas in close proximity to the portal vein, dorsocaudal to the pylorus. • The left lobe of the pancreas is located between the stomach and transverse colon and medial to the splenic head. It may be seen cranial to the gastric fundus and caudal to the left liver from the left of the patient caudal to the ribs. It is often difficult to identify these parts of the pancreas, especially in normal dogs (Hecht and Henry 2007). • It should be noted that gas within the GI tract may hamper evaluation of the pancreas. • The pancratic body and left limb should not exceed 1 cm in width (8.5 mm and 9.5 mm, respectively) in the cat, regardless of age, whereas the left pancreatic duct should not exceed 2.5 mm (Larson et al. 2005). Excessive probe pressure may displace the duodenum, affecting its normal anatomical orientation to the right kidney. Remember that the normal pancreas may not be visible because it is often isoechoic (similar) to the surrounding mesenteric fat. Figure 12.2. Normal pancreas. (A) Normal right pancreatic limb in the sagittal plane in a dog (boundaries identified by the crosses, +). Note the tubular hypoechoic structure within the midpancreatic parenchyma ( arrow). Color flow Doppler can aid in differentiating whether this structure is vessel (pancreaticoduodenal artery or vein) or pancreatic duct. (B) Right pancreatic limb in the sagittal plane in a cat. The pancreas is typically isoechoic to the surrounding mesentery ( asterisk). In the authors’ experience, the echogenicity of the pancreatic parenchyma can vary in normal animals without clinical signs or laboratory evi- dence of pancreatitis. The pancreas can range in echogenicity from mildly hypoechoic to mildly hyperechoic to the surround- ing mesentery, but is typically isoechoic to the surrounding mesentery in the normal state. Pancreatic echogenicity is especially dependent on gain and acoustic output settings. Decreasing the gain settings can aid in pancreatic identification. Serosal margins of the pancreas are typically hyperreflective and can be used to identify the organ’s boundaries. Identification of the descend- ing duodenum along the right dorsolateral aspect of the patient while fanning and scanning medially and laterally along the length of the descending duodenum will aid in identification of the right limb. The sonographer can then follow the right limb to the body of the pancreas. To identify the left limb of the pancreas, the sonographer can begin scanning and fanning in the sagittal plane along the left lateral cranial abdominal wall at the level of the last rib. Here, the gastric fundus and spleen can be easily identified and the sonographer can move caudally along the medial and lateral aspects of the spleen to the cranial pole of the left kidney in search of the organ. Pearl: Remember that the normal pancreas may not be visible because it is often isoechoic to the sur - rounding mesenteric fat and it is a small structure (i.e., well under 1 cm in width). However, the find - ings of moderately hyperechoic (bright white) peri- pancreatic fat and peritoneal fluid adjacent to an enlarged hypoechoic pancreas should prompt a sus- picion of pancreatitis.

231 POCUS: G ASTROINTESTINAL T RACT AND P ANCREAS It must be stressed that a significant number of dogs with pancreatitis will not have ultrasonographic evidence of pancreatitis , and the success of diagnosing acute pancreatitis will vary with sonographer experience (Hess et al. 1989). Failure to detect evidence of pancreatitis during the POCUS GIT and pancreas examination does not rule out acute pancreatitis, and further testing should be pursued if the history and other clinical findings support a diagnosis of acute pancreatitis. Pancreatitis is typically found more often in the left limb of the pancreas in cats. This patient’s entire pancreas was severely hypoechoic and enlarged. (C) Color flow Doppler evaluation of the right limb of the pancreas in a cat with mild pancreatitis and renal disease. In this case, the blue vessel represents the pancreaticoduodenal artery and the red vessel represents the flow within the pancreaticoduodenal vein. Recall that blood flowing away from the transducer is blue and blood flowing toward the transducer is red.

232 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER POCUS GIT and Pancreas Findings and Their Significance Small Bowel To be able to identify intestinal lesions, it is important to gain familiarity with the normal ultrasonographic appearance of the bowel. • In adults, the normal small intestine typically has five ultrasonographicaly identifiable layers, which tend to resemble a “hamburger” on cross‐section (Figures 12.4, 12.5; see also Figure 16.9). • The five layers from the lumen to the serosal surface include the hyperechoic luminal–mucosal gas interface, hypoechoic mucosa, hyperechoic submucosa, hypoechoic muscular layer, and hyperechoic subserosa and serosa. • When thinking of the ultrasonographic layers of the GI tract, the mnemonic “the sun is bright and it’s dark at midnight” may be helpful in remembering that layers starting with an “s,” like the sun, are bright (submucosa and serosa are hyperechoic), while layers starting with an “m,” like midnight, are dark (mucosa and muscular layer are hypoechoic) on the ultrasound image. Figure 12.5. Normal small bowel. Normal image of small bowel in the transverse plane, in a 5‐year‐old Jack Russell terrier with a two‐month duration of vomiting and radio - graphically evident pyloric outflow obstruction. Note the anechoic luminal small bowel fluid in some of the small bowel adjacent to the urinary bladder (UB). A small amount of anechoic peritoneal fluid was also noted ( arrow), consis- tent with modified transudate. Surgical and histopatholog - ical diagnosis was giant hypertrophic gastropathy (not shown). The small bowel was normal and the patient had a successful outcome with partial gastrectomy. Pearl: Normal small bowel looks like a “hamburger” in transverse orientation. Figure 12.4. Normal layering of small bowel. Normal image of adjacent loops of small bowel in both sagittal and transverse planes in a 9‐year‐old diabetic, female spayed miniature pinscher who presented for acute vomiting due to foreign body ingestion. Luminal GI contents can vary in echogenicity. In this example, the small bowel is predomi - nantly empty with mild admixed gas and chyme causing the hyperechoic lumen. There are five layers of the normal small intestine that are most sonographically evident and easily identified. From lumen to serosal surface, the layers are as follows: the luminal‐mucosal layer (L) is hyperechoic and represents the gas–mucosal interface, the hypoechoic mucosa (M), the hyperechoic submucosa (SM), the hypoechoic muscular layer (ML), and the hyperechoic subserosa/serosa (S). A small amount of anechoic peritoneal effusion (asterisk) was noted due to pancreatitis. Care should be taken not to confuse this finding with an increase in thickness of the mus- cularis layer. Pearl: Use the mnemonic “the sun is bright and it’s dark at midnight” to remember that layers starting with an “s” like the sun are bright (submucosa and serosa are hyperechoic [bright]) while layers starting with an “m” like midnight are dark (mucosa and muscular layer are hypoechoic [dark]) on the ultra - sound image.

233 POCUS: G ASTROINTESTINAL T RACT AND P ANCREAS Foreign Bodies The acoustic appearance of GI foreign bodies detected ultrasonographically varies depending on their physical properties. The margins of foreign objects that allow sound to pass through them can be visualized within the GI lumen whereas objects that reflect or attenuate sound often have a hyperechoic interface and produce shadowing beyond their superficial sur - face (Figures 12.6 and 12.7) (Tidwell and Penninck 1992; Sharma et al. 2011). • The majority of ultrasonographically detectable GI foreign bodies typically involve a well‐defined hyperechoic, hyperreflective acoustic interface with strong distal acoustic shadowing (Tidwell and Penninck 1992; Garcia et al. 2011). • This is in contrast to intraluminal gas, which tends to result in reverberation artifact (Figures 12.8 and 12.9; see also Figures 16.9–16.13) (Tidwell and Penninck 1992; Tyrrell and Beck 2006; Sharma et al. 2011). However, there is some overlap in the shad- owing seen with foreign bodies and intraluminal gas that may render the identification of a foreign body difficult (Tidwell and Penninck 1992). • The acoustic shadowing of foreign bodies may be masked by air, but manipulation of bowel with the probe and changes in patient position can aid evaluation. • Dilation of the intestine orad to a distally shad - owing structure that has a hyperechoic interface between the mucosa and lumen lends support to the presence of intestinal obstruction and suggests the need for surgical exploration (Garcia et al. 2011). • GI foreign bodies should be considered and ruled out when ultrasonographic findings suggest mechanical obstruction or GI irritation. • In the face of appropriate history and physical examination findings, the ultrasonographic detec - tion of peritoneal effusion, gas distension, and abnormal motility (particularly hyperperistalsis with failure to advance intraluminal contents) war- rants a careful search of the GIT for foreign bodies (Tidwell and Penninck 1992; Sharma et al. 2011). Linear Foreign Bodies Linear foreign bodies often appear as persistent echogenic or hyperechoic linear structures within the center of plicated small intestinal loops that do not move with peristalsis and remain static throughout the examination (Figures 12.10 and 12.11; see also Figures 16.9–16.13). • The finding of bowel plication is strongly sugges - tive of a linear foreign body and should prompt careful evaluation of the intestine (longitudinal and transverse images) at sites where plication is seen (Tidwell and Penninck 1992; Garcia et al. 2011). • Intestinal corrugation has also been associated with linear foreign bodies (Tidwell and Penninck 1992) but is less specific than plication. Care should be taken to avoid mistaking bowel plication for corrugation (a sign of spasticity and inflamma - tion/enteritis which may be seen with toxins, pri - mary enteropathy or underlying infectious causes) (Figure 12.12) (see later). 234 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Intestinal Obstruction The ultrasonographic diagnosis of intestinal obstruc - tion may be indirect based on the presence of a combined segmental luminal (fluid) distension, hyper- motility in the absence of luminal content progression (Ogata et al. 1996; Manczur et al. 1998), nonuniform intestinal peristalsis and the presence of hyper‐ and hypomotility in the same animal (Schmutz et al. 1997; Manczur et al. 1998). • Patients with these ultrasonographic findings should be carefully evaluated for luminal foreign bodies, intussusception, or even obstructive neo - plasia as their presence further supports a diag - nosis of intestinal obstruction (Tidwell and Penninck 1992; Penninck 2008a; Garcia et al. 2011). • The ultrasonographic presence of any two of the above findings has a reported sensitivity of 100% and specificity 98.5% for the diagnosis of intestinal obstruction in cats and dogs (Garcia et al. 2011). However, the presence of only intestinal hyper‐ or hypomotility and concurrent segmental intestinal dilation without progression of luminal content may result in a false‐positive diagnosis of intestinal obstruction (Garcia et al. 2011). Thus, it is impera - tive to continue to search for the presence of foreign bodies, intussusception or mass lesions that would further support mechanical obstruction and sur - gical decision making. 235 POCUS: G ASTROINTESTINAL T RACT AND P ANCREAS • In the transverse plane, the lesion has a series of multilayered concentric rings (bull’s eye or target lesion). In the longitudinal plane, the multilayered lesion has linear streaks of hyperechoic and hypoechoic tissue (Figures 12.13 and 12.14; see also Figure 16.13) (Penninck et al. 1990; Larson and Biller 2009; Garcia et al. 2011). • The outer layer of affected intestine may be thickened and signs of bowel obstruction are often present. • Fluid distension oral to the site of invagination, increased peristalsis without signs of content progression, and signs of hypo‐ or normal motility distant from the intussusception may also be noted (Larson and Biller 2009; Garcia et al. 2011). Septic Peritonitis and Pneumoperitoneum Septic peritonitis (often secondary to GI perforation) is a life‐threatening emergency that may be challenging to diagnose presurgically. • The AFAST examination (see Chapters 6 and 7) is particularly helpful in identifying peritoneal effusion (a common finding in patients with septic peritonitis). • Moderate amounts of fluid are easily detectable via ultrasound. Ultrasound‐guided fine needle aspira- tion may subsequently provide the definitive diag- nosis of sepsis (see Chapter 43). • In addition to the presence of fluid, which may be anechoic, anechoic with hyperechoic particles suspended throughout or echogenic and swirling, ultrasound may also detect the presence of intra - peritoneal gas in cases of GI or other hollow organ perforation (Boysen et al. 2003). • Although radiographs are indicated for the detec - tion of pneumoperitoneum, survey radiographs may fail to detect the presence of small‐volume intraperitoneal gas. Ultrasound has been used suc- cessfully to diagnose pneumoperitoneum in both people and veterinary patients (Boysen et al. 2003). • In dogs and cats, the ultrasonographic detection of intraperitoneal gas is characterized by Figure 12.9. Corrugated small bowel. Corrugation and plication can be difficult to differentiate. Notice the lack of deep invagination of the serosal margin. It is important to evaluate the bowel from different angles in both the sagittal and transverse planes to aid in differentiation of corrugation from plication and reverberation artifact from a linear foreign body. This can be achieved in real time with investigative fanning and scanning of the bowel loop in question. The authors recom - mend video documentation of such investigations for the medical record. 236 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER reverberation and comet‐tailing artifacts inter - posed between the nondependent abdominal wall and organs such as the liver and stomach, stomach and body wall or kidney and body wall (Figure 12.15) (Boysen et al. 2003). However, it should be noted that air‐filled bowel can be difficult to differentiate from intraperitoneal air. Careful identification of the peritoneal lining and the enhanced peritoneal strip sign (EPSS) will help differentiate intraperitoneal air from air‐ filled bowel (see later) (Kim et al. 2014). In cases where there is a high index of suspicion for small‐volume intraperitoneal gas or if the etiology of the suspected gas is unclear, ancillary diagnos - tics such as abdominal radiography or computed tomography should be considered. • Detection of the EPSS aids in the diagnosis of pneu- moperitoneum. The EPSS is the linear enhance - ment and thickening of the peritoneal lining with either dirty shadowing or multiple reflection arti - facts. It occurs where the peritoneum comes in contact with free abdominal gas. The associated shadowing or reflection artifact is transmitted through the peritoneal cavity and underlying soft tissue structures (Figure 12.16) (Grechenig et al. 1999; Kim et al. 2014). The small bowel is plicated and bunched with deep invag - inations of the serosa/subserosa. The presence of such a pattern should also prompt strong recommendations for surgical intervention. However, depending on patient positioning and the area of abdomen evaluated, detection of a false‐positive EPSS may occur in proximity to the linea alba of dogs positioned in dorsal recumbency, particularly if the linea alba is focally thickened (Kim et al. 2014). • In people and animals, pneumoperitoneum may be ultrasonographically apparent by the detection of reverberation or comet‐tailing artifacts between the anterior abdominal wall and the liver in the right upper quadrant with an 85% sensitivity and 100% specificity (Pattison et al. 1997; Muradali et al. 1999; Ferrell and Graham 2003; Chao et al. 2015). The authors have seen similar sonographic find - ings within the left dorsal aspect of the dog bet - ween the fundus and left liver. To increase the chances of detecting air between the fundus and left liver, the animal should remain in right lateral recumbency for a minimum of 10–15 minutes to allow intraperitoneal gas to rise to the nongravity‐ dependent sites. • Scanning cranially along an imaginary line of the diaphragmatic crura and at the approximate level of the costophrenic angle, between the ribs Figure 12.13. 238 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER while fanning, may aid in the detection of small amounts of intraperitoneal gas trapped between the liver and diaphragm. Furthermore, in the authors’ experience, evaluating the mid‐highest point of the abdomen, regardless of recumbency, may aid in the detection of a small volume of intraperitoneal gas. • Regardless of patient positioning, particular attention should be paid to the nongravity‐ dependent areas of the abdomen when looking for intraperitoneal gas (as gas rises) (Asrani 2007). • If the history and physical examination are supportive of acute GI disease and an AFAST examination is performed to look for septic peritonitis, it is also reasonable to look for the presence of intraperitoneal gas (particularly along the nongravity‐dependent body wall as gas rises) while simultaneously searching for fluid, which might alternatively be seen along the gravity‐ dependent aspects of the patient as fluid falls or settles. • Failure to detect gas does not rule out GI perfora - tion. Its presence in patients with supporting his - tory and clinical findings expedites the decision for exploratory surgery. Functional Ileus Ultrasonographically, GI motility can be recorded as the number of gastrointestinal contractions observed over a one‐minute time period. • To determine the number of contractions per minute, the number of contractions are recorded Figure 12.15. The patient had been on chronic nonsteroidal antiinflammatory therapy for arthritis. Immediately adjacent to the stomach is a loculation of anechoic fluid with echogenic particles noted in suspension (labeled FF and identified by the cross marks, +). (B) Intraperitoneal gas in the same patient. Pearl: Serial AFAST (and POCUS GIT and pancreas) examinations after resuscitation and rehydration are helpful (four hours post admission out to 12 and 24 hours) to detect initially occult peritonitis or bowel per- foration because peritoneal fluid and gas will often develop over time and as the patient becomes hydrated. Pearl: AFAST and POCUS GIT and pancreas exami- nations are helpful initial screening tests for penu - moperitoneum (Shanaman et al. 2013; Chao et al. 2015). Although CT is generally considered the gold standard for detection of pneumoperitoneum, abdominal radiography (including horizonal beam techniques) are good ancillary tests when pneumo - peritoneum is suspected (Chao et al. 2015).

239 POCUS: G ASTROINTESTINAL T RACT AND P ANCREAS twice over a three‐minute time period, averaged, and then divided by 3 to get the number of contrac- tions per minute (Penninck et al. 1989; Sanderson et al. 2017). • Fasting or anorexia of 12–24 hours duration decreases GI motility in dogs. Thus, knowing when the animal last ate is important when interpreting GI motility. If possible, GI motility should be assessed within six hours of ingesting a meal (Sanderson et al. 2017). • Caution should be exercised when diagnosing hypomotility based on the presence of food within the GI tract, as food can be ultrasonographically detected in the GI lumen of healthy dogs following 24 hours of fasting. However, the absence of GI contraction in the presence of food supports a diag- nosis of ileus (Sanderson et al. 2017). • Normal contractility varies depending on the sec - tion of GIT evaluated. The mean number of peristaltic contractions of the stomach and proximal duodenum is 4–5 contractions per minute. The number of contractions of the small intestine in the midabdomen is more variable and ranges from one to six contractions per minute (Penninck et al. 1989; Sanderson et al. 2017). • Certain GI disorders are associated with changes in intestinal motility, including mechanical bowel obstruction, gastric ulcers, severe pancreatitis, inflammatory bowel disease, and neoplastic processes (Garcia et al. 2011). Functional ileus, dur- ing which the lumen of the bowel remains patent, may also be caused by pain, metabolic dister - bances, poor perfusion, and sedative agents (Sanderson et al. 2017). • A generalized decrease in GI motility is reported in small animals with functional and chronic mechanical ileus, whereas a generalized increase in motility is most commonly reported in cases of acute mechanical obstruction (Penninck 2008a). • There is considerable overlap in motility changes between dogs that do and do not have small intestinal obstruction. Changes in motility alone do not indicate the need for surgery (Sharma et al. 2011; Garcia et al. 2011). • If the emergency clinician notes increased or decreased GI motility in a patient with clinical signs of GI disease, further diagnostics (abdominal radiographs or complete abdominal ultrasound examination) should be considered as several sur - gical conditions (foreign bodies, intussusception, and neoplasia) are frequently associated with altered GI motility (Penninck 2008a; Garcia et al. 2011). A thorough evaluation of the GI tract to rule out these conditions is warranted. Decreased intestinal motility due to functional ileus is commonly seen in postoperative patients. • This condition results in a transient cessation of coordinated propulsive motility, most commonly following abdominal surgery (Koscienly and Kalff 2011). • In people, it is associated with abdominal disten - sion, nausea, vomiting, and the inability to pass stools or tolerate a solid diet. 240 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER • In addition to the discomfort reported in people, postoperative ileus may predispose patients to wound dehiscence, intussusception, and pulmonary and thromboembolic complications (van Bree et al. 2012). • Several predispositions are associated with acute ileus following postoperative abdominal surgery in people, including intestinal handling during surgery, anesthetic agents, and opioid analgesics (Kehlet 2008; van Bree et al. 2012). • Many small animals are routinely fasted pre‐ and postoperatively, which can also contribute to ileus (Sanderson et al. 2017). Unless otherwise contraindicated, food should be reintroduced to patients as soon as possible following surgical procedures. • If the impression of ileus is due to fasting, reintro- ducing solid food within 24 hours of fasting should promote GI motility (Sanderson et al. 2017). However, if reintroduction of solid food fails to stimulate motility in the patient that has been fasted for less than 24 hours, other causes of functional ileus should be considered. It is currently unknown if liquid diets have the same effect on GI motility as solid diets following a period of fasting. • Long‐term ileus following abdominal surgery is believed to result from inflammation of the intestinal muscularis externa (Kalff et al. 1999). • Postoperative ileus involving the entire gastroin- testinal tract can occur even if only part of the intestine had been handled or is inflamed (van Bree et al. 2012). • If postoperative ileus is noted, measures should be taken to ascertain the underlying cause (opioids, postoperative surgery, abdominal pain, electrolyte imbalances, and peritonitis). • Therapeutic interventions should be implemented and include feeding soon after surgery, early ambulation, epidural analgesia (decreases the need for systemic opioid analgesia which is often associ- ated with ileus), nonsteroidal antiinflammatory agents, and minimally invasive surgery (Behm and Stollman 2003; van Bree et al. 2012). Corrugated Intestine Although not always easy to do, it is important to differ- entiate corrugated bowel from plicated bowel as the two pathologies have different etiologies. • Plicated bowel. Plicated bowel is usually associated with intestinal linear foreign bodies that cause the small intestine to bunch around a linear object, resulting in an asymmetrical intestinal pattern (see Figures 12.10, 12.11, 16.9–16.13). The loop of small intestine may weave as it cinches together and con- tracts around the linear foreign body. The finding of plicated bowel may indicate the need for sur - gery, even if the linear foreign body is not ultraso- nographically detected (Tidwell and Penninck 1992) (see Figures 12.9, 12.11, 16.9–16.13). • Corrugated bowel. In contrast, corrugated bowel is a very nonspecific ultrasonographic finding that sug- gests intestinal dysfunction or inflammation, which could result from several different causes (perito- nitis, enteritis, pancreatitis and pancreatic neoplasia, diffuse abdominal neoplasia, enteritis, thrombosis/ infarction, protein‐losing enteropathy, and acute renal failure) (Moon et al. 2003) (see Figure 12.9). • Corrugated intestine. Corrugated intestine occurs secondary to abnormal spastic peristalsis of the bowel resulting in an abnormal wavy (corrugated) pattern to the wall (Moon et al. 2003). The overall direction of the intestine (and serosal margin) tends to appear straight, in contrast to bunched or weaved with pli- cated bowel (see Figures 12.9, 12.12, 16.9–16.13). • Both conditions are most apparent in the sagittal (longitudinal) plane of the small intestine and may be evident in a single loop or sporadically throughout the scan in several loops. • If corrugated bowel is noted in the unstable patient, a POCUS examination of the pancreas and a search for peritoneal fluid using AFAST is warranted as the condition is commonly associated with pancre- atitis and peritonitis. Pancreatitis is particularly common when corrugation of the duodenum is noted (Moon et al. 2003). • If POCUS of the pancreas and/or AFAST examination are unremarkable, or if the patient is stable, a complete abdominal ultrasound exam (or other diagnostic tests) may be indicated to search for other pathol - ogies associated with corrugated bowel, including enteritis (parvovirus, inflammatory bowel disease, lymphocytic plasmacytic enteritis), pancreatic neo- plasia, diffuse abdominal neoplasia, thrombosis/ infarction, protein‐losing enteropathy, and acute renal failure (Moon et al. 2003). Pearl: In differentiating corrugated from plicated bowel, overall direction of the intestine tends to appear straight with corrugated bowel (as with enter- itis or pancreatitis). In contrast, the serosal margin follows the contour of the bunching with plicated bowel (as with surgically indicated linear foreign body) (see Figures 12.10, 12.11, 12.12, 16.9–16.13).

241 POCUS: G ASTROINTESTINAL T RACT AND P ANCREAS Pancreatitis Acute pancreatitis is generally a clinical diagnosis sup- ported by history and physical examination findings. If suspected, a POCUS pancreas examination may further support the diagnosis of pancreatitis. However, ultrasonographic findings may be inconsistent and may not reliably produce sufficient pancreatic paren - chymal change. • A normal ultrasonographic finding does not rule out pancreatitis. • Ultrasound has limited sensitivity (68%) for the detection of pancreatitis, even in severe acute cases (Hess et al. 1998). • Evidence of acute pancreatitis includes an enlarged and diffusely hypoechoic pancreas (Figure 12.17) (Lamb and Simpson 1995; Hecht and Henry 2007). • Variable amounts of peritoneal effusion may be present, and may be amenable to sampling for cytological evaluation. • Surrounding mesenteric fat often appears hyper - choic (bright) due to inflammation, necrosis, and saponification (see Figure 12.17) (Hecht and Henry 2007; Penninck 2008b). • Corrugation of the duodenum or jejunum, and focal pain at the scan site may be present (Hecht and Henry 2007). • Extrahepatic biliary obstruction may accompany pancreatits with bile duct and gallbladder disten - sion. These findings in patients with appropriate history and clinical findings warrant the initiation of therapy for acute pancreatitis. One disadvantage to a POCUS pancreas examination is that the entire bil- iary and pancreatic ductal system requires a greater time commitment and skill level that is typically beyond that of the nonradiologist veterinarian. • If the preliminary POCUS pancreas examination is negative, a complete abdominal ultrasound may be warranted. • When suspected or diagnosed, recheck of the pancreas in 1–3 days should be considered as ultrasonographic signs may become evident with time. Further, follow‐up evaluation will aid in monitoring response to treatment and progres - sion or resolution of changes. Peritoneal Effusion See Chapters 6 and 7. Gas artifacts may be difficult to distinguish from the shadowing associated with some GI foreign bodies. • The stomach is easy to identify due to the presence of rugal folds, but can be difficult to completely image due to luminal ingesta and gas. Luminal contents, or lack thereof, can also affect wall measurements. For example, an empty stomach may give the impression of having a thickened wall. • In dogs, the descending duodenal wall is thicker than other small intestinal segments and can normally measure up to 6 mm in large‐breed dogs. For the remainder of the small bowel, greater than 5 mm (4 mm for the ileum) in dogs and 2.5 mm in cats would generally be considered as thickened (Penninck et al. 1989; Newell et al. 1999). • In cats, the ileum is identified by its bright submu- cosal layer. • The colon can often be differentiated from the small intestinal wall by its thinner wall and lack of motility in normal instances. • Using an acoustic window such as the spleen can enhance imaging of the intestine. Quick Reference of Normals and Rules of Thumb Gastrointestinal T ract • Normal stomach wall thickness. Dogs 3–5 mm (higher in some giant breeds); cats 2 mm interrugal (up to 4.4 mm if rugal fold is measured) (Nyland et al. 2002). Measure from the hyperechoic outer serosal margin to the inner hyperechoic mucosoluminal surface. • Duodenal wall thickness. In dogs, the descending duodenal wall is thicker than other small intestinal segments and can normally measure up to 5 mm in large‐breed dogs (Newell et al. 1999). Measure from the hyperechoic outer serosal margin to the inner hyperechoic mucosoluminal surface. • Small intestinal measurements. Small bowel wall measurements, other than the duodenum, of greater than 4 mm in dogs and 2.5 mm in cats would gener- ally be considered as abnormally thickened (Newell et al. 1999). Measure from the hyperechoic outer serosal margin to the inner hyperechoic mucosolu- minal surface. • Remembering the five layers of the small intestine. Use the mnemonic “the sun is bright and it’s dark at midnight” to remember that on the US image, layers starting with an “s” like the sun are bright (submu- cosa and serosa are hyperechoic [bright]), while layers starting with an “m” like midnight are dark (mucosa and muscular layer are hypoechoic [dark]). • Direct evidence of GIT foreign bodies. The majority of ultrasonographically detectable GIT foreign bodies typically involve a well‐defined hyperechoic, hyperreflective acoustic interface with strong distal acoustic shadowing (Tidwell and Penninck 1992; Garcia et al. 2011). • Linear GIT foreign bodies: plication versus corrugation. The finding of bowel plication is strongly sugges- tive of a linear foreign body and should prompt careful evaluation of the intestine (longitudinal and transverse images) at sites where plication is seen (Tidwell and Penninck 1992; Garcia et al. 2011). Intestinal corrugation has also been associ- ated with linear foreign bodies (Tidwell and Penninck 1992) but is less specific than plication. • Corrguated versus plicated. In differentiating corru- gated from plicated bowel, overall direction of the intestine tends to appear straight with corrugated bowel (medical causes – enteritis/pancreatitis) in contrast to bunched or weaved with plicated bowel (surgical causes – linear foreign body) (Tidwell and Penninck 1992; Moon et al. 2003). • Indirect evidence of obstruction. Suspect obstruction with the finding of a severely dilated jejunum with luminal dilation measuring greater than 1.5 cm, which may highlight the need for a more extensive and complete abdominal ultrasonographic evalua- tion, abdominal radiographs or exploratory sur - gery. Measure from serosal to serosal surface. • Normal peristalsis – counting contractions. Determine the number of contractions per minute by recording the number of contractions over a three‐minute time period and average to get the number of con- tractions per minute (Penninck et al. 1989). ◦ The mean number of peristaltic contractions of the stomach and proximal duodenum is 4–5 contractions per minute. ◦ The mean number of peristaltic contractions of the jejunum averages 1–3 contractions per minute. ◦ The mean number of peristaltic contractions in other areas of small intestine is variable and ranges from one to six contractions per minute (Penninck et al. 1989; Sanderson et al. 2017). ◦ The large bowel (colon) normally has no peristalsis.

243 POCUS: GASTROINTESTINAL TRACT AND P ANCREAS • Ileus. A generalized decrease in GI motility is reported in small animals with functional and chronic mechanical ileus, whereas a generalized increase in motility is most commonly reported in cases of acute mechanical obstruction (Penninck 2008a). However, because of considerable overlap in motility findings, motility alone does not indi- cate the need for surgery (Sharma et al. 2011; Garcia et al. 2011). Pancreas • The right pancreatic limb is generally easiest to image in dogs and is the lobe more commonly affected by pancreatitis (Nyland et al. 2002; Hecht and Henry 2007; Penninck 2008b). • The left pancreatic limb is generally easiest to image in cats. • The reference range for pancreatitic thickness in dogs is 3.5–16 mm (Respess et al. 2012). • Identification of the pancreas can be challenging for the novice sonographer because it is isoechoic to adjacent tissues. As a result, its identification commonly relies on the observance of its duct and vasculature. • Historically, it has been thought that a normal pan- creas is generally not seen; however, the normal pancreas is in fact frequently imaged with high‐ frequency transducers and newer machines. • Pancreatitis is particularly common when corruga- tion of the duodenum is noted (Moon et al. 2003). • Even in cases of severe acute pancreatitis, the sensitivity of ultrasound may only be 68% (Hess et al. 1998). Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 247 Introduction In the grand scheme of things, reproductive ultraso- nography probably gets the short end of the stick since most of our patients in the United States lack their reproductive organs (testicles, ovaries, and uterus) through surgical sterilization. However, one should not assume that reproductive sterilization has taken place simply because the altered pet is more common. It is very important to confirm your patient’s reproductive status since many adopted dogs and cats have unknown medical histories. The sexual status of the male is typi- cally easy to ascertain from the physical examination; however, do not overlook cryptorchidism. Ultrasonographically, the majority of the reproduc- tive tract may be imaged. In females, POCUS repro- ductive includes the ovaries, uterus, cervix, and mammary glands (see Chapters 14 and 15) and for males, the prostate, scrotum, and testes (Figure 13.1). Of these structures, the uterus makes up the vast majority of POCUS reproductive examinations. This chapter, however, will focus on the male reproductive tract. What the POCUS Reproductive – Male Can Do • Help determine causes of scrotal swelling. Screen for: ◦ testicular torsion ◦ orchitis ◦ epididymitis ◦ cryptorchidism ◦ prostatic pathology. What the POCUS Reproductive – Male Cannot Do • Cannot differentiate between different types of testicular tumors. • Cannot differentiate benign versus malignant prostatic conditions. • Cannot fully screen for intraabdominal free fluid. 249 POCUS: REPRODUCTIVE – MALE problems including cryptorchidism. Interestingly, most male scans will be performed on dogs since the feline male seems immune to most reproductive conditions. The Prostate All male dogs have a prostate, neutered or not (Figure 13.4). It is the dog’s only accessory sex gland and it increases in size and weight with age due to glandular hyperplasia (Johnston et al. 2001a). Interestingly, the neutered male is more prone to pros- tatic neoplasia (prostatic adenocarcinoma) than the intact male (Root‐Kustritz 2010). Finding an enlarged prostate in a neutered male of any age should be con - sidered neoplastic until proven otherwise. Ultrasound may be helpful as an adjunctive test for aspirates and biopsies, but a digital rectal examination is invaluable for determining the presence of often painful prostatic enlargement in neutered males. Intact male dogs, on the other hand, have several possible conditions such as benign prostatic hypertrophy, bacterial prostatitis, prostatic abscesses, prostatic cysts, and paraprostatic cysts. Thus, the POCUS reproductive – male examina - tion can be helpful in sorting through these conditions. The feline prostate is a rather small structure of rare clinical importance and is rarely, if ever, imaged. Still, imaging the bladder and surrounding structures may be useful. Imaging the Prostate ‐ Dorsal and Standing Positioning • Dorsal. Place the dog in dorsal recumbency. Find the prostate by locating the urinary bladder. Move your probe to longitudinal orientation and then follow the bladder caudally until it narrows into the trigone region. Now, focus on the urethra (an anechoic linear stripe in longitudinal, anechoic circle in transverse). Once you have the urethra in the long axis, follow it caudally a short distance to the prostate. • Standing. The standing or lateral positions may also be used for prostatic imaging and standing is actually preferred by many sonographers. • A healthy prostate is bilobed and symmetrical. The symmetry is readily appreciated in transverse ori - entation. Except for ductal tissue, the prostatic parenchyma is homogeneous in appearance. The echogenicity is similar to the surrounding fat but has a finer echotexture (Lattimer and Essman 2007). • Stay transverse and assess symmetry (normal) and for homogeneous echogenicity other than the “butterfly.” • Some veterinary radiologists more easily image the prostate with the dog in a standing position. Prostate of the Castrated Male The normal dog prostate ultrasound appearance after involution, shrinking in size as a response to castration, has not been strictly defined or classified; however, Figure 13.4. The normal prostate gland in a castrated dog in the longitudinal plane. The prostate (denoted by the cal - iper marks) is of medium echogenicity similar to that of the normal canine uterus. Source: Courtesy of Robert M. Fulton, DVM, Richmond, VA. Pearl: Do not walk the patient (dogs) or give a litter box (cats) before the POCUS reproductive – male examination. The urine‐filled bladder improves imaging by providing an acoustic window and serves as a landmark in identifying caudal abdom - inal structures. Pearl: A hyperechoic “butterfly” pattern is typically apparent in the transverse view. The “butterfly” cor- responds with distribution of relatively more hyper- echoic (brighter) ductal tissue than the hypoechoic glandular connective tissue (Mattoon and Nyland 2002; Davidson and Baker 2009).

In general, the prostate in the castrated dog appears as a smooth, homogeneous swelling around the proximal urethra with total width being approximately 3–4 times the width of the urethra. The overall echogenicity is similar to that of the uterine body in the female (see Figure 13.4). Benign Prostatic Hypertrophy (BPH) Ultrasonographic appearance : enlarged, uniformly hyperechoic with a smooth margin. The enlargement may be different between dorsal and ventral areas, but is symmetrical when viewed in the transverse plane (Figure 13.5A). In time, the expected symmetry and uniform echogenicity of BPH may be lost as the condition progresses into the cystic stage (Lattimer and Essman 2007). Prostatitis Ultrasonographic appearance: a wide variety depending on severity of disease. The shape is generally normal but the echogenicity may increase or decrease and some degree of mottling (mixed echogenicity) is appreciated. A hypoechoic rim may be evident in some dogs. If prostatitis is severe enough, surrounding fat may become hyperechoic (bright) (Lattimer and Essman 2007). Prostatic Abscesses and Cysts Ultrasonographic appearance: abscesses and cysts may be found within or attached to the prostatic parenchyma. They are typically thin‐walled structures with either anechoic or hypoechoic centers. The presence or absence of acoustic enhancement in the far‐field helps differentiate fluid from soft tissue. Septation and echo- genic fluid are more suggestive of prostatic abscess than cyst(s) (Lattimer and Essman 2007). Gas formation by bacteria may be present with some abscesses. Air will typically be represented by multiple hyperechoic foci within the prostatic parenchyma and may be con - fused with tissue mineralization as may be found with some malignancies. Acoustic shadowing with gas is typically weaker than that seen with mineral. Paraprostatic Cysts Ultrasonographic appearance : in contrast to prostatic cysts, which are found within the prostatic parenchyma, paraprostatic cysts are found adjacent to the gland and may appear confluent with it. They are thin‐walled structures of varying size often appearing similar to the urinary bladder. The fluid contained within the paraprostatic cyst may be anechoic to echoic with or without intraluminal debris (Lisciandro 1995; Davidson and Baker 2009). Paraprostatic cysts are thought to be remnants or associated with remnants of the Müllerian duct (Lisciandro 1995; Smith 2008; Davidson and Baker 2009). Prostatic Neoplasia Ultrasonographic appearance : prostatic neoplasia may show similarities to prostatitis, abscesses, or cysts (see Figure 13.5B). Calcification and severe loss of sym - metry are suggestive of malignancy. Calcification will result in bright echoes with strong acoustic shadow - ing. This finding should prompt the pursuit of an aspi- rate or needle biopsy. Additionally, there is often severe Figure 13.5. Benign prostatic hypertrophy in the transverse plane. Pearl: When a paraprostatic cyst is suspected, it is often immediately helpful to catheterize the patient and radiographically perform a positive contrast study to define the location of the urinary bladder compared to the suspect paraprostatic cyst.
