The ultrasonographic appearance of the prostate should not be the sole determinant in making a specific diagnosis. Digital rectal examination will provide clues in firmness, symmetry, and pain, and tissue sampling, either by aspirate or biopsy, is typically required to make the definitive diagnosis while culture is recom - mended for suspect cases of bacterial infection. Fine needle aspiration has been shown to diagnose pros - tatic carcinoma in about 50% of cases and biopsy has been reported to improve diagnosis to as high as 89% (Johnston et al. 2001a). Scrotum and Testicles The descended scrotal testicles are easy to image using ultrasound. Keeping with previous probe positioning recommendations, begin with longitudinal orienta - tion. A thin, hyperechoic line, the mediastinum testis, is easily identified in the center of the organ (Figure 13.6). By placing both testicles side by side, transverse imaging allows for assessing differences between them regarding echogenicity and texture. The epididymis begins dorsocaudally and is hypoechoic to the testicular parenchyma (Davidson and Baker 2009). Cryptorchidism Descent of testicles normally occurs by 10 days after birth; however, in the young puppy and kitten, the tes- ticles can move between the scrotum and inguinal canal (Hoskins and Taboada 1992). Most clinicians will allow up to 6 months of age, by which time the inguinal canal has closed and any movement is precluded, to confirm cryptorchidism (Johnston et al. 2001b). Cryptorchidism (“hidden testis”) is a heritable, developmental defect in which descent of one or both testes does not occur by 6 months of age. Unilateral cryptorchidism is more common than bilateral. Retained testes are smaller than scrotal testes with size directly correlated with the degree of retention. Testes retained within the abdomen are smaller than those retained within the inguinal canal (Johnston et al. 2001b) (Figure 13.7). • Ultrasonographic scan and appearance : the cryptor - chid testes, while smaller than the scrotal testes, often will retain its normal anatomical structure, including the mediastinum testes with normal expected echogenicity (see Figure 13.7). The retained testicle may be located anywhere from the inguinal canal to the ipsilateral kidney (Davidson and Baker 2009); however, the inguinal location is more common. The cryptorchid testes can be diffi - cult to find (Johnston et al. 2001b). • The POCUS examination is often performed in lat- eral recumbency with the contralateral side down. The ipsilateral leg is raised to allow access to the inguinal region. With the probe in longitudinal ori- entation, a systematic scan is advanced from the inguinal canal to the caudal pole of the ipsilateral kidney. The lateral positioning allows for gravity to pull viscera away from the inguinal and retroperi - toneal areas of interest, improving ultrasono - graphic imaging. The POCUS examination may also be performed in dorsal recumbency. Orchitis and Epididymitis Orchitis (inflammation of the testicle) and epididy - mitis may occur singly or in combination and are typically painful conditions. 253 POCUS: REPRODUCTIVE – MALE however, the immunocompromised individual, children, and pregnant women are considered to be at higher risk and should avoid exposure (Johnston et al. 2001a,b). Care must be taken to protect oneself and other members of the healthcare team by following standard procedures such as wearing exam gloves and avoiding contact with or aerosolization of body fluids. Proper disinfection of surfaces and equipment is mandatory. Rapid slide agglutination tests (RSAT) are available for quick screening tests and agar gel immu - nodiffusion (AGID) can be used to confirm suspected cases. Serological tests have their limitations as B. canis evokes little humoral response. Recent advances in molecular biology have yielded PCR tests but are not yet widely available. A positive identification of the causative organism from blood culture is the definitive proof for brucellosis (Hollett 2010). T esticular T orsion Testicular torsion is more appropriately termed torsion of the spermatic cord. Dogs will typically present with signs of an acute abdomen including abdominal pain, vomiting, dysuria, hematuria, pyrexia, anorexia, leth - argy, or stiff gait. Other physical examination findings may be related to concurrent testicular neoplasia such as truncal, symmetrical alopecia or a pendulous pre - puce seen with Sertoli cell tumors. Ultrasonographic appearance: the testicle of the affected cord is typically enlarged and has a uniform hypoecho- genicity. There may or may not be fluid associated with the epididymis. Absence of blood flow when interro - gated with color flow or power Doppler imaging is the most supportive sign ultrasonographically; definitive diagnosis is made at the time of surgery which is the treatment of choice (Johnston et al. 2001b). T esticular T umors Testicular neoplasia is the most common tumor type in male dogs, second only to skin tumors. Tumors may be unilateral or bilateral and different tumors may be present within the same testicle. The three most common types of tumor are Sertoli cell tumor, seminoma, and interstitial (Leydig) cell tumors. Dogs with testicular neoplasia commonly present with testicular enlargement as the only sign; however, dogs with Sertoli cell tumor may present with bone marrow toxicity (anemia), symmetrical truncal hair loss, and male feminization due to excessive estrogen produc - tion (Johnston et al. 2001b). Testicular tumors may appear as focal masses of varying degrees of distinc - tion from surrounding parenchyma with varying degrees of echogenicity (Davidson and Baker 2009). Ultrasonographic appearance is not specific for tumor cell type and cannot differentiate between benign and malignant conditions (Feeney and Johnston 2007). The Global FAST approach may be used for staging (see Chapter 36). Miscellaneous Scrotal Swellings • Hernias: herniation of small bowel into the scrotum may be detected by finding the normal bowel layers adjacent to the testes; intestinal peristalsis may also be present, helping with the ultrasono - graphic diagnosis (see additionally Chapter 34) (Mattoon and Nyland 2002). • Hematomas, abscesses, and sperm granulomas: may all appear similar to other extratesticular pathology. Pearls and Pitfalls, The Final Say Given the external location and relatively simple anatomy, the testicles are easy to image. Still, make sure to systematically evaluate the three main areas. • Scrotal space – evaluate for fluid, intestines (as in the case of inguinal hernia) or other extratesticular structures, and position of the testicle based upon the epididymis (head caudal, body dorsal, tail dorsocranial). • Testicular parenchyma – evaluate for symmetry in size and shape, tumors, overall echogenicity. • Epididymis – evaluate for focal or diffuse swelling, position (see above), surrounding fluid. Remember, a scrotum that does not contain testicles is not always synonymous with castration; do not forget about cryptorchidism. The prostate is slightly more challenging to image than the testicles, but use the proximal urethra as a guide to lead you directly to it. Evaluate for changes in symmetry and echogenicity in transverse planes. Thoroughly image all edges as paraprostatic pathology can extend well beyond the expected prostatic location. Quick Reference of Normals and Rules of Thumb Given the large variation in size of dogs between breeds, there are no objective measurements to apply across our patients. Symmetry, rather, is the best rule of thumb. The testicles should be ultrasonographically symmetrical to each other, and the prostate should be ultrasonographi- cally symmetrical about its median plane. In general, the prostate in the castrated dog appears as a smooth, homogeneous swelling around the proximal urethra, with total width being approxi- mately 3–4 times the width of the urethra. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 255 Introduction In the grand scheme of things, reproductive ultraso- nography probably gets the short end of the stick since most of our patients lack their reproductive organs (testicles, ovaries, and uterus) through surgical sterili- zation. However, one should not assume that reproduc- tive sterilization has taken place simply because the altered pet is more common. It is very important to confirm reproductive status since many adopted dogs and cats have unknown medical histories. For instance, a pet owner may assume their female is spayed when in reality she may have never been observed to go into heat. When sexual status is questionable, the shaving of hair and evaluation for surgical spay and neutering scars is helpful, as are other physical examination find- ings such as the lack of mammary development in an older female dog or cat. With ultrasound, most of the reproductive tract may be imaged. In females, this includes the ovaries, uterus, cervix, and mammary glands, and for males, the prostate, scrotum, and testes (see Chapter 13). Of these struc- tures, the uterus makes up the vast majority of POCUS reproductive – female examinations. However, other important conditions of the female and male reproduc- tive tracts are discussed in this chapter and Chapter 13. What the POCUS Reproductive – Female Can Do • Diagnose pregnancy. • Aid in the diagnosis of pyometra, mucometra, and hydrometra. • Aid in the diagnosis of pseudopregnancy. • Aid in the medical management of pyometra. What the POCUS Reproductive – Female Cannot Do • Cannot definitively differentiate pyometra from mucometra and hydrometra. • Cannot provide an accurate fetal count. • Cannot fully screen for intraabdominal free fluid. Indications • Any ill intact female cat or dog to rule out pyometra. • Acute abdomen, especially in intact females with abdominal pain. POCUS: Reproductive – Female Robert M. A ¼–½ inch lime green linear tattoo is commonplace (Figure 14.1). Cats may also have a partial amputation of their left ear tip identifying them as sterilized. Note: An AFAST and the assignment of an abdom- inal fluid score should be minimally performed to screen for any effusions or other obvious AFAST target organ pathology. The Global FAST approach provides even more information regarding the thorax (TFAST), including heart (TFAST) and lung (Vet BLUE), as a quick assessment test for localized versus disseminated disease and comorbidities and complications.

256 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER • Dystocia. • Vaginal discharge. • Uncertainty of pregnancy. • Mammary gland abnormalities. Objectives • Be able to image the basic features of the female reproductive tract. • Identify common ultrasonographic reproductive pathology of the female. • Diagnose pregnancy. Reproductive Conditions of the Female Female reproductive anatomy is shown in Figure 14.2. The major structure involved in most concerning conditions of the bitch or queen is the uterus, and two of its major problems are pyometra and dystocia. Fortunately, the enlarged uterus is very accessible with ultrasound and recognizable by the novice sonogra - pher with minimal training. These conditions and other less common uterine and mammary conditions will be discussed but dystocia is covered in a separate chapter (see Chapter 15). Patient Positioning and Probe Selection Patients are best evaluated in dorsal recumbency with a curvilinear probe and a urine‐filled bladder; how - ever, lateral recumbency and standing position may also be used. Depending on the ultrasound machine, use a medium or comparable abdominal preset. Primarily focusing on longitudinal orientation rather than transverse orientation is usually easier when beginning because the female anatomy is more recognizable. However, performing the POCUS Reproductive – Female examination in standing may be less stressful for some patients. Imaging the Normal Ovary The ovaries lie just caudal to the kidneys. To image the kidneys, start in longitudinal orientation and visualize the ipsilateral kidney. Slide the probe caudally and then fan through this area immediately behind the kidney (Figure 14.3). The normal ovary is often diffi - cult to visualize as it is nearly isoechoic to surrounding tissues but will usually have a subtle cystic appearance (Figure 14.4). For this reason, a linear probe providing greater detail may be useful, especially in small dogs and cats. In large dogs, linear probes may not be able to image deep enough. Overlying gas from small intestine and large bowel can interfere with imaging in this area. Figure 14.1. Spay tattoo. Lime green tattoo scar indi - cating this female dog has been spayed. 257 POCUS: R EPRODUCTIVE – F EMALE Ovarian disease is uncommon in the dog and cat and the reader is referred to additional texts regarding ovarian pathology. Most ovarian disease is associated with changes in size (larger) and echogenicity (often hyperechoic), or cystic change (single or multiple anechoic structures) and is at least screened for using the POCUS reproductive – female examination. Imaging the Normal Uterus Begin the examination with the animal in dorsal recumbency. Keep in mind the normal caudal abdom- inal anatomy. The female reproductive tract lies in bet- ween the urinary bladder and colon (Figure 14.5) (Feeney and Johnston 2007). However, performing the POCUS reproductive – female examination in standing (or lateral recumbency) may be less stressful for some patients. • Place the ultrasound probe in longitudinal orienta- tion just cranial to the pubis where you would expect to find the urinary bladder. • Direct by rocking and sliding the probe caudally to the trigone of the bladder, fanning longitudinally and following urine (normally anechoic [black]) until it triangulates and narrows into the urethra. 259 POCUS: R EPRODUCTIVE – F EMALE • Approximately one‐third of the way along the urinary bladder, depending on bladder size, the uterine body will bifurcate into its two horns. • Follow the uterine horns cranially as they make their way caudal to the kidneys, using combinations of longitudinal and transverse views. This can be chal- lenging given the many twists and turns the uterine horns can make. If you are having problems tracing nongravid, nonfluid‐filled uterine horns, then they are probably not clinically relevant. Although rare, some females may have abnormalities of the tubular reproductive tract such as uterine atresia (not formed), more common in cats. Atresia may involve both or only one uterine horn (Johnston et al. 2001b). Cystic Endometrial Hyperplasia‐Pyometra Cystic endometrial hyperplasia (CEH)‐pyometra com- plex is the most common and important uterine dis - order in bitches. CEH‐pyometra occurs during the luteal phase of diestrus although there are some reports of it occurring during anestrus (Verstegen et al. 2008). General classifications of the complex have been sug - gested according to criteria outlined by Dow and DeBosschere. Dow’s classification scheme uses gross pathology findings and histological lesions while DeBosschere’s scheme also uses the degree of inflammatory reaction, fibroblast proliferation, and endometrium to myometrium ratio. Ultrasonography has been shown to be valuable in the diagnosis of CEH‐pyometra and an efficient tool in the identification of more severe disease as described in both Dow’s and DeBosschere’s schemes (Bigliardi et al. 2004). As pyometra should be included in the differential diagnosis for any intact bitch, regardless of the present- ing signs, the focused female reproductive examination for pyometra is indicated for any ill intact female dog or cat and should be considered in combination with AFAST (the Global FAST approach is better). Ultrasound has a higher sensitivity than radiography for deter - mining the presence of uterine enlargement and fluid accumulation (Feeney and Johnston 2007). The ultra - sound scan is similar to that for dystocia with a primary difference of searching for a fluid‐filled uterus rather than a gravid (fetus‐filled) uterus. Pyometra The initial physical examination finding of purulent vaginal discharge should be an immediate trigger for performing an ultrasound examination to determine the presence of pyometra. Conversely, the finding of a fluid‐filled uterus should trigger a more thorough search for purulent vaginal discharge that may be subtle or initially overlooked on physical examination. • Begin the scan in dorsal recumbency. Start over the urinary bladder in longitudinal orientation, moving along the ventral midline from the caudal abdom - inal region to the xiphoid as described with the dys- tocia evaluation. However, performing the POCUS reproductive – female in standing (or lateral recum- bency) may be less stressful for some patients. • Follow the midline evaluation with the lateral to the mammary gland scan on both the left and right sides to help differentiate the fluid‐filled uterus from the urinary bladder and fluid‐distended small bowel. • Careful scanning should be performed along each horn as thoroughly as possible to avoid a false‐neg- ative evaluation for pyometra. The amount and echogenicity of fluid can vary greatly independent of the pyometra being “open” (cervix open, vaginal discharge) or “closed” (cervix closed, no vaginal discharge), although a “closed” pyometra gen- erally leads to a greater degree of fluid distension. Echogenicity of intraluminal fluid in pyometra ranges from anechoic (pure black) to viscous and echogenic (Figure 14.10). In cases with echogenic fluid, its movement may be characterized by slow, swirling patterns (Mattoon and Nyland 2002). Pearl: In the nongravid or fluid‐filled uterus, it may not be possible to image the uterine horns for their full length. Figure 14.9. 261 POCUS: REPRODUCTIVE – FEMALE One form of segmental uterine pathology that is likely misdiagnosed as CEH‐pyometra has been termed pseudoplacentational endometrial hyperplasia (PEH). First reported in 1914, PEH also occurs during the luteal phase, with the endometrium remodeling in a way that is very similar to the normal histology of the endometrium at normal placentation sites in preg- nancy (Schlafer and Gifford 2008). While histologically different, clinical presentation and management are the same as for CEH‐pyometra. PEH is likely to form approximately two months post estrus compared to the typical two weeks postestrus occurrence more common with CEH‐pyometra. Surgical versus Medical Management The old adage holds true: “Don’t let the sun set on a pyometra.” Often spoken by a surgeon, this does not mean that all cases of pyometra should be immediately addressed with the scalpel. The unstable, compromised, septic patient should be resuscitated before operation. By optimizing patient status for anesthesia through the initiation of appropriate antibiotics, correction of hypo- volemia, hypoglycemia, and acid–base and electrolyte abnormalities, a favorable outcome is more likely. Detailed preoperative management is beyond the scope of this chapter but may be found in other reference materials (Johnston et al. 2001a,b; Traas 2008). While surgery remains the best option for the vast majority of cases, medical management has been shown to be a viable therapeutic option for the valuable breeding bitch (Verstegen et al. 2008). Because of the potent drugs and unfamiliarity with protocols by most general practitioners and emergency and critical care veterinarians, medical management is best referred to a small animal specialist in therio- genology or other veterinarian experienced in repro- ductive work. Stump Pyometra A stump pyometra should always be on the differential of any acute abdomen in a female spayed dog what- ever matter their age and its location would be ana- tomically between the urinary bladder and the colon. Stump pyometra may occur following ovariohyster - ectomy if a portion of the uterine horns or uterine body is not removed and the animal has increased progesterone concentrations. Progestins may come from endogenous sources such as residual ovarian tissue, sex hormone‐secreting adrenal tumors, or exogenous sources such as progestational compounds used to treat dermatitis, or may be potentially absorbed from creams used for treatment of meno- pausal symptoms in women (Howe 2006). Stump pyometra will not occur in a patient that has under - gone ovariectomy as there is no “stump.” The entire uterus is left intact. Common in European nations, the procedure is beginning to gain popularity in the United States. The same concerns for the development of pyometra (endogenous or exogenous progestin exposure) exist for stump pyometra but at least one study of 72 bitches that underwent ovariectomy did not show any incidence of pyometra over a 6–8‐year follow‐up (Howe 2006). The POCUS reproductive –female examination for stump pyometra is identical to that for pyometra but the primary area of interest is the caudal abdomen, specifically the region between the trigone of the bladder and colon. At this location, search for an area of mixed echogenicity indicative of complex mass effect (England et al. 2003; Davidson and Baker 2009). Other local diseases mimicking or causing a stump pyometra include stump granuloma caused by excess residual devitalized uterine body tissue, use of inappropriate suture material, or poor sur - gical asepsis. Additionally, hematoma formation caused by poor surgical technique or a coagulopathy can serve as a nidus for infection. The finding of free fluid suggestive of acute hemorrhage or peritonitis is another indication for the AFAST scan and assign- ing an abdominal fluid score (see Chapters 6 and 7) and the Global FAST is a more thorough examination for staging (see Chapter 36). Free fluid may only be characterized by abdominocentesis and subsequent fluid analysis. If the case is not urgent, that is, does not have a septic abdomen or large bleed, then a complete detailed abdominal ultrasound may be warranted. Uterine Torsion Uterine torsion in the dog and cat is uncommonly reported. However, the ultrasonographic appearance is as expected for pyometra. The diagnosis of uterine torsion is typically made at surgery (Misumi et al. 2000; Chambers et al. 2011). An AFAST and an assigned fluid score help screen for effusions including secondary hemoabdomen, and a Global FAST can assess for Pearl: Always use ultrasound for guided cystocen- tesis for obtaining urine with a suspect pyometra case. Failure to do so may result in inadvertent aspi- ration of the pus‐filled uterus and contamination of the abdomen.

262 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER thorax‐related complications, including aspiration pneumonia, lung edema, and volume depletion (see Chapter 36), and help direct fluid resuscitation. Mounting of Postoperative Recently In‐heat Spayed Females In‐heat (estrus) spayed females should be kept away from male dogs for two weeks postoperatively because they remain receptive to interested males. Mounting postoperatively can lead to trauma and rupture of the surgical site and insemination of the peritoneal cavity, leading to potentially life‐threat - ening sterile or septic peritonitis (Morley 2006). AFAST and fluid scoring would be the scan best suited to determining whether obvious peritonitis exists (evidence of free fluid), with subsequent char - acterization of ascites by abdominocentesis. Pseudopregnancy All bitches experience the same progesterone profile whether they become pregnant or not. As the proges - terone falls at the end of diestrus, some bitches will expe- rience overt signs of imminent whelping with fully developed mammary glands and milk letdown, nesting behavior, and even abdominal contractions (Johnston et al. 2001c). Although rare, the queen may also show signs of pseudopregnancy. The owners may be convinced their female dog has not been bred but we are all aware of unsupervised receptive females left in the backyard becoming pregnant. A POCUS reproductive – female examination will reliably confirm or refute the presence or absence of fetuses during midgestation and later. Pregnancy Diagnosis Pregnancy is ultrasonographically characterized by segmental fluid distension of the uterine horns. The hallmark is the fetal structures with the segments of fluid (Figure 14.11). These segments are the fetal vesicles. Fetal heart rate can typically be detected ultrasonographically after day 21 post luteinizing hormone (LH) surge. A more thorough discussion of fetal development can be found in Chapter 15. Mammary Glands Due to its superficial location and small thickness, the mammary gland is best imaged with a high‐frequency linear probe. However, if using a curvilinear probe, use the highest frequency available. The normal developed mammary gland at parturition is of a homogeneous appearance. The larger blood vessels may be noted entering the gland. With disease such as mastitis and neoplasia, there is loss of the homogeneous appear - ance (Mattoon and Nyland 2002). The ultrasonographic appearance of mammary gland neoplasia can be quite variable depending on its severity. Small mammary tumors may appear as poorly defined hypoechoic structures with acoustic enhancement artifact, and larger tumors may appear hyperechoic, sometimes with the presence of cysts (Figure 14.12). The spread of tumor tissue among the mammary glands can be successfully detected by ultrasound, and it is very sensitive for detecting such lesions of the mammary gland. 263 POCUS: R EPRODUCTIVE – F EMALE can also be successfully scrutinized for abnormal changes. Ultrasound, however, cannot determine whether lymphadenopathy is due to metastatic spread of tumor tissue or inflammatory reaction (Zuki and Boyd 2004). Pearls, Pitfalls, The Final Say The POCUS reproductive – female examination can lend insight to many disorders such as pyometra, hydrome- tra, and mucometra. Because these diseases are charac- terized by fluid, ultrasound is a sensitive imaging modality for these conditions. Be careful not to confuse the urinary bladder or fluid‐filled gastrointestinal tract (as with small bowel obstruction or severe diarrhea dis- tending the colon) with a diseased uterus. Similar evalu- ation of the uterus can help diagnose pregnancy and ultrasound is a fast, noninvasive method to do so. Quick Reference of Normals and Rules of Thumb • In anestrus, there is no uterine luminal fluid in nor- malcy; however, in estrus there may be a thin echo- genic stripe also considered as a normal finding (Mattoon and Nyland 2002; Verstegen et al. 2008). • The nongravid uterus is tubular, homogeneous in echotexture, with a lumen that is not readily seen and is differentiated from small intestine by lack of peristalsis and intraluminal gas, and absence of the layered appearance characteristics (Mattoon and Nyland 2015). Uterine width varies from 3 to 5 mm in cats and 5 to 10 mm in dogs. • A sonographic hallmark of pyometra is diffuse or segmental fluid dilation of the uterus. • Abdominal radiography is the most accurate way of determining the number of puppies or kittens in the litter (Davidson and Baker 2009). When talking to clients, avoid confirming numbers in the litter using ultrasound because of its inaccuracy. • Normal ultrasonographic layering of the small bowel in the fetus may be used as a guideline for full‐term maturation of puppies and kittens (Mattoon and Nyland 2002) – see Chapter 15. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 265 Introduction Canine and feline dystocia cases are challenging with the clinician having to juggle maternal, fetal, client, and breeder factors. While POCUS dystocia examination cannot help in managing all these elements, it is a valuable tool to gain insight into the fetal side of things and, when combined with the Global FAST approach, the maternal side of things. Assessing fetal development, viability, and fetal stress helps the clinician to make critical decisions in the management of dystocia. What the POCUS Dystocia Can Do • Help assess fetal maturity. • Screen for the presence of fetal stress. • Help manage dystocia by using serial examina- tions for the screening of fetal distress. What the POCUS Dystocia Cannot Do • Cannot provide an accurate fetal count. • Cannot consistently allow the scrutiny of every individual fetus for fetal stress. • Cannot fully screen for intraabdominal free fluid. Indications • Parturition in any dog or cat. • Diagnosed dystocia. • Vaginal discharge during pregnancy. • Green vaginal discharge not followed by passage of a puppy or kitten. Objectives • Discuss final fetal organogenesis. • Discuss fetal heart rate in relation to fetal stress. Dystocia Dystocia: from the Greek dys, meaning difficult, and tokos, meaning birth, or, more simply put, a difficult birthing. More specifically, dystocia is defined as the inability to expel fetuses through the birth canal dur - ing parturition and may result from maternal or fetal factors that prevent delivery from taking place (Jutkowitz 2005). Dogs and cats, like many mammals, tend to undergo parturition during the relative safety of night time. Therefore, dystocia often occurs outside normal business hours for the small animal clinician and becomes the responsibility of the overnight emergency veterinarian. A synergistic relationship between melatonin and oxytocin may, in part, explain this phenomenon (Sharkey et al. 2009). If the clinician presented with a dystocia has been managing the pregnancy from conception, they have a huge body of clinical information that can greatly aid important decision making, particularly in relation to deter - mining if pregnancy is term and parturition is immi- nent. Many times, however, the managing clinician is novel to the pregnancy and must rely on often POCUS: Dystocia Robert M. For either party, ultrasound is an invaluable tool to man - age parturition, including dystocia. Two primary pieces of vital information that POCUS can help deter- mine during parturition and dystocia management are fetal maturation and fetal stress. Fetal Maturation: Imaging Puppies and Kittens In Utero The pregnant bitch is often scanned in dorsal recum - bency. However, during term gestation when the gravid uterus may place undue pressure on the bitch’s diaphragm, scan in lateral recumbency (or standing position) (Figure 15.1) Dorsal recumbency has the advantage of allowing the uterine horns to fall away from each other and allows for a more systematic approach of scanning the entire uterus. Lateral recum- bency results in less pressure on the diaphragm but the uterine horns stack on top of each other. From either position, start with the probe in longitudinal orientation along the ventral midline near the pelvic brim. Fan the probe laterally to both sides. Return to the starting position, slide the probe crani - ally and repeat the lateral scanning movements. Repeat this process until most of the abdomen has been scanned and you have the general layout of the uterine horns and fetuses. Upon finding a fetus, align the probe along its long axis parallel to its spine to examine fetal abdominal and thoracic structures. • Start with the fetal abdomen and find the liver, which is generally the easiest to image because of its size and location adjacent to the thorax. • After identifying the liver, look caudally for the kid- neys (Figure 15.2) and small intestine (Figure 15.3). These are some of the last organs to form and serve as a guide for fetal maturation. As they develop, the kidneys begin to appear similar to adults with distinct cortical and medullary regions (see Chapters 10 and 16). The intestines are the final organ to develop their ultrasonographic identity and typically mark the end of fetal organogenesis (Mattoon and Nyland 2002; Gil et al. 2015) (see also Figures 12.4 and 16.9, and Chapters 12 and 16). There are four sonographic phases of fetal intestinal maturation beginning between days 39 and 44 of gestation as measured from the luteinizing hormone (LH) surge, with the final phase of fetal intestinal Pearl: Fetal heart rate is a key indicator of fetal stress. This final phase is characterized not only by intestinal layering (see Figures 12.4 and 16.9), but also by consistent and frequent peristalsis. The three visible bowel wall layers are the hyperechoic mucosal surface (intestinal lumen), the hypoechoic combined mucosa, submucosa, and muscularis, and the hyperechoic serosa. As ultrasound technologies continue to improve, it may be possible in the future to differentiate the middle layer into its com- ponent parts, thus giving a more accurate determina - tion of final, functional fetal maturity. In phase three of sonographic intestinal maturation, the intestines develop peristalsis but this is only intermittent and it may take over one minute of visualizing the intestines to see peristalsis. In the fourth final phase, intestinal motility is constant and visible immediately with ultra- sound (Gil et al. 2015). After scanning the fetal abdomen, follow the fetal trunk cranially into the thorax, which is readily identi- fied by the ribcage. There the beating heart is readily identifiable in the live, unstressed fetus. Pitfall: As the onset of consistent intestinal peri - stalsis may be as much as four days from natural delivery, visualization of intestinal motility should not be the sole determinant for C‐section. Here the fetal heart should be easily recognized by its fluttering chambers. The fetal heartbeat is the hallmark characteristic of fetal vitality. Fetal Stress Determining Fetal Heart Rate One of the most sensitive indicators of fetal stress is heart rate. There are two ways to determine fetal heart rate. The first, the “eyeball method,” is simple but lacks accu- racy. Visualize the fetal heart and count how many beats per minute. The second method is to use M‐mode imaging. This is preferred as it is more accurate and allows for better documentation. The M‐mode image may be digitally saved or printed for the medical record. Using M‐mode is more time‐consuming and technically more challenging when first learning the technique but in time it becomes much more expe- dient. In comparison, the eyeball method is generally an estimate while the M‐mode method is an accurate measurement of fetal heart rate (Figure 15.4). Fetal Heart Rates and Fetal Stress With increasing fetal stress come decreasing fetal heart rates. Specific values for heart rate in relation to fetal stress can vary among clinicians. From a clinical view- point, Traas (2008) uses the following guidelines. • Fetal heart rates of 160–180 beats/min indicate mild distress and clinical intervention should be considered. • Fetal heart rates between 140 and 160 beats/min indicate moderate distress and high risk of fetal death if not delivered within the next 2–3 hours. • Fetal heart rates less than 140 beats/min indicate severe distress and that immediate intervention (C‐ section) is required because fetal death is imminent. A study by Zone and Wanke (2001) suggests more conservative values. • Fetal heart rates between 180 and 220 beats/min indicate mild distress. • Fetal heart rates less than 180 beats/min indicate severe fetal distress. An additional marker of fetal stress is fetal bowel movements. All fetuses under severe stress exhibit bowel movements (Zone and Wanke 2001), which may be seen ultrasonographically as an echogenic character to the amniotic fluid. Similar echogenicity of the amniotic fluid may also be seen with premature pla- cental separation and hemorrhage (Lopate 2008). • Avoid telling a client the number of puppies or kit- tens in a litter based on a fetal count using ultra- sound because of its unreliability. The most accurate way of determining the number of puppies or kit- tens in a litter is by radiography (Davidson and Baker 2009). Pearl: The fetal heart can be difficult to image in fetal death because of both lack of heart movement and varying degrees of fetal decomposition. Intrauterine gas typically representing fetal death and decomposition may also be evident during ultrasound by dirty shadowing and air reverbera- tion artifacts, which further interfere with fetal cardiac imaging. Pearl: Normal canine or feline fetal heart rates should be greater than 200 beats/min and often well above 220 beats/min. Fetal cat heart rates are often around 265 beats/min (Jutkowitz 2005). Pitfall: Know how your ultrasound machine is set in M‐mode to determine heart rate. Some measure a single cycle while others measure two cycles and take the average. Pitfall: As they pass over a fetus, segmental uterine contractions may result in transient reduction of fetal heart rate (Lopate 2008). Pearl: When evaluating for fetal stress, bear in mind that stress may be variable within the litter and that a single individual may not reflect the general status of others. There may be fetal death in one or two fetuses, yet the others are healthy. Pearl: Normal fetal heart rate is approximately dou- ble the dam’s heart rate (Mattoon and Nyland 2015).

269 POCUS: Dy STOCIA • If uterine rupture or hemorrhage is a possibility, then an AFAST and assigned fluid score should be performed (see Chapters 6 and 7). Clinical intervention, whether surgical or medical, should not be solely premised on ultrasonographic findings since ultrasound cannot evaluate all forms of dystocia. Abdominal radiography should also be used to assess fetal size relative to the mother’s pelvic diam- eter to rule out forms of mechanical dystocia. Bloodwork should be used to rule out metabolic causes of dystocia. History (duration of time between births, duration of hard pushing), physical examination find- ings, and the owner’s observations and expectations must all be included the decision‐making process. Serial POCUS Dystocia during Medical Management The use of ultrasound for monitoring signs of fetal stress during medical management is superior to tradi- tional means. Moreover, its use carries the potential to positively influence the decision‐making process regarding medical versus surgical management, thus optimizing the chance for a favorable outcome for the fetuses, bitch, client, and veterinarian. Pearls, Pitfalls, The Final Say Ultrasonography is a very useful clinical tool for managing dystocia. The most important relevant skill is also perhaps the easiest to learn and that is deter - mining the fetal heart rate. A steady hand is required to visualize the small fetal heart but once this skill is developed, measuring fetal heart rate becomes quick and easy. Imaging the remainder of the fetal structures takes a little more time to develop the fine motor and visual interpretation skills, and is machine dependent, requiring greater ultrasound detail, but sonographer proficiency will come with time and practice. Using POCUS to assess fetal maturity can aid in the timing of C‐sections and other clinical interventions. Figure 15.4. M‐mode of fetal heart rate. Note that variability exists in litters where one fetus may be severely distressed and another normal. • Normal ultrasonographic layering of the small bowel coupled with peristalsis in the fetus may be used as a guideline for full‐term maturation of puppies and kittens (Mattoon and Nyland 2002). • In anestrus there is no uterine luminal fluid in nor - malcy; however, in estrus there may be a thin echo- genic stripe also considered as a normal finding (Mattoon and Nyland 2002). • Abdominal radiography is the most accurate way of determining the number of puppies or kittens in the litter (Davidson and Baker 2009). Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 271 Introduction Pediatric patients are commonly presented to the vet- erinarian due to signs referable to the abdominal cavity. Abdominal disorders can rapidly progress to serious conditions in pediatric dogs and cats; anorexia or fasting can result in hypoglycemia, vomiting can result in aspiration pneumonia, diarrhea can result in intussusception, and perforation from a foreign body can cause peritonitis. Congenital anomalies can first become clinically apparent in the pediatric patient. Dietary indiscretions are common. Parasitic infestation and viral infectious disease have the greatest incidence in pediatric patients. Contagious diseases result in con- finement in an isolation ward where continuous moni- toring can be difficult. Rapid, accurate diagnostic evaluation permits timely effective intervention. Physical examination findings, fecal examination for cytology, parasites and viral antigens, fecal culture for pathogenic bacteria, and abdominal radiography can all contribute useful diagnostic information. Cageside POCUS pediatrics and its abdominal ultrasound provide valuable clinical information about the peritoneal cavity, great vessels, abdominal viscera, and lymph nodes and can usually be obtained without sedation or anesthesia unless the patient is markedly painful. Ultrasound thus greatly facilitates prompt and ongoing diagnostic evalua- tion of the pediatric patient with abdominal disorders. What POCUS Pediatrics Can Do • Support or negate clinical suspicions based on less sensitive evaluations of physical examination, lab- oratory testing, and abdominal radiography. • Confirm/support the presence of an absolute indi- cation for surgery (e.g., intussusception, obstruc- tive foreign body, perforated bowel). • Provide support for further diagnostics (suspected vascular anomaly, upper or lower urinary tract disorders). What POCUS Pediatrics Cannot Do • Cannot replace a complete detailed abdominal ultrasound scan performed by a veterinary radiol- ogist or trained specialist. Indications • Acute abdomen. • Abdominal free fluid (urine, blood, transudate, exudate). • Protracted vomiting or diarrhea not responsive to supportive care. • Unexplained clinical deterioration. Objectives • Perform a basic ultrasound exam in a structured format. • Answer important clinical questions especially in confirming or refuting clinical suspicions based on physical examination, laboratory findings, and abdominal radiography to better direct pediatric care. • Answer important clinical questions when delays exist in being able to schedule a complete abdom- inal ultrasound by a veterinary radiologist or trained specialist. Equipment Pediatric patients are best evaluated using an ultra- sound machine equipped with a curvilinear (micro- convex) variable frequency scanhead (6.0–8.0 MHz) POCUS: Pediatrics Autumn P . Patient Preparation The pediatric patient should be gently placed in dorsal recumbency, ideally in a small padded V‐trough, and restrained by assistant(s) holding the fore‐ and hindlimbs (Figure 16.1A). Permit the pediatric patient to become accustomed to this restraint before initiating clipping or scanning; this usually minimizes strug - gling and resultant aerophagia. If sedation or analgesia is required, the use of a reversible narcotic agent such as hydromorphone or butorphanol is preferable. However, lateral recumbency or standing positioning is now being used for AFAST, TFAST, and Vet BLUE and provides another option, especially in stressed or critical pediatric patients. Figure 16.1. 273 POCUS: PEDIATRICS Clipping hair is usually minimally necessary in the pediatric patient. Clipping the cranioventral abdominal hair, using a quiet set of electric clippers with a #40 blade in the direction of hair growth, rather than against it, minimizes cutaneous trauma. Wetting the clipped skin with tepid water, tincture of zephran or 70% isopropyl alcohol, followed by a liberal amount of ultrasound gel, permits the best acoustic coupling of the scanhead to the patient, improving the image obtained. Care should be taken to avoid excessive chilling of pediatric patients secondary to the application of cool, room‐tempera- ture liquids and gels followed by evaporation. Alcohol‐based hand sanitizer is another coupling medium option that is less noxious. Fasting as much as is safely possible in the pediatric patient minimizes gastric ingesta obscuring imaging of the liver and gastrointestinal gas accumulation inter - fering with visualization of other abdominal viscera. Preventing urination immediately prior to the exami- nation permits better evaluation of the urinary bladder and dorsal sublumbar structures. Nauseated patients should be closely monitored for vomiting or regurgita- tion and immediately repositioned to ventral recum- bency with the head lowered should it occur to help prevent aspiration pneumonia. Serial evaluations can provide useful information when the clinical status of the pediatric patient has changed. clinicopathological deterioration, progres- sive lethargy or obtundation, acute or progressive pain, changes in abdominal palpation findings, or refractory vomiting or diarrhea warrant repeat evalua- tion for ultrasonographic findings indicating that gas- trointestinal obstruction, intussusception, visceral perforation, and/or peritonitis have occurred. Ultrasound of the Normal Pediatric Abdomen Regardless of the clinical history, the abdomen should always be evaluated completely and methodically, in a clockwise direction starting with the liver. Performing a complete abdominal scan in an organized fashion saves time and often identifies disorders that might otherwise be missed if only a focused study (i.e., bladder scan) is done. The complete scan should only take 10–15 minutes (Baker 2009). To begin, place the scanhead under the xiphoid with the beam in the sagittal plane. Visualization of the liver is achieved by fanning the beam from the patient’s right to left. The gallbladder is seen on the right; the left liver lobes are seen ventral and sometimes caudal to the stomach (see Figure 16.1B). Turning the scan- head to transverse allows for visualization of the liver between the stomach and gallbladder. This view is good for evaluation of the hepatic border, echogenicity of hepatic parenchyma, and the portal architecture (see Figure 16.1C). The portal vessels have more echogenic walls than the hepatic veins (see Figure 16.1D). Evaluation of the body and left limb of the pancreas is actually possible at this point, by looking caudal to the stomach. In sagittal, point the scanhead directly into the dog (Figure 16.2). This visualizes the pancreatic trapezoid where the body and the left limb of the pancreas are located. The spleen appears in the near‐field; the splenic vein divides the pancreatic body from the left limb. Realize that if the pancreas is normal, it is isoechoic to the surrounding mesentery and not visualized readily (Figure 16.3A). The normal pancreas can be visualized in the pediatric patient at times, due to the paucity of fat within the abdomen; lack of gastric gas is also helpful (see Figure 16.3B). Continuing in the sagittal plane, scan to the left past the stomach to the spleen. The spleen will be visual- ized ventrally in the near‐field, confirmed by the Pearl: Electronic warming devices (warm water blankets, 3M™ Bair Hugger™) may cause electronic interference with the ultrasound equipment (a wavy screen); warm water blankets or fluid bags are superior for preventing hypothermia (Penninck 2002a; Baker and Davidson 2006). Pearl: Serial examinations are very helpful and should be used in patients with worsening signs when ultrasound findings are initially equivocal or indeterminate. Pearl: Always do the POCUS pediatrics examina- tion in the same manner each time, going in a clock- wise direction. Pearl: Portal veins have more echogenic walls than hepatic veins.

Following the spleen transversely down the left body wall, you will see the left kidney. Pearl: Remember “SLiCK” for the order of echogenicity between spleen, liver, and kidney. In other words, the spleen (S) is normally more echogenic (brighter) than the liver (Li), which is normally equal or slightly more echogenic (brighter) than the cortex of the kidney (CK). Once visualization of the left kidney is achieved, turn to the sagittal plane and evaluate the renal border, cor- tical echogenicity, and pelvic architecture (see Figure 16.4B). Dilation of the renal pelvis is best seen in the transverse plane. Bear in mind that mild renal pelvic dilation can be associated with fluid loading and diuresis (Figure 16.5). The adrenal is located medial to the cranial pole of the kidney. In sagittal, scan medially from the kidney in order to visualize the linear aorta and the renal artery. The left adrenal is located cranial to the left renal artery and caudal to the left cranial mesenteric artery. Evaluate bladder wall and lumen contents and, dorsal to the bladder, the major vessels (caudal vena cava and aorta) (see Figure 16.6B). Sublumbar lymph nodes will be seen at the aortic bifurcation into the iliac arteries, adjacent to the bladder wall. The abdominal lymph nodes are readily visible in pediatric patients due to nonspecific immune stimulation at that period of development; this is usu - ally considered normal if their appearance is homoge - nous (see Figure 16.6C). The bladder should be scanned in both the transverse and sagittal planes. Sagittal scanning of the urinary bladder caudally will allow visualization of the proximal urethra (and pediatric prostate in the male) (Figure 16.7A). The pediatric uterus is best seen in transverse, dorsal to the bladder and adjacent to the colon (see Figure 16.7B). The testes should be found in the scrotum after 6 weeks of age (see Figure 16.7C). At the edge of the right ribcage, within the renal fossa of the liver, the right kidney will be found. The right kidney should be evaluated as was the left (renal border, cortical echogenicity, and pelvic architecture). By scanning sagittally between the right kidney and the caudal vena cava using a fanning technique, the right adrenal is visualized just lateral to the caudal vena cava (Figure 16.8A). Returning to the transverse plane in the cranial midabdomen at the mesenteric root, scan for mesen - teric lymph nodes and small bowel wall architecture. It may take 2–3 craniocaudal passes to evaluate the entire bowel in a thorough fashion. Canine and feline small bowel has distinct layering and motile ingesta in the lumen. Normally, the small bowel appears sonograph- ically as four distinct layers. The bowel lumen appears hyperechoic, as the mucosal interface is echogenic. The compression of gas and ingesta also visually strengthens this hyperechoic line. The layer just outside the lumen is the mucosa; it is hypoechoic and normally the thickest appearing section. Outside the mucosa is the submucosa, which is hyperechoic to the mucosa and about one‐third the thickness. The muscularis, the bowel muscle layer, is outside the submucosa and appears as a very thin hypoechoic black line. The out - ermost layer, the serosa, is not seen as linearly as the other wall layers, but is very hyperechoic and about the same thickness as normal muscularis (Figure 16.9). Figure 16.7 . 279 POCUS: P EDIATRICS Common Pediatric Abdominal Disorders Gastrointestinal Disease Abdominal ultrasonography provides additional and complementary information about the presence or absence of fluid in the peritoneal cavity (hemorrhage, effusion), intraabdominal gas suggesting bowel perfo- ration (or postoperative), the appearance of gastrointes- tinal contents (appropriate vs foreign), gastrointestinal tract motility (ileus vs hyperkinetic), gastrointestinal wall morphology (infiltrative, disrupted or edematous), and mesenteric lymph node appearance (anticipated pediatric reactivity vs pathological). Peritonitis/Peritoneal Effusion Pediatric patients have a small amount of free, scant, anechoic peritoneal fluid that appears in an abdominal ultrasound (best visualized lateral to the spleen when in dorsal recumbency) and represents normalcy. Increased fluid volume or echogenicity can indicate hemorrhage, septic peritonitis (exudative), transuda - tive ascites, or rupture of the gallbladder or urinary tract (see Figure 16.9D). 280 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER or urinary tract rupture are usually accompanied by evidence of inflammation causing progressively increased echogenicity (brightness) of the serosal sur - faces over time (Figure 16.10A). Blunt trauma resulting in hemoabdomen is best eval- uated with FAST ultrasound (see also Chapters 6 and 7). Rupture or crushing trauma to the liver or infarction of the spleen is readily differentiated from normal homogenous parenchyma (see Figure 16.10B). The localization and normal appearance of fluid‐filled vis- cera (bladder, gallbladder) can be reassuring but does not eliminate the possibility of an occult rupture; serial evaluation is advised along with the accumulation of clinical data (e.g., ultrasound‐guided centesis for peri- toneal fluid evaluation) (Penninck 2002b; Baker 2012). Gastrointestinal Foreign Body: Nonobstructive versus Obstructive A common clinical dilemma results from the ingestion of foreign objects by pediatric patients. Foreign bodies can cause gastrointestinal inflammation and perfora - tion even if they are not obstructive. Obstruction and/ or perforation are absolute indications for laparotomy, albeit an invasive and expensive procedure. On the other hand, an unnecessary (negative) laparotomy in the pediatric patient can increase morbidity and mortality from anesthetic events, hypotension, hypo - volemia, and surgical trauma, and is less likely to be tempered by the acquisition of meaningful biopsies as would occur in the adult pet. 281 POCUS: PEDIATRICS Unless radiopaque, gastrointestinal foreign bodies are often difficult to confirm radiographically; they are usually suspected clinically based on intraluminal gas and fluid accumulation proximal to the mechanical obstruction caused by their presence. Serial radiog- raphy can support progression of a nonobstructive foreign body but requires time. Contrast radiography can complicate subsequent endoscopy or laparotomy, and can be difficult to accomplish in the vomiting patient. Ultrasonography can provide supportive information and sometimes confirm the diagnosis if the foreign body has a characteristic appearance (such as a ball, a trichobezoar or a linear foreign body). Typically, a bright interface associated with strong shadowing suggests a foreign body. Fluid distension and peristalsis proximal to the object can confirm the suspicion. Balls have a rounded interface with uni- form acoustic shadowing (see Figure 16.10C) whereas other foreign bodies may have more irregular hyper - echoic borders with distal shadowing (see Figure 16.10D). Trichobezoars have irregular bright interfaces and strong shadowing. Linear foreign bodies produce bowel plication recognized as undula- tion (Figure 16.11A) and must be differentiated from undulation of the bowel wall which more commonly represents milder forms of enteritis. Complete obstruc- tion results in pronounced dilation of the bowel cranial to the object. Pyloric obstruction can result in gastric atony and distension (Penninck 2002b; Baker and Davidson 2006). Do not mistake gastric ingesta for a foreign body (see Figure 16.11B), or an empty stomach with prominent rugal folds as abnormal (see Figure 16.11C). Anatomical Obstruction Enteric duplication or agenesis can be confirmed ultrasonographically in pediatric patients. Duplication is rare and can occur anywhere in the intestinal tract; the clinical signs may be nonspecific (abdominal distension, discomfort). A fluid‐filled juxtaintestinal formation with variable peristalsis and contents can be seen. Enteric agenesis usually results in severe, life‐ threatening clinical signs in the neonatal period. Ultrasonographic findings usually include marked fluid and gas distension of bowel proximal to the defect (see Figure 16.11E). Pyloric stenosis secondary to hypertrophic gastritis has been reported in the pediatric dog. Focal circum- ferential thickening of the pylorus primarily involving the muscularis is typical (Penninck 2002b; Baker and Davidson 2006). Bowel Perforation Intestinal perforation can result in focal changes in bowel wall layer ratios, with thickening of the muscu- laris and submucosal layer due to inflammation and edema. A focal hypoechoic mass can be visualized where total effacement has occurred (Figure 16.12A). Hyperechoic slashes within the hypoechoic wall can represent gas trapping. Free abdominal air denotes bowel perforation unless the patient has recently undergone a laparotomy or laparoscopy or has a pene- trating abdominal wall wound. Free abdominal air is best visualized ventral to the spleen when the patient is in dorsal recumbency (see Figure 16.12B) and in nongravity lateral sites when in lateral recumbency; radiography can confirm the suspicion (Penninck 2002b; Baker 2009). Gastroenterocolitis Mild to moderate thickening of the gastrointestinal wall with preservation of wall layering and moderate mesenteric lymphadenomegaly are the most common ultrasonographic findings with nonspecific pediatric gastroenterocolitis, such as that resulting from dietary indiscretion or bacterial overgrowth. More severe pathology, such as extensive bowel edema or hemor - rhage accompanying severe infectious gastroenteroco- litis, can be associated with changes in fluid volume within the bowel lumen, wall thickening, corrugation, and loss of normal wall layering (Figure 16.13A; see also Figure 16.12C,D). These changes can be regional or diffuse. Fluid distension of the bowel with general- ized decreased motility can be seen with functional ileus accompanying gastroenterocolitis. Pearl: Ultrasound is now considered the best clinical tool for noninvasive diagnosis of intestinal obstruction. Pearl: Do not mistake gastric ingesta for a foreign body or an empty stomach with prominent rugal folds as abnormal. Pearl: Abdominal radiography should be used to definitively document free abdominal air suspected in an ultrasound examination (see Chapter 12).

283 POCUS: P EDIATRICS Several breeds of dogs have a reported genetic predilection for small intestinal disease. An immunop- roliferative enteropathy is seen in the Basenji, which is characterized by lymphangiectasia, intermittent diarrhea, weight loss, hypoalbuminemia and hyper - globulinemia, and lymphoplasmacytic mucosal infiltrates throughout the gastrointestinal tract. Histopathology is diagnostic, but abdominal ultraso - nography can identify bowel in which disruption of the normal layering has occurred. Chinese sharpei dogs have been identified with a lymphoplasmacytic‐ eosinophilic infiltrative enteropathy that is characterized by poor weight gain, weight loss, or intermittent diar - rhea episodes, with onset of signs typically between 2 and 6 months of age. Infiltrative enteropathies can be characterized ultrasonographically as having changes in the normal bowel wall echogenicity and layering (Penninck 2002b; Baker and Davidson 2006). Intussusception Intussusception is not uncommon in young dogs and cats, occurring most frequently at the ileocecocolic junction in dogs and in the jejunum in cats. Pediatric patients are prone to intussusception because they lack the intrinsic enteric neural mechanisms for aboral motility present in adult animals; instead, Figure 16.12. 284 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER gastrointestinal motility is pressure dependent and based on the sequential ingestion of food. Fasting or vomiting results in ileus and increases the risk of intussusception. The classic transverse ultrasonographic appearance of intussusception is a multilayered series of concen - tric rings representing the invaginated bowel wall layers; the outer layer can be edematous (hypoechoic) and the inner layers more normal in appearance (see Figure 16.13B). Discomfort is typically displayed when scanhead pressure is placed over the affected area of bowel. Doppler evaluation of the bowel and associated mesenteric vessels can provide information about bowel viability. Serial examinations are important when evaluating the pediatric patient with a palpable abdominal mass, unanticipated clinical deterioration or increased abdominal pain (Penninck 2002b; Baker and Davidson 2006). Enteric Parasites Enterocolitis from intestinal parasites can be severe in pediatric patients with high worm burdens. Small bowel helminths can be visualized ultrasonographically as dou- ble‐walled structures within the fluid‐filled lumen (see Figure 16.13C). Movement of helminths can be appreci- ated with real‐time ultrasonography (Penninck 2002b). Figure 16.13. (A) Small bowel wall thickening and loss of normal layering ( arrow). 285 POCUS: P EDIATRICS Enteric Thrombosis A serious consequence of hypercoagulopathic entero - colitis is mesenteric thrombosis resulting in bowel ischemia. Doppler imaging is necessary to identify the thrombus; the resultant hypoechoic bowel wall appearance is visible with real‐time ultrasonography (Baker 2009) (see also Section V). Congenital Herniation A developmental anomaly resulting in extrusion of a portion of the gastrointestinal tract outside the body wall, occurring within the umbilical canal (omphalo - cele) or lateral to the umbilical canal (gastroschisis), has been reported in humans and occurs in both dogs and cats (see Figure 16.13D). The condition is usually hopeless in small pediatric patients presented to the veterinarian hours after birth; however, a 30–70% survival rate is reported in humans with immediate postpartum surgical intervention. Diagnosis is made prepartum with abdominal ultrasound, based on the recognition of fetal gastric wall (rugal) structures or intestinal contents in an abnormal location. Earlier surgical intervention before inevitable septic contami - nation occurs may improve the prognosis in veterinary patients. Congenital peritoneopericardial diaphragmatic her- nias occur in both the dog and cat; ultrasonography provides an additional modality for their diagnosis. As with other diaphragmatic hernias, careful evaluation for continuity of the echogenic diaphragm differenti - ates a true hernia from mirror image artifacts (see Figure 16.14F). Evaluation of the pericardial contents can be made from the subcostal (across the liver) or intercostal (using the heart as an acoustic window) approach (Figure 16.14A). Abnormal pericardial con- tents can include falciform fat, liver, gallbladder, and/ or intestines (see Figure 16.14B). Umbilical hernias can be significant if large enough to permit bowel evisceration and strangulation (see Figure 16.14B). Omentum can become trapped in an open umbilical hernia in immature dogs and cats; closure of the hernia then results in a benign mass effect often alarming to clients. Evaluation of a pain - ful or enlarging umbilical mass usually permits Figure 16.14. (A) Intercostal imaging in the pediatric canine. (B) Peritoneopericardial diaphragmatic hernia. 286 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER differentiation of omentum from entrapped bowel, which has a typical enteric appearance. Congenital inguinal hernias can similarly be con- firmed by ultrasonographic identification of intestinal structures within the subcutaneous space of the affected groin. This can be a dynamic finding. Mesenteric fat may alternatively be entrapped through the hernia and sometimes becomes strangulated (see Figure 16.14C). Congenital hiatal hernias are more difficult to con- firm with ultrasound because of the inherent difficulty in imaging the gas‐filled stomach and the intermittent (sliding) nature of the disorder. Stomach wall with characteristic rugal folds can be imaged crossing the diaphragm into the thoracic cavity (Suter 1984; Baker and Davidson 2006). Acquired Herniation Traumatic diaphragmatic herniation can result in the presence of stomach, liver, spleen, intestines, and falciform fat in the thorax, usually accompanied by effusion of fluid enhancing imaging (see Figure 16.14D). Failure to identify a contiguous diaphragmatic image supports the diagnosis. Metabolic Conditions of the Pediatric Patient Congenital Portosystemic Shunts Portosystemic shunts are congenital malformations of the hepatic portal venous drainage system and can have either a familial, that is, genetic, or random occur- rence. Congenital portosystemic shunts can be either intrahepatic or extrahepatic; breed predilections for extrahepatic shunts include Yorkshire terrier, Maltese, poodle, miniature schnauzer, dachshund, Lhasa Apso, Pekingese, pug, and shih tzu, whereas intrahepatic shunts are more commonly identified in large‐breed dogs such as golden retrievers, German shepherds, Irish wolfhounds, Irish setters, and samoyeds. Portosystemic shunts are uncommon in cats. Ultrasonography provides a rapid and noninvasive method for screening patients suspected to have con- genital portosystemic shunts. Although scintigraphy is considered the most reliable noninvasive method of documenting a portosystemic shunt, its availability is limited to specialty and university practices, and its use requires special handling of the radioactive patient for at least 12 hours. The liver may be small and diffi- cult to image in patients with congenital portosystemic shunts (see Figure 16.14E). Imaging the liver from the standard ventral approach can be improved in some cases by using the left ventral intercostal or right dorsal intercostal approaches (Figure 16.15A). The presence of ascites can facilitate the study, as can adding fluid to the stomach, and positioning the patient to shift gas away from the scanhead and shift abdominal organs caudally (see Figure 16.15B). Ultrasound evaluation of portosystemic anomalies can be facilitated by positive pressure ventilation under anesthesia for the same reason. Extrahepatic shunts most commonly arise from the portal vein, splenic vein or left gastric vein in the dog, and from the left gastric vein in the cat. Identification of a shunting vessel emptying into the caudal vena cava is difficult but confirmatory. These shunts are often tortuous; Doppler helps identify altered blood flow (see Figure 16.15C,D). Intrahepatic shunts can be more difficult to identify because of patient size, bowel gas, and liver size. Clipping the hair coat intercostally on the right can allow for transverse vessel stacking (of the aorta, vena cava, and portal vein) and visuali- zation of ductal shunts (Figure 16.16). There can be right and left shunting of the ductus (Nyland and Hager 1985; Nyland et al. 2002a; Baker and Davidson 2006; Baker 2009). Seizure Disorders Pediatric patients with focal, partial or grand mal seizures for which no metabolic or toxic etiology can be identified can benefit from intracranial ultra- sound. Scanning the brain through the fontanelle, usually partially open in pediatric patients, permits noninvasive evaluation of the ventricles (Baker, personal communication). Evaluation of a normal littermate facilitates recognition of excessive cerebral spinal fluid accumulation by serving as a control (Figure 16.17). Pearl: Fluoroscopic evaluation can be more infor - mative in dynamic hiatal hernia cases. Pearl: Evaluation of a normal littermate facilitates recognition of excessive cerebral spinal fluid accumulation by serving as a control. Pearl: Thoracic radiography or positive contrast peritoneography can be used to confirm the diag- nosis if ultrasound findings are not conclusive (Suter 1984).

287 POCUS: P EDIATRICS Genitourinary Disorders Young dogs and cats are commonly presented to the vet- erinarian for perceived genitourinary system disorders. While gastrointestinal disorders account for most acute presentations, perceived urogenital disorders account for many others. Clinical differentiation between the characteristics of normal pediatric housebreaking and immature renal function and true urogenital disease can be challenging and is facilitated with ultrasound Renal Agenesis Congenital renal agenesis resulting in the absence of a kidney can be confirmed with ultrasound, but is usu - ally an incidental finding. The contralateral kidney typically has normal internal anatomy, but is enlarged as a consequence of obligatory hypertrophy (Baker and Davidson 2006). Renal Dysplasia Until reliable genetic markers are available for all of the various breed‐specific congenital renal dysplasias, ultrasound provides the best method of screening young dogs and cats for these likely heritable disorders. Early ultrasonographic screening is possible in breeds in which morphological changes are grossly evident (i.e., cairn terriers, German shepherd dogs, Persian cats). The kidneys lack normal corticomedullary inter- face and the renal border can be irregular (Figure 16.18A). The condition is usually bilateral (Baker 2009). Figure 16.15. 290 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER some ectopic ureters insert initially into the bladder and additionally tunnel distally to terminate in an abnormal site. Visualization of the dilated ureter usu- ally occurs near the urinary bladder (see Figure 16.18B). Visualization of the bladder neck and proximal urethra may be obscured by the pubic bone, making identification of such termination difficult. Hydronephrosis can eventually result from an uncorrected ectopic ureter due to flow impedance at the abnormal site of insertion (see Figure 16.18C). Urinary tract infection is commonly associated with ectopia, due to accompanying urethral sphincter mechanism anomalies, and if not detected and treated, can progress to pyelonephritis and ureteritis. Infection and its associated inflammation in the tract can further alter the ultrasonographic appearance of the kidneys, bladder, ureters, and urethra. Contrast‐enhanced computed tomography is the most sensitive and specific modality for the diagnosis of ectopia but, like double‐contrast radiography, requires anesthesia, making initial evaluation with ultrasound desirable when ectopia is suspected clini- cally. Endoscopic evaluation of the vestibule, vagina, bladder, and ureters can also confirm the diagnosis; laser correction of intramural ectopia is possible. The condition is thought to be heritable, and is more common in females (Lamb 1988; Nyland et al. 2002b; Baker and Davidson 2006; Baker 2009). Ureterocele A ureterocele is an uncommon congenital dilation of the ureter near the bladder, appearing as a cystic struc- ture within the bladder lumen or wall. The ureterocele occurs most commonly in association with an ectopic ureter. Diagnosis can be made by scanning the urinary bladder in the transverse plane and watching for strong peristalsis of the tunneling ureter (Lamb 1988; Nyland et al. 2015; Baker and Davidson 2006; Baker 2009) (see Figure 16.18D). Urinary T ract Infection Puppies are frequently presented to the veterinarian because of owner concerns about difficulty achieving housebreaking and the perception that urination is excessively frequent (pollakiuria). Historical differentiation between a history of true pollakiuria and dysuria associated with cystourethritis and the normal frequency of urination in pediatric dogs with immature renal concentrating abilities can be difficult. A urinalysis/urine culture with urine obtained by ultrasound‐guided cystocentesis can be diagnostic. The bladder can appear normal in acute urinary tract infection. Chronic urinary tract infection can induce bladder wall thickening (greater than 1–2 mm in a fully distended bladder), especially in the cranioventral portion of the bladder (Figure 16.19A). Similarly, early pyelonephritis can have a normal ultrasonographic appearance; chronic pyelonephritis can produce a dilated renal pelvis, sometimes accompanied by poor corticomedullary definition, increased echogenicity, reduction in renal size, and irregular renal contour (Nyland et al. 2002b; Baker and Davidson 2006) (see Figure 16.19B). Urolithiasis Cystic calculi (radiopaque or radiolucent), visualized as discrete hyperechoic focal echogenicities in the dependent portion of the bladder, occur most com- monly in pediatric patients with urinary tract infection (struvite or triple phosphate uroliths) and portosys- temic shunts (ammonium biurate uroliths); the presence of a cystic calculus without urinary tract infection in the pediatric patient should actually prompt evaluation for developmental hepatic vascular anomalies. Both urinary tract infection and cystic cal- culi are more common in female pediatric patients (Nyland et al. 2002b; Baker and Davidson 2006) (see Figure 16.19C,D). Patent Urachus The urachus permits the flow of urine from the bladder into the allantoic sac of the fetus, and nor - mally atrophies at birth. A patent urachus in the neonate is characterized clinically by urine drib- bling from the umbilicus. The fluid‐filled urachus can be identified ultrasonographically, extending cranially from the cranioventral bladder wall (Figure 16.20A). If an incompletely patent urachus is present in the neonate, a urachal diverticulum may result, seen as a divot in the apex of the bladder (see Figure 16.20B). Urachal diverticula can predis- pose the bladder to recurrent infection because of abnormal bladder flow in the region, and surgical excision can be indicated (Nyland et al. 2002b; Baker and Davidson 2006). Pearl: Both urinary tract infection and cystic calculi are more common in female pediatric patients.

291 POCUS: P EDIATRICS Cryptorchidism Ultrasound localization of cryptorchidism can con - firm the condition in pediatric patients with bilateral involvement whose neutering status is unknown, and assist the surgeon in planning the approach (i.e., inguinal vs cranial abdominal). Retained testes can torse and present as an acute abdomen. The retained testis can be positioned anywhere between the ipsi - lateral kidney and the scrotum. A systematic evalua - tion of the region from the caudal renal pole to the inguinal canal can identify an oval, homogeneously echogenic structure with a mildly hyperechoic border representing the parietal and visceral tunics (see Figure 16.20C). The epididymis is usually distinctly less echoic than the testicular parenchyma, as in the scrotal testis. The cryptorchid testis will maintain the anatomical structure, the mediastinum testis (a hyperechoic slash), and normal testicular echo - genicity despite being reduced in size compared to a scrotal testis, unless malignant transformation has occurred (Eilts et al. 1988; Baker and Davidson 2006) (see Figure 16.20D). Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 297 Introduction The thoracic FAST (TFAST) examination was first pub- lished in 2008, focusing on the diagnosis of pneumo- thorax in a large prospective study of 145 dogs with blunt and penetrating trauma (Lisciandro et al. 2008). The study also documented other intrathoracic injuries by detecting free fluid (pleural and pericardial effu- sion) and lung injury. TFAST was the first standard- ized, nonecho ultrasound examination of the thorax for veterinarians. The original study did not publish the diaphragmatico‐hepatic (DH) view but this view is advantageous on a number of fronts including serving as an acoustic window via the liver and gallbladder into the thorax for pleural and pericardial effusion and lung pathology along the pulmonary‐diaphragmatic surface (Boysen et al. 2004; Lisciandro et al. 2009; Lisciandro 2011, 2012, 2014a,b, 2016; Boysen and Lisciandro 2013; McMurray et al. 2016). Moreover, the caudal vena cava is imaged for volume status during fluid resuscitation, which is helpful for detecting right‐ sided cardiac strain/failure/overload, the abdominal cavity is surveyed for free fluid, and the liver and gall- bladder for any soft tissue abnormalities (Quantz et al. 2009; Nelson et al. 2010; Lisciandro 2011, 2016, 2019; Lisciandro and Armenise 2014; Darnis et al. 2018). Since day 1 in 2005 when the author developed AFAST and TFAST, the two examinations have been combined and referred to as combination (Combo) FAST, learning quickly by experience that by doing only one or the other FAST examination, serious condi- tions are easily missed (Lisciandro 2012). Moreover, the author has advocated that AFAST and TFAST be used first line as an extension of the physical exam. With the more recent addition of a more comprehen- sive lung examination, called Vet BLUE (Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2017), the author has since changed the term from Combo FAST to Global FAST, which is AFAST, TFAST, and Vet BLUE combined into a single ultra- sound format (Lisciandro 2012, 2019; Lisciandro and Armenise 2014). The use of AFAST, TFAST, and Vet BLUE extends beyond trauma to triage (nontrauma) and tracking (monitoring). In 2016, a prospective nontrauma case series applied AFAST and TFAST in combination to 100 cases (82 dogs, 18 cats). The authors found that 75% of cardio- vascularly unstable or respiratory‐compromised patients were positive for free fluid. They also docu- mented a positive rate of approximately 10% for those considered to be stable. Interestingly, this nontrauma study had a median time post presentation to the AFAST‐TFAST studies of 1.75 and 2.5 hours for unstable and stable patients, respectively, with an overall median time of two hours (range 0–12 hours) (McMurray et al. 2016). In other words, AFAST‐TFAST generally were not used first line as part of initial patient assessment. One has to wonder during the interval of ~2 hours bet- ween presentation and AFAST‐TFAST examination: How accurate and appropriate were the types of resus- citation? The ordered therapy? The diagnostic testing? Despite the much lower positive rate of ~10% in the stable patients, it is important to realize that missing a serious condition in one out of 10 dogs and cats, your patients, would be considered significant to many POCUS: TFAST – Introduction and Image Acquisition Gregory R.
