298 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER clinicians and pet owners. Moreover, Vet BLUE was not included and could have potentially added more positive studies by surveying more lung. Lastly, the study was important in (1) documenting the clinical rel- evance of applying AFAST and TFAST in combination (Lisciandro 2012), (2) the high frequency of positive examinations in unstable patients, and (3) that AFAST‐ TFAST proficiency could be attained with proper training and proctored examinations although there was only a single sonographer involved in the scanning (McMurray et al. 2016). Before we begin this chapter, it is important to acknowledge that TFAST is far more than a “flash exam” of the thorax (Lisciandro and Mann 2019). It is also important to acknowledge that relative to AFAST and Vet BLUE, TFAST is the most challenging to learn. TFAST is more complex because of the probe handling and machine manipulation to acquire images that involves the dynamics of a beating heart and phases of respiration as well as interpretation of air‐related arti- facts. TFAST, like AFAST, is a cerebral approach, assess- ing the thorax and its components of thoracic wall, pleural cavity, pericardial sac, lung and volume status in a standardized goal‐directed manner with clearly defined acoustic windows. Moreover, TFAST is gener- ally completed in a matter of minutes (Lisciandro et al. 2008, 2009; Lisciandro 2011, 2014a; Boysen and Lisciandro 2013; McMurray et al. 2016). The standard- ized approach helps rule in and rule out easily identi- fied serious conditions that would otherwise be missed or delayed in their detection based on less sensitive means of physical examination, blood and urine test- ing, and radiography (see Table 18.1). TFAST (and Global FAST) gives diagnostic power (evidence‐based) to the attending veterinarian by actually “seeing” the problem list by “seeing” the conditions. Lastly, since his internship, the author has abided by the axiom to “never send a patient out the door with something you could have easily diagnosed.” The Global FAST approach is the new “quick assessment test” that mod- ernizes this statement. What TFAST Can Do • Can rapidly detect with high accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity pneumothorax in traumatized dogs and cats. • Can determine the degree of pneumothorax (in other words, its severity) as “partial” versus “mas- sive” by finding the “lung point.” • Can detect and monitor pleural effusion, initially and serially. • Can detect and monitor pericardial effusion, ini- tially and serially. • Can determine the presence or absence of cardiac tamponade. • Can be used as a soft tissue examination of the heart. • Can detect and monitor lung contusions initially and serially; however, lung contusions are better detected, tracked and scored using the Vet BLUE lung contusion scoring system (see Chapters 22 and 23). • Can detect thoracic wall, pleural space, and lung pathology through the presence of the “step sign.” • Can assess volume status and contractility (fractional shortening, FS%) by using the TFAST right pericardial site (PCS) view to evaluate the left ventricular short‐axis “mushroom” view. • Can assess left cardiac strain/failure/overload by using the TFAST right PCS view to evaluate the left atrial to aortic ratio (LA:Ao) on short‐axis. • Can assess right cardiac strain/failure/overload by using the TFAST right PCS view to evaluate the right ventricular to left ventricular ratio (RV:LV) on long‐axis. • Can screen for right atrial and auricular masses at the TFAST left PCS view. • Can screen for intracardiac and extracardiac masses at any of the TFAST echo views. • When combined with Vet BLUE, can assist in respiratory distress evaluation, rapidly deter - mining pulmonary versus cardiac causes. • When combined with Vet BLUE, can assist in respiratory distress cases by rapidly supporting different types of lung disease including forms of pulmonary edema (cardiogenic, noncardiogenic), pneumonia, pulmonary thromboembolism, and neoplastic conditions. • Can be used to serially monitor intrathoracic con- ditions including pleural, pericardial, heart and lung conditions at point of care in place of serial radiography or computed tomography (CT). What TFAST Cannot Do • Cannot reliably characterize pleural fluid; sample acquisition (thoracocentesis) and fluid analysis is necessary. • Cannot reliably characterize pericardial fluid; sample acquisition (pericardiocentesis) and fluid analysis is necessary. • Cannot fully replace thoracic radiography (TXR). • Cannot fully replace complete echocardiography.

299 POCUS: TFAST – I NTRODUCTION AND I MAGE A CQUISITION • Cannot fully replace computed tomography (CT). • Cannot diagnose nonthoracic causes of respiratory distress, the so‐called nonrespiratory lookalikes within the peritoneal cavity – hemoabdomen, canine anaphylaxis, and causes of acute abdomen; and retroperitoneal space conditions – bleeding from adrenal, vena cava, and aortic sources and other renal‐related or spinal‐related sources of free retroperitoneal fluid, without AFAST. • TFAST is limited in its pulmonary evaluation because it has only two acoustic windows for lung compared to the nine acoustic windows of Vet BLUE. Indications • Blunt and penetrating trauma. • Nontrauma triaged cases (weakness, collapsed, “ain’t doing right” (ADR), changes in breathing patterns). • All respiratory distress. • Trauma cases for lung contusions. • Nontrauma cases for evidence of various forms of alveolar‐interstitial edema and pulmonary hemorrhage. • Pneumothorax (PTX) for detecting and assessing severity using the “lung point” in standing or sternal, tracking pneumothorax using the “lung point,” and deciding whether thoracocentesis is indicated by the “TFAST PTX 1/3s Rule” for the “lung point” as the upper third, middle third, and lower third of the thorax (see Chapter 18). • Pleural effusion for detecting, tracking, and esti - mating its severity using the PCS view measure - ments at the level of the costochondral junction (see Chapter 18). • Pericardial effusion for detecting, tracking, and estimating its severity using widest measure - ments at the DH view and PCS view measure - ments at the level of the costochondral junction (see Chapter 18). • Surveying at‐risk small animals for pneumothorax, pleural effusion, and pericardial effusion, including any and all postinterventional/procedural cases (thoracic surgery, thoracoscopy, lung lobe aspi - rates, other at‐risk procedures, mechanical ventila- tion, and post anesthesia). Objectives • Understand TFAST and its five acoustic windows. • Be able to perform TFAST image acquisition. • Understand the principle that air rises (nongravity dependent) and fluid falls (gravity dependent) (Figure 17.1). • Understand the pitfalls and artifacts of each of the TFAST views. What Clinical Questions are Answered using TFAST Binary Answers – Y es or No, Unremarkable or Abnormal • Does the patient have pleural effusion (PE) – free fluid in the pleural space? • Does the patient have pericardial effusion (PCE) – fluid in the pericardial sac? • Does the patient have cardiac tamponade? • Does the patient have pneumothorax – free air in the pleural space? • Does the patient have evidence of systolic dysfunction? • Does the patient have evidence of right‐sided heart dysfunction/strain/failure/overload? • Does the patient have evidence of left‐sided heart dysfunction/strain/failure/overload? • Does the patient have any intracardiac abnormalities? • What is the patient’s volume status? • Does the patient have any obvious lung pathology? TFAST and Its Five Acoustic Windows TFAST consists of five acoustic windows (views) hav- ing exact clarity as follows: bilaterally the chest tube site (CTS) and PCS views, plus the single DH view (Figure 17.2) (Lisciandro 2014b, 2016; McMurray et al. 2016). The DH view is part of the TFAST, AFAST, and Vet BLUE formats, providing a large amount of clinical information including screening for pleural and peri- cardial effusion, lung conditions, cardiac problems, and patient volume status, and within the abdomen for soft tissue screening of the gallbladder and liver and for ascites (Lisciandro 2011, 2014a,b, 2016; Boysen and Lisciandro 2013; McMurray et al. 2016). The strengths of the respective views are as follows. • The CTS views are for pneumothorax, free air in the pleural cavity, because air rises (see Figures 17.1 and 17.2), and it is best practice to have your patient in standing or sternal for the “lung point” (see Chapter 18). • The PCS views are for detecting pleural and peri- cardial effusion, free fluid in the pleural cavity and pericardial sac, because fluid falls because it is gravity dependent (see Figures 17.1 and 17.2), and for the TFAST echo views. • The DH view is for pleural cavity, pericardial sac, heart and lung imaging with less air interference than the transthoracic TFAST views, taking advantage of the acoustic window of the liver and gallbladder; for ascites and soft tissue abnormalities of the liver and gallbladder; and volume status via the caudal vena cava and hepatic veins. Peforming TFAST – General Set‐Up Ultrasound Settings and Probe Preferences • Curvilinear (microconvex) probe with a range of 5–10 MHz. A linear probe may also be used for lung ultrasonography (see Chapters 22 and 23) and a phased‐array probe for cardiac imaging, although the curvilinear probe is sufficient and faster without probe changes during TFAST. • Presets of either the abdominal or cardiac settings may be used depending on how your ultrasound machine performs. Most ultrasound machines per- form well on the abdominal preset for the entire Global FAST, which is favored by the author and much faster than switching presets. • The focus cursor, on most machines, should be placed at the level of the region of interest, gener - ally midscreen or across from the “lung line” when evaluating lung (see Chapter 5). Ultrasound Screen Orientation The abdominal preset and all others on your machine likely are consistent with cranial (the head) to the left of the screen and caudal (the tail) to the right of the screen. When using cardiac presets, the orientation is switched, which is very confusing for the noncardiolo- gist sonographer. The cardiac preset may be main- tained but the orientation changed back using the reverse button on the machine or rotating the probe 180° to maintain the consistency of orientation with the head always to the left (cranial) of the screen and the tail to the right (caudal). 302 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER The important point here is to note that commonly, the head is no longer to the left of the screen when chang- ing to a cardiac preset (unless you reverse the marker or modify your probe orientation), and the change in orientation must be acknowledged by the sonographer for proper spatial awareness and interpretation (see Figures 1.6 and 5.3). Machine Positioning Where the machine is located is hugely important for imaging the patient accurately and for the safety of the sonographer, assisting staff, and patient. The machine and the head of the patient should always be in the same sightline (see Figure 5.3). When this rule of thumb is violated, spatial orientation for the sonographer may be affected as well as the performance of ultrasound‐ assisted and ultrasound‐guided procedures. Moreover, the sonographer and assisting staff are generally looking at the ultrasound screen and not the head of the patient so if the patient is becoming cyanotic or decompensating, it may not be recognized when their head is facing the other way. Moreover, if the patient turns to bite or scratch the sonographer and assistant(s), it is more difficult to move quickly out of the way. Pain is a powerful teacher, and insisting on the patient’s head and machine in the same sightline was a lesson learned the painful way (dog bite) by the author when developing TFAST in 2005. Patient Positioning In patients that present standing or in sternal, it is gen- erally a good idea to perform TFAST prior to any patient restraint in case the patient is hemodynami- cally fragile. By beginning with TFAST (and Vet BLUE), intrathoracic life‐threatening conditions that can potentially become catastrophic with patient restraint or transport are initially detected and promptly addressed, such as need for centesis for PTX, PE or PCE. When critical patients present in lat- eral recumbency, TFAST and AFAST are generally per- formed without moving the patient, and before moving the patient to sternal or standing to evaluate the contralateral hemithorax for the opposing CTS and PCS views. Right lateral recumbency (versus left lateral recum- bency) is generally preferred because it is the stan- dard positioning for electrocardiographic and echocardiographic evaluations and may be arguably more reliable for gallbladder, caudal vena cava, and hepatic venous imaging, although sonographers skilled at performing TFAST and AFAST in left lateral may disagree. In either lateral, the four AFAST views and the ipsilateral TFAST PCS view can be performed at nearly the same depth setting (7–15 cm) on the abdominal preset prior to going to a more shallow depth (4–8 cm) for the CTS view. Thus, six of the eight TFAST‐AFAST views are rapidly completed (Figure 17.3). If PTX is suspected, move to sternal or standing to search for the lung point to more accu- rately assess the degree of PTX (see lung point sec- tion) and perform thoracocentesis immediately if unstable as per clinical judgment. A modified lateral‐sternal recumbency position is another option to allow the patient to ventilate more efficiently when in respiratory distress. The modified lateral‐sternal position is acquired by allowing the thorax to be in sternal while having the forelegs posi- tioned laterally toward the sonographer (Figure 17.4). The position gives an estimate of the abdominal fluid score without the patient having to be in purely a lat- eral recumbent position (see Figure 6.4). Dorsal recumbency should never be used for several important reasons, including the increased stress in dorsal recumbency for respiratory and hemodynami- cally fragile patients, and the invalidation of the AFAST‐applied fluid scoring system (validated only in lateral recumbency; see Chapters 6 and 7). When moving a patient into dorsal recumbency, their venti- lation is changed by the weight of the abdominal organs against the diaphragm and reversing the least gravity‐dependent, most aerated lung to become the most gravity‐dependent position within the thorax. The combination negatively affects ventilation. In addition, dorsal recumbency causes the weight of the abdominal organs to compress the cauda vena cava and aorta, affecting circulation and, most importantly, venous return to the heart (see Figure 6.5). Thus, if your patient had a known or unknown preload problem prior to being moved to dorsal recumbency, their status could catastrophically change if placed and restrained in dorsal recumbency. In human medi- cine, it has been said, “Death begins in radiology. Never send a human patient to radiology without a good physical exam and an EFAST (essentially a Global FAST).” The same could be said in veterinary medicine when deciding on the safety of dorsal recum- bency positioning for your patient. Pearl: A tip for gaining a TFAST PCS view is to place a rolled towel under the forelegs of a sternally recumbent patient (see Chapters 19 and 39). By doing so, the sternum is elevated off the tabletop, optimizing maneuverability of the ultrasound probe (see Figures 19.2 and 39.28).

The author pre- fers smaller amounts of 70% isopropyl alcohol and larger amounts of alcohol‐based hand sanitizer, a Mississippi State Radiology Department trick. Acoustic coupling gel may also be used, but it is gooey and does not wipe off or evaporate like hand sanitizer (and with hand sanitizer your hands may be a little dry but always clean!). As for alcohol, it is much more noxious to the patient’s skin and to the patient’s lungs when enclosed in oxygen cages. Furthermore, alcohol should not be used if electrical defibrillation is anticipated since it presents a burn/fire hazard and thus is even more dangerous in oxygen‐enriched environments. Of note, some manufacturers do not recommend isopropyl alcohol placed directly on the probe head because it can damage (desiccate) the rubber footprint (see Figure 4.13). Thus, placing a small amount of acoustic cou - pling gel on the probe head may be an easy protective solution (check manufacturer recommendations). 305 POCUS: TFAST – INTRODUCTION AND IMAGE ACQUISITION T o Dim or Not Dim the Lights The author rarely dims lights. This is also a risk/ benefit decision because when lights are dimmed in critical patients requiring life‐saving interventions, it can be difficult to locate equipment. Poor lighting also may affect how rapidly staff can move around when vision is decreased. Image quality in human studies has been shown to be acceptable in ambient light with most ultrasound machines (Breitkreutz et al. 2010). Performing the TFAST Chest Tube Site View The chest tube site (CTS) views are applied bilaterally for the diagnosis of pneumothorax (PTX) because they are the highest point, least gravity‐dependent site (air rises), on the thoracic wall over the pleural cavity, where air would accumulate in PTX (collapsed lung away from the intercostal space that is occupied with free air) (Figure 17.5). The TFAST CTS view is analo- gous to human PTX protocols (Kirkpatrick et al. 2004; Reissig et al. 2011) in which the most anterior, least gravity‐dependent chest region over the pleural cavity is imaged first. The premise is that if lung is observed in opposition to the intercostal space, then PTX is not present in spontaneously breathing patients, especially when in standing and sternal (versus lateral in which pockets can bubble, causing the “double lung point” effect) (Copetti and Cattarossi 2007; Volpicelli et al. 2013). The orientation for all lung ultrasound is the “gator sign” (Figures 17.6 and 17.7) (Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2017) explained in more detail in the “gator sign orientation” section. The CTS view has historically been defined as directly dorsal to the xiphoid process between the eighth and ninth intercostal spaces (ICS); however, experience has taught us that most often this location is likely to be the “transition zone” of the pleural (thorax) and peritoneal (abdominal) cavities (Figures 17.8 and 17.9). We refer to this as the “cau- dodorsal transition zone” (CdTZ). This is important because the CdTZ can be a confusing region to eval- uate for PTX because of the motion of the lung, the pleural cavity, and air shadowing coupled with abdominal structures moving simultaneously. We now teach that the sonographer first locates the CdTZ by finding the “curtain sign” where the linear caudal border of dirty shadowing of lung moves to and fro obscuring abdominal contents (Figure 17.9) (Neelis et al. 2015). From the CdTZ, the probe is then moved (slid) cranially 2–3 intercostal spaces to move away from the CdTZ and more clearly evaluate for “lung sliding” without the diaphragmatic reflection and its adjacent abdominal structures (see Figure 17.12). When PTX is suspected, the probe is moved through Vet BLUE views – “TFAST PTX 1/3s Rule,” middle third and lower third of the thorax – searching for the “lung point,” defined as where lung recontacts the thoracic wall (Lisciandro 2011; Lisciandro et al. 2008) (see Figure 18.5). Any evidence of lung recontacting the thoracic wall sup- ports the presence of the “lung point,” most com- monly by observing the resumption of “lung sliding” or B‐lines (see Chapter 18 for more detail). Being confused in the CdTZ can lead to many errors, including mistaking movement of the diaphragmatic reflection and its adjacent abdominal structures as “lung sliding” or a “step sign” (see Step Sign section) and also mistaking abdominal structures for some of the Vet BLUE lung ultrasound signs, such as the rugal folds of the stomach as a shred sign (pseudo shred sign) or the liver as a tissue sign (pseudo tissue sign), or air and fluid in the stomach lumen for B‐lines (pseudo gastric B‐lines), or the gallbladder for free fluid (see Pitfalls TFAST, Chapter 18, and Pitfalls Vet BLUE, Chapter 23) (see Figures 23.20, 17.9, 3.2, and 3.6). Optimizing the Image at the CTS View and the Gator Sign Pitfalls – Machine Settings Depth Setting At the CTS view, depth is generally set between 4 and 8 cm. For smaller patients start with 4–5 cm and for large canine patients increase to 7–8 cm (and sometimes up to 9–10 cm in giant‐breed dogs) (Figure 17.10; see also Figures 17.6 and 17.7). As a general rule, have a little more depth for an overview and to see your land- marks and then decrease depth accordingly (magnify). Gain Turning down the gain in the near‐field is important, as the contrast is better for recognizing “lung sliding.” A common mistake is making the screen along the pulmonary‐pleural interface (lung line) too bright (too white) (see Figure 17.10B) or undergained (too dark) through the far‐field (see Figure 17.10C). The ideal image at the CTS view is to have some gain to be able to see whether artifacts and suspected pathology extend through the far‐field (Figure 17.10A).

308 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Angle of Insonation The angle of insonation is very useful for imaging lung. A 90° angle of the ultrasound beam to the aerated pulmonary‐pleural interface (PPI) produces a sharp, crisp hyperechoic (bright white) “lung line” with dis - tinct A‐lines (“A” for “air”) (Figure 17.11) (Lisciandro 2014b,c). An angle that deviates from 90° makes the PPI and its “lung line” appear less distinct with softer grays, but despite losing the crisp detail of the “lung line” (as in Figure 17.11E), this imaging strategy is helpful for imaging “lung sliding” (see Tricks of the Trade section below) (Lisciandro 2014b,c). Pitfall – Probe Positioning and Orientation Longitudinal or Perpendicular to Ribs The “gator sign” orientation must be acquired with the probe held stationary perpendicular to the long axis of the ribs, or what some sonographers would describe as a longitudinal orientation (parallel to the long axis (spine) of the patient’s body) (Figure 17.12) (Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2017). Without clearly establishing the “gator sign” orientation, the PPI and “lung line” cannot be accurately located. There are two ways to describe the PPI. The first is where lung is directly opposed to the intercostal space, preferred by the author and referred to as the “lung line,” which also serves accu - rately our terminology when pleural space disease is present. The second description is where parietal and visceral pleura are directly opposed; however, in dis - ease states, such as pleural effusion, there is separation of the two pleura so again the “lung line” seems to be a better descriptor (see Figures 17.9, 17.10, and 17.12). Transverse or Parallel to Ribs Some lung sonographers will advocate rotating the probe so that it is parallel to the long axis of the ribs, or in transverse orientation to the patient’s long axis. However, this can be a dangerous proposition because it is easy to lose sight of where the PPI and “lung line” are located (see Figures 22.5 and 41.21). The spine of the scapula, subcutaneous emphysema, and even air in the stomach can be easily mistaken for the lung surface (see Figures 18.12, 18.13, and 41.21). When moving to the transverse orientation of lung, the lung sonogra - pher must always continually double‐check by return- ing to the “gator sign” orientation and reconfirming that the “lung line” is being accurately tracked. Pitfall – Subcutaneous Emphysema and Fat In people, subcutaneous emphysema (SQE) and fat seem to be a much bigger problem than in small ani - mals. The presence of SQE is low in trauma cases (Lisciandro et al. 2008) but presents an imaging problem by causing shadowing by air proximal to the “gator sign” so the “gator sign” cannot be imaged. However, in most cases of SQE, gently applying probe pressure Figure 17 .7 . The “one‐eyed gator.” Unlabeled in (A) with an illustrative overlay in (B). The pulmonary–pleural interface, referred to as the “lung line” by the author, is evident as a hyperechoic line on either side of the rib. 311 POCUS: TFAST – I NTRODUCTION AND I MAGE A CQUISITION Pitfall – Lateral Recumbent Positioning Being Over the Top The probe should be placed at the highest point where air would rise along the thoracic wall (see Figure 17.5); however, when your patient is in lateral recumbency, this will not likely be the uppermost dorsal third of the thorax because of the barrel‐shaped nature of the canine and feline thorax. By not appreciating this con - cept, the probe is mistakenly placed on the other side of the highest point or lower than it should be (Figure 17.13). The easiest way to prevent this is to look at your patient’s thorax. At eye level, double‐check as to whether you are at the highest point where air would rise or incorrectly over the backside of the thorax (see Figure 17.13). Furthermore, in lateral recumbency, the CdTZ is found similarly as when standing or sternal and evaluation for “lung sliding” is identically performed 2–3 intercostal spaces cranial to the CdTZ (see Figures 17.8 and 17.9). 313 POCUS: TFAST – I NTRODUCTION AND I MAGE A CQUISITION Double Lung Point The “double lung point” has been described in people with smaller volume pneumothorax and occurs when the free air does not completely pocket at the highest point within the pleural cavity (Volpicelli et al. 2013). The smaller volume of free air in the pleural space gets pushed into different locations or, as the author likes to put it, bubbles unevenly. The effect is having “lung sliding” interposed with an absent “lung sliding” (the pneumothorax) in the same field of view. This effect is seen in people in supine positioning. It may be immediately eliminated in small animals by moving them to sternal or standing, when possible, when pneumothorax is suspected (see Figure 18.8). The effect is also more problematic with positive pressure ventilation. Figure 17 .12. Anatomy at the CTS view and the “gator sign” orientation. 314 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER T ricks of the T rade for Imaging “Lung Sliding” These are a few strategies that we have learned over the past several years. • Obliquing or ricocheting the echoes. Change the angle of insonation from 90° to ~75° or in other words, fan the probe slowly, making the PPI and “lung line” less hyperechoic, or rather more gray than white, and then hold the probe stationary and observe for “lung sliding” (see Figures 17.11 and 22.8). This is called “obliquing the echoes” or you may think of as “ricocheting the echoes (ultrasound beam)” off the highly reflective surface of air whether in aerated lung or in the presence of pneu- mothorax (see Figures 17.11 and 22.8) (Lisciandro 2014b; Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2017). • One‐eyed gator. Move the rib to the center of the screen. Observe for lung sliding on either side of the rib. This is called “scattering the echoes” because essentially you are having echoes reflect off the rib (bone) and scatter to its sides and before then striking the reflective surface of air at different angles (see Figures 17.7 and 22.8) (Lisciandro 2011, 2014b,c: Boysen and Lisciandro 2013). • Combine obliquing and ricocheting the echoes with the one‐ eyed gator. Do both – change the angle of insonation and place the rib centered in the screen simulta - neously (see Figures 17.7, 17.11, and 22.8). The author typically does both maneuvers to start TFAST and not waste any time for efficiently observing for the presence or absence of “lung sliding.” • Butorphanol. It is also helpful to give light sedation that calms the patient and is safe, low risk and short‐acting, and generally does not induce pant - ing. We can accept the limited risk and benefits of subcutaneous butorphanol that generally reduces patient anxiety and slows their breathing pattern without causing panting. Figure 17 .13. If pneumothorax is suspected, it’s best to avoid searching for the “lung point” in lateral because of phenomena like the “double lung point” and move the patient to standing or sternal position. See Chapter 18 for the “lung point” and the “parking garage versus skyscraper effect” (see Figure 18.8). Although shown on a dog, the TFAST concept is analogous for cats. 315 POCUS: TFAST – INTRODUCTION AND IMAGE ACQUISITION T roubleshooting Inconsistent Imaging of the Pulmonary‐Pleural Interface and “Lung Line” • Manipulating the machine is another option. ◦ Make sure the focus cursor is directly across from the PPI and “lung line” (see Figure 5.12). ◦ Turn down the overall gain to make the near‐ field darker, providing more contrast along the PPI (see Figure 17.10). ◦ Change from the abdominal preset to the cardiac preset, which is rarely done by the author but a consideration. The cardiac preset, however, will change the screen orientation by reversing and making the head to the right and tail to the left of the screen unless you use the reverse button present on many machines, or turn the probe 180° to revert back to having the head to the left and tail to the right on the screen, as is done with all other ultrasound imaging. • Watch the patient’s breathing pattern while observing for “lung sliding”; during breath holding or apnea, “lung sliding” will not be seen. Thus, “lung sliding” is best appreciated if the sonogra- pher is paying attention to when the patient inspires and expires during each spontaneous breath (or when administered positive pressure ventilation). • If “lung sliding” is not observed then the “lung point” is sought by moving through the Vet BLUE views in the middle third (perihilar lung region) and lower third (middle lung region) of the thorax (see Chapter 18, PTX section) and best practice is to move your patient into sternal or standing position when possible (see Figure 18.8). • Use the opposing hemithorax as a control, meaning if you can clearly see “lung sliding” on the opposing hemithorax with the same settings, then likely PTX is present on the suspected side, especially if a “lung point” is determined. Summary – How to Image the Chest T ube Site View Step by Step in Standing or Sternal Recumbency • Find the CTS view by going directly dorsal to the xiphoid and into the uppermost dorsal third of the thorax over aerated lung (see Figures 17.8 and 17.9). • Adjust depth to 4–5 cm to 7–8 cm (and even 9 cm in giant breeds) (see Figure 17.10). • Acquire the “gator sign” orientation (see Figure 17.12). • Adjust gain for a good‐looking image (see Figure 17.10). • Find the CdTZ, defined as having the pleural cavity (thorax) to the left of the screen and the peritoneal cavity (abdomen) to the right of the screen. The “curtain sign” is your landmark (see Figures 17.8 and 17.9). • After finding the “curtain sign”, find the proximal generally most hyperechoic line representing the PPI or, in other words, the aerated lung surface referred to as the “lung line” to the left of the screen away from the abdominal structures (see Figure 17.12). • Follow the “lung line,” sliding the probe cranial away from the CdTZ 2–3 intercostal spaces in order to eliminate the abdominal cavity from view, which may not be possible in small canine patients and cats (see Figure 17.8). • At this location, 2–3 intercostal spaces cranial from the CdTZ, observe for “lung sliding,” the to‐and‐ fro movement with inspiration and expiration along the intercostal space, or the sliding of parietal and visceral pleura over one another (see Figure 17.12). “Lung sliding” has been likened to an Etch‐a‐Sketch® cursor being moved back and forth over the same line (Lisciandro 2011; Lisciandro et al. 2008, 2014, 2017; Boysen and Lisciandro 2013). • The angle of insonation is important (see Figure 17.11). Oblique or ricochet the echoes off the “lung line” to help bring out “lung sliding” if not observed with 90° angle of insonation. • If “lung sliding” is still not obvious, add on the “one‐eyed gator sign” by placing the rib in the center of the screen, called scattering the echoes (see Figure 17.6) (see Tricks of the Trade above). Performing the TFAST Pericardial Views The PCS views are bilaterally applied in the region of the third to fifth intercostal spaces, generally at the level of the costochondral junctions, with the objective Pearl: “Lung sliding” is now the accepted term in human medicine (Volpicelli et al.2012), replacing the term “glide sign” previously used in veterinary medicine (Nyland and Mattoon 2002; Lisciandro et al. 2008; Lisciandro 2011) (see Figure 17.12). Pearl: Make sure your patient and ultrasound machine are in the same sight line for sonographer, staff, and patient safety (see Figure 5.3).

With the heart identified and depth increased to always see the hyperechoic pericardium in the far‐field (see Figure 17.14), the TFAST caudal and then cranial “slide” are performed to screen for smaller volume pleural effusions within the “cardiac‐diaphragmatic pouch,” the area between the caudal heart and diaphragm, and the cranial heart and thoracic inlet within the “cardiac‐cervical pouch” (Figure 17.17; see also Figure 17.2). We refer to this probe maneuver as the “TFAST slide” and it is identically performed at the left and right TFAST PCS views. Think anatomy as you perform the “TFAST slide.” Sliding caudally brings you over the diaphragm and the liver, which are readily recognized because of their similarity to the FAST DH view. By identifying the liver and diaphragm, small‐volume effusions may be appreciated in the “cardiac‐diaphragmatic pouch” caudally. In the presence of PE, the PE will separate lung from thoracic wall, creating fluid stripes and tri - angulations and a “curtain sign” of pleural effusion (Neelis et al. 2015) (see Figure 18.25). PE is described in more detail in Chapter 18. Right TFAST Pericardial Site View Locating the Heart The apical beat is palpated with an opened left non - probe (helper) hand and the probe is held in the right hand with the patient in right lateral recumbency as described at the left TFAST PCS view (see Figure 17.16). The probe is placed on the underside of the patient over the strongest palpable apical beat (see Figure 17.16). The “TFAST slide” is performed simi - larly to the left TFAST PCS view for PE, however, TFAST short‐axis and long‐axis views are acquired there too (Figure 17.18). Optimizing the TFAST Cardiac Image – Depth, Gain, Presets, and Focus Cursor Depth Depth should be set so that the heart is always imaged in its entirety using the hyperechoic line in the far‐ field, the pericardium, as a mandated landmark (see Figures 17.14 and 17.15). By not imaging the heart in its entirety, identifying heart chambers becomes con - fusing and lends itself to mistaking fluid‐filled heart chambers for pleural and pericardial effusion or other pathology. Enough depth to clearly see the heart in its entirety is the most important fundamental imaging concept for TFAST. Gain Moving from lung (Vet BLUE) to TFAST, your image likely will be undergained (too dark) and generally the gain will need to be increased. In contrast, when moving from AFAST to TFAST, the gain for similar soft tissue densities of abdominal organs to heart requires minimal if any change (see Figure 17.10). Presets Often TFAST echo views (as with AFAST and Vet BLUE) are acceptable on the abdominal presets, but for small abdomen, medium abdomen, and large abdomen (or pediatric and adult) the frequencies for each preset will be different, depending on your machine. The bottom line for presets is that you have to learn what you like on your machine, stay consistent with cardiac orientation so as to know where to expect cardiac structures, and ultimately recognize which direction on the screen is cranial and caudal (see Figures 1.6, 17.25, and 17.26). Focus Cursor The image may not look as good as you would like, then you realize the focus cursor was left in the near‐ field because you were looking at lung and forgot to move the cursor to the center of the cardiac image. Get into the habit of checking the position of the focus cur- sor (see Figure 5.12). Freezing and Rolling the Cine Ball This skill is mandatory for optimizing image interpre - tation, especially for cats that have much higher heart rates than dogs; higher feline heart rates make eyeball- ing their TFAST echo views more prone to error. The “freeze” button captures images and, depending on how your machine is set up, saves several frames retro- spectively, for frame‐by‐frame review. The “cine ball” is usually a roller ball on the machine’s keyboard but may be buttons. In either case, they permit frame‐by‐ frame capture that allows for post hoc review without the stresses of real time, especially in unstable or frac - tious patients. How to Image the Right TFAST Pericardial Site View Step by Step Right TFAST PCS Short‐axis Views • Locate the heart by palpating for the apical beat and placing the probe on the thoracic wall where the strongest palpated apical beat is found. This holds true for both lateral and standing or sternal recumbency (see Figure 17.16). • Place the probe under the laterally recumbent (right side down) patient on the short‐axis line with the marker toward the elbow. We start on short‐axis views because it is easier to understand on what level you are by memorizing our TFAST echo chart (see Figures 17.16, 17.19, 17.20, and 17.25). You may also do the TFAST echo views in a standing patient, which the author prefers and does >95% of the time in stable dogs and cats. Echo measurements are validated in standing dogs (Chetboul et al. 2005). • Wait through a couple of breaths if the heart is not immediately in view because your acoustic window may be intermittent (especially in sternal or standing patients) between inspiration and expi- ration from lung (air) interference. • Make sure you have adequate coupling medium on the thorax with the hair parted before starting your approach. Without this strategy, you may get a nice acoustic window but without ample cou- pling medium you have to remove the probe from the patient to apply more medium, and you may not get a great acoustic window a second time. • If the heart is not located after a couple of breaths, while remaining on the short‐axis line, move the probe ventrally to get closer to the sternum and away from aerated lung (air rises). • If the heart is not in view, likely it is an intercostal space cranial to where you are so slide one space cranially, looking for the beating heart. • Once the heart is located, identify where you are on the left ventricular short‐axis views (see Figures 17.19, 17.22, 17.23, and 17.25) and then fan along the short‐axis line. These are generally very small hand movements of just a few millimeters while fanning that take you through the full range of short‐axis views. You must memorize the short‐axis views on the echo chart so you know what direction to direct the probe, toward the heart base (more dorsal) or toward the heart apex (more ventral or toward the sternum), to get your images. The author images right TFAST PCS echo views according to the rogue version. These short‐axis levels are named from the apex to the heart base from the “bull’s eye” to the “batman sign” to the “mush- room” to the “windshield wipers” to the “fishmouth” to the “Mercedes‐Benz sign” (circle in the middle of the screen) that represents the aorta. The “Mercedes‐ Benz,” created by the three aortic semilunar valves, is often difficult to appreciate with the curvilinear (micro- convex) probe in most patients. Thus, the “circle in the middle” on the next level toward the heart base (dorsal) from the “fishmouth” is the key to identifying the aorta. The “circle in the middle” is unique to the heart base region and is therefore an important landmark. Right TFAST Pericardial Site Long‐axis Views • After working through all the short‐axis cardiac levels (short‐axis cardiac ladder), move to where the mitral valves are located at either the “wind- shield wipers” or the “fishmouth.” • While on the mitral valves, rotate the marker toward the patient’s spine but angled a little crani- ally to get on the long‐axis line (see Figures 17.16, 17.19, and 17.24). Once on the long‐axis line, fan one way and then the other while maintaining the footprint parallel to the long‐axis line to get the long‐axis four‐chamber views. • While the fan is occurring cranially and then cau- dally, watch the left ventricle to see it “open up” with its mitral valves appearing as “windshield wipers” (and if the left ventricle is closing down then fan the other direction). These movements are generally just a few millimeters, a very tight window, while fanning through this view. • The long‐axis four‐chamber view has a hyper - echoic focal point at the interventricular septum and then a thin white line extending from it repre- senting the intraatrial septum (see Figure 17.24). • A very small fanning from the long‐axis four‐ chamber view will get you to the LVOT, an anechoic

330 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER circle representing the aorta (and possibly the Mercedes‐Benz sign) and/or a hypoechoic (black) linear tract through the circle representing the LVOT (see Chapters 19–21). • The Mercedes‐Benz sign is often difficult to appre- ciate with the curvilinear (microconvex) probe in most patients, so the “circle” is the key to identi- fying the aorta, dependent on the view (short axis versus long axis). Pitfalls at the TFAST Pericardial Views Machine Settings Screen Orientation Make sure that you are aware of the screen orientation and which side of the screen is cranial. In abdominal presets and all other imaging, cranial is to the left of the screen. When changing to the cardiac preset, the screen orientation marker will be reversed. Either push the reverse button on your screen or rotate the probe 180° to maintain screen left as cranial if you prefer. Depth Always have enough depth to see the landmark of the bright pericardium in the far‐field. Artifacts There are three major artifacts that are the most rele- vant at the PCS views. Edge Shadowing Can produce hypoechoic and anechoic regions on either side of the heart, being a rounded structure. Scan by the axiom that “One view is no view” and combine multiple views (PCS and DH) to improve your interpretation. Mirror Image With dry lung against the far side of the heart, mirror image artifact is not uncommon in which the heart is partially or completely mirrored in the far‐field. Slice‐thickness and Side‐lobe With rounded borders to cardiac chambers, slice‐ thickness and side‐lobe artifacts can mimic soft tissue abnormalities. Anatomy – Left TFAST Pericardial Site View The left TFAST PCS view is unique in that commonly an anechoic stripe is present between the heart and the thoracic wall representing pericardial fat (Lamb 2000) (see Figures 18.25 and 18.26). The best way to interpret this is to combine views and observe for the complete dirty shadowing from aerated lung in the absence of pleural effusion during the “TFAST slide” maneuver. If the stripe does not continue into the “cardiac‐ diaphragmatic pouch” caudally or the “cardiac‐ cervical pouch” cranially during the “TFAST slide” or is not supported by findings at combined views (DH view), then the suspect finding is likely not pleural effusion but rather pericardial fat as seen radiographi- cally (Lamb 2000). A fat pad also exists in many patients in between the apex of the heart that is triangular but variably echogenic (shades of gray) (see Figures 18.25 and 18.26). To differentiate the pericardial fat pad from pleural effusion, the probe is swept dorsally to see if dirty shadowing from the thoracic wall obscures imaging or when free fluid is present the effect is absent along with a “curtain sign” of pleural effusion (Neelis et al. 2015) (see Figure 18.25). Furthermore, combine multiple views, especially the DH view, because this will interrogate the “cardiac‐diaphragmatic pouch” from a different scanning plane. Performing the TFAST Diaphragmatico‐Hepatic View The TFAST DH view is performed identical to the AFAST DH view and the DH view should look nearly identical whether the patient is in lateral, right lateral or left lateral recumbency (Figure 17.27; see also Figures 6.8–6.12). Typically, three structures (the “Big 3”) are rapidly located to get a feel for the depth and proportions of the view: gallbladder, “cardiac bump,” and caudal vena cava. The best way in which to start the view is to begin at 10–15 cm depth, depending on the size of the patient (10 cm smaller to 15 cm larger patients), so that time is not wasted trying to find the Big 3 structures while being at too shallow a depth. Once structures are identified, the depth may be reduced so the caudal vena cava is at the limit of the far‐field. In severe respiratory compromised sternally (or standing) positioned small animals, the subxiphoid location is modified to accommodate the patient and may be used subcostally off midline and not immedi- ately caudal to the xiphoid if safer. Importantly, the

331 POCUS: TFAST – I NTRODUCTION AND I MAGE A CQUISITION caudal vena cava will be more difficult to image and the heart will look different because of the oblique angle. However, the basic interrogation for free intraab- dominal, pleural, and pericardial fluid may be com - pleted, with some interrogation of the liver depending on what side the patient is imaged (the gallbladder is on the patient’s right side). The gallbladder lies to the right of midline so it may be difficult to view from a modified left subcostal view, especially in cats. The TFAST DH view is part of AFAST, TFAST, and Vet BLUE (see Chapters 6 and 22). The reader is referred to Chapter 6 in which the DH view is outlined in great detail. Briefly, the DH view is performed as follows. • The DH view begins with longitudinal placement of the probe with the probe marker towards the patient’s head immediately caudal to the xiphoid Figure 17 .27 . 332 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER process. Stay longitudinal because transverse planes are confusing (see Figure 4.3). • The probe is then directed far more cranially than most sonographers expect, being almost parallel to the sternum (see Figure 17.27). Attempting to bring the curved white (hyperechoic) line, representing the diaphragm‐pulmonary interface as close (to the probe head) as possible in the near‐field is another helpful tip. Don’t direct toward the spine as you will get too much gastrointestinal tract and often there is lots of gas shadowing. • Depth should be adjusted so that the diaphragm courses through the distal two‐thirds of the image on the screen so that the near‐field is two‐thirds abdomen and the far‐field one‐third thorax (see Figures 6.8–6.12 and 17.27). This allows for ade- quately screening both the abdomen and thorax. • The gallbladder, if not in view, is sought by fanning toward the tabletop (when in right lateral recum- bency) or when the patient is standing and the sonographer is on the patient’s left, fans toward the patient’s right side (or the assistant if standing on the other side of the patient) because the gall- bladder is located to the right of midline in both dogs and cats. • In this same plane or close by, and making sure that the probe is immediately against the xiphoid, look for the caudal vena cava (CVC) as it traverses the diaphragm in both canines and felines (see Figures 6.8–6.12 and 17.27). • The CVC is recognized by the two hyperechoic (bright white) lines that make up the near wall (short line) and far wall (long line) with reverbera- tion artifact (A‐lines) parallel hyperechoic lines to the far wall extending through the far‐field, dependent on depth setting and the presence or absence of dry lung against the CVC’s far wall (see Figures 6.9, 6.11, and 6.12). • The mantra at the DH view is to see the Big 3 (gall- bladder, “cardiac bump”, CVC) as a general over - view and for proper depth setting before starting the fanning and rocking (see Figure 17.27). • Once the Big 3 have been identified and the image looks good, then in a sequential way specifically interrogate in the same order every time as follows. ◦ Check the abdominal cavity for free fluid by fanning through the gallbladder (and its adja- cent liver) in both directions, then followed by… ◦ Rocking the probe toward the sternum to best image the cardiac bump, where the muscular apex of the heart is very near or immediately against the diaphragm for pericardial effusion, then followed by… ◦ Imaging along the diaphragm for pleural effu- sion, and lung pathology along the pulmonary‐ diaphragmatic interface. Soft Tissue Findings at the DH View If the canine and feline gallbladder is not visualized, its rupture, displacement (diaphragmatic herniation), or the presence of gallbladder stones, mineralization, sludge, mucoceles, and emphysematous cholecystitis should all be considered within the clinical context of the patient’s history, presenting complaint, and other diagnostic findings (see Chapters 6 and 8). Pitfalls of the Diaphragmatico‐ Hepatic View See Chapter 6. Summary of TFAST Views and Their Clinical Utility TFAST now consists of five acoustic windows that include the bilaterally applied CTS and PCS views and a single midline DH view. The premise here is that fluid falls (gravity dependent) and air rises (nongrav- ity dependent) (see Figure 17.1). Thus, it is easy to remember the clinical utility of the TFAST views. The right and left CTS views are best used to rule out PTX and serve as a single‐point survey for lung conditions. Vet BLUE should always be performed to search for the “lung point” when applicable (see Chapter 18) and for more comprehensive lung screen- ing assessment. The right and left PCS views are used to screen for the presence of pleural and pericardial effusions, and assess volume status and contractility (FS%), and left‐ and right‐sided strain/failure/overload through the four TFAST echo views (see Chapter 18). The single DH view is a first‐line view for pericar - dial and pleural effusions because of less lung inter - ference using the acoustic window of the liver and gallbladder (Lisciandro 2016a). The view is also used to assess CVC characterization and size, hepatic venous distension, and gallbladder wall edema (cardiac gallbladder) for volume status and right‐ sided heart strain/failure/overload (Nelson et al. 2010; Lisciandro 2011, 2014a,b, 2016; Lisciandro and Armenise 2014; Darnis et al. 2018). See also Chapters 6, 18, 26, and 36.

333 POCUS: TFAST – INTRODUCTION AND IMAGE ACQUISITION Recording TFAST Findings on Goal‐directed Templates Recording your findings is imperative for a successful ultrasound program. See Chapter 18 and Appendix I. Pearls and Pitfalls, The Final Say TFAST is more than a “flash exam” of the thorax (Lisciandro and Mann 2019). The TFAST examination rapidly answers many important clinical questions to help with decision making not only for patient resus- citation but also directing diagnostic efforts and patient management. TFAST is a superior imaging modality for pneumothorax, pericardial effusion, and soft tissue conditions of the heart which are suspected or completely missed radiographically. TFAST can help determine patient volume status and be used as a tracking tool for pleural and pericardial effusions and pneumothorax. For the TFAST Chest T ube Site • You can’t reliably image lung if you can’t obtain the “gator sign” orientation. • Use the “Tricks of the Trade” for manipulating the echoes either by the “one‐eyed gator sign” and scattering the echoes or by the angle of insonation and ricocheting the echoes, or do both to enhance the observation of “lung sliding.” • Understand that gain, focus cursor, angle of insonation, and depth play a large role in image quality. • Observe the CdTZ on every patient when defining the CTS view so that you become used to the pit- falls of lung ultrasound and avoid mistaking abdominal structures for lung pathology. For the TFAST Pericardial Sites • Always image the heart in its entirety with enough depth to be able to identify the hyperechoic peri- cardium as your landmark in the far‐field to avoid mistaking heart chambers for pleural and pericar - dial effusion and other pathology. • Always start with the TFAST short‐axis views for right PCS views. • Learn to fan along the short‐axis and long‐axis TFAST echo lines. If you understand this concept you will quickly excel in TFAST echo image acquisition. • Memorize the TFAST echo chart because it will help you know where you are and what direction you should go for image acquisition. • The DH view should always be used because of its advantageous acoustic window via the liver and gallbladder into the pleural and pericardial spaces. Eyeballing TFAST Echo Views • Especially in cats, the “freeze and roll the cine ball” maneuver must be mastered because the faster feline heart rate makes “eyeballing” more error prone. Quick Reference of Normals and Rules of Thumb • If any evidence of lung, most commonly lung sliding and B‐lines, observed against the intercostal space at the TFAST CTS view rules out PTX, espe- cially in the preferred standing or sternal position. • B‐lines in trauma are lung contusions until proven otherwise. • Always image the heart in its entirety using the hyperechoic (bright white) pericardium as a land- mark in the far‐field. • Adhere to the axiom that “One view is no view” for the accurate diagnosis of pleural effusion and peri- cardial effusion. • The FAST DH view is likely nearly 100% sensitive and 100% specific for detecting clinically relevant pericardial effusion in dogs and cats. • Dogs and cats have no pleural or pericardial effusion that is evident in normalcy; however, pericardial fat mimics pleural effusion espe- cially (1) along the heart at the left TFAST PCS view as an anechoic stripe (linear) between the heart and intercostal spaces, and (2) as an echo- genic triangulation (fat pad) within the cardiac‐ diaphragmatic pouch. • The “eyeball method” is accepted in people as a screening test for obvious cardiac abnormalities. • A left atrial to aortic ratio (LA:Ao) that is >2:1 would be obviously abnormal in both dogs and cats. • A right ventricular to left ventricular ratio (RV:LV) on the four‐chamber long‐axis view approximating a ratio of 1:1 would be obviously abnormal in both dogs and cats. • An abnormal fractional shortening (FS%) for dogs and cats would be <20%.

Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 337 Introduction TFAST is an examination of the thorax that extends beyond the “flash mentality” because with its cerebral approach, a tremendous amount of clinical information may be gained in a matter of minutes, similar to the AFAST examination. Chapter 17 reviews image acquisition principles, to which the reader is referred. This chapter will discuss the clinical integration of TFAST and its five acoustic windows as they relate to pleural and pericardial effusion, pneu- mothorax, the TFAST echo views for cardiac condi- tions, and the caudal vena cava for volume status combined with other TFAST findings. Before beginning this chapter, it is important to acknowledge the uniqueness of the thorax, with its two major organs, compared to the abdomen, with more than six major organs, regarding effusions and free air. First, there is only one major fluid‐filled struc- ture within the thorax that the sonographer can mis- take for free fluid and that is your patient’s heart. The heart, unlike the abdominal organs, is not as forgiving regarding misguided centesis (sticking a needle in your patient’s heart versus the liver or spleen or urinary bladder). Second, the other major thoracic organ, lung, is air‐filled and occupies most of the thorax, posing problems not only with its direct imaging but also interfering with the imaging of the heart and pleural cavity because ultrasound does not transmit through air but rather reflects. Thus, transtho- racic acoustic windows are much more challenging and intimidating to many sonographers who are com- fortable imaging the abdominal cavity, but lack confidence in tackling the thorax. Free fluid in the thorax also differs from the abdominal cavity and retroperitoneal space, in which free fluid commonly images as anechoic (black) trian- gulations. Whereas pleural effusion often behaves sim- ilarly, pericardial effusion is contained within the pericardial sac and is rounded (not triangulated) in appearance. Then finally, we can have pathological free air in the pleural cavity, called pneumothorax, which involves an array of intimidating air‐related artifacts that must be differentiated from aerated lung. Get ready for a wild but achievable TFAST ride through the small animal thorax! What TFAST Can Do • Can rapidly detect pneumothorax in traumatized dogs and cats with high accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. • Can determine the degree of pneumothorax (in other words, its severity) as “partial” versus “mas- sive” by finding the “lung point.” • Can detect and monitor pleural effusion, initially and serially. • Can detect and monitor pericardial effusion, ini- tially and serially. • Can determine the presence or absence of cardiac tamponade. • Can be used as a soft tissue examination of the heart. • Can crudely detect and monitor lung contusions initially and serially. Findings at the Chest Tube Site View Concept of Wet versus Dry Lung Lung Sliding and A‐lines Indicate Dry Lung and Rule Out Pneumothorax “Lung sliding” is defined as the to‐and‐fro motion of the lung along the intercostal space represented by the bright white, hyperechoic, (proximal) line or the pulmonary–pleural interface (PPI) or where the parietal and visceral pleura slide across one another (micro description) or where the “lung line” and inter- costal space slide across one another (macro descrip- tion) (see Figure 17.6). All these descriptions are synonymous and are descriptive in normalcy. However, when pleural space disease exists, the PPI is most commonly disrupted by fluid, air, abdominal organs, or soft tissue and we refer to the lung surface as the “lung line.” “Lung sliding” has replaced the veterinary term of “glide sign” (Volpicelli et al. 2012). In normalcy, “lung sliding” of aerated lung is accom- panied by strong air reverberation artifacts called A‐lines (remember “A” is for “air”). The observation of A‐lines is dependent on your angle of insonation (make it as close to 90° to the lung surface as possible) and your machine settings (frequency, depth, focus cursor), explained in more detail in Chapter 17. Primary A‐lines are identified by their equidistance from one another as parallel lines (or bars) through the far‐field (see Figure 17.6). Their spacing is approxi- mately the distance from the probe head to the first soft tissue–air interface (in normalcy aerated lung against the thoracic wall or pneumothorax when air is in the pleural space). A‐lines are also present, dependent on settings and your machine’s software, as secondary and tertiary A‐lines or, in other words, as A‐double prime and A‐triple prime (A’‐, A”‐, A”‐) lines (see Figure 17.6). The key is the presence of repeated horizontal parallel lines (or bars) from the “lung line” through the far‐field. The presence of “lung sliding” with A‐lines defines the term “dry lung” and, with its absence, pneumothorax (PTX) (Lichtenstein et al. 2000; Kirkpatrick et al. 2004; Volpicelli et al. 2006; Lisciandro 2011, 2014a,b, Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2017). Importantly, “lung sliding” is a real‐time finding. It requires correlating with phases of respiration, the to‐ and‐fro movement in concert with inspiration and expiration. The presence of “lung sliding” differenti- ates “dry lung” from PTX since both conditions have strong A‐lines because both have air immediately adja- cent to the thoracic wall and its intercostal space. In PTX there are strong A‐lines but no “lung sliding” (Volpicelli et al. 2012; Lisciandro 2011; Lichtenstein et al. 2000; Kirkpatrick et al. 2004) (Figure 18.1). Moreover, the finding of the “lung point” (described later) increases the sensitivity and specificity of a PTX diagnosis (Lichtenstein et al. 2000; Lisciandro et al. 2008, Lisciandro 2011, 2014a) (see Figures 18.5 and 18.6). B‐Lines and Wet Lung Rule Out Pneumothorax B‐lines have also been referred to as “ultrasound lung rockets” and represent forms of alveolar‐interstitial edema; however, in trauma, B‐lines are lung contu- sions until proven otherwise (Ball et al. 2009; Lisciandro 2011, 2014a,b; Lisciandro et al. 2014; Dicker et al. 2019). You cannot see the B‐line artifact when PTX is present because free air in the pleural space images as A‐lines, a uniquely different artifact (Lichtenstein et al. 1999; Ball et al.2009; Lisciandro 2011). B‐lines are now the preferred nonvisual term for artifacts historically referred to as comet‐tail artifact, ultrasound lung rockets, and ring‐down artifact (Lichtenstein et al. 1997, 1999, 2009; Volpicelli et al. 2012; Louvet and Bourgeois 2008). It is important to note that B‐lines are created differ- ently from true comet‐tails. Comet‐tails were first used to describe the ultrasound artifact created by strong reflectors (metal) of the ultrasound beam, whereas B‐lines are created by the large difference in acoustic

B‐lines are defined as laser‐like hyper - echoic (bright white) vertical streaks that oscillate in synchrony with phases of respiration while obliter - ating A‐lines and extend through the far‐field of the ultrasound screen without fading (Figure 18.2). Their laser‐like appearance is why they have also been referred to as “ultrasound lung rockets” (Lichtenstein 2007, 2010b; Lisciandro 2011, 2014a,b). B‐lines, despite extending through the far‐field, represent a superficial fluid–air juxtaposition along the very outer 1–3 mm of lung surface in people (Volpicelli et al. 2006; Soldati et al. 2011), which likely holds true for all mammalian lung. B‐lines are referred to as “wet lung” since they most commonly represent forms of alveolar‐interstitial edema (Volpicelli et al. 2006; Lisciandro 2011, 2014a,b, Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2017). Importantly, B‐lines are nonspecific and thus their presence is referred to as alveolar‐interstitial syndrome (AIS) because their distribution with a regional pattern‐ based approach must be used for their causative inter- pretation, that is, Vet BLUE (see Figure 18.2). In people, older lung (>65 years of age) and fibrosis along the lung surface from chronic respiratory diseases can also cause B‐lines that are not truly representative of AIS (Shyamsundar et al. 2013). In trauma, B‐lines are lung contusions until proven otherwise and a Vet BLUE B‐line scoring system and lung contusion severity score have been developed (Ball et al. 2009; Lisciandro 2011; Dicker et al. 2019). See Chapters 22 and 23 for more detail and Figure 23.29. Pseudo B‐lines The “Shimmy Line” or Z‐line The “shimmy line,” a term coined by the author, is a tight band of horizontal A‐lines extending through the far‐field that may appear at first glance as a B‐line(s) (Figure 18.3). However, the “shimmy line” does not swing like a pendulum with inspiration and expira - tion and lacks the discrete laser‐like hyperechoic character of a B‐line, and “shimmy lines” do not extend through the far‐field (Lichtenstein 2010b; Neto et al. 2016; Lee 2016). In the author’s experience, these lines are generally observed with really “dry lung” and are most often seen at angles of insonation of 90° to strongly aerated lung surface. Since they are in fact created off the thoracic wall and its reflective fascial planes, they do not swing to and fro with inspiration and expiration, they fade, unlike true B‐lines, they do not obliterate A‐lines, unlike true B‐lines, and are in essence short comet‐tails (Soldati, personal communi- cation). These “shimmy lines” have also been referred to as “Z‐lines” and clinically mean nothing, having no relevant lung pathology implications, and thus were given the last letter in the alphabet for that reason (Lichtenstein 2010b; Lee 2016). It is important to note that the use of the “Z‐line” nomenclature is controver- sial and for many lung sonographers the line nomen - clature adds further confusion over merely stating that “shimmy lines” lack the characteristics of B‐lines and are inconsequential. Moreover, in our experience, they are overlooked when using the definition of B‐lines. With fairly minimal experience with your machine and its settings, you will be able to readily differentiate the B‐line(s) from a “shimmy line.” Gastric “Pseudo B‐lines” The presence of fluid immediately adjacent to air at the outer surface of lung creates the B‐line artifact. The same artifact can be similarly created within the gastric lumen when liquid (fluid) ingesta and air are juxta - posed (see Figures 3.6 and 18.3). Typically, these “pseudo gastric B‐lines” are seen at the TFAST CTS view since air rises within the gastric lumen to its least gravity‐dependent region as air similarly rises within the pleural cavity (see Figure 18.3). The “pseudo gastric B‐lines” are a major reason why we now teach to find and move away from the caudodorsal transition zone (CdTZ) at the TFAST CTS view (and during Vet BLUE) to avoid mistaking these lines for lung pathology. Moreover, abdominal structures such as the rugal folds of the stomach and liver may be mistaken for “pseudo shred sign” and “pseudo tissue sign,” respectively (see Figures 23.13, 23.16, and 23.20 and Chapters 22 and 23). Nodule “Pseudo B‐lines” Nodules along the surface of the lung, due to their difference in acoustic impedance of soft tissue and aer- ated lung, cast “pseudo B‐lines” through the far‐field (see Figures 3.6 and 18.3). Usually, it is obvious that there is a nodule(s) in the near‐field from which the “pseudo B‐line” is cast. However, nodule “pseudo B‐lines” may be associated with nodules that are very Figure 18.2. TFAST Pneumothorax: A‐lines with Absent “Lung Sliding” “Dry lung,” A‐lines with “lung sliding,” and PTX look identical on B‐mode still images. The difference must be made in real time or on cine clips. The difference between “dry lung” and PTX is the presence and absence of “lung sliding,” respectively (Lichtenstein et al. 2000, Lichtenstein 2007; Kirkpatrick et al. 2004; Lisciandro et al. 2008; Volpicelli et al. 2012). The CTS view was selected because if “lung sliding” is observed at the CTS view, the highest reasonable point over the pleural cavity, then PTX is immediately ruled out (Lisciandro 2008). The same strategy of the least gravity‐dependent or highest reasonable point over the anterior chest is used in human medicine (Lichtenstein et al. 1999, 2000; Lichtenstein 2007; Kirkpatrick et al. 2004). Lung Point: Improves the Diagnosis, Semiquantifies the Degree, and Helps Monitor PTX (Figures 18.5 and 18.6) Effect of Positioning When PTX is suspected, move your patient to standing or sternal if possible for several important reasons. First, standing or sternal is generally safer because your patient as a rule can ventilate more easily and efficiently. Second, the “lung point” is better categorized by using greater differences in height between the most and least gravity‐dependent sternum and upper limits of the pleural cavity, referred to by the author as the “parking garage‐sky - scraper concept” (Figures 18.7 and 18.8) (Lisciandro 2011). Third, air rises to the least gravity‐dependent regions of the thorax and the cap of air within the pleural cavity is more evenly distributed (not “bub - bled”) than in a patient in lateral recumbency, elimi - nating confounding findings such as the “double lung point” and the “reverse sliding sign” (Volpicelli et al. 2013; Hwang et al. 2018) (see Figure 18.6). Recently, a newer concept that shows promise has been described, referred to as the “double curtain sign” and the “reverse curtain sign” observed at the CdTZ in standing or sternal (Boysen et al. 2019). Lateral recumbency in small animals would correlate with supine posi - tioning in people. Thus this “parking garage effect” places minimal differences between levels for locating the “lung point” (see Figures 18.7 and 18.8). Second, respiration is important because in either spontane - ously breathing patients or those being supported with positive pressure ventilation (PPV), the type of ventilation changes how free air in the pleural space (PTX) behaves. During PPV , the free air in the pleural cavity is pushed or “bubbled” unnaturally into differ - ent regions with each breath, whatever the posi - tioning. This PPV effect does not occur in spontaneously breathing small animals in which the free air within the pleural cavity more naturally rises to the least gravity‐dependent region, and collapsed lung falls into gravity‐dependent regions, especially when the patient is in standing or sternal positioning (see Figure 18.7). Searching for the Lung Point Improves Sensitivity The “lung point” is defined as the point along the thoracic wall where there is evidence of lung recontact- ing intercostal spaces (see Figures 18.5–18.8), in other words, the transition zone of free air within the pleural space and lung reopposed to the thoracic wall. Most commonly, the “lung point” is found through the observation of “lung sliding” or B‐lines; however, any ultrasonographic evidence of lung recontacting the thoracic wall determines the “lung point,” including the “shred sign,” “tissue sign,” “nodule sign,” “wedge sign” (see Chapters 22 and 23 and Figures 23.2, 23.5, 23.7–11), and the “lung pulse,” explained in greater detail in the next section (Lichtenstein et al. 2000, 2003; Lichtenstein 2007). The sonographer must consider this lung information because “lung sliding” with “dry lung” differs from the condition of B‐lines or “wet lung” in which the lung likely has forms of alveolar‐ interstitial edema. Moreover, the findings of consolida- tion (shred sign, tissue sign, wedge sign, nodule sign) indicate that lung function, ventilation, is even more severely compromised. In the presence of significant pleural effusion, such as hemothorax in trauma, the “lung point” will be affected because the PE displaces air and lung floats on the PE, making positioning again important for expected findings. The Lung Point Semiquantitates Degree of PTX The location of the “lung point” with your patient in sternal or standing semiquantitates and thus catego - rizes the degree of PTX (Lichtenstein et al. 2000; Sargsyan et al. 2001; Lisciandro 2011). Although not yet published at the time of writing this chapter, degree of PTX likely correlates with the location of the “lung point,” most effectively in standing or sternal posi - tioning over lateral recumbency. We have used a systematic approach, referred to as the “TFAST PTX 1/3s Rule,” of an upper third, middle third, and lower third for location of the “lung point” with the patient in standing or sternal position and designating each third as trivial, moderate, or severe (Lisciandro 2011, 2014a) (Figure 18.9, Table 18.3). The use of this TFAST systematic approach is important for several clinically relevant reasons. • It allows for decision making on whether thoraco - centesis should be performed. • It provides a tracking or monitoring tool (static, resolving or worsening). • It minimizes iatrogenic lung trauma via empirical thoracocentesis. We use the rule of thumb that a “lung point” in the upper third is “trivial PTX” and thus PTX can be moni- tored by tracking the location of the “lung point” over time; a middle third is “moderate PTX” and treatment (minimally thoracocentesis) should be seriously con - sidered; and a lower third is “severe PTX” (serious) that mandates treatment (thoracocentesis) (see Figure 18.9). Use of the TFAST PTX 1/3s Rule for Pneumothorax Monitoring The location of the “lung point” serves as a monitoring tool, using its distance from the CTS view (Lichtenstein et al. 2000; Sargsyan et al. 2001; Lisciandro 2011). 351 POCUS: TFAST – CLINICAL INTEGRATION Missing PTX on TFAST T ricks of the T rade The original TFAST study evaluated 145 dogs and showed that with experience and in slower breathing patients, PTX could be diagnosed with ~95% sensi- tivity and specificity (Lisciandro et al. 2008). The major reasons for missing PTX during TFAST include the following. • Panting patients – administer butorphanol routinely for respiratory patients because it is safe and serves as an anxiolytic without causing hemodynamic com- promise and panting, while also being short‐acting. • Not incorporating the author’s Tricks of the Trade by manipulating the echoes during image optimi- zation either by using the “one‐eyed gator sign” – rib in the middle of the screen – or obliqu- ing or ricocheting the echoes by changing the angle of insonation (see Figures 17.7 and 17.11) • Not having proper machine settings, especially regarding depth and gain (see Figure 17.10), • Not searching for the “lung point.” • Improper training. Through our continued understanding of these factors, we have been able to markedly improve training, including accelerating the learning curve and gaining proficiency in the accurate diagnosis of PTX (Lisciandro 2011, 2014a,b; Dicker et al. 2019). False Negatives It is possible to mistake “lung sliding” for abdominal structure movement at the CdTZ, when in fact the patient has PTX. Sliding cranial 2–3 intercostal spaces away from the CdTZ and searching for the “lung point” eliminates this error (see Figures 17.8 and 17.9). A helpful intervention is the use of subcutaneous injectable butorphanol (or other cardiovascular and respiratory forgiving form of sedation) that is low risk, fairly rapid onset, short‐acting, and does not cause panting, while serving as an anxiolytic and slowing breathing patterns. False Positives It is also possible to mistake “lung sliding” in PTX for panting or rapid shallow breathing in dogs and cats (Lisciandro et al. 2008). Sliding cranial away from the CdTZ and searching for the “lung point” helps elimi- nate this confounder (see Figures 17.8 and 17.9). A helpful intervention is the use of subcutaneous injectable butorphanol (or other cardiovascular and respiratory forgiving form of sedation) that is low risk, fairly rapid onset, short‐acting, and does not cause panting, while serving as an anxiolytic and slowing breathing patterns. Use of M‐mode and Power Doppler for Detecting PTX The demand for still image documentation of PTX in people has resulted in the use of M‐mode and power Doppler ultrasonography (Cunningham et al. 2002; Lichtenstein 2007, 2010b). The reason for these alternate modalities is that still images are easier to archive and consume less data than storing cine clips for PTX documentation. M‐mode has not only proven helpful as an adjunct to B‐mode but is also now used as a primary diagnostic modality in peo- ple (Lichtenstein 2007, 2010b). Use of M‐mode: Seashore Sign, Stratosphere Sign, and Rain Sign When using M‐mode, “dry lung” is represented by the “seashore sign,” likened to the graininess of sand along the shoreline (Figure 18.10) (Lichtenstein 2007, 2010b). The “seashore sign” is created by the movement of “lung sliding” and rules out PTX and supports “dry lung.” In contrast, when no “lung sliding” exists along the “lung line,” as in PTX, a “stratosphere sign” (also called the “bar code sign”) is observed (Lichtenstein 2007, 2010b). A couple of considerations when using M‐mode for lung are to reduce the frame speed to “slow” or as low as possible to minimize confounding thoracic wall movement, and use different transducers such as linear or phased array rather than a curvilinear (micro- convex) probe. Another variable is the actual ultra - sound machine and its software; some ultrasound machines may perform better using M‐mode for lung than others. Despite these modifications, the author remains more confident with using B‐mode for observing the presence or absence of “lung sliding” and when PTX is suspected, in searching for the “lung point” in B‐mode. Use of Power Doppler and the “Power Slide” The use of power Doppler seems to have never made the mainstream in human medicine. In short, the presence of the colored pixels of power Doppler along the “lung line” supports the movement of “lung sliding” and the absence of colored pixels suggests the diagnosis of PTX (Cunningham et al. 2002). Thus, power Doppler in theory could be used for medical records as a still image (Figure 18.11). In the author’s experience, as with M‐mode, there is generally too much thoracic wall movement in spontaneously breathing small animals for power Doppler to be as reliable as B‐mode (Lisciandro 2014a), and M‐mode is superior as an adjunct technique, making power Doppler the lesser of the three modalities (Table 18.4). Other Confounders Subcutaneous Emphysema and Its Effects on TFAST The presence of subcutaneous emphysema (SQE) is problematic because ultrasound does not transit (image) through air and, depending on where the SQE is present, any or all of the acoustic windows of TFAST may be affected (Lisciandro et al. 2008; Lisciandro 2011). In the only study to the author’s knowledge reporting SQE, only 7/145 (~5%) cases were affected (Lisciandro et al. 2008). If the sonographer is unable to displace the SQE with probe pressure and is thus unable to observe the “gator sign” orientation, then TFAST evaluation of lung (and pleural cavity) will be indeterminate. In other words, if the “gator sign” cannot be imaged then the TFAST sonographer cannot confidently interrogate lung (or image the pleural cavity) (see Table 18.2). Displacing SQE with gentle probe pressure is successful for acquiring the “gator sign” orientation and PCS views in most small ani - mals, thus allowing for TFAST lung, cardiac, and pleural cavity examination (Lisciandro et al. 2008). In human medicine, some sonographers have referred to SQE as having E‐lines, with “E” standing for emphy - sema (Lichtenstein 2010b; Lee 2016; Neto et al. 2016). However, the “line language” becomes confusing since often there are no “lines” at all in SQE; and air per - forms as air – A‐lines or dirty shadowing dependent on the angle of insonation. The use of “E‐lines” is not preferred by the author (Figures 18.12 and 18.13). Figure 18.11.
