The “Step Sign” of TFAST and the CTS View The term “step sign” was coined in the original TFAST study to describe the ultrasound finding of a disruption to the expected linear continuity of the PPI (Lisciandro et al. 2008: Lisciandro 2014a; Dicker et al. 2019) (Figure 18.14). The “step sign” often correlated with abnormal findings on thoracic radiography (TXR) that included pleural space abnormalities such as pleural effusion and diaphragmatic hernia, thoracic wall abnormalities such as intercostal tear(s), rib fracture(s), and subcostal hematomas, and other intrathoracic abnormalities including comorbidities such as an anterior mediastinal mass, severe left atrial enlarge- ment, and others (Lisciandro et al. 2008). The “step sign” also can be seen as a normal finding at the CdTZ and is described in Chapter 17 (see Figure 17.9). “Step sign” rule‐outs are summarized in Table 18.5. The upshot is that when a “step sign” is observed at the CTS view away from the transition zone of pleural and abdominal cavities, a potentially serious abnor - mality should be suspected. Vet BLUE for more com- prehensive lung evaluation and radiography should be pursued and the “step sign” placed into clinical context with other findings. The term “step sign” has also been used to describe disruption of the expected linear continuity of long bones as a sonographic feature of bone fractures and an accurate screening test for rib fractures in foals and skull and long bone fractures in children (Picandet et al. 2007; Barata et al. 2012; et al. Parri 2013) (see Figures 35.7 and 35.9). Summary for the CTS View Three Major Lung‐related Findings There are three major findings at the CTS view: (1) “lung sliding” and A‐lines, referred to as “dry lung” representing normal aerated lung at the periphery and immediately ruling out PTX; (2) B‐lines, referred to as “wet lung” most commonly representing forms of alveolar‐interstitial edema at the periphery, immedi- ately ruling out PTX; and (3) pneumothorax, A‐lines with absent “lung sliding” and a “lung point.” • “Lung sliding” and A‐lines also referred to as “dry lung.” ◦ Expect for adult dogs and cats, and puppies and kittens >6 weeks of age to have a “dry lung” profile with absent B‐lines (Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2017, 2018; Lisciandro and Fosgate 2018). • B‐lines, also referred to as ultrasound lung rockets and “wet lung.” ◦ Immediately rules out PTX at that specific point on the thoracic wall because the artifact cannot be observed when air is in the pleural space (PTX) (Lichtenstein et al. 2000; Kirkpatrick et al. 2004; Lisciandro et al. 2008; Lisciandro 2011). ◦ Represent various forms of alveolar‐interstitial edema; however, in trauma cases B‐lines repre- sent lung contusions until proven otherwise (Lisciandro et al. 2008; Lisciandro 2011; Ball et al. 2009; Dicker et al. 2019). ◦ The Vet BLUE B‐line scoring system provides a way in which to score the degree of lung contu- sions in trauma patients. See the Vet BLUE Lung Contusion Severity Score in Chapters 22 and 23 (Lisciandro 2011, 2014b; Dicker et al. 2019). • Pneumothorax as A‐lines with absent “lung sliding.” ◦ Search for the “lung point” (Lisciandro et al. 2008; Lisciandro 2011). Pericardial Effusion General TFAST Considerations Regarding Pericardial Effusion Several years ago, we posed the question “How would you teach me to accurately diagnose pericardial effu- sion (PCE) using ultrasound?” Colleagues would reply, “It just looks like pericardial effusion” and text- books would read, “Imaging features of pericardial effusion are the presence of a sonolucent space bet- ween the epicardium and pericardial/mediastinal interface, an influence of gravity on the localization of fluid” (Bonagura and Fuentes 2015), a virtually mean- ingless answer from a teaching standpoint, especially for the nonradiologist, noncardiologist sonographer. From such answers, the author realized that TFAST tenets for the accurate diagnosis of PCE needed to be created and that knowledge of cardiac anatomy on both short‐ and long‐axis views was imperative to pre- vent mistakes (Lisciandro 2016). The left ventricular short‐axis view is a most con- fusing and dangerous proposition as a primary view because of the crescent‐shaped right ventricle that mimics the rounding of PCE within the pericardial sac (Figure 18.15). Moreover, the FAST DH view needed to become a primary view in small animals. The FAST DH view is advantageous because it avoids air interference from transthoracic views and directly images for PCE without the confusion of cardiac chambers and for these reasons is the number 1 view in human medicine (see Figure 18.18) (Lisciandro 2014a, 2016, 2019). Pericardial Effusion and Pleural Effusion are Quite Different The differences between PCE and PE ultrasono- graphically are significant and must be acknowl- edged by the sonographer on a number of fronts. First, the sonographer must understand the intratho- racic anatomy to accurately differentiate PCE from PE and recognize when both are concurrently pre- sent. Second, thoracic radiography is generally a good test for pleural effusion but unreliable for peri- cardial effusion (Guglielmini 2012; Côté 2013). Lastly, the prevalence of PCE is likely much higher than previously reported because historically unless the patient underwent advanced imaging, either complete echocardiography or CT, the diagnosis of PCE was missed because thoracic radiography is unreliable (Guglielmini et al. 2012; Côté et al. 2013). Now that TFAST and AFAST have become first‐line imaging tests for many clinicians, and ultrasound is arguably the gold standard test for PCE, cases of PCE are captured as part of initial patient assessment rather than being missed or delayed. In 2005, pre‐ FAST, the author’s practice had three documented cases of PCE in comparison to when TFAST became a first‐line test, after which 28 documented cases were detected (Lisciandro 2014a, 2016). The true preva- lence of PCE is likely higher than reported pre‐FAST, as are likely many other cardiac‐related conditions, such as intracardiac masses, pulmonary hyperten- sion, dilated cardiomyopathy, left atrial tear in chronic mitral valve disease, caval syndrome, and others, because unless a complete echocardiogram or CT was performed, the condition was missed. The bottom line is that we were using the wrong imaging modality as our screening test. T able 18.5. Rule‐outs for the “step sign” of lung. 359 POCUS: TFAST – C LINICAL I NTEGRATION Accurate TFAST Diagnosis of Pericardial Effusion The sonographer should have a set of rules to follow for the accurate sonographic diagnosis of PCE. The only major fluid‐filled structure in the thorax that can be mistaken for PCE (or PE) is your patient’s heart. And it’s not generally a good thing for your patient to perform centesis on their heart chamber. These are the TFAST tenets that will be subsequently explained in greater detail. • Always, always, always image the heart in its entirety with enough depth to see the bright hyperechoic pericardium, your habitual landmark, in the far‐ field. By adhering to this tenet, the probability of mistaking the heart for PCE (or PE) is greatly reduced (Figure 18.16; see also Figure 18.15). We call this the “DeFrancesco Rule.” • Image toward the muscular apex of the heart where there are no confusing heart chambers. Pericardial effusion rounds the muscular apex of the heart, referred to as the “racetrack sign” and “bull’s eye sign” (Lisciandro 2014a, 2016). 361 POCUS: TFAST – C LINICAL I NTEGRATION Does My Patient have Cardiac T amponade? Defining Cardiac T amponade The question increases the anxiety of the sonogra - pher when finding PCE. Cardiac tamponade occurs when intrapericardial pressure exceeds right atrial and right ventricular pressures, causing their col - lapse seen on either short‐axis or long‐axis views (Figure 18.20). In real time, the right atrium and right ventricle often dynamically collapse with a rip - pling effect. As a result of cardiac tamponade, obstructive shock occurs in which blood cannot be pumped from the right heart to the lung and right‐ sided congestive heart failure ensues. Different degrees of cardiac tamponade can be present (see Chapters 19–21) with more severe forms being life‐ threatening and warranting emergent pericardio - centesis (see Chapters 21 and 43). Using the Characterization of the Caudal Vena Cava and Hepatic Veins By definition, obstructive shock secondary to cardiac tamponade will result in a distended caudal vena cava (CVC), referred to as FAT or fluid‐intolerant CVC, along with hepatic venous distension because the hepatic veins drain into the CVC, referred to as the “tree trunk sign” (Lisciandro 2014a, 2016) (see Figures 18.20D and 36.8). If the patient survives, in time hepatic venous congestion becomes chronic and right‐sided congestive heart failure develops with ascites (modified transudate) (see Figures 6.8, 6.9, Figure 18.17 . The presence of a nonhemoabdomen ascites supports a long‐standing presence of PCE because the ascites occurred over time, supporting a more chronic process (see Figures 6.8, 6.9, 6.10, 6.11, 18.18C,D, and 18.20 and see Chapter 7) (Stafford Johnson et al. 2004). 365 POCUS: TFAST – CLINICAL INTEGRATION ascites (Stafford Johnson et al. 2004). This is another example of how targeted POCUS exams can miss important clinical information that could have a pro- found effect on patient management. With the Global FAST approach, ascites may be rapidly ruled in or out and the CVC and its associated hepatic veins charac- terized using AFAST (see Chapter 36). Moreover, AFAST and its target organ approach rapidly screens for obvious soft tissue abnormalities, such as obvious liver masses or other abdomen‐related pathology. In another canine pericardial effusion study of 107 dogs, 50–66% had evidence of pulmonary metastasis based on surgical and necropsy findings as the gold standard, of which only 33% were detected via thoracic radiography (TXR) (MacDonald et al. 2009); Vet BLUE screens for any obvious lung abnormalities including pulmonary metastasis and may prove better than three‐view TXR (Kulhavy and Lisciandro 2015). These studies make a strong case for initially staging all canine PCE cases using the Global FAST approach over targeted POCUS exams, in which important information is often missed (satisfaction of search error) or delayed in its detection (see Figure 18.20). See Patient Staging in Chapter 36 and Figure 36.23. In summary, there are different degrees of cardiac tamponade and the best approach is as follows. • Look at your patient. Are they hemodynamically stable? If the answer is yes, then take a few breaths and relax. If the patient is unstable, then emergent pericardiocentesis is indicated as a life‐saving intervention (see Chapters 19–21and 43 and Section IX). • Look at the CVC (see Figure 18.20). It is a nonecho option that is often less stressful for the patient because it can be performed rapidly without the air interfer- ence and restraint needed for echocardiography, including TFAST echo views and POCUS heart. ◦ If the CVC has a bounce, then the patient does not have obstructive shock, in other words, does not have cardiac tamponade (see Figures 7.12 and 18.20 and Table 7.6). And if a CVC bounce is present, do Global FAST (and an electrocar - diogram) to look for another reason for weak- ness and shock because it’s unlikely to be primarily due to the PCE! ◦ If the CVC is FAT, then there is evidence of obstructive shock or cardiac tamponade. Look at your patient. Are they stable or unstable? An unstable patient requires emergent pericardio- centesis versus a stable patient that favors peri- cardiocentesis as an elective procedure (see Figures 7.12 and 18.20 and Table 7.6). In human medicine, it has been shown that an unre- markable inferior vena cava (IVC) rules out cardiac tamponade and a FAT or distended IVC is only 40% specific, meaning that even if the IVC is FAT or dis- tended, the patient still may not have cardiac tam- ponade requiring emergent pericardiocentesis (Himelman et al. 1988; Candotti and Arntfield 2014; Tchernodrinski and Arntfield 2015). Moreover, in weak hypotensive people with PCE and a non‐dis- tended IVC, it is possible that the PCE is not the cause because there is no cardiac tamponade (Himelman et al. 1988; Candotti and Arntfield 2014; Tchernodrinski and Arntfield 2015). So again, look at your patient and do Global FAST to look for other causes! When Should Emergent Pericardiocentesis Be Performed? Chronic versus Acute PCE Emergent pericardiocentesis should be performed in hemodynamically unstable cases with obstructive shock. The procedure is straightforward and complica- tions are most commonly related to arrhythmias over cardiac puncture or bleeding (Humm et al. 2009). With that being said, we now capture acute PCE that was historically missed, and some of these dogs have acute cardiac chamber rupture, in which the pericardial sac is protective by keeping the hemorrhage in a closed system. Clinically, this is important because pericardi- ocentesis may be indicated, but the PCE and cardiac tamponade may recur quickly, ranging from minutes to the next several hours. Tearing the pericardium, the so‐called “rough pericardiocentesis” to create an inex- pensive temporary pericardial window, would be con- traindicated in these cases as they may exsanguinate into their pleural space. Management also is different and likely requires a pericardial catheter for intermit- tent as needed pericardiocentesis of which the blood, often without anticoagulant, could be repeatedly auto- transfused with an inline blood filter, and the patient potentially kept alive for definitive surgical interven- tion (Morges et al. 2011; Higgs et al. 2015; Ployart et al. 2013; Robinson et al. 2016). Pearl: When performing pericardiocentesis, leave a small volume of fluid in the pericardial sac if complete echocardiography will be subsequently performed because the pericardial fluid provides an acoustic window for the detection of a pericardial or heart‐ based mass (Scansen 2011).

366 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Other Pericardial Effusion Subsets Left Atrial Rupture/Tear The author captures the complication of left atrial tear/ rupture (LAT) several times a year because TFAST is an extension of the physical exam (actually the Global FAST approach is used as an extension of the physical exam). TFAST‐Global FAST is performed on all cardiac patients and suspects (Figure 18.21). The complication is fascinating because it has been traditionally over - looked. LAT is also covered in Chapter 21 from the veterinary cardiologist perspective. The classic presen- tation in the author’s experience is acute respiratory signs, usually with respiratory distress but sometimes just persistent relentless coughing. The PCE most often has a clot (Reineke et al. 2008; Nakamura et al. 2014) and the key to an accurate diagnosis is PCE in a mitral valve heart disease dog with a severely enlarged left atrium. Look for the severely enlarged left atrium (LA:Ao >2:1) not only via the right TFAST PCS short‐ axis echo views, but also advantageously (generally less patient stress) via the DH view (see Figures 17.27, 18.17C, and 18.32B). The LAT aspects which are important from the non- cardiologist perspective are as follows. • LAT is routinely missed by radiography. • Most patients are small dogs with chronic mitral valve disease. ◦ Dachshunds and Shetland sheepdogs are most common (DeFranceso, personal communication). • Pericardial effusion in a dog with the appropriate clinical profile and a severely enlarged left atrium. • A clot present within the PCE is a hallmark for LAT but variably present (Reineke et al. 2008; Nakamura et al. 2014). • LAT dogs often have only mild pulmonary edema (use Vet BLUE). ◦ The Vet BLUE B‐line scoring system guides loop diuretic usage. ◦ Vet BLUE prevents overtreating with loop diuretics. • Emergent pericardiocentesis is generally avoided, but in the unstable patient it may be needed and care should be taken not to tear open the pericar - dium (author experience, <5% of cases). • Treatment includes lowering left atrial pressure by including pimobendan and afterload reducers such as amlodipine (Suzuki et al. 2011). • Most LAT cases survive hospitalized care, but the long‐term prognosis is guarded because of their unpredictable clinical course. In a small case series, 10/11 were discharged with a median survival of 203 days, found to be better for those with first‐ event congestive heart failure. The left atrium can heal and these dogs survive several months or more (Nakamura et al. 2014). Cardiac Chamber Rupture and Pericardial Effusion: Traumatic and Nontraumatic Cardiac chamber rupture can be caused by trauma (blunt and penetrating) and nontrauma (usually a ruptured tumor). Trauma‐induced PCE has been reported and successfully treated surgically in both penetrating (projectiles and foreign bodies) and blunt trauma (Witt and Mayhew 2011; Elliott and Mayhew 2011), and neoplastic causes have had successful out- comes (Ployart et al. 2013; Treggiari et al. 2017). Keys for success include early detection, patient stabiliza- tion and management, and a willing surgeon. Catheterization of the pericardial sac and initial and repeated autotransfusion will likely be required for patient stabilization. Gallbladder Wall Edema: the “Cardiac Gallbladder” Gallbladder wall edema (GWE) has gained a lot of press regarding its use in the triage setting, espe- cially with anaphylactic dogs (see Chapters 6 and 7). However, GWE may also be a result of right‐ sided cardiac conditions and right‐sided congestive heart failure (Nelson et al. 2010; Lisciandro 2014a, 2019) (Figures 18.22 and 18.23). The terms “anaphylactic gallbladder” and “cardiac gall- bladder” have been created by the author for these patient subsets (Figure 18.22; see also Figure 7.12) and the author has a case series of dogs and cats with PCE, dilated cardiomyopathy, right‐sided congestive heart failure (congenital, pulmonary hypertension, tricuspid disease) and volume over - load from fluid therapy (Nelson et al. 2010; Lisciandro 2014a, 2019). Thus, in the acute setting Pearl: Some cardiac and systemic conditions result in a small rim of hemodynamically benign pericar - dial fluid (often <5 mm) that is clinically silent. TFAST provides a monitoring tool by measuring the widest dimension at the DH view in standing or sternal positioning (so gravity dependent) with “trivial” <5 mm, “mild” 5 mm–1 cm, “moderate” >1 cm–<2 cm, and “severe” >2 cm, similar to human medicine (Candotti and Arntfield 2014; Tchernodrinski and Arntfield 2015).

369 POCUS: TFAST – C LINICAL I NTEGRATION So why the increased prevalence of PCE? We have historically been using the wrong test as our first line‐ screening. Ultrasound is arguably the gold standard test for PCE and with widespread use of TFAST, these cases are now being captured. Pleural Effusion General TFAST Considerations Regarding Pleural Effusion Pleural effusion (PE) has major important differences from pericardial effusion. First, PE is generally uncon- tained and unrestrained within the pleural cavity and thus, it often appears triangulated ultrasonographi - cally, similar to free intraabdominal fluid. In contrast, PCE is contained and restrained within a much smaller Pearl: If PCE remains an uncertainty and the patient is hemodynamically stable, then arrange for complete echocardiography for confirmation (or perform serial TFAST examinations or both). 371 POCUS: TFAST – CLINICAL INTEGRATION For example, feline congestive heart failure and its associated modified transudate is most commonly anechoic and bilateral in contrast to feline pyothorax that can almost appear as echogenic as soft tissue and have very little fluid movement, being purulent, of high viscosity, and compartmentalized with adhe- sions. Furthermore, pressure atelectatic lung can mimic masses so care must be taken not to overinterpret PE‐ related soft tissue abnormalities but rather wait until after thoracocentesis and reevaluate along with more advanced imaging, such as detailed nonthoracic ultra- sound study, thoracic radiography, or CT. In general, blood and transudates tend to be anechoic while exu- dates, including chylous/pseudochylous/purulent effusions, tend to more echogenic. Third, TXR is complementary to ultrasonography for detecting PE (unlike PCE in which TXR is unreliable) (Guglielmini et al. 2012; Côté et al. 2013). Following a set of TFAST sonographic rules or tenets helps maxi- mize the probability of an accurate PE diagnosis. Accurate TFAST Diagnosis of Pleural Effusion The sonographer should have a set of rules to follow for the accurate TFAST diagnosis of PE (as with PCE). The only major fluid‐filled structure in the thorax to be mistaken for PE is your patient’s heart. And it is not generally a good thing for your patient to perform cen- tesis on their heart chamber. These are the TFAST tenets that will be subsequently explained in greater detail. • Always, always, always image the heart in its entirety with enough depth to see the bright pericardium, your habitual landmark, in the far‐field. By adhering to this tenet, the probability of mistaking the heart for PE (or PCE) is greatly lessened (see Figures 18.15 and 18.16). • One view is no view! Combine views. This is an axiom from human medicine. • Use the “TFAST slide” maneuver, sliding caudal from the heart toward the diaphragm and then cranial from the heart toward the cervical region, to evaluate the “cardiac‐diaphragmatic pouch” and “cardiac‐cervical pouch,” respectively (see Figures 17.2, 17.17, and 17.18). • Rotate from a position of perpendicular to the ribs to parallel to the ribs for a “one view is no view” approach during the “TFAST slide” – the “Boysen maneuver.” • Use the DH view where heart chambers are avoided as confounders and with the advantage of much less air (lung) interference over transthoracic views (Lisciandro 2014a, 2016). TFAST “Slide” for Pleural Effusion Left PCS View After identifying the location of the heart from the left PCS view, the “TFAST slide” is performed (see Figures 17.2, 17.17, and 17.18). The “TFAST slide” is com- posed of a caudal slide and then a cranial slide from the heart toward the diaphragm and from the heart toward the neck, respectively. The caudal “TFAST slide” interrogates the “cardiac‐diaphragmatic pouch,” the most gravity‐dependent region in the standing or sternal patient. With minimal training, the sonographer can easily recognize the liver and diaphragm to the right of the screen and then image between it and the heart for PE. The probe is next slid cranially across the heart past the cranial thoracic border of the heart to the “cardiac‐cervical pouch,” the most gravity‐dependent region in the standing or sternal patient cranial to the heart. Pleural effusion is characterized by the separation of the parietal and visceral pleural, in other words dis- ruption of the PPI or the “lung line” displaced away from the thoracic wall and often accompanied by the “curtain sign” (Neelis et al. 2015). If PE is questionable in either pouch, then the “Boysen Maneuver” can next be performed by rotating the probe parallel to the long axis of the ribs at either of the TFAST cardiac pouches, especially helpful for detecting small amounts of pleural effusion (Boysen, personal communication). Pitfalls at the Left PCS View Anechoic/Hypoechoic Stripes If small anechoic/hypoechoic stripes (1–5 mm) are seen in between the heart at its most ventral left short‐axis view (referred to as the hammerhead view) and the thoracic wall in the near‐field, the linear anechoic/ hypoechoic stripe is unlikely to be pleural effusion (Figure 18.25) but rather pericardial fat (Lamb 2000). Pleural effusion will be best identified away from this pitfall by performing the “TFAST slide” into the “cardiac‐diaphragmatic” and “cardiac‐cervical pouches” and finding anechoic‐hypoechoic triangula- tions away from the heart (Figures 18.26). Another way to rule out PE is if the stripe is lost because of dirty shad- owing from air in lung during the “TFAST slide” into these pouches, by moving slightly dorsal so that you are not imaging the lowest extreme of the pleural cavity (Neelis et al. 2015), or by adding the “Boysen maneuver.”

374 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Combining Views DH View The key to performing the DH view is to rock the probe toward the head of the patient in the longitudinal ori - entation (see Chapter 6). The pocketing of fluid will occur in the “cardiac‐diaphragmatic pouch” imaged through a different plane and direction from the TFAST PCS views. The “lung line” will separate from the dia- phragmatic surface and PE is triangulated with no rounding as seen with the “racetrack sign” of PCE (Figure 18.27; see also Figure 18.24). The DH view is very useful for the diagnosis of PE in that air interfer - ence is minimized through the acoustic window through the liver and gallbladder into your patient’s thorax. The appearance of PE is quite different from PCE because there will be triangulations with PE in contrast to the rounding and “racetrack sign” with PCE. The DH view will look different from normalcy because the hyperechoic line created by aerated lung immediately against the soft tissue diaphragm is lost with fluid (PE) against the diaphragm. Moreover, aerated and atelectatic lung will be wafting in the tri - angulations of PE, which is not a feature of PCE. The dog in Figure 18.27 has a serious, likely vascular intrathoracic injury that is missed on thoracic radiog - raphy. By documenting the injury, trauma sequelae may be better detected if complications occur over time like intrathoracic CVC obstruction and ascites, and the complication, kinked CVC syndrome, is treat - able with surgery (Cornelius and Mahaffey 1985; Lisciandro et al. 1995; Fine et al. 1998). Recently, it was shown that PCE detected in any degree with or without PE using ultra- sound was 100% specific for congestive heart failure in cats presenting to veterinary hospitals at North Carolina State and Iowa State (Ward et al. 2018) (see Figure 18.28). Using TFAST echo views and CVC and hepatic venous characterization (and, better, Global FAST), other important feline patient information may be obtained, and generally in the same amount of time as a targeted POCUS exam or thoracic “flash” that only addresses the binary question of the presence or absence of PE. Other findings during TFAST may include the suspicion for intrathoracic masses (see Chapters 19–21). Use of Radiography for the Diagnosis of Pleural Effusion If the TFAST sonographer cannot confidently diagnose PE, the use of TXR should be incorporated into the work‐up, or nonthoracic ultrasound or complete echo- cardiography by someone more skilled, or combina- tions thereof. However, TXR has limitations in that it is unreliable for PCE, especially with the presence of PE that obscures the cardiac silhouette, and is unreliable and generally ineffective for pulmonary evaluation (see Figure 18.28). Conversely, PE actually enhances imaging of the heart and its chambers and the presence of PCE; it also enhances imaging of the “lung line” for the six Vet BLUE lung ultrasound signs, and the presence or absence of PCE, which is especially helpful in the diagnosis of congestive heart failure in cats (see Chapters 19–21). Overall Pitfalls of Imaging the Heart • Using the left ventricular short‐axis views between the “mushroom” view and the heart base and its “Mercedes‐Benz” sign can be very confusing and lead to mistaking the crescent‐shaped right ven- tricle for PCE. • The difficulty in getting a good acoustic window to visualize the heart transthoracically in cases of severe respiratory distress. • Mirror artifact off the far side of the heart when “dry lung” is immediately against the pericardium in the far‐field. Definitive Characterization of Pleural and Pericardial Effusions Requires Sampling Ultrasound’s strength is imaging fluid and fluid‐filled structures, but it cannot reliably characterize or diag- nose the etiology of the fluid. Fluid acquisition via tho- racocentesis or pericardiocentesis with fluid analysis and cytology is necessary because there are many differ- ent types of effusion (transudate, modified transudate, exudates [pyothorax, chylous, and pseudochylous], and neoplastic). Before pursuing sample acquisition, the risks and benefits must be weighed by the attending veterinarian (Table 18.6). Ultrasound‐guided or assisted thoracocentesis and pericardiocentesis are described in Chapters 43 and 21. Measuring and Monitoring Pleural Effusion Attempts have been made in cadaver models to mea- sure PE from the sternum through cardiac cut‐out ta- bles to the lateral thorax. However, atelectatic lung in cadaver dog and cat models lacks the respirophasic dynamics and the floating of aerated lung in live breathing patients (Newitt et al. 2009; Shimali et al. 2010). The author suggests measuring patients in sternal or standing at the 4th–5th intercostal space at the level of the costochondral junction with the maximum respirophasic distance from the thoracic wall to the heart. A method will need to be developed from live patients using consistent methodology and comparison to actual volumes aspirated in live dogs and cats with PE. Pearl: Use the DH view to determine the presence and absence of PCE as likely it is a sole view for both dogs and cats (Lisciandro 2016). Pearl: Use the DH view as a nonecho alternative for cardiac tamponade because in a patient with a CVC that has a “bounce”, cardiac tamponade is ruled out by definition. If a FAT distended CVC is pre- sent, then look at your patient. In people, a FAT IVC, analogous to the CVC, is 92–97% sensitive but not specific (40%) (Himelman et al. 1998; Candotti and Arntfield 2014; Tchernodrinski and Arntfield 2015). Thus, when a collapsible “bounce” to the IVC is found in people with PCE, cardiac tampon- ade is unlikely. The IVC (and CVC) provides a non- echo view option that is often easier to acquire (and generally safer and faster) than echo views in dis- tressed, unstable, and hemodynamically fragile patients.

377 POCUS: TFAST – CLINICAL INTEGRATION Other Pleural Cavity Findings During TFAST Diaphragmatic Herniation Through repetition in performing the DH view, the loss of the expected curvilinear continuity of the diaphragm will often be appreciated in the presence of both traumatic and congenital types of diaphragmatic herniation (Figures 18.29 and 18.30). Additionally, the lack of finding the gallbladder at its expected location can be helpful in triggering suspicion that the diaphragm is herniated (or ruptured). The axiom of “one view is no view” is also helpful because visuali- zation of the heart may be obscured by solid organs or viscous structures (air‐filled/fluid‐filled) including liver, gallbladder, spleen, loops of small intestine and stomach, which become readily apparent with minimal training to the nonradiologist sonographer experi- enced with AFAST and its target organ approach. Furthermore, this observation will help guide therapy and avoid blindly performing thoracocentesis into abdominal structures before a confirmatory thoracic radiograph with or without contrast is acquired (see Figures 18.29 and 18.30). Masses Diagnosis of masses within the thorax during TFAST can be problematic and may require advanced training. Lung may develop pressure atelectasis in PE cases, and atelectatic lung may appear as a tissue sign mim- icking a mass lesion. Moreover, the lung may in fact have forms of pathological consolidation and nodules. The best strategy is to reimage after thoracocentesis, allowing time for spontaneous breathing and/or positive pressure ventilation to reexpand normal atel- ectatic lung to better differentiate if the suspect lesions persist or resolve. Additional Clinical Relevance of the DH View The DH view also serves as a soft tissue evaluation of the gallbladder and liver, screens for ascites, character- izes the CVC and its associated hepatic veins, and determines lung surface pathology along the pulmonary‐diaphragmatic interface (see Chapters 7, 22, 23, and 36 for more detail). TFAST Echo Views TFAST Cardiac Evaluation The TFAST screening for soft tissue cardiac abnormal- ities (and Vet BLUE for lung surface conditions) is analogous to the AFAST target organ approach, meaning that TFAST cardiac evaluation is a rule‐in test (Figure 18.31). In other words, if the condition is seen, then it likely exists and gold standard confirmation would be indicated next with a higher probability of having a positive test. However, if the condition is not seen, then it is possible that it was missed since detec - tion is user dependent and the patient may require more expert or sophisticated interrogation or the gold standard test for diagnosis. These conditions include dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM), hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), pulmonary hypertension (PHT), left‐sided cardiac conditions/volume overload/failure, right‐sided cardiac conditions/volume overload/failure, intracar- diac masses, heartworms, and LAT in chronic mitral valve disease. The TFAST echo views are eyeballed, meaning they are subjectively assessed in most instances (Ferrada et al. 2012a, 2014; Atkinson et al. 2017). There is evi - dence on the human side that eyeballing works well in screening for obvious disease and a recent interna - tional point‐of‐care echocardiography consensus state- ment advocated for the eyeball method (Ferrada et al. 2012a, 2014; Atkinson et al. 2017). The sonographer looks to see if basic echo views appear to be unremarkable or not, a simple binary question as a screening test. Will more subtle conditions be missed? Possibly, but consider how much you are missing every day on traditional training of physical examination and radiography. You have nothing to lose so look and see if the heart has PCE, chamber abnor - malities, soft tissue problems, intracardiac (within its chambers), extracardiac, and intramural masses, or parasitic organisms (heartworms), as well as valvular conditions such as asynchrony from ruptured chordae tendinae or vegetations. Moreover, the TFAST echo views may be evaluated in standing in dogs and cats (Chetboul et al. 2005; Loughran et al. 2019). The three major TFAST echo views plus a fourth bonus view are as follows (see Figure 18.31). • The left ventricular short‐axis view (LVSA) at the level of the chordae tendinae, same as for M‐mode measurements, to assess volume and contractility. • The left atrial to aortic ratio on short‐axis view (LA:Ao) for left‐sided cardiac conditions, the so‐ called “quick peek” view for left‐sided cardiac con- ditions (heart strain/failure/overload). 383 POCUS: TFAST – CLINICAL INTEGRATION Chapters 36 and 37 (see Figure 36.7). The Global FAST non‐echo fallback views work in the opposite direction too. For example, “dry lung” or absent B‐lines in all Vet BLUE views rule out left‐sided CHF (Lisciandro 2016: Ward et al. 2017; Vezzosi et al. 2017) and a “bounce” or fluid‐responsive CVC rules out right‐ sided CHF (Himelman et al. 1988; Candotti and Arntfield 2014; Tchernodrinski and Arntfield 2015). Thus, if there is no evidence for congestive heart failure on Global FAST nonecho fallback views, then echo views can wait in critical patients until they are more stable. The Global FAST Approach is Key to Averting Satisfaction of Search Error The use of Global FAST automatically helps avoid sat- isfaction of search error by applying AFAST, TFAST, and Vet BLUE as a single examination. In respiratory compromised or distressed patients or those that may be hemodynamically fragile, Global FAST may be per- formed entirely in standing and then, only if indicated, performed in part in lateral recumbency when the patient is more stable if needed. Recording TFAST Findings on Goal‐directed Templates To achieve success with TFAST you must record your patient data, save images for review and learning and teaching purposes, and review final outcomes, espe- cially comparing to subsequent imaging. Entries should be marked “indeterminate” and “not assessed” as they are important for learning and training pur - poses (Figure 18.34). “Indeterminate” means that the DH view was imaged but the findings were inconclu- sive. “Not assessed” means that the DH view was never evaluated for whatever reason (patient too stressed, fractious, or because of triaging other cases). For example, if the DH view was marked as an “inde- terminate” entry and then subsequently you found out there was a pneumothorax, a pneumoabdomen, a diaphragmatic hernia, or an emphysematous gall- bladder, then lessons are learned regarding the limi- tations of TFAST in addition to modifying teaching paradigms. On the other hand, if you don’t record your data, then you can’t measure performance. If you can’t measure performance, then you can’t evaluate and improve. See Chapter 45 and the Appendices for additional examples of goal‐directed templates. Quick Reference of Normals and Rules of Thumb • Any evidence of lung, most commonly “lung sliding” or the presence of B‐lines, that is observed at the TFAST CTS view rules out clinically relevant PTX, especially in the positioning of standing or sternal. • B‐lines in trauma are lung contusions until proven otherwise. • Always image the heart in its entirety using the hyperechoic (bright white) pericardium as a land- mark in the far‐field. • Adhere to the axiom that “one view is no view” for the accurate diagnosis of PE and PCE. • The FAST DH view is likely nearly 100% sensitive and 100% specific for detecting clinically relevant PCE in dogs and cats. • Dogs and cats have no pleural or pericardial effu- sion that is evident in normalcy; however, pericar - dial fat mimics pleural effusion especially (1) along the heart at the left TFAST PCS view as an anechoic stripe (linear) between the heart and intercostal spaces, and (2) as an echogenic triangulation (fat pad) within the cardiac‐diaphragmatic pouch. • The “eyeball method” is accepted in people as a screening test for obvious cardiac abnormalities. • A left atrial to aortic ratio (LA:Ao) that is >2:1 would be obviously abnormal in both dogs and cats. • A right ventricular to left ventricular ratio (RV:LV) on the four‐chamber long‐axis view of >1:2 or ~1:1 would be obviously abnormal in both dogs and cats. • An abnormal fractional shortening (FS%) for dogs and cats would be <20%. • Sonographic striation of the gallbladder wall in dogs and cats can be due to right‐sided congestive heart failure (most commonly pericardial effusion), referred to as a “cardiac gallbladder” (Lisciandro 2019). • TFAST right‐sided cardiac markers that screen for obvious right‐sided cardiac problems include the RV:LV , characterization of the CVC and hepatic veins, and gallbladder wall edema, that is, sono- graphic striation and the “cardiac gallbladder” (Lisciandro 2016, 2019).

384 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Pearls and Pitfalls, The Final Say • TFAST should be used as a first‐line imaging test, as a quick assessment test as an extension of the physical exam, to “see” your problem list, and to rule in and out important potentially life‐threatening conditions. • TFAST has clear advantages over thoracic radiog- raphy for pericardial effusion, pleural effusion, cardiac conditions including abnormal chamber ratios, soft tissue abnormalities, and includes one of the AFAST views, the DH view, that provides information regarding ascites, soft tissue abnor - malities of the liver and gallbladder, and volume status via the CVC. • TFAST can not only diagnose but also monitor pneumothorax using the “lung point” concept. • TFAST is not a “flash exam” of the thorax. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 389 Introduction Focused cardiac ultrasound (FCU) or focused echocar- diography are terms used to describe a limited ultra- sound examination of the cardiovascular system, typically performed by a noncardiology specialist and as an adjunct to the physical examination, to recognize specific sonographic signs that represent a narrow list of potential diagnoses in specific clinical settings (Spencer et al. 2013). Most commonly, FCU is per - formed in symptomatic or at‐risk small animal patients in the acute or primary care setting. Unlike complete echocardiography, FCU is usually a time‐ sensitive exam investigating the cause of a patient’s clinical signs in order to make immediate treatment decisions by rapidly diagnosing potentially life‐threat- ening conditions and improving the management of a critically ill patient (Beaulieu 2007; Labovitz et al. 2010; Arntfield and Millington 2012). Frequently, FCU is part of a more comprehensive and integrated thoracic ultrasound including interrogation of the pleural space, anterior mediastinum, and lungs (see also Chapters 17, 18, 22, and 23). Recently, FCU has shown clinical utility in veteri- nary medicine as an aid in the diagnosis of heart failure (Ward et al. 2018) and other nontraumatic conditions causing cardiovascular instability and respiratory dis- tress (McMurray et al. 2016). Recent studies also support the assessment of the caudal vena cava as an aid in diagnosis of fluid responsiveness and volume status and as a noninvasive estimate of right atrial pressure (Nelson et al. 2010; Cambournac et al. 2018; Kwak et al. 2018; Marshall et al. 2018). See also Chapters 6, 7, 17, 18, 26, 36, and 37. With limited didactic and hands‐on training, noncardiologist or nonradiologist veterinarians can achieve an acceptable proficiency in identifying pleural and pericardial effusions, and detecting the presence of right and left atrial enlargement (Tse et al. 2012). Achievable goals discussed in the next three chapters include not only the detection of pleural and pericar - dial effusion, left and right atrial enlargement but also the assessment of significant abnormalities in contrac- tility, valvular anatomy, volume status, identification of obvious masses and right sided‐heart disease. Similar to other focused ultrasound exams, the FCU provides a rapid, point‐of‐care, safe (radiation sparing), noninvasive, and portable assessment of patients. FCU is indicated in dogs and cats presenting with respiratory signs or distress, significant arrhythmias and persistent or episodic hemodynamic collapse, especially to rap- idly rule out pericardial effusion with cardiac tampon- ade and pleural effusion, and to help diagnosis heart failure or other causes of hemodynamic compromise. The author finds FCU particularly useful for cats in respiratory distress to differentiate heart failure from other causes of respiratory distress (see also Chapters 17, 18, 22, 23, 36, and 37) because physical examination and radiographic findings are notoriously nonspecific in felines. In fact, up to 30% of cats in heart failure have no murmur or gallop sound on initial cardiac ausculta- tion (Rush et al. 2002). Furthermore, distribution of radiographic lesions is variable in cats with cardio- genic pulmonary edema caused by left‐sided heart POCUS: Heart – Introduction and Image Acquisition Teresa DeFrancesco CHAPTER NINETEEN

390 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER failure (versus the predictable perihilar distribution in dogs), and pleural effusion, a common manifestation of feline heart failure, obscures the cardiac silhouette, making radiographic assessment of heart size difficult. On the other hand, ultrasound is superior in detecting pleural and pericardial effusion (arguably the gold standard) (Reissig et al. 2011), and cardiac imaging is enhanced when effusions are present rather than diminished compared to thoracic radiography. Thus, a cat with pleural effusion may be clearly imaged with ultrasound with minimal stress, allowing more accu- rate assessment of heart chamber dimensions and spe- cifically left atrial size (Schober et al. 2014). In conclusion, the added diagnostic value of FCU was highlighted by a study in which the diagnostic accuracy of minimally trained first‐year medical stu- dents performing bedside echocardiography was superior to that of board‐certified cardiologists performing cardiac physical examinations for the detection and evaluation of selected valvular and non- valvular cardiac abnormalities (Kobal et al. 2005). The improved diagnostic accuracy of FCU in certain condi- tions over the cardiac physical examination alone is the reason why point‐of‐care thoracic ultrasound has been termed the “visual stethoscope of the 21st century” (Moore and Copel 2011). What Focused Cardiac Ultrasound Can Do • Identify severely enlarged cardiac chambers, even in the presence of pleural effusion, thus providing useful and timely corroborative evidence for either left‐ or right‐sided heart failure. • Assess left ventricular contractility by either the “eyeball method” or by measurement of its fractional shortening, thus helping with detection of left ventricular systolic failure and diagnosis of dilated cardiomyopathy in dogs. • Detect obvious thickened mitral or tricuspid valves and possibly ruptured chordae tendineae. • Assess severe left ventricular concentric hyper - trophy (thickening), thus helping with the diag- nosis of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in cats. • Detect severe left atrial enlargement and screen for left atrial thrombus or echogenic “smoke” in cats with aortic thromboembolism (ATE). • Detect heartworms in the right heart in cats with respiratory distress or in dogs with caval syndrome. • Detect pleural effusion and characterize its distribution. • Estimate the amount of pleural fluid, its location(s), identify a suitable site for thoracocentesis, and track (monitor) for recurrence of effusion. • Detect pericardial effusion, determine the presence of cardiac tamponade and possibly the etiology of the effusion. • Estimate the amount of pericardial fluid, identify a suitable site for pericardiocentesis, and track (mon- itor) for recurrence of effusion. • Assess the size and degree of respiratory variation of the caudal vena cava to determine if a patient is fluid tolerant or intolerant. What Focused Cardiac Ultrasound Cannot Do • Cannot be used as a stand‐alone diagnostic test for the definitive diagnosis of heart failure (echocardi- ography by itself can only diagnose heart disease, not failure). • Cannot replace complete echocardiography by a veterinary cardiologist or radiologist, and sonogra- phers should know their limitations. • Cannot provide proficient use of color flow, pulsed, continuous wave or tissue Doppler echocardiog- raphy (not covered). Indications • Respiratory distress, respiratory compromise, or uncharacterized tachypnea or dyspnea. • Congestive heart failure (left‐ and right‐sided) suspects. • Pericardial effusion with or without cardiac tam- ponade suspects. • Uncharacterized persistent or intermittent hemo- dynamic instability or collapse. • Uncharacterized syncope, collapse or generalized weakness. • Uncharacterized tachycardia (rapid heart rate) or significant cardiac arrhythmia. • Feline aortic thromboembolism. • Cardiovascular assessment of volume status and heart contractility. • Tracking (monitoring) using serial exams for recur- rence of pericardial or pleural effusions post cente- sis or during course of therapy. Objectives • Be able to perform basic echocardiographic views of the short and long axis at the right and left para- sternal and subxiphoid sites. • Be able to recognize normal heart anatomy including the atria, ventricles, and associated valves and walls. • Identify a severely enlarged left atrium (LA) in small animals with suspected left‐sided heart failure.

391 POCUS: HEART – INTRODUCTION AND IMAgE ACQUISITION • Identify severe right heart enlargement, caudal vena cava, and hepatic venous distension sugges- tive of right heart failure or possibly secondary to chronic pulmonary hypertension/cor pulmonale in a dog with respiratory distress. • Be able to qualitatively assess left ventricular (LV) systolic function as normal, hypo‐ or hyperdy- namic. Additionally, be able to measure left ven- tricular fractional shortening (FS%), a commonly used quantitative parameter of LV function. • Be able to measure the LV wall thickness in dias- tole, LV lumen in systole and diastole, and left atrial (LA) and aortic (Ao) dimensions, and know cut‐off values for normal and abnormal. • Identify pericardial effusion and cardiac tampon- ade. Additionally, identify the cause of the pericar- dial effusion. • Identify pleural effusion. • Identify masses within the heart, in heart walls or heart base, and pleural space, prompting confirma- tion by complete echocardiography or other advanced imaging technique or procedures. • Be able to assess extreme abnormalities in volume status as fluid tolerant or fluid intolerant. Additionally, be able to serially assess cardiac mea- surements in response to intravenous fluid resusci- tation and therapy. Ultrasound Settings and Probe Preferences The use of the cardiac setting (presets) on your ultra- sound unit generally provides more contrast in echo- genicity, making identification of cardiac chambers and assessing their motion (valves and walls) easier (than abdominal presets). Images in this chapter (cardiac preset) may be compared to cardiac images in Chapters 17 and 18 (abdominal preset). Most built‐in cardiac presets will also flip the left to right orientation of the image, which is different from other built‐in pre- sets. Cardiologists prefer viewing so that the cranial aspects of the heart and the marker indicator are on the right side of the screen, which is in the opposite orien- tation from all other ultrasound imaging. If you do not use a cardiac preset to image the heart, then the image on the screen will be a mirror image of what is typi- cally seen in cardiology and echocardiographic text- books (see Figures 19.3 and 19.6). Image quality of the heart is best with ultrasound machines (or settings) with high frame or sampling rates. Inadequate (too slow) frame or sampling rates are recognized by a real‐ time image that is choppy. • Use of curvilinear (microconvex) or phased‐array sector probes (3–10 MHz) is ideal for imaging the heart between ribs (creating an acoustic window). Use the highest megahertz (MHz) possible to obtain the highest resolution images. If given a choice, the phased‐array probe is preferred for cardiac imaging because of better temporal resolution and typically a small footprint, resulting in less rib (shadowing) interference. The curvilinear (microconvex) probe is a multipurpose probe that can be used for cardiac imaging and enhanced by using a cardiac preset. Linear probes generally do not image the heart well because of their long footprint and rib interference (ultrasound does not transmit through bone). • Adjust the depth setting so that the entire heart is visualized and the heart makes up the majority of the image of the screen. In large or giant breeds, this may require a depth of up to 30 cm, which is often not available in some of the compact ultrasound machines. The focus setting is placed in the area of interest or near distal edge of the cardiac image. • Adjusting the depth and optimizing the size of the heart on the image are important to avoid artifacts and misinterpretations. If the depth setting is too high relative to the heart size (small heart at top of image with a large void in the far field), a mirror (double image) artifact may result (and be con- fusing to the sonographer). How to Perform a Focused Cardiac Ultrasound Patient Positioning and Preparation • Depending on patient stability and comfort, the FCU can be performed with the patient in either lateral or sternal recumbency (or standing). If the Pitfall: If you are unable to image the entire heart, cardiac chambers, especially if enlarged, may be easily misinterpreted for pleural and pericardial effu- sions, leading to the potentially catastrophic mistake of performing centesis on a heart chamber (see also Chapters 17, 18, 43, and 44) and cardiac chamber dimensions may not be accurately measured. Pearl: Adhere to the axiom “One view is no view” to avoid misinterpreting normal heart anatomy for pleural or pericardial effusions, especially when the necessary depth for imaging the heart in its entirety is not possible on your ultrasound machine.

392 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER patient is in respiratory distress, the exam is per - formed in sternal recumbency (or standing) while the patient receives flow‐by oxygen. • In a dog or cat with respiratory distress, the exam performed in sternal or standing recumbency will be more challenging because of lung interference and chest wall motion. Commonly, one may see “quick peeks” of the heart in between respiration cycles. • The heart is best visualized when closest to the thoracic wall because of less lung (air) interfer - ence (ultrasound does not transmit through air). Thus, lateral recumbency with the probe posi - tioned on the thorax of the patient’s recumbent side is ideal (Figure 19.1; see also Figures 19.3, 19.6, and 19.7). • The heart also can be visualized from the nonre - cumbent side of the thorax, especially if the animal has a narrow thoracic confirmation (see Figure 19.7). • Focused cardiac ultrasound can be performed on a special table designed for echocardiography (“echo table”) that elevates the patient off the tabletop and has a cut‐out hole where the heart is, facilitating probe maneuverability and enabling a more com - fortable and complete focused evaluation (see Figure 19.1). • Typically, generous amounts of alcohol and acoustic coupling gel are applied while parting the hair to allow the coupling agents to reach the skin. • Shaving is usually unnecessary but may be warranted if the patient has extremely thick hair. Shaving minimizes the amount of alcohol and acoustic coupling gel needed to obtain acceptable ultrasound images and because of the cooling effects of alcohol, may be best for hypothermic patients. • The use of alcohol is contraindicated when electrical defibrillation is anticipated (ventricular fibrillation, cardiopulmonary arrest) because the alcohol pres - ents a serious fire hazard. Right Parasternal Short‐axis Views • Place the probe at the right 4th–5th intercostal space near the costochondral junction or at the site where there is a palpable heart beat (place your hand on the patient’s thorax) preempting probe placement. • To obtain the LV short‐axis views, position the probe so that the marker on the probe is pointing towards the elbow (marker toward the elbow) (see Figure 19.3). 396 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER • An important first view to obtain will be the LV short‐axis view just below the mitral valve, also called the LV “mushroom” view, as it is most help- ful for the assessment of contractility and left ven - tricular chamber dimensions (see Figure 19.3A). • Rotate and fan the probe until the LV short‐axis “mushroom” view of the LV is as round and sym - metrical as possible. • The LV in the “mushroom” view should normally have a circular appearance and the RV should be crescent shaped (see Figure 19.3A). Flattening of the interventricular septum (IVS) suggests right ventricular volume or pressure overload (see Figure 20.9A). • Now fan upward above the mitral valve to visu - alize the heart base in short‐axis view. In other words, from the LV “mushroom” view, angulate or fan the probe upward towards the cervical spine until the aorta and aortic valves are in view in cross‐section. • Rotate and angulate the probe so that the cross‐sec- tion of the aorta is round and all three cusps of the aortic valves are visible (see Figure 19.3B), recog - nized as the “Mercedes‐Benz” sign (or the “peace sign” or “Y”). At the heart base, the probe can be angulated to optimize for either the left atrial appendage (looks like a “whale tail”) or the pulmonary artery (PA) (see Figure 19.4). The diam- eter of the PA should normally be the same as the diameter of the aorta in this view. • When comparing the diameters of the left atrium (LA) and aorta (Ao), the image should be opti - mized for the left atrial appendage. Normally, the diameters of LA and Ao in this view, whether in 2D B‐mode or M‐mode, are similar in size (LA:Ao is 1:1) (see Figures 19.3B, 19.4, and 19.5). If the left atrium is greater than 1.3 times the aorta in dogs, then the left atrium is enlarged (see Figure 20.2); and greater than 1.6 in cats (LA:Ao >1.3:1 dogs, >1.6:1 cats) (Rishniw and Erb 2000; Abbott and Maclean 2006). In summary, the right parasternal short‐axis views at the heart base are helpful in assessing left atrial, pulmonary artery size, and the presence of a heart base mass (e.g., chemodectoma) (see abnormal examples in Chapter 20). Right Parasternal Long‐axis Views • To obtain the LV long‐axis views, start with the short‐axis (marker to the elbow) view and simply rotate the probe about 90° in a clockwise direction so that the marker on the probe is pointing towards the neck and head (see Figure 19.6). Note that the rotation of the probe is similar to the methodology of the TFAST echo views, but the screen orientation is opposite (see Figures 17.25 and 17.26). • The marker on the probe is pointed towards the neck and head to obtain the sagittal or long‐axis views with the probe angulated slightly caudally (see Figure 19.6). • The right (and left) parasternal long‐axis views are most helpful to estimate the size and relative pro - portions of the right and left heart. Pearl: Within this acoustic window, angulate or fan the probe just below and then through and above the mitral valve to get the various views. Pearl: In the short‐axis view, a left atrial diameter that is twice the aortic diameter is very suggestive of left‐sided heart failure in an animal with consistent clinical signs (see abnormal examples in Chapter 20). Pitfalls: Be cautious not to overinterpret normal fat at the heart base as a mass lesion. Adipose or fat tissue is quite hyperechoic with irregular borders. A heart base mass usually has a smooth border and is less echogenic (see Chapter 20).

398 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER The Atria In normalcy, the left and right atria are approximately the same size (1:1) with a neutral (nondeviated) inter - atrial septum. The Valves In normalcy, all cardiac valves should be thin with no evidence of prolapsing or areas of focal thickening. The semilunar valves (mitral and tricuspid) are gener- ally easy and less challenging to evaluate (than the aortic and pulmonary valves) by the inexperienced sonographer. Overall Long‐axis Assessment A semiquantitative assessment of LV contractility, mitral valvular anatomy, pericardial and pleural effusion can also be obtained in this view and is achievable for the noncardiologist or nonradiologist sonographer. • With slight angulation towards the animal’s head and slight counterclockwise rotation of the probe, one can also image the ascending aorta, aortic valves, left atrium, and left ventricular outflow tract (see Figure 19.6B). • The LA and Ao in this view should be the same size (LA:Ao should be 1:1). Normal Canine Cardiac Chamber Dimensions These vary based on body weight and breed (Table 19.1). In contrast to dogs, normal feline cardiac chamber dimensions do not vary based on body weight (Table 19.2). • To obtain cardiac chamber dimensions, freeze a loop (cine function) and scroll between systole (when the LV lumen is the smallest) and diastole (when the lumen is the biggest) to obtain a fractional shortening (FS%) using 2D B‐mode and to measure LV wall thicknesses. • Alternatively, M‐mode echocardiography can be used. The M‐mode view is an “ice pick” view with the cursor placed in the center of the LV short‐axis “mushroom” view or at the level of the mitral valve. Use of M‐mode enhances assessment of both LV contractility and its wall thickness (see Figure 19.5A). • For LV wall thickness, both the IVS and LV free wall (LVFW) are measured in diastole with either 2D B‐ mode or M‐mode echocardiography. • Normally, the RV free wall thickness (RVFW) is about half the thickness of the LVFW. • Normal values are stratified by body weight in dogs (see Table 19.1). In contrast to dogs, size is independent of weight in cats and thus feline IVS and LVFW thickness in diastole should be approx- imately 3–4 mm. 399 POCUS: H EART – I NTRODUCTION AND I MA g E A CQUISITION Fractional Shortening Values (FS%) Keep in mind that normal FS% can vary by breed and loading (~ volume status) conditions. In general, normal FS% is 28–45% in the dog and 30–50% in the cat. A FS% below 20% is suggestive of severe myocar - dial systolic failure and a FS% above 55% would be considered hyperdynamic LV function (see Tables 19.1 and 19.2). FS% LV internal dimensiond iastoleL VIDs ystole LVID diasstole 100 Left Parasternal Apical and Cranial Views The left cranial or basilar views allow additional and excellent views of the aorta, pulmonary artery, left atrium, right atrium and ventricle. These views are obtained with the probe positioned at the 3rd–4th intercostal spaces on the left side with analogous posi- tioning to the right parasternal view (see Figure 19.7). Image quality is best when moving the patient to left lateral recumbency so the heart falls against the thoracic wall (moving lung [air] out of the way since ultrasound does not transmit through air). However, depending on the dog’s thoracic conformation, left‐ sided views could be obtained with the dog remaining in right lateral recumbency immediately after obtain - ing right parasternal views or imaging in sternal recumbency. Not having to reposition the animal saves time. The main reasons to image from the left side are to further assess the right heart, further assess valvular anatomy and motion, discriminate pleural from peri - cardial effusions when present, and search for possible masses when indicated. Left Parasternal Apical View The left four‐ and five‐chamber apical views are obtained with the probe marker pointing towards the spine and the probe angulated up towards the neck about the fifth intercostal space near the costochondral junction (see Figure 19.7). • The left four‐chamber apical view allows simulta - neous visualization of both right and left ventricles and their atria. • The RV tricuspid and LV mitral valves should be thin with no evidence of prolapsing (see Figure 19.7A). • The left five‐chamber apical view is obtained with a slight angulation toward the head and a slight rotation of the marker towards the head until the aorta comes into view (see Figure 19.8). Left Parasternal Cranial View From the left apical view, the probe is moved one or two intercostal spaces cranially with the probe marker towards the spine angulated slightly to opti - mize the visualization of the right atrium and ventricle (see Figure 19.7B). • The left cranial view allows for optimal visualiza - tion of the right heart, including the right auricle and tricuspid valve. • This is the best view to visualize a small right auric- ular mass in a dog with pericardial effusion and cardiac tamponade (see examples in Chapter 21). Subxiphoid or Subcostal View • The transducer (probe) is positioned just caudal to the xiphoid, typically with the patient in right lat - eral recumbency, similar to the TFAST and AFAST diaphragmatico‐hepatic (DH) view (see Figure 19.9). • The marker is pointed towards the elbow and the probe angulated towards the head almost parallel with the body wall. Adjust the depth and rotate the probe until a four‐ or five‐chamber view is seen (see Figure 19.9A). Note: The view may not be pos- sible in some very large dogs depending on the depth limits of your ultrasound machine. • From the subcostal cardiac views, angulate the probe and decrease the depth to visualize the liver, caudal vena cava, and hepatic veins (see Figure 19.9B). The liver is assessed primarily for passive congestion (signs of right‐sided failure) as evidenced by caudal vena caval and hepatic venous Pearl: Cardiac chamber dimensions and LV systolic function can be influenced by the breed of dog, the patient’s volume and hydration status, the presence of a tachy‐ or bradyarrhythmia, and systemic inflammation. Pitfall: Interpretation of LV systolic function and cardiac size thus should be interpreted in the con - text of the patient’s complete clinical picture, with attention given to these confounding factors (breed, volume and hydration status, arrhythmias, and systemic inflammation).

400 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER distension with ascites between the liver lobes (see also Chapters 6–8, 17, and 18) (Nelson et al. 2010). • Hepatic venous distension is judged subjectively. The ability to see large anechoic vessels, larger branches and then smaller branches, extending peripherally into hepatic tissue is compatible with enlarged hepatic veins. The concurrent findings of ascites and an enlarged and hypoechoic liver add confidence to the diagnosis of right‐sided heart failure (see abnormal examples in Chapter 20 and also see also Chapters 6–8, 17, and 18). • Hepatic veins can be differentiated from portal veins in the liver because they have much less echogenic vessel walls and portal veins have hyperechoic (much brighter) walls (see also Chapters 6–8, 17, and 18). When measured at the same depth, portal veins and hepatic veins should be about the same size. • Now obtain an image of the caudal vena cava near the diaphragm from this subxiphoid view. The probe is angulated almost perpendicularly towards the spine with slight upward tilting of the tail of the probe as the caudal vena cava is slightly to the right of midline just below the spine (see Figure 19.9B). • Alternatively, the caudal vena cava can be imaged from the left sublumbar region with the patient in right lateral recumbency. The caudal vena cava is ventral (more right‐sided) than the pulsating aorta (see Chapter 26). • The caudal vena cava can be assessed for respiratory fluctuation in size as an indicator of volume status. Optimize the image by fanning through the caudal vena cava to obtain a sagittal view with the largest diameter. M‐mode can be useful to visualize respiratory fluctuations of the caudal vena cava (Figure 19.10). Be careful with translational motion of the probe with respirations. • Respiratory fluctuations are greater in animals that may be fluid responsive (generally >50–60% fluc - tuation). No respiratory fluctuations, only static distension, of the caudal vena cava are seen in ani- mals that have high right atrial pressure (Feissel et al. 2004; Beigel et al. 2013). Pearls and Pitfalls, The Final Say • Focused cardiac ultrasound can expedite diagnosis and treatments, especially in patients that are hemodynamically unstable or in respiratory distress. • The specific cardiac views and images differ depending on clinical need. The right parasternal and subxiphoid views are easier than the left‐sided views to acquire proficiency. • While canine normal values for cardiac chambers are listed based on body weight, these values can vary based on dog breed, body conformation, volume status, arrhythmias, and systemic diseases. • With training, one should be able to identify severe left atrial enlargement, decreased systolic function, right ventricular enlargement, pericardial effusion, and a dilated plethoric caudal vena cava. Quick Reference of Normals and Rules of Thumb • In normalcy, the LV should be 3–4 times larger than the RV in the right parasternal four‐chamber view (3:1). • If the RV is the same size as the LV , then severe right ventricular enlargement can be diagnosed (and its various rule‐outs considered). • In normalcy, the left and right atria are approxi - mately the same size or 1:1 with a neutral (nonde - viated) interatrial septum. • In normalcy, the LA and Ao in the short‐axis right parasternal view should be nearly the same size. • If the LA is greater than 1.3 times the aorta in dogs, then the LA is enlarged; greater than 1.6 times in cats (LA:Ao >1.3:1 dogs, >1.6:1 cats). Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 403 Introduction Focused cardiac ultrasound (FCU) can provide vital and noninvasive detailed information about cardiac structure and function, beyond the capabilities of the physical examination and thoracic radiographs. This valuable information can aid in the rapid diagnosis and improved management of suspected heart failure, pericardial and pleural effusion or other hemodynam- ically unstable patients. Even with limited experience, significant cardiac abnormalities such as marked chamber enlargements, pericardial effusion, and myo- cardial failure can be determined. The integration of other point‐of‐care information of the lung, pleural and peritoneal space will provide valuable corrobora- tive evidence of left‐sided or right‐sided congestive heart failure and justify loop diuretic usage (see Chapters 22, 23, and 36). What Focused Cardiac Ultrasound Abnormalities Can Do • Identify severely enlarged left atrium, providing useful and timely corroborative evidence for left‐ sided heart failure in a dog or cat with respiratory signs. • Identify severely enlarged right atrium and ven- tricle, providing useful evidence for right heart failure in a dog with ascites or severe pulmonary hypertension in a dog with respiratory distress. • Provide a qualitative or quantitive assessment of left ventricular chamber size, systolic function, and wall thickness to aid in the diagnosis of cardiomyopathies. • Detect obviously thickened or abnormal cardiac valvular anatomy, providing supportive evidence for degenerative valvular heart disease or infectious endocarditis. • Detect heartworms in the right heart in dogs with caval syndrome or in cats with respiratory distress. • Detect an obvious cardiac mass such as a heart base mass or right atrial hemangiosarcoma in a dog with respiratory or hemodynamic compromise. Assess the size and degree of respiratory variation of the caudal vena cava to determine if a patient is fluid tolerant or intolerant. What Focused Cardiac Ultrasound Abnormalities Cannot Do • Cannot be used as a stand‐alone diagnostic test for the definitive diagnosis of heart failure. Heart failure is a clinical diagnosis incorporating the FCU with the history, physical exam, and other imaging and diagnostic tests.
