404 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER • Cannot replace a complete and diagnostic echocar- diography by a veterinary cardiologist or other specialist. Ultrasound is a user‐dependent modality and sonographers should know the limitations of their ultrasound unit and skill level. • Cannot teach how to utilize more advanced echo - cardiographic features of heart assessment. Indications • Respiratory distress, uncharacterized tachypnea or other respiratory signs. • Body cavity effusions (pleural, pericardial or peri - toneal effusion) suspected or confirmed based on physical exam or other imaging. • Suspect right‐sided or left‐side heart failure based on physical exam or imaging. • Uncharacterized syncope, collapse, generalized weakness or hemodynamic instability. • Uncharacterized tachycardia (rapid heart rate) or significant cardiac arrhythmia. • Feline aortic thromboembolism (ATE). • Suspect heartworm caval syndrome in a dog. Objectives • Identify a severely enlarged left atrium (LA) in dogs and cats with suspected left‐sided heart failure and integrate the FCU findings with the lung and thoracic ultrasound exams (see Chapters 17, 18, 22, 23, 26, 36, and 37). • Identify severe right heart enlargement, caudal vena cava, and hepatic venous distension sugges - tive of right heart failure or possibly secondary to chronic pulmonary hypertension/cor pulmonale in a dog with respiratory distress. • Identify severely diminished left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction. • Know the FCU abnormalities of the common acquired heart diseases in dogs and cats – specifically, degenerative valvular heart disease and dilated cardiomyopathy in dogs and hypertro- phic cardiomyopathy in cats. • Know the common locations and FCU appear - ances of the common etiologies of cardiac neoplasia. Valvular Heart Diseases Degenerative Mitral Valve Disease Mitral valve disease (MVD) is the most common cause of heart disease in dogs. It is estimated that MVD accounts for 75–85% of all heart disease in dogs, so it is the most common cause of canine heart failure (Fox 2012). MVD is most prevalent in older, small‐breed dogs but can also affect large‐breed dogs to a lesser degree. Commonly affected breeds include the cavalier king charles spaniel, dachshund, chihuahua, toy poodle, beagle, cocker spaniel, maltese, pomeranian, shetland sheepdog, miniature schnauzer, whippet, and many small mixed breeds (Borgarelli and Buchanan 2012). Cats rarely get degenerative valvular heart disease. MVD causes pro- gressive degeneration and thickening of the mitral valve, leading to backwards blood flow from the LV to the LA due to mitral valve insufficiency. Over time, chronic mitral valvular insufficiency may lead to left‐sided congestive heart failure. Not uncommonly, MVD can manifest with acute fulminant heart failure as a result of a chordae tendineae rupture or, less commonly, as a result of a LA tear with pericardial effusion (see Figures 18.21, 18.32B, and 21.5). Dogs with a ruptured LA typi- cally present in severe respiratory distress and have a history of heart murmur and recent collapse episode (Reineke et al. 2008; Nakamura et al. 2014). Common FCU findings in MVD • Thickened mitral valve (MV) leaflets with possible prolapsing of an MV leaflet, usually the anterior mitral valve leaflet (Figure 20.1). Follow‐up echocardiography by a boarded spe - cialist after initial diagnosis by FCU will provide corroborative evidence of the initial diagnosis or feedback of an initial incorrect diagnosis. Figure 20.1. Right parasternal long‐axis view of severe left atrial enlargement in a dog with mitral valvular disease. Arrowhead highlights prolapsing of the anterior mitral valve leaflet.

405 POCUS: H EART ‐ A BNORMALITIES OF V ALVES , M YOCARDIUM , AND G REAT V ESSELS • In left‐sided congestive heart failure, severe LA enlargement is present typically with a LA:Ao ratio of >2:1. Left ventricular enlargement is also present (Figure 20.2). • In early left‐sided volume overload, the LV main - tains its systolic function and may appear to be hyperdynamic (higher than normal FS%). In later, end‐stage MV disease, LV systolic myocardial function becomes diminished. • Concurrent degeneration and thickening of the tricuspid valve is common. Infectious Endocarditis Infectious endocarditis (IE) is an uncommon disease in dogs and is rarely seen in cats. Despite its low prevalence, IE is a disease in which FCU can be extremely helpful in expediting a diagnosis. The diagnosis is difficult without the use of FCU or an echocardiogram because of its vague clinical signs and nonspecific clinical presentations. Animals usu - ally succumb to acute congestive heart failure because of extensive valvular damage and insuffi - ciency. They can also present with clinical signs related to other disease complications such as poly - arthritis, glomerulonephritis, thromboembolism, and lethal arrhythmias (MacDonald et al. 2010). Focused cardiac ultrasound is extremely helpful in diagnosing IE through detection of vegetative lesions on the valvular surfaces. The most commonly affected valves in the dog and cat are the aortic and mitral valves (MacDonald et al. 2010). In fact, the finding of an irreg- ular echogenic thickening or mobile mass on the aortic valve is highly suggestive of IE in a clinically ill dog or cat. Unfortunately, clearly distinguishing DMV disease (endocardiosis) from MV endocarditis can be difficult based solely on the ultrasound images. However, the finding of an independently oscillating focal lesion on the MV can be very suggestive of IE, especially in a sick dog. It is important to emphasize that the FCU findings need to be interpreted in light of the clinical presenta - tion and progression of clinical signs. Common FCE findings in IE • Vegetative lesion (irregular thickened and often mobile mass) on the “blood flow” side of the aortic and/or mitral valve (Figure 20.3). • Left atrial and ventricular volume overload are common due to valvular insufficiencies. Figure 20.2. Right parasternal short‐axis view of severe left atrial enlargement in a dog with mitral valvular disease. The left atrial (LA) diameter is more than twice the diameter of the aorta (Ao), LA:Ao ratio is >2:1. Ao, aorta; LA, left atrium; PV , pulmonary vein; RV , right ventricle. Pitfall: Many older small‐breed dogs with respiratory disease have concurrent MV disease. The size of the LA may be used to determine if respiratory clinical signs are due to heart disease or respiratory disease as well as the presence of car - diogenic pulmonary edema or pneumonia repre - sented by regional and pattern‐based distribution and numbers of B‐lines on lung ultrasound (see Chapters 22 and 23). usage (Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2016, 2017; Gargani et al. 2015; Ward et al. 2017; Vezzosi et al. 2017; Ward et al. 2018) (see Chapters 22 and 23). Pearl: The LA size in a dog with acute chordae ten - dineae rupture may not be severely enlarged. However, these dogs typically have severe cardio - genic pulmonary edema and clinical signs. Use of the Vet BLUE B‐line scoring system can help estimate extravascular lung water and guide loop diuretic Pearl: In a dog with severe cardiogenic pulmonary edema due to MVD, B‐lines are usually present in all lung fields (Lisciandro et al. 2014; Ward et al. 2017). Pearl: Pericardial effusion seen in a dog with congestive heart failure and cardiogenic shock may be a result of LA rupture as a complication of severe MV disease and LA dilation (see Figures 18.21, 18.32B, and 21.5) (Reineke et al. 2008; Nakamura et al. 2014).

406 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Myocardial Diseases Dilated Cardiomyopathy and Other Causes of Left Ventricular Myocardial Failure Left ventricular performance by FCU should be assessed in any hemodynamically unstable patient. Global assessment of LV contractility can be a qualitative “eyeball” assessment and/or a quantitative assessment by fractional shortening (FS%) or ejection fraction. The value of the “eyeball” assessment of LV function should not be underestimated. An experi - enced and trained clinician can make real‐time assess- ments of LV wall kinetics and chamber dimensions to make an immediate diagnosis. The simplest quantitative approach is to measure the LV end‐ diastolic dimension and the LV end‐systolic dimension for determination of the fractional shortening. This can be done in 2‐D or via M‐mode echo (see Figures 19.5, 36.6, and 37.5). Normal FS% is 28–45% in the dog and 30–50% in the cat. A FS% below 20% is suggestive of severe myocardial systolic failure and a FS% above 55% would be considered hyperdynamic LV function. Left ventricular systolic myocardial failure can be caused by a primary myocardial disease or could be the end‐result of various different insults or diseases. The most common cause of LV myocardial failure in veterinary medicine is breed‐associated dilated car - diomyopathy (DCM) in Doberman pinschers, Great Danes, and boxers with arrhythmogenic cardiomy - opathy with DCM phenotype (Stern and Ueda 2019). However, many other causes of LV myocardial failure are possible such as nutritional cardiomyopathies (carnitine, taurine, grain‐free diet), doxorubicin cardiomyopathy, tachycardia‐induced cardiomyop - athy, sepsis‐induced myocardial dysfunction, cardio - myopathy of volume overload in dogs with end‐stage MV disease, and end‐stage hypertrophic cardiomy - opathy (HCM), referred to as “burn‐out” HCM of cats (Meurs 2010). Dilated Cardiomyopathy Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is a common cause of heart disease and heart failure in certain large‐ and giant‐breed dogs (Figure 20.4; see also Figures 18.32B and 37.5). DCM is uncommonly diagnosed in cats. It causes myocardial failure and cardiac dilation. DCM is often breed associated and is usually identified when a dog is symptomatic with congestive heart failure. Commonly affected breeds include Doberman pin - schers, Great Danes, boxers, Irish wolfhounds, Labradors, and golden retrievers. Dogs with DCM may be young, middle‐aged or older and males are more commonly affected than females. Cardiac arrhythmias are often associated with DCM (Martin et al. 2009). Common FCU Findings in DCM • Dilated LV with spherical appearance in the long‐axis views with a markedly hypodynamic LV systolic function (poor contractility) (see Figure 20.4A). The internal dimension of the normal canine LV in diastole should not exceed 5 cm in dogs less than 120 lb. • Fractional shortening is typically <20% (normal FS% is 28–45% in dogs, 30–50% in cats) (see Figure 20.4B). • Dilated LA and increased LA:Ao ratio but not increased as much as in MVD. Ao, aorta; LA, left atrium; LV , left ventricle; Veg, vegetative lesion. Pearl: Predisposing factors such as chronic infections or bacteremia, congenital heart disease, and immu - nosuppressive therapy are common in dogs with IE. Pitfall: Infectious endocarditis is a clinical diagnosis usually in an extremely ill dog or cat. If IE is suspected based on FCU, a complete detailed echo - cardiogram and systemic evaluation is advised (see Chapter 36).

407 POCUS: H EART ‐ A BNORMALITIES OF V ALVES , M YOCARDIUM , AND G REAT V ESSELS • Not uncommonly, all four cardiac chambers may be dilated, especially if biventricular heart failure is present. • Normal MV anatomy with reduced MV motion. Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the most common cause of heart disease and heart failure in cats (Rush et al. 2002; Hall et al. 2007; Payne et al. 2015) but is extremely rare in the dog. Congestive heart failure is a common cause of respiratory distress in the cat. HCM is defined as LV hypertrophy in the absence of diseases that can lead to hypertrophy. A wall thickness of either the interventricular septum (IVS) or LV free wall of >6 mm in a cat is suggestive of HCM (Payne et al. 2013) (Figure 20.5). Other causes of LV hypertrophy that mimic HCM include systemic hypertension, hyperthy- roidism, congenital aortic stenosis, acromegaly, infil - trative disease and, importantly, “pseudohypertrophy” associated with volume contraction and dehydration (Luis‐Fuentes and Wilkie 2017). The “eyeball method” of FCU is more challenging in the feline species because they have higher heart rates than dogs. Thus, freezing and rolling the cine ball to move through captured frames improves FCU assessment and should become habitual for the feline FCU sonographer. Figure 20.5. Pearl: Tachyarrhythmias and sepsis syndrome may also markedly diminish myocardial function, caus - ing misinterpretation of echocardiographic find - ings. Reevaluation of myocardial function once arrhythmias and sepsis have resolved is advised for best patient assessment. Pitfall: Be careful not to overinterpret what may appear by the “eyeball method” to be subnormal LV systolic function in a large‐ or giant‐breed dog. These dogs have LV systolic function parameters that are lower than a small‐breed dog.

408 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy generally affects young, middle‐aged, and older cats and more com- monly affects males than females. Although the most commonly affected cat is the mixed‐breed cat, certain breeds, such as the Maine coon, ragdoll, Bengal, British shorthair, Sphinx, and Persian breeds, have a high prevalence of HCM (Luis‐Fuentes and Wilkie 2017). Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy typically causes heart failure due to LV diastolic dysfunction causing elevated filling pressures with normal, subnormal or even supranormal LV systolic function parameters. Cats in congestive heart failure secondary to HCM will usually have an enlarged left atrium (Schober et al. 2014; Ward et al. 2018). In cats with respiratory distress, lung ultrasound (Vet BLUE) provides an option to rapidly rule out left‐sided congestive heart failure in the absence of B‐lines even if there is evidence of some cardiac abnormalities. Other differentials such as feline asthma, neoplasia or upper airway obstructions are other common conditions caus- ing respiratory distress (Lisciandro et al. 2016; Ward et al. 2017, 2018). Loop diuretics are not indicated in the absence of B‐lines and the FCU or complete echocardio- gram may wait until the patient is more stable. Common FCU Findings in HCM • Concentric LV hypertrophy, including the LV pap- illary muscles. The LV hypertrophy can be either symmetrical or segmental (Figure 20.6A). • A LV wall in diastole measuring greater than 6 mm (>6 mm) is generally considered hypertrophic. In some cats with chronic HCM, LV walls may be high normal thickness because of a phenomenon called LV remodeling (Luis‐Fuentes and Wilkie 2017). • In a cat with suspect heart failure, the LA is severely dilated with typically a LA:Ao ratio >2:1 (see Figure 20.6B). • Variable amounts of pleural effusion are often a unique manifestation of congestive heart failure (HF) in cats (see Figure 20.5). • Small amount of pericardial effusion (typically <5 mm) without evidence of cardiac tamponade may be seen in cats with congestive HF as a consequence of their HF and is commonly not due to pericardial disease. In fact, the most common cause of pericardial effusion in cats is heart failure (see Figure 20.6A) (Hall et al. 2007; Ward et al. 2018). • Typically, HCM cats have normal to hyperdynamic (high FS%) LV function. However, in end‐stage or remodeled HCM, LV function can be diminished (lower FS%) (normal FS% in cats is 30–50%) (Payne et al. 2015). • Possible LA thrombus, most commonly within the left auricle, may be present. The thrombus can be adhered to the atrial wall or freely mobile (see Figure 20.6C). “Smoke” or a swirling appearance of blood in the LA can be seen in cats with severe LA enlargement and stagnant blood flow. This finding, known as spontaneous echo contrast, may be seen in cats that have suffered an aortic thromboembo- lism (ATE) or are at high risk for thromboembolism (Schober and Maerz 2006). Cardiac Neoplasia Primary and metastatic tumors of the heart are relatively uncommon. Despite the lower prevalence, FCU can be quite helpful in expediting a diagnosis. Cardiac tumors are more common in dogs than cats. Dogs usually present for clinical signs related to obstruction of blood flow in or out of the heart, compression of the airways or cardiac tamponade and pericardial effusion. Common owner complaints include respiratory signs such as coughing, retching, tachypnea, or dyspnea. They also present for col- lapse, weakness or abdominal distension. Occasionally, a dog with a cardiac neoplasia, usually a heart base tumor, will be asymptomatic. The clinically silent cardiac tumor usually is identified when an echocardiography or thoracic radiography is performed for another problem, such as a heart murmur (Guglielmini et al. 2016). When a mass lesion is identified in the heart or at the heart base, the etiology of the mass is typically deduced Pearl: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is diagnosed when LV hypertrophy is present in the absence of hyperthyroidism, hypertension, severe hypovolemia, including from dehydration, and aortic stenosis. Pitfall: Left atrial thrombus has clear edges and should be confirmed in multiple views. The edges of a thrombus should not be hazy. Be careful not to over- interpret a side‐lobe artifact in the LA for a thrombus (see Chapters 3 and 5, and Figures 3.7 and 15.17). Pitfall: Extreme hypovolemia causing “pseudohy- pertrophy of the left ventricle” can be confused with HCM in the cat. The LA size should be enlarged in a symptomatic HCM cat, while LA size will be normal to small in hypovolemia and LV pseudohypertro- phy. Moreover, the evaluation of lung using Vet BLUE is another strategy to rule out left‐sided congestive heart failure in the critical unstable cat (Lisciandro et al. 2016, 2017; Ward et al. 2017, 2018).

409 POCUS: H EART ‐ A BNORMALITIES OF V ALVES , M YOCARDIUM , AND G REAT V ESSELS by its location, shape, and echogenicity, and the clinical context (Rajagopalan et al. 2013). The most common cause of a cardiac neoplasia is hemangiosarcoma, typi- cally located in the right atrium or right atrial appendage (Waters et al. 1988; Boston et al. 2011). Dogs with a right atrial hemangiosarcoma typically present for signs asso- ciated with cardiac tamponade and pericardial effusion (MacDonald et al. 2009). The second most common cardiac tumor is an aortic body tumor (also called chemodectoma) at the heart base. Dogs with chemodec- tomas can also present with pericardial effusion and cardiac tamponade. Alternatively, these tumors can get quite large and cause airway compression or obstruction to blood flow. Cardiac tumors can also be located in the pericardium, left or right ventricle and on cardiac valves. Other less common types of cardiac neoplasia include lymphoma, mesothelioma, leiomysarcoma, fibrosar - coma, chondrosarcoma, myxosarcoma, hamartoma, thy- roid adenoma, and melanoma (Treggiari et al. 2017). Other less likely nonneoplastic causes of a cardiac mass in the dog are a fungal granuloma or an intracardiac thrombus (MacDonald et al. 2009; Treggiari et al. 2017). Figure 20.6. 410 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER German shepherd dogs, golden and Labrador retrievers are at increased risk for cardiac hemangiosar- coma while brachycephalic dog breeds (boxers, bulldogs, and Boston terriers) are at increased risk for aortic body tumors (MacDonald et al. 2009; Treggiari et al. 2017). With a high metastatic rate for some cardiac tumors, performing thoracic radiography and the use of Global FAST including Vet BLUE to stage the patient should be considered (MacDonald et al. 2009) (see Chapter 36). Common FCU Findings of Cardiac Neoplasia • Cardiac hemangiosarcoma is often an irregular mass of varying size and mixed echogenicity located in the wall of the right atrium or right atrial appendage. Concurrent pericardial effusion and cardiac tamponade is common and less commonly a splenic mass (Figure 20.7) (Waters et al. 1988; Boston et al. 2011). • Clinically significant heart base chemodectomas are usually large masses of homogeneous echogenicity with smooth borders located adjacent to the ascending aorta. Concurrent pericardial effusion is also common (Figure 20.8) (Rajagopalan et al. 2013). • Mesothelioma usually does not cause a discrete mass and is often associated with a thickened pericardium and pericardial effusion (MacDonald et al. 2009). Abnormalities of Great Vessels Pulmonary Hypertension Pulmonary hypertension (PHT) is defined as a systolic pressure in the pulmonary artery of greater than 30 mmHg or greater than ¼ of systemic blood pressure (Kellihan and Stepien 2010). PHT is a complex syndrome that can be caused by many diseases and is often idiopathic. PHT can be categorized into precapillary or postcapillary based on the disease causing the elevated pulmonary arterial pressure (PAP). Causes of precapillary PHT include heartworm disease, pulmonary embolus, chronic lung disease, primary or idiopathic PHT. PHT can also be due to postcapillary etiologies relating to increased left heart filling pressures, or pulmonary venoocclusive dis- ease (Kellihan and Stepien 2010). Common presenting complaints for PHT are syncope and dyspnea. Other clinical signs include worsening cough, increased respiratory rate, “can’t sleep or get comfortable,” lethargy, and decreased appetite (Johnson et al. 1999). Severe PHT can also result in right‐sided congestive heart failure and ascites. PHT can be difficult to diagnose without the aid of FCU or a complete detailed echocardiogram because radiographs and physical examination findings can be difficult to inter- pret and are nonspecific (Kellihan and Stepien 2010). In dogs with severe PHT due to heartworm disease, heartworms may be seen as double‐lined structures within the pulmonary artery. With caval syndrome, a severe form of heartworm disease, the heartworms will be seen in the right atrium and ventricle and caudal vena cava (Figure 20.9C; see also Figure 18.32E). Careful interrogation of the main pulmonary artery (PA) for a possible pulmonary embolism is advised. Common FCU Findings in Severe Pulmonary Hypertension • Severe RV hypertrophy (RV > LV) on the right parasternal long‐axis four‐chamber view. Its short‐ axis view is too variable for the noncardiologist sonographer as a sole view. • Flattening of the IVS in the LV short‐axis “mush- room” view (see Figures 20.9A and 37.6). • Small internal LV lumen suggests poor filling of the LV and low cardiac output due to the PHT. • Right atrial dilation, caudal vena caval, and hepatic venous distension may be seen in severe PHT and right‐sided congestive heart failure (Figure 20.10; see also Figure 37.6). • Main PA enlargement (larger than the aorta) (see Figure 20.9B) (Sutherland‐Smith et al. 2018). Assessment of the Caudal Vena Cava Caudal vena cava (CVC) diameter and its respiratory variations can be used to estimate right atrial filling pressures and guide volume responsiveness (Feissel Pearl: Most masses at the heart base are chemodec- tomas, tumors of the chemoreceptors in the aorta. Other possible causes of a heart base mass include ectopic thyroid gland tissue, hemangiosarcomas, and mesothelioma (Treggiari et al. 2017). Pearl: FCU findings of right‐sided congestive heart failure typically include right ventricular and right atrial enlargement, caudal vena cava and hepatic venous distension, and ascites. Pearl: A right atrial hemangiosarcoma is typically best seen from the left parasternal view optimized for the right atrium and auricle. Make sure to fan through the entire mass to estimate the mass size and extent of involvement. If a mass is very large, it can be seen in any view and may compress the atria or great vessels, impinging the inflow and/or out- flow of blood (see Figure 18.32F). Pitfall: In an extremely overweight dog or cat, be careful not to overinterpret adipose tissue at the heart base as a cardiac mass. Pearl: With acute PHT such as in an acute pulmonary thromboembolism (PTE), the right ventricle will be enlarged. Other FCU findings of more chronic PHT include a RV that is eccentrically hypertrophied, PA enlargement, and diminished RV function. RV hypertrophy results from chronic severe PHT. Pitfall: With severe chronic PHT, the RV papillary muscles will also be severely hypertrophied. In the right parasternal short‐axis views, these RV papil- lary muscles can mistaken for a mass or thrombus (see Figures 20.9A and 37.6).

This section will pri - marily focus on the assessment of the CVC as it relates to elevated right heart filling pressure. Elevated right atrial pressures can result from right‐sided congestive heart failure due to structural acquired or congenital heart diseases, severe PHT, and pericardial effusion with cardiac tamponade. Elevated right atrial pressure can also result from excessive volume expansion in a critically ill patient (Nelson et al. 2010). In spontaneously breathing ani - mals, the CVC normally collapses during inspiration. In patients with severely elevated right atrial pressure (>15 mmHg), the CVC diameter will be increased with no respiratory fluctuations noted (see Figures 20.10 and 37.6). Hepatic veins will also be distended and ascites may be seen between the liver lobes. The visualization of a dilated nonfluctuating CVC can be quite helpful to expedite the diagnosis of right‐sided congestive heart failure in a dog with ascites or cat with large‐volume pleural effusion. It is important to know that the degree of respiratory fluctuation can be affected by the depth and volume of the breath in a spontaneously breathing patient. In a patient who is panting or taking short shallow breaths, the fluctuations may not accurately correlate with right atrial filling pressure. However, the respiratory Figure 20.9. Conversely, a distended and plethoric (blood‐filled) CVC would sug- gest fluid intolerance and elevated right atrial pressure (see also Figures 7.12, 7.13, 26.1, 26.4, 36.7, and 36.11). A long‐axis view of the CVC as it crosses the diaphragm is the author’s recommended view from a subxiphoid transducer position (the same as the FAST diaphragmatico‐hepatic [DH] view). The view allows easy qualitative assessment of the CVC, hepatic veins and presence of ascites in the abdomen and thorax, and screens for both pleural and pericardial effusion. M‐mode assessment of the CVC can be helpful in visu- alizing the respiratory fluctuations. There are a few other views that can be used to visualize the CVC at the porta hepatis and cranial and caudal to the right kidney (Darnis et al. 2018; Marshall et al. 2018) (see Chapter 26). The advantage of the subxiphoid view (FAST DH view) is that the respiratory fluctuations can be better assessed at the level of the diaphragm and the CVC can be easily imaged in most dogs and cats (Figure 20.11). 414 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Cardiopulmonary Arrest Both the American Heart Association and the European Resuscitation Council recommend the use of ultra- sound in cardiac arrest situations (Link et al. 2015; Soar et al. 2015). Point‐of‐care ultrasound (POCUS) is help- ful in the diagnosis of any possible correctable causes of cardiac arrest while resuscitation is ongoing (see Table 37.1). Possible reversible causes of cardiac arrest in which ultrasound can aid in the diagnosis include hypovolemia, tension pneumothorax, cardiac tampon- ade, and pulmonary thromboembolism. Additionally, ultrasound can be used to assess myocardial motion and prognosis. The use of ultrasound should not delay the onset or the intervals between cardiac compres- sions. Typical protocols propose use brief 10‐second ultrasound exams of the heart and lungs after each continuous two‐minute round of chest compressions and basic life support. Cardiac standstill visualized by the FCU suggests no return to spontaneous circulation despite electrical activity. If cardiac standstill is docu- mented, it would be reasonable to terminate resuscita- tion efforts. Conversely, if coordinated cardiac motion is observed, continue CPR while searching for its cause. Pearls and Pitfalls, The Final Say The images obtained from the FCU can expedite the diagnosis of structural heart disease in patients pre- senting with clinical signs suggesting left‐sided and right‐sided heart failure. These patients are typically in respiratory distress or can be hemodynamically unstable. The FCU is a low‐stress, low‐impact, nonin- vasive tool that will lead to expedited treatment and improved patient care. Even without the use of advanced echocardiographic techniques, such as 2D and M‐mode, FCU images of significant cardiac abnor- malities such as marked chamber enlargements and myocardial failure can be determined. Quick Reference of Normals and Rules of Thumb • Fractional shortening (FS%) is typically <20 % in DCM with normal FS% being 28–45% in dogs and 30–50% in cats. • Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in cats is supported by a LV wall measured in diastole to be >6 mm. In some cats with chronic disease, LV walls may be high normal thickness because of a phenomenon referred to as LV remodeling. • In a cat with suspected heart failure, the LA is severely dilated with typically a LA:Ao ratio >2:1. • Variable amounts of pleural effusion are often a unique manifestation of congestive heart failure in cats. • Small amounts of pericardial effusion (typically <5 mm) without evidence of cardiac tamponade may be seen in cats with congestive heart failure. In fact, the most common cause of pericardial effusion in cats is heart failure (~75%). • Extreme hypovolemia can be mistaken for HCM in cats, a phenomenon referred to as “pseudohyper - trophy of the left ventricle.” • Features of severe pulmonary hypertension include: (1) severe RV hypertrophy (RV > LV) on the right parasternal long‐axis four‐chamber view, (2) flat- tening of the IVS in the LV short‐axis “mushroom” view”, (3) small internal LV lumen suggests poor filling of the LV and low cardiac output due to the PHT, 4) right atrial dilation, CVC, and hepatic venous distension in severe PHT and right‐sided congestive heart failure, and 5) main pulmonary artery enlargement (larger than the aorta). • The most common cause of a cardiac neoplasia in dogs is hemangiosarcoma, typically located in the right atrium or right atrial appendage. • Most masses at the heart base are chemodectomas, tumors of the chemoreceptors in the aorta. Other possible causes of a heart base mass include ectopic thyroid gland tissue, hemangiosarcomas, and mesothelioma. • Left atrial to aortic ratio (LA:Ao) >2:1 is extremely suggestive of left‐sided heart failure in a dog or cat with respiratory distress, especially with the presence of B‐lines providing further supportive evidence using the Vet BLUE regional, pattern‐ based approach (see Chapters 22 and 23). B‐lines are nonspecific and must be placed into a regional, pattern‐based approach, i.e. Vet BLUE. • Normally the LV is 3–4 times the size of the RV . An RV that is larger than the LV with a distended and nonfluctuating CVC is extremely suggestive of right‐sided heart failure, especially in a dog with ascites. • Normal LV chamber size, wall dimensions and sys- tolic function can vary based on body weight, breed of dog, heart rate/rhythm, volume status and systemic disease. Careful clinical integration of all influences on chamber dimensions is advised before making assessments of LV size and function.

Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 417 Introduction Pericardial effusion (PCE) is an excess of fluid in the pericardial sac. The normal pericardial sac has a small amount of clear serous fluid that is usually not detect- able with ultrasound. Abnormal accumulations of pericardial fluid develop as a result of many disease processes. Neoplastic and idiopathic PCE disorders are the most common in the dog, particularly large‐breed and brachycephalic dogs (MacGregor et al. 2005; MacDonald et al. 2009; Boston et al. 2011). Less com- monly, PCE may be caused by a left atrial tear (mitral valve disease dogs), coagulopathies, uremia, systemic inflammation, infectious pericarditis (e.g., coccidioido- mycosis), trauma or foreign bodies (Reineke et al. 2008; Nakamura et al. 2014; Covey and Connolly 2018). In cats, PCE is most commonly a manifestation of congestive heart failure (Hall et al. 2007). Much less commonly, lymphoma and feline infectious peritonitis (FIP) can result in pericardial effusion in cats. Cardiac tamponade is a frequent consequence of PCE in the dog and a life‐threatening condition. Cardiac tamponade results when the intrapericardial pressure is higher than the right ventricular filling pressure. This high intrapericardial pressure causes poor right ventricular filling, low cardiac output, and right heart failure. Both the amount of the effusion and its rate of formation determine the degree of hemody- namic compromise. A dog can have cardiac tampon- ade and poor cardiac output with a small amount of pericardial effusion if the rate of accumulation of the effusion is fast. Common clinical signs include collapse, lethargy, cough, vomiting, inappetence, abdominal distension and possible difficulty breathing. Dogs with chronic mitral valve disease that have suffered a left atrial tear will be acutely dyspneic and extremely weak (Reineke et al. 2008; Nakamura et al. 2014). While there are some classic physical examination findings such as muffled heart sounds, weak pulses, jugular venous distension and abdominal distension, these can be nonspecific. Focused cardiac ultrasound (FCU) can provide a rapid and accurate diagnosis, especially in a dog with cardiac tamponade and small‐ volume pericardial effusion. Despite some suggestive findings such as globoid cardiomegaly, thoracic radi- ography is often not a valuable imaging modality for the diagnosis of PCE (Côté et al. 2013). FCU is a sensitive diagnostic test for pericardial effusion; peri- cardial effusion can be reliably recognized with a 95% degree of accuracy by noncardiologists with POCUS training (Tse et al. 2013; Ceriani and Cogliati 2016). What Focused Cardiac Ultrasound Pericardial Effusion Can Do • Detect the presence of PCE and cardiac tamponade. • Based on the absence or presence of a mass (its location, size, shape, echogenicity, and behavior), suggest the suspected etiology of the PCE. • Estimate the amount and echogenicity of PCE (small, moderate, large) and identify an optimal site for POCUS‐assisted or POCUS‐guided pericardiocentesis. 418 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER • Monitor for recurrence of the PCE, which is not uncommon with a right atrial mass and highly probable with hemangiosarcoma. What Focused Cardiac Ultrasound Pericardial Effusion Cannot Do • Care should be taken to not overzealously defini - tively diagnose the etiology of the pericardial effusion without corroborative or confirmatory evidence. Indications • Collapse, weakness, and hemodynamic compromise. • Vague clinical signs with muffled heart sounds and weak pulses. • Sudden‐onset collapse and dyspnea in a dog with advanced mitral valve disease. • Abdominal distension and jugular venous distension. • Globoid radiographic appearance to the cardiac silhouette. Objectives • To accurately identify pericardial effusion and dis- tinguish it from pleural effusion. • To identify right atrial collapse, the sonographic finding of cardiac tamponade, in a dog with peri - cardial effusion. • To be familiar with the two most common neo - plastic causes of pericardial effusion in the dog, specifically a right atrial mass (likely a hemangio - sarcoma) or heart base mass (likely a chemodectoma) (Treggiari et al. 2017). • To be familiar with the FCU findings of a left atrial tear in a dog with advanced mitral valve disease. • To know that PCE in the cat is often associated with congestive heart failure and is managed medically. • To know the indications for and be familiar with how to perform an emergency pericardiocentesis in a dog with cardiac tamponade and PCE (see also Chapter 43). Pericardial Effusion The pericardium consists of a tough fibrous parietal layer and a membranous visceral layer adhered to the epicardium. In normality, the parietal and visceral layers are seen as one hyperechoic (bright white) line adjacent to the epicardium. When there is PCE, the two layers separate. PCE is typically seen as an anechoic (black) space encircling the heart between the myocar- dium and the highly echogenic parietal layer of the pericardium (Figure 21.1). Occasionally, the PCE could have a more echogenic appearance, suggesting increased cellularity to the fluid, such as in a left atrial tear or infectious pericar - ditis. Multiple views of the heart as well as visualizing the entire heart are necessary to avoid mistaking a dilated atrium or ventricle for pericardial (or pleural) effusions, resulting in a catastrophic error and performing centesis of a cardiac chamber (see also Chapters 17 and 18). In the smaller compact ultra - sound units, the maximum depth of 13 or 15 cm may not allow viewing of the entire heart in a large‐breed dog. In these cases, viewing the fluid and heart from multiple views is of the utmost importance. The axiom “One view is no view” is sage advice when diagnosing pericardial effusion (see also Chapters 17 and 18 and Figures 18.18, and 18.19). PCE is seen from all standard views including the subxiphoid (Lisciandro 2016), right parasternal, and left‐sided views (Figure 21.2). Neoplasia, most commonly right auricular hemangio - sarcoma and heart base chemodectoma, is the most common cause of pericardial effusion in an older dog. The presence of a possible cardiac mass is generally better evaluated prior to pericardiocentesis depending on patient stability. Figure 21.1. 419 POCUS: H EART – P ERICARDIAL E FFUSION AND P ERICARDIOCENTESIS Pleural effusion is often present concurrently with PCE. The distinction between pleural and pericardial effusion can be challenging. Moderate‐ to large‐volume PCE is seen as circumferential anechoic space encircling the ventricles in short‐axis view, while pleural effusion will be seen as angular anechoic spaces near the heart and between the lung lobes. PCE should taper as it nears the top of the left atrium in the long‐axis views as the pericardium attaches to the top of the atrium (Figure 21.3A). The parietal pericardium is usually the most hyperechoic (brightest) structure within the thorax. You can turn down the gain of the ultrasound machine and generally the last linear echo structure is the pericar- dium. If no PCE is present then the pericardium (the last white line) should be adjacent to the epicardial surface of the heart. Lastly, pleural effusion is gravity dependent and will shift to the recumbent side down. As previously mentioned, multiple views are key for interrogation of the pleural and pericardial spaces (see also Chapters 17 and 18 and Figures 18.18 and 18.19). Common FCU findings in Pericardial Effusion • Anechoic fluid around the heart that is delineated by the pericardium, which appears as a bright white (hyperechoic) linear echo in the far‐field (mostly because of acoustic enhancement) (see Figures 18.19, 21.1, 21.3A,B). • Echocardiographic criteria for cardiac tamponade are right atrial and possibly right ventricular dia - stolic collapse (see Figures 18.19, 18.20, and 21.3A). • Cardiac tamponade and obstruction of right heart filling are further corroborated by a distended and nonfluctuating caudal vena cava (see Figures 18.20 and 21.2). • A heart base mass is usually best visualized in the right‐sided parasternal views (see Figures 20.8 and 21.3A) while a right atrial or auricular hemangio - sarcoma is typically best seen from a left‐sided parasternal view optimized for the right atrium and auricle (Figure 21.4). If a mass is very large, it can be seen in any view and may compress the atria or great vessels, impinging the inflow or out - flow of blood (see Figure 18.32F). • Nonstandard views may be best to fully determine the extent of the mass. • PCE caused by a left atrial tear in a dog with mitral valve disease will have an increased echogenicity representing a tubular-shaped blood clot. The left atrium is typically enlarged and the mitral valve will be thick and abnormal (Figure 21.5; see also Figures 18.21 and 18.32B). Pericardiocentesis The main indication for pericardiocentesis is the urgent and life‐saving removal of PCE from a dog with cardiac tamponade and hemodynamic compro - mise. If time and patient conditions allow, an attempt Figure 21.2. Subxiphoid (or diaphragmatic hepatic) view of pericardial effusion and ascites in a dog. The pericardial effusion is depicted by the arrowheads. The caudal vena cava (*) is distended and nonfluctuating, suggestive of cardiac tamponade. CdVC, caudal vena cava. Pearl: If patient stability allows, search for a mass when PCE is present (prior to pericardiocentesis). Masses are seen more easily with pericardial fluid around them. Pitfall: Furosemide and vasodilators are contraindi- cated in the setting of cardiac tamponade. Typically, fluid expansion with intravenous crystalloids is used to transiently improve cardiac output while awaiting pericardiocentesis. Medical treatment with diuretics and other conventional medications, how- ever, is indicated for the management of PCE in cats with congestive heart failure. Pitfall: Some very obese cats will have a large fat deposit on their pericardium that can be misdiag - nosed as pericardial effusion or a mass. Fat has a more echogenic (brighter) appearance than fluid.

420 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER to identify a possible mass prior to pericardiocentesis is warranted as the mass may be missed after centesis. While there is some risk associated with this procedure, the risks are typically outweighed by the benefits. The removal of the pericardial fluid is the only therapeutic maneuver that will allow the heart to fill normally and significantly improve cardiac output. Medical management of cardiac tamponade with diuretics and vasodilators is harmful. In addition, the fluid analysis of the PCE may have some limited diagnostic utility (MacDonald et al. 2009; Cagle et al. 2014). PCE without evidence of cardiac tamponade does not need to be urgently removed. Small‐volume PCE is commonly a manifestation of heart failure in the cat and occasion - ally the dog (Ward et al. 2018). When PCE without cardiac tamponade is thought to be a manifestation of heart failure, then conventional heart failure medical management is advised. The complications associated with pericardiocente - sis are uncommon but significant (Humm et al. 2009). Cardiac puncture, pneumothorax, arrhythmias, and potential death should be discussed as potential com - plications. If a specialty center is close by and the dog’s condition is reasonably stable, these cases are often referred to a center that commonly performs pericar - diocentesis. Pericardiocentesis is typically performed on the right hemithorax because it is considered safer due to the cardiac notch, the space between the right cranial and middle lung lobes, and reduced chance of lacer - ating a coronary artery. It is of the utmost importance that the patient does not move during the procedure. Sedation is sometimes needed but some patients are so hemodynamically compromised that sedation is not necessary. The larger the volume of PCE, the safer the procedure because there is more distance between the needle and the heart. In human medicine, ultrasound guidance has decreased the complication rate of pericardiocentesis (Tsang et al. 1998; Lindenberger et al. 2003). In veterinary medicine, ultrasound is most commonly used either to assist or to guide pericardiocentesis. Ultrasound‐guided pericardio- centesis is real‐time visualization of the needle draining the pericardial sac while ultrasound‐assisted pericardio- centesis helps to find the optimal location for catheter insertion into the pericardium with intermittent ultra - sound monitoring the fluid drainage. The author prefers the ultrasound‐assisted method because moderate‐ to large‐volume PCE is most common and the preference is to introduce and maintain a soft catheter in the pericardial sac for the duration of draining the fluid rather than a sharp needle that is often used for ultrasound‐guided cen- tesis (Degirmencioglu et al. 2013). The author performs ultrasound‐guided pericardiocentesis for small‐volume pericardial effusion usually for diagnostic purposes under heavy sedation. Ultrasound‐assisted Pericardiocentesis with an Over‐the‐Needle Catheter • A short peripheral intravenous (IV) catheter is placed for administration of drugs (sedation, anti - arrhythmic drugs, or IV fluids). • The sedated patient is placed in sternal or left lat - eral recumbency, depending on the preference of the veterinarian performing the procedure. • A large area on the right hemithorax (3rd to 8th intercostal space from just below the costochondral junction [CCJ] to midthorax) over the heart is clipped. • Prior to surgically prepping the skin, the optimal location is chosen for the introduction of the cath - eter with the aid of the ultrasound (Figure 21.6A). The optimal site should be at or above the CCJ to avoid the internal thoracic artery, and where there is a clear and central view of the PCE with minimal lung interference. 423 POCUS: HEART – PERICARDIAL EFFUSION AND PERICARDIOCENTESIS A Luer‐Slip 3 cc syringe is connected to the cath- eter. Once the catheter tip is through the skin, at least 1 cc of negative suction is applied to the syringe. The catheter is inserted perpendicular to the chest wall and advanced through the subcuta- neous tissues and intercostal muscles until dark red hemorrhagic fluid fills the syringe, signaling that you have entered the pericardial space (see Figure 21.6C). • Pleural effusion is often present together with PCE. Pleural fluid is typically serosanginous or pink in color. One should continue to advance the catheter until the dark red fluid fills the syringe. If there is any doubt about the location of the cath- eter (pleural or pericardial space), you can inject a small amount of agitated saline and ensure that the catheter is located in the correct space and not in the pleural space or right heart (Schussler and Grayburn 2010). • Once in the pericardial sac, the catheter is advanced over the needle stylet. The needle stylet is then removed. Extension tubing, a three‐way stopcock, and a large syringe are quickly attached to the hub of the catheter and drainage of the fluid begins. The fluid should come easily with minimal nega- tive suction (see Figure 21.6D). • You should try to completely drain the PCE. Complete emptying of the fluid will be noted by the absence of more fluid with gentle negative suction. Arrhythmias will often be noted as the catheter tip will be touching the epicardium when little fluid is in the pericardial sac. • Careful monitoring of the ECG during insertion of the needle and during the centesis is advised. If arrhythmias are noted, slight retraction of the needle/catheter should result in resolution of the arrhythmia. • After the pericardiocentesis, the dog should be monitored with FCU for possible reeffusion, espe- cially if a right atrial mass is identified. Reeffusion within a few hours is not uncommon with hemor - rhaging right atrial hemangiosarcomas. Ultrasound‐guided pericardiocentesis is very sim- ilar to ultrasound‐assisted with a few differences. With ultrasound‐guided centesis, the sonographer will hold the probe with their nondominant hand and a reason- ably long centesis needle with the dominant hand. The needle hub is connected to extension tubing, three‐way stopcock, and syringe. An assistant will apply negative suction with the syringe as the needle is advanced into the skin and subcutaneous tissues. The sonographer will watch the insertion of the needle into the pericar - dial space that should coincide with fluid filling the collection system and syringe. The sonographer will continuously watch while the needle is in the pericar - dial sac while the fluid is drained, exercising caution to keep the needle tip from touching the heart. Pearls and Pitfalls, The Final Say Focused cardiac ultrasound is the most sensitive and specific diagnostic modality that is readily available to vet- erinarians to diagnose PCE and cardiac tamponade. Physical examination, chest radiographs, and electrocardi- ography will suggest the diagnosis of PCE but POCUS will: • provide a definitive diagnosis of PCE • provide a diagnosis of cardiac tamponade (right atrial collapse in diastole, distended caudal vena cava [CVC]) • possibly determine the cause of the PCE (often a cardiac neoplasia) • aid in pericardiocentesis. A significant challenge is in accurately distinguishing PCE from pleural effusion, a severely dilated cardiac chamber or excessive pericardial fat. Always try to view the entire heart with fluid encircling it from mul- tiple views and transducer positions. Also try to iden- tify a mass if possibly prior to pericardiocentesis. Scan the right atrium (including the auricle) and heart base carefully for possible hemangiosarcoma or che- modectoma, respectively. Pericardiocentesis, either by Pearl: Most PCEs are hemorrhagic and can be similar in appearance to blood. If you are concerned about an accidental right ventricular puncture and frank blood, wait to see if the hemorrhagic fluid clots. PCE should not clot while blood from a cardiac puncture will clot after a couple of minutes. You may also feel the rhythmic pulsation of the heart on the catheter. Pearl: Even if you are unsuccessful in advancing the catheter into the pericardial sac, just the puncture of the pericardium will likely relieve the cardiac tam- ponade. The PCE will often drain into the pleural space. Reevaluating the amount of PCE and the presence of right atrial collapse after an attempted pericardiocentesis is advised.

Quick Reference of Normals and Rules of Thumb • Always increase your depth to be able to see the heart in its entirety using the hyperechoic (bright white) pericardium in the far‐field as your landmark. • Mirror image of the heart is possible with excessive depth that can be confounding to the sonographer. • Pericardial effusion is most commonly caused by neoplasia in dogs and congestive heart failure in cats. • Pericardial effusion is most commonly hemorrhagic and differentiated between true cardiac puncture and pericardial effusion by the presence and absence of a clot, respectively. • Pericardial effusion is most accurately diagnosed sonographically through the use of multiple views, being careful not to mistake a cardiac chamber for pericardial (or pleural) effusion. • The safest echocardiogram views for the diagnosis of pericardial effusion are those in which the cham- bers are clearly identified with pericardial effusion clearly outside the heart and in between it and the pericardial sac. • Cardiac tamponade is a life‐threatening condition requiring emergent pericardiocentesis. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 425 Introduction The Vet BLUE protocol was developed in 2010 after finding pulmonary pathology at the TFAST chest tube site view and was first described in our first edition (Lisciandro 2014a,b). Vet BLUE added seven more acoustic windows (views) beyond TFAST for lung evaluation and is the veterinary modification of the BLUE Protocol (Bedside Lung Ultrasound Examination) in humans (Lichtenstein and Meziere 2008). Vet BLUE (Veterinary Brief Lung Ultrasound Exam) is designed so that its regional pattern‐based approach may be applied rapidly and at the point of care in any respiratory small animal (Lisciandro 2014a,b; Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2017, 2018; Ward et al. 2017). Without the delay of radiography and computed tomography, Vet BLUE helps guide therapy to stabilize the patient for continued work‐up (Ward et al. 2017, 2019; Dicker et al. 2019). Vet BLUE findings may be correlated to thoracic radiography (TXR) and computed tomography (CT). Moreover, Vet BLUE is consistent with how most veterinarians interpret thoracic radiog- raphy with its regional pattern‐based approach of Caudodorsal, Perihilar, Middle, and Cranial lung region views (Lisciandro 2014b; Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2017; Ward et al. 2017, 2018b, 2019). So why the delay in the uptake of lung ultrasound (LUS) use in small animal veterinary medicine? It is true that ultrasound waves do not transmit through air but rather are reflected, and therefore ultrasonog - raphy does not allow visualization of aerated lung parenchyma in the way that is allows visualization of nonviscous soft tissue and fluid‐filled structures. However, the surface of the lung is visible on ultra- sound, and the epiphany is that LUS is extremely sensitive for lung surface pathology (Volpicelli et al. 2006, 2012; Lichtenstein and Meziere 2008; Rademacher et al. 2014; Kulhavy and Lisciandro 2015; Ward et al. 2017, 2018b; Dicker et al. 2019). Furthermore, many types of lung pathology, including alveolar‐interstitial edema, consolidation, and nodules, cause easily recog- nizable LUS artifacts that can be detected with high sensitivity and specificity (Kulhavy and Lisciandro 2015; Ward et al. 2017, 2018b; Dicker et al. 2019). In fact, Vet BLUE may actually be more sensitive than TXR for detecting alveolar‐interstitial edema, metastatic nodules, and lung contusions (Kulhavy and Lisciandro 2015; Lisciandro et al. 2016; Ward et al. 2018b; Vezzosi et al. 2017; Dicker et al. 2019); and per - forms well when compared to CT for many respiratory conditions in people and lung contusions in dogs (Volpicelli et al. 2006; Dicker et al. 2019). For example, CT is sensitive enough to reliably detect metastatic lung nodules as small as 1–2 mm in contrast to radiog- raphy, which has a threshold of 7–9 mm (Nemanic et al. 2006). In this same study, TXR compared to CT only detected metastatic nodules in 9% of cases. Vet BLUE gives you another option for cost‐effective pulmonary metastasis screening as a same‐day, same‐patient visit, rapid, point‐of‐care imaging modality. In a comparative study with TXR, Vet BLUE outperformed TXR and was shown to detect nodules POCUS: Vet BLUE – Introduction and Image Acquisition Gregory R. Lisciandro and Stephanie C. 426 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER at the lung surface that were smaller than 1 mm (Kulhavy and Lisciandro 2015). In people, it has been shown that most acute lung pathology extends to the lung surface and is thus detected by LUS (Lichtenstein and Meziere 2008; Volpicelli et al. 2006, 2012). Through our published and unpublished Vet BLUE research, we have found similar findings: acute conditions make it to the lung surface in dogs and cats (Lisciandro 2012, unpublished data). There is no reason to suspect that this differs from any other mammalian lung (Smith et al. 2012; Yarto and Lisciandro 2017, unpublished data). The limitation of any LUS examination is that in order to be visualized, pathology must extend very near to the peripheral, lung referred to as the “lung line” by the authors, which in people represents the outer 1–3 mm of lung (Volpicelli et al. 2006). Thus, if the pulmonary pathology occurs centrally within the lung and/or does not extend to the “lung line” at the acoustic window being used, then the pulmonary lesion will not be imaged regardless of pro- tocol used. Thus, a major limitation of LUS is that it can only detect peripheral lesions present in an acoustic window being imaged; however, you will quickly find out how much Vet BLUE improves your current respiratory diagnostic and monitoring practice – the limitation approximates triviality. In this chapter, we will cover how to perform the Vet BLUE lung ultrasound examination including relative anatomy, basic artifacts, the Vet BLUE B‐line scoring system, and briefly its regional pattern‐based approach. We will also cover its comparison to the other veteri- nary LUS protocols and differences in B‐line scoring. Chapter 23 integrates the six Vet BLUE lung ultra- sound signs with practical clinically relevant Vet BLUE applications. Enjoy the ride into this new imaging frontier! We have made proactive lung ultrasound relevant and no small animal veterinarian has done as much proactive lung ultrasound as we have … 1000+ exams over 16 years. What Vet BLUE Can Do • Provide a standardized regional pattern‐based approach for lung ultrasound examination. • Provide a systematic manner in which to record findings. • Can rapidly rule out clinically relevant alveolar‐ interstitial edema including left‐sided congestive heart failure by the finding of absent B‐lines at all Vet BLUE views. • Can rapidly detect signs of alveolar‐interstitial syn- drome (cardiogenic or noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, pneumonia, or other causes of increased extravascular lung water) with the finding of B‐lines at Vet BLUE views. • Can “score” the degree of alveolar‐interstitial edema by using the Vet BLUE B‐line scoring system. • Can justify the use of loop diuretics in patients with left‐sided congestive heart failure using the Vet BLUE B‐line scoring system. • Can guide loop diuretic therapy for patients with left‐sided congestive heart failure using the Vet BLUE B‐line scoring system. • Can “score” the degree of lung contusions using the Vet BLUE B‐line lung contusion scoring system. What Vet BLUE Cannot Do • Provide a definitive diagnosis for underlying cause of lung pathology. • Detect centrally (deeper) located lung pathology or conditions that are not in contact with the lung sur- face at a Vet BLUE acoustic window. • Replace a complete physical examination, thoracic radiography, or CT imaging when indicated. Indications • Point‐of‐care screening for patients with respiratory‐related clinical signs (tachypnea, respiratory distress, cough) and for patients at risk for respiratory complications. • Rapid assessment of patients with respiratory‐ related clinical signs deemed too unstable for TXR or CT, or when additional imaging is delayed because of lack of resources. • Serial monitoring of respiratory patients using a rapid, noninvasive, radiation‐sparing, point‐of‐ care imaging modality. • Use as a guide for diuretic therapy by monitoring persistence or resolution of B‐lines and the Vet BLUE B‐line scoring system. • Use as a guide for fluid resuscitation or for detec- tion of volume overload (cardiogenic pulmonary edema) in at‐risk hospitalized and critically ill patients. • Use in hospitalized patients for the presence and absence of volume overload, aspiration pneu- monia, atelectatic lung, pulmonary thromboembo- lism, and others. Objectives (T able 22.1) • Be able to perform Vet BLUE and understand the principles of image acquisition and its pitfalls.

427 POCUS: VET BLUE – INTRODUCTION AND IMAGE ACQUISITION • Be able to recognize normal appearance of aerated lung by A‐lines with lung sliding at the pulmonary– pleural interface, also referred to as the “lung line.” • Be able to recognize LUS artifacts associated with alveolar‐interstitial syndrome by the presence of B‐lines (previously called ultrasound lung rockets). • Be able to recognize the shred sign, tissue sign, nodule sign, and wedge sign. • Be able to integrate the Vet BLUE regional pattern‐ based approach with the patient’s clinical profile for an evidence‐based working diagnosis by “see- ing” the condition. Patient Preparation T o Clip or Not? Hair is generally not shaved but rather parted, with acoustic coupling medium applied as directly to the skin as possible, minimizing air trapping (see Figure 5.2). Isopropyl alcohol is often used alone or as a com- ponent of the coupling medium. Isopropyl alcohol should not be used when electrical defibrillation is anticipated (fire/burn hazard) or if prohibited by the transducer manufacturer due to risk of probe head damage. Commercially available acoustic coupling gel may be used on the probe head while the isopropyl alcohol is used to wet and part the hair, maximizing transducer–skin contact. Alcohol‐based hand sanitizer, which has the advantage of being an excellent cou- pling medium, is much less noxious (not as chilling) to the skin and lungs (irritating fumes) than isopropyl alcohol, and wipes off much more easily than commer- cially available acoustic coupling gel. If the sonogra- pher prefers clipping, clip in patients with longer hair using the smallest clipping width possible from ven- tral to dorsal so that the hair may be feathered to cover the clipped area, making clients much happier. 428 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Lights On or Off? Imaging quality is generally sufficient without dim- ming lights in most indoor environments. Dimming lights potentially detracts from finding important equipment and avoiding hazards during resuscitation when time is critical. In all of the published AFAST, TFAST and Vet BLUE studies, lights were rarely dimmed for the ultrasound examinations (Lisciandro et al. 2008, 2009, 2014, 2017, 2018). In a human prospec- tive study evaluating the efficacy of ultrasound during cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), similar favor - able conclusions regarding ambient light were reached (Breitkreutz et al. 2010a,b; McEntee et al. 2011). However, depending on the machine and sonogra- pher’s preference and the clinical situation, lighting may be appropriately dimmed for image optimization. Patient Positioning Standing and Sternal are Safest Vet BLUE is most often performed in standing position because its nine acoustic windows are readily acces- sible in this position (Figure 22.1). Moreover, standing is generally safer and more comfortable for the patient. Sternal recumbency is also used in fragile respiratory or compromised patients. A roll of towels may be placed under the forelegs to access more ventral Vet BLUE (and TFAST) acoustic windows, especially help- ful in felines (see Figures 19.2 and 39.28). When patients present recumbent, Vet BLUE may be performed on the exposed hemithorax along with the FAST dia- phragmatico‐hepatic (DH) view, with the opposing hemithorax performed by moving the patient to sternal/standing or to their opposing side. Most importantly, sternal or standing is preferred for patients with confirmed or suspected respiratory dis- ease, those that are respiratory compromised or respiratory distressed, and those that are questionably stable and hemodynamically fragile. Dorsal recumbency should never be used in unstable or questionably stable patients (Sigrist et al. 2004, 2011; Lisciandro et al. 2008, 2011; Boysen and Lisciandro 2013). A Vet BLUE/TFAST approach should be per - formed first before any significant restraint to rule out obvious pulmonary conditions, pleural effusion, and other pleural space‐occupying conditions, pericardial effusion, cardiac abnormalities, and ascites (see Chapters 17 and 18). Excessive restraint or placing a hemodynamically fragile patient in dorsal recumbency is risky because the additional restraint and stress/ anxiety can lead to increased oxygen demand, which is then compounded by the reduction of tidal volume and venous return through the weight of abdominal organs on the diaphragm and the caudal vena cava, respectively (see Figure 6.5). In human medicine, it is suggested to “never send a patient to radiology without a good physical exam and an extended FAST (EFAST)”; in other words, first perform a good physical exam and a Global FAST. Machine Positioning The ultrasound machine and head of the patient should be in the same sightline for better spatial orien- tation and overall safety (see Figure 5.3). For example, if the patient is decompensating (cyanotic, open‐mouth breathing) or turns to bite the sonographer or the animal holder, adjustments can be more easily made if the patient’s head is in the sightline of the ultrasound screen. If the patient’s head is facing in the opposite direction and away from the machine, the holder and sonographer are at risk for injury and the patient for unwitnessed decompensation – for example, if the patient is open‐mouth breathing or becoming cyanotic, the sonographer and the assistant cannot see the patient’s head directly. Ultrasound Settings and Probe Preferences Curvilinear Probe on Abdominal Preset versus Other • A curvilinear (microconvex) probe with a fre- quency of 5–10 MHz is generally preferred for Vet BLUE, and this same probe may be used for the entire Global FAST examination. Linear probes will provide the best detail along the lung surface; how- ever, most clinically relevant lung pathology is easily appreciated with the curvilinear probe, and curvilinear probes fit best within the contours of rib spaces. Phased‐array probes have a “pinpoint” focal point and excellent temporal resolution, and are thus preferred for cardiac ultrasound. However, preliminary studies in which the author is involved suggest that phased‐array probes are inferior to curvilinear probes for visualization and enumera- tion of B‐lines. • Depth is set at 4–8 (up to 9–10) cm for most patients. Depth settings that are too low (“too close” to the lung) make it possible to miss lung lesions that fill the screen, and depth set- tings that are too high (“too far away” from the lung) make it possible to miss smaller lung surface pathology (see Chapter 23). Depth may be decreased (magnify) to investigate smaller lung pathology and to view details of the pulmonary–pleural inter- face (PPI), also referred to as the “lung line,” but then should be again increased to the general guide- lines of 4–8 cm (and 9–10 cm for giant breeds) (Figure 22.4). • The focal zone cursor, featured on most ultrasound machines, should be placed at the level of the PPI represented by the hyperechoic line where the vis- ceral and parietal pleura meet in normalcy in the absence of pleural space disease or where the “lung line” is located in pleural space conditions (see Figures 22.2 and 22.3). • Appropriate gain settings are very important. “Overgaining,” making the image too bright (too white), makes it difficult to see the PPI (see Figure 17.10) and artifacts along the lung surface. In gen- eral, the gain setting for Vet BLUE should be less than that for soft tissue during TFAST and AFAST, such that the screen is darker with more contrast. However, gain must also be high enough so that imaging is possible through the far‐field of the screen to accurately identify B‐lines and deeper lesions (see Figure 17.10). • Because the abdominal preset is generally used for the rest of the Global FAST examination, this preset is also often used for Vet BLUE. However, the cardiac preset may provide more contrast and be preferred by some sonographers. The author, how- ever, does the entire Global FAST on the abdom- inal preset and with a single probe type (curvilinear). • The “gator sign” is the same intercostal orientation as for the TFAST CTS view and used for all lung ultrasound orientation (see Figures 22.2 and 22.3). See the Probe Orientation section below. How to Do a Vet BLUE Exam Lung Orientation and the Gator Sign The “gator sign” is an orientation where the probe head is positioned perpendicular to the long axis of the ribs, or in the longitudinal plane for lung. The standard orientation for all lung ultrasound (LUS) begins with the observation of the “gator (alligator) sign” (Figures 22.2 and 22.3). The “gator sign” is created by the rounded rib (alligator’s eyes) with a proximal hyperechoic line in between (alligator’s bridge of nose) creating the image of a partially submerged alligator peering over the water at the sonographer. The space between the rib (alligator’s eyes) is the intercostal region with the hyperechoic line (alligator’s bridge of nose) created by the strong air–soft tissue interface rep- resenting the PPI and the “lung line (surface)” (see Figures 22.2 and 22.3). The author prefers the term “lung line” because when pleural space conditions are present, the integrity of the PPI is lost, and the term “lung line” is more accurate for what is being located and evaluated. The “gator sign” orientation is the starting point for all lung ultrasound (Lisciandro 2011; Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2017; Ward et al. 2017). This orientation is the same as described for the TFAST CTS view (Lisciandro et al. 2008; Lisciandro 2011; Boysen and Lisciandro 2013) (see Figure 17.12). The “gator sign” orientation also allows observation of the to‐and‐fro motion of “lung sliding” (Volpicelli et al. 2012), previously referred to as the “glide sign” in the veterinary litera- ture (see Figure 22.2) (Nyland and Mattoon 2002). “Lung sliding” represents the to‐and‐fro sliding of visceral and parietal pleura during inspiration and expiration, or “lung sliding” along the intercostal space. Its appearance resembles the back‐and‐forth movement of an Etch‐a‐Sketch® cursor (see Figures 22.2 and 22.3) (Lisciandro et al. 2008, 2014a,b; Lisciandro 2011). Probe Orientation: Rotate or Not Some sonographers advocate rotating the probe parallel to the ribs to get another plane of lung during LUS (Figure 22.4). Caution should be exercised unless the sonographer has an extensive knowledge of LUS imaging and its anatomical borders and pitfalls. Rotating the probe and losing sight of the “lung line” can lead to misinterpretations of abdominal structures, dorsal and ventral borders of the pleural cavity Pearl: Consider Vet BLUE as an “extension” from the TFAST CTS view, applied to three additional transthoracic lung regions per hemithorax plus the FAST DH view providing a more comprehensive lung ultrasound examination.

If transverse orientation is attempted, the lung sonogra - pher must always double‐check by appreciating the “gator sign” while rotating the probe from longitudinal to transverse and then returning to longitudinal, the author’s recommended methodology (see Chapter 41). Thus, the Vet BLUE acoustic windows are referred to as “lung regions.” Naming of the Nine Acoustic Windows There are eight bilaterally applied transthoracic acoustic windows plus the ninth acoustic window as the DH view. • Caudodorsal (Cd) lung region, right and left • Perihilar (Ph) lung region, right and left • Middle (Md) lung region, right and left • Cranial (Cr) lung region, right and left • Diaphragmatico‐hepatic view, single acoustic window Defining the Locations of the Nine Acoustic Windows (Views) T ransthoracic Views Caudodorsal Lung Region (Cd, point 1) This is defined as directly dorsal to the xiphoid in the upper third of the thorax in its 9th–10th intercostal space near the highest point over the pleural cavity with lung. The Cd view starting point is the same acoustic window used for the TFAST CTS. At this region, the sonographer looks for the caudodorsal transition zone (CdTZ) where pleural and abdominal cavities meet because you will move cranial, away from this region to start Vet BLUE. 437 POCUS: V ET BLUE – I NTRODUCTION AND I MAGE A CQUISITION Perihilar Lung Region (Ph, point 2) This is defined as the point in the middle third of the thorax between the 6th and 7th intercostal spaces approximating the perihilar region on a thoracic radiograph. The Ph (point 2) is found by “drawing” a line from the Cd (point 1) to the elbow. This is done with your acoustic coupling medium and your hand by roughing the hair along this “Vet BLUE line.” Halfway from the Cd (point 1) is the Ph (point 2) (Figure 22.11). Middle Lung Region (Md, point 3) This region is defined as the lower half of the thorax over the heart approximating the 4th–5th intercostal spaces. If the heart is in view and obscuring lung, then sweep immediately dorsal in that same intercostal space(s), finding the “lung line” and then performing the Vet BLUE examination (Figure 22.12). Cranial Lung Region (Cr, point 4) This is defined as the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd intercostal spaces – in other words, in the region caudal to the thoracic inlet and cranial to the heart. The foreleg often needs to be gently extended cranially to get this view (see Figure 22.11). The soft tissue and vessels of the thoracic inlet help define the Cr (point 4). Identify the thoracic inlet’s soft tissue structures, the cranial transition zone (CrTZ) (Figure 22.13), and then slide caudally over the first three intercostal spaces. The author recommends always extending the foreleg from the elbow region rather than the paw because some dogs (and cats) do not like their paws touched and become stressed or bite when their paws are handled. Performing the Vet BLUE Order of Vet BLUE The Vet BLUE acoustic windows are generally per - formed in the following order moving from dorsal to ventral and cranial: left Cd → Ph → Md → Cr view, then DH, followed by right Cd → Ph → Md → Cr views. The reason for beginning dorsal is to rule in or rule out pneumothorax (PTX); and when suspected the “lung point” is automatically sought by moving ven - trally along the subsequent Ph and Md lung regions. However, in most patients in which PTX is unlikely, the repetition of performing Vet BLUE after Vet BLUE after Vet BLUE on a daily basis will help the sonogra - pher become confident with observing “lung sliding” while also learning how to optimize image acquisition with the Tricks of the Trade (see Chapter 17) and adjustments in the focus cursor, gain, depth, etc. The protocol detailed below includes numerous updates and methodological improvements from the original Vet BLUE examination described in 2014 (Lisciandro 2014b; Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2017; Ward et al. 2017, 2019). 445 POCUS: VET BLUE – INTRODUCTION AND IMAGE ACQUISITION Performing Vet BLUE Step by Step (Figure 22.16) • Locate the Cd, Point 1 lung region, which is the same methodology as for the TFAST CTS view by palpating the xiphoid and then moving dor - sally to the upper third of the thorax. To recog- nize the pitfall, slide more dorsally to see the difference between being over the PPI and the “lung line” and being over the hypaxial and epaxial muscles along the vertebral column and proximal rib heads. • Place the probe perpendicular to the long axis of the ribs and appreciate the hyperechoic PPI and “lung line” (air). • Identify the “gator sign” orientation with two ribs and an interposing intercostal space starting with depth of 4–8 cm for smaller and larger patients (and giant breeds up to 9–10 cm), respectively. • With the probe stationary and the angle of insonation 90° to the PPI, make the “lung line” sharp and hyperechoic as a crisp, bright white line. The gain may need to be turned down more than was used on soft tissues, but have some gain through the far‐field so that artifacts may be seen through the entire screen. Too much gain results in poor detail along the “lung line” (see Figure 22.6). • Find the CdTZ where pleural and abdominal cav- ities meet by identifying the “curtain sign” and then slide 2–3 intercostal spaces cranially away from abdominal structures and the diaphragm (see Figures 22.9 and 22.10). This is the starting Caudodorsal lung region (Cd, point 1). • From here, slide an intercostal space caudally first, being aware of how close you are to the abdominal cavity, then return to your starting point, and then slide an intercostal space cranially before return- ing to your Cd (point 1) starting point. You have surveyed three intercostal spaces at the Vet BLUE Cd view. • From the Vet BLUE Cd starting point, draw your Vet BLUE line to the patient’s elbow using your acoustic coupling medium and a finger to roughen the hair coat along this line so it is obvious (see Figure 22.11B). • Along your Vet BLUE line, halfway to the elbow is Ph (point 2). Survey three intercostal spaces as done at Cd. Slide caudally first, being aware of pos- sible abdominal structures coming into view, and then slide cranially. You again surveyed three inter- costal spaces. • Along your Vet BLUE line, move to the elbow region for the Md (point 3). If heart is observed and obscuring lung, the probe is swept immediately dorsal until the heart is just out of view and a “gator sign” and “lung line” are identified as per - formed for the previous two views. The method- ology is repeated – slide caudally first, being aware of abdominal structures possibly coming into view, and then slide cranially. You have again surveyed three intercostal spaces. • Now begin the final Cr (point 4) by gently extend- ing the foreleg cranially to allow room to slide the probe into the axillary region (see Figures 22.10 and 22.11). The probe is held similar to all other views perpendicular to the ribs directly over the space with minimal rocking. • Slide cranial dorsal through the axillary region and identify the thoracic inlet of cervical soft tissue and vessels, keeping in mind the “check mark” track of the Vet BLUE line. Vessels, jugular vein, and carotid arteries are identified on B‐mode by pulsation and their linear and circular anechoic appearance being blood‐filled (fluid). Generally, color flow Doppler is not necessary but may be used. This is the cranial transition zone (CrTZ) and is located to the left of the screen. • By sliding too ventral, the “gator sign” will be lost in pectoral muscles that have a pennate appearance sonographically. To recognize the pit- fall, slide ventrally and image the pectoral mus- cles to become familiar with their pennate appearance (see Figures 22.17D, 34.1, 35.1, and 35.14). • Slide caudally from the CrTZ and see in the follow- ing order: rib 1, intercostal space 1, rib 2, intercostal space 2, rib 3, intercostal space 3. You have now surveyed the first three intercostal spaces of Cr (point 4). • The transthoracic Vet BLUE acoustic windows have been completed on the left hemithorax and the same methodology is performed on the right hemithorax (see Figure 22.12). • The DH view is the nontransthoracic acoustic window that provides a deep window into lung along the pulmonary–diaphragmatic interface and is invaluable in identifying lung pathology not evi- dent at the three transthoracic acoustic windows (see Figure 22.14). In summary, three intercostal spaces have been surveyed at each of the respective Vet BLUE views. Always slide caudally first so that the question may
