447 POCUS: VET BLUE – INTRODUCTION AND IMAGE ACQUISITION be asked “how close am I to the transition zone of pleural and peritoneal cavities (to prevent mistaking abdominal structures for lung pathology)?” The lung sonographer also quickly becomes attuned to the variability in amount of liver, stomach wall and lumen, and gallbladder that is viewed along the pleural‐peritoneal transition zone of points Cd‐1, Ph‐2, and Md‐3 and how easily these structures can be mistaken for pathology. The methodology described here is improved from our original publi- cation by better recognizing pitfalls and being a more repeatable LUS examination and will soon be published. Vet BLUE is a proactive screening test that is regional and pattern based. The findings within each region may be recorded and followed over time. In contrast, the scanning of every intercostal space loses regional- ity and a pattern‐based approach and lacks specific Vet BLUE data points for monitoring (see Vet BLUE B‐line Scoring and Comparison to Other Lung Ultrasound Formats below). Trouble Shooting Avoiding the Phenomenon of Drifting Drifting occurs by the weight of your hand moving the probe into a different location than where you think you are imaging by watching the screen and ignoring the external position of the probe on your patient. Make a habit of placing fingers (or part of your hand) of your probe hand on the patient’s thoracic wall, so‐called “kickstanding” of the probe, so that you can comfortably maintain contact with your patient and thus prevent drifting away from where you think you are imaging (see Figure 5.9). Moreover, V‐troughing the patient with your helper hand (nonprobe hand) prevents your patient from swaying and losing probe‐to‐skin contact and thus your nice acoustic window, which delays the study and often leads to sonographer frustration (see Figure 5.7). Confounders of Lung Ultrasound Adhering to the following axiom serves the lung sonographer well: If you cannot appreciate the “gator sign” orientation and accurately identify the “lung line” then you cannot be certain that you are in fact looking at lung. Confounders include the following. Imaging Outside the Boundaries of the Pleural Cavity Caudally Abdominal structures including the liver, stomach and its rugal folds, and the gallbladder. • The liver can be mistaken for lung consolidation, a “pseudo tissue sign,” defined in Chapter 23. • The stomach wall can be seen as an anechoic stripe mimicking and thus potentially being mistaken for pleural effusion, although pleural effusion gener - ally occurs ventrally with aerated lungs rising (floating) dorsally and would never be noted at the least gravity‐dependent region. • The stomach and its rugal folds can be mistaken for a “pseudo shred sign,” defined in Chapter 23. • The stomach and its gastric luminal contents (ingesta having fluid and air) can create “pseudo gastric B‐lines,” defined in Chapter 23 (see Figures 18.3 and 22.10). • The gallbladder, depending on its luminal con- tents, can be mistaken for lung pathology or pleural/pericardial effusion. Dorsally The hypaxial muscles along the rib heads and spine (Figures 22.17 and 22.18). Ventrally The pectoral muscles and soft tissue along the sternum including vessels. Muscle has an ultrasonographically pennate appearance (see Figures 22.17, 34.1, 35.1, and 35.14). Cranially The thoracic inlet and its soft tissue including vessels (see Figure 22.17). Craniodorsal The periscapular muscles and the scapula. The bony scapula is a smooth surface and can mimic the “lung line” (see Figures 22.17 and 41.21C). Subcutaneous Emphysema • Air between the skin and intercostal space, subcu- taneous emphysema (SQE), will obscure the “lung line” by dirty shadowing, often with A‐lines as expected at any strong air–soft tissue interface

453 POCUS: V ET BLUE – I NTRODUCTION AND I MAGE A CQUISITION Figure 22.23. Composite of three different published lung ultrasound formats. The composite emphasizes how important critical thinking is when determining what lung ultrasound format works best for the patient. In each row is a different LUS format illustrated with “theory” and “reality” to show what the actual acoustic windows survey. In row (A), the Vet BLUE theory and reality has acoustic windows that are the same. The Vet BLUE B‐line scoring system (0, 1, 2, 3, >3, and infinity [∞]), explained in detail in Chapter 23, is applied to each of its nine views, thus there are nine scores. In row (B), the ZigZag Intercostal Continuum (ZZIC) method is applied to every intercostal space; however, this is impossible because of the scapula and its associated musculature especially in a standing (sternal) patient so “theory” and “reality” are quite different. The scor- ing system is per hemithorax, thus two scores, making it difficult to assess the degree of alveolar‐interstitial edema (B‐lines). For example, once >3 B‐lines are observed, focally or diffusely over an individual hemithorax, the ZZIC score is the same, “>3,” when degrees of edema are radically different (focal score of >3 is much less edema than diffusely >3). Moreover, with a Vet BLUE pattern‐based approach, the patient with the score of >3 B‐lines focally over a middle lung region likely has aspiration pneumonia, and the patient with >3 B‐lines diffusely likely has left‐sided congestive heart failure. These differences are lost with a per hemithorax scoring system. In row (C) is the four‐quadrant approach, and the amount of lung is markedly different between “theory” and “reality.” The black and tan dachshund is in fact the published four‐quadrant format (Rademacher et al. 2014). The methodology is sliding cranially and caudally as shown with arrows and each quadrant is scored. The asymmetry of amount of lung coupled with sliding over the same lung may contribute to a higher score than the patient really has (like - wise, it is possible Vet BLUE underestimates and the ZZIC loses semiquantitation inherently through a per hemithorax approach). It is worth taking the time to think out these three formats. Source: Reproduced with permission from Dr Gregory Lisciandro, Hill Country Veterinary Specialists and FASTVet.com, Spicewood, TX. 454 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER induced PTX, presumably intubated and mechanically ventilated although this is unclear from the publica- tion (Hwang et al. 2018). However, the use of positive pressure ventilation has important implications on LUS findings because free air in the pleural space is unnaturally pushed into different regions (see Figures 18.7 and 18.8). In both LUS formats, the canine thorax was divided into four quadrants: caudal dorsal, caudal ventral, cranial dorsal, and cranial ventral. The level of the elbow was defined as the border between dorsal and ventral in the left‐sided CHF study (Rademacher et al. 2014) and the shoulder in the PTX study (Hwang et al. 2018). Using these landmarks as LUS bound- aries, the reality is an asymmetrical division of lung (see Figure 22.23). In both LUS four‐quadrant formats, the dorsal regions encompass more potential lung than the ventral regions, and the caudal dorsal and caudal ventral regions are in reality over very little lung (see Figure 22.23). The four‐quadrant left‐sided CHF study used a linear probe (versus microconvex with Vet BLUE) and the average time per examination was 10 min- utes (Rademacher et al. 2014), much longer than a Vet BLUE (<2 minutes) (Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2017; Ward et al. 2017). Each quadrant was evaluated using a “sliding” methodology, moving the probe caudal to cranial and then cranial to caudal within each of the four quadrants (see Figure 22.23). Numbers of B‐lines were totaled per quadrant. The authors found that 31% of unaffected dogs had at least one B‐line, with a mean number of 0.9 +/‐ 0.3 B‐lines per normal dog. In contrast and as expected, in left‐sided CHF there was a much higher mean number of B‐lines per patient (6.2 +/‐ 3.8). A major difference between the four‐quadrant CHF approach and Vet BLUE is that by “sliding” over each quad- rant, the overlapping of previously imaged lung is possible, which may account for the higher numbers of B‐lines seen in normal dogs in that study (Rademacher et al. 2014) than in Vet BLUE studies (Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2017; Ward et al. 2017, 2018a, 2019), or conversely Vet BLUE may underestimate. Importantly, locations of LUS‐detected cardiogenic pulmonary edema correlated with locations found on thoracic radiography (Rademacher et al. 2014) similar to Vet BLUE studies (Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2017; Ward et al. 2017, 2018b). However, the four‐ quadrant approach does not inherently correlate LUS regions and their respective findings to thoracic radiography as Vet BLUE does. Moreover, with the disproportionality of lung in the four‐quadrant approach, degrees of alveolar‐interstitial edema likely seem more difficult to appreciate. The other four‐quadrant approach study evaluated experimentally induced PTX and compared three imaging modalities – LUS, thoracic radiography (TXR), and computed tomography (CT) – within 30 minutes (Hwang et al. 2018). This study presents an interesting approach, but unless the reader is experi- enced in LUS, they may overlook its nuances. Briefly, thoracostomy tubes were placed under general anes- thesia and it is unclear whether ventilation was con- trolled via positive pressure ventilation (PPV) or these dogs were spontaneously breathing. This is important because PPV manipulates how free air within the pleural cavity is distributed because PPV presumably pushes (redistributes) the free air (PTX) unnaturally into pockets (see Figures 18.7 and 18.8). Moreover, their four quadrants are unequal and asymmetrical regarding amount of lung surveyed and lack the ability to find a “lung point” (see Figure 18.9). In fact, their caudal dorsal and caudal ventral quadrants are over very little if any lung. Their methodology, how- ever, provides an interesting approach for diagnosing PTX. Historically, the CdTZ has been avoided because the respirophasic dynamics for observing “lung sliding” are confounded by the complexity of movement by the lung, its “curtain sign,” and the adjacent abdominal structures. However, Hwang and colleagues suggest that the CdTZ region is an effective site for detecting small‐volume PTX, supported by comparative imaging of TXR and CT, and more recent research has shown similar more understandable findings (and technique) using the CdTZ with PTX diagnosed using the “reverse curtain sign” and “dou- ble curtain sign” (Boysen et al. 2019). Zigzag Intercostal Continuum Approach The Zigzag Intercostal Continuum (ZZIC) Approach (author’s term) was published by investigators who evaluated dogs with different stages of degenerative mitral valve disease based on the ACVIM classification system (Vezzosi et al. 2017). The study was well done, but without critically reviewing the methodology, its nuances and weaknesses may not be appreciated by the reader. Dogs were not shaved but rather the hair was parted and isopropyl alcohol and acoustic coupling gel were used for imaging the entire hemithorax. Every intercostal space was eval- uated using a linear probe (see Figure 22.23). The study found that significant numbers of B‐lines were only detected in dogs with stage C degenerative mitral valve disease with active left‐sided congestive heart failure, a well‐founded and clinically relevant

455 POCUS: VET BLUE – INTRODUCTION AND IMAGE ACQUISITION finding. Dogs with preclinical degenerative mitral valve disease (B1, B2) and dogs with treated/com- pensated stage C disease had none to rare B‐lines, again a well‐founded and clinically relevant finding. LUS correlated with findings of cardiogenic pulmonary edema on TXR similar to findings on the other studies (Rademacher et al. 2014; Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2016, 2017; Ward et al. 2017, 2018b). In fact, it was suggested that LUS may have been more sensitive than TXR for detecting cardiogenic pulmonary edema by finding B‐lines in some dogs that had unremarkable TXR lung, similar to other studies (Rademacher et al. 2014; Lisciandro et al. 2016; Ward et al. 2017, 2018b). The LUS examination methodology, though, has important features that should be critically consid- ered. The ZZIC scoring system was an estimation of total number of B‐lines per hemithorax (numerous/ confluent vs absent/rare), and inherently lacked the ability to assess the presence and number of B‐lines at any discrete views other than per hemithorax. Thus, the ZZIC not only is deficient in being able to semiquantitate degree of cardiogenic pulmonary edema (numbers of B‐lines), but it also lacks a regional pattern‐based approach and is unable to dif- ferentiate causes of alveolar‐interstitial edema (dis- tribution of B‐lines) (see Figure 22.23). Secondly, similar to the four‐quadrant approach, the ZZIC in theory appears to be an extensive lung evaluation, but the scapula and its associated musculature pre- vent much of the cranial dorsal thoracic lung being evaluated (see Figure 22.23). Thirdly, and very impor - tantly and similar to the four‐quadrant approach, knowledge of the pitfalls of LUS along its caudal, cranial, dorsal, and ventral boundaries is essential to avoid mistaking each of these regions for lung pathology, important for lung sonography training (see Figure 22.17). Moreover, extreme margins of highly reflective aerated lung inherently lend them- selves to creating artifact by the ultrasound striking reflective margins and thin portions of lung (author’s experience). Some final questions not specifically covered in the ZZIC methodology should be considered. How does the lung sonographer image every intercostal space dorsal to ventral in a thickly coated breed with no shaving and isopropyl alcohol and coupling gel? How cold does a smaller patient get with the amount of isopropyl alcohol over each hemithorax? Moreover, are there any patient problems with the resultant nox- ious fumes if the patient is placed in a closed environ- ment like an oxygen cage? Where do you accurately restart your ZZIC study when the patient moves? How were ZZIC sonographers trained to recognize the caudal, cranial, ventral, and dorsal borders of the lung along the thorax? These features of the ZZIC method- ology were recognized in part by the author when evaluating both LUS methods, ZZIC and Vet BLUE, in dolphins (see Chapter 41). Recording Vet BLUE Findings on Goal‐directed Templates Recording your findings is imperative for a successful ultrasound program. See Chapter 23. Pearls and Pitfalls, The Final Say • Vet BLUE is a regional pattern‐based approach that is standardized with exact clarity to its acoustic windows. • Vet BLUE is correlative to the manner in which most veterinarians view thoracic radiography. • The caudodorsal transition zone is important to be able to identify because the lung sonographer may easily mistake abdominal structures without recog- nizing this pitfall. • The first three Vet BLUE acoustic windows of Caudodorsal, Perihilar, and Middle are along the Vet BLUE line to the elbow and importantly the sonographer always slides caudally first to ask “How close am I to the transition zone of the pleural and peritoneal cavity abdominal cavity?” • All Vet BLUE acoustic windows survey three inter- costal spaces. • The cranial transition zone is identified by soft tissue structures of the neck and the probe then slides caudally over the first three intercostal spaces for a repeatable and accurate Cranial lung region. • Boundaries to lung should generally be avoided, but the sonographic appearance of these structures should be known to the lung sonographer to avoid mistaking them for lung pathology. • The pulmonary–pleural interface and “lung line” are optimized by adjusting depth, gain, and focus cursor with a depth of 4–8 cm for small to large patients (up to 9–10 cm in giant breeds), respectively. • There are major differences in lung imaged and scoring systems between Vet BLUE, the four‐quad- rant approach, and the ZigZag Intercostal Continuum that must be understood.

456 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Quick Reference of Normals and Rules of Thumb • Expect adult dogs and cats and puppies and kit- tens >6 weeks of age to have “dry lung” artifacts predominate (absent B‐lines). In other words, no more than a single B‐line at only one of the eight transthoracic Vet BLUE views. • Numbers of B‐lines correlate to the degree of alve- olar‐interstitial edema in human lung and likely similar in other mammalian lung including small animals. • “Absent B‐lines All (Vet BLUE) Views (ABAV)” rules out clinically relevant left‐sided congestive heart failure in both dogs and cats (and likely for all mammalian lung) (see Chapter 23). • The Volpicelli Strong Positive Model is an effective screening test to rule in left‐sided congestive heart failure in cats (see Chapter 23). • Shred sign in gravity‐dependent Vet BLUE views supports aspiration and bacterial bronchopneu- monia (see Chapter 23). • Wedge sign in the dorsal nongravity‐dependent Vet BLUE views supports pulmonary thromboem- bolism (see Chapter 23). • Nodule sign supports neoplastic, granulomatous processes including fungal, parasitic and bacterial, and abscessation (see Chapter 23). Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 459 Introduction Over thirty 30 years ago, a physician, Roy Filly, MD, dubbed the ultrasound probe “the modern stetho- scope.” Although lung ultrasound (LUS) has been uti- lized by large animal veterinarians for decades, especially on the equine side, there has been no easily understandable lung language until the first edition of this book (Lisciandro 2014b). The lung language that we propose, including the terms “dry lung,” “wet lung,” shred sign, tissue sign, nodule sign, and wedge sign to describe specific findings, allows clear commu- nication of findings between colleagues. The use of lung ultrasound in veterinary practice is proving to be an invaluable tool to assess patients for pulmonary disease. Lung ultrasound artifacts and their integration into a regional pattern‐based approach have provided a new tool that in human medicine replaces the subjec- tivity of lung auscultation as well as the unreliability of supine chest radiography and breathing patterns (Volpicelli et al. 2012). The ultrasound probe is the “visual stethoscope” and allows the sonographer to “see” versus hearing (and guessing) as to the type of lung pathology (Filly 1988, Lichtenstein and Mezière 2008; Volpicelli et al. 2006; Lisciandro 2011, 2012, 2013, unpublished data; Moore and Copel 2011; Lisciandro et al. 2014; Gillman and Kirkpatrick 2012). Vet BLUE (Brief Lung Ultrasound Exam) is a protocol for lung ultrasound that provides an additional imaging modality which serves as both a practical pulmonary screening test and an adjunct for the often problematic interpretation of radiographic lung. The use of the ultrasound probe as a visual stetho- scope allows point‐of‐care imaging of lung ultrasound artifacts and signs along the lung surface, providing evidence‐based clinical information. Vet BLUE lung ultrasound when used in clinical practice may function as a screening test or a primary and ancillary imaging modality as well as a point‐of‐care monitoring tool without the restraint and risk of radiographic studies (see Table 23.1). In this chapter, we describe our lung language, including the six Vet BLUE lung ultrasound signs and their clinical applications. We use the term “B‐lines” in place of “ultrasound lung rockets” (Volpicelli et al. 2012; Lisciandro et al. 2014). We expand on the information from the first edition of this textbook add- ing years of additional information we have learned about lung ultrasound since its publication. Enjoy the ride into this new frontier! What Vet BLUE Can Do • Can rapidly rule out clinically relevant alveolar‐ interstitial edema by the finding of “dry lung.” • Can rapidly rule out left‐sided congestive heart failure in patients with respiratory distress by the finding of “dry lung all (Vet BLUE) views” abbrevi- ated as ABAV (Absent B-lines All Views). • Can rapidly detect signs of alveolar‐interstitial syn- drome (cardiogenic and noncardiogenic pulmonary edema) using the “wet lung” (B‐lines) principle. • Can rapidly and preemptively detect the development of alveolar‐interstitial syndrome using the “wet lung” principle in patients at risk for volume overload (fluid resuscitation, transfu- sion administration, mechanical ventilation, kidney failure, hypoalbuminemia, heart disease, POCUS: Vet BLUE – Clinical Integration Gregory R. Lisciandro and Stephanie C. Lisciandro CHAPTER TWENTY-THREE

460 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER etc.) and those at risk for pulmonary hemorrhage (coagulopathic). • Can guide loop diuretic therapy using the Vet BLUE B‐line scoring system by counting B‐lines at each respective Vet BLUE view and combining with numbers of positive Vet BLUE regions. • Can rapidly and often preemptively detect the development of acute lung injury/acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and its related subsets. • Can rapidly and often preemptively detect aspira- tion pneumonia in at risk patients. • Can screen for pulmonary thromboembolism (PTE) and be used as a tool to trigger thromboprophy- laxis and thrombolytics. • Serves as a rapid point‐of‐care pulmonary metas- tasis check. • Can detect lung surface pathology not evident on thoracic radiography. • Can help when combining with Global FAST and its TFAST echo views to differentiate true respiratory conditions from nonrespiratory look‐alikes. • Can provide evidence‐based information to help determine your next best diagnostic test in work‐ups. • Can detect lung patterns in trauma patients that support pulmonary contusions. • Can provide a Vet BLUE lung contusion severity score by numbers of B‐lines at each respective Vet BLUE view combined with the number of positive Vet BLUE regions. • Can provide an evidence‐based working diagnosis for respiratory and nonrespiratory conditions that helps keep patients alive for subsequent imaging and gold standard testing and treatment. • Can be used for monitoring response to therapy (serial exams) in many lung conditions, including cardiogenic and non‐cardiogenic pulmonary edema, pulmonary contusions, pulmonary hemor- rhage, pneumonias, neoplasia, and granulomatous disease. What Vet BLUE Cannot Do • Cannot give a definitive diagnosis. Vet BLUE pro- vides regional pattern‐based evidence for certain lung conditions similar to interpretative conclu- sions using thoracic radiography (TXR) and computed tomography (CT) although likely with higher sensitivity for lung surface pathology. • Cannot detect lung pathology that is deep to the peripheral margin of lung or pathology that is not present at one of its views. Vet BLUE is limited to lung disease that makes it to the lung periphery and must also be present at the view being used. • Cannot fully replace TXR or CT but may be used as an adjunctive diagnostic aid, a screening test, and a monitoring tool for many diagnosed conditions. Indications • A screening test for patients with respiratory signs, respiratory compromise or distress, and for patients at risk for respiratory complications. • Point‐of‐care rapid assessment for patients too unstable for TXR or CT, or when additional imaging is delayed because of lack of resources. 461 POCUS: V ET BLUE – C LINICAL I NTEGRATION • Monitoring response to therapy in many respiratory patients as a rapid, noninvasive, radiation‐sparing, and point‐of‐care imaging modality. • As a guide for loop diuretic usage by using the Vet BLUE B‐line scoring system. • Use as a guide for fluid resuscitation or for early detection of volume overload (cardiogenic pulmonary edema) in at‐risk hospitalized and crit- ically ill patients, especially when combined with the Global FAST approach including its TFAST echo views. Objectives • Apply the simple “wet lung” and “dry lung” lung ultrasound concepts in a regional pattern‐based approach following the Vet BLUE protocol; thus, be able to categorize respiratory distressed patients into probable causes including upper airway versus lower airway, lung disease versus congestive heart failure, and nonrespiratory (so‐called respiratory look‐alikes) versus respiratory causes. • Recognize additional lung conditions through rec - ognition of the Vet BLUE visual lung language of shred sign, tissue sign, nodule sign, and wedge sign. • Preemptively anticipate thoracic radiographic findings by using the Vet BLUE visual lung lan - guage in a regional pattern‐based approach. • Make evidence‐based decisions regarding therapeutic course (initial assessment as well as monitoring) in patients with respiratory disease or affected animals. The Global FAST exam includes Vet BLUE combined with AFAST and TFAST. We recommend always performing the complete Global FAST approach because a problem list is “seen,” and thus, the interpre- tation and clinical integration of Vet BLUE findings are optimized. For example, a nodule sign found during AFAST in a younger outdoor cat in central Texas with an enlarged spleen (>10 mm in thickness) and no other apparent masses may dictate fungal serology as the next best test because of the high suspicion of histo - plasmosis. Multiple nodule signs on Vet BLUE in a dog with a hemoabdomen and cavitated splenic mass may support metastatic disease. A dog with dilated cardio- myopathy (DCM) will present with a dry cough and unremarkable TXR but on TFAST has obvious poor contractility (DCM) that would otherwise be missed. By only performing Vet BLUE, satisfaction of search error often occurs, and essential information is missed, as in the cases mentioned above. See Chapters 36 and 37 for staging the patient on day 1 (Table 23.1). Important Considerations and Limitations of Vet BLUE and Lung Ultrasound Before beginning this chapter, there are several points that must be appreciated by the lung sonographer and those using the Vet BLUE protocol. • Significant, acute, common, clinically relevant pulmonary disease most likely extends to the lung periphery in dogs and cats and other mammalian lung, similar to what has been found in people (Lichtenstein and Mezière 2008; Lichtenstein 2010a; Soldati et al. 2011; Volpicelli et al. 2012; Lisciandro 2012, unpublished data; Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2016, 2017; Ward et al. 2017, 2018b). However, if lung pathology doesn’t extend in close proximity to the “lung line” (outer ~1–3 mm of human lung), the lung’s peripheral surface at an acoustic window being used during lung ultrasound, then it will be missed (Volpicelli et al. 2006) (Figure 23.1). • Centrally located lung disease will be missed (occult lesion) by lung ultrasound because ultra - sound cannot image through aerated lung (Soldati et al. 2011; Volpicelli et al. 2006, 2012; Kulhavy and Lisciandro 2015; Dicker et al. 2019) (see Figure 23.1). In (B) is the lung anatomy and what is being missed in (A) because the pathology does not touch the “lung line.” The stars represent lung pathology such as alveolar‐interstitial syndrome that does not extend to the lung surface and thus will go unde - tected during LUS. 462 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER • B‐lines in most instances represent forms of alveolar‐interstitial edema, referred to as alveolar‐ interstitial syndrome (AIS), but B‐lines are nonspe- cific for the cause of alveolar‐interstitial edema (Lichtenstein et al. 1997; Lichtenstein and Mezière 2008; Volpicelli et al. 2006, 2012). • Alveolar‐interstitial syndrome is referred to as a “syndrome” because B‐lines are nonspecific and thus may represent forms of cardiogenic and non- cardiogenic pulmonary edema, pneumonia, hem- orrhage and other inflammatory conditions (Soldati et al. 2006; Lisciandro 2011, 2014a,b; Volpicelli et al. 2012; Rademacher et al. 2014; Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2017; Ward et al. 2017, 2019). In trauma patients, the finding of AIS supports lung contusions until proven otherwise (Ball et al. 2009; Lisciandro et al. 2008; Lisciandro 2011, 2014a,b; Dicker et al. 2019). Think of AIS most com- monly as “wet lung” with the presence of B‐lines. • Vet BLUE can effectively detect AIS that correlates with radiographic lung (Rademacher et al. 2014; Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2016, 2017; Ward et al. 2017, 2018b; Vezzosi et al. 2017; Szymczak et al. 2018), and with higher fre- quency than TXR and comparable to CT in human, canine, and feline lung (Volpicelli et al. 2006, 2012; Lichtenstein 2010b; Ward et al. 2018b; Dicker et al. 2019). • Vet BLUE can effectively detect pulmonary contu- sions with higher sensitivity and specificity than TXR and fares well compared to the gold standard of CT (Dicker et al. 2019). • Alveolar‐interstitial edema (B‐lines) represents extravascular lung water, and precedes alveolar flooding, a more serious and more difficult lung condition to treat; thus B‐lines serve as an early warning sign to alter therapeutic course (Lichtenstein et al. 2009a; Lichtenstein 2010a; Lichtenstein and Karakitosos 2012; Jambrik et al. 201; Soldati et al. 2011; Shyamsundar et al. 2013; Lisciandro et al. 2016; Ward et al. 2017, 2018b; Vezzosi et al. 2017). • Infiltrative lung conditions such as lung consolida- tion and nodular disease are sonographically detected through observation of the shred sign, tissue sign, nodule sign, and wedge sign (Lichtenstein et al. 2004, 2009b; Lichtenstein 2010a,b; Volpicelli et al. 2012; Lee et al. 2015; Kulhavy and Lisciandro 2015; Ward et al. 2017, 2019). Vet BLUE Visual Lung Language Most Normal to Least Normal A composite of the Vet BLUE visual lung language is illustrated in Figure 23.2 (Lichtenstein 2010b; Lisciandro 2014b; Lee et al. 2015). • Dry lung – normal aerated lung surface, A‐lines with “lung sliding” (Figure 23.5). Dry lung only to be confounded with pneumothorax, which is A‐lines without “lung sliding” (Figure 23.6). • Wet lung – alveolar‐interstitial syndrome, B‐lines (Figures 23.3, 23.4, 23.7). There are other causes of “wet lung” that are far less common, one of which is pleural thickening from pulmonary fibrosis and senescent lung, which is more common in people than small animals (Tardella et al. 2012; Shyamsundar et al. 2013; Wang et al. 2017) as well as types of “pseudo‐ B‐lines” (see Nodular Disease). • Shred sign – air bronchogram (Figure 23.8). • Tissue sign – hepatization (Figure 23.9). • Nodule sign (mass sign) – nodule (mass if >3 cm) (Figure 23.10). • Wedge sign – infarct, PTE (Figure 23.11). Dry Lung versus Wet Lung: A‐lines, Lung Sliding, and B‐lines A‐lines with “lung sliding” represents “dry lung” at its surface (see Figure 23.5; see also Figures 17.6 and 22.3). A‐lines with no “lung sliding” represent pneumo- thorax (PTX) (Figure 23.6). B‐lines represent “wet lung” and most commonly forms of alveolar‐interstitial edema (Figure 23.7). B‐lines are nonspecific in that they cannot tell you what type of alveolar‐interstitial edema is present. Thus, the presence of B‐lines is commonly referred to as alveolar‐ interstitial syndrome (AIS) and a regional pattern‐based approach, Vet BLUE, is used to place their presence into clinical relevance (see Figure 23.13). B‐lines less com- monly are caused by senescent lung and fibrosis, more relevant to people who live longer than our small animal patients (Shyamsundar et al. 2013); and must be differentiated from “pseudo B‐lines” (see Figure 23.10). Shred Sign, Tissue Sign, Nodule Sign, and Wedge Sign Shred sign is lung consolidation seen as a fractal (irreg- ular) line from the expected linear continuity of the “lung line” with hyperechoic foci (air) within the con- solidation. The shred sign represents an air broncho- gram (see Figure 23.8) (Lichtenstein et al. 2004, 2009b; Lisciandro 2014b; Lichtenstein 2010a; Lee et al. 2015; Neelis et al. 2015). Tissue sign is lung consolidation similar to the shred sign, but more severe. 468 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Lung Ultrasound Artifacts Further Defined: “Lung Sliding, ” A‐lines, and B‐lines “Lung sliding” is the “to and fro” respirophasic movement of the visceral and parietal pleura over one another. The macrodescription preferred by the author is the “to and fro” respirophasic movement of the “lung line” (surface) along the intercostal space. In other words, as the patient inspires and expires, the expanded (inspiration) and contracted (expiration) lung surface will slide along the intercostal space and is imaged as “sliding” using ultra- sound (see Figure 23.5). The absence of “lung sliding” diagnoses PTX (see Figure 23.6). Panting, shallow breathing, and apnea will all confound “lung sliding” which along with PTX is explained in more detail in Chapters 17 and 18 (Lichtenstein et al. 2000; Kirkpatrick et al. 2004; Lisciandro et al. 2008). A‐lines are air reverberation artifact and “A” stands for air, a good way to remember A‐lines. These are equidistant horizontal lines parallel to the intercostal space and extending from the first reflective hyper - echoic surface, generally the “lung line” of aerated lung in normalcy, that then repeat themselves and their equidistant spacing through the far‐field of the ultra - sound screen (Figure 23.12; see also Figures 17.6, 17.12, 18.6, 22.2, 22.3, 23.3, 23.5, 23.6) (Volpicelli et al. 2006, 2012; Lichtenstein 2009a). A‐lines indicate a strong aer- ated presence and are observed in either “dry lung” or pneumothorax (air in the pleural space) with the differentiating feature being the presence or absence of “lung sliding.” The A‐lines of PTX are also parallel to the pulmonary‐pleural interface and where the “lung line” is expected, but lung is collapsed and displaced from the thoracic wall (see Figure 23.6). A‐lines may also be present in “dry lung” in patients with pleural effusion, thus the term “lung line” is used by the author when lung is not directly opposed to the thoracic wall. A‐lines, air reverberation, are also possible when air is present in other regions, such as free air in the perito - neal cavity, pleural cavity, pericardial sac, retroperito- neal space, stomach, etc. B‐lines usually represent forms of alveolar‐interstitial edema and are most commonly the ultrasonographic result of a small amount of fluid next to a small amount of air at the outermost periphery of lung. Simplistically, the strong difference in acoustic impedance creates the vertical lines that synchronously swing in real time with respirophasic movement, although it’s a bit more complex than this, These laser‐like strongly hyper - echoic lines do not fade while obliterating A‐lines and must extend through the far‐field of the ultrasound screen (Lichtenstein et al. 1997; Volpicelli et al. 2006, 2012; Lisciandro et al. 2008, 2014, 2017; Lisciandro 2011, 2014a,b). Despite the artifact extending through the far‐field of the screen, they are caused by the very out- ermost surface of lung (Volpicelli et al. 2006; Lichtenstein et al. 2009a). The term “B” for B‐lines has an unknown basis other than the letter “B” follows “A” in the alphabet; however, the author likes to remember B‐lines as approximating Kerley B lines that represent pulmonary interstitial edema on radiographs (Volipicelli et al. 2006, 2012; Louvet and Bourgeois 2008; Lichtenstein et al. 2009a,b; Lisciandro 2011). Importantly, B‐lines are nonspecific for the type of alveolar‐interstitial edema, thus referred to as alveolar‐interstitial Figure 23.12. “Dry lung” – A‐lines and “lung sliding.” Correlative line drawing with labeled B‐mode images. Conversely, absent B‐lines rule out left‐sided congestive heart failure in dogs and cats in a rapid, highly sensitive manner (Lisciandro 2014b; Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2016, 2017; Rademacher et al. 2014; Ward et al. 2017; Vezzosi et al. 2017) and likely for all mammalian lung (Yarto and Lisciandro 2017, unpublished data). Counting numbers of B‐lines has been shown to cor- relate with degree of pulmonary edema on the gold standard test of CT in human lung (Volipcelli et al. 2006). In one comparative study in dogs and cats, Vet BLUE fared better than three‐view TXR for detecting AIS (Ward et al. 2018b) and in another, Vet BLUE exceeded TXR and compared favorably with CT (Dicker et al. 2019). Thus, the Vet BLUE B‐line scoring system, described below, is clinically relevant (Figures 23.14 and 23.15). Lastly, in humans, in whom pulmonary fibrosis is much more common, thickened pleural sur- faces can also cause B‐lines, as does senescent lung (Tardella et al. 2012; Shyamsundar et al. 2013). Expectations for Frequency of Wet Lung Artifacts in Normalcy Adult canine and feline lung and puppies and kittens >6 weeks of age carry the expectation of having infre - quent numbers of B‐lines during Vet BLUE (Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2016, 2017, 2018; Ward et al. 2017, 2018b). Expect adult dog, adult cat, and puppies and kittens >6 weeks of age to have predominantly “dry lung” arti - facts at all nine acoustic windows of Vet BLUE, meaning the absence of B‐lines (Lisciandro 2014b; Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2016, 2017, 2018; Ward et al. 2017). The low frequency of B‐lines is nearly the same between adult dogs, adult cats, and puppies and kit - tens >6 weeks of age with no more than a single B‐line at a single Vet BLUE view about ~10–12% of the time (Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2017, 2018). The upshot is that every B‐line is potentially significant in feline and canine lung >6 weeks of age and should be recorded on the patient’s Vet BLUE template for comparison to later studies. Vet BLUE B‐line Scoring System Counting B‐lines During Vet BLUE First and foremost, the author’s clinical research has shown that during Vet BLUE dogs, cats, and puppies and kittens (and dolphins) have predominantly “dry lung” artifacts, A‐lines, at all Vet BLUE views (Figure 23.16) (Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2017, 2018; Ward et al. 2017; Yarto and Lisciandro 2017, unpublished data). Thus, B‐lines are unexpected and when observed expected to be only sporadically present in low num - bers (Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2016, 2017; Ward et al. 2017, 2018; Yarto and Lisciandro 2017, unpublished data). Exceptions are in regions where lung is very thin (lung Figure 23.14. Vet BLUE B‐line scoring system. Numbers of B‐lines correlate with the degree of alveolar‐interstitial edema in human lung and likely the same holds true for all mammalian lung. Thus, counting B‐lines is clinically relevant. Expect “dry lung” artifacts, A‐lines, and “lung sliding” to predominate (Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2016, 2017, 2018). Single B‐lines are uncommon. When single B‐lines are present in multiple views, they are abnormal and should be recorded on goal‐directed templates and placed into clinical context. The lung sonographer knows, however, that lower numbers mean lesser degrees of alveolar‐interstitial edema, and conversely more B‐lines mean greater degrees (severity) of alveolar‐interstitial edema. The Vet BLUE B‐line scoring system counts the maximum number over a single intercostal space at each of the Vet BLUE acoustic win- dows (views) (see Figure 23.15). The scoring is 1, 2, 3, as weak positives, and >3 and infinity (∞), as strong positives. They found that numbers of B‐lines correlated with the degree of alveolar‐intersti- tial edema when compared to the gold standard test of CT in human lung. Thus, the author developed a simple, easy to remember Vet BLUE B‐line scoring system (Lisciandro 2014b; Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2016, 2017; Ward et al. 2017, 2018b): the highest number of B‐lines over a single intercostal space at each Vet BLUE view is recorded as 0 (negative), 1 (a single B‐line), 2 (two B‐lines), 3 (three B‐lines), >3 (more than three B‐lines but not confluent over the entire intercostal space), and infinity, when confluent over an entire intercostal space, referred to by some sonographers as “white lung” (see Figures 23.14, 23.15, and 23.16) (Gargani and Volpicelli 2014). Consider B‐line scores of 1–3 as weak positive and scores of >3 and infinity as strong positives (Volpicelli Strong Positive Model). The use of this scoring system helps gauge how much AIS is present at that regional view (acoustic widow). B‐lines have not only shown good clinical cor- relation for detection of AIS (cardiogenic pulmonary edema and lung contusions) in both dogs and cats (Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2016, 2017; Ward et al. 2017, 2018b; Dicker et al. 2019), but also interobserver agreement is high (kappa values >0.85) in two differ - ent studies (Ward et al. 2017; Dicker et al. 2019). Vet BLUE findings should be recorded on goal‐directed templates (see below and Table 23.5). Other B‐line Scoring Systems Volpicelli Strong Positive Model ‐ Cardiac Bias The Volpicelli Strong Positive (VSP) model differs from the Vet BLUE B‐line scoring system in that only >3 and infinity B‐lines are scored as “positive” (see Figure 23.17). In other words, B‐line numbers of 1, 2, and 3 are discredited, when in fact the expectation dur- ing Vet BLUE is to have rare B‐lines (see Figure 23.18) (Ward et al. 2017). The VSP model has strengths in evaluating human patients especially in left‐sided congestive heart failure because only the most strongly positive acoustic windows are counted; however, this is not universally accepted for the evaluation of B‐lines (Volpicelli et al. 2006; Lichtenstein 2009a; Gargani and Volpicelli 2014; Lee et al. 2015). The VSP model does have a place as it proved useful in diagnosing felines with left‐sided congestive heart failure using the VSP criteria and with ≥2 Vet BLUE views being positive bilaterally (Ward et al. 2017). Using this VSP scoring modification with a left‐sided congestive heart failure bias in felines, Vet BLUE had the same sensitivity (89%) and specificity (87%) as TXR (Ward et al. 2017). The advantage of using VSP scoring modification during Vet BLUE is that pulmonary imaging is rapid without restraint, which effectively rules in left‐sided CHF Figure 23.18. The upshot is that by understanding the scoring strategy and placing regional findings into a pattern‐based approach, the lung sonographer has dif- ferent ways to integrate LUS findings during Vet BLUE (Jambrik et al. 2004; Volpicelli et al. 2006; Gargani and Volpicelli 2014; Wang et al. 2017). Why are They Called B‐lines? There are two answers to this: (1) “B” follows “A” in the alphabet, and (2) “B‐lines” are named for radio- graphic Kerley B‐lines that represent interlobar edema (pulmonary edema) (Louvet and Bourgeois 2008; Lisciandro 2011, 2014b; Lisciandro et al. 2014). Why are They Not Comet‐tails? The “wet lung” artifact has been published as comet‐ tail artifacts (Lichtenstein et al. 1997). However, comet‐ tail artifact (CTA) is a poor descriptor because the CTA was first described by the reflective artifacts extending beyond metallic buckshot in a human liver, which does not represent the ultrasonographic phenomenon of alveolar‐interstitial syndrome having fluid next to air with the artifact not reflective but rather due to strong differences in acoustic impedance (between air and fluid) (Lichtenstein et al. 1997; Volpicelli et al. 2006; Lichtenstein 2010b). CTAs observed during LUS have no defined clinical relevance and in the author’s expe- rience are often created by small (<1 mm) lung surface irregularities and also found along extreme thin mar - gins of aerated lung. Comet‐tail Artifact The comet‐tail artifact is an extension of LUS artifact that comes off the thoracic wall (parietal pleura) or lung surface (visceral pleura) but does not extend through the far‐field in laser‐like fashion as defined for B‐lines (Lichtenstein 2007, 2010b; Lichtenstein and Mezière 2008). It is imperative to have enough gain through the far‐field to be able to differentiate between comet‐tails and B‐lines (Lichtenstein et al. 2009a; Lichtenstein 2010a; Lisciandro 2014b; Gargani and Volpicelli 2014) (see Figures 17.10 and 22.6). Comet‐tail artifacts observed during LUS have no defined clinical relevance and in the author’s experience are created by small (<1 mm) lung surface irregularities and also along extreme thin margins of aerated lung, and are rarely observed during Vet BLUE. Six Signs-Further Information Shred Sign – Air Bronchogram The shred sign is the irregularity (fractal, shredding) and lack of the expected linear continuity of the pulmonary–pleural interface and its “lung line” that represents lung consolidation along the intercostal space (Figure 23.19; see also Figure 23.8) (Lisciandro 2014b; Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2017; Ward et al. 2017). Importantly, the lung consolidation has air within the consolidation and thus shred sign represents an air bronchogram (Lichtenstein et al. 2004; Lichtenstein and Mezière 2008; Lisciandro 2014b; Neelis et al. 2015). These air bronchograms appear as hyperechoic (bright white) flecks or foci throughout the consolidation and can be dynamic or static (Lisciandro 2014b; Lichtenstein et al. 2004, 2009b; Neelis et al. 2015). Remember, air on ultrasound is white (hyperechoic) which is the opposite of radiography! The air bronchogram may still have air exchange occurring with air movement during phases of respiration, referred to as a “dynamic” air broncho- gram, or have stagnant air, referred to as a “static” air bronchogram (Lichtenstein et al. 2004; Lichtenstein 2009a,b; Gillman and Kirkpatrick 2012; Mongodi et al. 2016). The movement of air through these airways can be difficult to appreciate in spontaneously breathing dogs and cats; however, with controlled positive pressure ventilation (under anesthesia, mechanical ven- tilation), the differentiation of “dynamic” from “static” may be made by observing whether the air “slides” or wisps through the hyperechoic foci (air bronchograms). Thus, a shred sign is consolidation with aeration and must be placed into clinical context for developing an accurate working diagnosis since the sign is nonspe- cific in and of itself. Generally, shred signs in gravity‐ dependent Vet BLUE regions in nontrauma patients represent bacterial bronchopneumonia or aspiration pneumonia until proven otherwise (Lisciandro 2014b; Ward et al. 2017, 2019). Tissue Sign – Hepatization of Lung In contrast to the shred sign, the tissue sign is a gradation of more severe consolidation because lung in the tissue sign lacks aeration and thus the consolidation appears like liver (see Figures 23.9 and 23.19) (Lichtenstein Pearl: To best integrate Vet BLUE, the lung sonogra- pher must place findings into clinical context, perform serial examinations, and record Vet BLUE data on goal‐directed templates (see Table 23.5).

476 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER 2009a,b; Lichtenstein et al. 2010b; Lisciandro 2014b; Neelis et al. 2015). The airways are fluid‐filled or infil- trated or obstructed “upstream” to cause the tissue sign. The term “hepatization” has historically been applied to this lung ultrasound finding (Neelis et al. 2015). Color flow Doppler is a good option to document whether pulsatile blood flow is present through the lung with a tissue sign to differentiate a lung lobe torsion (no flow with fluid bronchograms) from a mass (pulsatile blood flow) (Hecht and Penninck 2015). Nodule Sign The nodule sign is an organized infiltrating mass. It is a step up in severity from the shred sign and tissue sign because now the abnormal consolidation is in fact organized consolidation along the lung surface within its parenchyma. The nodule sign is generally charac- terized by a hypoechoic or anechoic circle or oval along the “lung line” with pseudo B‐lines extending through the far‐field with respirophasic synchrony (see Figures 23.10, 23.19, 23.35, and 23.26) (Lisciandro 2014b; Neelis et al. 2015). A nodule sign that does not oscillate to and fro with respirophasic movement is more likely originating from the thoracic wall (Neelis et al. 2015). The effect is similarly created as for alve- olar‐interstitial edema, with strong differences in acoustic impedance but rather than fluid next to air is soft tissue cuffed by air. Thus, B‐lines associated with the nodule sign are referred to as pseudo B‐lines since they do not represent AIS. Thus, when vertical streaks are seen on lung ultrasound, the sonographer should follow them to the “lung line” to look for the nodule sign. By definition, nodules are generally considered ≤3 cm and a mass >3 cm. The author has not created a “mass sign” as an additional descriptor but certainly the term could be applied for nodule signs that are >3 cm (Alpert et al. 2015). In some instances, the nodule sign may be associ- ated with adjacent inflammation (edema, hemorrhage) and pathology and thus with other Vet BLUE lung ultrasound signs including B‐lines, shred sign, tissue sign, and wedge sign. The nodule sign is only ultraso- nographically apparent if these nodules (and masses) are located at the periphery of lung within the exam- ined acoustic window (see Figure 23.1). Centrally located (deeper) nodules (and masses) that do not touch the “lung line” at the LUS acoustic windows will be missed. However, in a pilot study, Vet BLUE per - formed better than TXR for pulmonary metastasis (Kulhavy and Lisciandro 2015) and three‐view TXR has been shown to perform poorly when compared to the gold standard of CT (Nemanic et al. 2006; Armbrust et al. 2012; Alexander et al. 2012). In another study evaluating pulmonary contusions, Vet BLUE outper - formed TXR and fared well compared to CT (Dicker et al. 2019). The million dollar question is how well does Vet BLUE fare when compared to CT? Certainly we can answer that it performs likely better than TXR for many respiratory conditions (Kulhavy and Lisciandro 2015; Ward et al. 2018b; Dicker et al. 2019). Use of Vet BLUE for Detecting Pulmonary Nodules A pilot comparing Vet BLUE to three‐view TXR showed that all three‐view TXR studies that had nodules deter- mined by a blinded, board‐certified radiologist had nodules on Vet BLUE; however, several cases that had the nodule sign on Vet BLUE were not apparent on TXR (Kulhavy and Lisciandro 2015). The gold stan- dard test of CT has been shown in small animals to be able to detect nodules as small as 1–2 mm (Nemanic et al. 2006; Armbrust et al. 2012) and clearly is a better test than three‐view TXR (Nemanic et al. 2006; Eberle et al. 2010; Armbrust et al. 2012; Alexander et al. 2012). In fact, in one study evaluating dogs with osteosar - coma (OSA), of the 11 dogs with metastatic disease seen on CT, only two had metastasis detected by TXR (Eberle et al. 2010). Interestingly, another study found no difference in detecting nodules between traditional film screen and computed radiography (Alexander et al. 2012). Comparative studies have shown that the threshold for radiography to detect nodules is some- where between 3 and 7 mm, a wide range (Armbrust et al. 2005; Nemanic et al. 2006; Alexander et al. 2012), and clearly TXR greatly underestimates the numbers of nodules compared to CT (Nemanic et al. 2006; Eberle et al. 2010; Armbrust et al. 2012; Alexander et al. 2012). One study determined that in the case population, the right middle and left and right caudal lung regions most commonly had nodules compared to other lung lobes (Alexander et al. 2012). In our experience, Vet BLUE and lung ultrasound can readily detect lung surface nodules <1 mm. The author is a collaborator in ongoing research comparing these three imaging modalities to help answer the clinical question: How good is Vet BLUE as a pulmonary metastasis check? The author would answer, from experience and preliminary clinical research, “very good” and better than three‐view TXR. Another impor- tant factor that must be considered is how often lung metastases reach the lung surface, because if nodules are not along the “lung line” at one of the nine Vet BLUE acoustic windows, then the pulmonary metas- tasis will be missed (see Figure 23.1).

477 POCUS: VET BLUE – CLINICAL INTEGRATION The answer is to perform Global FAST on all cancer‐aged patients to “stage” their disease on day 1 (see Chapters 36 and 37). By doing so, you provide more clinical information to your client regarding their pet. Moreover, the client may better decide on cost/benefit for the recommended work‐up. The Global FAST approach serves as a same‐day screen- ing test to let the owner know whether the disease has obviously spread (or is disseminated) versus appearing localized. The same approach may be used for staging any disease (infectious) as being localized or disseminated as well as screening for comorbidi- ties and complications. Wedge Sign The wedge sign represents lung infarction (PTE) (Lisciandro 2013, unpublished data). This is arguably the most abnormal or severe Vet BLUE sign by repre- senting a pie‐shaped region of vascular necrosis (see Figures 23.11 and 23.19; see also for case examples Figures 37.9 and 37.10) (Mathis et al. 2005; Mastruzzo et al. 2008). The wedge sign may also be considered a subset of the shred sign and tissue sign. In gravity‐ dependent Vet BLUE acoustic windows, the wedge sign would be difficult to distinguish from bacterial and aspiration pneumonias and other ventral pathology; however, in the least gravity‐dependent left and right Caudodorsal and Perihilar Vet BLUE views, the wedge sign is very convincing for PTE, giving cli- nicians a means to justify and trigger thromboprophy- laxis and thrombolytics, and a way to monitor and track PTE (resolving, worsening with more wedge signs, or static) (Mastruzzo et al. 2008). See Chapter 25 and Chapter 37 for CPR. Summary In summary, the Vet BLUE six lung ultrasound signs are arranged by degree of lung infiltration/consolida- tion, beginning with unremarkable “dry lung” fol- lowed by “wet lung” (B‐lines representing AIS), followed by degrees of lung consolidation with shred sign (consolidation with aeration), tissue sign (consol- idation without aeration), nodule(s) sign (organized infiltrate), and lastly the wedge sign, representing lung surface infarction (pie‐shaped vascular wedge of necrosis) (see Figures 23.5, 23.6–11, and 23.19). The diaphragmatico‐hepatic (DH) view should not be underestimated as an integral part of Vet BLUE as it can detect lung pathology that was missed or ques- tionable at the eight transthoracic Vet BLUE views (Figure 23.21). Combinations of any and all of the signs may be pre- sent in severely diseased dogs and cats, especially in dogs with heartworm disease (Dirofilaria immitis). Lastly, the visual system provides veterinarians with a Vet BLUE visual lung language to freely communicate findings during conversation and within medical records. Other Lines: Are They Really Lines? The use of a pulmonary line nomenclature is not nec- essarily the best way proceed with teaching lung ultrasound to veterinarians and is not fully accepted in human medicine. The author has earmarked C‐ lines, E‐lines, I‐lines, and Z‐lines for discussion, but there are many more types of LUS lines (Lichtenstein and Mezière 2008; Lichtenstein 2007, 2009a, 2010a,b; Lee et al. 2015; Lee 2016). The author prefers the Vet BLUE visual lung language over creating esoteric “lines” for all possible LUS findings (Figure 23.22). A similar visual lung language is also used in human point‐of‐care ultrasound textbooks and published reviews (Lee et al. 2015; Lichtenstein 2010a). The visual lung language system eliminates the need for so many different lines, many of which are not really lines at all, e.g., C‐lines, E‐lines, I‐lines, Z‐lines (Lisciandro 2014b). C‐lines C‐lines are not lines because consolidation is most often a fractal irregular effect that deviates from the expected normal linear continuity of the “lung line” (see Figure 23.22) (Lichtenstein and Mezière 2008; Lichtenstein 2007, 2010a,b). The author prefers the terms shred sign, tissue sign, nodule sign, and wedge sign because they are visual, each has clinically rele- vant implications and are more descriptive than lump- ing them all into a general category of C‐lines. “C‐lines” are nonspecific and too generalized. Pearl: Abdominal structures are situated farther cra- nially in standing dogs and cats than you would think; thus, finding caudal Vet BLUE transition zones and sliding cranially away from them helps to avoid mistaking abdominal structures for lung pathology (Figure 23.20).

479 POCUS: V ET BLUE – C LINICAL I NTEGRATION E‐lines E‐lines are a moot point if the lung sonographer focuses on the basic premise for all LUS – if you cannot image the “gator sign” orientation, then you can’t accurately image lung. E‐lines make the simple far more complicated and in most instances of subcutaneous emphysema (SQE), there are no lines at all but rather the expected air‐related principle of the dirty shadowing effect and/or A‐lines (see Figures 18.12, 18.13, and 23.22). Moreover, most SQE is readily recognized during physical exam. I‐lines I‐lines are comet‐tail artifacts that most often originate from the lung surface but fade, unlike B‐lines. Comet‐ tail artifacts observed during LUS generally have no defined clinical relevance and in the author’s experi - ence are created by small (<1 mm) lung surface irregu- larities and also observed along extreme thin margins of aerated lung (Figure 23.23). Z‐lines Z‐lines are yet another example where simply abiding by the definition of B‐lines avoids the addition of the “Z‐line.” Z‐lines are potentially mistaken for B‐lines because they are vertical streaks, but they fade and do not oscillate with respirophasic movement and do not obliterate A‐lines (see Figure 23.22). They are most commonly created by the reflective fascial planes in the near‐field (intercostal muscles and those more superficial) away from the pulmonary–pleural inter - face (PPI). Thus, “Z‐lines” do not oscillate in syn - chrony with phases of respiration. In the author’s experience, these Z‐lines, called “shimmy lines” by the author, go unnoticed by most sonographers once B‐lines are learned on your machine. The letter “Z” was given to these “lines” by Lichtenstein because they have no clinical relevance other than being a confounder (Lichtenstein 2010b; Lee 2016). See also Chapter 17. Clinical Use of Regional Pattern‐based Vet BLUE Approach The Vet BLUE regional pattern‐based pattern approach may be used for ruling in (specificity) and ruling out (sensitivity) respiratory and nonrespiratory look‐alike causes (Table 23.2). 481 POCUS: VET BLUE – CLINICAL INTEGRATION become known in time as more comparative imaging studies are published. To illustrate the Vet BLUE regional pattern‐based pattern approach, examples of nonrespiratory look‐alikes, left‐sided congestive heart failure, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, pneumonia, nodular disease, and pleural effusion are shown on several figures using lateral thoracic radiographs with Vet BLUE illustrative overlays (Figure 23.24; see also Figures 23.25, 23.26, 23.28, and 23.29). “Dry Lung” Conditions The finding of “dry lung all (Vet BLUE) views” or “absent B‐lines all (Vet BLUE) views (ABAV)” is impor- tant in patients with respiratory distress (Lisciandro et al. 2016) (Figure 23.25). The finding effectively rules out any clinically relevant left‐sided congestive heart failure in dogs and cats with 88–96% sensitivity and likely holds true for all mammalian lung (Lichtenstein 2009a; Lisciandro et al. 2016; Ward et al. 2017). The finding of absent B‐lines also rules against the use of loop diuretics because no clinically relevant alveolar‐ interstitial edema exists (Rademacher et al. 2014; Lisciandro 2014b; Lisciandro et al. 2016, 2017; Ward et al. 2017, 2019; Vezzosi et al. 2017). The patient may have heart disease, but no clinically relevant left‐sided congestive heart failure is present. Rule‐outs for “dry lung all (Vet BLUE) views” or ABAV are summarized in Table 23.3. Importantly, ABAV respiratory conditions will most commonly include upper airway disease, feline asthma, tracheo- bronchitis/bronchitis, severe pneumothorax, and PTE and lung pathology that does not make it to the “lung line” (lung surface) or pathology that is not present at any of the Vet BLUE acoustic windows or other LUS formats being used. For nonrespiratory look‐alikes, in other words conditions that present with respiratory signs that are not truly respiratory, the categories include: (1) cardiac such as arrhythmias, dilated cardio- myopathy, pulmonary hypertension, right‐sided congestive heart failure, and pericardial effusion, (2) uncharacterized hypotension such as internal hemor - rhage (hemoabdomen, hemothorax, hemoretroperito- neum), gastric dilation‐volvulus (GDV), sepsis, canine anaphylaxis, and (3) miscellaneous causes such as high fever, pyrexia, heat stroke, severe metabolic acidosis, and anemia (Lisciandro 2012, 2013, unpublished data; Hnatusko et al. 2019). “Wet Lung” Conditions Left‐sided Congestive Heart Failure Most cases of canine left‐sided congestive heart failure have a dorsal perihilar distribution (think the classic perihilar edema on the thoracic radiograph) or generalized distribution of B‐lines (alveolar‐inter - stitial edema), unless the dog is a Doberman, which often have a random patchy alveolar‐interstitial pattern like felines (Fox 1988; Benigni et al. 2009). Early cardiogenic pulmonary edema has been reported to be asymmetrical and more right‐sided (caudodorsal lung fields) than left (Guglielmini et al. 2009). The Volipcelli strong positive (VSP) model was used to better categorize pulmonary edema as car - diogenic or noncardiogenic with manipulation of the Vet BLUE B‐line scoring system (Figure 23.26; see also Figures 23.14–17). The VSP model is more con- servative, making only B‐lines scores of >3 and infinity “positive,” thus discrediting scores of 1, 2, and 3 (see Figures 23.16 and 23.18). However, if the Vet BLUE sonographer understands the VSP model cardiac bias, then the VSP model helps to rule in left‐ sided congestive heart failure (L‐CHF) from other causes of respiratory distress, especially for cats (Ward et al. 2017). 483 POCUS: V ET BLUE – C LINICAL I NTEGRATION Numbers of B‐lines Guide Loop Diuretic Usage Numbers of B‐lines and the Vet BLUE B‐line scoring system help direct loop diuretic usage (Jambrik et al. 2004; Volpicelli et al. 2006; Lisciandro 2011; Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2016, 2017; Shyamsundar et al. 2013; Gargani et al. 2015; Gargani 2019) (Figure 23.27). Studies in dogs have shown that LUS‐detected cardiogenic lung edema correlates with findings on TXR (Rademacher et al. 2014; Vezzosi et al. 2017; Ward et al. 2017, 2018b) and has been suggested as a point‐of‐care, low‐impact imaging modality for patient monitoring (Rademacher et al. 2014; Ward et al. 2017, 2018b; Vezzosi et al. 2017). Conversely, when low B‐line numbers exist, much less aggressive (and delaying) loop diuretic therapy appears to be supported by several studies (Rademacher et al. 2014; Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2016, 2017; Ward et al. 2017, 2018b; Vezzosi et al. 2017). Moreover, for patients receiving aggressive loop diuretic therapy, including by constant‐rate infusion, Vet BLUE may be performed as often as hourly as a more reliable test than lung auscultation and radiography (Rademacher et al. 2014; Gargani et al. 2015; Lisciandro et al. 2016; Vezzosi et al. 2017; Ward et al. 2018b). Noncardiogenic Pulmonary Edema Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema (NCPE) has histori- cally been described as symmetrical caudodorsal distri- bution of alveolar‐interstitial infiltrate on TXR (Bouyssou et al. 2017), for example neurogenic (post seizure), asphyxiation/choked, electrocution, drown - ing, smoke inhalation, ARDS, and transfusion‐related lung injury (TRALI) (Figure 23.28). A recent retrospec - tive study came to contradictory TXR pattern conclu - sions, but the study evaluated small animals with presumed NCPE in very low, diluted numbers by sev- eral subsets of patients (49 dogs, 11 cats). The conclu - sions drawn were that NCPE may be more randomly distributed and asymmetrical, being more right‐ than left‐sided (Bouyssou et al. 2017). In the author’s experi- ence, NCPE remains a top differential in small animals with a predominantly caudodorsal “wet lung” distri - bution; and integrating Global FAST findings helps increase the probability of a correct working diagnosis, especially incorporating TFAST echo views and charac- terization of the caudal vena cava and hepatic veins. The wedge sign would be difficult to differentiate from pneumonia in gravity‐dependent Vet BLUE views, but when in Caudodorsal and Perihilar views, PTE should be strongly suspected and placed into clinical context with other supportive information. Subpleural lesions similar to the wedge sign have supported the diagnosis of PTE in people (Mathis et al. 2005; Mastruzzo et al. 2008; Nazerian et al. 2014); however, in the author’s experience PTE in dogs is much more wedge‐shaped (triangular) than that described in people (Lisciandro 2013, unpub- lished data). Other Diffusely Wet Conditions Lung contusions, pulmonary hemorrhage in coagulo- pathic patients, feline anaphylaxis, canine pulmonary hypertension, allergic and irritant pneumonitis, dirofi- lariasis (canine heartworm disease), feline histoplas- mosis, and feline Alurostrongylus and Paragominus infections are additional conditions which the author has encountered that may mimic left‐sided CHF, being diffusely “wet lung” using the VSP model. Metastatic neoplasia, although appearing to have diffuse “wet lung”‐like artifacts, has in fact “pseudo B‐lines” cre- ated by strong differences in acoustic impedance bet- ween soft tissue cuffed by aerated lung (Soldati, personal communication). These “pseudo B‐lines” likewise oscillate in synchrony with phases of respira- tion so careful evaluation of the “lung line” to evaluate for surface nodules and other Vet BLUE LUS signs is important. Moreover, several nodules of various sizes should be detected during Vet BLUE to draw the final conclusions for nodular lung. Care should be taken to avoid overinterpreting small blips along the “lung line,” where divisions of lung lobes and parts of lung contact one another, that may mimic small nodules (see Figure 23.23). Repeating the Vet BLUE in 10–14 days is a viable option as well. Close observation of the “lung line” from which the B‐line originates is important to rule in and out the presence of the nodule sign for neoplastic disease, abscesses and granulomatous disease. Using the Vet BLUE “Wet Lung” versus “Dry Lung” Concept for Monitoring During Fluid Therapy Combining numbers of B‐lines using the Vet BLUE B‐line scoring system with numbers of positive views, B‐lines are “sentinels” for developing lung edema and serve as a rapid point‐of‐care, low‐impact monitoring tool for detecting increased extravascular lung water (EVLW) (Jambrik et al. 2004; Lichtenstein et al. 2009a; Lichtenstein and Karakitsos 2012; Shyamsundar et al. 2013; Gargani et al. 2015; Gargani 2019). The gold standard test for EVLW of transpul- monary thermodilution cardiac output (PICCO) is invasive and of limited availability (Anile et al. 2017). Thus, Vet BLUE and its simple B‐line scoring system coupled with numbers of positive regional views carries tremendous potential for estimation of EVLW in our small animal patients (Anile et al. 2017). Moreover, the finding of increased EVLW (B‐line, alveolar‐interstitial edema) anticipates the possible development of alveolar flooding (shred sign, tissue sign, air bronchograms, and lung consolidation), which is far more difficult to treat. Moreover, unrecognized EVLW risks overt patient decompensation (labored breathing, respiratory distress) before being detected by more traditional means of lung auscultation and vital signs. By recognizing the development of B‐lines in patients receiving intravenous fluid therapy, the attending clinician can modify the clinical course, especially regarding fluid therapy and loop diuretics, and further investigate causes. Lung Contusions and Vet BLUE Using Vet BLUE for Scoring Severity of Lung Contusions in T rauma Numbers of B‐lines combined with number of positive Vet BLUE views semiquantitates overall lung contu- sion severity, providing a Vet BLUE lung contusion severity score (Lisciandro 2011, 2014b; Lisciandro 2012, unpublished data; Dicker et al. 2019). In other words, the more B‐lines at higher numbers of positive Vet BLUE regional views, the more severe the lung contu- sions are in that patient. Focally, numbers of B‐lines in a Vet BLUE view also semiquantitate the degree of lung contusions within that region of lung, and the dis- tribution of lung contusions is also appreciated by combining positive views with numbers of B‐lines. In severe lung contusions, shred sign and tissue sign are present (Dicker et al. 2019). For example, a puppy that has a crush injury from being stepped on by a large adult presents in overt and severe respiratory distress. The puppy is found to have >3 B‐lines at all Vet BLUE views, including the DH view, indicating severe pulmonary contusions. This patient information is gained immediately following the physical exam with minimal to no restraint and little patient risk (no restraint and no transport to radiology). In contrast, a dog that has been bluntly traumatized by an automobile or was kicked by a horse has only >3 B‐lines at only two of nine Vet BLUE views – the left Caudodorsal and Perihilar lung region views (absent at the other seven Vet BLUE views). The Vet BLUE sonog- rapher can readily appreciate the difference in severity of the lung contusions between the puppy being stepped on and the hit‐by‐car or kicked by a horse examples. Serial Vet BLUE and scoring may then be used as a mon- itoring tool for assessing worsening, resolving, and static lung contusions (Figure 23.30). Comparative Imaging: Vet BLUE, Radiography, and Computed T omography The use of Vet BLUE does not negate the need for radiographical studies. Radiography is generally a better imaging test for fractures, bone lesions, pro- jectile foreign bodies, thoracic wall injuries, and her - niations; and CT is generally considered the gold

492 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER standard imaging test for most patients. However, Vet BLUE provides a lower risk, lower impact, point‐ of‐care first‐line imaging test for the critical and unstable patient that exceeds radiography for lung surface pathology and may be used diagnostically for many common respiratory conditions while com - paring favorably with CT for many conditions. Moreover, Vet BLUE may be subsequently used as a cost‐effective monitoring tool. In traumatized canine lung, Vet BLUE is more sensitive than TXR and fares well when compared to CT (Figure 23.31) (Dicker et al. 2019). The limitations of Vet BLUE when com - pared to CT were found to be the missing of deeper (away from the lung surface) lung contusions and those associated with the mediastinum (Dicker et al. 2019). Vet BLUE Examples Dogs Heart Disease Patient Before and After Anesthesia Preanesthetic evaluation with the Global FAST approach helps detect morbidities while at the same time establishing a baseline of data imaging points to which future studies post anesthesia may be com- pared. A practical common example is the mitral valve disease dog coming in for an anesthetic procedure that has “dry lung” before the procedure and is coughing post procedure (Figure 23.32). By having a preproce- dure baseline, the cause of coughing is better deter - mined with serial Vet BLUE plus the Global FAST approach. Choked on Rawhide The first example is a patient with Dry Lungs (D) all views and used for comparison for the subsequent examples of different respiratory conditions. Let’s work through the following example of a dog that has choked on a rawhide that presents stable but with an increased respiratory rate. There are three common scenarios causing the increased respiratory rate: (1) stress, anxiety, oropharyngeal and tracheal irritation, (2) noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, and (3) aspiration pneumonia. Think about the Vet BLUE profiles for each. In (1) the dog will have “dry lung” (D) (see Figure 23.25), or in other words be dry all Vet BLUE views with ABAV . In (2) the dog will likely have a predominantly dorsal or generalized distribution of “wet lung” (W) (see Figure 23.26). In (3) the dog will likely have a predominantly ventral gravity‐dependent distribution of “wet lung” (W) (see Figures 23.29 and 23.34). Vet BLUE profiles may be established within 90 seconds in most patients and an evidence‐based approach is used point of care, leading to more accu- rate assessment and treatment. Additional imaging and testing is then triggered as indicated, but impor - tantly can be delayed until the patient is more stable. Cats Abdominal Breathing and Nostril Flaring The respiratory distressed feline presents with similar breathing patterns of abdominal breathing and nostril flaring (Figure 23.33). A physical exam and watching the patient spontaneously breathe without restraint is good practice. However, if you can place a stethoscope on the patient, you can place an ultrasound probe. In these felines, the Vet BLUE‐TFAST approach (always better to use Global FAST with AFAST performed with the cat in standing or sternal) is very helpful and can cut to the chase diagnostically by “seeing” the condition. There are four common conditions in cats to be con- sidered: (1) feline asthma, (2) left‐sided CHF, (3) pleural effusion, and (4) metastatic disease. Each of these has radically different Vet BLUE profiles that, in fact, would have already been sorted out in about the time it took me to type this paragraph. In (1) the cat has feline asthma and will have “dry lung” all views, absent B‐lines all (Vet BLUE) views (ABAV), ruling out left‐sided CHF (Lisciandro et al. 2016; Ward et al. 2017). In (2) the cat has left‐sided CHF and will have “wet lung” in most if not all Vet BLUE views (Lisciandro et al. 2017; Ward et al. 2017). In fact, the VSP model works as well in cats with left‐sided CHF as three‐view TXR (Ward et al. 2017). In (3) the cat has pleural effusion and will have free fluid identified during Vet BLUE‐TFAST (Ward et al. 2018a). In (4) the cat with metastatic disease has nodules of various sizes in multiple views during Vet BLUE coupled with mammary gland tumors (Kulhavy and Lisciandro 2015). A good physical exam and an AFAST help search for additional supportive information to formulate a working diagnosis. Each of these four felines has radically different Vet BLUE profiles despite very similar breathing patterns and lung auscultation.
