497 POCUS: VET BLUE – CLINICAL INTEGRATION “dry lung,” lung sliding and A‐lines rule against aggressive loop diuretic therapy and for delaying or administering lower doses. “Wet lung” gives evidence‐ based information that loop diuretics are potentially indicated because left‐sided CHF may be present. Additional findings of the shred sign and tissue sign suggest marked to severe lung consolidation that must be placed into clinical context. The nodule sign gener - ally suggests neoplastic or granulomatous disease (fungal, parasitic) and the wedge sign in Caudodorsal and Perihilar lung regions suggests PTE. Atelectatic lung can cause “wet lung” artifacts as well as forms of consolidation due to pressure atelectasis, making repeat or serial examinations after thoracocentesis necessary to see if the Vet BLUE lung findings resolve or persist. Considering Pressure Atelectatic Lung This is a very good clinical question. Are the Vet BLUE lung signs of “wet lung,” shred sign, and tissue sign in fact a result of pressure atelectasis? Each could very well be, so the best strategy is to treat and reassess. As a general rule, atelectatic lung resolves post thoraco- centesis in spontaneously breathing patients within three hours (three‐hour rule), as shown in a recent pilot study of 63 dogs (Lisciandro and Fosgate 2018). Clinical studies in feline cases are warranted, but at least the “three‐hour rule” derived from dogs gives the attending clinician a general guideline and stresses the importance of serial (repeat) Vet BLUE exams. Persistence of abnormal Vet BLUE findings of >3 hours suggests that the lung lesions are more than pressure atelectasis, placed into clinical context and used to develop a more streamlined diagnostic plan (lung lobe aspirate, different types of fluid analysis testing, direct airway evaluation and sampling, CT, etc.). The use of this TFAST‐Vet BLUE approach in cats (and dogs) provides clear advantages over TXR because TXR is a less reliable evaluation of the lung surface and intrathoracic abnormalities in the presence of pleural effusion, and ineffective for diagnosing pericardial effusion (ultrasound is arguably the gold standard test) (Guglielmini et al. 2012; Côté et al. 2013). Monitoring Applications for Vet BLUE Vet BLUE for Left‐sided Congestive Heart Failure and Volume Overload Effective uses of Vet BLUE include determination of whether clinically relevant left‐sided heart failure is present (Lichtenstein and Mezière 2008; Lichtenstein and Karakitsos 2012; Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2016, 2017; Lee et al. 2015; Ward et al. 2017) and evaluating the current status of the patient’s lung relative to degrees of alveolar‐interstitial edema (left‐sided congestion, extravascular lung water) (Gargani et al. 2007; Peris et al. 2010; Jambrik et al. 2010). In probably any and all mammalian lung, the finding of “dry lung all (Vet BLUE) views” (or ABAV) rules out with high sensi- tivity (>96%) any clinically relevant left‐sided CHF (Lichtenstein and Mezière 2008; Lichtenstein et al. 2009a; Volpicelli et al. 2012; Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2016, 2017; Ward et al. 2017). Conversely, the presence of B‐ lines supports the diagnosis of left‐sided CHF, espe- cially when using the VSP model, and in dogs when distributed in the upper (dorsal) lung views of the Caudodorsal and Perihilar areas (pneumonia being predominantly ventrally distributed, being gravity dependent) (Ward et al. 2017, 2019). Assessment of the LA:Ao ratio is by far the most important additional piece of information, the so‐called “quick peek” echo view. Interestingly, in people discharged after having left‐sided CHF, those with persistent B‐lines are more likely to return sooner with recurrence of left‐sided CHF than those having “dry lung” on their exit exams (Gargani et al. 2015). It is so important to realize that a dog or cat with “dry lung all (Vet BLUE) views” (ABAV) can have other intrathoracic pathology that is missed without always combining Vet BLUE and TFAST (see Table 23.4). A good example is PCE that often results in respiratory distress in both dogs and cats. Being predominantly a right‐sided phenomenon in dogs, the Vet BLUE profile is expected to be “dry lung” all views (ABAV) whereas in cats lung likely would be wet because their most common cause for PCE is congestive heart failure (Hall et al. 2007; Ward et al. 2018a), so by only performing Vet BLUE as a standalone format, the PCE is missed. In canine PCE, Global FAST should be performed as the patient may have a midabdominal mass that is missed and AFAST with an abdominal fluid score allows you to rule in and rule out effusion, whether a modified transudate or a hemoabdomen, and semiquantitate the volume when present. Another example that is very common is the coughing dashchund or Shetland sheepdog that has respiratory signs and some with per- sistent cough. The Vet BLUE is dry all views (ABAV), but the dog has a left atrial tear/rupture, a serious com- plication of chronic mitral valve disease, that would be missed and treatment potentially erroneously pursued as increased cardiogenic edema without Vet BLUE. Moreover, think about this hemodynamically fragile patient being restrained in radiology risking the patient coding (cardiopulmonary arrest, CPA), or having an

498 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER unremarkable thoracic radiograph that missed the PCE caused by the left atrial rupture/tear (Guglielmini et al. 2012; Côté et al. 2013). For efficiency, we recommend doing a Vet BLUE‐ TFAST blend by, for example, doing a left Vet BLUE from Caudodorsal (Cd) to Perihilar (Ph) to Middle (Md) to Cranial (Cr) lung regions then sliding caudally over the left TFAST PCS and imaging the heart and interrogating for pleural effusion followed by the DH view from the patient’s left side. After the DH, move to the patient’s right side and make the depth shallow (4–8 cm) for Vet BLUE performing the right Cd to Ph to Md to Cr before ending at the right TFAST PCS, and its most time‐consuming echo views. However, prior to the TFAST right PCS, the sonographer already knows if the lungs are predominantly wet or dry, and where the lung pathology exists, if any, if any pleural effusion (PE) or PCE is present, and how the caudal vena cava and hepatic veins are characterized. Thus, by our rec- ommended Vet BLUE‐TFAST order, the sonographer gains a good idea of how important the TFAST echo views at the right PCS view are by ending at them. Vet BLUE for Pulmonary Hypertension Dogs with pulmonary hypertension (PHT) not uncom- monly have alveolar‐interstitial edema (Kellihan et al. 2015; Kulhavy and Lisciandro 2018). This is very impor- tant to recognize because the PHT‐pulmonary edema is refractory to loop diuretics and the “quick peek approach” will miss the problem, a danger in POCUS heart examination without a Global FAST approach. These TFAST right‐sided cardiac markers (R‐SCMs) are defined as (1) an enlarged right ventricular to left ven- tricular ratio on long axis (RV:LV), (2) a FAT caudal vena cava with hepatic venous distension, (3) gallbladder wall edema, and (4) ascites at the FAST DH view. The findings of an increased RV:LV and a FAT caudal vena cava with hepatic venous distension (tree trunk sign) should always warrant a complete detailed echocardio- gram. The true sensitivity and specificity of TFAST R‐ SCMs are under study for detecting different subsets of right‐sided heart disease, but a recent study suggested that the nonecho TFAST R‐SCMs, i.e., excluding the RV:LV , were not effective as a screening test for canine PHT, concluding that a complete echocardiogram is necessary to rule in or out this subset of right‐sided canine heart disease (Vientós‐Plotts et al. 2019). However, it should be kept in mind that the addition of TFAST echo views (and POCUS heart – focused cardiac ultrasound), including an increased right ventricular to left ventricular ratio (RV:LV), interventricular flattening at the short‐axis left ventricular mushroom view, and an increased pulmonary artery to aortic ratio on short‐axis (PA:Ao), may increase the effectiveness of this type of first‐line screening test for PHT in dogs (see Figures 37.6, 17.25 and 17.26). Vet BLUE for Pneumonias Vet BLUE may be used for tracking (monitoring) pneu- monias by recording findings at the regional views and expecting in resolving pneumonias to see the most consolidated/abnormal lung signs resolving to B‐lines followed by “dry lung” (A‐lines and “lung sliding”). On the other hand, worsening pneumonia will progress from alveolar‐interstitial edema (“wet lung”) of B‐lines to shred sign to tissue sign and possibly, depending on the type of pneumonia, nodule sign. Findings must be recorded and of course a definitive diagnosis sought through gold standard testing to make sure that the diagnosis is correct (bronchoalveolar lavage [BAL], blind BAL, endotracheal wash, fungal testing, lung lobe aspi- rates, lung biopsy, additional imaging studies). The Vet BLUE examination provides a monitoring tool to trigger additional intervention, testing, and imaging along the patient’s clinical course that is low cost, effective, and gives clinicians more confidence using this ancillary imaging modality. Vet BLUE should be combined with Global FAST because other comorbidities may be devel- oping that will be otherwise missed. For example, a feline patient had respiratory signs and maybe a more conservative approach was pursued and on recheck, the spleen is now enlarged (>1 cm) and a splenic aspirate, a safer procedure than a lung lobe aspirate or less costly than a thoracic CT, is performed, yielding the diagnosis of feline histoplasmosis. Without this Global FAST approach, tunnel vision takes the feline down a different path possibly with delays and more risk (and more cost). Vet BLUE for Nodular Disease Vet BLUE may also be used to monitor response to therapy by measuring changes in the size and numbers of nodule(s) (neoplastic, fungal, bacterial or other types of granulomas). The use of Vet BLUE and lung ultrasound in this manner can help determine whether the chemotherapy or antifungal or anthelminthic or antibiotic therapy is working more effectively and with less cost than serial thoracic radiography or CT, carrying the potential that medication strategies may be changed sooner than later. The advantage of Vet BLUE over other published formats is that Vet BLUE has discrete defined regions that may be evaluated, scored and findings recorded that can then be com- pared and followed.

499 POCUS: VET BLUE – CLINICAL INTEGRATION The Future of Proactive Vet BLUE and Lung Ultrasound in Small Animals The use of proactive Vet BLUE lung ultrasound is novel. Historically, lung ultrasound in small animals has primarily been utilized as a secondary imaging pulmonary modality based on thoracic radiography, ironically a less sensitive modality. We are not rein- venting the wheel, and large animal practitioners, especially on the equine side, have been using LUS for a couple of decades, but their approach generally lacks a visual easily understandable lung language and dis- crete regions like Vet BLUE in which locations may be scored and patient data recorded for future comparison. Vet BLUE through its standardization serves as a platform for clinical research regarding the sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy of the regional pattern‐based LUS examination for acute and chronic respiratory conditions, and continues to accelerate the long overdue general use of LUS in small animals. Finally, Vet BLUE may be the greatest advancement for respiratory medicine and possibly veterinary medicine this decade, regarding its impact on care. It is worth learning and implementing Vet BLUE on a daily basis. Recording Vet BLUE Findings on Goal‐Directed Templates Case Examples of Vet BLUE Advantage over Thoracic Radiography Vet BLUE has advantages over TXR on several fronts, including being low impact, point‐of‐care imaging and extremely sensitive for lung surface pathology. 500 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Common diseases make it to the lung surface, and thus Vet BLUE is an effective means to rapidly categorize veterinary patients using its regional, pattern‐based approach, ranging from left‐sided CHF to pneumonia to pulmonary thromboembolism to nonrespiratory look‐alikes to different types of nodular disease. Moreover, through the recording of results, lung con- ditions may be tracked or monitored using Vet BLUE. Some everyday examples are presented below. Aspiration Pneumonia and Other Bacterial Pneumonias The finding of the shred sign in gravity‐dependent Vet BLUE views, Cranial and Middle lung regions, strongly supports the presence of aspiration pneumonia and bacterial pneumonias (Figure 23.34; see also Figures 23.29 and 23.32). Nebulous TXR findings may be better clarified through the use of Vet BLUE. The bulldog cross has an expiratory TXR and coupled with its conformation is problematic in interpretation. However, a Vet BLUE clearly shows “dry lung” at all Vet BLUE views except the right and left Middle (Md) and Cranial (Cr) lung regions that rule in aspiration pneumonia until proven otherwise. The case could have been a hospitalized vomiting parvoviral puppy or pancreatitic dog, any postoperative case, a dog with laryngeal paralysis, a dog with CHF with worsening respiratory signs, a brachiocephalic breed, etc. The list goes on and on. The use of Vet BLUE as a screening test is obvious and detection of the shred sign is readily learned with proper training. The cough is so intermittent that the decision to treat conservatively is made, a historically typical approach in the author’s experience. In this sce- nario, the dog is sent home with antibiotics and fails therapy. A few days later the client phones the veteri- narian who changes the antibiotic and again the dog fails therapy. Now 5–7 days later, failing two different antibiotics, the dog returns for imaging. The patient is scheduled for an endotracheal wash or referred for BAL with airway sampling and testing. The diagnosis may be made (or not, further delayed) and results from the BAL (or other airway sampling), including culture, further delay definitive care. The upshot is that the diagnosis has been delayed for several days and pos- sibly up to two weeks. Let’s consider another sce- nario – the client determines that the cough is no big deal and watches the dog’s respiratory signs worsen for the next three weeks until ultimately rechecking at the point of respiratory distress. Thoracic radiographs now have severe changes in the lungs. The respiratory disease has become advanced and the opportunity to treat and cure, diminished.

501 POCUS: V ET BLUE – C LINICAL I NTEGRATION The new paradigm involves the Global FAST approach because Vet BLUE by itself misses other comorbidities in the thorax and abdomen that may have significant relevant consequences for patient care. In the new approach, Vet BLUE clearly shows multiple nodules, some as large as 5.2 mm and 7.2 mm in diam- eter, that are missed on the TXR (Figure 23.36). This important clinical information is garnered on day 1 of care, immediately following the complete detailed abdominal ultrasound. Digital radiography has been purported to detect nodules as small as 3 mm, but TXR misses these larger 5.2 and 7.2 mm nodules. These Vet BLUE findings trigger fungal testing on day 1 (or a lung lobe aspirate), and the diagnosis of coccidioido - mycosis is expediently made, giving the opportunity to treat (and monitor) when the disease is early in its course. Pearls and Pitfalls, The Final Say • Vet BLUE is the most studied lung ultrasound examination in veterinary medicine. • Vet BLUE provides a regional pattern‐based approach that surveys three intercostal spaces at each transthoracic view. • The identification of the transition zones helps to avoid mistaking abdominal structures for lung pathology and makes the examination more repeat- able between colleagues and with recheck examinations. • Vet BLUE is the fastest and safest way in which to rule out left‐sided CHF in both dogs and cats. 505 POCUS: VET BLUE – CLINICAL INTEGRATION • Vet BLUE has a “visual lung language” that helps with communication of findings. • Vet BLUE has a B‐line scoring system to better estimate the degree of alveolar‐interstitial edema. • Vet BLUE and its B‐line scoring system help to direct diuretic usage in left‐sided CHF patients. • Vet BLUE has a lung contusion scoring system. Quick Reference of Normals and Rules of Thumb • Expect adult dogs and cats and puppies and kit- tens >6 weeks of age to have “dry lung” artifacts predominate (absent B‐lines). In other words, no more than a single B‐line at only one of the eight transthoracic Vet BLUE views. • Numbers of B‐lines correlate to the degree of alve- olar‐interstitial edema in human lung and likely in other mammalian lung, including small animals. • “Absent B‐lines all (Vet BLUE) views (ABAV)” rules out clinically relevant left‐sided CHF in both dogs and cats (and likely for all mammalian lung). • The Volpicelli Strong Positive model is an effective screening test to rule in left‐sided CHF in cats. • Shred sign in gravity‐dependent Vet BLUE views sup- ports aspiration and bacterial bronchopneumonia. • Wedge sign in the dorsal nongravity‐dependent Vet BLUE views supports pulmonary thromboembolism. • Nodule sign supports neoplastic, granulomatous processes including fungal, parasitic and bacterial, and abscessation. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 511 Introduction Vascular access is a requirement for nearly every emergent and/or critical case, and the more emergent or critical the patient, the more difficult obtaining vascular access seems to be. Moreover, many elective procedures require vascular access for administration of sedatives, analgesics, anesthetics, medications, and emergency drugs. Factors like anatomical conforma- tion and local hematoma formation from failed intra- vascular catheter attempts can potentially jeopardize patients’ safety and add to their discomfort. Ultrasound guidance for vascular access is point‐of‐care and non- invasive, increases reliability, and is generally unaf- fected by common complications like patient size, obesity, local hematoma formation, and peripheral edema that can frustrate blind catheterization proce- dures (also referred to as the landmark technique). As a result, ultrasound‐guided central venous catheter placement has become standard of care in human med- icine for both adult and pediatric patients across mul- tiple disciplines and is similarly recommended for arterial catheterization (Miller et al. 2002; Milling et al. 2005; Wigmore et al. 2007; Ringold and Kelmer 2008; Froelich et al. 2009; AIUM 2013; Mustapha et al. 2016). Although sparsely described in the veterinary litera- ture, ultrasound guidance during these procedures delivers the same advantages as in human medicine (Ringold and Kelmer 2008; Chamberlin et al. 2013; Izer et al. 2017; Pavlisko et al. 2018). Through comparison with traditional blind catheteri- zation, ultrasound‐guided techniques have documented greater success rates with fewer complications in the emergency, critical care, and anesthesia settings. Furthermore, ultrasound guidance is less invasive than surgical cut‐down techniques, which often sacrifice the vessel and risk neuropraxia (Miller et al. 2002; Karakitsos et al. 2006; Pirotte and Veyckmans 2007; Ringold and Kelmer 2008; Theodoro et al. 2010). Perhaps most importantly, ultrasound‐guided vascular access tech- niques have been shown to be achievable by minimally trained, nonradiologist clinicians (Miller et al. 2002; Froehlich et al. 2009) and veterinarians (Ringold and Kelmer 2008; Chamberlin et al. 2013). Veterinary Central Venous Catheterization The author’s veterinary study describing ultrasound guidance for central venous catheter placement dem- onstrated that the procedure was technically easy and rapid, with a median time of 1.9 minutes without hematoma formation and 4.3 minutes with hematoma formation. Ultrasound guidance additionally had a relatively shallow learning curve among nonradiolo- gist residents and faculty involved in learning and then performing the procedure. Despite complicating factors such as iatrogenic perivascular hematoma formation and cardiovascular collapse post cardiac arrest, ultrasound‐guided central venous catheter placement was achievable with a 100% success rate across all participants in the study (Chamberlin et al. 2013). And, now with a realistic training model also described within this chapter, learning this ultrasound‐ related skill is even more practical. 512 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Veterinary Arterial Catheterization The most common site in veterinary medicine for arterial catheter placement is the dorsal pedal artery, which is a challenging target in small or unstable patients. The larger femoral artery is an excellent alternative and thus also may be used for obtaining direct blood pressure as well as respiratory and acid– base laboratory values; this larger artery is also the preferred access site for cardiac catheterizations and other interventional radiology procedures (Ringold and Kelmer 2008; Kweon et al. 2012; Izer et al. 2017; Pavlisko et al. 2018). Ultrasound guidance may be used to visually place femoral arterial catheters in veterinary patients. The target vessel and the insertion of the stylet, guidewire, and catheter are not only imaged during real‐time ultrasound for greater accuracy during cath- eter insertion, but the procedure helps identify and avoid nearby anatomical structures, thus minimizing complications over the traditional blind landmark tech- niques (Ringold and Kelmer 2008; Chamberlin et al. 2013). In fact, higher intravascular pressures make peri- arterial hematomas larger and more common; repeated attempts are virtually impossible using the landmark technique at the same site. Perivascular fluid (like a hematoma) does not hinder but in fact often enhances target vessel imaging in the far‐field through acoustic enhancement artifact. Ultrasound thus delivers a huge advantage in these situations. Applications for Peripheral Vessels While distal and peripheral vessels are commonly used by veterinarians for short‐term simple vascular access, ultrasound‐guided catheterization of vessels like the cephalic vein or dorsal pedal artery in cats and dogs is generally of minimal benefit due to their small limb radius and the shallow depth of tissue between skin sur- face, vessel of interest, and underlying bone. Ultrasound machines are also generally unable to image that closely in the near‐field. Although acoustically permeable “stand‐off” blocks are used for denser superficial mus- culoskeletal structures such as tendons, ligaments, and bones, they are generally cumbersome and thus ineffec- tive for catheterizing superficial and distal limb vessels in dogs and cats (see Chapters 34 and 35). Recent T raining Advancements A novel, simple, affordable, realistic training model has recently been described for teaching and practicing ultrasound‐guided vascular access (Rippey et al. 2015). A recipe for creating these useful chicken breast phan- toms is provided later in this chapter. In summary, ultrasound guidance for central venous and arterial catheterization delivers the potential to provide significant benefits in patient care by facili- tating vessel cannulation success rates, especially when patient factors like hypotension, conformation, or hematomas make vascular access particularly chal- lenging. Recent training advances, experience, and knowledge should help accelerate providers’ profi- ciency and comfort with ultrasound guidance as a core skill for veterinarians. What POCUS Central Venous and Arterial Catheterization Can Do • Rapidly identify the jugular vein or femoral artery for catheterization independent of vascular col- lapse, peripheral edema, obesity, patient size, and local hematoma formation. • Guide central venous or femoral arterial catheter placement, preventing damage to adjacent struc- tures otherwise unrecognized via the traditional blind landmark method. • Provide a less invasive option over surgical cut‐ down procedures. • Facilitate the use of central venous catheters, which allow more rapid fluid and drug delivery to central circulation and simplify repeated blood sampling. • Enable administration of hyperosmolar or other fluids that cause peripheral phlebitis, and allow for otherwise incompatible fluid administration via multilumen central venous catheters. • Enable early goal‐directed therapy including central venous pressure (CVP) measurement and central venous oxygen saturation. • Facilitate arterial catheterization which allows arterial blood sampling, direct arterial blood pressure measurements, and interventional radi- ology techniques. • Enable and then confirm a reliable “clean stick” for safe and successful cannulation of a desired vein or artery, particularly useful for interventional or high‐flow procedures such as hemodialysis. What POCUS Central Venous and Arterial Catheterization Cannot Do • Cannot guide cannulation of superficially located small veins and arteries. • Cannot replace adequate ultrasound training because vascular ultrasound techniques are operator dependent.

513 POCUS: C ENTRAL V ENOUS AND A RTERIAL C ATHETERI z ATION Indications • Failure or anticipated failure in obtaining any vascular access by traditional blind landmark tech- niques due to cardiovascular collapse, hypoten - sion, or hematoma formation. • Inability to identify the target vessel (central vein or femoral artery) due to cardiovascular collapse, hypotension, or hematoma formation. • Requirement for central venous access for administration of caustic or high osmolarity drugs poorly suited for peripheral administration, and/ or administration of parenteral nutrition and mul - tiple incompatible drugs or transfusion products by use of multilumen central venous catheters. • Requirement for frequent blood sampling for criti- cally ill and fractious animals. • Requirement for arterial sampling and access for direct arterial blood pressure readings and/or respiratory and acid–base monitoring when tradi - tional distal arterial sampling sites are compro - mised or unavailable. • Requirement for cannulation of large vessels with minimal trauma for interventional radiology, hemodialysis, and other special procedures. Objectives • Ultrasonographically recognize the regional vascu- lature and anatomy of the neck. • Use ultrasound guidance for central venous placement using the jugular vein. • Ultrasonographically recognize regional vascula - ture and nerves of the hindlimbs. • Use ultrasound guidance for femoral arterial cath - eterization and direct arterial sampling. • Be aware that a simple model (phantom) can be made locally using inexpensive, readily available supplies that provides hands‐on training with realistic images including normal tissue planes and echogenicity. Placement of an Ultrasound‐ guided Central Venous Jugular Catheter Equipment and Materials Probe Most of the probes commonly used in small animal medicine can be used to gain vascular access. Linear array probes with a minimum frequency of 7.5 MHz are preferred because of their superior detail at shallow depths. Curvilinear (microconvex) 5–8 MHz probes are the most widespread probe type in veterinary medi - cine, having the ability to magnify to a depth of <4 cm. • Some ultrasound machines have a “needle enhancement” feature; these can be helpful and are most commonly featured with linear probes. • Probes should be cleaned and disinfected according to manufacturer guidelines before and after use in ultrasound‐guided vascular access. • Although not required, color flow Doppler ultra - sound is helpful to gain confidence in differenti - ating vein from artery. However, most sonographers become proficient with ultrasound‐guided proce - dures using only B‐mode. In fact, several large studies recommend against using color flow Doppler because the pulse in the artery can also make the vein move, which can lead to operator confusion (Bowra 2006). Pearl: Utilizing “Small Parts” or “Vascular” presets on your machine can improve imaging detail. Pearl: For aseptic ultrasound imaging, the probe may be placed in a sterile surgical glove or sterile obstetric sleeve as a protective barrier that is filled with acoustic coupling gel (Figure 24.1). Figure 24.1. Sterile probe preparation. Sterile probe prepa- ration using a sterile glove barrier. Acoustic coupling gel is on the probe inside the glove. Alcohol with or without sterile acoustic coupling gel is applied to the patient’s skin for optimal imaging at the probe‐glove‐skin interface.

514 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Central Venous Catheter Selection There are different styles of central venous cathe- ters available, including the through‐the‐needle Venocath® (Hospira, Inc., Lake Forest, IL) and Seldinger‐type designs (Mila International, Erlanger, KY; Cook, Inc., Bloomington, IL) which come in variable lengths with variable numbers of lumens (single, double, triple). Central Venous Catheter Line Length Premeasuring from the insertion site to the patient’s 4th–5th rib is imperative to prevent catheter‐associated complications because advancing the central line too far risks placing the catheter into the right heart and/ or pulmonary artery. Excessive advancement of the catheter can cause direct injury to the heart or coiling and knotting of the central line, rendering it irretriev- able (Mitchell and Clark 1979; Kusminsky 2007). The central venous catheters placed using the Seldinger technique are preferred; however, both central venous catheter designs can be unquestion- ably foreign and intimidating to the novice. Sacrifice a Venocath or single‐lumen Seldinger‐technique central venous catheter for familiarity with the device; the latter includes several components including a needle or stylet, a guidewire, a dilator, and the actual central venous catheter (used sequentially). Some excellent supplementary step‐by‐step descriptions are available including Silverstein and Hopper’s Small Animal Critical Care Medicine, Hackett and Mazzaferro’s Veterinary Emergency and Critical Care Procedures (2012 edition includes online videos), as well as other video demonstrations available on YouTube. How to Place an Ultrasound‐ guided Central Venous Jugular Catheter Static versus Dynamic and One‐ versus T wo‐person T echniques As with any medical procedure, there are multiple ultrasound‐guided vascular access techniques avail- able to the veterinarian. Each technique has inherent advantages and disadvantages with regard to comfort, efficacy, and safety. The points for ultrasound‐guided central venous catheter placement reviewed below relate to how much the probe is used during actual catheter placement (static vs dynamic or real‐time placement vs combinations thereof) and probe orienta- tion (transverse [out of plane] vs longitudinal [in plane] vs combinations thereof). Because needle guides (devices that attach to the probe) are too cumbersome for vascular access techniques, only free‐hand descrip- tions are used in this text (Ringold and Kelmer 2008; Chamberlin et al. 2013). Static T echnique The static technique uses ultrasound as a screening tool to localize structures (vessels, nerves, etc.) prior to blindly placing the catheter in the traditional landmark manner. This technique has been described in the human literature as acceptable, though it is less suc- cessful than the dynamic technique. The static tech- nique may be an option for the novice who has difficulty coordinating both the probe and the stylet as guided by the ultrasound image during catheter introduction. Dynamic T echnique In the dynamic technique, ultrasound is used to actu- ally guide the catheter into the vessel using ultra- sound in real time. Because this method tracks the target vessel and the surrounding structures in rela- tion to the sharp stylet, it is safer and typically more successful than the static technique, especially when a single operator manipulates both the catheter and the ultrasound probe. Note that an assistant is gener - ally still needed to place digital pressure in the jugular furrow to “hold off the vein,” just like during the traditional blind technique. The novice sonogra- pher performing the dynamic technique may be tempted to have an assistant maneuver the probe; however, communication and coordination between Pearl: In general, it is best to use a 16 gauge central venous catheter for larger dogs (>7.5 kg) and an 18 gauge central venous catheter for smaller dogs and cats (<7.5 kg). Pearl: Premeasure the catheter to the fourth or fifth rib on the patient and note the length on the catheter (most central venous catheters have length demar - cations printed on them). Confirm central venous catheter location with postprocedure radiographs. Pearl: Sacrifice a Venocath or Seldinger‐technique catheter for familiarity and practice with the device.

515 POCUS: CENTRAL VENOUS AND ARTERIAL CATHETERIzATION the person placing the catheter and the person holding the probe is often a source for error. With minimal training to develop comfort with ultrasound imaging and coordinating both the probe and stylet, the one‐person technique will quickly prove more successful and lead to fewer errors than the static or two‐person options (Milling et al. 2005; Chamberlin et al. 2013). Traditionally, jugular vein catheterization is aban- doned when hematomas obscure palpable and visual landmarks. However, ultrasound becomes more effec- tive when imaging through fluid in such circumstances (acoustic enhancement artifact) and permits continued attempts for central venous catheter placement at the discretion of the attending veterinarian. Moreover, stylets, needles, and catheter components may be ultrasonographically visualized in real time, providing distinct advantages over both the static and blind land- mark methods. Coated needles have been specifically developed for increased ultrasonographic visualiza- tion (Havel’s, Mila). Honing Y our Skills Simple and affordable homemade models using Jello® or commercially available phantoms are great practice options (Wells and Goldstein 2010; Rippey et al. 2015), and a description for a recently published realistic phantom model using chicken breast filets and balloons is included in this chapter. We have found the chicken breast phantom model hugely helpful in accelerating the perfection of ultrasound‐ guided catheterization skills. The dynamic real‐time technique is subsequently described. Keep in mind the aforementioned options because it is not uncommon for any veterinary procedure to become modified based on the particular circumstances at that time, such as bailing on the dynamic technique because the static technique lends itself better to the situation at hand. Anatomy The external jugular veins are the preferred central venous catheter sites in veterinary patients. Each jugular vein runs ventrolaterally on the left and right sides of the neck superficially under the skin, traversing from the angle of the mandible to the thoracic inlet. Each jugular vein is bounded throughout its slightly angulated course ventrally by the sternocephalicus muscle and laterally by the cleidocervicalis muscle. Patient Preparation Place the patient in lateral recumbency consistent with typical positioning for jugular catheterization, then clip hair and aseptically prep the skin as fully as pos- sible, depending on patient stability. • All attempts should be made to adequately shave over the jugular furrow (ventrolateral cervical region) to give ample room to aseptically prep the skin over the central venous catheter insertion site and com- fortably protect the site post insertion (neck wrap). • Liberal local use of 70% isopropyl alcohol, either by itself (which is often sufficient) or in combination with acoustic coupling gels mentioned below, improves probe contact or greatly enhances image quality while maintaining a clean catheter insertion site. However, the attending veterinarian should keep in mind the following precautions. • Alcohol‐induced hypothermia (external cooling) may occur in any patient, especially smaller animals. • The inherent flammability of alcohol also poses burn risks to the patient in the event of electrical defibrillation. Sterile acoustic coupling gels are commercially avail- able and ideal (Aquasonics, Parker Laboratories, Fairfield, NJ). Although it lacks viscosity and tends to fall off the site, sterile K‐Y® Jelly (Johnson and Johnson, New Brunswick, NJ) serves as a replacement option to sterile commercially available acoustic coupling gel. Orientation • Verify the ultrasound probe‐to‐screen marker ori- entation so that direction is accurate during the procedure. • The ultrasound monitor must be located in a com- fortable line of sight and generally the head of the patient and the ultrasound screen should be in the same sightline. Pearl: Excess alcohol and gel should be wiped off the hair and skin as soon as it is no longer needed. Pitfall: It is unsafe for the patient, not to mention difficult, fatiguing and uncomfortable for the sonog- rapher, to insert a central venous catheter (or arterial catheter) when craning to look over your shoulder at the ultrasound screen (Bowra 2006).

516 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER • With the nondominant hand of the person placing the central venous catheter, the ultrasound probe is placed in the jugular groove in transverse orienta - tion just caudal to the desired catheter entry point on the skin, searching for the anechoic (black) cir - cles of the vessels (Figure 24.2A). • Structures (particularly artery versus vein) are most easily identified by their anatomical location and by intermittent gentle probe pressure (com - pression technique) since veins will collapse (flat - ten) while arteries will not flatten but remain relatively circular (see Figure 24.2). • Color flow Doppler, when available, may be help - ful in the learning phases to gain confidence in dif- ferentiating vein from artery. However, color flow Doppler is not required as proficiency may be obtained without it, and in fact it is not recom - mended in several larger published human studies and protocols (Bowra 2006). • Color flow Doppler does not identify artery and vein by color but rather is generally coded as “red” flow- ing towards the probe and “blue” flowing away. The sonographer can either remain in transverse orien- tation (needle out of plane) throughout the catheter placement (often easier for the novice and advanta - geous in short‐necked animals) (Blaivas et al. 2003), rotate the probe 90° to a longitudinal alignment (needle in plane), obtaining an anechoic (black) linear tract representative of the jugular vein (Figure 24.3), or use combinations of transverse and longitudinal views. In either transverse or longitudinal views, the probe is placed just caudal (closer to the heart) to the desired catheter entry point on the skin. For safety and by convention when using longitudinal orientation (very important), the ultrasound probe marker should point rostrally, thus positioning the probe marker on the same side as the catheter insertion site. T ransverse Orientation With the jugular vein identified, move the ultrasound probe and alter image depth and focus so that the vessel appears in the center of the ultrasound screen as an anechoic circle (transverse orientation), thus “land- marking” the jugular vein’s position (Figures 24.2 and 24.4). With the dominant hand, insert the stylet (or Figure 24.2. Compression technique to discriminate jugular vein from carotid artery. (A) Transverse image depicting normal probe pressure (no significant compression) with both the jugular vein and carotid artery visible. (B) Transverse image depict- ing the disappearance of the jugular vein with gentle probe pressure (compression) while the lumen of the carotid artery remains visible (circular). The compression technique is effective and reliable in discriminating between arteries and veins. Pearl: As with traditional landmark techniques, having an assistant “hold off” the jugular vein by applying digital pressure at the thoracic inlet can prove helpful in visualizing as well as cannulating the jugular vein. Sensible Use of a Short T emporary Jugular Catheter In emergency resuscitation situations, in which time is critical for rapid venous access and a full‐length central venous catheter may be too cumbersome, an excellent intermediate option is to use ultrasound guidance to percutaneously place a short large‐bore (18 gauge or larger) 1.5 inch catheter in the jugular vein. The tempo- rary short catheter permits rapid administration of resuscitative fluids through a large central vein (jugular). This short jugular catheter may be tempo- rarily secured with any combination of tape, adhesive catheter covers, or one or two looped sutures incorpo- rating both the catheter’s hub and the patient’s skin. Be careful because the skin over the vessel is highly mobile in this area and the short catheter can come out of the jugular vein into the subcutaneous space during patient movement. If you have resuscitated the patient and you don’t have a long central venous catheter in stock, place another short peripheral catheter for fluid/ drug administration, but consider leaving the short jugular catheter secured with a saline lock. Be smart! The short, large‐bore catheter in the jugular vein may be used after initial stabilization as a conduit using the central venous catheter kit’s guidewire for a long central line, taking advantage of this temporary catheter to complete a modified Seldinger technique with a single or multilumen central venous catheter or the Venocath. Of course, time and patient stability per- mitting, a true central venous catheter may be placed at the outset (see above). The responsible use of a central venous catheter is a welcome addition to patient care in any emergency and critical care center or 24‐hour general practice. Please note, however, that significant hemorrhage or other complications can occur if the catheter is dislodged or severed, so 24‐hour veterinary surveillance and monitoring is warranted. Equipment For special procedures such as cardiac catheterization, use equipment (stylets, catheters) designed for that procedure. For general blood pressure monitoring and sampling (including via the femoral artery), arterial access can be maintained with standard short catheters (18–24 gauge, 1–1.5 inches) commonly used for peripheral (cephalic, saphenous) venous access. Procedure The dynamic real‐time technique with combinations of longitudinal and transverse orientation is described here, as briefly outlined under the central venous cath- eter section. Anatomy The femoral artery is a continuation of the external iliac artery and courses along the medial aspect of the femur. Proximally, the femoral artery lies cranial to the femoral vein and caudal or medial to the saphenous nerve within the femoral triangle (formed by the sartorius muscle cranially, pectineus muscle caudally, and iliopsoas and vastus lateralis muscle Pearl: In general, it is best to use a 16 gauge central venous catheter for larger dogs (>7.5 kg) and 18 gauge central venous catheter for smaller dogs and cats (<7.5 kg). See the equipment section above. Pearl: It is extremely important to secure any arterial catheter via tape and/or padding around the limb to prevent dislodgment and life‐threatening hemorrhage while moving anesthetized or even awake patients.

Distal to the femoral triangle, these vessels are covered by the caudal belly of the semimembranosus muscle and course caudodistally in relation to the femur, crossing the mid to distal third of the femoral diaphysis at an angle of approximately 35° (Ringold and Kelmer 2008). Patient Preparation Place the patient in lateral recumbency with the non- dependent hindlimb abducted, extended, and immo- bilized by tethering it to the table by appropriate physical and/or chemical restraint techniques to allow access to the dependent limb’s inguinal region (proximal medial thigh). Shave the medial thigh, giving ample room to aseptically prep the skin over the femoral artery insertion site. Liberal local use of 70% isopropyl alcohol either by itself (which is often sufficient) or in combination with the gels mentioned below improves probe contact and greatly enhances image quality while maintaining a clean central venous catheter insertion site. The attending veterinarian should keep in mind the following precautions. • Alcohol‐induced hypothermia (external cooling) may occur in any patient, especially smaller animals. • The inherent flammability of alcohol is environ- mentally dangerous (fire, explosion) and poses burn risks to the patient in the event of electrical defibrillation. Sterile acoustic coupling gels are commercially avai- lable and ideal (Aquasonics, Parker Laboratories, Fairfield, NJ). Although it lacks viscosity and tends to fall off the site, sterile K‐Y Jelly can be used instead of sterile commercially available acoustic coupling gel. Orientation Verify the ultrasound probe‐to‐screen marker orienta- tion so that direction is accurate during the procedure. The ultrasound monitor must be located in a comfort- able line of sight. • Using the nondominant hand, place the ultrasound probe over the femoral triangle in transverse orien- tation relative to the axis of the proximal limb, proximal to the desired entry point on the skin, searching for the anechoic (black) circles of the vessel lumens (Figure 24.9). • Structures (particularly artery vs vein) are most easily identified by anatomical location (the femoral artery is cranial to the femoral vein) and by intermittent gentle probe pressure because veins flatten (collapse) and arteries remain relatively circular (maintain their lumen and do not collapse) (Figure 24.10). Generally, the pulsatile motion of the artery is often observable in B‐mode without the use of color flow Doppler. Color flow Doppler, when available, may be helpful in the learning phases to gain confidence in differen- tiating femoral artery from vein. • Once the artery is identified, move distally along the femoral triangle to approximately middiaphy- sis of the femur in case multiple attempts are needed. By starting distally, the proximal femoral artery is spared and may be used for repeated attempts if necessary. • Using a #11 scalpel blade or an extra 18 gauge to nick the skin 3–5 mm lateral to the vessel may facilitate getting the stylet through tough skin. Pearl: For aseptic ultrasound imaging, the probe may be placed in a sterile surgical glove or sterile obstetric sleeve as a protective barrier that is filled with acoustic coupling gel (see Figure 24.1). Pearl: Excess alcohol and gel should be wiped off the fur and skin as soon as it is no longer needed. Pearl: It is difficult and potentially hazardous to insert a central venous catheter or arterial catheter when craning to look over your shoulder at the screen (Bowra 2006). Pearl: Remember that the colors do not identify the vessel but rather are generally coded as red with flow toward the probe and blue with flow away from the probe. Pearl: Color flow Doppler ultrasound imaging for pulsatile arterial flow is not 100% reliable because the artery’s “jump” can transmit misinterpreted motion to the nearby vein, causing misidentification (Bowra 2006).

524 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER General Comments regarding Transverse versus Longitudinal Orientation As with any intravenous catheter placement, regardless of ultrasound guidance, the most challenging aspect of the procedure after finding the vein or artery is pene- trating the superficial vessel wall without the vessel sliding or rolling away. The longitudinal approach provides direct visuali- zation of the stylet entering the skin while directing the stylet toward the jugular vein and during pene- tration of the lumen. It is easier to maintain visualiza- tion of the sharp tip of the stylet and relevant structures using the longitudinal orientation, avoid- ing complications such as inadvertent puncturing of the vessel’s far wall and damage to other structures. The longitudinal approach is thus considered the saf- est orientation because it allows visualization of the stylet tip through the entire central venous catheter placement process. On the other hand, some users find the longitudinal approach to be more difficult when redirecting the catheter if the vessel rolls away because of the diffi- culty discerning in real time which direction the stylet goes relative to the target vessel (medial vs lateral). Once this occurs, the sonographer may need to partially or fully rotate back to transverse orientation to deter - mine how to redirect the stylet into the target vessel. The transverse approach provides better visualization of the vessel of interest relative to other structures and more efficiently helps visualize redirection of the stylet when the vein or artery rolls. Moreover, transverse orientation is better suited where space is limited (i.e., for smaller or short‐necked patients). However, there is a greater risk of losing track of the stylet’s sharp tip and thus inadvertently damaging surrounding structures. On the other hand, if the probe is placed too far rostrally over the stylet’s midpoint or even as high as the hub (which can definitely occur while the clini- cian’s attention is divided between the probe, the stylet, and the ultrasound image), then visualization of the sharp tip of the stylet within the narrow fan of the ultrasound beam will be lost. It is easier to lose track of the tip of the stylet in transverse than longitudinal orientation as mentioned above, thus risking damage to other structures. How to Make a Realistic Practice Phantom Ultrasound‐guided vascular access has a shallow learning curve but the opportunity to gain proficiency before attempting the technique in an emergent or unstable patient supports patient safety and operator success. A simple model (phantom) using inexpensive, readily available supplies was recently developed that provides hands‐on training with realistic high‐fidelity images including normal tissue planes and echo- genicity. The author has used this easily constructed model in international settings to successfully teach ultrasound‐guided vascular access to veterinary care providers of varying levels of experience. The mate- rials and techniques are highlighted here, and more details including videos are available at www.vascular‐ access.info (Rippey et al. 2015). Supplies A photograph of the supplies needed to construct the chicken breast phantom model is shown in Figure 24.12. • Modeling balloons (the long thin ones used to make balloon animals work best to simulate veins, available at party or hobby shop retailers) and/or Pezzer tubes (arteries). • Colored fluid (simulated “blood”). • 60 cc catheter‐tipped syringe, to load the blood into the balloon simulated vessels. • Plastic cling wrap, i.e., Saran Wrap®. • Acoustic coupling gel. • IV catheters (short and/or long). • Boneless skinless chicken breasts (not too thick, or the catheter is too short to feed effectively). • Exam gloves (both for the user and to put the ultra- sound gel and probe into – the image quality remains good while your probe is further protected from contact with the chicken). Pearls and Pitfalls, The Final Say Real‐time ultrasound‐guided vascular access can be technically challenging at first but has a relatively shal- low learning curve. It has been shown that proficiency may be readily mastered by the nonradiologist veteri - nary sonographer with minimal training (enabled by simple and affordable models), the procedure is fast and has the potential to become an invaluable asset to your practice. A few key points. • Place the ultrasound screen in a line of vision that is comfortable for you. This is safest for your patient as well. • Liberal use of 70% isopropyl alcohol is generally sufficient for good image quality; however, some probe heads will incur damage (check manufac - turer’s guidelines), and alcohol may excessively cool the patient and increase risk of burns if electrical defibrillation is required. • For initial emergency resuscitation, a short, large‐ bore (18 gauge, 1.5 inch) catheter can be placed in the jugular vein for rapid easy vascular access and high fluid rates. Just be careful because the skin over the vessel is highly mobile in this area, and the short catheter can come out of the jugular vein into the subcutaneous space during patient movement. • The short catheter also provides an excellent con - duit after initial stabilization for a guidewire and replacement with a true central venous catheter using a modified Seldinger technique. • Color flow Doppler can sometimes be helpful but is not required for vasculature structure identification, and it has some inherent artifactual problems if a patient is uncooperative because movement com - promises its diagnostic utility. • The compression technique during B‐mode is often adequate to discriminate veins (which collapse with compression) from arteries (which do not collapse). • Focus on keeping the sharp tip of the stylet and the target vessel visible in the field of view at all times for success and safety. Using combinations of transverse and longitudinal orientation is some - times helpful. • Move the stylet (or needle in some kits, see above) slowly, and look for tenting as the tip lands on the superficial proximal wall of the vessel. • Models or phantoms can be made with Jello (incor- porating embedded objects like grapes or tomatoes as targets), polony, or chicken breasts and mod - eling balloons (Wells and Goldstein 2010; Rippey et al. 2015; www.vascular‐access.info). • Phantoms also can be purchased for practicing stylet orientation and tracking. Starting with a large dog with more easily recognized and larger anatomy instead of a pug or a cat may also be helpful. Figure 24.14. Chicken breast model assembly part II. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 529 Introduction Throughout this textbook, you are learning image acquisition and the ultrasonographic appearance of fluid (cavitary effusions to fluid‐filled organs to viscus organs), various soft tissues (muscle to solid organs to nerves), bone and air (lung to viscus organs). Imaging fluid‐filled vessels is another skill to add to your arma- mentarium with the potential to improve patient care and outcome. POCUS vascular is not meant to be a standalone examination without the Global FAST approach. Applying Global FAST should be an extension of your physical examination and POCUS vascular an add‐on so that major easily detected conditions within the abdomen, retroperitoneal space, and thorax are not missed. Moreover, most thromboem- bolic disease is a result of another disease process, which may be treatable. And, by using Global FAST as a more effective surveillance system and a first‐line evaluation, the triggering of thrombopro- phylaxis and thrombolytics becomes more evidence based by “seeing” the problem(s) for decision making. This chapter will briefly review the major sites and principles for the detection (or suspicion) of venous and aortic thrombosis and thromboembolism in small animals, of which very little is known. The use of POCUS and FAST ultrasound has the ability to change another traditionally difficult paradigm. What POCUS Vascular Can Do • Identify fluid‐filled vessels and distinguish veins from arteries using the compression technique. • Screen for sonographic evidence of venous thrombosis, arterial thrombosis, and pulmonary thromboembolism. • Screen for abnormalities in veins and arteries supported by their distension, collapse and soft tissue thrombi within using the general principles of obstruction to flow within a conduit. • Provide a means to dictate thrombolytics and throm- boprophylaxis and monitor response to therapy. • Develop your use of color Doppler. What POCUS Vascular Cannot Do • Cannot identify superficially located small veins and arteries without a stand‐off device. • Cannot replace adequate training because vascular imaging often requires more knowledge of your ultrasound machine, imaging techniques, probe changes, and ultrasonographic anatomy. Indications • Add‐on to all at‐risk patients for venous and arterial thrombosis and pulmonary thromboembolism. • Edematous limbs. POCUS: V ascular – Veins and Arteries Gregory R. 530 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER • Acute respiratory signs. • Post heartworm treatment. • Patients undergoing chemotherapy. • Total hip replacement surgery, and other postsur - gical invasive bone procedures. Objectives • Distinguish between veins and arteries using the compression technique with and without the use of color Doppler. • Understand how to use color flow Doppler. • Survey major vessels for evidence of venous and arterial thrombosis and thromboembolism. Equipment, Materials, and General Preparation Probe Most curvilinear (microconvex) probes with fre- quency ranges of 5–10 MHz on abdominal presets that are commonly used in small animal practice may be used for vascular imaging of the larger vessels within the abdominal cavity. However, for more superficial vessels, especially with limbs, linear transducers with a minimum frequency of 7.5 MHz are preferred because of their superior detail at shallow depths. Additionally, the “Small Parts” or “Vascular” presets on your machine will optimize the imaging detail with either probe type, and a stand‐off device further optimizes image quality and may be mandatory for superficial vessels (see Chapters 30–35). Patient Preparation In general, shaving of hair is not required for POCUS, but in thickly coated patients or those in which imaging is not satisfactory for the detail required for interrogation of the area of interest, shaving will likely improve your image. Parting the hair is often helped by wetting the hair first with 70% isopropyl alcohol, which is then reapplied to the skin as needed with the addition of either alcohol‐based hand sani- tizer or commercially available acoustic coupling gel, dependent on sonographer preference. Maximize probe head to skin contact with ample coupling medium using combinations of 70% isopropyl alcohol, commercially available gel, and alcohol‐ based hand sanitizer. General Principles and Compression T echnique By combining principles you will have a better proba- bility of being correct in your assessment of venous and arterial thrombosis, thromboembolism and the degree of their obstruction. As with any obstructive process to unidirectional flow within a conduit, the proximal side will have dilation and the distal side attenuation. Importantly and generally counter to logic, the acute nascent thrombus (clot) is poorly echo- genic and often anechoic (like blood), being difficult to directly image. Thus, color Doppler is important to apply to the vessel(s) of interest to enhance imaging of the thrombus as well as the deviations of expected blood flow within an unobstructed vessel. Physically, pressure compression is important for a couple of rea- sons: (1) veins, being a lower pressure system and thin- ner‐walled, collapse before arteries in normalcy, and (2) veins, when obstructed, become less compressible. The use of the compression technique is often ade- quate for differentiating vein from artery (Figure 25.1). This principle is used as a diagnostic strategy for detecting deep venous thrombosis (DVT) in the lower limbs of people using B‐mode, often without color flow Doppler (Crisp et al. 2010; Kory et al. 2011). However, importantly, venous blood can be sluggish and echogenic, especially in larger veins, mimicking soft tissue, advocating for the use of color Doppler in veterinary patients (Nyland and Mattoon 2015; Nyland et al. 2015). Color Doppler There are a few different types of color Doppler but most commonly color flow Doppler, which gives an overview of flow, will be used by the nonradiologist. Color flow Doppler is necessary for two major reasons: acute thrombi often are poorly echogenic and not obvious with gray‐scale B‐mode imaging, and to dif- ferentiate sluggish venous flow from a thrombus (Nyland and Mattoon 2015; Nyland et al. 2015). However, color flow Doppler has some limitations including patient movement (panting, trembling, or struggling), which leads to motion artifacts causing the Doppler colors to “jump” to other areas. Similarly, the color flow Doppler gain setting has a profound effect (aliasing) on image quality and overgaining leads to a similar problem with colors “jumping” to other areas (Figure 25.2). Color flow is also affected by other basics such as the angle of insonation and the focus cursor. Learn how to adjust the gain, place the focus cursor across from the area of interest, and manipulate the

531 POCUS: V ASCULAR – V EINS AND A RTERIES angle of insonation for best imaging using color flow Doppler. In most machines, the color flow Doppler gain is the same wheel or button as the overall B‐mode gray‐scale gain. Vessel Orientation and Slice‐thickness Artifact Vessels are imaged in their longitudinal (also referred to as long‐axis) and transverse (also referred to as short‐axis) planes. Longitudinal elongates the vessel as a tube and transverse brings the vessel into the shape of a circle or oval (Figure 25.3). Slice‐thickness artifact can occur in larger veins that are within solid organs (primarily hepatic veins and the caudal vena cava passing through the liver) and mimic a thrombus when imaged in longitudinal planes. To help differentiate slice‐thickness artifact from a true thrombus, rotate the probe to the transverse plane, which will as a rule elim- inate the artifact (Figure 25.4) (Nyland and Mattoon 2015; Nyland et al. 2015). Porta Hepatis Anatomy It is important to learn the anatomy of the closely asso- ciated aorta, caudal vena cava (CVC), and portal vein imaged via the 10–12th intercostal spaces in a transverse plane with the probe oriented parallel to the ribs. At this porta hepatis view, the aorta, CVC, and portal vein may be imaged side by side from cranial to caudal within the same view (see Chapter 26) (see also Figures 16.15, 16.16, 26.2, 26.5, and 39.3). 532 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Venous and Arterial Thromboembolism Central and Deep Venous Thrombosis Central venous thrombosis is seen in small animals, often in the CVC (see Figure 25.6) and splenic veins. Other venous thrombosis sites detected ultrasonograph- ically in small animals include hepatic, portal, renal, jugular cranial vena cava and pulmonary veins (Nyland and Mattoon 2015). Venous thrombosis is relatively unstudied in small animals in terms of prevalence and causes. However, neoplastic, inflammatory (immune‐ mediated disease, pancreatitis, sepsis), cardiac, and infectious diseases, including parasitic, and glucocorti- coids are common risk factors as they relate to Virchow’s triad (hypercoagulability, endothelial injury, and stasis or turbulence of flow) (Goggs et al. 2009; Laurenson et al. 2010; Nyland and Mattoon 2015; Nyland et al. 2015). 533 POCUS: V ASCULAR – V EINS AND A RTERIES Hepatic veins as a general rule are inapparent in lateral and standing and sternal recumbency during FAST examinations. Anecdotally, hepatic venous distension occurs to some extent in dogs and cats placed into dorsal recumbency (Lisciandro 2014, unpublished). Principles of upstream venous distension due to down- stream obstruction to flow and echogenic material within the venous lumen are characteristic. However, acute nascent clots may appear as anechoic as the blood in the venous lumen, and thus not apparent with B‐mode gray‐scale imaging (Nyland and Mattoon 2015). Furthermore, hepatic veins can have slice‐thick- ness artifact mimicking a thrombus, and thus rotating the probe to the transverse plane will help eliminate the artifact (see Figure 25.4) (Nyland and Mattoon 2015). When hepatic venous distension is thought to be a thrombus, color flow Doppler should be added to differentiate sluggish flow from obstruction (Nyland and Mattoon 2015). In another example, the use of color flow Doppler is also shown contrasting B‐mode and color flow Doppler in a case of aortic arterial thromboembolism in a dog. Also, direction of flow is important to consider depending on whether imaging veins or arteries (Figures 25.5 and 25.6) (see also Figures 16.6, 26.2, 26.3, 26.6, 26.7, and 39.3). Obstruction of the hepatic venous system, when severe enough, leads to hepatic venous congestion and ascites (see Chapters 6, 7, 19–21, and 26). The Global FAST approach surveys for other causes of hepatic venous congestion, such as right‐sided congestive heart failure including pericardial effusion, dilated cardiomyopathy, and pulmonary hypertension, while incorporating lung (Vet BLUE) and the CVC and hepatic veins. More directed POCUS examinations might then follow, such as POCUS heart, POCUS caudal vena cava, and POCUS kidney. Splenic Venous Thrombosis Anatomically, the splenic vein is part of the portal system and joins with the cranial and caudal mesen - teric veins and the gastroduodenal vein to form the portal vein. Concurrent diseases have been docu - mented in 80 dogs with splenic venous thrombosis (SVT) detected by ultrasound (Laurenson et al. 2010). In this case series, 33% of the dogs had concurrent splenic infarction (see Chapter 9), and 18 % had concurrent portal venous thrombosis, of which 64% had ascites (Laurenson et al. 2010). SVT was found to be most prevalent in dogs with concurrent neoplasia (54%) with 25% having round cell neoplasia (lympho - sarcoma > leukemia > mast cell > histiocytic > mela - noma). Concurrent nonneoplastic conditions included systemic inflammatory response syndrome (26%), dis- seminated intravascular coagulation (20%), pancrea - titis (18%), immune‐mediated anemia (16%), and renal failure without proteinuria (14%), with many dogs having more than one concurrent condition. Interestingly, dogs with protein‐losing nephropathy and hyperadrenocorticism made up <10% of cases. Exogenous steroid administration was also common among SVT dogs (43%) (Laurenson et al. 2010). 534 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER The SVT was commonly detected in the region of the splenic hilus (Figure 25.7) (see also Figures 9.11, 16.10B, and 39.8). The splenic hilus is easily recognizable dur - ing a POCUS spleen because of the obvious splenic venous branching forming a “Y” shape or “whale tail” effect in both dogs and cats (see Chapters 9 and 39, Figure 39.8). The splenic artery runs along the splenic vein, but splenic arterial branches are difficult to image and the splenic artery is less conspicuous than its vein. Color flow Doppler is needed to differentiate sluggish splenic flow from a true thrombus (Nyland and Mattoon 2015). With repetition, the nonradiologist performing Global FAST and POCUS will be able to recognize the splenic vein and the splenic hilus as abnormal (and its parenchyma as abnormal from splenic infarction), thus capturing the case for a complete detailed abdominal ultrasound, other indi - cated testing, and triggering adjustment in clinical course including treatment. Global FAST is important to stage the patient including detecting concurrent effusions and obvious soft tissue abnormalities of the abdominal organs, heart, and lung surface (see Chapters 36 and 37). Portal Venous Thrombosis The portal vein is closely related to the splenic vein and CVC. Principles are similar to other centrally located venous thrombosis and if portal vein thrombosis is severe enough, ascites and shunting of the collateral venous system will occur. Renal Vein Thrombosis The renal vein courses a short distance from the CVC to its respective kidney in close proximity with the renal artery (see also Figures 16.6, 26.8–10). This retroperito- neal region of interest will also have the abdominal aorta (and adrenal glands) typically in view. Invasive adrenal tumors are a common cause for thrombi in the adjacent CVC and occasionally in the renal artery. Secondary changes in the kidney are also expected, including hypoechoic cortical regions from the infarc - tion that over time will lead to hyperechoic renal paren- chymal triangulation, loss of corticomedullary detail, and contracture of the renal parenchyma. In acute renal vein thrombosis, renal enlargement and perinephric fluid may also be present (Nyland et al. 2015). The principal objective for the nonradiologist novice and intermediate sonographer is to be able to recognize the region as abnormal (and everything else is bonus information), capturing the case for additional imaging. In patients with suspect adrenal tumors, staging with Global FAST is indicated before letting the patient leave your care (see Chapters 36 and 37). Deep Venous Thrombosis Deep venous thrombosis is a fascinating translational topic from people, being bipeds, to veterinary medi - cine, in which the vast majority of our patients are quadrupeds. The prevalence of DVT in veterinary medicine is completely unknown. Moreover, no stan - dardized systematic ultrasonographic surveillance approach has been developed for dogs and cats, unlike people in which DVT is prevalent and leads to potentially catastrophic pulmonary thromboembolism (PTE). However, the opposing femoral artery and vein may be easily imaged during AFAST at its cysto‐colic (CC) view with a curvilinear (microconvex) probe. In the CC view, the urinary urine‐filled bladder serves as a stand‐off and acoustic window for the femoral artery and vein (Figure 25.8). The CC view may be helpful to screen for abnormalities in high‐risk dogs and cats. So what is the required proficiency of the nonradiolo- gist performing ultrasound scans for DVT? One study demonstrated that emergency physicians who had undergone a 10‐minute training session on the tech - nique of two‐point compression ultrasonography could detect DVT in people with a sensitivity and specificity of 100% and 99% (Crisp et al. 2010). In another prospec- tive study, intensivists performed bedside compression ultrasonography and findings were compared to a formal vascular study (the gold standard) with high sensitivity and specificity of 86% and 96%, and an accuracy of 95%. The prevalence of DVT in these patients was 20% (Kory et al. 2011). Importantly, bedside‐intensivist ultrasonographic compression scans could be performed promptly while formal vascular studies took a median time of 13.8 hours from ordering to their execution by the radiology department (Kory et al. 2011). The use of ultrasound has become the standard at most institutions. Deep vein thrombosis is a common and severe problem in human medicine, annually affecting 1–5 patients out of every 1000 in the United States (White 2012). Moreover, 2 million people are affected annu- ally, resulting in 600 000 hospitalizations. Of these, 200 000 deaths result from the most dreaded complica- tion of PTE (Crisp et al. 2010). To our knowledge, no studies have reported the clinical relevance, if any, of DVT in peripheral limbs in veterinary medicine. It seems plausible that DVT probably exists but is unrec- ognized in small animals, and may explain sudden death or rapid deterioration in critically ill small animal patients (see Chapters 36 and 37). However, we now have some tools to survey for PTE and DVT. Future veterinary studies with standardized protocols are required to determine whether POCUS vascular and lung ultrasound studies will be helpful in diag- nosing these conditions in small animals (Szatmári et al. 2001; Dean and Ku 2008). Pulmonary Thromboembolism Preexisting PTE factors are similar to those for other sites of venous thromboembolism (Goggs et al. 2009; Crisp et al. 2010; Kory et al. 2011; White 2012) (Table 25.1). Pulmonary thromboembolism is a frequent life‐threatening problem in people and early detection is key for patient survival, triggering treatment including thrombolytics and prophylaxis. Computed tomography contrast angiography (CTPA) is consid- ered the gold standard test, but many PTE patients are too unstable for CTPA. Moreover, small PTE at the lung periphery may not be detected by CTPA. Dependent on where the PTE is located, ultrasound carries some advantages, being low impact for the patient, rapid and cageside. POCUS evaluations including cardiac (POCUS heart, TFAST) and pulmonary (Vet BLUE) assessment can be helpful (see Figures 23.11, 37.6, 37.9, and 37.10). Supportive evidence for PTE includes acute right ventricular dilation in an acutely respiratory‐ distressed or hypoxemic patient (POCUS Heart, TFAST). Thrombi or “echogenic smoke” or heartworms (dirofilariasis) may be seen within the right heart and T able 25.1. The wedge sign may be seen along the lung periphery during Vet BLUE in upper lung regions (see Chapters 22 and 23) (see Figures 23.11, 37.6, 37.9, and 37.10). These different locations for PTE argue for the use of Global FAST with POCUS add‐on imaging and for having a baseline Global FAST recorded on goal‐directed templates for every patient admitted for care (and even at‐risk outpa- tients). Furthermore, Global FAST should become part of the work‐up for dogs and cats with heartworm. Having this baseline information recorded is invalu- able for comparison to future studies (see Chapters 36 and 37). For example, knowing on admission that an at‐risk patient with pancreatitis has an unremarkable long‐axis right ventricular to left ventricular ratio, and that their lung surface is smooth without any Vet BLUE lung ultrasound signs, is key for those developing respiratory signs, some subtle (Liska and Poteet 2003; Tidwell et al. 2007). Finding cardiac and pulmonary PTE evidence, changes from the patient’s initial Global FAST profile that you recorded, gives evidence‐based information that PTE treatment is likely indicated. Arterial Thromboembolism and Thrombosis Arterial thromboembolism (ATE) and aortic thrombosis (AT) are most commonly located in the distal aorta at or in close proximity to its bifurcation to the hindlimbs in both dogs and cats (Fuentes 2012; Williams et al. 2017). However, causes are different between the two species. In dogs, ATE appears to be less frequently documented than AT in a recent review article (Williams et al. 2017). Most canine cases of AT (~50%) are idiopathic (Winters et al. 2012; Williams et al. 2017); however, a number of diseases have been reported as causing ATE/AT in dogs including cardiac, hyperadrenocorticsim, protein‐losing nephropathy, infectious diseases, including ehrlichiosis and spirocercosis, immune‐mediated diseases, gluco- corticoid administration, and others. In cats, cardiac disease is most common and results in ATE rather than AT. In felines, the bifurcation of the distal aorta is the classic location (with a saddle thrombus), with the right subclavian artery as the second most common feline arterial thromboembolic site. Other more common feline causes are hyperthyroidism and pulmonary neo- plasia (Fuentes 2012). The bottom line is that ATE and AT are typically a result of fulfillment of Virchow’s triad. The diagnosis often requires the use of color flow Doppler to enhance imaging of the poorly echogenic nascent clot similar to venous thrombosis/thrombo- embolism in which early stage thrombi often have poor contrast to the normal blood‐filled vessel lumen (Szatmári et al. 2001; Zwingenberger and Wisner 2008). Furthermore, familiarity with the anatomy of the region is important as well as correlating the anatomy to patient positioning. An air‐filled or stool‐filled colon can interfere with imaging and patient positioning and restraint can carry risk, especially with patients moved to dorsal recumbency. These factors must be consid- ered during POCUS vascular assessment. Principles of venous blood flow obstruction likewise apply to arterial obstruction, including vessel dilation upstream and vessel attenuation downstream although vasoconstriction is more intense than with venous events. Ultrasonographic strategies used by physicians for ATE include looking for “smoke” representing proximal turbulent blood flow as well as proximal dilation of the vessel. Importantly, color flow Doppler has its limitations including patient movement and adjusting the color flow Doppler gain to prevent motion artifact and overgaining, which both lead to the same problem of Doppler colors “jumping” to other areas, thwarting accurate interpretation. With that being said, the identification of ATE in dogs and cats may be made with caution by nonradiologists, keeping in mind that mistakes may impact unfavorably on patient prognosis and therapy (Lake‐Bakaar et al. 2012). A readily identi- fiable aortic thrombus in a dog is shown without the use of color flow Doppler (Figure 25.9) (see also Figure 25.5) and a saddle thrombus in a cat (Figure 25.10). If ATE is suspected but not confirmed, a complete detailed abdominal ultrasound evaluation by a veteri- nary radiologist or specialist skilled in ultrasound or other advanced imaging (CT, MRI) may be indicated. However, a Global FAST approach can be helpful in surveying for additional information and comorbidi- ties. A similar approach is used in people for gaining additional supportive evidence as well as rapidly detecting complications and comorbidities (Nazerian et al. 2014; Squizzato et al. 2015). Future study is needed regarding the sensitivity, specificity, and accu- racy of ultrasonographic diagnosis of ATE/AT in dogs by nonradiologists. Pearls and Pitfalls, The Final Say The use of ultrasound to survey for vascular abnor - malities is exciting for a traditionally difficult problem in veterinary medicine – the detection of venous and arterial thrombosis and thromboembolism.
