Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 Introduction In the last decade a lot of attention has been given to the evaluation of volume status using ultrasonog- raphy of the inferior and/or superior vena cava and the effect of passive leg raising on the caval size and its collapsibility in people. Besides the evaluation of the larger vessels, adding evaluation of certain basic cardiac images and of the lungs, pleural space and abdomen allows for a more complete assessment of the cardiovascular system in an emergency and criti- cal care setting. In this chapter, the focus will be on ultrasonography of the caudal vena cava (CVC) in small animals and three published methodologies. The reader is referred to the chapters on cardiac, pulmonary and thoracic ultrasonography for inte- grating additional POCUS information for complete patient volume assessment (see Chapters 17, 18–23, 36 and 37). POCUS caudal vena cava (POCUS CVC) by no means replaces a complete physical examination and other traditional volume assessment measures, but rather serves as an adjunct for confirming or refuting clinical suspicion. By using POCUS CVC, the clinician has another tool for assessing patient volume status that is noninvasive, rapid, repeatable, permits comparison of findings (serial examinations), and requires minimal patient restraint and stress in con- trast to the traditional use of central lines for central venous pressure, which is no longer advocated in human medicine (Marik and Cavallazzi 2013). Moreover, POCUS CVC is easily taught to students and veterinarians and does not require any additional equipment besides your ultrasound machine. Over the past 10 years, we’ve been developing the use of POCUS in our emergency and critical care (ECC) service and have lead research regarding the assessment of the CVC in dogs (Darnis et al. 2018, 2019). Indeed, POCUS CVC and cardiovascular‐ pulmonary POCUS integration have allowed us to objectivate clinical findings that better dictate therapeutic decisions, reassuring the attending vet- erinarian. Most importantly, POCUS examinations in our experience seem to positively affect the prog- nosis of small animals presented to our service. What POCUS Caudal Vena Cava Can Do • Provide various methodologies for assessing the CVC including three studied methods: subxiphoid CVC view, intercostal CVC view, paralumbar CVC view. • Identify hypovolemic patients by demonstrating flat CV , a decreased CVC to aorta ratio, and high variability in CVC dimensions across the respiratory cycle. • Identify hypervolemic patients by demonstrating a fat CVC, an increased CVC to aorta ratio, a low var- iability in CVC dimensions across the respiratory cycle, and prominent hepatic vessels. POCUS: Caudal Vena Cava Kris Gommeren, Elodie Darnis, and Anne‐Christine Merveille CHAPTER TWENTY-SIX

542 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER • Help guide fluid resuscitation and track and mon- itor volume status throughout initial stabilization as well as during hospitalized care. What POCUS Caudal Vena Cava Cannot Do • Replace complete echocardiography. • Replace the physical examination. • Replace clinical integration of the complete patient profile including POCUS cardiovascular and pulmonary findings. • Serve as a single POCUS assessment for volume status. Indications • Assessment of volume status. • Patients with a suspicion of cardiovascular com- promise: shock, collapse, respiratory compromise or distress. • Patients with conditions associated with large shifts in intravascular volume: severe gastrointes- tinal losses, anaphylaxis, internal hemorrhage, acute renal injury, post removal of large quantities of cavitary fluid. • During fluid resuscitation to evaluate the efficacy of treatment. • During transfusion or hemodialysis. • Whenever an acute circulatory change is noted: development of tachycardia, decrease in arterial blood pressure. Objectives • Evaluate the CVC through one or more of the fol- lowing methods. ◦ Subxiphoid CVC view, visualizing at the level where the CVC crosses the diaphragm in a longitudinal orientation in a cineloop allowing evaluation of size and size change throughout the respiratory cycle. ◦ Intercostal CVC view, visualizing a cross‐section of both the CVC and the aorta in a single frame, recording a cineloop allowing evaluation of size and size‐change throughout the respiratory cycle and comparison with the size of the aorta. ◦ Paralumbar CVC view, visualizing the CVC and the aorta in a single frame in either a longitudinal or a transverse orientation. At this location the effect of respiratory movement on the venous system will often be negligible. • Be able to integrate POCUS CVC with basic echo- cardiographic views. ◦ Right parasternal view – long axis. ◦ Right parasternal view – short axis. – Transverse or short‐axis ventricular view for fractional shortening (FS%). – Transverse or short‐axis left atrium (LA) and aortic (Ao) view for the LA/Ao ratio. • Evaluate chamber sizes and systolic function including heterogeneous and homogeneous motion. • Evaluate wall thickness of the ventricles – pseudohypertrophy versus true hypertrophy. • Identify pericardial effusion and evaluate the presence of pericardial tamponade. • Identify pleural effusion. • Identify intraabdominal and retroperitoneal effusions. How to Do a POCUS Caudal Vena Cava Ultrasound Settings and Probe Preferences The entire POCUS CVC procedure can be performed using a curvilinear (microconvex) 5–7 MHz probe. Most views can be obtained at 7 MHz, except for the subxiphoid CVC and intercostal CVC views in larger breed dogs, in which a 5 MHz probe will improve the depth penetration and generally allow better CVC visualization. Most inter- pretations are made cageside, based on the subjective “eyeball approach” of real‐time ultrasonography, but still images and captured cineclips that encompass an entire respiratory cycle are advised for CVC and aortic measure- ments, review, and interpretation. Patient Positioning and Preparation As for most of the POCUS techniques, clipping hair is generally not required for imaging. Rather, hair is parted and isopropyl alcohol and additional acoustic coupling medium are applied to the exposed skin. In rare cases insufficient image quality occurs in dogs with unclipped hair. These tend to be outdoor dogs with longer, thick haircoats, especially during wintertime. The Three Methods for POCUS Caudal Vena Cava Three different methods have been described and studied in the veterinary literature: the subxiphoid

543 POCUS: C AUDAL V ENA C AVA CVC view (Darnis et al. 2018, 2019; Finnerty et al. 2017); the intercostal CVC view (Meneghini et al. 2016; Darnis et al. 2018); and the paralumbar CVC view (Cambournac et al. 2018; Darnis et al. 2018). Placing the patient in left lateral recumbency is preferred, especially for the intercostal CVC view, in contrast to right lateral recum- bency for basic echocardiography. These three methods may also be acquired in a standing patient; however, in our experience, especially when obtaining the subxi- phoid CVC view, dogs will tend to move when pressure is exerted behind their xiphoid process. As the CVC is a low‐pressure vessel, it can easily be compressed through excessive probe pressure, leading to erroneous measurements. A simple technique is to exert ample pressure while locating the CVC followed by minimal pressure without compromising the quality of the image for best characterizing the CVC and taking measurements. The benefits and downsides of each of our three described POCUS CVC methods are determined by the ease of acquisition of the image, the motion arti - facts observed at each respective region, and the degree of size change generated by intrathoracic pressure changes during the patient’s respiratory cycle. We typ- ically assess all three POCUS CVC methods since their acquisition only demands a couple of minutes; and by comparing these methods, the probablity of misinter - preting volume status is lessened in our opinion. Subxiphoid Caudal Vena Cava View The CVC is assessed in a longitudinal orientation as it crosses the diaphragm (Figure 26.1) (Darnis et al. 2018). The CVC is easily located slightly right from midline, just next to the gallbladder. The hepatic veins dorsally drain into the CVC (see Figures 20.10, 36.7, and 36.8). In the case of right‐sided congestive heart disease, these vessels also become more apparent (see Figure 36.9). In deep‐chested dogs, a lower frequency probe might be required (5 MHz) due to the deeper location of the CVC. At the subxiphoid CVC view, pressure changes during the respiratory cycle are maximal because of its proximity to the thorax, and therefore this location is ideal to evaluate dynamic changes in the CVC. However in our experience, B‐mode evalua- tion of the CVC is more reliable than M‐mode because of movement of the diaphragm and CVC during phases of respiration (see also Figures 20.11, 36.11, and 36.12). Moreover, the subxiphoid CVC view does not allow comparison of the size of the CVC to the aorta. The CVC:Ao ratio is helpful to negate the effect of body size on CVC evaluations in dogs (Cambournac et al. 2018; Darnis et al. 2018). Intercostal Caudal Vena Cava View This CVC approach starts from a view of the porta hepatis at which a transverse orientation of the CVC, portal vein, and aorta can all be imaged on a single view (Figure 26.2; see also Figure 16.15) (Meneghini et al. 2016; Darnis et al. 2018). At the intercostal CVC Figure 26.1. Subxiphoid CVC view in a healthy dog. The probe is placed longitudinally immediately caudal to the subxiphoid process and angled cranially to visualize the diaphragm as at the FAST DH view (see Chapters 6 and 7). The probe is then fanned to the right of midline until the CVC is identified where it crosses the diaphragm. The probe is then slowly fanned off either side of the CVC and returned to the position where the CVC is subjectively felt to be at its widest diameter with an image similar to that shown. Diaph, diaphragm. Figure 26.2. Hepatic CVC view at the porta hepatis of a healthy dog. To locate the porta hepatis, the probe is placed parallel to the ribs for transverse orientation of the CVC and aorta at the 10th to 12th right intercostal space immediately ventral to the epaxial muscles in the upper third of the thorax. Ao, aorta; CVC, caudal vena cava; PV , portal vein.

544 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER view, size changes of the CVC can be observed throughout the respiratory cycle, while at the same time motion artifacts are rather small in comparison to the subxiphoid CVC view. Therefore, the intercostal CVC view theoretically would be better for both the “eyeball method” and actual measurements of CVC size while additionally providing CVC:aortic ratios since the aorta is imaged. However, due to the proximity of the caudal lung field as well as the stomach, the intercostal CVC view can be complicated by aerated lung or gas in the stomach. This problem is most often encountered in dogs presented with respiratory com - promise and distress (caudal lung field tends to expand along with aerophagia) and deep‐chested dogs. Whenever air interference occurs with visualization of the porta hepatis, a “modified view” is used by sliding the probe further caudally until the left kidney is located. At this level, a transverse orientation of both the CVC and aorta is visible within the same acoustic window, but at a cost of losing the portal vein that is often not visible within this “modified window.” At the modified view, the “eyeball method” and actual mea - surements may be similarly made (Darnis et al. 2018). Paralumbar Caudal Vena Cava View This approach is the most caudal position for the evaluation of the canine CVC (Figure 26.3; see also Figure 26.6) (Cambournac et al. 2018; Darnis et al. 2018). At this location, the CVC and aorta are located rather superficially and can be evaluated in a transverse or longitudinal plane. The major advantage of the para - lumbar CVC view is the lack of both motion artifacts and interference by aerated lung or gas‐filled stomach or intestines. This makes it easy to acquire both B‐ and M‐mode cineloops for measurements of the CVC and aorta. However, its superficial location makes the para- lumbar CVC view sensitive to pressure artifacts, so the probe should be gently manipulated with as little pressure as possible. Moreover, due to its distance from the thorax, size changes of the CVC are much less dynamic, unless the patient is severely respiratory dis- tressed. For this reason, fluid responsiveness should not be primarily evaluated at the paralumbar CVC view (Darnis et al. 2018). Image Acquisition and Measurements for POCUS Caudal Vena Cava Subxiphoid Caudal Vena Cava View In order to visualize the CVC at the level of the diaphragm, the probe is placed under the subxiphoid process, angled cranially in a longitudinal orientation (Figure 26.4; see also Figure 26.1). The diaphragm and the liver are identified on the screen. Typically, the Figure 26.3. Paralumbar CVC view with both longitudinal (A) and transverse (B) orientations in a healthy dog. To obtain the paralumbar CVC view the probe is moved caudally under the last rib pointing in a cranial direction from behind the last rib, allowing visualization of the right kidney. The probe is slowly moved or fanned medially off the right kidney until the CVC and aorta are identified. The probe is slowly rotated and fanned to obtain a longitudinal orientation in (A) where the CVC and Ao are parallel to each other within the same acoustic window, and (B) transverse orientation where the CVC and Ao become oval. Ao, aorta; CVC, caudal vena cava.

545 POCUS: C AUDAL V ENA C AVA probe must then be fanned slightly to the right of midline, without excessive pressure, to bring the gallbladder and CVC into view. Here the CVC is then identified at the point where it crosses the diaphragm. As soon as the CVC is visualized, the probe can be slowly fanned and/or slightly rotated to obtain the optimal view, in essence where the CVC has a maximal diameter, and where the vessel wall can be followed over a longer distance (Darnis et al. 2018). In spontaneously breathing patients, The maximal diameter of the CVC is seen during expiration, as the positive intrathoracic pressure will prevent blood moving towards the heart across the diaphragm, thus causing blood to pool within the abdominal CVC. Conversely, the CVC has its minimal diameter at the end of inspiration, as the negative intrathoracic pressure draws the blood from the abdominal CVC into the thoracic CVC and the right atrium. Measurements are performed where the ventral wall of the CVC crosses the diaphragam perpendicular to its dorsal wall (Figure 26.4) (Darnis et al. 2018). Intercostal Caudal Vena Cava View In order to obtain this view, the probe is placed just below the right epaxial muscles in the upper third of the thorax (see Figures 26.2 and 26.5) (Meneghini et al. 2016; Darnis et al. 2018). The probe should be some - where between the 10th and 12th right intercostal spaces, parallel with the ribs. If aerated lung obscures the image, then the sonographer has two options: the probe is angled caudally and/or moved an intercostal space caudally, or the probe is placed more dorsally over the epaxial muscles and then slowly slid ventrally into the respective intercostal space until the porta hepatis is visualized (Meneghini et al. 2016; Darnis et al. 2018). Alternately, after the right kidney is identi- fied, the probe can be angled cranially or moved an intercostal space cranially. When the porta hepatis is visualized, a transverse image of the aorta, CVC, and portal vein can be identi- fied as three hypoechoic round (aorta and possibly the CVC and portal vein) to oval (CVC and portal vein) structures within the same view (see Figure 26.5B). The vessels are ordered from left to right as aorta, CVC, and portal vein. Note the CVC at this location often is ovoid rather than circular, thus the size of the vessel rather than its diameter should be evaluated (Darnis et al. 2018). The size of the CVC is calculated via measurement of its short and long axis using B‐mode (see Figure 26.5B) (Darnis et al. 2018). The diameter of the aorta is typically measured at the same moment as the CVC because the dimensions of the aorta do not change with respiration, and change only minimally between systole and diastole. If a simultaneous electro- cardiogram (ECG) tracing is available, we tend to mea- sure the aorta at the beginning of systole, when its size is maximal (Darnis et al. 2018). Ideally, an acoustic window is obtained that visualizes part of the right kidney, as well as the CVC and the aorta, which are located parallel to each other. Measurements may be made in B‐ or M‐mode. The vessel distance from the diaphragm is greatest at this CVC view, thus the CVC and aorta are least affected by intrathoracic pressure changes throughout the respiratory cycle. However, in brachycephalic dogs, often having exaggerated nega- tive intrathoracic pressure due to their unique airway conformation, respiratory variations might be observed (Darnis et al. 2018). Use of Allometric Scaling Formulas for CVC Assessment CVC evaluation in small animals still requires further scientific validation in actual clinical settings. However, the authors have established reference values that may be used for the CVC using the three described POCUS CVC methods in healthy dogs (Darnis et al. 2018). Reference values for the hepatic and paralumbar CVC views, expressed via allometric scaling, are presented in Table 26.1. The subxiphoid CVC view had poorer repeatability, and therefore no references values have been calculated, although absolute CVC height values have been recently sug- gested (see Tables 7.6 and 36.2). The poorer subxiphoid CVC view measurement repeatability is likely due to several factors: movement of the diaphragm causing difficulties in performing both B‐ and M‐mode measurements, a more pronounced effect of the force of respiratory movement on CVC imaging, and variability in the observed angle at the diaphragm of the CVC during measurement (see also Figures 36.11 and 36.12). Although at first glance it seems to indicate that the subxiphoid CVC view is of less clinical utility than the other two views, changes observed in a clinical setting seem to be more pro- nounced at the subxiphoid view (see cineloops on the Companion Website). Therefore, the subxiphoid CVC view merits further investigation, as it may be the best view to make “eyeball method” evaluations (Darnis et al. 2018, 2019). Integration of POCUS CVC Findings The main purpose of a POCUS CVC is the evaluation of volume status and indirectly cardiovascular function of the patient (see Chapter 36 for integration of information). Both the CVC and right heart are closely related (referred to as fallback view in the Global FAST approach), as right‐sided cardiac disease often leads to hepatic venous congestion, which shares several char - actersitics with hypervolemia, such as distended CVC and hepatic veins. Additionally, hypervolemia also causes right atrial dilation, and right ventricular dilation in more chronic and severe situations, and the left heart may also be involved (see also Figures 36.7 and 36.8 and Chapter 36). Therefore, evaluation of volume status should always include a cardiac and lung evaluation and a survey for effusions (see Chapters 17–21 and 36). Lastly, abnormalities sus- pected during POCUS CVC at the authors’ critical care department trigger a complete detailed echocardio- gram by the cardiology department. 549 POCUS: CAUDAL VENA CAVA and dynamic changes of the inferior vena cava as fat (distended without collapsability) or flat (attenuated without collapsability) (Perera et al. 2010; Ferrada et al. 2012a,b; Lee et al. 2016). Of note, IVC sonographic assessment is usually performed in people at the sub- xiphoid view. When the flat versus fat inferior vena cava distinc- tion is not clearcut in people, several approaches exist to avoid fluid overload. The first technique is the comparison of inferior vena cava (IVC) parameters while administering a true or “virtual” fluid bolus by passive leg raising, or by actively changing intratho- racic pressures in ventilated patients (Vieillard‐Baron et al. 2004; Monnet et al. 2016a). Passive leg raising carries the benefit that only a “virtual” bolus is admin- istered, and consequently the risk of active and true volume overload is minimized because no fluids are actually administered. Although effective in people, this technique is unlikely to become commonplace in companion ani- mals because of differences between anatomy and blood volume in the hindlegs of bipeds and quad- rapeds for the following reasons. First, the amount of blood pooled in the venous system of hindlegs of companion animals is unlikely to be similar to humans. Second, veterinary exam and triage tables are not designed to comfortably raise our patient’s hindlimbs. Moreover, such patient positional changes and lack of patient understanding of the procedure would more likely induce a stress response affecting POCUS CVC findings. Third, although thoracic pressures can be manipulated in ventilated small animals, this repre- sents a minority of our emergency and critical care case population, most of which are spontaneously breathing. Consequently, we are left to evaluate the effect of the administration of intravenous fluid boluses on CVC assessment. Furthermore, to scientifically detect CVC differences, actual measurements will need to be correlated to the “eyeball method.” In people, a minimal change of ~15% in IVC diameter is generally accepted as a positive reaction to fluid loading condi- tions. Whether the same threshhold exists in small ani- mals remains to be determined. Pearls and Pitfalls, The Final Say We have evaluated three different POCUS CVC method- ologies for assessing the CVC in dogs. Each has its own limitations including distance from the thorax, effect of respiratory patterns and patient status, and reliability and repeatability of measuring the CVC and aorta dependent on location of each view. Until further studies correlate the utility of these three POCUS CVC method- ologies to clinical cases, we do not know which is best. However, to make an accurate volume status assessment, POCUS cardiovascular and pulmonary findings must be combined with POCUS CVC findings. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 Introduction The nonophthalmologist veterinarian is often faced with the challenges of having to assess eye conditions that require urgent attention, such as those that might need emergent referral and/or specific medications or surgery to save vision or the globe. Using ocular ultra- sonography to obtain evidence‐based information and increase the probability of an accurate diagnosis over solely traditional clinical diagnostic means is an unde- rutilized option for the nonophthalmologist veteri- narian in busy general or emergency and critical care practices. While a complete ocular ultrasound exam by a veterinary ophthalmologist or radiologist may be indicated when there is ocular opacity and/or extraoc- ular inflammation or injury, a POCUS eye examination can help alleviate the practitioner’s frustration of not being able to visualize intraocular and periorbital structures. The use of ocular ultrasonography by non- ophthalmologist veterinarians can help answer impor- tant clinical questions quickly when a complete clinical eye examination alone does not reveal a diagnosis. What POCUS Eye Can Do • Provide a diagnostic window into an eye not ame- nable to direct examination by traditional means. • Provide anatomical information about an opaque or inaccessible eye without resorting to more costly imaging methods. • Diagnose or support a clinical diagnosis of anterior or posterior lens luxation, intraocular masses, ret- inal detachments, and scleral rupture. • Expedite referral for salvage of vision or the globe by detecting otherwise occult conditions. • Assist in providing an initial prognosis for vision and the globe. What POCUS Eye Cannot Do • Cannot substitute for a full clinical ocular examination. • Cannot provide a diagnosis in the absence of a basic level of clinician skill and knowledge of ocular anatomy and disease. • Cannot overcome any inherent mechanical limita- tions of your ultrasound machine and probe. Indications • Opaque eye: cannot visualize through the cornea or anterior chamber because of corneal, anterior chamber, or other structural opacity (Figures 27.1, 27.2, 27.3) (see also Table 27.3). • Bulging eye: to differentiate exophthalmos (pro- truding normal‐sized globe) from buphthalmos (enlarged globe), and determine the presence and sonographic characterization of a retrobulbar mass (Figure 27.4) • Cloudy eye: cannot visualize the fundus because of opacities in the normally clear ocular media POCUS: Eye Jane Cho CHAPTER TWENTY-SEVEN Note: While ocular ultrasound can significantly assist in diagnosis, it cannot always allow for a specific etiological diagnosis due to variations in ultrasound appearances and a wide variety of pos- sible pathology. Note: Use Global FAST to help determine if the ocular problem is localized or part of disseminated disease. Global FAST surveys the abdomen (AFAST), thorax (TFAST) including heart (TFAST) and lung (Vet BLUE) and also helps assess patient volume status (see Chapters 6, 7, 17, 18, 22, 23, 36, and 37).

554 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER (cornea, anterior chamber, lens, and vitreous) (see Figures 27.1–3). • Traumatized eye: especially with swollen perioc - ular structures preventing examination of the eye, to evaluate for injury to the globe or its struc - tures (with great caution) (see Figures 27.25 and 27.26A). Objectives • To identify the location, size, and shape of normal and abnormal ocular and periocular structures, allowing for a more correct ophthalmic diagnosis. • To better define the existence of pathology war - ranting specific treatment, especially emergent treatment, thus optimizing preservation of vision and the globe. Ultrasound Settings For imaging the globe, the ultrasound probe with the highest frequency available should be used. A 7.5– 10 MHz probe is preferable. • A 7.5 MHz probe is adequate for imaging deeper structures (orbit). A 5 MHz probe may be accept - able for detecting deeper large lesions at the expense of losing detail. Higher MHz (7.5–12 MHz) provides better detail in the nearer fields. However, a newer modality called high‐resolution ultra - sound (HRUS), also called ultrasound biomi - croscopy, uses very high‐frequency probes of 35–50 MHz to image the very near parts of the eye (<1 cm) in great detail, but is only rarely available and requires sedation or anesthesia. Figure 27 .1. Corneal opacity. Various types of corneal opacity can make directly viewing the intraocular structures difficult or impossible, including (A) corneal edema, (B) corneal pigmentation, and (C) other types of corneal scarring.

555 POCUS: E YE • A probe with a small scan head diameter (linear or sector) is preferred. • If the machine allows, a “Small Parts” or “Eye” or similar setting optimizing focus in the very near field (1–5 cm) is preferred. • Reduced depth of the image (using a “depth” dial if present on your machine) also helps to magnify small structures. • If the machine has a foot pedal, install prior to the eye exam, to allow hands‐free freezing of images. Patient Eye Preparation • Ideally, a sterile, viscous, aqueous‐based ultra - sound gel that is nontoxic to the eye and ocular sur- faces should be used. The author routinely uses Aquasonic 100 (Parker Laboratories, Fairfield, NJ) ultrasound gel, a very commonly used and readily available gel, on the intact ocular surface, with no ill effects (Dziezyc and Hager 1988). Aquasonic is also available in sterile form. Gel such as K‐Y ® (which is less viscous and thus tends to fall off the eye, making its use more difficult) or ophthalmic 2.5% methylcellulose gel can be used. Clean the probe well and dry it according to manufacturer’s instructions before placing it on the eye. In cases of possible globe rupture, a sterile gel such as individual packets of K‐Y should be used and the Figure 27 .2. Opacities in the anterior chamber. Various types of pathology can render the anterior chamber cloudy or opaque, obscuring the rest of the intraocular structures, including (A) hyphema, (B) hypopyon, and (C) fibrin and other structures. Pearl: Gain can be turned up or down during the exam to highlight certain structures. This can be used to better define differences in echogenicity, but care should be taken to not “create” or “remove” lesions while adjusting gain.

556 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER probe should be placed on intact eyelid or periocu- lar skin and not the eye (see later in this chapter). • If a stand‐off is needed for imaging the anterior, most superficial parts of the eye, either a thicker layer of gel or a water‐filled glove may be used, though the latter can be unwieldy to handle. • All gel should be gently and completely flushed off the ocular surfaces with sterile saline eyewash immediately after the exam. Fluorescein staining of the cornea after the exam is also recommended to ensure that no corneal damage has occurred dur - ing the examination. How to do the POCUS Eye First, topically anesthetize the cornea with several drops of ophthalmic proparacaine, tetracaine, or another appropriate topical ophthalmic anesthetic. Note that this is likely stored in the refrigerator. If adequate topical anesthetic effect is not achieved with 10–15 drops over two minutes, additional chemical restraint may be needed. This should be tailored to the patient, and titrated to the lightest sedative/anesthetic plane needed. No specific sedation or anesthetic protocols are required, although a reversible one may be preferable. Figure 27 .3. Ocular opacities. Structural opacities in the eye can prevent direct viewing of the anatomy of the eye behind the opacity, such as (A) iris adhesions that close the pupil, (B) cataract, and (C) other abnormal structures or masses in the anterior chamber (in this case, a formed blood clot with fibrin).

557 POCUS: E YE Unless the patient is excessively mobile or very painful, sedation and/or general anesthesia are typically unnecessary, and may make examination more difficult due to resulting changes in globe position. Second, regarding restraint, the animal should be able to sit, lie sternal, or stand normally in a com - fortable position. If sitting or standing, make sure the animal is not allowed to scoot or slide back - wards. At least one assistant is needed to hold the animal’s head still. Either that assistant or the sonog - rapher can hold the eyelids open (Figure 27.5). An additional assistant may be needed to work the freeze button. Third, regarding probe pressure and positioning, avoid pressing the probe directly onto the cornea. Maintain a layer of ultrasound gel 3–10 mm thick bet - ween the probe and the cornea (Figure 27.6). Be mindful of the direction of the patient’s gaze. By keeping the probe correctly oriented, you will be more likely to properly localize ocular and periocular structures. Figure 27 .4. The bulging eye. Exophthalmos and buphthalmos can clinically look very similar on initial inspection. Both dogs have one eye that is bulging, but further examination would be needed to differentiate a globe that is merely large versus one that is being pushed out of the orbit. Ocular ultrasound can help determine the nature of the problem, and thus the correct course of action. The eye in (A) is exophthalmic, and (B) is buphthalmic. Figure 27 .5. Ocular ultrasound setup. An assistant should hold the patient in a comfortable position in which the patient cannot slide backwards. This person can also hold the patient’s eye open for the exam. Another assistant should be available to freeze the image if needed. Pearl: Maintain a layer of ultrasound gel 3–10 mm thick between the probe and the cornea. This tech - nique will allow better imaging of the near fields (cornea, anterior chamber, iris) and be more com - fortable for the patient.

558 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Fourth, regarding probe positioning, several views can be used, including vertical, horizontal, and lateral, and behind the orbital ligament (viewing posterior to ante- rior). Begin by placing the probe vertically (bisecting the globe into medial and lateral halves) on the central cornea (Figure 27.7) to image the globe from the ante - rior to the posterior pole. Sweep the probe, moving the point of contact from one side of the cornea to the other, imaging the entire globe. Alternately, pivot the angle of the probe while keeping the probe contact point stationary. A second viewing angle to consider is horizontal, with the probe placed parallel to the floor (bisecting the globe into top and bottom halves). The probe is then swept/angled from top to bottom (Figure 27.8). A third (and less commonly used) view places the probe parallel to the iris from the lateral aspect of the globe (bisecting the globe into anterior and posterior halves), sweeping/angling the probe from front to back (Figure 27.9). A fourth possible angle is a retrobulbar one from behind the orbital ligament, producing a lower quality image directed from the back to the front of the eye (Figure 27.10). This view may be worth con - sidering if the cornea might be ruptured, or the lids are extremely thickened or swollen, but you need to proceed with caution to prevent causing addi - tional damage. Figure 27 .6. Probe with aqueous‐based gel. Do not use alcohol‐based gel, which may be harmful to the cornea . Apply a large amount of coupling gel that is safe for eyes (see text for specifics) to the ultrasound probe before applying to the eye. The probe should not be pressed onto the eye, but held with a 3–10 mm “stand‐off layer” of gel between the probe and the cornea if possible, to allow for better imaging of the most superficial structures. Pearl: Look at the position of the other eye and the facial muscles for help in orienting the images of the eye being evaluated. Figure 27 .7 . Vertical probe position. The initial view should be with the probe held vertically, dividing the globe into lat- eral and medial halves, and either tilting the probe from side to side or moving it from side to side (changing the contact point on the eye) to image the whole structure. Note the thick layer of gel that is maintained between the probe and the eye. Figure 27 .8. Horizontal probe position. This view divides the globe into upper and lower halves, providing additional directional information on intraocular structures.

559 POCUS: E YE In summary, these additional views can provide further information as to the location and orientation of lesions if needed, although generally not all views are necessary to make most urgent clinical decisions. Performing the scan first at higher gain, then at lower gain, will allow for differentiation of smaller, more subtle, and lower‐intensity lesions. Ultrasonographic Findings in a Normal Eye When imaging using the vertical or horizontal probe posi- tion, under your layer of gel, the most superficial structure seen will be the cornea, represented by a single bright 1 mm thick curved line or (depending on your probe fre- quency) two very thin bright parallel curved lines (the anterior and posterior corneal surfaces) about 1 mm apart (Figure 27.11). If there is not enough stand‐off space bet- ween the probe and eye, it may not be visible at all. Just posterior to this is the anechoic anterior chamber. This should always be anechoic as it is filled with the aqueous humor, an acellular solution, and is normally about 3–5 mm deep in the central axis (Cottrill et al. 1989). It is bordered posteriorly by the iris and axial anterior lens capsule, and peripherally by the iridocor- neal angle (which is not typically seen in any detail with standard ultrasound). The iris might be visible as a thin linear area of increased echogenicity at the peripheral anterior lens but is often not distinguishable from the adjacent struc- tures (Figure 27.12). It should be thin with an approxi - mately flat anterior surface, with no asymmetrical thickness (medial vs lateral), though it may be slightly thicker when the pupil is dilated and thinner when the pupil is constricted. Figure 27 .9. Lateral probe position. This view places the probe so that it divides the globe into anterior and posterior sections. It is easiest to access from the lateral sclera where the limbus is most exposed. This view is not commonly used but may allow for further orientation of intraocular structures. Figure 27 .10. Probe position from behind orbital ligament. If possible, palpate the orbital ligament and feel for the slight depression behind it. You may need to palpate the other side to locate the ligament, as orbital injury is often what necessi- tates this view. Shaving or completely wetting down the skin in this area before applying gel will improve the image. Orient the probe forward. Note that the probe will be in contact with the skin and a thick gel layer is not necessary with this view. Images obtained using this view will not be of as good quality as those obtained with corneal contact. Pearl: If imaging through skin, shaving or thor - oughly wetting down the skin hairs improves the image quality. Important: In cases where globe rupture is sus - pected (gross hyphema, hypotony [low intraocular pressure], or visible globe deformation/deflation), if imaging is required, it is preferred to image through closed lids or intact skin, rather than through the cornea, to prevent contamination of the intraocular space. Do not press on the globe or lids, as this will easily further damage the eye. Pearl: The normal anterior chamber is always anechoic (uniformly black).

560 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER The lens is directly behind the iris, and the anterior lens capsule may not be distinguishable from the iris where they are in contact. The lens capsule is a thin bright line surrounding the lens in an oval shape. It should be smooth and curvilinear, though it appears brightest along the central axis of the image (at the central anterior and posterior lens capsules, when the vertical and horizontal views are used) and often “dis- appears” towards the periphery (see Figure 27.11). The ability to see even a part of the lens capsule with its characteristic appearance allows the user to reliably locate the lens, especially when the lens is not in a normal position. The lens material inside the capsule is generally fairly echolucent, but it can be more echo - genic than the aqueous in front of it and the vitreous behind it, and may not be uniform. Nuclear sclerosis and cataracts may appear as variable echogenic struc - tures within the normally hypoechoic lens. The lens should always be centered in the visual axis. The lens zonules, small structures that attach the lens equator to the ciliary body, are generally not visible on ultrasound. The ciliary body, which is the posterior continuation of the iris, may be seen as a small mound of echogenic tissue peripheral to the lens equator, but is also often not easily distinguishable from the iris, or even visible. The posterior chamber is defined as the space between the iris and the lens (not the retina), and as such is actually a very small and thin space in front of and to the sides of the lens that is not easily discernible on ultrasound. Posterior to the lens is the large, gel‐like, uniformly echolucent vitreous body, composed mainly of water and collagen fibers. No echogenic structures should be present in the vitreous (see Figure 27.11). However, various vitreal abnormalities (asteroid hyalosis, vitreal strands) may be ultrasonographically present without being a clinically significant cause for disease (Labruyère et al. 2008). Posterior to the vitreous is the posterior eye wall, a smooth and echogenic curved line representing the back of the globe. The posterior eye wall is made up of three thin layers (the retina, choroid, and sclera) that are normally so closely opposed to each other as not to be ultrasonographically distinguishable from each other. 561 POCUS: E YE Behind the globe, it may be possible to identify the hypoechoic optic nerve, originating just ventral to the back of the globe and sometimes appearing as two thin parallel and occasionally curved lines extending towards the posterior orbit (see Figure 27.12). Note that it is normally off center from the axis of the ante - rior segment, more so in dogs than in cats. It may also appear as a hypoechoic linear (or possibly curvilinear) structure without the brighter borders. It is often surrounded by a thin layer of bright fat and the hypoechoic extraocular muscle bellies, all oriented as a cone towards the posterior orbit. The diameter of the optic nerve sheath may be measured in the retrobulbar tissues. In general, these structures are not nearly as easy to discern as the intra- ocular structures. Finally, a very bright line representing the ventrome- dial bony wall of the orbit may be seen behind these retrobulbar soft tissue structures. This is a smooth and bright line that curves away from the globe ventrally. Normal ocular findings are listed in Table 27.1 and abnormal findings in Table 27.2. Clinical Significance and Implications of Abnormal Findings Anterior Lens Luxation Clinical Findings • History: acute change in the eye (trauma is not required). • Signalment: terrier breeds most commonly affected; also poodles, but can occur in any dog breed; cats may also be affected. • Eye exam: corneal edema – usually most pro- nounced in the center or wherever the lens is touch- ing the cornea; may not be able to visualize iris or anterior chamber well; directing focal light from the side may highlight a relucent (brightly reflec- tive) “rim” of the luxated lens in the peripheral anterior chamber (Figure 27.14); pupil dilated with a poor pupillary light response (PLR); cannot see fundus well; high intraocular pressure (IOP) – often over 30–40 mmHg; menace response and vision is variable. Ultrasonographic Findings • Lens in anterior chamber – usually can only see the thin bright line of the axial anterior lens cap- sule just behind the cornea, or the posterior lens capsule just in front of pupil; sometimes can see an echolucent lens‐shaped structure with a thin bright border in anterior chamber right behind the cornea and anterior to the normal lens loca- tion (Figure 27.15). 564 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER • No lens in normal location (posterior lens capsule is not just anterior to center of globe) – reliable finding. • Mobile, thin, somewhat amorphous strands in vitreous (in posterior segment) might be present. • Possible retinal detachment (see Retinal Detachments below). Actions • Measure IOP (preferably with an applanation or rebound tonometer, not with a Schiotz tonometer). Avoid using the center of the cornea where the lens is likely to be touching the cornea inside. If acute glaucoma (IOP >25 mmHg) is present (onset of ocular pain and high IOP <24 hours), immedi - ately refer to ophthalmologist for evaluation and possible surgery. Vision might be able to be saved if the lens can be surgically removed or possibly repositioned before the retina has been perma - nently damaged by high IOP . • If available, start the antiglaucoma medications 0.5% timolol every 12 hours and/or 2% dorzol - amide q8h (or the combination drop timolol/dor - zolamide q8h), +/‐ oral methazolamide 1 mg/lb up to q8–12h. The latter may be difficult to find and can be considered optional. • Short‐term glaucoma treatment like a dose of IV mannitol might be worth considering especially if IOP increase is very high and recent, if vision may still be present, and/or referral to an ophthalmolo- gist for lensectomy surgery is imminent. • Do not give mydriatics (tropicamide, atropine) as this may exacerbate glaucoma. Do not give miotics (latanoprost, pilocarpine, etc.) as these will block the normal flow of aqueous humor, trapping the lens in the anterior chamber and exacerbating glaucoma. Figure 27 .13. 566 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Posterior Lens Luxation Clinical Findings • History: variable; typically the chief complaint will not implicate lens disease; chronic or acute. • Signalment: variable. • Eye exam: variable, as it depends on the cause of the posterior lens luxation. An aphakic crescent may be visible (Figure 27.16), and the lens may luxate any - where posteriorly, though most commonly it will luxate ventrally and posteriorly. If due to trauma, there may be hyphema, posterior segment bleeding, retinal detachment, globe rupture, etc. If due to chronic glaucoma, there may be blindness, buph - thalmos, mydriasis, a deep anterior chamber, retinal degeneration, optic nerve cupping, etc. If due to previous primary anterior lens luxation, there may be focal axial corneal edema, a deep anterior chamber, and possibly other signs of previous glau- coma. If due to chronic anterior uveitis (seen more in cats), other signs of uveitis may be present (aqueous flare, fibrin in anterior chamber, iris hyperemia, etc.). Ultrasonographic findings (Figure 27 .17) • No lens in normal position just behind iris and in anterior half of globe. • Thin curvilinear lens capsule in posterior segment, in characteristic lens shape. • Lens position is variable and may be gravity dependent. • Mobile, thin, somewhat amorphous strands in vitreous may be present (vitreal degeneration). • If present, ultrasonographic signs of vitreal hemor- rhage, retinal detachment, scleral rupture, buph - thalmos, etc. Figure 27 .16. Aphakic crescent. This illustrates the clinical appearance of an aphakic crescent when visible. A posteri - orly and ventrally luxated lens (which happens to be a cata - ract) is in the lower pupil, allowing for the appearance of an aphakic (“without lens”) area in the upper part of the pupil (in this case) where the lens is absent. A corresponding ultra- sonographic appearance would be seen depending on the lens location. Figure 27 .17 . Posterior lens luxation. In this eye with chronic glaucoma and buphthalmos, the lens zonules have broken down, allowing the lens to become mobile and rest in the dependent part of the globe along the posterior eye wall as shown in (A). Note that there is no lens visible in its normal location. In (B) is the normal B‐mode image of the eye for comparison.

567 POCUS: EYE Actions • Measure IOP , and treat glaucoma if needed. Do not give mydriatics (atropine, tropicamide) if the IOP is high, as this may exacerbate glaucoma. Miotics (latanoprost, pilocarpine) are not specifically con- traindicated and may help to keep the lens trapped in the posterior segment. • Topical antiinflammatories may be needed if there are clinical signs of anterior uveitis. • Based on clinical signs and history, need to deter - mine primary cause as discussed above. The poste- rior location of the lens, alone, does not necessarily require specific treatment but is more an indicator of possibly more significant ocular pathology that must be identified and addressed. Consider referral to a veterinary ophthalmologist. Retinal Detachment Clinical Findings • History: possible acute or subacute vision loss (may not be noticeable to owner if unilateral). • Signalment: variable. • Eye exam: reduced or absent PLR, menace and dazzle; hyphema (blood in anterior chamber); rest- ing mydriasis (in affected eye), especially with aniso- coria; possible retinal hemorrhages or generalized red color from behind pupils; visible retinal detach- ment seen on fundic exam (best seen using indirect ophthalmoscopy, rather than direct ophthalmoscopy (for examination techniques see Cho 2019). Ultrasonographic Findings • If intraocular bleeding is present, this may be visible as echogenic structures (see Intraocular Hemorrhage section below). • The retinal detachment itself is seen as a thin bright continuous curvilinear structure in the posterior segment that can be followed back to the optic nerve head, often making a V‐ or Y‐shape or “gull wing” appearance (Figure 27.18A). • This linear structure is almost always attached at the ora serrata (junction between retina and ciliary body) (Figure 27.18B). • Often accompanied by other echogenic structures (vitreal strands, hemorrhage, asteroid hyalosis) in the posterior segment. • Retinal detachments may be bullous (retina sepa- rated from the posterior eye wall) or “flat” (retina close to the posterior eye wall) (Figure 27.18C). • Retinal detachments may be completely detached (only attached at the optic nerve head and ora serrata) or partial (still attached to the choroid in some areas). • It is possible to see discontinuities (tears or holes) in the detached retina, but not common. • The subretinal space is more often echolucent (indi- cating a serous retinal detachment) than echogenic (indicating subretinal blood, cells or a mass), and is very often more echolucent than either the retina or the posterior eye wall. • The presence of vitreal blood and vitreal mem- branes/degeneration can make identification of a retinal detachment, especially a partial detach- ment, much more difficult (see Figure 27.26). These findings can significantly reduce image contrast, causing a missed diagnosis of detach- ment, or a false positive if vitreal membranes are oriented to masquerade as a detachment (Gallhoefer et al. 2013). • If available, the use of contrast enhancement may improve the ability to differentiate a detached retina from vitreal membranes by identifying vas- cularization within the suspect structure(s), and may be more useful than using Doppler (Labruyère et al. 2011). • Seeing attachment points of a suspected retinal detachment (especially at the optic nerve and ora serrata) greatly increases the chance that a sus- pected detachment is truly a retinal detachment. Sweeping the probe across a suspect area in differ- ent directions will improve your ability to see this. Actions • Measure blood pressure especially if retinal detach- ment is nontraumatic and bilateral; treat systemic hypertension (systolic blood pressure >180 mmHg) if present and consistent with clinical signs. • Look for signs of anterior or posterior uveitis (miosis, aqueous flare, hypotony, iris hyperemia, etc.). If present, and cornea is fluorescein negative, and if patient will not be seen by a veterinary oph- thalmologist within 48–72 hours, begin topical treatment, such as NeoPolyDex drops or ointment, or 1% pred acetate suspension q6–12h, and systemic nonsteroidal antiinflammatories. If patient will be seen immediately, therapy may be delayed until examination. • If hyphema is present, measure IOP , and treat with antiglaucoma medications if IOP >25 mmHg (0.5% timolol q12h and/or 2% dorzolamide q8h, or the combination drop timolol/dorzolamide q8h), +/‐ oral methazolamide 1 mg/lb up to q8–12h). The latter may be difficult to find and can be considered optional.

568 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER • Note that other differentials for retinal detachment include primary retinal detachment, systemic disease (systemic infection, neoplasia) as well as idiopathic/ immune‐mediated pathologies, so a complete physical exam and/or additional laboratory testing and imaging (thoracic radiographs, +/‐ abdominal radiographs or ultrasound) for systemic disease may be indicated if other clinical signs are abnormal. • Consider referral to a veterinary ophthalmologist for further evaluation and possible advanced addi- tional treatment. 569 POCUS: E YE Intraocular Masses Clinical Findings • History: variable; many owners are unaware of the eye looking abnormal and the eye is often not pain- ful until either uveitis, glaucoma or hyphema develops; signs referable to these secondary prob - lems are often the presenting complaint. • Signalment: variable, but generally middle‐aged to older animals. • Eye exam: variable but any of the following: deformed globe in advanced cases (outward focal bulging of eye wall); hyphema; focal peripheral corneal edema if mass is touching inside of cornea (Figure 27.19A), dyscoria, iris thickening, presence of a visible mass in either anterior or posterior segment (pigmented or nonpigmented, and espe - cially near eye wall) (Figures 27.20 and 27.21); lens subluxation; focal retinal detachment associated with a solid‐looking structure; any of the above with glaucoma. Ultrasonographic Findings • A bulge in the normally spherical eye wall might be seen in advanced cases, with a mass as described below just under the area of the bulging eye wall. • Hyphema might be seen as indistinct, echogenic material in the anterior chamber. • Dyscoria would be difficult to appreciate on ultra - sound, but an area of iris thickening might be seen if thickening is marked (see Figures 27.19B and 27.20C). • The most common type in dogs (uveal melanoma) usually appears as an attached, rounded, uni - formly echogenic structure in the area of the iris or ciliary body (less commonly the choroid) with a sharp border, possibly slightly pushing the lens off‐ center (see Figure 27.19B,C). • Differentiate masses from uveal cysts, which would be very thin‐walled, echolucent within, and either free‐floating or attached to the posterior iris, pupil margin or ora serrata. • Masses are often broad‐based (on the eye wall) and not pedunculated (see Figure 27.21). Pearl: Retinal reattachment surgery, while not as commonly performed in animals as it is in humans, is increasingly available for animals with primary retinal detachment. Figure 27 .19. Anterior chamber mass in a dog. (A) The left eye of this 9‐year‐old dog has focal corneal edema, obscuring a large dark mass of the iris. The corneal edema has resulted from the mass growing large enough to contact and damage the corneal endothelium. The eye is buphthalmic and blind, and the IOP is 43 mmHg. (B) A large, uniformly echogenic mass is present in the anterior chamber of the same eye, originating from the iris and slightly pushing the lens to the right side of the image. Note the rounded, relatively distinct border between the mass and the anterior chamber and lens. The lens itself, as well as the vitreous, is otherwise normal and echolucent. Left is lateral in this image. (C) Subgross photo of the globe in (A) and (B). The eye was enucleated and a large, solid, pigmented mass is visible in the lateral anterior chamber. Some dis - tortion of the globe shape is present but this is a common processing artifact. The mass was diagnosed histopathologically as a uveal melanocytoma. Pearl: The prognosis for vision is better if the subreti- nal space is echolucent (transudate) and worse if echogenic (blood, cells, mass). The prognosis also worsens with increasing duration of the detachment. Pearl: If retinal detachment is present and associ - ated with trauma, the prognosis for vision is guarded to poor (Book et al. 2008).

570 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER • Doppler might show blood flow within a mass but absence of Doppler‐confirmed blood flow does not rule out neoplasia. • Masses may also be seen with vitreal hemorrhage, vitreal strands, and possibly retinal detachment. • Intraocular masses would be rarely associated with a foreign body (Welihozkiy et al. 2011). Actions • Look for signs of uveitis and hyphema; if anterior uveitis or hyphema is present and cornea is fluo - rescein negative, begin topical antiinflammatories, such as NeoPolyDex drops or ointment, or 1% pred acetate suspension q6–12h. 571 POCUS: E YE by a veterinary ophthalmologist immediately, top- ical therapy can be delayed until examination. • Measure IOP; if glaucoma present (IOP >25 mmHg), begin antiglaucoma medications, such as 0.5% timolol q12h, 2% dorzolamide q8h, or dorzolamide/ timolol q8h, if not being seen by an ophthalmologist within 24 hours. Do not give mydriatics (tropicamide, atropine) as this may exacerbate glaucoma. • Most intraocular neoplasms (such as melanoma, ade- noma) are primary and late to metastasize; however, a minimal systemic work‐up with baseline bloodwork, urinalysis, and thoracic radiographs, with or without abdominal imaging (ultrasonography, radiography), is indicated if systemic illness is present since intraoc- ular neoplasia (such as lymphosarcoma, hemangio- sarcoma, etc.) may represent metastatic disease. • Enucleation may ultimately be needed for both diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. • Consider timely referral to a veterinary ophthal - mologist as necessary for confirmation and defini - tive therapy. Intraocular Hemorrhage Clinical Findings • History: variable; possible vision loss, possible trauma, change in appearance, possible history of coagulopathy. • Signalment: variable. • Eye exam: hyphema (see Figure 27.2A), red or red‐ black haze visible inside eye from behind iris and lens, inability to visualize any fundic details; pupil may be any size and may still be responsive to light. Since the possible causes of intraocular hemorrhage include retinal detachment, posterior segment mass or injury, trauma, systemic hypertension, coagulop- athy and possibly vascular disease, accompanying history and clinical signs vary with the underlying cause. IOP may be low, normal or high. Ultrasonographic Findings • If hyphema is present, diffuse echogenic material will be present in the anterior chamber. • Variably sized and shaped structure(s) within the vitreous with poorly defined borders that are semi‐ mobile (try jiggling the eye) but not completely gravity dependent; can be multifocal; may be densely and uniformly echogenic, anechoic, hypoechoic or heterogeneous; may be composed of multiple point‐like echoes; are often near the eye wall (where the original bleeding occurred) (see Figure 27.26). • Differentiate on ultrasound from asteroid hyalosis, which tends to have a lucent peripheral vitreal border and is generally uniform (Figure 27.22) but both have partial mobility and may also have concurrent vitreal strands. • May be associated with retinal detachment, intraocular masses and scleral rupture (see corresponding sections in this chapter). The presence of echogenic blood in any location could greatly obscure the ultrasonographic visi - bility of both normal structures and actual lesions. • Need to differentiate from a solid intraocular mass, which will not be mobile at all, will always be attached to the eye wall, and will typically have a more distinct interior border than a hemorrhage. Pearl: All the above ophthalmic medications are human drugs, and drops are generally available at human pharmacies. Pearl: In the absence of trauma, two of the most common causes for spontaneous intraocular bleeding in older dogs are retinal detachment and intraocular neoplasia. In cats, neoplasia and hyper - tensive retinopathy with retinal detachment are the most common in the author’s experience. Figure 27 .22. Optic nerve and asteroid hyalosis. Asteroid hyalosis, a common finding in older dogs, is typically seen as an amorphous, fairly uniform, semimobile echogenic material in the normally echolucent vitreous. It is often denser in the center of the vitreous, leaving the more peripheral vitreous echogenic.

572 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Actions (T able 27 .3) • Look for signs of hyphema and uveitis (aqueous flare, miosis, hypotony); if uveitis is present and cornea is fluorescein negative, start topical ste - roids, such as NeoPolyDex drops or ointment or 1% prednisone acetate q6–12h, and consider systemic antiinflammatories. If IOP is low‐normal and uveitis is present, consider topical mydriatic cycloplegics (atropine q12–48h); IOP should be monitored. • If not associated with trauma, and especially if seen with hyphema, pursue a timely work‐up for coagulopathy including clotting times, platelet count, etc. • If not associated with trauma, and seen with retinal detachment, especially if bilateral, measure blood pressure; if hypertensive (systolic blood pressure >180 mmHg), then start systemic antihypertensive therapy. • Measure IOP , and treat with antiglaucoma medica- tions if IOP >25 mmHg (0.5% timolol q12h and/or 2% dorzolamide q8h, or timolol/dorzolamide q8h), +/‐ oral methazolamide 1 mg/lb up to q8–12h). 573 POCUS: EYE Suspected Retrobulbar Masses/ Exophthalmos Distinguishing between exophthalmos and buphthal- mos is key to choosing the right treatment plan when the eye is “bulging” (see Figure 27.4). Clinical Findings of Exophthalmos (Pushed‐Out Eye) • History: variable, may be acute or gradual onset. • Signalment: variable due to the varying etiologies. • Eye exam: globe protrudes and has reduced retro- pulsion (compare to the other side by palpating gently with an index finger on each closed eye) but is not enlarged in size (see below); globe deviation, not necessarily with strabismus; elevated nictitans; secondary lagophthalmos and central corneal exposure; indentation of sclera may be seen on fundic exam but fundus is otherwise normal; vari- able changes in vision and in IOP – most cases still have intact vision and normal IOP . • Physical exam: also look for possible ipsilateral dental disease or evidence of inflammation in soft palate; pain on opening mouth (variable); local lymphadenopathy; ipsilateral nasal disease; sneez- ing and nasal discharge; palpable periocular/ orbital bony abnormalities. Clinical Findings Supportive of Buphthalmos (Large Eye) • History: gradual or chronic onset. • Signalment: for dogs, a breed predisposed to pri- mary glaucoma, for example any terrier breed, bas- sett hound, cocker, beagle, sharpei, Siberian husky, shih tzu, Dalmatian, Great Dane, etc. For cats, clinical signs and history of chronic or recurrent uveitis. Secondary glaucoma can occur with any age or breed having prior intraocular disease. • Eye exam: enlarged (and not just pushed out) globe; signs of chronic glaucoma including blindness, episcleral injection, diffuse corneal edema, corneal striae, negative PLR, mydriasis, high IOP , hyperreflective tapetum, thin retinal ves- sels, dark and/or cupped optic nerve head. Ultrasonographic Findings of Retrobulbar Mass/ Exophthalmos • Affected globe is normal size. • Globe indentation by the mass may be seen (Figure 27.24B,C). • Mass effect of variable echotexture behind the globe (Figure 27.24B,C). • Variably discrete mass borders. Pearl: Intraocular bleeding is a nonspecific finding. Differentials include systemic disease (systemic hypertension, coagulopathy, vasculitis, etc.), ocular disease (uveitis, retinal detachment, neoplasia, pos- sibly lens luxation, etc)., trauma, etc. Referral is indi- cated unless the cause is definitively identified, treated, and managed. Note: Differentiate exophthalmos from buphthal- mos using ultrasound by measuring globe at widest front‐to‐back diameter and compare to normal eye (normal typically around 19–21 mm) (Figure 27.23). Buphthalmos is only caused by glaucoma, and is thus distinctly different in pathology from exophthalmos. Pearl: Cases of buphthalmos still warrant timely referral to a veterinary ophthalmologist for glau- coma treatment for the affected blind eye and glau- coma prophylaxis for the remaining sighted eye. Pearl: Indentation is more consistent with a mass or cyst rather than cellulitis. Pearl: Echogenicity versus echolucency is often not predictive of the etiology of a retrobulbar mass (Mason et al. 2001). Pearl: Cellulitis/abscesses usually have very indis- tinct borders and variable echogenicity, and oblit- erate/obscure normal structures; cystic structures typically are more sharply marginated with anecho- lucent/anechoic interior; neoplastic masses tend to be more discrete (than cellulitis/abscess) and more uniform, but may have cavitation, indistinct bor - ders, and variable echogenicity and even be occult via ultrasonography (Mason et al. 2001).

574 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER • The mass may be attached to or separate from the globe. • Most common differentials include abscesses (gen- erally acute onset and very painful on opening mouth), soft tissue or bony neoplasia (generally gradual onset and of varying degrees of pain – may not be painful at all). • Other less likely differentials include cysts (including sialoceles), foreign bodies, cellulitis or inflammation of retrobulbar tissues (sialoadenitis, extraocular muscle myositis), bony orbital masses, hamartomas, vascular anomalies, parasitic disease. These may be very difficult to distinguish (Welihozkiy et al. 2011). • Bony destruction is more indicative of neoplasia, and is more easily detected using radiography. Actions • If neoplasia is suspected, initiate a work‐up to screen for metastatic disease including baseline bloodwork, urinalysis, skull and thoracic radiog - raphy with or without abdominal imaging (ultra - sonography, radiography); referral to a veterinary ophthalmologist or surgeon may be necessary. • If an orbital abscess is suspected supported by find- ings of pain, ipsilateral soft palate swelling, gross dental disease, leukocytosis, lethargy, +/‐ fever, perform an oral exam and appropriate imaging, such as dental and skull radiographs, with appli - cable dental treatment; if found, oral abscess explo- ration, drainage, cytology, biopsy, and culture as indicated; systemic antibiotics and analgesics; advanced imaging and referral to a veterinary oph- thalmologist, surgeon, or dentist, as per clinical impression may be necessary (Hartley et al. 2007). Fine needle aspiration of suspected retrobulbar masses carries the risk of hemorrhage, possible iatrogenic globe puncture or nerve damage, but is often diagnostic for neoplasia and infection when the needle is appropri - ately placed. Aspiration aided by simultaneous ultra - sound can reduce these risks. Vascular anomalies, although extremely rare, may develop significant bleeding when aspirated or biopsied, and may not be amenable to typical hemorrhage control maneuvers. Most cases of primary orbital/periorbital neoplasia are malignant, for example nasal or third eyelid adeno- carcinoma, soft tissue sarcomas, osteosarcoma, squamous cell carcinoma, meningioma, glioma, lym - phoma (Kern 1985; Attali‐Soussay et al. 2001). Figure 27 .23. Measuring globe size. The probe has been placed so that the maximal length of the globe from anterior to posterior (the A‐P diameter) can be measured, and the image frozen for measurement. In (A), the normal eye, the normal A‐P diameter measured is 2.10 cm. In (B), an image of the fellow eye which is glaucomatous and blind, this same measurement is 2.57 cm. Note: These are additional images from the dog in Figure 27.19. In (C) is the normal B‐mode image of the eye for comparison. Pearl: Check ultrasonographically or on fundic exam, if visible, for any motion of the mass relative to the globe; if the mass stays separate from the globe when the gaze is redirected, it is more likely to be noninflammatory (neoplasia or a cystic structure). Pearl: A lateral orbital location may be more sugges- tive of abscess than neoplasm.

575 POCUS: E YE Suspected Globe Rupture Clinical Findings • History: suspected or known trauma (vehicular trauma, being struck by objects like doors, furniture or toys, fights with other animals including clawed cats and larger dogs, etc.); out - door animals. • Signalment: variable. • Eye exam: acute ocular pain; globe deformation, gross hypotony, chemosis, subconjunctival hem - orrhage; other periocular injuries, lid swelling and bruising; hyphema and/or anterior uveitis (Figures 27.25 and 27.26; see also Figure 27.2); blood, fibrin and dark brown‐black uveal tissue may be mounded externally at site of rupture Figure 27 .24. 576 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER (which might be located somewhere behind the front exposed part of the eye and thus not visible externally) (Rampazzo et al. 2006); orbital or skull fractures. Ultrasonographic Findings Extreme care should be used in approaching ocular ultrasonography in these cases, if at all. Avoid any direct contact with the suspected ruptured area; use sterile gel and adequate topical and anesthesia (see above) or the retrobulbar angle for probe placement; avoid any pressure at all to the globe and excessive restraint. • Globe not spherical like normal. • Globe may be smaller than the other eye (compare diameter of each eye). • Eye wall may not be clearly visible in all views – intraocular structures may seem to blend in with adjacent extraocular structures consistently in one location (see Figure 27.26B,C). • Will often be accompanied by sonographic evi - dence of retinal detachment, vitreal hemorrhage, and/or lens luxation or loss (see above corresponding sections). • The interior of the whole globe may appear hetero- geneously echogenic (due to the presence of blood and fibrin) with no discernible normal structures except for the lens, which will remain echolucent against this echogenic background if present. Actions • Evaluate first for life‐threatening trauma such as skull fractures, traumatic brain injury, cavitary hemorrhage, lung contusions, pneumothorax, etc. with a basic trauma work‐up. • Do not aggressively clean off adherent mucus‐like material from the eye surface. This may be fibrin that is actually sealing the defect, and removing it may cause a releak of intraocular contents as well as acute pain. • Administer systemic pain medications, systemic antiinflammatories and analgesics, systemic antibi- otics, and topical ophthalmics (antibiotics, atro - pine; drops preferred, avoid ointments) as dictated by patient. Figure 27 .25. Traumatic globe rupture in a dog. This unfortunate dog had been kicked by a moose, causing major ocular injury. Note that the corneal contour of this left eye is not spherical but rather appears squashed into a flatter shape by the eyelids. This is because the globe has lost its tension and shape due to a large rent at the limbus. Hyphema obscures all the intraocular structures, but a care - fully performed ocular ultrasound (not shown) from behind the orbital ligament might reveal a posterior rent and the presence of a retinal detachment, lens luxation or lens extrusion. Important: In cases of suspected globe rupture, extreme caution should be exercised when considering ocular ultrasonography. Avoid any direct contact with the suspected ruptured area and if ultrasound imaging is necessary (to confirm or clarify clinical suspicion) use only sterile gel after adequate topical anesthesia, or the retrobul - bar view, if at all. Any pressure at all to the globe or resis - tance by the patient may be painful and will cause further eye damage. The patient may be better served by avoiding ultrasound altogether and simply referring to an ophthal - mologist for definitive care. Pearl: Stabilize animal systemically first before working up the eye! Pearl: If the eye is too painful to be imaged with top- ical anesthesia and other clinical signs are sugges - tive of globe rupture, the patient may be better served by avoiding ultrasound altogether due to the potential for causing further damage. Pearl: Stabilize the critical patient before addressing the ocular component. Pearl: The owner’s ability to give topical medica - tions may be limited due to patient pain. Due to the possibility of further injury in the act of topical drug administration, topical medications may not be worth the trouble.

578 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER • Very carefully place an E‐collar to prevent self‐trauma. • If a penetrating foreign body is seen, leave it in place if immediate, timely referral is possible; if a foreign body is clearly visible, very mobile and loose enough to fall out on its own before referral to an ophthalmologist is possible, it may be very care- fully removed in the clinic under clean conditions with at least topical anesthesia; however, there is risk of damaging the eye and causing leakage of intraocular contents, allowing for intraocular infec- tion, bleeding, and increased risk of loss of the eye. • Many cases will require enucleation, but referral to a veterinary ophthalmologist may provide options for salvaging the globe and possibly vision. Pearls and Pitfalls, The Final Say • Important to correlate ultrasound findings with clinical ophthalmic signs! Always do a complete ocular examination first when presented with an ocular complaint. • Very helpful to compare the abnormal eye to the other eye as a control, especially when the other eye is unaffected. • Adjust magnification (depth) to a level adequate to distinguish lesions. • Adjust gain both by increasing and decreasing to help distinguish real findings from artifacts. • Unless you are very comfortable with your diag- nosis and treatment plan, it is wise to adhere to the following statement: if an eye is diseased enough to require ultrasound, it should most likely be referred to an ophthalmologist for follow‐up. • Use Global FAST to help determine if the ocular problem is localized or part of disseminated dis- ease. Global FAST surveys the abdomen (AFAST), thorax (TFAST) including heart (TFAST) and lung (Vet BLUE) and also helps assess patient volume status (see Chapters 6, 7, 17, 18, 22, 23, 36, and 37). Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 Introduction Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the gold standard for brain imaging. However, this technique involves high costs such as equipment acquisition and mainte- nance, making it difficult to perform as a routine any- where, especially in veterinary medicine. Moreover, MRI requires some form of chemical restraint, which is commonly inhaled general anesthesia via endotracheal intubation, which carries patient risk. On the other hand, transcranial ultrasonography (TCUS) has the advantage of being noninvasive and low cost, which has great value in the diagnosis of brain disorders such as hydrocephalus, tumors, congenital malformations, and traumatic processes, and can be performed without the need to anesthetize the patient. Transcranial ultrasonography is considered a screen- ing method for neuroimaging examination in many situations. It may be applied to cases of trauma, patients with anesthesia limitations and owners’ eco- nomical restrictions, before patients are imaged by computed tomography (CT) or MRI. In human medicine, TCUS has been compared to CT and MRI in children in order to detect the cause of head- ache. While CT and MRI were able to detect tumors as the primary disease in 3.8% of these cases, TCUS was less effective, detecting tumors as primary disease in 2.2% of cases. However, the low cost, lower patient risk, and convenience through point‐of‐care imaging appli- cations make TCUS an option in clinical practice not only as a screening test but also when measurements and monitoring are needed (Abrão et al. 1998; Wang et al. 2002). In children, the temporal, parietal, and suborbital acoustic windows are commonly utilized when performing TCUS (Wang et al. 2002). These acoustic windows may be used for animals but the breg- matic fontanelle and temporal bone have been most studied as acoustic windows for TCUS in veterinary medicine (Gallagher et al. 1995; Lorigados and Pinto 2013; Cintra et al. 2014). Both human and veterinary protocols additionally use the foramen magnum as an acoustic window to assess the caudal fossa. Despite many published veterinary studies (Hudson et al. 1998; Carvalho et al. 2007; Duque et al. 2009) some neurologists still remain uncomfortable with the potential use of TCUS. However, many small animal patients have suitable transcranial acoustic windows that allow screening for structural lesions with the advantages of being a rapid, safe (no anesthesia requirement and minimal restraint), point‐of‐care, imaging application. One of the main indications for TCUS is ventricular system evaluation. Ventricular measurements may be used clinically and compared to normal published reference values (Table 28.1). What POCUS Brain Can Do • Screen for anatomical abnormalities of the brain. • Screen for structural abnormalities of the brain. • Provide monitoring measurements (ventricular system, focal lesions). What POCUS Brain Cannot Do • Account for variables of skull bone thickness. • Account for anatomical variations between patients and species. • Differentiate between malignant and benign lesions. 580 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Indications • Any small‐breed dog or cat with neurological signs and accessible transcranial acoustic windows. Objectives • Understand how to image the three transcranial acoustic windows. • Appreciate basic ultrasonographic brain anatomy. • Understand the value and limitations of transcra- nial Doppler ultrasound (TCUS). How to do POCUS Brain Probe T ype Real‐time B‐mode TCUS probe requirements are as follows. • Linear probes of 5–10 MHz with depth range of 1.0–4.0 cm for neonates with or without an open rostral fontanelle. • Curvilinear (microconvex) probes of 2–6 MHz with high resolution and depth range of 1.0–6.0 cm for mature small‐breed dogs without an open breg- matic fontanelle. Acoustic Windows for POCUS Brain Three transcranial acoustic windows may be used for POCUS brain: rostral, temporal, and suboccipital. Rostral Acoustic Window The rostral window is used in patients with an open bregmatic fontanelle, including puppies <1–3 months old, kittens <5 months old, and many toy breeds. However, even in a closed bregmatic fontanelle having a thin frontal bone, an acoustic window may be pre- sent because ultrasound can image through thin bone. T emporal and Suboccipital Acoustic Windows The temporal window is located above zygomatic arch, and the suboccipital window should be used in all cases (Figures 28.1, 28.2, 28.3, and 28.4). Ultrasonographic Anatomy The brain is surrounded by the bones of the skull and during fetal development, fibrous sutures appear bet - ween them. These sutures extend to intersections called the fontanelles. Compared to humans, at birth most dogs and cats have either a very small fontanelle (approximately 0.5–3 mm) or one that is completely ossified. The toys and chondrodystrophic breeds are exceptions, in which the fontanelle between the frontal and parietal bones is relatively greater in size and can remain open for up to three months or in some cases remain persistently open throughout life.
