The contours of the bone can be identified as a hyperechogenic (bright white) arcuate line in the near‐field of the image, with brain parenchyma (gray and white brain matter) appearing with moderate degrees of echogenicity. The encephalon is contained in a cavity inside the skull, whose rostral border is limited by a bony plate, called the ethmoid, and caudally limited by the occipital bone. Laterally, the cavity is limited by the temporal, parietal, and frontal bones. The dome of the cavity (calvaria) is formed by the frontal and parietal bones, and the base is formed by the ethmoid, prephe- noid, and basisphenoid bones. Its most prominent internal anatomical feature is the cerebellar tentorium, which is a large projection at the junction of the dorsal and caudal walls, forming the middle portion of the cerebellum in the transverse fissure of the brain (Hudson et al. 1989; Cartee et al. 1993; Homco 1996). The hippocampus can be seen caudo- medial to the lateral ventricle with greater echogenicity (brighter) when compared to the thalamus (darker). The third ventricle appears as a hypo‐ to anechoic (dark to black) area around the interthalamic adhesion (Homco 1996). These structures can be more easily seen in longitudinal and transversal planes using the rostral acoustic window. Transverse planes of this acoustic window with a rostral direction (see Figure 28.18) image the dorsal portions of the caudate nucleus close to the telencephalic region (Carvalho and Andrade neto 2005). The lateral ventricles are located in a paramedian region in the cerebral hemispheres. The third ventricle lies within the diencephalon and hints toward the mes- encephalic aqueduct. The fourth ventricle lies within the rhombencephalon and communicates with the outer spaces of the cerebral fluid. The third and fourth ventricles in the dog and cat under normal conditions are too small to be measured sonographically. The cor- pus callosum and callus groove sometimes are not seen, but are represented by a dorsal hyperechoic (bright white) line with less intense echoes. All these anatomical landmarks are best viewed at the rostral window on sagittal and transverse planes (see Figures 28.18–25). When the ventricles are distended, they appear as anechoic cavities and may or may communicate with one another, particularly in their rostral portion. 592 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER through the rostral fontanelle in the transverse plane, should not exceed 0.15 cm in neonatal dogs and similar in normal adults. This ventricular diameter should be measured in a transverse plane at the level of the inter- thalamic adhesion. Ventriculomegaly is considered when the dorsoventral measurement of the lateral ven- tricles is greater than or equal to 0.35 cm at this point. The use of corresponding longitudinal planes help better interrogate this three‐dimensional structure of the ventricles. Another applied measurement is the distance between the dorsoventral point of the ven - tricle to the surface of the brain which ranges from 1.63 to 2.06 cm in young dogs (Hudson 1998). At the inter - thalamic adhesion level in longitudinal plane obtained through the rostral acoustic window, the thickness of the cerebral mantle is measured as the distance from the ceiling of the ventricle to the surface of the brain (see Figure 28.17). In a dorsal plane obtained at the temporal acoustic window, it is also possible to measure the width of lat- eral ventricles. The measurement should be made bet- ween the septum pellucidum and the lateral wall of the ventricle (see Figure 28.8). In a study of 37 normal adult dogs (mesaticephalics), the mean lateral ven - tricle width obtained in the anterior parietotemporal region was 0.27 ± 0.03 cm (Spaulding et al. 1990). There are some noteworthy differences between the neonatal brain and the adult brain of animals. The ten- torium of the cerebellum is cartilaginous, allowing its visibility through access through the dorsal midline in puppies. The grooves and spines, however, are less developed in puppies than in adult dogs. The hippo - campus is a prominent structure in the encephalon of adult animals, but is not clearly visible in the neonate brain for similar reasons (Carvalho et al. 2007). However, no references exist in the literature establish- ing the anatomical differences expected in elderly adult animals. Pearls and Pitfalls, The Final Say POCUS brain is an alternative imaging modality to be considered in neurological patients, especially in cats and small‐ and toy‐breed dogs that have viable tran - scranial acoustic windows. POCUS brain may be used for both initial assessment and serial monitoring, being economical, fast, safe, and radiation sparing, and carries less patient risk and cost when compared with CT and MRI. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 Introduction Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a common occurrence in veterinary medicine and is associated with a high rate of morbidity and mortality in both humans (Ghajar 2000) and small animals (Dewey 2000). TBI is most fre- quently caused by road traffic accidents, but can also be due to falls, kicks, gunshot wounds, and animal bites; nontrauma causes include metabolic, toxic, hyp- oxic, infectious, vascular, and space‐occupying lesions (Vianna and Arias 2013). Successful outcome depends upon the severity and location of injury, appropriate management, and timely identification of complica- tions. Advanced imaging has been the gold standard evaluation of TBI but is limited by availability, patient risk, and expense. Moreover, many veterinarians are unfamiliar with the potential use of ultrasound for central neurological evaluation despite published veterinary studies (Hudson et al. 1989; Carvalho et al. 2007; Duque et al. 2013). The fact that ultrasound cannot pass through bone has contributed to this reluc- tance. However, many small animal patients have suit- able transcranial acoustic windows that allow for both screening for structural lesions and assessing vascular perfusion along with the advantages of being a rapid, safe, point‐of‐care, imaging application. With the brain being bathed in cerebral spinal fluid which is circulated through a system of ventricles and the subarachnoid space, the organ is structurally ame- nable to sonographic assessment since ultrasound’s strength is imaging fluid. As a result, dilation of its ventricular system is easily appreciated, and standard- ized measurements may be performed and used clini- cally with normal reference values (Table 29.1). A more challenging ultrasound skill, transcranial Doppler ultrasonography (TCDUS), used for vascular mapping and flow measurements, is also discussed in this chapter, involving the vasculature itself and some vascular‐derived factors, using Doppler for the assessment of brain perfusion and the degree of intra- cranial pressure. Traditional methods used most fre- quently for such monitoring cerebral perfusion and intracranial pressure are technically challenging, inva- sive, and can cause complications (Werner et al. 1995). On the other hand, TCDUS of cerebral arteries has dis- tinct advantages of being not only noninvasive with less patient risk, but also a low‐cost, readily available imaging method when compared to computed tomog- raphy (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Transcranial Doppler ultrasonography was intro- duced to human medicine in the early 1980s (Berg et al. 2008; Carvalho Andrade Neto 2014), and is a method which may be used repeatedly, allowing real‐ time measurement of blood flow velocity in the major cerebral arteries without the need for contrast agents (CT and MRI). More recently, TCDUS has been used to confirm changes in cerebral hemodynamics in several neurological disorders of people and small animals, and can provide the Doppler velocimetry parameters of velocity, resistive and pulsatility index (PI) in the various cerebral arteries (Carvalho et al. 2007). Normal RI reference ranges have been determined in dogs as 0.55 ± 0.04 for cerebral arteries (Seo et al. 2005) and 0.5–0.78 for the basilar artery (Saito et al. 2003). The clinical significance of the RI is that it has been shown to correlate with the degree of intracranial pressure (ICP) (Fukushima et al. 2000a,b) with RI measure- ments (ICP = –37.35 + 109.85 × RI) investigated in POCUS: Brain – Clinical Integration Cibele F. 596 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER veterinary and human medicine literature (Fukushima et al. 1999). Thus, TCDUS has the potential to be a use- ful tool for monitoring TBI cases for the presence of ICP and its changes during treatment (McCormick et al. 2017). What POCUS Brain Can Do • Screen for structural abnormalities of the brain. • Evaluate brain perfusion via TCDUS. • Serve as a monitoring tool for intracranial pressure (ICP). What POCUS Brain Cannot Do • Account for variability of skull bone thickness. • Account for variables that affect TCDUS including hematocrit, blood glucose, ventilatory status (oxy- genation, carbon dioxide levels), and cardiac output. • Account for anatomical variations between patients and species. Indications • Any small animals with neurological signs and accessible transcranial acoustic windows. • Patients with suspect or confirmed TBI, increased ICP , or central neurological disease. Objectives • Be aware of the 3 transcranial acoustic windows. • Be able to appreciate basic ultrasonographic brain anatomy. • Be familiar with the required transcranial color Doppler ultrasound (TCDUS) images. • Be familiar with Doppler velocimetry indices. • Understand the value and limitations of transcra- nial color Doppler ultrasound (TCDUS). 597 POCUS: B RAIN – C LINICAL I NTEGRATION How to do POCUS Brain Probe T ype Both real‐time B‐mode and TCDUS probe require - ments are as follows. • Linear probes of 5–10 MHz in neonates with or without an open rostral fontanelle with depth range of 1.0–4.0 cm. • Microconvex probes of 2–6 MHz with high resolu - tion for more mature small‐breed dogs with breg - matic fontanelle with depth range of 2.0–6.0 cm. • Color flow and pulsed Doppler for TCDUS. Acoustic Windows for POCUS Brain Three transcranial acoustic windows may be used for POCUS brain. • Rostral acoustic window. • Temporal acoustic window. • Suboccipital acoustic window. Rostral Acoustic Window The rostral window is used in patients with an open bregmatic fontanelle: puppies <1–3 months of age and kittens <5 months of age, and many toy breeds. The window is accessible when a closed bregmatic fonta - nelle has a thin frontal bone. T emporal and Subocciptal Acoustic Windows The temporal window is located above the zygomatic arch, and the suboccipital window should be used in all cases. T echnique for POCUS Brain Each acoustic window should be scanned in all planes if possible. At the rostral window, sliding the probe in the ros - tral to caudal direction, the sonographer obtains transverse planes (Figure 29.1). At the rostral window, fanning the probe in lateral direction, the sonographer obtains sagittal planes (Figure 29.2). Figure 29.1. Finally, at the suboccipital window, the sonographer obtains transverse and sagittal planes (Figure 29.4). T ranscranial Ultrasonography without Color Flow Doppler – Imaging the Parenchyma Publications exist documenting normal ultrasono - graphic findings using transcranial ultrasonography in healthy dogs (Hudson et al. 1989, 1991) and corre - lating transcranial ultrasound images with encephalic anatomy (Carvalho et al. 2009; Cintra et al. 2014). In smaller dogs and cats with thin skull bones and those with an open bregmatic fontanelle, it is possible to see several anatomical landmarks sonographically (Figure 29.5) including various sulci, the interhemi - spheric fissure, ventricular system (lateral ventricle, third and fourth ventricles and the mesencephalic aqueduct that connects the third and fourth ventricles), cerebellum, caudal brainstem, and medulla. T ranscranial Ultrasonography with Color Flow Doppler – Imaging the Vasculature The brain’s main arterial anatomy is composed of the vertebrobasilar system and the cerebral arterial circle (Figure 29.6A). Vascular anatomy can be further assessed by TCDUS (Figure 25.6B). The temporal window is the best acoustic window to assess the cerebral arterial circle. The additional arteries within the cerebral arterial circle are best assessed by TCDUS via the rostral window. The suboccipital window is the best to assess the vertebrobasilar system, in both the transverse and sagittal planes. A few reports have described vascular anatomy and its reference values (Spaulding et al. 1990; Saito et al. 2003; Duque et al. 2010; Carvalho and Andrade Neto 2014). TCDUS can be used to confirm changes in cerebral hemodynamics (Werner et al. 1992, 1993, 1995; Carvalho et al. 2012a). In a temporal approach, directing the probecaudally, we obtain dorsal planes. Color Doppler is performed (as a kind of guide) to identify the cerebral arterial circle (Figure 29.7). Once the vessels are identified, pulsed Doppler is initiated, paying attention to the optimal angle of insonation (>60°) to maximize signal. Freeze the image when you get three similar sequential waveforms (Figure 29.8), and then measure a representative spectral waveform to determine the patient’s peak systolic velocity, end‐diastolic velocity, and resistive index (Figure 29.9, Table 29.2). Sonographic Features of Traumatic Brain Injury from Trauma Head trauma is the most common cause of bleeding in the subarachnoid space of small animals (Braund 2003; Vianna and Arias 2013; De LaHunta et al. 2014), with the possible complications of epidural and sub - dural hematomas, and intracerebral and intraventric - ular hemorrhage. Clinical consequences of focal lesions vary with location, regional extent and collat - eral damage, i.e. coup contrecoup phenomenon (Braund 2003). Epidural and subdural hematomas generally are seen as hypoechoic lesions (Figure 29.10); however, brain edema and demyelinization appear similar sonographically and may be concurrently present. Intraventricular hemorrhage is identified by the presence of echogenic debris within the lateral ventricle cavities (Figure 29.11). Intraparenchymal hemorrhage Figure 29.2. Over time, hemorrhage organization can sonographically appear as a mass effect and perile - sional edema may be seen as a hypo‐ or anechoic halo around the lesion (Figure 29.13). Any intracavitary lesion can cause a space‐occupying “mass effect” that may result in disruption of cerebral spinal fluid circulation or both effects may lead to increased intra - cranial pressure (ICP) (Figure 29.14) because of the Monro–Kellie Doctrine. Real‐time imaging in B‐mode and TCDUS may be used for assessing injury and its potential ramifica - tions, including via estimating ICP TCDUS (Carvalho et al. 2012a). Furthermore, vasospasm secondary to TBI (Werner et al. 1995) may be assessed through map- ping with color flow Doppler, and calculations of Doppler velocimetry using TCDUS. POCUS brain findings may also be clinically integrated with the patient’s modified Glasgow Coma Score (Platt et al. 2001) for decision making. Sonographic Features of Brain Pathology from Nontrauma Hydrocephaly Prevalence studies of central neurological disease in dogs indicate that congenital anomalies constitute approximately 6% of total diagnoses, with hydroceph- alus accounting for ~50% of these cases, making hydro- cephalus one of the more common canine congenital defects (Spaulding et al. 1990). Small‐breed and brachy- cephalic dogs are most commonly affected by hydro - cephalus (Spaulding et al. 1990), with many patients presenting with nonspecific signs. Moreover, the sig - nificance of the degree of ventriculomegaly can be dif- ficult to determine. Although POCUS brain imaging may demonstrate ventriculomegaly (Figure 29.15), B‐ mode parameters may not be sensitive and specific enough for accurate monitoring during treatment and clinical course of these patients (Spaulding et al. 1990). 600 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Reports in the veterinary literature better correlate TCDUS resistive index (RI) of the basilar artery to clinical signs in hydrocephalic dogs than B‐mode (Fukushima et al. 1999, 2000a,b). One clinical study showed that with experimentally induced acute hydro- cephalus in cats, a 22% reduction in the blood flow of the brain, cerebellum, and encephalic trunk occurred, and differed in variable ways in each part of the encephalon (Hochwald et al. 1975). Thus, TCDUS is a more accurate method of cerebral hemodynamic assessment than B‐mode with the potential to monitor treatment of hydrocephalus by measuring the RI of the cerebral arteries (Figure 29.16), combined with other clinical information. In summary, TCDUS measurement of the RI is likely more useful than B‐mode measurements of the lateral ventricles (Carvalho et al. 2009). Strokes Cerebrovascular diseases in dogs are defined as brain abnormalities caused by blood supply impairment (Garosi 2010), which often affect the cognitive and neu- rological status of the dog. Previously considered uncommon in animals, cerebrovascular disease is being recognized with greater frequency in veterinary medicine since brain imaging techniques such as ultra- sonography, CT and MRI have become more readily available. Stroke is currently one of the leading causes of human death (Lillehei et al. 1984; Garosi 2010) but its overall occurrence in dogs is not well known. Stroke, also referred to as a cerebrovascular accident (CVA), is the most common clinical manifes - tation of cerebrovascular disease, and can be broadly divided into ischemic stroke and hemorrhagic stroke (Braund 2003). Once the diagnosis of ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke is confirmed, potential under - lying causes should be sought and treated. In one study of 42 small‐breed dogs showing acute onset of clinical signs with no progressive focal cerebral dysfunction with the diagnosis of cerebrovascular disease confirmed at necropsy, coexisting diseases included cerebral amyloid microangiopathy, endo - crinopathy, coagulopathy, neoplasias, and hyperli - pemia with published antemortem sonographic features (Figure 29.17) (Carvalho et al. 2012b). However, further studies are needed to fully investi - gate the potential of TCDUS to monitor the treatment and clinical course of this patient subset. Encephalitis As a representative example of inflammatory disease of the canine central nervous system (CNS), granulo - matous meningoencephalitis (GME) is the second most common inflammatory CNS disease in dogs, following canine distemper. GME is an acute, nonsuppurative, and progressive disease that mainly affects small‐ and toy‐breed dogs, especially young and middle‐aged ter- riers and poodles (mean age 5 years; range 6 months to 12 years); thus POCUS brain has the potential to eval - uate and monitor this disease. Lesions are often restricted to the CNS and most commonly occur within the white matter of the cerebrum, cerebellum, caudal brainstem, and cervical spinal cord. Figure 29.4. 602 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Three types of GME have been described based on the site of the lesions: focal, disseminated, and ocular (Fisher 2002). Historically, the presumptive diagnosis of GME has been based on nonspecific findings of history, laboratory testing, advanced imaging (CT and MRI), and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis. Disseminated GME may be confounded with infection and inflamma- tion, and focal GME with neoplasia and nonneoplastic space‐occupying lesions such as inflammatory/ infectious/parasitic‐related granulomas, cysts, and infarcts. Ocular GME may be confounded by other causes of optic neuritis. In general, CT scan and MRI, although useful diagnostic imaging tools for detecting brain injuries, cannot differentiate benign space‐occu- pying masses from neoplastic lesions and their expense and need for chemical restraint make serial examination often impractical. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 Introduction Peripheral nerve blocks of the forelimb are used to pro- vide analgesia in both medical and surgical situations. Peripheral nerve blocks are indicated for the alleviation of perioperative pain, chronic pain, and traumatic pain of the shoulder, brachium, antebrachium, carpus, meta- carpus, and phalanges. Peripheral nerve blocks may be used as a primary analgesic procedure or more com- monly as part of a multimodal analgesic approach to small animals with acute and chronic pain as inpatients and outpatients. Moreover, the use of POCUS nerve blocks allows the clinician to more accurately locate target nerves, thus better insuring success and avoiding nearby structures such as blood vessels and body cav- ities, thus minimizing complications. The use of POCUS nerve blocks provides clear advantages over blind tech- niques. In fact, ultrasound‐guided nerve blocks are becoming standard of care in human medicine. What POCUS Nerve Blocks – Forelimb Can Do • Can assist with accurately performing nerve blocks over blind techniques. • Can help avoid complications by imaging nearby structures such as vessels and body cavities, and other structures to be avoided. What POCUS Nerve Blocks – Forelimb Cannot Do • Cannot replace the need for familiarity with the anatomy at each nerve block location. • Cannot replace ultrasound‐guided skills and the hand–eye and spatial coordination necessary for needle placement and advancement. Indications • Regional anesthesia of the forelimb during proce- dural anesthetic events, and nonprocedural options for acute and chronic pain. • Part of multimodal anesthesia of the forelimb. • The paravertebral approach is indicated to provide analgesia/anesthesia to the shoulder and proximal brachium. • The subscalene approach is indicated to provide analgesia/anesthesia to the shoulder, brachium, and elbow. • The axillary approach is indicated to provide analgesia/anesthesia to the distal brachium and elbow. • The radial, ulnar, median, and musculocutaneous nerve block (RUMM) is indicated to provide anal- gesia/anesthesia to the antebrachium, carpus, metacarpus, and digits. Objectives • Be able to identify relevant anatomy of the forelimb. • Be able to perform the regional blocks of the forelimb. • Know the clinical utility of each of the three approaches, and what part of the forelimb is anes- thetized in each. 610 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER How to Perform POCUS Nerve Blocks – Forelimb Approaches and Locations The nerves of the forelimb via the brachial plexus may be blocked at different locations by different approaches – the paravertebral, subscalene and axil- lary (Table 30.1). Relevant Anatomy of the Brachial Plexus • The brachial plexus is formed by the ventral roots of the spinal nerves C6, C7, C8, and T1 (Evans and de Lahunta 2013). Occasionally the brachial plexus receives contributions from C5 and T2. • The ventral branches of C6 and C7 emerge through the intervertebral foramen of C5–6 and C6–7, respectively, and course through the muscles in the intertransverse space towards the medial aspect of the scalenus muscle. • The ventral roots of C8 and T1 emerge through the intervertebral foramen of C7–T1 and T1–T2, respec- tively. The branches of C8 course ventrally parallel to the cranial aspect of the first rib, and the branches of T1 course lateral to the axillary artery. • The nerve branches then descend into the cervical area bordered laterally by the deep fascia of the neck and medially by the prevertebral fascia. Probe T ype Used to Perform Forelimb Blocks • Ultrasound machine with a linear transducer (probe) of ≥10 MHz. • 2–4 cm depth depending on animal size. Materials Needed to Perform Forelimb Blocks • Clippers and skin preparation solutions. • Sterile gloves. • Sterile drapes. • Local anesthetic (in sufficient quantity). • 50 mm 21 gauge isolated unipolar needles (for cats and dogs weighing less than 15 kg). • 100 mm 21 gauge isolated unipolar needles (for dogs weighing more than 15 kg). • Sterile transducer (probe) drapes and gel. • Multiparametric monitor (electrocardiogram [ECG], noninvasive blood pressure [NIBP], pulse oximetry [SpO2], temperature). • Emergency drugs. Ultrasound‐guided Brachial Plexus: Paravertebral Approach The brachial plexus paravertebral approach consists of the deposit of an anesthetic solution at the ventral roots of spinal nerves C6, C7, C8, and T1 (Bagshaw et al. 2009). The paravertebral approach provides analgesia/anes- thesia to the entire forelimb, but it is indicated for proce- dures involving the shoulder and proximal brachium. T able 30.1. 611 POCUS: N ER v E B LOCKS – F ORELIMB Ultrasound Probe Placement and Block T echnique • C6 and C7 block . Place the probe parallel to the longitudinal axis of the cervical spine, immediately below the lateral border of the transverse process of C6. • C8 through T1 block . Place the probe parallel to the longitudinal axis of the cervical spine, cranial to the first rib and above the costochondral joint. • The block is performed using an in‐plane needle advancement (Figure 30.1). • Check through gentle aspiration for extravascular needle placement and abort if blood is aspirated or if resistance to the injection occurs. • During anesthetic injection, the needle should be repositioned if necessary to obtain a homogeneous distribution of anesthetic around the target nerve. Drugs and Volume Administered • Drug and concentration: bupivacaine 0.5%, ropiva- caine 0.5%, levobupivacaine 0.5%. • Suggested volume: 0.05 mL/kg per branch. Scan of Brachial Plexus at the Paravertebral Space Scanning of the Paravertebral Spaces C5–6 and C6–7 The transverse process of C6 is the most prominent landmark. Scanning of the C8–T1 Complex The most relevant landmark is the first rib, which is seen as a hyperechoic semicircular line, and a sharp acoustic shadow, which extends medially. The acoustic window allows visualization of the C8–T1 nerve com - plex, medial to the belly of the scalenus muscle (Figures 30.4 and 30.5). Ultrasound‐guided Brachial Plexus Block through an Axillary Approach The brachial plexus block through an axillary approach consists of instillation of local anesthetic solution around the nerves responsible for innervation of the forelimb in the axillary space (Figure 30.9). The target nerves are the musculocutaneous nerve, axillary nerve, radial nerve, and median‐ulnar nerve trunk (Campoy et al. 2010; Ansón et al. 2015). The axillary approach provides analgesia/ anesthesia to structures located distal to the midbrachial region, and it is indicated for procedures involving the distal humerus, elbow, antebrachium, and carpus. 614 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER • Once positioned, gently direct the ultrasound beam until a transverse view of the axillary vessels and nerves is obtained. • Identify the axillary fascia surrounding these structures. • The brachial plexus block in the axillary space is performed with an in‐plane technique. • The needle is introduced through the belly of the superficial pectoral muscle and lateral to the jugular vein, in a caudodorsal direction. • Check for extravascular needle placement and avoid injection if resistance is perceived . If necessary, the needle should be repositioned to obtain a homogeneous distribution around the target nerve. Drugs and Volume Administered • Drug and concentration: bupivacaine 0.5%, ropiva- caine 0.5%, levobupivacaine 0.5%. • Suggested total volume: 0.15–0.2 mL/kg. Scan of the Axillary Space The axillary artery, represented as a pulsatile and anechoic circle structure, is the main reference of the image. The axillary vein, situated caudal to the artery, is an ovoid and anechoic structure, easily collapsible when gentle pressure is applied with the transducer. The acoustic window permits identification of the nerves of the brachial plexus, located cranial and slightly dorsal to the axillary vessels (Figures 30.10 and 30.11). Ultrasound‐guided Radial, Ulnar, Median, and Musculocutaneous (RUMM) Nerve Block The RUMM block desensitizes the antebrachium, carpal joint, and forepaw. It consists of the instilla - tion of anesthetic solution over the radial, musculo - cutaneous, median, and ulnar nerves at the middle third of the brachium (Portela et al. 2013; Castiñeiras et al. 2015). Figure 30.9. Axillary approach. Ultrasound‐guided axil - lary plexus block being performed in a dog. A linear probe is positioned in the axillary space, between the manubrium of the sternum and the supraglenoid tubercle of the scapula, with a ventrodorsal orientation in a parasagittal approach. The needle is introduced in‐plane, in a cranio - caudal direction. Source: Used with permission from Otero and Portela (2019). Pearl: In order to achieve a deep and long‐lasting block, the local anesthetic must be injected after puncturing the axillary fascia. Note: The protocol generally provides analgesia for up to eight hours. Since the phrenic nerve could be blocked with this technique, bilateral blocks should be avoided. There is a potential risk of producing an iat- rogenic pneumothorax if the needle pierces the parietal pleura at the thoracic inlet, therefore it is important to avoid introducing the needle caudal to the brachial artery. Pearl: Under probe compression, veins initially col- lapse while arteries do not. Pearl: The axillary approach to block the brachial plexus promotes block of the ipsilateral phrenic nerve. This block does not significantly impair ven- tilation in animals without respiratory compromise unless performed bilaterally. Pearl: The nerves that supply the thoracic limb run through the axillary space from medial to lateral and should be memorized. For this reason, when the ultrasound probe is placed parasagittal to this area in a ventrodorsal orientation, a transverse view of the nerves and vessels is obtained.

Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 Introduction Peripheral nerve blocks of the hindlimb are indicated for numerous clinical and surgical procedures, and they can in some cases replace neuraxial anesthesia techniques. The nerves that innervate the hindlimb, mainly the femoral and sciatic nerves, can be blocked from their emergence from the intervertebral foramen to their distal branches in the thigh region. The specific nerve to be blocked should be chosen according to the area to be desensitized. The use of POCUS nerve blocks and the use of ultrasound for visualizing structures may reduce both failure and complication rates associ- ated with many of the blind techniques. What POCUS Nerve Blocks – Pelvic Limb Can Do • Can assist with accurately performing nerve blocks over blind techniques. • Can help reduce complications by imaging nearby structures such as vessels and body cavities, and other structures to be avoided. What POCUS Nerve Blocks – Pelvic Limb Cannot Do • Cannot replace the need for familiarity with the involved anatomy at each nerve block location. • Cannot replace ultrasound‐guided skills and the hand–eye and spatial coordination necessary for needle placement and advancement. Indications • Regional anesthesia of the pelvic limb during pro- cedural anesthetic events, and nonprocedural options for acute and chronic pain (Table 31.1). • Part of multimodal anesthesia of the pelvic limb. • Combination of psoas compartment with lumbosa- cral trunk block is indicated to provide analgesia/ anesthesia to the hip, thigh, and knee. • The combination of femoral and sciatic nerve block is indicated to provide analgesia/anesthesia to the femur area and knee. • The combination of saphenous and sciatic nerve block is indicated to provide analgesia/anesthesia to the to the knee, tibia and tarsus. Objectives • Be able to identify regional anatomy of the pelvic limb and caudal vertebral column. • Be able to perform regional blocks of the pelvic limb. • Know the clinical utility of each of the lumbar plexus nerve blocks, including the psoas compartment nerve block, the femoral nerve block, and the saphenous nerve block. • Know the clinical utility of each of the sacral plexus nerve blocks, including, the lumbosacral trunk block and the sciatic nerve block • Be able to choose the correct approach relating to the area to be blocked (Table 31.1). 620 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER How to Perform POCUS Nerve Blocks – Pelvic Limb Approaches and Locations The femoral nerve can be blocked as it passes through the psoas compartment or when it exits the muscle at the level of the femoral triangle on the medial aspect of the thigh. Additionally, the saphenous nerve, the main sensory component of the femoral nerve, can be blocked during its passage through the medial aspect of the thigh. Relevant Anatomy of the Lumbar Plexus • After exiting the intervertebral foramen, the ven- tral branches of the fourth, fifth, and sixth lumbar spinal nerves penetrate the iliopsoas muscle and interconnect to form the lumbar plexus (Evans and de Lahunta 2013). • The most important nerves of the lumbar plexus are the femoral and obturator nerves. • The femoral nerve and its ramification, the saphe- nous nerve, penetrate the belly of the iliopsoas muscle and course between the sartorius and pec- tineus muscles, lateral to the iliac fascia in the proximal third of the femoral triangle. • At the level of the thigh, the saphenous nerve, already separated from the femoral nerve, is located cranial to the femoral artery, sharing the same interfascial space. Materials Needed to Perform Pelvic Limb Blocks • Clippers and skin preparation solutions. • Sterile gloves. • Sterile drapes. • Local anesthetic (in sufficient quantity). • 50 mm 21 gauge isolated unipolar needles (for cats and dogs weighing less than 15 kg). • 100 mm 21 gauge isolated unipolar needles (for dogs weighing more than 15 kg). • Sterile transducer (probe) drapes and gel. • Multiparametric monitor (electrocardiogram [ECG], noninvasive blood pressure [NIBP], pulse oximetry [SpO2], temperature). • Emergency drugs. Ultrasound‐guided Femoral Nerve Block in the Psoas Compartment The ultrasound‐guided femoral nerve block in the psoas compartment consists of the injection of local anesthetic between the major and minor psoas mus- cles, at the level of the seventh lumbar vertebra (L7). Due to its proximity to the femoral nerve, the obturator nerve is blocked when local anesthetic is injected in the psoas compartment (Echeverry et al. 2012a,b; Mahler 2012; Tayari et al. 2017). Ultrasound Probe Placement and Block T echnique for the Psoas Compartment • Place the probe perpendicular to the long axis of the spine in line with the ventral side of the sub - lumbar muscles at the level of L7 (Figure 31.1). • Once the probe is in place, the lumbar vertebrae are visualized and, ventral to them, the iliopsoas muscle. • The iliac artery is an important reference and can be identified medially and ventrally to the psoas compartment (Figures 31.2 and 31.3). • Once the target is identified, measure the insertion depth using calipers and the centimeter scale on your screen, and calculate the angle of entrance of the needle. • An in‐plane approach is suggested to perform the femoral nerve block in the psoas compartment. • Check for extravascular needle placement and avoid injection if resistance is perceived or blood is aspirated. If necessary, the needle should be repositioned to obtain a homogeneous distribution around the target nerve. Ultrasound‐guided Femoral Nerve Block in the Inguinal Region The block of the femoral nerve consists of the injection of local anesthetic on the femoral nerve after exits the psoas compartment and enters the femoral triangle (Campoy et al. 2010; Echeverry et al, 2010). Probe T ype • Linear transducer (probe) of ≥10 MHz. • 1–2 cm depth depending on the animal size. Ultrasound Probe Placement and Block T echnique • Place the probe on the medial aspect of the thigh and center the femoral artery in the middle of the screen (Figure 31.4). • Identify the iliac fascia below the femoral vessels. • Once the nerve complex is identified in a craniolat- eral position in relation to the femoral artery, per - form the block as close as possible to the belly of the psoas muscle. • Introduce the needle from the cranial border of the probe, and advance it through the belly of the sar - torius muscle in a craniocaudal direction. • Once the tip of the needle is on the target nerve and after negative aspiration has been obtained, inject an aliquot of the calculated volume. Scan of the Femoral T riangle The femoral artery is identified as a pulsatile anechoic (black) round structure in between the medial femoral fascia and the iliac fascia. The femoral nerve is located below (lateral to) the caudal portion of the sartorius muscle, always cranial and lateral to the femoral artery, and in its own interfascial space. It is always slightly more echogenic than the surrounding structures (Figures 31.5 and 31.6). Ultrasound‐guided Saphenous Nerve Block in the Distal Thigh Region The saphenous nerve, the main sensory branch of the femoral nerve, can be blocked in the middle third of the thigh region, where it shares the same interfascial space with the femoral artery, to provide analgesia of the stifle without affecting the motor function of the quadriceps muscle (Shilo et al. 2010; Costa‐Farré et al. 2011). Probe T ype • Linear transducer (probe) of ≥10 MHz • Depth set at 1.5–2 cm. Ultrasound Probe Placement and Block T echnique • Place the probe perpendicular to the long axis of the limb, on the medial aspect of the thigh, at the junction between the proximal and middle thirds (Figure 31.7). • Identify the femoral artery and move the probe to place it in the center of the image (Figure 31.8). • The saphenous nerve runs cranial to the femoral artery, until it branches at the level of midthigh. Note: This block usually provides analgesia/anes - thesia for up to eight hours. Motor weakness of the quadriceps muscle is generally observed after this block. The superficial circumflex iliac artery is located medially (superficially) to the femoral nerve and can be used as a landmark to identify the femoral nerve at the femoral triangle (Garcia‐Pereira et al. 2018). Through its intrapelvic path, the lumbosacral trunk is located on the medial aspect of the ilium in relation - ship with the gluteal vessels under the superficial and medium gluteal muscles. The main nerves arising from the lumbosacral trunk are the sciatic nerve, formed by the tibial and peroneus nerves, the cranial and caudal gluteal nerves, and the caudal cutaneous femoral nerve. Ultrasound‐guided Lumbosacral T runk Block Block of the lumbosacral trunk consists of the injection of local anesthetic on the origin of sciatic nerve involving at the same time the cranial and caudal glu - teal nerves and the caudal cutaneous femoral nerve (Shilo et al. 2010). Probe T ype • Linear transducer (probe) of ≥10 MHz for (for cats and dogs weighing less than 15 kg): 2–4 cm depth. • Microconvex transducer (probe) 5–8 MHz (for dogs weighing more than 15 kg): 3–6 cm depth. Ultrasound Probe Placement and Block T echnique • Place the probe perpendicular to the long axis of the ilium over its greater ischiatic notch (Figure 31.10). • Identify the caudal gluteal vessels and pelvic fascia (Figure 31.11). • The lumbosacral trunk will be visualized over the medial aspect of the ilium, lateral to the caudal glu- teal artery. • Introduce the needle in‐plane through the gluteal muscles from medial to lateral, and advance in a ventrolateral direction. Ultrasound‐guided Sciatic Nerve Block in the Lateral Thigh Region The block of the sciatic nerve is performed immediately distal to the greater trochanter, between the biceps fe - moris and the abductor muscles in the lateral aspect of the thigh (Campoy et al. 2010; Echeverry et al. 2010). 628 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Pearls and Pitfalls, The Final Say • Lumbar plexus block combined with a parasacral plexus block can be successfully used for hindlimb amputation. • These blocks are being used in small animals in lieu of epidural anesthesia with fewer side‐effects. • Invasive surgeries of the pelvic limb can be per - formed without giving opioids to the animal and still maintain an excellent analgesic plane. • Lumbar plexus block (i.e., psoas compartment block) produces deep muscular relaxation of the entire limb, so animals should be carefully evalu- ated during recovery until they can accommodate the limb. • With practice, the pelvic limb can be blocked in less than five minutes. 629 Point-of-Care Ultrasound Techniques for the Small Animal Practitioner, Second Edition. Edited by Gregory R. Lisciandro. © 2021 John Wiley & Sons, Inc. Published 2021 by John Wiley & Sons, Inc. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 Introduction Peripheral nerve blocks of the trunk are indicated to provide perioperative analgesia in animals having intrathoracic, thoracic wall, abdominal or mammary surgery. The nerves involved in the sensory innerva- tion of the abdominal and thoracic wall can be blocked to alleviate pain related to intraabdominal and intra- thoracic surgeries, and lesions associated with the abdominal and thoracic wall. Ultrasound guidance is a useful tool for identifying location of these nerves, to monitor needle placement, and visualize local anes- thetic spread. The use of POCUS nerve blocks improves success while reducing complications over blind techniques. What POCUS Nerve Blocks – T runk Can Do • Can assist in accurately performing nerve blocks, reducing the subjectivity of blind tech- nique blocks. • Can help to reduce complications by visually iden- tifying nearby structures such as blood vessels and body cavities, or other important anatomical struc- tures to be avoided. What POCUS Nerve Blocks – T runk Cannot Do • Cannot replace the need for familiarity of the anatomy at each nerve block location. • Cannot replace ultrasound‐guided skills and the hand–eye and spatial coordination necessary for needle placement and advancement. Indications • To treat acute or chronic pain originating in the abdominal and thoracic wall, and the peritoneal and pleural cavities. • Important part of a multimodal anesthetic/anal- gesic strategy for the trunk. • The thoracic paravertebral block is indicated to provide analgesia/anesthesia to the thorax (wall and cavity). • The ultrasound‐guided intercostal blocks are indi- cated to provide analgesia/anesthesia to the thoracic wall and ribs. • The transversus abdominis plane (TAP) block is indicated to provide analgesia/anesthesia to the abdominal wall and parietal peritoneum. Objectives • Be able to identify regional anatomy of the thoracic and abdominal walls and the associated paravertebral regions of the thoracic and lumbar spine. • Be able to perform regional blocks of the trunk. • Know the clinical utility of each of the approaches to block the trunk, including the thoracic paraver - tebral, intercostal, and transverse abdominal plane blocks (Table 32.1). 630 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Ultrasound‐guided Thoracic and Abdominal Wall Blocks Relevant Anatomy of the T runcal Nerves • The thoracic spinal nerves (13 pairs) exit the spinal canal through their respective intervertebral foramina (Evans and de Lahunta 2013). • When located in the paravertebral space, they have a dorsal branch, a ventral branch, and the ramus com- municans of the sympathetic chain (Figure 32.1). • The ventral branch crosses the paravertebral space to reach the intercostal space as the intercostal nerve. • Along its route to the ventral midline, the inter - costal nerve gives several cutaneous motor and sensory ramifications, the latter responsible for the innervation of the middle and ventral regions of the thoracic wall. • The communicating branch carries autonomic fibers and connects the spinal nerve with the thoracic sympathetic chain. • The limits of the thoracic paravertebral space are as follows. ◦ Dorsal: internal intercostal membrane. ◦ Ventral: parietal pleura. ◦ Medial: intervertebral foramen, intervertebral discs, and vertebral bodies. ◦ Lateral: there is no clear lateral limit. • The abdominal wall is innervated by the ventral branches of the caudal intercostal (T9 to T12), costoabdominal, cranial iliohypogastric, caudal iliohypogastric, and ilioinguinal nerves (Evans and de Lahunta). • The nerves of the abdominal wall run embedded in a fascial plane located between the obliquus inter - nus abdominis and transversus abdominis mus- cles, known as the transversus abdominis plane (Castañeda‐Herrera et al. 2017). Ultrasound‐guided Thoracic Paravertebral Block This technique produces an ipsilateral somatic and sympathetic nerve blockade and it is used to provide perioperative analgesia of the thoracic wall and cavity (Monticelli et al. 2017; Portela et al. 2017). Probe T ype • Linear transducer (probe) of ≥10 MHz for (for cats and dogs weighing less than 30 kg): 2–4 cm depth. • Microconvex transducer (probe) 5–8 MHz (for dogs weighing more than 30 kg): 4–7 cm depth. Materials Needed • Clippers and skin preparation solutions. • Sterile gloves. • Local anesthetic (in sufficient quantity). • 20 gauge 75 mm Tuohy needle attached to an extension line. • Sterile transducer (probe) drapes and gel. • Permanent marker. T able 32.1. Approach to the trunk, where on the trunk analgesia/anesthesia is provided, and important nearby structures. Approach Where analgesia/ anesthesia is provided Important nearby structures Comments Thoracic Paravertebral Block Dermatome in concordance with the injected thoracic level Spinal nerve (dorsal, ventral and sympathetic rami communicans) at the site of injection This block provides excellent quality of analgesia in animals undergoing thoracotomies Intercostal block Dermatome in concordance with the intercostal nerve blocked Intercostal nerve This block does not provide visceral analgesia. Useful block to alleviate pain from rib fractures Transversus abdomins plane (TAP) block Dermatomes from T9 to L3 Abdominal wall and parietal peritoneum This block provides good‐quality postoperative analgesia in patients undergoing laparotomies and mastectomies. It can also be used to provide analgesia in cases with pancreatitis

631 POCUS: N ERVE B LOCKS – T RUNK • Multiparametric monitor (electrocardiogram [ECG], noninvasive blood pressure [NIBP], pulse oximetry [SpO2], temperature) • Emergency drugs. Ultrasound Probe Placement and Thoracic Paravertebral Block T echnique • Place the probe parallel to the long axis of the spine, close to the dorsal midline, and gradually slide laterally until the two consecutive transverse processes of the respective thoracic paravertebral spaces are included on the screen. • To allow a better angle for the needle entrance, the probe should be rotated to an oblique orientation to show the transverse process cranially and the neck of the immediately caudal rib (Figure 32.2). • Once the probe is in place, the following echo - graphic features should be recognized: transverse process, parietal pleura, internal intercostal mem - brane, and paravertebral space. • Once the target is identified, measure the insertion depth using calipers and the screen’s centimeter scale and calculate the angle of entrance of the needle. • An in‐plane approach is suggested to perform the block. • The needle is advanced in a medial‐ventral‐ cranial direction until its tip is positioned bet - ween the internal intercostal membrane and the parietal pleura. • Check for extravascular needle placement and avoid injection if resistance is perceived or blood is aspirated . Drugs and Volume Administered • Drug and concentration: bupivacaine 0.5%, ropiva- caine 0.5%, levobupivacaine 0.5%. • Suggested volume: 0.05 mL/kg per site. Figure 32.1. Truncal anatomy. Schematic of the components of the paravertebral space and the relationship between its anatomical structures. VB, ventral branch of the spinal nerve; DB, dorsal branch of the spinal nerve; IIM, internal inter - costal membrane; EF, endothoracic fascia; PP , parietal pleura; VP , visceral pleura; RC, ramus communicans of the sympathetic chain; SG, sympathetic ganglion; LC, levator costae muscle; EI, external intercostal muscle; II, internal intercostal muscle. Figure 32.2. Thoracic paravertebral block. Dog positioned in sternal recumbency. The needle is introduced in‐plane from the caudal aspect of the transducer (probe) and advanced in a medial‐ventral‐cranial direction until its tip is positioned between the internal intercostal membrane and the parietal pleura. Source: Modified and used with permis - sion from Otero and Portela (2019). Pearl: During local anesthetic injection at the thoracic paravertebral space, a ventral displacement of the pleura during injection is associated with a successful block. Note: The protocol generally provides analgesia/ anesthesia for up to eight hours. An oblique orienta- tion of the transducer (probe) helps to introduce the needle to the desired endpoint. Pearl: The authors currently suggest blocking at least 3–5 thoracic paravertebral segments associated with the location of the incision(s) when ultrasound guidance is used in animals undergoing lateral thoracotomies.

Ultrasound‐guided Intercostal Block The intercostal block consists of injection of a local anesthetic solution alongside the caudal border of the rib, between the internal intercostal muscle and the parietal pleura. Probe T ype • Linear transducer (probe) of ≥10 MHz. • 2–4 cm depth depending on the size of the animal. Materials Needed • Clippers and skin preparation solutions. • Sterile gloves. • Local anesthetic (in sufficient quantity). • 22 gauge 50–75 mm spinal needles. • Prefilled extension line. • Sterile transducer (probe) drapes and gel. • Multiparametric monitor (electrocardiogram [ECG], noninvasive blood pressure [NIBP], pulse oximetry [SpO2], temperature). • Emergency drugs. Ultrasound Probe Placement and Intercostal Block T echnique • Place the probe perpendicularly to the long axis of the rib, at the level of the angle of the rib (Figure 32.5). • Once the probe is in place, the following echo - graphic features should be recognized: ribs, parietal pleura, internal intercostal muscle. • The needle is advanced in‐plane in a caudocranial direction until its tip is positioned between the internal intercostal muscle and the parietal pleura. • Check for extravascular needle placement and avoid injection if resistance is perceived or blood is aspirated. Drugs and Volume Administered • Drug and concentration: bupivacaine 0.5%, ropiva- caine 0.5%, levobupivacaine 0.5%. • Suggested volume: 0.05 mL/kg per site. Figure 32.3. Thoracic paravertebral block. 634 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER • Prefilled extension line. • Sterile transducer (probe) drapes and gel. • Multiparametric monitor (electrocardiogram [ECG], noninvasive blood pressure [NIBP], pulse oximetry [SpO2], temperature). • Emergency drug. Ultrasound Probe Placement and T ransversus Abdominis Plane Block T echnique • Place the probe parallel to the caudal edge of the last rib (subcostal approach) and in cranial to the ilium crest (umbilical approach) (Figure 32.8). • Identify the muscular planes and the parietal perito- neum. Individualize the Transversus abdominis plane. • The needle enters in‐plane until its tip is between the obliquus internus and transversus abdominis muscles. • Inject a small aliquot to check the instillation site of the anesthetic. In case of an intramuscular injec - tion, withdraw or insert the needle a few millime - ters to the targeted place. Repeat this maneuver until the objective is achieved. • Check the extravascular and extraabdominal posi - tion of the needle. • Inject the calculated volume of local anesthetic in the intermuscular plane. To increase the distribution surface of the anesthetic, the needle can be moved in a caudodorsal direction as the injection is made. Drugs and Volume Administered • Drug and concentration: bupivacaine 0.25%, ropi - vacaine 0.25%, levobupivacaine 0.25%. • Suggested volume: 0.25–0.3 mL/kg per point accounting for a total volume per animal of 1 to 1.2 mL/kg corresponding. Scan of the Abdominal Wall See Figures 32.9 and 32.10. Pearls and Pitfalls, The Final Say • Thoracic paravertebral blocks might require more time to be performed, compared to other blocks, until good skills are developed. • Thoracic paravertebral blocks usually provide complete analgesia for lateral thoracotomies, sig - nificantly reducing the need for opioids in the peri- operative period. • Transversus abdominis plane (TAP) block is a very useful and simple procedure, indicated to control pain after any abdominal surgical procedures, that Figure 32.8. Transverse abdominal plane (TAP) block. Dog positioned in dorsal recumbency for a transversus abdomi - nis plane block. The linear transducer (probe) is positioned caudal and parallel to the last rib for the subcostal approach and then slid caudally to the midabdomen for the midab - dominal injection. The needle is introduced in‐plane from the cranial edge of the transducer (probe). Source: Reproduced with permission from Otero and Portela (2019). Pearl: Among the muscles of the abdominal wall, the internal abdominal oblique is the thickest. Note: The protocol generally provides analgesia/ anesthesia for up to six hours. This block has been also used to provide analgesia in animals suffering from pancreatitis. Pearl: Due to the high volume required for bilateral blockade of the abdominal wall (1.0–1.2 mL/kg), it is always recommended to calculate the maximum dose allowed for the chosen anesthetic and then complete the volume with a sufficient amount of saline solution. The final concentration will vary but the final dose of local anesthetics will be the same in all animals. Pearl: To desensitize the abdominal wall bilaterally, the transverse abdominal plane procedure should be performed on both hemiabdomens.

635 POCUS: N ERVE B LOCKS – T RUNK should be applied bilaterally and is best performed preoperatively. • In order to obtain a complete spread to the entire abdomen, two injections per hemiabdomen are recommended: one cranial, caudal and perpendic - ular to the last rib (subcostal) and the other at the midabdominal region. • In small dogs and cats, the abdominal wall is very thin, so it is mandatory to introduce the needle very superficially (close to the probe) in order to avoid intraabdominal punctures. • Transversus abdomins plane block performed after surgery could be more complicated because the pneumoperitoneum could make it difficult to visu- alize the normal landmarks. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 Introduction Ultrasound examination of the spine is a valuable tool when performing different regional anesthetic approaches. Ultrasound allows differentiation of the bony structures and the contents of the spinal canal, such as ligaments, meninges, spinal cord, and nerve roots. Additionally, it is useful to determine the path and depth of needle introduction. Neuraxial blocks can be achieved by an intrathecal or an epidural approach. The epidural space can be accessed at differ- ent levels such as in the sacrococcygeal, lumbosacral (LS), lumbar or thoracic intervertebral spaces. These approaches are summarized in Table 33.1. What POCUS Nerve Blocks – Neuroaxial Can Do • Can assist in the identification of intervertebral space to perform epidural anesthesia/analgesia through a sacrococcygeal, lumbosacral or thoraco- lumbar approach. • Can assist in intrathecal needle placement, avoid- ing bone contact. • Can assist epidural/intrathecal injection in patients with abnormal spinal anatomy. • Provides the only available method for confirma- tion of epidural/intrathecal drug administration in real time before drug injection. What POCUS Nerve Blocks – Neuroaxial Cannot Do • Cannot replace the need for familiarity with the involved anatomical landmarks. • Cannot avoid laceration of dura mater during needle handling. • Cannot replace ultrasound‐guided skills and hand–eye and spatial coordination necessary for needle placement and advancement. Indications • Surgeries involving perineal region, tail, pelvic limbs, abdominal wall/cavity, and thoracic wall/cavity. • Treatment of postoperative pain. • Treatment of pain associated with traumatic events. • Treatment of chronic pain. Objectives • Be able to identify regional anatomy of the vertebral column. • Be able to identify the contents of the spinal canal. • Be able to guide the needle using an in‐plane technique. • Know the clinical utility of each of the neuroaxial approaches – sacrococcygeal, lumbosacral and thoracolumbar. • Know the difference between epidural and intra- thecal anesthesia/analgesia. • Understand the “ultrasound‐signs” of epidural/intra- thecal drug administration; color flow Doppler test, dural sac collapse and enlargement of epidural space. This approach allows the identification of two parallel hyperechoic (bright white) lines flanked by an acoustic shadow produced by the high impedance of the surrounding bones (see Figure 33.3). The hyperechoic line that is observed in the roof of the vertebral canal is the representation of the interarcuate ligament, in close contact with the dura mater, and is called “the dorsal complex (see Figure 33.3).” Occasionally, a hypoechoic (dark) line can be visualized between these structures, which is fatty tissue lodged in the dorsal aspect of the vertebral canal. The line on the floor of the vertebral canal repre- sents the dura mater and the longitudinal dorsal ligament, and is called “the ventral complex” (see Figure 33.3). Due to the scarce adipose tissue in the ventral aspect of the vertebral canal and the weight exerted by the dural sac, these structures are visualized as a single hyperechoic (bright white) line. Depending on the level of the spine scanned, between the dorsal and ventral complexes the subarachnoid space and the spinal cord or cauda equina can be distinguished (Otero et al. 2016; Viscasillas et al. 2016). Longitudinal Ultrasound Scan of the Lumbosacral Area A longitudinal ultrasound scan of the vertebral column allows identification of the intervertebral level and direction of the needle when an in‐plane neuraxial blockade is performed. Collapse of the Dural Sac During injection of a solution into the epidural space, the fluid distends the space between the interarcuate ligament and the dura mater. Thus, collapse of the dural sac during injection is a real‐time confirmation sign of epidural injection (Otero et al. 2016). Epidural Space Enlargement After injection, the fluid remaining in the epidural space can be identified as a typical anechoic (black) pool between the interarcuate ligament and the superficial longitudinal ligaments and the dura mater, and this can be used as confirmation of epidural injec- tion (Otero et al. 2016) (Figure 33.18). Pearls and Pitfalls, The Final Say • Ultrasound offers several advantages when used to guide needle placement for neuraxial anesthesia/ analgesia. • Ultrasound provides real‐time images. • It is noninvasive, safe, and avoids exposure to radiation. • Ultrasound real‐time approaches may be beneficial in animals with abnormal spinal anatomy. • It has been shown in human medicine that in expert hands, the use of ultrasound for epidural needle insertion reduces the number of puncture attempts, improves the success rate of epidural access on the first attempt, and reduces the need to puncture multiple levels. 647 Point-of-Care Ultrasound Techniques for the Small Animal Practitioner, Second Edition. Edited by Gregory R. Lisciandro. © 2021 John Wiley & Sons, Inc. Published 2021 by John Wiley & Sons, Inc. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 Introduction The skin, soft tissue, and large parts of the musculo- skeletal (MSK) system are relatively superficially located compared to visceral organs and are therefore easily accessible using ultrasound. In recent years, ultrasound has gained popularity in evaluation of soft tissues for the presence of lesions, especially tumors. However, soft tissue ultrasound can be used for a wide range of other etiologies, including further evaluation of areas of palpable soft tissue thickening or decrease in soft tissue, areas of abnormal soft tissue function or anatomy, and when the patient has experienced physical trauma (vehicular, ballistic, foreign body, animal abuse, etc.). The advantages of ultrasound include its wide avail- ability, relatively low cost, the benefit of performing real‐time imaging, the ability to perform dynamic eval- uations of structures, and the lack of ionizing radia- tion. Ultrasound can not only differentiate between fluid‐filled structures and masses in the soft tissue but can also detect mineralization of or within the soft tissue before it can be detected with radiography or computed tomography. Many lesions have a nonspe- cific appearance on ultrasound but ultrasound allows better characterization of the soft tissue lesion and, if indicated, provides the ability for ultrasound‐guided sampling. This chapter will cover basic ultrasound imaging of the normal soft tissue including normal expected anatomy of the skin, subcutaneous tissue and fat, muscle, fascia, bone, and salivary glands. Additionally, ultrasound characteristics of abnormalities of soft tissues are described and illustrated. What POCUS Musculoskeletal – Soft Tissue Can Do • Provide diagnostic access to a soft tissue structure which is not accessible to direct evaluation. • Provide anatomical information about soft tissue structures to better formulate a treatment plan and provide prognostic information. • Help in differentiating between various soft tissue injuries. • Help in decision making if an immediate intervention is necessary, such as surgical correction of abdominal wall rupture with vascular impaired intestine. • Allow for ultrasound‐guided aspiration of abnormal content such as fluid within or adjacent to soft tissue structures. • Evaluate soft tissue structures to assess if they move normally. including movement together or independent of each other. What POCUS Musculoskeletal – Soft Tissue Cannot Do • Cot substitute for a thorough physical and clinical evaluation as these will guide where the ultrasound examination is to be performed. • Cannot substitute for lack of anatomical knowledge for the area examined. POCUS: Musculoskeletal – Soft Tissue Susanne M. Stieger‐Vanegas CHAPTER THIRTY-FOUR

648 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER • Cannot overcome depth limitations of the ultra- sound transducer (probe), which may limit access to soft tissue structures deep within the body. • Cannot overcome physical limitations of ultra- sound such as penetration through gas‐containing structures, bone, and structures which limit the travel of ultrasound waves and cause strong distal shadowing, such as surgical implants, stones, etc. • Cannot always differentiate between different eti- ologies because many pathologies have a similar ultrasound appearance. • Cannot always replace a musculoskeletal ultra- sound study performed by a radiologist or veteri- narian specifically trained in musculoskeletal ultrasound. Often a close working relationship with other specialists and a multidisciplinary approach are crucial for successful management and outcome for the patient with soft tissue injuries. Indications Soft tissue injuries can be caused by a wide variety of disease, some of which may occur acutely and some chronically; however, despite being chronic, the patient might present acutely due to pain, swelling, asym- metry or decreased appetite and lethargy similar to an acute injury. Common soft tissue injuries in veterinary patients involve the musculoskeletal system, the thoracic or abdominal wall or superficial soft tissues and can be caused by a wide range of reasons such as traumatic injuries including vehicular, ballistic, foreign body trauma or due to animal abuse. These causes can result in visible superficial injuries or injuries which may not be as easily noted on a physical examination. Performing an ultrasound of an area where pain or swelling is noted on clinical examination or a site of known trauma can provide valuable information com- plementing the clinical examination. Commonly noted soft tissue injuries include edema, cellulitis, fistulous tracts without or with visible foreign bodies, tendon injuries, and fractures. One of the most common rea- sons to use ultrasound to evaluate an area of soft tissue injury is to attempt to differentiate between the various types of soft tissue lesions. Objectives The reasons for performing a soft tissue ultrasound include the screening and diagnosis of soft tissue injuries, therefore providing more information about the location, shape, margination, internal characteris- tics, and vascularity of the lesion. Furthermore, regional lymph nodes may be included in the assessment and this can be helpful in the decision‐ making process. Thus, ultrasound can provide clini- cians with a higher certainty of the extent and type of soft tissue lesion, thus providing a prompt diagnosis, which may alter and improve the management and treatment of a patient. Equipment and Settings for POCUS Musculoskeletal – Soft Tissue Usually minimal preparation of the patient is necessary when performing a soft tissue ultrasound. Preferentially, the ultrasound transducer (probe) with the highest frequency available, providing adequate depth for the anatomy in the area of interest, should be used. In some cases, lower frequency transducers with a smaller contact surface might be used in small patients or in areas with limited physical space to gain good images of the area of soft tissue injury. It can be useful having a stand‐off pad available to increase image depth if very superficial structures are imaged or to compensate and enhance contact in an area of a very uneven surface (see Chapter 35, Figure 35.1). Stand‐off pads are made of an acoustically trans- parent medium. If no stand‐off pad is available, ultra- sound gel can be placed into a glove and used instead. When using a glove filled with ultrasound gel as a stand‐off pad, ensure that only minimal air is mixed into the gel while filling an area of the glove, as the presence of air bubbles results in image degradation. T ransducer • Linear array transducer (probe) with a wide range of frequencies. • A small or large curvilinear transducer with a wide range of frequencies to evaluate deeper soft tissue structures or to access areas where only limited surface contact is available and the larger footprint of the linear transducer limits contact. • A “hockey stick” transducer often works well where access to an area of interest for ultrasound examination is very small. Settings • Adjustments of gain, frequency, and focal zone are crucial and the focal zone(s) may have to be adjusted frequently during an imaging examination.

649 POCUS: MUSCULOSKELETAL – SOFT TISSUE • It can be helpful to have a dual image function available so that contralateral structures can be compared at the same time. • Doppler function, whether conventional, power or microvascular, is helpful to evaluate for vascular flow in a lesion. • Video capabilities to allow storage of images of areas that were evaluated dynamically or where the lesion extends over a greater length than can be captured in one image. Patient Preparation • Frequently, minimal preparation is necessary. • Often ultrasound examination does not require anesthesia; some patients require sedation while other patients tolerate the examination well without sedation. However, sedation or anesthesia may be recommended in cases of extensive soft tissue injury for pain management and should be consid- ered before the ultrasound examination is started. • Depending on the location of the soft tissue, the patient can be placed in dorsal or lateral recum- bency. If a lesion of the abdominal wall or inguinal area is suspected, it can be helpful to perform the examination with the patient spatial standing while considering where gravity‐dependent regions are located. Standing (or sternal) position may increase abdominal pressure therefore further displacing abdominal organs, which may help in outlining abdominal organs, which move into abnormal locations and help to identify their poten- tial incarceration within a hernia. • Clipping of the hair in an area of interest to improve transducer (probe) contact, thereby reducing the presence of artifacts and optimizing the image. However, soft tissue ultrasound may be performed without clipping, especially in longer‐haired patients, where the hair can be parted to gain direct access to the skin. • To achieve a good contact between the transducer and skin, 70% isopropyl alcohol should be applied, the hair parted, and ultrasound coupling gel should be used. In patients with skin injuries, sterile water or sterile ultrasound gel or alternatives such as K‐Y® jelly, should be used instead of 70% isopropyl alcohol or commercially available ultrasound gel for patient comfort and to prevent wound contamination. • In patients where fine needle aspirates or biopsies are planned, sterile ultrasound gel can be used or the examination can alternatively be performed using sterile water or 70% isopropyl alcohol. • When fine needle aspirates or biopsies are performed, clean the patient’s skin appropriately with the necessary level of hygiene. Importantly, ultrasound coupling gel during fine needle aspiration or biopsy can cause significant artifacts on cytological speci- mens (Molyneux and Coghill 1994; Lalzad et al. 2012) and should therefore be removed prior to the fine needle aspiration or biopsy. Sterile saline solution or alcohol can be used to achieve transducer contact. How To Do the POCUS Musculoskeletal – Soft Tissue Once the area of interest is prepared, it is easiest to start the soft tissue ultrasound a short distance away from the area of interest within normal anatomy. As a standard when performing a soft tissue ultrasound, both sagittal and transverse plane images should be acquired. In a sagittal image, the probe is usually ori- ented towards the patient’s head or proximal in the limb. In transverse images, the patient’s left side of the image is oriented towards the right side of their body and the opposite for the patient’s right side. However, some veterinarians change this based on their preference or dominant hand. Make it a habit to first perform the scan with a higher depth to gain a general overview of the soft tissue lesion and then to zoom in (decrease depth) on the area of interest to best evaluate anatomical detail. Furthermore, the highest frequency possible that provides the necessary depth penetration should be used for optimal detail. Remember that increasing the frequency improves spatial resolution while reducing penetration, whereas lower frequency has better depth penetra- tion with less spatial resolution. It is important to scan the entire area or lesion until normal anatomy is again noted. When scanning superficial injuries, use only light pressure so that the area of interest is not compressed, which distorts the structure. It is also helpful to hold the transducer (probe) so that part of your hand such as a finger or ulnar aspect of your arm rests on the patient’s body, which will help to stabilize the probe during scanning and prevent “drifting” while focusing on the screen (see Chapters 4 and 5) or placing too much pressure on the lesion while scanning. Additionally, it can be helpful to gently move the area of interest, so that the lesion can be evaluated dynamically. This is especially important in areas where the normal function of structures is disrupted, such as body wall, muscle and tendon injuries.

650 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Ultrasonographic Findings of Common Soft Tissue Structures Dermis and Epidermis The dermis and epidermis may only be differenti - ated ultrasonographically if a high‐frequency trans - ducer is used. The first layer adjacent to the head of the transducer (probe) is hyperechoic (bright white) and is more correctly termed the “epidermal echo” (Figure 34.1). Deep to the epidermis layer, the dermis is noted, which is heterogeneously hypoechoic (dark) with small hyperechoic reflectors (white) caused by the collagen fibers. Deep to the dermis is the subcutaneous tissue, which is also heteroge - neous in echogenicity and hypoechoic relative to the dermis and epidermis. Fascia The fascia is the next deeper layer to the subcutaneous tissue and is usually relatively linear, thin and hyper - echoic (see Figure 34.1). Muscle The ultrasonographic appearance of muscle is relatively distinct. Normal muscle is diffusely hypoechoic. In the transverse plane, perpendicular to the long axis of the muscle, the muscle has a speckled appearance (see Figure 34.1). Bone The cortical surface of bone is usually smooth except in areas of attachments of tendons and ligaments. The surface of bone is hyperechoic, causing complete distal acoustic shadowing because ultrasound cannot transmit through bone (see several examples in Chapter 35). Salivary Gland On ultrasound, the normal salivary gland is usually homogeneous and tends to be hyperechoic in comparison to adjacent muscle tissue. Dependent on the fat content of the salivary gland, it might appear more hyperechoic relative to other adjacent structures. The salivary glands are usually well defined from sur- rounding adjacent soft tissue structures. Parotid Salivary Gland The parotid salivary gland is located cranioventral to the ear and at the cranioventrolateral aspect of the ster- nomastoideus muscle and has an irregular triangular shape. The excretory duct of the parotid salivary gland runs rostrally and ends opposite the second maxillary molar tooth. Mandibular Salivary Gland The mandibular salivary gland is round to ovoid and is located at the caudoventral angle of the mandible, ventral and often mildly caudal to the parotid salivary gland. The mandibular salivary gland parenchyma is uniformly hypoechoic (Figure 34.2). At the rostroven - tral aspect of the mandibular salivary gland, the man - dibular lymph nodes can be found, which are normally smaller than the adjacent mandibular salivary gland but can be similar in echogenicity. The excretory duct of the mandibular salivary gland exits the hilus of the gland running along the ventrolateral aspect of the mylohyoid muscle and rostrally to the sublingual car - uncle, which is a small papilla at the base of the fren - ulum of the tongue seen on visual and physical examination of this area. Sublingual Salivary Gland The sublingual salivary gland is located at the rostral aspect of the mandibular salivary gland and is smaller and less distinct than the mandibular salivary gland. 1 2 3 4 5 6 Figure 34.1. 651 POCUS: M USCULOSKELETAL – S OFT T ISSUE The dorsal aspect of the sublingual salivary gland is in part covered by the parotid salivary gland. The sublin- gual salivary gland in the dog has a monostomatic and polystomatic part. The monostomatic aspect of the sublingual and the mandibular gland are in part connected by a common tissue capsule. The monosto - matic aspect of the sublingual gland empties into the sublingual duct, which runs together with the mandib- ular duct rostrally to the sublingual caruncle lateral to the base of the frenulum. The mandibular and sublin - gual salivary glands may open together or separately at the sublingual caruncle. When separate, the man - dibular gland opening tends to be located rostral to the sublingual gland opening. The rostral, polystomatic aspect of the sublingual salivary gland is strongly lobulated and extends dif - fusely along the sublingual duct on the medial aspect of the mandible rostrally. The polystomatic aspect of the sublingual gland has multiple small ducts, which empty directly into the oral cavity at the medial aspect of the mandible. Zygomatic Salivary Gland The zygomatic salivary gland is ultrasonographically more challenging to scan because it is located ventro - medial to the eye and caudal or adjacent to the zygomatic arch. The salivary duct of the zygomatic gland ends at an opening at the dorsolateral aspect of the maxillary first to second molar teeth adjacent to the opening of the parotid salivary gland. Common Soft Tissue Lesions Cellulitis and Edema Cellulitis is a frequent pathological condition of the subcutaneous tissues caused by an infection. Cellulitis is usually a clinical diagnosis and patients may present with a focal area of increased tempera - ture (heat), hyperemia, swelling, and leukocytosis. Edema may palpate similarly compared to cellulitis but patients usually do not have a fever, hyperemia, or leukocytosis. Edema is frequently caused by congestive heart failure but can also be secondary to lymphatic disease. The ultrasonographic appearance may vary dependent on the severity and chronicity of the cellulitis or edema but most commonly cellu - litis has a heterogeneous echogenicity created by a mixture of hyperechoic and hypo‐ to anechoic tissue (Figure 34.3) referred to as striated or having a cob - blestone appearance in people. Additional features of cellulitis include skin thickening and increased vascularity that may be better detected using color Doppler ultrasound (Figure 34.4). Larger focal fluid accumulations are not typical for either cellulitis or peripheral edema and other conditions such as seroma, abscess, or cystic structures should then be considered. In summary, cellulitis and edema have similar ultra- sonographic findings and the difference between the two is usually based on combining clinical findings and clinical impression. Figure 34.2. Seroma is usually identified by its simple fluid appearance, meaning the fluid is anechoic (black), with either no wall or a thin, hyperechoic circumferential wall surrounding the seroma (Figure 34.5). Remember that distal to a fluid‐ filled structure such as a seroma, distal acoustic enhancement will be noted. Ultrasound‐guided fluid sampling and fluid analysis with cytology and culture may be needed to differentiate between the sterile and infected seromas. Hematoma Hematomas can occur nearly anywhere for a wide range of reasons. A hematoma is an accumulation of blood outside the vascular system secondary to hemorrhage. In the early stage, a hematoma may appear similar in echogenicity to a seroma, but frequently echogenic particles are noted within the hematoma’s anechoic fluid. Sedimentation of these particles within the hematoma may be noted in addition to hyperechoic septations dividing the hematoma into smaller areas. Additionally, hematomas may have components consisting of anechoic fluid and other parts with het - erogeneous hypoechogenicity suggesting organiza - tion of the hematoma. In later stages, the hematoma may be heterogeneously hypoechoic and well defined from adjacent soft tissue. In these stages of organization, it can be difficult to diffeentiate the hematoma from a soft tissue mass (e.g. granuloma or neoplasia). Figure 34.5. Features of a body wall seroma.
