654 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Abscess Abscesses often can be diagnosed clinically without the need for ultrasonographic imaging. However, in cases where an extension into deeper tissues is sus - pected, where large vessels are in close proximity to the abscess, or where there is concern for adjacent osteo myelitis, ultrasound imaging can be helpful. An abscess has a mixed central echogenicity sur - rounded by thickened, hypo‐ to hyperechoic tissue (Figure 34.6). Additionally, within or adjacent to an abscess gas may be noted by the presence of gas rever- beration artifacts. As a reminder, gas appears on ultra- sound as a bright reflective surface with shadowing, which obscures the underlying anatomy; when the amount of gas is small, a short acoustic shadow or reverberation (ring‐down) artifact may be noted, whereas when the amount of gas is large, a long rever- beration artifact can be seen. Movement or gentle pressure on the abscess can result in movement of the particles within the abscess, helping to differentiate an abscess from a soft tissue mass. Color Doppler allows further soft tissue evaluation for the presence or absence of vascular flow, allowing differentiation bet - ween abscess (no vascular flow) and soft tissue mass (vascularity) (Figure 34.7). Ultimately, sampling will often be necessary and ultrasound guidance allows for planning a safe route for aspiration and/or drainage of the abscess by avoid- ing associated structures including major blood ves - sels, nerves, and body cavities, thus reducing the risk of complications. Using ultrasound guidance for aspi - ration and drainage is becoming standard of care in human medicine for these reasons. Foreign Body Foreign bodies are frequently not visualized on initial clinical examination. Radiopaque foreign bodies can be well visualized using radiography but many foreign bodies are not radiopaque and are therefore missed on radiographic examination. Ultrasound is an excellent imaging modality for identifying foreign bodies. The echogenicity and pattern visualized secondary to a foreign body are very dependent on foreign body com- position, size, and time post injury. Fluid surrounding the foreign body, when present, can be a helpful visual clue for foreign body localization (Figure 34.8). However, highly echogenic fluid with intralesional echogenic tissue strands from an abscess may obscure visualization of the foreign body. In general, foreign bodies are always hyperechoic with or without distal acoustic shadowing (Mohammadi et al. 2011). Distal acoustic shadowing may be seen in approxi - mately 60–75% of patients with wooden, thorn and grass awn foreign bodies and in over 90% of cases with broken glass or metallic foreign bodies. Moreover, broken glass or metallic foreign bodies often also cause comet‐tail artifacts, which are characterized by a thin band of reverberation artifacts. Grass awns may be directly identified by their spindle shape and hyper - echogenicity within the soft tissue (Figure 34.9) (Gnudi et al. 2005). Lastly, minimally invasive ultrasound‐guided tech- niques have been described for foreign body removal (Stades et al. 2003; Staudte et al. 2004; Della Santa et al. 2008). When using ultrasound guidance, it is best to use small‐sized surgical instruments because distal acoustic shadowing caused by the surgical tools often reduces the ability to visualize the foreign body during the ultrasound‐guided procedure. The most commonly involved glands are the zygomatic, parotid, and man - dibular involved salivary glands. Despite a variety of implicated causes including ascending infection from the oral cavity and trauma to the head and neck, fre - quently no inciting cause is apparent. Generally, swelling in the area of the gland is noted on physical examination. On ultrasound, the affected salivary gland may be enlarged and is often heteroge - neously hypoechoic (Figure 34.10). If the salivary ducts are dilated, they can be visualized on ultrasound. If visualized, the dilated ducts can be followed along their expected anatomical path and, if present, sialoliths are visualized as hyperechoic, distally acoustic shadowing structures. A sialocele, also referred to as a salivary mucocele, is the accumulation of saliva in the submucosal or subcu- taneous tissues that most commonly occurs in the head and neck due to damage to the duct or capsule of a salivary gland. Not uncommonly, these injuries are overlooked or not considered to be serious as they truly are, because other more serious injuries are present. However, diagnosis of the abdominal wall injury can be critical as it can lead to visceral and, less commonly, vascular compromise. Abdominal wall ruptures can lead to inguinal herniation, which is best diagnosed early as herniation can lead to strangulation of the intestines, and displacement of the urinary bladder into the hernia can lead to urinary bladder wall com - promise and inability to urinate and compress the urinary bladder. The abdominal wall consists of superficial to deep layers; the outer layer is the skin, followed by the sub- cutaneous tissue, fat, muscles, and fascia, with the innermost layer being the peritoneum. Ventral on either side of midline and separated by the linea alba is the rectus abdominis muscle. On the inner surface of the abdominal wall, the thin, hyperechoic peritoneum is located. In the near‐field, the dermis and subcuta - neous fat are recognized as explained previously. Abdominal wall rupture or herniation is commonly very noticeable on ultrasound as separation of the abdominal wall layers can be seen (Figures 34.14 and 34.15; see also Figure 16.14). Furthermore, Doppler ultrasound can be used to evaluate the extent of vascular perfusion in displaced abdominal organs. If a transient or dynamic herniation is present along the abdominal wall such as at the umbilical or inguinal region, eliciting a cough by tracheal palpation may adequately increase the intraabdominal pressure to better diagnose the condition. Neoplasia of Superficial Structures Benign Neoplastic Masses Lipomas are benign fat‐containing masses, which occur frequently in subcutaneous and intramuscular locations, and are considered the most common soft tissue neoplasm. They are heterogeneously hyper - echoic to isoechoic to surrounding subcutaneous fat and tissue (Figure 34.16). Lipomas are often ovoid in shape, well defined from surrounding tissue, and tend to have low vascularity and therefore only minimal blood flow is seen using color Doppler. Lipomas tend not to have distal acoustic shadowing or acoustic enhancement as fluid‐filled structures would (Nyman et al. 2006). Although lipomas are common, it is important to remember that ultrasono - graphically they can appear similar to the less com - monly occurring low‐grade liposarcoma. Malignant Neoplastic Masses Malignant superficial masses can be primary or met - astatic neoplasias. A wide range of superficial masses are reported including mast cell tumors, melanoma, squamous cell carcinoma, soft tissue sarcoma, tumors of the skin glands or follicles, and epitheliotropic lymphoma. Frequently, these masses are hypoechoic on ultrasound and the vascularity is variable. Masses with heterogeneous echogenicity and irregular bor - ders (Figure 34.17; see also Figure 14.12) are more likely to be malignant than benign tumors (Nyman et al. 2006). Fine needle aspirates or biopsies are needed to differentiate between the various superficial neoplasias. Moreover, the Global FAST approach can rapidly screen for other abnormalities (see Chapters 36 and 37). Figure 34.13. Suspected mandibular salivary gland rup - ture secondary to blunt trauma. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 Introduction In the last 20 years, ultrasound has emerged as an alternative imaging modailty for the musculoskeletal (MSK) system. The soft tissues and MSK structures are often located relatively superficially and therefore are ultrasonographically accessible. Musculoskeletal emergencies are often a result of trauma such as a vehicular accident, high‐rise or foreign body injury. These patients frequently have serious internal injuries, which require more immediate attention, so that the MSK trauma is often assigned a lower priority in the initial triage and treatment. However, MSK injuries often require surgical interven- tion and long‐term treatment, and affect the prognosis for the patient. Moreover, these MSK‐related factors can be costly and affect the owner’s decision regarding further treatment. Therefore, early evaluation of MSK injuries is critical for a timely diagnosis, assessing prog- nosis, and developing a treatment plan and POCUS MSK carries the potential to provide such information. Emergency veterinarians are generally less familiar with imaging MSK and soft tissue compared to other ultrasound applications like FAST examinations, which are used to rapidly survey for internal injuries. However, many principles learned from FAST exami- nations, such as recognizing free fluid, soft tissue and bony structures and their associated artifacts, can translate to POCUS MSK. In this chapter, we will describe basic POCUS MSK applications in the immediate care and emergency setting as an adjunct to patient evaluation as well as including some nonemergent and moni- toring applications. What POCUS Musculoskeletal – Bones and Joints Can Do • Provide imaging of bone, muscle, and tendons. • Provide imaging of bone, muscles, tendons and joints that would be otherwise delayed by patient status and risk of transport to radiology. • Provide structural information regarding the integ- rity of cortical bone (detect cortical disruption). • Provide ultrasound‐guided access to the bone, including its medullary area, for sampling. • Provide structural information about muscles and tendons for the presence of partial or complete muscle or tendon tears. • Provide an imaging modality for monitoring soft tissue injury site(s) for healing and scarring. • Provide structural information about joints, including their associated bone surface and sur - rounding soft tissue. • Evaluate for the presence of cartilage defects and the thickness of the joint capsule and qualitatively and quantitatively evaluate synovial fluid in regard to its echogenicity and volume. • Evaluate MSK structures dynamically for normal and abnormal movement and for the presence of partial or complete tendinous, ligamentous and POCUS: Musculoskeletal – Bones and Joints Susanne M. What POCUS Musculoskeletal – Bones and Joints Cannot Do • Cannot substitute for a thorough clinical evalua- tion which preemptively guides the location and objectives for the applicable POCUS MSK examination. • Cannot overcome depth limitations of the available ultrasound transducer (probe). • Cannot overcome physical limitations of ultra- sound, including the penetration of air, ballistic materials, and intact bone, or associated implants that reflect ultrasound, such as metallic implants (plates, screws, wires, rods, etc.). • Cannot replace a detailed MSK study by a skilled sonographer with specialized training. Indications • For cooperative higher risk patients due to comor - bidities and critical patients that need imaging but are intolerant of chemical restraint. • For guiding determining MSK problematic sites and thus helping plan and guide therapeutic intervention(s). • For patients with surgical metallic implants when the MSK region of interest is superficial to the reflective metallic implant. • For differentiating soft tissue hypoechoic fluid‐ filled structures from soft tissue masses using color Doppler. • For more safely performing diagnostic and therapeutic interventions using ultrasound guidance to more accurately direct needles and devices while avoiding larger blood vessels, nerves, and cavities, for example avoiding the axillary nerve and associated vessels and the pleural cavity when targeting an axillary mass. • For draining or obtaining a sample(s) from fluid‐ filled structure (s) including a cyst or abscess in soft tissue. • For obtaining or draining fluid from a joint or bursa. • As an adjunct to MRI because ultrasound provides better axial resolution and thus better images smaller lesions and smaller sized veterinary patients when limited by currently available MRI scanners. • For real‐time dynamic evaluation of MSK struc- tures and their functionality, especially injuries missed in resting muscle or tendon that are only detected if dynamic stress and limb motion is applied, such as collateral ligamentous injuries and dynamic widening of the joint space. Objectives POCUS MSK provides some basic ultrasound scanning principles for identifying and localizing MSK injuries. Moreover, POCUS MSK can help characterize the type of injury and what structures are involved and be com- plementary to radiography and MRI. The information acquired using POCUS MSK also assists in specific treatment(s) and interventional procedure(s), and serves as a low‐impact, cost‐effective, point‐of‐care dynamic and static imaging modality for many MSK conditions. Equipment and Settings Clipping Hair and Coupling Medium If possible, the area of interest should be clipped of hair. A mixture of 70% isopropyl alcohol and water should be applied to the scanning area followed by acoustic coupling gel to optimize the image quality while lim- iting artifacts. In patients with dermal injuries, sterile water, sterile saline solution, and K‐Y® jelly may be used individually or in combination instead of irri- tating isopropyl alcohol and commercially available coupling gel. Remember that ultrasound waves do not

T ransducer (Probe) T ypes The transducer with the highest frequency available while providing adequate imaging depth should be used. It is advantageous to have a variety of probes with various contact surfaces (footprints) available during POCUS MSK, as smaller probes allow access to small or very curved areas, whereas larger probes pro- vide a better general overview, allowing the imaging of a larger area of tendon or muscle and associated structures. Interchanging probes during scanning may be needed for gaining the most POCUS MSK information. • Linear array transducer (probe) with a wide range of frequencies (8–20 MHz). The footprint of most linear array transducers is larger and straighter when compared to curvilinear (microconvex) probes. • A small curvilinear (microconvex) transducer (probe) with a wide range of frequencies to eval - uate deeper MSK structures or to access areas where only limited surface contact is available. • A “hockey stick” transducer (probe) for accessing very small acoustic windows, and this probe can also be used for intraoral applications. Stand‐off Pads A stand‐off pad can be helpful to artificially increase depth if very superficial structures are to be imaged while at the same time improving contact (acoustic coupling) when uneven surfaces are being imaged (Figure 35.1). Stand‐off pads are commercially avail - able and made of an acoustically transparent medium; however, makeshift stand‐offs may be assembled by placing ultrasound gel into a glove. Settings • Adjustments of gain, frequency, and focal zone are crucial and the focal zone(s) may have to be adjusted frequently during an imaging examination. • A dual image function can be helpful so that con- tralateral structures can be compared at the same time. • Doppler function, either conventional color flow, power or microvascular, is advantageous to eval- uate for the presence of vascular flow in a MSK structure • Video storage of POCUS MSK areas evaluated dynamically can be useful when a lesion is moni- tored over time, as still images may lack the complete information of a lesion. Minimizing MSK‐related Artifacts Anisotropy and Off‐axis Side‐lobe Artifacts Importantly, muscles and especially tendons should always be imaged perpendicular to their fiber structures otherwise the tendons and their myotendi- nous junctions will be artifactually reduced in echo- genicity (hypoechoic). When the perpendicular angle to the fiber is not ultrasonographically maintained, anisotropy and off‐axis artifact result (Cook 2016) (Figure 35.2). Structures such as tendons, including their myoten- dinous junction, are strongly reflective surfaces and therefore more affected by anisotropy artifact than muscles, nerves, and other tissues. Anisotropy artifact must be recognized and minimized by the sonogra- pher for accurate MSK image interpretation. For example, tendinous structures imaged at oblique angles may falsely appear hypo‐ to anechoic due to the anisotropy artifact, resulting in misinterpretation, including falsely identifying a tendon injury or fluid accumulation in areas where the structures are in fact normal. Off‐axis artifacts include the secondary lobe artifacts commonly referred to as side‐lobe artifact in which a nearby out‐of‐view structure reflects enough beam to create a “ghost image” within the primary field of view (Mattoon and Nyland 2015). Acoustic Shadowing, Acoustic Enhancement, and Reverberation Artifacts Similar to other body areas, acoustic shadowing (dirty/incomplete and clean/complete), acoustic enhancement, and reverberation artifacts can occur (see Chapter 3). Acoustic shadowing occurs when a sound wave is attenuated by a very dense object, such as bone, that reflects nearly all the sound waves. However, acoustic shadowing also occurs secondary to dense foreign bodies or calcifications. Acoustic enhancement is caused by the sound wave traveling through an anechoic fluid that results in an area of increased echogenicity (hyperechoic) distal to the fluid‐filled structure when compared to adjacent tissues. Reverberation artifacts result when sound waves are reflected back and forth between a highly echogenic structure’s surface and the probe surface, resulting in an image with evenly spaced parallel horizontal lines off the structure through the far‐field, referred to as A‐ lines and ring‐down artifact. These lines are usually less echogenic than the previous line moving from near‐ to far‐field. This common artifact is associated with reflectors of ultrasound, such as air, glass and metallic objects like projectiles and needles in soft tissue (see Chapters 22, 23, 30–33). Furthermore, similar to other body areas, MSK structure(s) should be habitually evaluated in both transverse and longitudinal planes to reduce the prob- ability of misinterpreting an artifact for a true lesion. Pearl: Anisotropy artifact is an angle‐generated artifact produced in tissue that contains multiple, parallel linear sound interfaces, most commonly in tendons and ligaments, that leads to preferen- tial reflection of the beam in one direction. Clinically, the area of interest is more (falsely) hypoechoic. Pearl: Off‐axis artifacts include the side‐lobe artifact generated by lateral beams from the primary beam striking an “out of sight structure” creating a “ghost image” that is falsely placed within the primary beam that can confound interpretation (see Chapter 3). Alter or eliminate this artifact by chang- ing probes, dropping the focal point, or lowering the gain. The artifact will disappear whereas true pathology will persist (Mattoon and Nyland 2015).

Furthermore, and unique to MSK imaging, recording position of the limb or area that was scanned as either in full or partial extension or flexion is important. Imaging of incompletely stretched muscles and tendons will have an effect on the echo- genicity of the targeted structure. Each body area should be carefully evaluated from proximal to distal or dorsal to ventral in both transverse and longitudinal planes. Normal Bone Normal bone has a highly reflective, hyperechoic (bright white), smooth surface with complete distal acoustic shadowing due to the reflection of the ultra- sound wave back to the probe from the cortical margin of the bone. Normal bone has a smooth, hyperechoic cortex along the diaphysis to epiphysis, which changes along the joint margins to a thin hypoechoic curvilinear area representing the joint cartilage. The transition bet- ween the osseous and cartilaginous surfaces is smooth. In the area of the attachments of tendons and ligaments, the normal bone surface is more irregular. If the sonog- rapher is not familiar with the ultrasonographic anatomy of the area evaluated, comparison with the contralateral limb can easily be performed. Normal Joint The normal joint is most easily evaluated in longitudinal (sagittal) planes with a high‐frequency probe; how- ever, as previously noted, all structures should also be evaluated in transverse planes. It is important to hold the probe very lightly to reduce pressure on the normal joint structures. Increased pressure during ultrasound examination of the joint can cause compression of the synovia and joint fluid, resulting in lack of visualiza- tion of the synovial fluid. The joint fluid (synovial fluid) is anechoic and often only present in small quan- tities. When performing a joint ultrasound, it is impor- tant to also evaluate the extraarticular and intraarticular structures of the joint. The joint capsule is overall thin, often mildly hypoechoic with an articular thin, hyper - echoic lining, which is usually well defined from the synovial fluid. Normally, only minimal vascular flow is noted in the synovia when using Doppler ultra- sound. Mild synovial folding might be normally pre- sent in various joints. The articular cartilage is a thin, well‐defined, hypoechoic line along the articular, hyperechoic surfaces of the bones. The thickness of the articular cartilages varies minimally between the var - ious joints. Normal Skeletal Muscle Normal skeletal muscle has a very characteristic ultra- sound appearance and can easily be differentiated from subcutaneous fat bone and vascular structures. In some cases, the nerves within or adjacent to the muscle tissue can also be differentiated using ultrasound (see Chapters 30–33). Normal muscle has a relatively heterogeneous echogenicity with hypoechoic muscle bundles sur - rounded by hyperechoic epimysium and perimysium. In transverse imaging planes, normal muscle has a more speckled (“starry night”) appearance and in a longitudinal view relative to the length axis of the muscle, the muscle has a more pennate appearance sim- ilar to barbs on a feather (see Figure 35.14A) (Stevenson 2013). Within the muscle, a strong hyperechoic linear area consistent with the myotendinous junction may be noted into which the adjacent muscle bundles converge. From the myotendinous junction, the fibers can be fol- lowed into the tendon of the muscle. It is important to remember to evaluate ultrasonographically whether the movement of the muscle is normal or abnormal. Normal T endon Normal tendon fibrils have a hyperechoic (bright white) echogenicity interposed with hypoechoic sig- nals resulting from the surrounding connective tissue. In a longitudinal image, a strong linear, hyperechoic fiber pattern is noted. On a transverse image, well‐ defined hyperechoic tendon fibrils interspersed with hypoechoic connective tissue are seen. Normal Ligament Similar to tendons, normal ligaments have a linear, hyperechoic (bright white) fiber pattern (Figure 35.3). In small animals, the ligaments are often evaluated most easily in a longitudinal view. As ligaments are often ori- ented in a curved pattern, alignment of the probe is cru- cial to reduce the occurrence of anisotropy artifacts. Normal Nerve In veterinary patients, small nerves may not be dis- cernible and differentiated from surrounding tissue. Larger nerves may be identified as a round to oval structure consistent with hypoechoic nerve fascicles

In a transverse image, the nerve may appear as a round, small struc - ture with an “onion ring” or “honeycomb” pattern (Figure 35.4) (see also Chapters 30–33). In a longitudinal image, the nerves have a linear fiber structure and can be noted as small, mildly mixed echogenic tubes. Normal Cartilage Normal hyaline cartilage will be seen as a homoge - neously anechoic layer covering an articular bone sur- face (Figure 35.5). The hyaline cartilage has a very thin, superficial and deep hyperechoic layer, which allows differentiation of the cartilage from adjacent bone and joint fluid. Normal Subcutaneous Tissue Superficially a bright echogenic line caused by the dermis and epidermis is followed deep by a hypoechoic area created by fat that often has a more recogniz - able heterogeneous and granular appearance (see Figure 34.1). Hematoma formation is recognized by a hypoechoic or mixed echogenic area and adjacent soft tissue swelling can be used to guide the ultrasound examination. It is important to remember that very irregular shaped and deeper located bones, such as tarsal, carpal, vertebra, are not well evaluated using ultrasound, necessitating additional imaging tech - niques for their proper evaluation. Osteomyelitis and Bone T umors Osteomyelitis and bone neoplasia can vary in ultrasono- graphic appearance. Often, on ultrasound, the cortical margin of the bone may be more irregular and contain small defects compared to adjacent normal areas of bone and additionally, a fine hyperechoic (bright white) band of tissue might be noted next to the cortex, indi - cating a periosteal response (Figure 35.10). The adjacent soft tissue might be increased in thickness, more hetero- geneous in echogenicity and texture (Figures 35.11 and 35.12). In osteomyelitis, the adjacent inflamed tissues may be reduced in echogenicity (Figure 35.13). Importantly, osteomyelitis and bone neoplasia can have similar ultrasonographic features and therefore ultrasound‐guided fine needle aspirates or bone biopsies are generally recommended for further evalu- ation of the lesion. Ultrasound can be useful for identi- fying the cortical defect through which a needle can be guided for optimal sampling. In osteomyelitis, the degree of cortical lysis is gener- ally less severe than in some forms of bone neoplasia. In advanced primary bone neoplasia, often large, het - erogeneous and irregular defects are present in the cortex of the diaphyseal to the metaphyseal aspect of the bone in addition to irregular, hyperechoic perios - teal new bone formation (Codman’s triangle). As a reminder, the Codman triangle is not pathognomonic for neoplasia and this triangular periosteal response can also be seen in inflammatory processes. The adja - cent soft tissues are often very heterogeneous and can be highly vascularized. Figure 35.4. Normal and peripheral nerve sheath tumor of axillary nerve. Comparison images of the right (A) and left axilla (B). The normal right axillary nerve shown in (A) is noted as a small round, hypoechoic structure between the right axillary vein (V) and artery (A). On the left side, the axillary nerve shown in (B) is enlarged and mildly heterogeneous in echogenicity and similarly located between the right axillary vein (V) and artery (A). In mild injuries, only an increase in size (swelling) of the muscle may be present that may only involve a portion of the muscle body. In more severe injuries, areas of reduced echogenicity consis - tent with hematoma and/or seroma formation may also be noted. In earlier acute phases, a hematoma may appear relatively anechoic whereas in later chronic phases, hematomas become heterogeneous and hyperechoic secondary to coagulation. Intrinsic injuries can be caused by a wide range of traumas affecting the myotendinous junction of the muscle (see Figure 35.14). These injuries can range from mild to severe, involving only a small area or resulting in complete rupture of the muscle at its myotendinous junction (Draghi et al. 2013). T endon Injuries The injured tendon is often mixed or reduced in echo - genicity with loss of normal fiber structure. Frequently, an increase in the size of the tendon (focal or diffuse) can be noted. Additionally, tenosynovitis may be present, recognized as an increased amount of fluid causing distension of the tendon sheath (Figure 35.15). The fluid can be variable in echogenicity, ranging from anechoic to mixed echogenic secondary to inflammation, hemorrhage or infection. The synovial layer of the tendon sheath might be increased in thickness and have an irregular border. If concern about an infectious teno- synovitis exists, sampling and analysis of the fluid should be performed as hemorrhage and an infectious process can have a similar ultrasonographic appearance (see Figure 35.15). Common Sites of Muscle and T endon Injuries in Small Animal Patients Supraspinatus Muscle (Supraspinatus T endinopathy) The most common site of supraspinatus injuries, espe- cially in the dog, is the tendon of insertion at the greater tubercle of the humerus. In an acute injury, an area of decreased echogenicity and loss of normal fiber struc - ture may be noted in this area (Figure 35.16). Importantly, the aspect of the tendon immediately proximal to the greater tubercle normally has an area of decreased echogenicity, in part due to its different fiber anatomy at this location. In chronic lesions, areas of increased echogenicity without and with distal shadowing can be noted. When areas of hyperecho - genicity with distal shadowing are present, areas of mineralization secondary to chronic fiber disruption should be suspected. Biceps and Achilles T endon Rupture Injuries to tendons can be partial or complete (Figures 35.17 and 35.18). When a partial tendon rup - ture is identified, it is important to evaluate the extent of it, as partial rupture can develop into complete rup- ture of a tendinous structure. Often a “core” lesion may be noted, which is an area of hypoechogenicity and fiber loss within the tendon (see Figure 35.17). Adjacent soft tissue should always be evaluated, including tendon sheaths and adjacent joints. It is important to remember that tendinous structures are not well vascularized and healing is often slow, requiring a long duration of stabilizing support and/ or exercise restriction. Iliopsoas Muscles This type of injury can be challenging to diagnose; however, it is not uncommon in active (sporting) dogs and can be associated with a significant level of patient pain and discomfort. If a lesion is suspected, the entire length of these muscles from the lumbar spine and the pelvis to the lesser tubercle of the femur needs to be eval - uated, as lesions can occur anywhere along this path. Moreover, lesions frequently occur bilaterally and thus a comparison with the contralateral side might look similar if both are equally injured. Muscle Atrophy Atrophied muscle is smaller when compared to the contralateral limb or body area. Often a heterogeneous, patchy and striped echogenicity with hypoechoic areas in between may be noted (Figure 35.19). In human patients, it has been demonstrated that when a muscle atrophies, such as in neuromuscular disorders, the muscle tissue gets replaced by fat and fibrous tissue, resulting in increased echogenicity of the muscle. 680 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Pearls and Pitfalls, The Final Say • Correlate POCUS MSK findings with clinical find - ings because some diseases, such as osteomyelitis and bone neoplasia, appear ultrasonographically similar and additional tissue sampling is necessary for a definitive diagnosis. • Compare the suspected lesion with the contralat - eral side or adjacent normal tissue, especially when the contralateral side or adjacent area is not affected. • Routinely evaluate MSK lesions both statically and dynamically to evaluate for conditions more recog- nizable with changes in flexion and extension, the presence of adhesions, and to ensure normal movement (function) of the tissue. • POCUS MSK can provide additional information regarding bone healing, specifically when the degree of vascularization is of concern, and when there is concern whether infection exists. Ultrasound‐guided sampling of regions of concern containing fluid may then be pursued using color flow Doppler to avoid vascular structures. • Image POCUS MSK in two steps. First, evaluate the area of interest as an overview, and then second, magnify (decrease depth) so that smaller lesions may be detected and not overlooked. • Acute muscle injuries often present with subtle findings of focal swelling and minor fiber inhomo- geneity that will change over time, emphasizing the importance of serial POCUS MSK examination and comparison(s) and the need for saving and archiving these images. • When imaging tendons, anisotropy artifact is common and avoided by continuous adjustment of the imaging plane and ensuring that the tendon is scanned at its maximum echogenicity. By not scanning in this manner, artifactual anisotropy resulting in areas of decreased echogenicity within a tendon might be misinterpreted as a lesion. • POCUS MSK may be used as an ancillary tech - nique to other imaging modalities to more com - pletely evaluate the extent of a lesion, such as skull fracture and traumatic brain injury. Head injuries with suspected brain involvement can initially be quickly evaluated with a POCUS MSK and POCUS brain, followed by computed tomography and/or MRI after patient stabilization. • POCUS MSK is effective for detecting injuries such as rib fractures, but assessment for related intratho- racic injury should not be overlooked, including the Global FAST approach, followed by additional imaging as indicated such as thoracic radiography and computed tomography when the patient is sta- bilized for complete trauma evaluation. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 685 Introduction This chapter covers two major principles: the use of Global FAST for patient monitoring, and the use of Global FAST for staging disease. The Global FAST approach is the combination of AFAST and its abdom- inal fluid scoring system, its target organ approach; TFAST for pleural and pericardial effusion, its TFAST echo views, and its target organ approach to the heart; and lastly Vet BLUE for detection of alveolar‐interstitial edema and other lung surface pathology. The Global FAST approach consists of exact clarity to its 15 acoustic windows with clear objectives on its goal‐directed templates (Boysen and Lisciandro 2013; Lisciandro and Armenise 2014; Lisciandro 2014a,b,d, 2019b) (see Figures 36.3, 36.4, 37.1, and 37.2). Furthermore, Global FAST provides a set of unbiased imaging data points that avoid satisfaction of search error and picking and choosing POCUS examinations based on the preconceived bias of the clinician. For example, the finding of sonographic gallbladder wall edema in a collapsed dog may erroneously lead to the diagnosis of canine anaphylaxis when the patient in fact has pericardial effusion as its cause for the sono- graphic gallbladder wall edema and its collapse (see Figure 7.12, 7.13, 18.22, 18.23, 36.8, and 36.9) (Lisciandro 2014a,d, 2019a). A Vet BLUE with “dry lung” all views (absent B‐lines) rules out left‐sided congestive heart failure with high sensitivity in both cats (96%) and dogs (89–96%) (see Table 23.3) (Lisciandro et al. 2016) but without TFAST, the dilated cardiomyopathy or the intracardiac mass is missed (see Figure 18.32) while without AFAST, the low‐grade hemoabdomen with a midabdominal mass is missed (Figure 36.1). Expanding further on the case of pericardial effusion with gallbladder wall edema, referred to as a “cardiac gallbladder” (Lisciandro 2019a), the Global FAST approach provides even more clinically relevant information, allowing assessment of volume status via the caudal vena cava (CVC) at the FAST diaphrag- matico‐hepatic (DH) view and its characterization. In this case, the CVC is determined to be FAT, or dis- tended CVC (fluid intolerant, high central venous pressure) along with hepatic venous distension (tree trunk sign), which is indirect evidence for cardiac tam- ponade and obstructive shock (Himelman et al. 1988: Candotti and Arntfield 2015; Lisciandro 2014a,d, 2016). Moreover, the TFAST echo views provide direct evi- dence for cardiac tamponade and obstructive shock through the observation of right atrial and ventricular collapse. The AFAST screens for the presence of a non- hemoabdomen ascites (better prognosis) and Vet BLUE for the presence of pulmonary metastasis (poor prog- nosis) (see Figures 18.20 and 36.21) (Stafford Johnson et al. 2004; MacDonald et al. 2009). The Global FAST approach is clearly more informa- tive than a “flash exam,” which consists of no defined acoustic windows other than a sweep of the abdomen and thorax to answer a single binary question of fluid positive or fluid negative. Furthermore, it is important to critically consider whether the terms “AFAST”, “TFAST” and “Vet BLUE” are being misused for “flash- ing” (Lisciandro and Mann 2019). 687 POCUS: GLOBAL FAST – P ATIENT MONITORING AND STAGING potentially detrimental to patient care by missing the big clinical picture (Narasimhan et al. 2016). The POCUS targeted examination, focused organ or system exam clearly has its place, but should be performed after a Global FAST. The cases at the end of this chapter further emphasize this point (see Figures 36.18–24). The use of Global FAST for patient monitoring con- tinues to evolve from its original concept with the publication of subsequent clinical studies (Lisciandro 2012, 2016; Boysen and Lisciandro 2013; Lisciandro and Armenise 2014; Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2016, 2017, 2019; McMurray et al. 2016; Ward et al. 2017, 2018a,b, 2019: Dicker et al. 2019; Hnatusko et al. 2019; Lisciandro and Lisciandro 2019; Vientós‐Plotts et al. 2019). Global FAST is advantageous over the individual use of POCUS Heart, POCUS Caudal Vena Cava, Vet BLUE, and AFAST by integrating important global patient information (see Figures 36.5, 36.18– 24). Integration of other relevant findings increases the probability of being correct. Conversely, when selecting individual POCUS exams, important patient information is potentially overlooked to the detri- ment of the patient through selective imaging and satisfaction of search error. A good example would be performing a POCUS Heart along with a POCUS Caudal Vena Cava for volume status during fluid resuscitation. The patient is assessed as volume contracted based on poor left ven- tricular filling and a flat caudal vena cava warranting more aggressive fluid therapy; however, the question always raised is where is the volume loss? In other words, where is the “leak in the tank”? By applying Global FAST, the AFAST component detects free intraabdominal fluid with an abdominal fluid score (AFS) of 4. The fluid is sampled and evaluated, docu- menting a hemoabdomen. The postinterventional life‐ threatening bleed is detected before overt patient decompensation but likely missed with POCUS Heart and POCUS Caudal Vena Cava. To the detriment of the bleeding patient, they will likely worsen with a more aggressive fluid resuscitation approach based on only a POCUS Heart and POCUS Caudal Vena Cava. The AFAST findings rapidly provide a complete global evaluation and trigger blood transfusion and interven- tions to stop the otherwise occult ongoing hemorrhage missed by targeted POCUS Heart and POCUS Caudal Vena Cava. Moreover, the clinical question of “Where is the volume loss (“leak in the tank”)?” is automatically evaluated by Global FAST that includes searching for effusion within the peritoneal and pleural cavities, ret- roperitoneal space, pericardial sac, and lung (Tables 36.1 and 36.2). The patient can often “leak” large volumes of effusion in the peritoneal and pleural cavities and retroperitoneal spaces, forgiving areas, before the “leak in the tank” is recognized, and in bleeding patients, large volumes that are potentially catastrophic before being recognized without ultra- sound based on less sensitive means of physical exam, vital signs, laboratory testing, and radiography (Lisciandro et al. 2009; Perera et al. 2010; Bilello et al. 2011). The pericardial sac and lung differ in that they are unforgiving areas for “leaks” because much smaller volumes lead to obvious negative changes in patient status, including poor cardiac output and obstructive shock (pericardial effusion) and deterioration in venti- lation (“wet lung”) from increased extravascular lung water, respectively. The use of the Global FAST approach for staging patients for localized versus disseminated disease is helpful for conveying prognostic information to clients and also for following response to treatment. For example, fungal granulomas may be tracked during antifungal therapy using Vet BLUE. Moreover, the Global FAST approach helps dictate the next best diag- nostic test for the general practitioner as well as the specialist. For example, a cat may have lung nodules on Vet BLUE and an enlarged spleen on AFAST with the suspicion of disseminated fungal disease diverting the lung lobe aspirate to a potentially less risky splenic aspirate, or the combination of Global FAST findings triggers fungal testing or a lung lobe aspirate (see Figures 23.35–23.37). In patients suspected of having neoplastic processes, use Global FAST to rapidly stage the patient for local- ized versus disseminated disease (see Figures 36.19– 36.21). For example, a splenic mass deforming the splenic capsule, a serious finding, is detected using POCUS abdomen with a “flash approach,” the general ultrasound sweep of the abdominal cavity without any standardization. The client is given the news of a can- cerous process, which likely triggers much anxiety compounded by the prospect of an overwhelming and costly diagnostic “staging” work‐up. As a result, many of these cases are euthanized (Lux et al. 2013). A new approach is Global FAST the same day before the patient departs, looking for obvious dis- seminated disease. For the splenic mass, peritoneal hemorrhage is screened for by AFAST and its fluid scoring system, and when hemoabdomen is present, the free fluid is categorized as a small‐volume bleeder versus large‐volume bleeder, thus helping with decision making on the need for a blood transfusion (Lisciandro et al. 2009; Boysen and Lisciandro 2013). Moreover, liver masses and pericardial effusion are rapidly screened for via the DH view, pleural and

If the patient is negative on the Global FAST staging, a very different presentation may be made to the owner of encourage- ment and the possibility of cure with the diagnostic steps of X, Y, and Z. The conclusion is that “Your pet is a surgical candidate!” Conversely, departing clients left to “think about it” often despair about the potentially catastrophic dis- ease process that is suspected along with being guilt ridden and torn between pursuing treatment or not. When patients stage with obvious disseminated dis- ease using the Global FAST approach, the patient– client–veterinarian bond is strengthened through the helping of patient and client in the pet’s final stages of life, rather than the client feeling abandoned (see Figures 36.22, 36.23). The author has been on both ends of this spectrum, being a general practitioner the first half of his 28‐year career and an emergency veteri- narian and specialist the second half. Case examples are presented at the end of this chapter and the reader is referred to specific AFAST, TFAST, Vet BLUE, and POCUS chapters for more detail. The Global FAST approach is a game‐changer for patient evaluation and one of the most impactful para- digm changes for better patient care this decade. 691 POCUS: GLOBAL FAST – P ATIENT MONITORING AND STAGING What Global FAST – Patient Monitoring and Staging Can Do • Can rapidly assess patient volume status by inte- grating the TFAST echocardiography views with the “Global FAST nonecho fallback” strategies of the FAST DH view for caudal vena cava and hepatic venous distension characterization and Vet BLUE for “wet lung” versus “dry lung.” • Can rapidly screen for effusions causing hypovole- mia, by surveying the peritoneal and pleural cav- ities, retroperitoneal space, pericardial sac, and lung. • Can trigger ultrasound‐guided procedures with the finding of free fluid and soft tissue abnormalities. • Can rapidly semiquantitate and categorize intraab- dominal hemorrhage as small‐volume bleeder versus large‐volume bleeder by assigning a numerical fluid score (0–4) and decision making for the need for transfusion therapy and surgical interventions. • Can rapidly semiquantitate and categorize non- hemorrhagic effusions as small‐volume effusion versus large‐volume effusion by assigning a numerical fluid score. • Can rapidly estimate urinary bladder volume using the AFAST cysto‐colic formula and with serial mea- surements estimate urine output noninvasively. • Can rapidly screen for obvious soft tissue abnor - malities using the AFAST target organ approach. • Can semiquantitate pleural effusion. • Can semiquantitate pericardial effusion. • Can rapidly screen for left‐ and right‐sided cardiac strain/failure/overload using the TFAST echocar - diography views. • Can rapidly screen for cardiac soft tissue abnormalities. • Can rapidly screen for lung conditions and catego- rize them by the distribution of the six Vet BLUE lung ultrasound signs. • Can semiquantitate degree of pneumothorax (PTX) and track its severity using the TFAST “lung point” concept and TFAST PTX 1/3s Rule. • Can help determine need for and guide use of vasopressors using the Global FAST volume status approach. • Can help determine need for and guide use of throm- boprophylaxis and thrombolytics using the Global FAST approach for pulmonary thromboembolism. What Global FAST – Patient Monitoring and Staging Cannot Do • Cannot replace the physical examination but rather serves as an extension of the physical exam. • Cannot replace blood pressure and electrocardio- graphic monitoring. • Cannot replace arterial and venous blood gas eval- uation and other respiratory function assessment. • Cannot definitively characterize effusions and mass lesions based on echogenicity because sam- pling and fluid analysis with cytology and tissue sampling and testing are required, respectively. • Cannot replace advanced imaging, including complete detailed ultrasound studies of the abdomen and thorax, computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Indications • All hospitalized patients on fluid therapy. • All perioperative patients using Global FAST as their preanesthetic screening test. • All postinterventional cases for the presence of complications. • All patients with serious conditions (neoplasia, sepsis, infectious diseases, i.e., fungal) for staging as localized versus disseminated disease. • Any patient with suspect stability, uncharacterized forms of shock, and uncharacterized hypotension. • All patients with cardiopulmonary arrest (CPA) or those needing cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR). • All patients with return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) as part of advanced life support and post‐ CPR resuscitation. Objectives • Understand the clinical utility of combining AFAST, TFAST, and Vet BLUE as a single examina- tion called Global FAST as an extension of the physical examination for any abnormal or preinter- ventional patient. • Understand how staging using Global FAST helps “see” your problem list and better determine your next best test(s). • Understand how Global FAST may be used periop- eratively and postinterventionally for detecting comorbidities and complications otherwise missed without ultrasound. • Understand how Global FAST can detect left‐ and right‐sided strain/failure/volume overload so that adjustments may be made during resuscitation efforts. • Understand how Global FAST can trigger throm- bolytics and thromboprophylactics. • Understand how Global FAST may be used for patient monitoring.

692 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Ultrasound Settings, Probe Preferences, Patient Positioning, and Preparation Ultrasound Settings and Probe Preference A curvilinear (microconvex) probe with a frequency range of 5–10 MHz. The appropriate abdominal preset with a depth range of 3–15 cm is generally acceptable for the entire Global FAST examination in most dogs and cats. Changing probes is unnecessary and often pro - longs the completion of the Global FAST examination. Optimizing Image Quality and Probe–Skin Contact Hair is generally not shaved but rather parted for probe‐to‐skin contact (minimizing air trapping) (Figure 36.2) with the use of isopropyl alcohol and/or alcohol‐based hand sanitizer, and/or acoustic cou - pling gel (see Figures 5.2 and 39.29). The author uses minimal amounts of isopropyl alcohol primarily to wet and part the hair (also strips out air and lipid in hair follicles) followed by alcohol‐based hand sanitizer or acoustic coupling gel. Smaller amounts of isopropyl alcohol are less noxious to your patient by minimizing the coolness and wetness of alcohol along with its fumes, especially when the patient is then placed in an oxygen cage. Alcohol‐based hand sanitizer has the added benefit of being easily wiped off while also evaporating quickly. Isopropyl alcohol should not be used if electrical defibrillation is anticipated because it poses a burn/fire hazard. The clinician should be aware that isopropyl alcohol may cause probe head damage (see Figure 4.13). Patient Positioning and Most Efficient Ways to Perform Global FAST There are a couple of highly efficient ways to perform the 15 acoustic windows (views) of Global FAST in standing/sternal and lateral recumbency that mini - mize depth changes and moving to different sides of the patient (Figure 36.3). Figure 36.2. Global FAST with low patient impact imaging with minimal restraint. The photo shows the low impact of Global FAST imaging on a patient that is unshaved and unrestrained. The sonographer is starting with the Vet BLUE part of Global FAST. See also Figure 37.23. Pearl: The author generally does not shave patients and does not dim the lighting when performing any part of Global FAST, which is supported by similar findings regarding environmental lighting and that ultrasound imaging is generally not compromised (Breitkreutz et al. 2007, 2010).

693 POCUS: G LOBAL FAST – P ATIENT M ONITORING AND S TAGING In fact, Global FAST may be reduced to six achiev - able probe maneuvers as follows. AFAST A single maneuver for all five AFAST views: fan, rock cranially, and return to the starting position. TFAST Three maneuvers. • “TFAST slide” caudal and cranial into the “cardiac‐ diaphragmatic pouch” and “cardiac‐cervical pouch” respectively. • Right TFAST pericardial site (PCS) short‐axis views. • Right TFAST PCS long‐axis views. Vet BLUE Two maneuvers. • Three intercostal spaces (ICS) – one caudal and one cranial from the primary for the Caudodorsal, Perihilar, and Middle lung region views. • Sliding from the cervical region, the cranial transition zone, across the first rib, first ICS, second rib, second ICS, and third rib, third ICS for the Cranial lung region view. Lateral Recumbency When a patient presents in lateral recumbency and is best left in that position for initial Global FAST exami- nation, AFAST is generally performed followed by Figure 36.3. Global FAST standing position. Shown is an efficient manner in which to perform Global FAST in a standing patient. The sonographer starts from the left side and performs Vet BLUE first (1–4) and then performs the TFAST left PCS view (5) followed by the FAST DH view (6). By performing the DH View from the left side, the gallbladder is imaged by fanning toward the patient’s right side which gives much easier hand motion for the right‐handed sonographer. After the DH View, the AFAST is completed by performing the SR view (7) followed by the CC view (8) and the HRU view (9) and a focused spleen (not shown) as illustrated in (A) and (C) for cats and dogs, respectively. The sonographer then moves to the patient’s right side as shown in (B) and (D) and performs the right Vet BLUE (10–13) and then the TFAST right PCS view (14) with its most time‐ consuming TFAST echo views. Finally, the HR5th bonus view is performed (15). Another advantage is that by performing in this order, the sonographer has a good idea of how important the TFAST echo views are because lung has been surveyed (Vet BLUE) including pneumothorax and alveolar‐interstitial edema, the thorax has been surveyed for pleural and pericardial effu- sion, and the CVC and its associated hepatic veins have been characterized. If there is no free fluid detected on AFAST then lateral recumbency is not necessary for fluid scoring. The AFAST views look identical independent of positioning and are performed with the same probe maneuvers as if the patient were in lateral recumbency. 694 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER TFAST and its PCS views with depth and gain settings that are similar, thus rapidly completing six of eight views (Figure 36.4). The use of the DH view first is the author’s choice in lateral recumbency because it rap - idly surveys the thorax for pleural and pericardial effusion and pulmonary conditions, the caudal vena cava for volume status, the liver and gallbladder for obvious soft tissue changes including gallbladder wall edema, and the abdomen for the presence of ascites. As a single view, the DH view provides a huge amount of clinically relevant patient information including sur - veying the thorax without the air interference of lung at transthoracic TFAST views. Findings at the DH view can dictate whether the TFAST is performed next followed by Vet BLUE or AFAST is completed before moving to TFAST and Vet BLUE. • The AFAST DH view is performed with lots of depth (10–15 cm) depending on the size of the patient. The higher depth setting allows for a quick overview to see your expected big three landmarks of diaphragm, heart (“cardiac bump”), and caudal vena cava. Depth may then be magnified (decreased) to place the caudal vena cava nearer to the bottom (far‐field) of the screen. • Depth and gain setting are generally similar bet - ween AFAST and the TFAST PCS views and both the left TFAST PCS and right TFAST PCS views are evaluated in this order (see Figure 36.4). • After completing the TFAST PCS views, depth is decreased and the gain turned down for more con- trast for lung for the ipsilateral TFAST CTS view for pneumothorax (PTX) and continuing through the ipsilateral Vet BLUE. Right lateral (over left lat- eral) is advantageous because of the cardiac notch and the heart falling against the thoracic wall for the most valuable of the TFAST echocardiography views, the right PCS view for the left ventricular short axis (LVSA), the short‐axis left atrial to aortic ratio (LA:Ao), and the long‐axis four‐chamber (LA4C) view for the right ventricular (RV) to left ventricular (LV) ratio (RV:LV). • Left lateral recumbency is used when the patient presents in this position and is most comfortable in left lateral. The AFAST applied abdominal fluid scoring system is validated in either lateral recum- bency; however, the TFAST echocardiography Figure 36.4. Now the sonographer has a better idea of patient stability by assessing for pleural and pericardial effusion, lung disease, cardiac conditions, and volume status before moving the patient to right lateral recumbency as shown in (C) and (F). 695 POCUS: GLOBAL FAST – P ATIENT MONITORING AND STAGING views are generally more reliable in right lateral recumbency but may be attempted from left lateral. • An imaging trick is to slide the probe closer to the sternum and then direct the scanning plane to the expected location of the heart, attempting to avoid air interference from lung. Standing or Sternal Most patients are less stressed and Global FAST is low impact in standing (or sternal) position and the entire Global FAST format may be performed in < 6 minutes (360 seconds for 15 views is ~25 seconds per view), keeping in mind that eight of the 15 views are transthoracic Vet BLUE views, which are typically faster (~15 seconds) than AFAST and TFAST views. Again, Global FAST is performed without shaving hair and with minimal patient restraint (see Figures 36.2 and 36.3). Beginning on the left side (author preference) of the patient, the left Vet BLUE transthoracic views are per - formed first, starting at the Caudodorsal lung region and then moving ventrally and cranially through the subsequent Vet BLUE views. Vet BLUE requires less depth, more magnification, and lower gain (darker screen with more contrast) than soft tissue imaging of AFAST and TFAST. Following the left Vet BLUE, depth is increased to see the landmark of the pericar - dium in the far‐field, gain is generally increased, and the left TFAST PCS view is performed with its “TFAST slide” caudally and then cranially, within the respec- tive cardiac pouches (see Chapter 17). The FAST DH view with nearly same settings as the PCS view is performed next and double checks the “cardiac‐dia- phragmatic pouch.” While standing, the AFAST spleno‐renal view, cysto‐colic view, hepato‐renal umbilical view, and focused spleen are then per - formed with identical image acquisition as in lateral recumbency and as shown in Chapter 6. In other words, there is no difference in the look of the AFAST views between positioning as target organs are fanned through in nearly identical imaging planes. AFAST, Vet BLUE, and TFAST have now been completed on the left side. The right Vet BLUE is then performed, requiring a depth change (less depth, magnified) and a gain change (less gain, darker for more contrast along the “lung line”). As on the left side, Vet BLUE begins with the Caudodorsal lung region view followed by the Perihilar, Middle, and Cranial lung regions before blending with the right TFAST PCS echocardiography views (LVSA, LA:Ao, LA4CV) (Figures 36.5 and 36.6). The HR5th bonus view is performed last with fanning, rocking, and returning to the starting point as with the other AFAST views; however, this view is not part of the AFAST‐applied abdominal fluid scoring system. Now the entire Global FAST has been completed and standing‐sternal is the positioning of choice for the detection of pleural and pericardial effusion because it is safer and gravity dependency is ventral bilaterally at the TFAST PCS views and FAST DH view. As for ascites, if the standing‐sternal patient is negative for free intraabdominal fluid, then lateral recumbency is only necessary to repeat the FAST DH View and TFAST echocardiography views in patients with ambiguity in standing‐sternal. If the patient is positive for ascites, then when safe to do so, the patient is placed into either lateral recumbency and then three minutes are allowed to pass so that fluid may distribute, prior to assigning an AFS (Lisciandro et al. 2009). Why Start Left and then Move Right for the Global FAST Blend? The author prefers beginning with the left side of the patient as described. By moving from left to right with the Vet BLUE‐TFAST blend, the sonographer already has ruled pneumothorax in or out, knows not only whether lung is wet (B‐lines) or dry (A‐lines) but also to what degree by using the Vet BLUE B‐line scoring system (plus the presence of any other Vet BLUE lung ultrasound signs). Furthermore, the sonographer knows whether pleural and/or pericardial effusion are present, what the liver and gallbladder look like, if there is obvious ascites, and the characterization of the caudal vena cava before arriving at the most time‐con- suming right TFAST PCS view where the TFAST echo- cardiography views are performed (see Figure 36.6). Thus, the sonographer knows how important these TFAST echocardiography views are because if lung is dry (absent B‐lines all views) and the caudal vena cava has a fluid‐responsive appearance, then the TFAST echo views for left‐ and right‐sided heart failure are less important on the initial survey. TFAST echocardi- ography views may wait until the patient is more stable or less stressed, and if the patient has no pleural effu- sion (PE), pericardial effusion (PCE), or PTX and has “dry lung” then the restraint for TFAST echocardiog- raphy views is less risky. Never Dorsal Recumbency Dorsal recumbency should not be used for several rea- sons but most importantly because of increasing patient risk. A hemodynamically fragile patient that is unknowingly placed in dorsal recumbency undergoes significant negative changes in ventilation and

696 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER circulation, specifically venous return (see Figure 6.5). Add to these respiratory and cardiovascular stresses the increased oxygen demand in a struggling, anxious patient, and the patient risks acute and potentially cat- astrophic decompensation. When considering trauma, many dogs and cats have concurrent lung contusions and other thoracic‐related injuries (Powell et al. 1999; Sigrist et al. 2004; Lisciandro et al. 2008; Armenise et al. 2019); hemoabdomen (Boysen et al. 2004; Lisciandro et al. 2009; Lisciandro 2012); and in non - trauma, many hypotensive triaged patients have pleural and/or pericardial effusion and intracavitary bleeds often accompanied by anemia (McMurray et al. 2016; Lisciandro 2016a,b). Moreover, the abdominal fluid scoring system is not validated in dorsal recumbency and only subjective terms of mild, moderate, and severe have been used (Sutherland‐Smith et al. 2007; Stander et al. 2010). Global FAST for Patient Monitoring The use of Global FAST for volume status includes the following. • TFAST echocardiography (echo) views for left‐ and right‐sided strain/failure/overload. • TFAST PCS views and the FAST DH view for pleural and pericardial effusion. 697 POCUS: G LOBAL FAST – P ATIENT M ONITORING AND S TAGING • TFAST for pneumothorax. • TFAST for soft tissue lesions of the heart. • FAST DH view for caudal vena cava and hepatic venous characterization. • Vet BLUE for lung. • AFAST and its fluid scoring system. • AFAST for interrogation of the retroperitoneal space. • AFAST for soft tissue obvious abnormalities using the target organ approach. • AFAST cysto‐colic view for estimating urinary bladder volume over time with serial measure - ments used for noninvasive estimation of urine output. There is no need for a veterinary RUSH (Rapid Ultrasound in Shock) protocol or other similar proto - cols (Neri et al. 2007; Perera et al. 2010; Lichtenstein and Malbrain 2015) because Global FAST does every - thing RUSH does and more (Perera et al. 2010; Boysen and Lisciandro 2013; Lisciandro and Armenise 2014Lisciandro 2019b). The RUSH exam lacks an abdominal fluid scoring system, a “lung point” assessment for degree of pneumothorax (while also serving as a monitoring tool), and a urinary bladder estimation formula, and has much less lung evalua - tion (Lisciandro et al. 2008, 2014, 2017; Lisciandro 2011; Lisciandro and Armenise 2014; Lisciandro and Fosgate 2017). The view is used for subjective assessment of volume and contractility by looking at its maximum (diastole) left ventricular filling and the change in its filling between diastole (maximum) and systole (minimum) for an estimation of fractional shortening (FS%). In row (B) the short‐axis view from the right TFAST PCS view is used to assess the LA:Ao, screening for left‐sided cardiac strain/failure/overload. Shown with the arrows is the approximation of the comparative measurements (LA:Ao) with the expected normal ratio of ~1:1 in dogs and ~1.5:1 in cats. Obvious abnormal for either species would be > 2:1. In row (C) the LA4CV from the right TFAST PCS view is shown to assess the RV:LV , screening for right‐sided cardiac strain/failure/overload. Shown with the triangles is the expected ratio of the RV to LV as ~1:3–4 as the RV should be much smaller than the LV . Global FAST nonecho fallback views are important to further reinforce clinical impression regarding these TFAST echo views (see Figures 36.7 and 36.8). 698 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Global FAST for Volume Status Clarity, Rapidity, Standardization The use of Global FAST for volume status includes TFAST echocardiography (echo) views and pleural and pericardial effusion (Lisciandro et al. 2008; Lisciandro 2011, 2014a, 2016a; Boysen and Lisciandro 2013; McMurray et al. 2016) and pneumothorax (Lisciandro et al. 2008; Lisciandro 2011, 2014b; Boysen and Lisciandro 2013), the FAST DH views for caudal vena cava and hepatic venous characterization (Nelson et al. 2010; Boysen and Lisciandro 2013; Lisciandro and Armenise 2014; Darnis et al. 2018), Vet BLUE for lung (Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2017; Ward et al. 2017, 2018a; Dicker et al. 2019), and AFAST and its fluid scoring system and interrogation of the retroperitoneal space (Lisciandro et al. 2009; Boysen and Lisciandro 2013; Lisciandro 2011, 2014a, 2019b; Lisciandro et al. 2019a; McMurray et al. 2016; Armenise et al. 2019), and its cysto‐colic view for estimating urinary bladder volume, that over time may be used for noninvasive estimation of urine output (Lisciandro and Fosgate 2017). Integrating information is key for increasing the probability of an accurate assessment. Time is also important and Global FAST is 15 defined acoustic win- dows (views) with exact clarity that with its standard- ized methodology requires only six different probe maneuvers. Moreover, the Global FAST components of AFAST, TFAST, and Vet BLUE are the most studied in veterinary medicine with over 16 relevant publications at the time of writing (Lisciandro et al. 2008, 2009, 2014, 2017, 2019; Lisciandro 2016a; Lisciandro and Fosgate 2017; Ward et al. 2017, 2018a,b, 2019; Dicker et al. 2019; Hnatusko et al. 2019; Vientós‐Plotts et al. 2019). Integrating Echocardiography and the “Global FAST Nonecho Fallback Views” The use of Global FAST for volume status includes TFAST echocardiography (echo) views and the “Global FAST nonecho fallback views,” a term created by the author. The strategy of using “Global FAST nonecho fallback views” spares your patient the risk of echocar- diography and radiography, when your patient is criti- cal. For example, left‐ and right‐sided congestive heart failure is rapidly ruled out by the finding of “dry lung” all views during Vet BLUE (or absent B‐lines) (Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2016, 2017; Ward et al. 2017) and a nondistended CVC (bounce) and hepatic veins at the FAST DH view, respectively (Ferrada et al. 2012a,b; Boysen and Lisciandro 2013; Lisciandro and Armenise 2014; Tchernodrinski and Arntfield 2015). These “Global FAST nonecho fallback views” are generally easier (and faster) and require minimal patient restraint when compared to TFAST echocardiography views and radiography. In other words, don’t risk patient decompensation and the potential for cardiopulmonary arrest (CPA) in a patient that has unremarkable “Global FAST nonecho fallback views.” Heart disease may exist, but left‐ and right‐sided congestive heart failure are as a general rule ruled out. In other words, echocar- diography and radiology can wait until your patient is more stable. TFAST Cardiac Imaging The four TFAST echocardiography views and their clinical utility are explained below. Short‐axis Views The TFAST echocardiography views consist of two short‐axis views. Volume and Contractility Left ventricular short‐axis (LVSA) “mushroom” view. • Volume – subjective size of left ventricle in diastole (maximum size). • Fractional shortening percentage (FS%) – subjective changes in size from systole to diastole (change in size through the cardiac cycle). • Normal dog FS 25–45%; cat FS 30–50%. • Obvious abnormal. ◦ Heart that is both enlarged and fluttering, lack- ing robust contractions. ◦ LVSA internal maximum diameter > 5 cm in dogs (DeFrancesco, personal communication 2019). Left‐sided Strain/Failure/Overload Left ventricular short‐axis “Mercedes‐Benz” view. • Left ventricular short‐axis left atrial (LA) to aortic (Ao) ratio (LA:Ao). • Normal generally is a ratio of < 1.3:1 in dogs and < 1.6:1 in cats. • Obvious abnormal enlargement is LA:Ao > 2:1 in both dogs and cats. Long‐axis Views The TFAST echocardiography views consist of two long‐axis views. Right‐sided Strain/Failure/Overload Long‐axis four‐chamber view (LA4CV).

699 POCUS: GLOBAL FAST – P ATIENT MONITORING AND STAGING • RV:LV. • Normal generally is a ratio of approximately 1:3–4 in dogs and cats or, in other words, the RV should be 1/3 to 1/4 of the size of the LV . • Obvious abnormal enlargement is an RV:LV of approximately 1:1 in both dogs and cats. Abnormalities within the Ascending Aorta Left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) on long axis. • Any obvious soft tissue abnormalities in the LVOT including masses, dilation (aneurysm), and vegetation(s) on the aortic valves. Freeze the image and roll the cine ball through mul- tiple frames to get a more accurate assessment of the heart when it cannot be done in real time with the “eyeball method.” This is especially helpful in cats that have much higher heart rates than dogs, and in dogs with tachycardia, in which the “eyeball method” is problematic and more error prone. Nonecho Fallback Strategies for Right‐sided Heart Problems FAST DH View and Its Right‐sided Cardiac Markers The FAST DH view is the “Global FAST nonecho fall- back view,” often safer than TFAST echocardiography views for critical patients. By definition, right‐sided congestive heart failure results in a distended or FAT caudal vena cava along with concomitant hepatic venous congestion. The features of right‐sided congestive heart failure may be “seen” sonographically by observing what the author terms the four “TFAST right‐sided cardiac markers” (RSCM). Caudal Vena Cava Characterization of its dynamic changes over several respiratory cycles combined with its maximum height where it crosses the diaphragm (Figure 36.7 and Tables 36.3 and 36.4) (Nelson et al. 2010; Lisciandro 2011, 2014a,d, 2016a; Boysen and Lisciandro 2013; Lisciandro and Armenise 2014; Darnis et al. 2018; Vientós‐Plotts et al. 2019). • “FAT” (fluid intolerant) – distended with < 10% change in height. • “Flat” (fluid starved or hypovolemic) – small with < 10% change in height. • “Bounce” (fluid responsive) – normal sized with 35–50% change in height. Hepatic Veins Hepatic veins are normally unremarkable and incon- spicuous at the FAST DH view in patients positioned in lateral or standing‐sternal. Thus, hepatic venous dis- tension serves as a marker for increased central venous pressure, especially when combined with a “FAT” or distended CVC (Nelson et al. 2010; Ferrada 2012a,b; Lisciandro 2014a,d, 2016a, 2019a; Tchernodrinski and Arntfield 2015; Vientós‐Plotts et al. 2019). • “Tree trunk sign” (Figure 36.8) (Lisciandro 2014a,d, 2016a, 2019a; Vientós‐Plotts et al. 2019). Gallbladder Wall Edema (Lisciandro et al. 2019b) • “Cardiac gallbladder” (Figure 36.9) (Lisciandro 2014a,d, 2016a, 2019a; Vientós‐Plotts et al. 2019). • The finding of sonographic striation similar to the “gallbladder halo effect” in canine anaphylaxis, and when caused by anaphylaxis referred to as the “anaphylactic gallbladder”(Quantz et al. 2009). Ascites (Nelson et al. 2010; Lisciandro and Armenise 2014; Vientós‐Plotts et al. 2019) • Modified transudate confirmed when free fluid is safely accessible typically caudal or near the hepato‐renal umbilical (HRU) view for sampling with subsequent fluid analysis and cytology (see Figures 6.10, 6.19, 6.25, and 6.32). • In cats, unlike dogs, ascites is generally not pre- sent in right‐sided congestive heart failure but felines rather have pleural effusion that is often accompanied by degrees of pericardial effusion (Ward et al. 2018a). Ruling Out Right‐sided Congestive Heart Failure A dog or cat (or rabbit, gerbil, or ferret) with a fluid‐ responsive CVC (bounce) without hepatic venous dis- tension has as a rule no evidence of right‐sided congestive heart failure which serves as a helpful approach when the TFAST echocardiography view(s) are equivocal or are not possible due to patient status. Nonecho Fallback Strategies for Left‐sided Heart Problems Vet BLUE for Lung and Wet Lung Versus Dry Lung Findings By definition, left‐sided congestive heart failure results in pulmonary edema. Thus, if a dog or cat has absent B‐lines at all Vet BLUE views (ABAV), then the patient

See Figure 36.17 and Chapters 22 and 23 for greater detail. Assessing and Measuring the Caudal Vena Cava and Assessing Hepatic Venous Distension Where to Evaluate the Caudal Vena Cava? Multiple regions have been used to assess and mea - sure the CVC in dogs (Nelson et al. 2010; Lisciandro 2014a,d, 2016a; Meneghini et al. 2016; Tuplin et al. 2017; Bucci et al. 2017; Kwak et al. 2018; Cambournac et al. 2018; Darnis et al. 2018; Vientós‐Plotts et al. 2019) (Figure 36.10) (see Chapter 26). • Where the CVC traverses the diaphragm (subxi - phoid or FAST DH view) having the advantage of combining hepatic venous characterization and being closest to the right heart and pleural cavity, making it most predictive of central venous pressure (Nelson et al. 2010; Lisciandro 2014a,d; 2016; 2019a; Tchernodrinski and Arntfield 2015; Tuplin et al. 2017). This is the view detailed by the author in this chapter. • At the porta hepatis at the 11–13th intercostal spaces of the right hemithorax where hepatic veins are not assessed but rather the CVC is compared to the adjacent abdominal aorta. See more detail in Chapter 26 (Bucci et al. 2017; Darnis et al. 2018; Armenise et al. 2019). • Cranial to the right kidney (or left kidney). • Caudal to the right kidney where hepatic veins are not assessed but rather the CVC is compared to the adjacent abdominal aorta (Meneghini et al. 2016; Kwak et al. 2018; Marshall et al. 2018; Cambournac et al. 2018). See more detail in Chapter 26. Characterizing the Caudal Vena Cava and Hepatic Veins – “Eyeball Method” Assessing the CVC and its dynamic change in height over several respiratory cycles as “FAT,” “flat,” or hav- ing a “bounce” (Figure 36.11; see also Figure 36.9). Measuring the Caudal Vena Cava At the FAST DH view, two options are available in its longitudinal plane, M‐mode and B‐mode, each having limitations (Figure 36.12). Either is acceptable in the opinion of the author, who prefers the simplicity of the B‐mode measurement (see Figures 36.11 and 36.12). Table 36.3 is created from data from Darnis et al. 704 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER although only via subjective assessment, the finding of the “tree trunk sign” is currently used (Nelson et al. 2010; Lisciandro 2014a,d, 2016a, 2019a; Lisciandro and Armenise 2014; Vientós‐Plotts et al. 2019) (see Figures 36.7 and 36.9). Combining both the “eyeball method” and actual measurements at the FAST DH view would likely give the best overall assessment, but this is speculative and likely dependent on types of heart conditions. As a final note, the FAST DH view provides charac- terizations of both the CVC and hepatic veins at the same view, whereas other published CVC locations do not give hepatic venous characterization but rather compare size of the CVC to the adjacent abdominal aorta (see Figure 36.10 and also Figures 38.8 and 38.9 and Chapter 26 for greater detail). CVC methods further away from the diaphragm are at increasing dis- tance from the pleural cavity and right heart and are thus in theory less sensitive predictors of patient volume status. Global FAST for Volume Loss The Leak in the T ank Whenever a patient presents as volume contracted, the important question is always asked “Where is the fluid loss?” referred to as a “leak in the tank” by the RUSH examination (Perera et al. 2010). By finding the “leak in the tank,” the volume loss has a better chance of being corrected. For example, a postoperative dog may be mildly tachycardic, hypothermic, quiet and alert with a normal blood pressure. The focused cardiac ultrasound (FCU) or a POCUS caudal vena cava (CVC) exam may reveal volume contraction. An intravenous fluid bolus may be administered along with serial FCU or POCUS CVC. However, Global FAST not only rapidly detects the ascites but also trig- gers an abdominocentesis and a hemoabdomen is diagnosed along with categorization of a small‐ volume bleeder versus large‐volume bleeder (see Chapter 7). Another example would be a dog with acute hemorrhagic diarrhea syndrome (previously referred to as hemorrhagic gastroenteritis syndrome, HGE) (Busch et al. 2015; Mortier et al. 2015). The dog is stable, unremarkable on physical examination, with normal vital signs and blood pressure assessment, and is being treated for mild tachycardia with analgesia. However, Global FAST shows that the patient is volume contracted with poor left ventric - ular filling on the right TFAST PCS view and the CVC is flat at the FAST DH view. Fluid resuscitation is better approached with the checks and balances using the Global FAST approach. Global FAST Automatically Surveys for the Leak in the T ank Four Spaces Plus Lung and Maybe More Global FAST automatically surveys for internal volume loss by interrogating four spaces plus lung (see Maybe More section below) including: • the peritoneal cavity • the retroperitoneal space • the pleural cavity • the pericardial sac • the lung (extravascular lung water). Figure 36.10. Different locations for characterization of the CVC in dogs. Several locations have been studied in dogs for hypovolemia based on the characterization and measure - ments of the CVC. These are numbered as 1 FAST DH, 2 porta hepatis, 3 cranial to the right kidney (RK) and left kidney (not shown), and 4 caudal to the RK. It is important to understand a few concepts, the first being that volume status is likely best assessed as close as possible to the right atrium. Second, CVC characterization is correlated to the adjacent hepatic veins at site 1; however, for sites 2–4, the CVC is being compared to the aorta and although reproducibly mea- sured between different observers, the question must be raised as to how relevant volume status is with increasing distances from the patient’s right atrium. The author favors site 1 where the CVC traverses the diaphragm and also pro - vides information regarding hepatic venous distension. Clinical studies have shown that site 2 is measured well (CVC and aorta for their comparison) and has correlated with hypovolemia although the view is not part of Global FAST (see Chapter 26 for greater detail).
