705 POCUS: G LOBAL FAST – P ATIENT M ONITORING AND S TAGING The patient may lose marked volume in the three “forgiving areas” of the peritoneal cavity, retroperito - neal space, and pleural cavity before it is obvious to the attending veterinarian that the patient has developed serious complication(s). The “unforgiving areas” of the pericardial sac and lung are also surveyed; however, large “leaks” in these two regions lead to obvious changes in patient status because much smaller relative volumes of pericardial effusion will affect cardiac output and increases in extravascular lung water (B‐lines and Vet BLUE B‐line scoring system) in lung will quickly affect ventilation. The Vet BLUE examination has been shown to detect alveolar‐interstitial syndrome with higher frequency than thoracic radiography, providing clear advan - tages by being point‐of‐care, rapid and a regional pattern‐based approach (Lisciandro et al. 2016; Ward et al. 2017, 2018b; Dicker et al. 2019), and is comparable to computed tomography (CT) for lung contusions (Dicker et al. 2019). The detection of “leaks” in these areas can trigger interventions to better treat the patient by directing care with evidence‐based information by “seeing” the problem and assessing its degree through AFAST (abdominal fluid scoring system), TFAST (“lung point” for degree of pneumo - thorax) and Vet BLUE (B‐line and pulmonary contu - sion scoring systems). 706 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER their target organ approach, each automatically screens for plugs (obstruction of flow), thrombi (blood clots) in the urinary bladder and cardiac chambers, and various vessels including renal, splenic, hepatic, and the CVC, and other leaks such as a fluid‐distended gastrointes - tinal and urogenital tract that may be easily appreci - ated through the observation of distended fluid‐filled loops and thrombus in the urinary bladder. These find- ings can trigger investigative interventions ranging from the simple during physical examination (digital rectal examination for gastrointestinal bleeding and free catch urine samples) to more advanced imaging and diagnostic testing (D‐dimers, coagulation testing, advanced imaging). Through Global FAST, infarction potentially may be recognized within the spleen, lung, and renal cortex. Other obstructions to flow would be poor vascular tone such as in sepsis, and poor venous tone likely would be better recognized through CVC and splanchnic pooling during AFAST by a distended (or “FAT”) CVC with hepatic venous distension (“tree trunk sign”) and edematous small intestine, respec - tively (Lisciandro 2014a,d, 2016a, 2019a). Summary The objective of the Global FAST approach is to recog- nize deviations from what is expected at each of its 15 acoustic windows to allow further assessment with the potential to positively affect outcome (Blackbourne et al. 2004; Ollerton et al. 2006; Neri et al. 2007; Lisciandro et al. 2008, 2009, 2014, 2017; Lisciandro 2011, 2012; Boysen and Lisciandro 2013; Perera et al. 2010; Ferrada et al. 2011, 2012a,b; Lisciandro and Armenise 2014; Lichtenstein and Malbrain 2015; Tavares et al. 2019). There will always be exceptions, but this approach provides a solid foundation from which skills may be further developed. For example, the septic patient may have poor vascular tone resulting in poor ventricular filling on the left ventricular “mush - room” view, triggering intravenous volume expansion when in fact the patient requires vasopressors. 707 POCUS: G LOBAL FAST – P ATIENT M ONITORING AND S TAGING Global FAST Monitoring T ools Use of the AFAST‐applied Abdominal Fluid Scoring System for Ascites The use of the abdominal fluid score is important for semiquantitating intraabdominal small‐volume bleeder/effusion (AFS 1–2, < 3 with modification of AFS) versus large‐volume bleeder/effusion (AFS 3–4, ≥3 with modification of AFS) and estimating both hemorrhagic and nonhemorrhagic volume loss within the abdominal cavity. With hemoabdomen, the decisions for blood transfusion(s) may be made using AFS (see Chapters 6 and 7, and Table 7.3). This facet of Global FAST is not part of the RUSH exam. Use of TFAST for Estimating Pleural and Pericardial Effusion Pleural Effusion Studies have been performed in cadaver cats and dogs positioned in sternal using an off‐the‐sternum imaging methodology for measuring distance between the heart and the thoracic wall; however, the estimation formulas were unreliable (Newitt et al. 2009; Shimali et al. 2010). A suggestion by the author is to measure the distance of pleural effusion from the thoracic wall at the fourth or fifth intercostal spaces at the level of the costochondral junction and/or via the FAST DH view in a standing or sternal patient, although this methodology has never been studied (Figure 36.13). Ideally, such a method would need to be developed from spontaneously breathing subjects with lung natu- rally aerated rather than in cadaver studies because the dynamics of aerated lung floating in pleural effusion would presumably differ between antemortem and postmortem (Newitt et al. 2009; Shimali et al. 2010). Pericardial Effusion No studies to the author’s knowledge have been for - mulated to measure the volume of pericardial effusion in dogs and cats. Descriptors for amount of pericardial effusion have been published in people and include trivial < 0.5 cm, mild 0.5–1.0 cm, moderate > 1.0 and < 2.0 cm, and severe > 2.0 cm (Candotti and Arntfield 2015). The question remains: where to measure? A sug- gestion by the author is to measure the distance of pericardial effusion from the pericardial sac to the heart (visceral pericardium) at the fourth or fifth inter- costal spaces at the level of the costochondral junction with the patient in sternal‐standing, although this methodology has never been studied (Figure 36.14). Another methodology that would seem logical would be to measure the maximum distance in a standing or sternal patient between the pericardial sac and the heart (visceral pericardium) from the FAST DH view (see Figure 36.14). Use of Global FAST for Estimating Urine Output Formulas exist for estimating urinary bladder volume (Atalan et al. 2007; Lisciandro and Fosgate 2017) and the ellipsoid formula of length (cm) × height (cm) × width (cm) × 0.625 estimates the urinary bladder volume in milliliters (mL) (Figure 36.15). To the author’s knowledge, only a single study has been per- formed in cats (Lisciandro and Fosgate 2017). Thus, with serial measurements, urine output may be esti - mated noninvasively by change in volume over change in time (∆ urine volume/∆ time). Although not known for cats, residual urine volume in dogs has been reported to be < 0.2 mg/kg (Atalan et al. 1999). Dogs Figure 36.13. Use of Global FAST for Estimating Pneumothorax Using The “Lung Point” The use of the “lung point” serves as a means not only to assess the degree of PTX but also to monitor PTX (Lisciandro et al. 2008; Lisciandro 2011, 2014a; Lisciandro and Armenise 2014) (Figure 36.16). When PTX is sus - pected, the patient is best moved to sternal or standing position (if in lateral) and the sonographer continues with a Vet BLUE, searching for any evidence of lung recontacting the thoracic wall, most commonly “lung sliding” or B‐lines, but any Vet BLUE lung ultrasound signs can determine the location of the “lung point” (Lisciandro et al. 2008; Lisciandro 2011, 2014b; Lisciandro and Armenise 2014). In other words, when PTX is sus- pected at the Caudodorsal lung region, then the sonog- rapher continues to the Perihilar (Ph) lung region (middle third) followed by the Middle (Md) lung region (lower third), referred to as the TFAST PTX 1/3s Rule. If a “lung point” is not found at either, then the sonographer may slide even lower along the thoracic wall ventral to the Md lung region. If evidence of lung contacting the thoracic wall is found, then the sonogra- pher moves dorsal from that view until lung contact - ing the thoracic wall is lost (because of PTX). The transition zone of PTX and lung contacting the thoracic wall is the “lung point.” The TFAST PTX 1/3s Rule Figure 36.14. Use of the Vet BLUE B‐line Scoring System Numbers of B‐lines are counted as the largest number at each Vet BLUE view and scored as 0, 1, 2, 3, > 3, and infinity (∞). Consider scoring of 1, 2, and 3 as weak positives and > 3 and infinity (∞) as strong positives (Ward et al. 2017). The scoring system is detailed in Chapter 23 and may be applied to patients with alveolar‐interstitial syndrome (AIS) and lung contusions. In people, scoring num - bers of B‐lines is also used in pulmonary fibrotic conditions. This facet of Global FAST is not part of the RUSH exam. Figure 36.16. Estimating degree of pneumothorax and the TFAST PTX 1/3s Rule. (A–C) The patient with PTX is in lateral recumbency and because of the “parking garage effect” the free air bubbles into different regions, creating a “double lung point” phenomenon in which a “lung point” is potentially seen on either side of the collapsed lung. Moreover, if the patient is receiving positive pressure ventilation, the free air (PTX) is pushed into multiple locations unnaturally between the collapsed lung. In (D–F) the effect is eliminated or greatly reduced by moving the patient to standing or sternal position, thus creating a “sky scraper effect” in which the difference between the sternum and least gravity‐dependent chest tube site (CTS) view is greatest. Thus, it is unlikely a “double lung point” will be observed. In (F) the probe is moved along the lateral thoracic wall searching for the “lung point.” The TFAST 1/3s Rule is used to assess as trivial, moderate, and severe PTX, dependent on the location of the “lung point,” the upper 1/3, middle 1/3, and lower 1/3, respectively. In (G) the degree of PTX may be charac - terized as trivial, moderate, and severe depending on where the lung point is located. 710 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER B‐line Scoring for Estimating Degrees of Alveolar‐ Interstitial Edema and Extravascular Lung Water Numbers of B‐lines have been shown to correlate with degree of alveolar‐interstitial edema on computed tomography and directly correlate with extravascular lung water (Jambrik et al. 2004, 2010; Volpicelli et al. 2006; Gargani et al. 2015). In other words, greater numbers of B‐lines in most patients means greater degree of alveolar‐interstitial edema and extravascular lung water (EVLW) (Figure 36.17). This is important because the degree of EVLW corre - lates with survival in people, so by detecting increases in B‐lines, interventions may potentially take place prior to overt patient decompensation (Jambrik et al. 2004, 2010; Volpicelli et al. 2006; Lichtenstein and Karakitsos 2012; Shyamsundar et al. 2013). This facet of Global FAST is not part of the RUSH exam. See Chapters 22 and 23 for greater detail. Figure 36.17 . The Vet BLUE B‐line scoring system. The amount of extravascular lung water may be estimated by its direct correlation with numbers of B‐lines. In (A) a patient developing B‐lines may be determined as having left‐sided volume over- load or pneumonia (as well as other causes) based on the Vet BLUE regional pattern‐based approach and integrating TFAST echocardiography views and the Global FAST nonecho fallback views (see Tables 23.2, 23.3, and 23.4). In (B), a patient with left‐sided congestive heart failure, loop diuretic usage may be guided by the Vet BLUE B‐line scoring system. Lots of B‐lines (> 3 and infinity) at most Vet BLUE views dictates more aggressive loop diuretics than one or two positive Vet BLUE views with smaller numbers of B‐lines (0–3). In (C) lung contusions may be similarly semiquantitated by numbers of B‐lines combined with distribution of positive Vet BLUE views. 711 POCUS: GLOBAL FAST – P ATIENT MONITORING AND STAGING B‐line Scoring System for Guiding Diuretic Usage Numbers of B‐lines can help justify the need for loop diuretics (see Figure 36.17). In dogs and cats with absent B‐lines during Vet BLUE (likely holds true for all mammalian lung), loop diuretics should not be given empirically (Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2016, 2017; Rademacher et al. 2014; Ward et al. 2017, 2018b; Vezzosi et al. 2017). When B‐lines are present, their numbers and distribution help guide loop diuretic usage. In patients with small numbers of B‐lines, loop diuretics likely may be administered more conservatively versus patients with high numbers of B‐lines (> 3 and infinity) at many Vet BLUE views. Numbers of B‐lines most commonly represent alveolar‐interstitial syndrome, meaning B‐lines are nonspecific and must be placed in clinical context. For example, a predominance of B‐lines dorsally or generalized is more likely cardio- genic and noncardiogenic forms of lung edema, espe- cially when combined with TFAST echo views and other supportive evidence including physical exam findings, patient history, signalment, and other imaging. This facet of Global FAST is not part of the RUSH exam. See Figure 36.17, Table 23.4, and Chapters 22 and 23 for greater detail. B‐line Scoring System for Lung Contusions In trauma cases, numbers of B‐lines may be combined with numbers of positive Vet BLUE views and their distribution to assign a Vet BLUE lung contusion severity score to the patient (Lisciandro 2011, 2014b; Boysen and Lisciandro 2013; Dicker et al. 2019) (see Figures 23.30, 36.17). For example, a trauma patient with > 3 B‐lines at its left Ph and Md lung regions has focal contusions compared to another trauma patient that has > 3 B‐lines at all transthoracic Vet BLUE views as well as at the DH view. This facet of Global FAST is not part of the RUSH exam. See Chapters 22 and 23 for greater detail. Global FAST for Staging Disease – Localized Versus Disseminated Disease Having practiced veterinary medicine as a general practitioner and a clinical specialist for over 28 years and having trained 1000+ veterinarians throughout the United States, the following scenarios are not uncommon and drive home an important and necessary paradigm change. The “flash approach” of ultrasound for imaging patients is a huge detriment for patient care in the author’s opinion, likened to performing an incomplete physical examination. Moreover, the “flash approach” not only lends itself to desultory methodology but also obviates the mandatory requirement for recording patient data other than “fluid positive” or “fluid negative” and other freehanded data entries. Finally, the “flash approach” and targeted “POCUS” examination, without a standardized set of data imaging points provided by Global FAST, lends itself to the dangerous problem of satisfaction of search error. A case in point is canine anaphylaxis and its marker of sonographic striation of the gallbladder wall, discovered in a bril- liant study by Quantz (2009); however, its flaw was doing just a targeted or focused gallbladder examina- tion and not a Global FAST. By performing Global FAST, the added rule‐outs of pericardial effusion and right‐sided congestive heart failure, including dilated cardiomyopathy, and the unique canine complication of hemoabdomen would likely have been detected sooner than post‐study by other investigators (Lisciandro 2014a,d, 2016b; Lisciandro et al. 2019b; Hnatusko et al. 2019). Let’s look at several scenarios and the positive effect that the Global FAST approach has on patient care (Figure 36.18). Staging the Hemoabdomen Canine Hemoabdomen A retrospective study described numbers of canine hemoabdomen cases and those that proceeded to definitive surgical care. Of the 432 cases, only 86 were operated, or 20% (Lux et al. 2013). Many factors enter into the decision to pursue a diagnostic work‐up and the decision for definitive care; however, the author will describe a typical scenario that many veterinar - ians would recognize. The acute collapsed nontrau- matic hemoabdomen patient is triaged and because a physical exam is ambiguous, the ultrasound probe is used to “flash” the abdomen, answering a simple binary question of “fluid positive” or “fluid nega- tive” with or without an additional sweep of the abdomen for a “mass.” The subsequent discussion with the client goes as follows: “Your dog has a bleed within its abdominal cavity. The bleeding likely has a splenic tumor as its cause (Lux et al. 2013). The most likely diagnosis is a malignant tumor with a proba- bility of benign ranging from ~25% to 33% to malig- nant ranging from ~67% to 75% (Hammond and Pesillo‐Crosby 2008; Aronsohn et al. 2009; Levinson et al. 2009; Eberle et al. 2012; Lux et al. 2013; Lynch et al. 2015). We need to do X, Y, and Z for a cost of X.” This work‐up of X, Y, and Z is likely expensive, including blood work +/‐ coagulation profile, three‐ view thoracic radiograph as a pulmonary metastasis

712 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER check, and a complete detailed abdominal ultrasound to confirm the bleeding mass, its origin, and whether intraabdominal metastasis is apparent. The end‐result is that the patient is euthanized, given palliative care or not treated (Lux et al. 2013). So let’s think about this work‐up and the study’s data a bit more (Lux et al. 2013). If the ratio of benign to malignant is as poor as 25–33%% to 67–75% then likely there are many dogs with benign tumors being eutha - nized. If we think about the effectiveness of staging with a three‐view thoracic radiograph (TXR) study for pulmonary metastasis and pericardial effusion, common sites for hemangiosarcoma to metastasize, the literature has shown that there are real limitations to this approach. Three‐view TXR misses lung nod - ules, for which computed tomography is the gold stan- dard (Eberle et al. 2010; Alexander et al. 2012; Armbrust et al. 2012), and misses pericardial effusion, for which ultrasound is arguably the gold standard (Guglielmini et al. 2012; Côté et al. 2013). The questions must be asked: “If the patient is staged negative on Global FAST for any obvious metastasis, would the benign to malignant tumor fre - quency be improved?” and “Would we be able to better determine surgical candidacy and thus treat with the potential to cure benign splenic neoplastic disease?” The advantages of the Global FAST approach for staging this subset of patients with the most clinically relevant questions are as follows (Figure 36.19). AFAST • DH view – are there obvious liver metastases (target lesions)? • SR and HRU views – is there an obvious splenic or midabdominal mass? • What is the AFS? Determine small‐volume bleeder versus large‐volume bleeder to help with the decision regarding blood transfusion(s). Figure 36.18. Questions asked during staging with Global FAST. In (C,D) clinically relevant ques - tions are shown on overlays for the staging of disease and conditions as being localized or disseminated. The Global FAST approach provides a means to not only quickly screen for local versus disseminated disease but also to determine the diag - nostic path, including the next best test(s). Moreover, by “seeing” the problem list with evidence‐based information, treatment is potentially better directed. See the text for greater detail. TFAST • Is there pleural effusion? • Is there pericardial effusion? • Is there any obvious intracardiac mass? Vet BLUE • Are there any obvious lung nodules? • Any lung surface abnormalities? The attending clinician is searching for any obvious complications and signs of metastasis and thus is helped in their presentation of the condition to the client with the potential for hope and definitive care. The traditional work‐up will take place with more confidence for the possibility for definitive gold stan- dard treatment for the patient. Feline Bladder Masses As with dogs, cats have neoplasia as the top differential but the signalment, sex, and location generally differ, with bladder tumors more common in older males (versus middle‐aged female dogs) and nearer the apex (cats) than the trigone (dogs). Moreover, the prognosis may be guarded to good as well as in dogs (Wilson et al. 2007; Griffin et al. 2018). The staging of the cat would be identical and determining localized disease before the patient departs on day 1 affords the oppor - tunity to work up and treat. The clinically relevant questions are the same as for dogs. Staging Pericardial Effusion Canine Pericardial Effusion Pericardial effusion is far more prevalent than previ- ously recorded because we were using the wrong first‐ line screening test, namely thoracic radiography, which is unreliable (Stafford Johnson et al. 2004; MacDonald et al. 2009; Guglielmini et al. 2012; Côté et al. 2013). With first‐line use of AFAST and TFAST and the emphasis to look past the diaphragm for PCE and fol- lowing specific tenets for its accurate diagnosis (Lisciandro 2014a,d, 2016a, 2019a), the sonographer is less intimidated by the thorax and is becoming more confident in accurately diagnosing PCE. With increased detection comes the need to better understand the causes and prognoses for pericardial effusion in both the dog and cat. In the dog, it has been reported that a nonhemoab- domen ascites along with echocardiography negative for a heart mass carries a significantly better prognosis (605 days versus 45 days), thus emphasizing the impor- tance of a Global FAST approach over the “flashing of the thorax” in which the presentation to the client likely will involve neoplasia as a top differential (Stafford Johnson et al. 2004). The advantage with “flashing the thorax” or selectively imaging the heart lies more in the PCE diagnosis and that the finding carries a poor prognosis rather than staging the patient with the Global FAST approach in an attempt to pursue treatment. Moreover, pulmonary metastasis is com- monly missed by thoracic radiography, detecting only 33% of cases with thoracoscopy with necropsy as the gold standard comparison test (MacDonald et al. 2009). By staging with Global FAST, ascites may be easily screened for with high sensitivity and specificity, as well as lung nodules during Vet BLUE (Kulhavy and Lisciandro 2015). Staging with a more favorable prognosis helps direct the client to performing life‐saving pericardiocentesis (so more and more veterinarians will need to acquire this skill) and understanding that pericardiocentesis buys time for the client to make decisions, including gold standard testing of a complete detailed echocar - diogram and possibly surgery. Even slow‐growing, mildly inflammatory heart base tumors may be treated for months with pericardiocentesis and other minimal interventions. Moreover, dogs echo negative for cardiac masses may have foreign bodies, infectious and inflammatory causes, or acquired coagulopathies that have the potential to be cured. See Chapters 18, 20, and 21 for greater detail. The advantages of the Global FAST approach for staging this subset of patients with the most clinically relevant questions are as follows (Figure 36.21). AFAST • DH view – are there obvious liver metastases (target lesions)? • SR and HRU views – is there an obvious splenic or midabdominal mass? • What is the AFS? What is the fluid type? If non- hemorrhagic, a modified transudate carries a much better prognosis (Stafford Johnson et al. 2004). If

Feline Pericardial Effusion Unlike dogs, cats have congestive heart failure (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, HCM) as the top differential when PCE is detected (Hall et al. 2007; Ward et al. 2018a). In the largest published study, 75% of cats with PCE were ultimately diagnosed with heart failure most commonly from HCM (Hall et al. 2007). In another more recent study, the finding of PCE was 100% specific, meaning every cat with any degree of PCE was ultimately diagnosed with heart failure (Ward et al. 2018a). Thus, the clinically rele - vant questions differ with cats. Staging is important but in terms of cats with pleural effusion, “flashing the thorax” may be detrimental with a long list of dif - ferentials, when the observation of PCE places heart failure as the top differential and changes the presen - tation to the client as well as directing care along the lines of this treatable disease. Global FAST Approach Case Examples The use of Global FAST would have made me a better veterinarian if I had known then what I know now, having been on both sides of the equation as a primary care veterinarian and as a emergency veterinarian at referral practices. On the primary care side, the client felt guilty about not pursuing a work‐up for a pre - sumed cancerous condition, often leaving to “think about it (the plan and its cost without much hope),” never to return. On the flip side, as an emergency vet - erinarian, that same client saw me for the euthanasia because they felt too guilty to return to the primary care veterinarian. Either way, care is less than optimal, to the detriment of the patient. Now let’s look at three cases to illustrate the point. Case 1 The patient is a 13‐year‐old male (neutered at 6 months of age) Jack Russell terrier that presents with strangu - ria and hematuria (Figure 36.22). On physical exami - nation, the most significant finding by digital rectal examination is an asymmetrical enlarged and painful prostate. The top differential is straight forward as a prostatic adenocarcinoma. The diagnostic work‐up includes confirmation of the mass as well as staging the abdominal cavity by a complete detailed diagnostic abdominal ultrasound, a three‐view TXR as a pulmonary metastatic check, and blood and urine test- ing. The client departs to discuss with her family the patient assessment and proposed diagnostic work‐up with a top differential of prostatic neoplasia with a fairly guarded to poor prognosis. Let’s look at the client’s perspective. She got the dog before she was married and now it’s part of her family with three young children. She won’t return to the pri- mary veterinarian due to the guilt of not pursuing the work‐up with little hope. However, several days later, she told her story to a recent acquaintance, who hap - pened to be not only a veterinarian but a specialist in small animal internal medicine and skilled in advanced ultrasound, who offered to perform a Global FAST. Vet Figure 36.22. Jack Russell terrier with prostatic adenocarcinoma. Global FAST begins with the Vet BLUE as shown. The sonographer, a specialist in small animal internal medicine, readily detects multiple various sized nodules throughout the Vet BLUE examination. The patient has disseminated disease, which is important to tell the client on day 1, and set up a plan that includes palliative end‐of‐life hospice care. Source: Reproduced with permission from Dr Gregory Lisciandro, Hill Country Veterinary Specialists and FASTVet.com, Spicewood, TX.

At the first two Vet BLUE views, variable sized nod - ules were observed along the lung surface and were subsequently detected throughout the Vet BLUE. The remainder of the Global FAST along with a focused prostate and the clinical profile of the patient sup - ported metastatic disease to the lungs and sublumbar lymph nodes. The information provided by Global FAST was important on a number of fronts: the client is informed of the disseminated disease (and not left to feel guilty and not know), and palliative therapy is offered (instead of no therapy) and the dog made as comfort - able as possible, providing end‐of‐life time for the dog with its family. In this scenario, the client will return to the primary practitioner for end‐of‐life decisions rather than go elsewhere. A solid bond of trust has been formed between the client and her primary care veter- inarian and case management and care greatly improved. Global FAST may be continued for moni - toring progression as well as response to treatment, if attempted. Another possible scenario is that this same case is sent by the primary care veterinarian to a referral prac- tice and the pulmonary metastasis may or may not be detected initially. When detected initially, the client wonders why you, as the primary care veterinarian, didn’t spare them the trip and cost by detecting these nodules before referral. The Global FAST should have been performed on day 1 before the client departed. The other possibility is that the detection of the pulmonary metastases is delayed or missed by less sensitive imaging such as three‐view TXR (Armbrust et al. 2012; Alexander et al. 2012; Kulhavy and Lisciandro 2015). Case 2 The patient is Tootsie, a 15‐year‐old female spayed dachshund that had a gingival mass removed and biopsied at the time of her recent dental (Figure 36.23). The histopathology came back with the diagnosis of malignant melanoma and a three‐view TXR was rec - ommended to screen for metastatic disease to her lungs. The imaging was declined due to cost com - pounded by the information that the tumor was highly malignant (so why bother?). The client was instructed for home monitoring, including “watching” for cough- ing and changes in breathing that likely would occur with pulmonary metastasis. The “watching at home” creates client anxiety – every time Tootsie, the dog she loves dearly, coughs or breathes a little differently the owner wonders if her dog is succumbing to the highly malignant tumor. Global FAST imaging is offered to screen for not only pulmonary metastasis but any other obvious abnormalities in the abdomen and thorax, including the heart. The low‐impact study, requiring little to no Figure 36.23. Dachshund named Tootsie with malignant melanoma removed during dental. The dog has a tumor removed off the gingiva during a dental procedure and the histopathology returns with the diagnosis of malignant mela- noma. The dog is doing fine at home and returns for a recheck and discussion of the plan with the concerning diagnosis. The client decides not to pursue imaging and is instructed to mon- itor at home as their other option, thinking that good money is poorly spent for the recommended three‐view TXR. Every time Tootsie coughs or looks different to the owner, the client thinks her dog is going to succumb to metastasis. Option 2 is imaging with Global FAST on day 1. The dog is imaged at its home on a coffee table in the living room and the “lung line” has no pathology, including no nodules. The rest of Global FAST is unremarkable. The good news is given to the client and Global FAST examinations are carried out every three weeks to 16 weeks post dental. No evidence of disseminated meta- static is found and Tootsie is alive and doing well 12 months later. Another client–patient–veterinary bond has been solidified. Do Global FAST on day 1! On the other hand, if lung surface abnormalities were detected during Vet BLUE then three‐view thoracic radiograph would be indicated and likely agreed to by the owner. Case 3 The ultrasound probe is naive to the patient and a Global FAST approach is easily applied to this rat (Figure 36.24). The AFAST portion easily can detect ascites and soft tissue lesions of the target organs including caudal vena cava and hepatic venous dis - tension, TFAST screens for pleural and pericardial effusion with unlikely TFAST echo views because of the depth limits of the probe, and Vet BLUE easily screens for “wet lung” versus “dry lung” as well as lung surface pathology. The Global FAST was an unre- markable scan and the neurological rat was treated supportively and symptomatically. Global FAST may be used for monitoring. Global FAST for Urinary Obstruction and Renal Failure Global FAST is invaluable for the renal failure patient, including postrenal, renal, and pre‐renal causes. It is not uncommon for urinary obstructed dogs and cats to have free intraabdominal fluid and retroperitoneal and perirenal effusion (Nevins et al. 2015; Gerken et al. 2019. The prognosis in the vast majority is good with standard treatment as these typically are medically treated complications even with the confirmation of a uroabdomen. Serial Global FAST examinations are key to track the effusion, which is expected to resolve within 24–48 hours. See more detail in Chapters 10 and 37. Global FAST for Pulmonary Thromboembolism Global FAST carries the potential to detect pulmonary thromboembolism (PTE) in dogs and cats (and other mammalian species) through screening for acute right ventricle dilation and the wedge sign during Vet BLUE (Lisciandro 2013, unpublished data). More skilled sonographers may also survey the pulmonary arteries for saddle thrombi as well. The sensitivity and speci - ficity for this approach are unknown in veterinary medicine but it has proven effective in people in both detection and monitoring response to treatment appli- cations (Mathis et al. 2005; Mastruzzo et al. 2008). The Global FAST approach also has clear advantages over contrast pulmonary angiography using computed tomography that poses risk and requires specialized equipment (Goggs et al. 2014). Serial Global FAST examinations are key to track the progression and res- olution of PTE. See more detail in Chapters 25 and 37. 720 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER prior to any anesthetic procedures (Nomura and Watanabe 2017). Recording Global FAST findings pro- vides a baseline to which postanesthetic profiles may be compared and complications detected (Lisciandro et al. 2015; Lisciandro and Fosgate 2018). For example, the dental prophylaxis case that has concurrent but otherwise occult bladder stones is best detected before the dental, or the same case with a splenic mass, or with poor systolic function (dilated cardiomyopathy), or with small‐volume pleural or pericardial effusion. The use of Global FAST also includes patients ranging from a skin mass removal to an elective procedure to an emergency procedure. Global FAST Perioperatively The Global FAST approach may be used for moni- toring for volume status and complications, including those resulting in free fluid such as hemorrhage, infec- tion, inflammation, and vascular in the four spaces (peritoneal and pleural cavity, retroperitoneal space, pericardial sac) and lung (Lisciandro and Fosgate 2018). Moreover, Global FAST surveys for soft tissue abnormalities and cardiovascular and pulmonary complications, as outlined in Chapter 37, including the Hs and Ts of CPR and treatable forms of hypotension and shock. Lung Atelectasis and Gallbladder Wall Edema Lung atelectasis is common in anesthetized people, including for minor sedation events. It has been shown in a pilot study that dogs undergoing short anesthetic procedures maintained “dry lung” Vet BLUE profiles post procedure without obvious signs of atelectasis, such as B‐lines, shred sign, tissue sign (Lisciandro et al. 2015). However, dogs receiving tiletamine‐zolazepam trended toward more atelectatic lung, making a case for periodic positive pressure breath sighing during anes- thesia (Lisciandro and Fosgate 2018). In a more recent study of 63 anesthetized dogs, the following were important findings (Lisciandro and Fosgate 2018): • dogs with spontaneous breathing were more likely to develop signs of lung atelectasis than those on anesthetic ventilators • dogs undergoing anesthesia did not develop gall- bladder wall edema from splanchnic venous pooling • dogs receiving morphine as a premedication and during their procedure (even those that vomited) did not develop gallbladder wall edema • dogs receiving contrast agents did not develop gallbladder wall edema • a dog that received a blood transfusion did develop gallbladder wall edema (Lisciandro and Fosgate 2018). The Global FAST baseline is important for detecting preanesthetic complications and for comparison to perioperative findings for complications and for opti- mizing resuscitation and volume status. Use of Global FAST as Geriatric Health Screening The reader likely has a good idea of the potential for Global FAST to capture disease earlier in its course in older patients presenting once or twice a year for pre- ventive medicine. Global FAST and Saving Images The Global FAST approach takes ~7 minutes for the expe- rienced and properly trained sonographer to acquire its 15 acoustic windows (see Figures 36.3, 36.4, 37.1, and 37.2), which is ~20–25 seconds per view. The author recom- mends setting your machine for a minimum of 6‐second cine clips prospectively and performing each of the 15 views initially as a “pilot” and then repeating and recording the same view so every view is interrogated twice. Unless unrecognizable, the AFAST and TFAST views require no labeling as each are distinct when target organs are included and the heart is unique from the right and left TFAST PCS views. Vet BLUE poses the greatest challenge, which is easily surmountable by making each of its transthoracic views unique. The Caudodorsal lung regions are marked with the cau- dodorsal transition zone by including it at the beginning of the clip. The Perihilar lung regions are marked by only having intercostal spaces. The Middle lung region is marked (or identified) by including the heart at the beginning of its clip. Lastly, the Cranial lung region is marked by including the cranial transition zone of the thoracic inlet at the beginning of its clip. Moreover, performing the AFAST, TFAST, and Vet BLUE examina- tions in the same order every time maintains consis- tency, although the author performs the Global FAST order dependent on patient positioning (see Figures 36.3, 36.4, 37.1, and 37.2). Findings are always recorded on standardized goal‐directed templates (Figure 36.25).

Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 Introduction The use of point‐of‐care ultrasound (POCUS) for uncharacterized shock, cardiopulmonary arrest (CPA), advanced life support (ALS), and cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) has become an important inter - vention for rapidly addressing treatable causes of impending and actual CPA (Breitkreutz et al. 2007, 2010; Link et al. 2015; Soar et al. 2015; Henry et al. 2018). The American Heart Association’s (AHA) CPR guidelines have an important section entitled Knowing your Hs and Ts that lists these potentially treatable con- ditions (Neumar et al. 2010; Lisciandro and Armenise 2014; Andrus 2015; Link et al. 2015; Soar et al. 2015). The “Ruling Out the Hs and Ts Chart” (Table 37.1) is provided with the author’s modifications for small animals and provides the basis for this chapter. Using Global FAST can be lifesaving and helps delegate resources more accurately for those patients that can be saved if their treatable problem is detected soon enough. For example, according to the AHA CPR guidelines and clinical studies, pulseless electrical activity (PEA) in people is often due to a treatable underlying condition (Breitkreutz et al. 2007, 2010; Neumar et al. 2010; Link et al. 2015; Soar et al. 2015). In the author’s experience, these are conditions that are typically causing a pre- load problem or, in other words, poor venous return to the heart. Such conditions include pneumothorax, pericardial effusion, internal bleeding, pulmonary thromboembolism, anaphylaxis, hypoglycemia in a septic patient, and hyperkalemia in urinary obstruction, all treatable with potentially good outcomes for the patient. Thus, if these treatable conditions are detected quickly before the patient incurs significant complica- tions or dies, there is a chance for a favorable patient outcome. The Global FAST approach rapidly screens for many of these treatable conditions and forms of shock (see Tables 37.1, 37.3, and 37.4). What is the most effective screening method for cardiac assessment? A most telling prospective CPR study from several years ago documented that ~75% of people diagnosed with PEA (~51% of the total CPR study population) and ~35% of those with asystole had in fact on echocardiogram demonstrable coordinated cardiac contractions (Breitkreutz et al. 2007, 2010). 730 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER result, the terms “true PEA” and “true asystole” have been applied to people without coordinated cardiac contractions and “pseudo‐PEA” and “pseudo‐asystole” for those having coordinated cardiac contractions. The relevance of this is that people with coordinated cardiac contractions seen using ultrasound had increased survival (Breitkreutz et al. 2007, 2010). Tying this altogether, the Global FAST approach not only surveys for treatable causes of CPA but also assesses for coordinated cardiac contractions, thus helping to direct resources for those patients with treat- able conditions, while also serving as a missing link in the veterinary CPR efforts for improvement (Lisciandro and Armenise 2014; Boller and Fletcher 2012). Even more convincing when considering the AHA guide- lines, ultrasound is either the gold standard test or has higher sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy for most of these Hs and Ts of CPR over traditional approaches without ultrasound. For this reason, Global FAST should be standard of care for CPR and ALS protocols for our veterinary patients (currently lacking), carrying the potential to improve outcome by more accurately directing lifesaving interventions as in human guide- lines (Breitkreutz et al. 2010; Boller and Fletcher 2012; Lisciandro and Armenise 2014; Callaway et al. 2015; Soar et al. 2015; Link et al. 2015; Henry et al. 2018). The RUSH and FAST‐ABCDE ultrasound examina- tions have likewise been developed in people for these same reasons (Neri et al. 2007; Perera et al. 2010; Armenise et al. 2019); however, the Global FAST approach is fast and does more than the RUSH examination (see Table 36.1) and has distinct advan- tages over both RUSH and VetFAST‐ABCDE. Although VetFAST‐ABCDE is a more comprehensive head‐to‐ toe approach, it has additional aspects that are more challenging for nonradiologist sonographers and other related time‐consuming issues such as patient preparation and probe changes. Furthermore, the VetFAST‐ABCDE exam has many objectives that are generally lower yield, not primary causes for shock, CPA and CPR, and are often known based on physical examination, such as ocular injury, neurological status, laryngeal function, collapsing trachea, and tracheal cervical injury. Moreover, VetFAST‐ABCDE likely underestimates its time for completion. The Global FAST approach is a standardized protocol and has exact clarity to all its 15 acoustic windows that take <7 minutes to complete. POCUS eye, POCUS heart, POCUS MSK, POCUS brain, etc. are more often appropriate after resuscitation as add‐on examinations as clinical course dictates. More detailed information on Global FAST is provided in Chapters 6, 7, 17, 18, 22, 23, and 36, and clinically relevant POCUS chapters for the add‐on examinations. What Global FAST for T reatable Shock, ALS, and CPR Can Do • Can detect many of the AHA Hs and Ts of CPR within minutes when minutes count. • Can help dictate resources during CPA and CPR as well as post CPR. • Can rapidly trigger lifesaving ultrasound‐guided procedures. 731 POCUS: GLOBAL FAST – RAPIDLY DETECTING TREATABLE FORMS OF SHOCK, ALS, AND CPR • Can rapidly trigger life‐saving therapeutic inter - ventions by providing a more accurate diagnosis when Hs and Ts are detected. • Can determine return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) by direct visualization of synchronized heart contractions. • Can differentiate between ROSC and PEA. • Can differentiate between true asystole and pseudo‐asystole by “seeing” whether coordinated cardiac contractions are present. • Can assist in tracking (monitoring) resuscitation by detecting the presence or loss of ROSC and surveying for developing complications. • Can assist in tracking (monitoring) resuscitation by assessing volume status through the use of TFAST echo views, FAST DH characterization of the caudal vena cava (CVC) and hepatic veins, and lung through Vet BLUE. • Can guide use of vasopressors using the Global FAST (volume status) approach (see Chapter 36). • Can semiquantitate intraabdominal hemorrhage and need for blood transfusion using the AFAST‐ applied fluid scoring system (see Chapter 7). • Can assess urinary output using the AFAST cysto‐ colic view formula for urinary bladder volume estimation (see Chapters 7 and 36). • Can semiquantitate degree of pneumothorax and track its severity by finding the “lung point” and utilizing the TFAST PTX 1/3s Rule (see Chapters 17 and 36). What Global FAST for T reatable Shock, ALS and CPR Cannot Do • Cannot assess several of the AHA Hs and Ts of CPR, including electrolyte disturbances, blood glucose abnormalities (hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia), body (or core) temperature disturbances (hyper - thermia, hypothermia), intracranial hypertension and vascular accidents, and hypoxemia. • Cannot replace the physical exam. • Cannot replace blood pressure and electrocardio- graphic monitoring. • Cannot replace arterial and venous blood gas eval- uation and other respiratory function assessment. • Cannot characterize effusions based on echo- genicity, so, sampling and fluid analysis and cytology are required. Indications • Any patient with questionable cardiovascular stability. • Any patient with uncharacterized forms of shock. • Any patient with uncharacterized hypotension. • All patients with CPA. • All patients with ROSC as part of ALS and post‐ CPR resuscitation. Objectives • Understand the clinical utility of combining AFAST, TFAST, and Vet BLUE as a single examination called the Global FAST approach for critical patients. • Understand how the Global FAST approach may be used to rule out the Hs and Ts of the AHA CPR guidelines. • Understand how the Global FAST approach may be used for monitoring patients for complications and during resuscitation as a part of ALS. • Understand how the Global FAST approach does more than the RUSH (ultrasound) exam used in people. Ultrasound Settings, Probe Preferences, and Patient Positioning and Preparation Ultrasound Settings and Probe Preference A curvilinear (microconvex) probe with a frequency range of 5–10 MHz and abdominal preset(s) with a depth range of 3–15 cm is generally acceptable for the entire Global FAST examination in most dogs and cats. Optimizing Image Quality and Probe–Skin Contact Hair is generally not shaved but rather parted for as direct as possible probe‐to‐skin contact with the use of isopropyl alcohol, and/or alcohol‐based hand sanitizer, and/or acoustic coupling gel. The author prefers the use of minimal amounts of isopropyl alcohol to effectively part the hair followed by alcohol‐based hand sanitizer. The strategy is much less noxious to your patient by minimizing the cold wetness of isopropyl alcohol and its fumes, especially when moved to an oxygen cage. Alcohol‐based hand sanitizer is an excellent coupling medium and has the added benefit of being easily wiped off and evaporates quickly. Isopropyl alcohol should not be used if electrical defibrillation is anticipated because it poses a burn/fire hazard. The clinician should also be aware that isopropyl alcohol may cause probe head damage and contributes to hypothermia (see Figure 4.13).

732 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Patient Positioning and Most Efficient Ways to Perform There are a couple of highly efficient ways to perform Global FAST in standing and lateral recumbency that minimize depth changes and moving to different sides of the patient. Lateral Recumbency AFAST, beginning with its diaphragmatico‐hepatic (DH) view, is performed first followed by TFAST and its left and right pericardial site (PCS) views with depth and gain settings that are similar, thus rapidly completing six of the 15 Global FAST views (Figure 37.1). After com - pleting the TFAST PCS views, depth is decreased (mag- nify) for the ipsilateral TFAST chest tube site (CTS) view for performing Vet BLUE. Right lateral is advantageous because of the cardiac notch and the heart falling against the thoracic wall for the three major TFAST echo views (see Figures 37.1, and also 17.16, 17.20, 17.21, and 19.3). Left lateral recumbency is used when the patient presents in this position and is most comfortable in left lateral. The AFAST‐applied abdominal fluid scor - ing system is validated in either lateral recumbency but TFAST echo views are generally much easier in right lateral recumbency because of the heart falling against the thoracic wall along with the cardiac notch (see Chapters 17–21). Pearl: The author does not shave patients and does not dim the lighting when performing any part of Global FAST, which is supported by similar findings regarding environmental lighting in the FEEL protocol – that ultrasound imaging is generally not compromised (Breitkreutz et al. 2007, 2010). Moreover, dark environments are potentially haz - ardous when staff are moving around and not time efficient when attempting to locate equipment during CPR and ALS. Figure 37 .1. Global FAST in lateral recumbency. When the patient presents in lateral recumbency, the FAST DH view is per- formed first because it is a window into the thorax without the air interference of the transthoracic views and quickly assesses for obvious pericardial and pleural effusion, cardiac motion, and the CVC as well as providing a deep window into lung along the pulmonary–diaphragmatic interface and information within the abdominal cavity. (A–C) AFAST in a cat is performed first since it is rapid, followed by similar gain and depth setting for the TFAST pericardial site views, and then either in lateral the ipsilateral hemithorax may be evaluated using Vet BLUE and then moving the patient to the opposing lateral for the final Vet BLUE views (both shown) or the patient moved to sternal or standing (shown) to complete the Vet BLUE and HR5th bonus view (right kidney and associated liver). The analogous standardized order is shown in the dog in (D–F). There are 15 acoustic win- dows for Global FAST performed with the same microconvex probe and abdominal preset with only changes in depth, gain, and the focus cursor needed during most studies. 733 POCUS: GLOBAL FAST – RAPIDLY DETECTING TREATABLE FORMS OF SHOCK, ALS, AND CPR Standing or Sternal Recumbency Beginning on the left side of the patient, the left Vet BLUE transthoracic views are performed first followed by the left TFAST PCS view, the DH view, spleno‐renal (SR) view, cysto‐colic (CC) view, and the hepato‐renal umbilical (HRU) view and then the AFAST focused spleen (see Chapters 6–9). The sonog - rapher then moves to the right side of the patient and performs the right Vet BLUE followed by the right TFAST PCS views, ending with the HR5th bonus view (Figure 37.2). Beginning on the left side is advantageous because by the time the sonographer gets to the most time‐ consuming TFAST echo views at the TFAST right PCS views, lung, pleural effusion (PE) and pericar - dial effusion (PCE), caudal vena cava (CVC) assessment, and volume status have already been assessed before ending at the most time‐consuming TFAST echo views. Furthermore, the sonographer already has a good idea of how important these TFAST echo views are and can delay them in unstable patients, having already performed the “Global FAST nonecho fallback views” for left‐ and right‐sided congestive heart failure and volume status, being Vet BLUE and the CVC at the DH view, respectively (see Chapter 36). Dorsal recumbency should always be avoided for several reasons, most importantly because of increased patient risk (Boysen and Lisciandro 2013; Lisciandro 2014a,b,c; Lisciandro and Armenise 2014). A hemodynamically fragile patient that is unknowingly placed in dorsal recumbency undergoes significant negative changes in ventilation and circulation, specifically venous return. Add to these respiratory and cardiovascular stresses the increased oxygen demand in a struggling, anxious patient, and the patient risks acute and potentially catastrophic decompensation. Considering trauma, most dogs and cats have concurrent lung contusions and other thoracic‐related injuries (Powell et al. 1999; Sigrist et al. 2004; Lisciandro et al. 2008, 2009; Boysen et al. 2014; Lisciandro 2011) and considering nontrauma, many hypotensive triaged patients have pleural and/ or PCE and intracavitary bleeds often accompanied by anemia (McMurray et al. 2016; Lisciandro 2016a). Moreover, the abdominal fluid scoring system is not Figure 37 .2. Global FAST in standing (or sternal) positioning. When the patient is standing or sternal, Global FAST may be performed rapidly starting with the Vet BLUE-TFAST blend of left Vet BLUE, numbered 1–4, and then the left TFAST pericardial site view, numbered 5, and DH view, numbered 6, as shown in (A) and (D) in a cat and dog, respectively. AFAST may be continued in standing or sternal using the same external landmarks and probe maneuvering as in right lateral recumbency, or the patient moved to right lateral recumbency as shown in (B) and (E). The patient is then turned and the machine moved or the sonogra- pher moves to the opposing side of the patient so the patient, its holder, and sonographer are all facing the ultrasound screen to perform the right Vet BLUE, numbered 10–13, and right TFAST echocardiography views, numbered 14, followed by the final AFAST view, numbered 15 as shown in (C) and (F). If the AFAST is negative in standing or sternal, then lateral recumbency is generally unnecessary for AFAST fluid scoring. If AFAST is positive in standing or sternal, then when acceptably stable, move the patient to either lateral recumbency, right lateral shown here in (B) and (E), wait 3-minutes to allow fluid to re-distribute, and then abdominal fluid score, repeating the AFAST, numbered 6–9. 736 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER of a right TFAST PCS view with an attenuated left ven- tricular short‐axis “mushroom view” combined with a flat or fluid‐starved CVC helps quickly determine that the patient has hypovolemia (see Figures 17.25, 17.26, 36.7, 36.8, 36.9, and 37.4). Whenever hypovolemia is determined, then the search for a “leak in the tank” is pursued, and the Global FAST approach automatically does this by imaging the peritoneal and pleural cavities, retroperitoneal space, pericardial sac, and lung (Lisciandro 2011, 2012, 2016a; Lisciandro and Armenise 2014; McMurray et al. 2016). Moreover, the AFAST‐applied fluid scoring system is invaluable in semiquantitating volume of blood (and any other effusions) and the patient as a small‐volume versus large‐volume intraabdominal bleeder (Lisciandro et al. 2009, 2015, 2019a; Lisciandro 2011, 2012, 2016b; Boysen and Lisciandro 2013). Although no definitive formula exists for estimating pleural and pericardial effusion in clinical situations (Newitt et al. 2009; Shimali et al. 2010), distances can still be measured for each and estimations as trivial (>0.5 cm), mild (0.5–1 cm), moderate (1–3 cm), and severe (>3 cm) may be made at the suggested level of the costochondral junction at the TFAST PCS views from the intercostal space to the heart in standing and sternal small animals (see Figures 36.13, 36.14). Combining the Global FAST approach findings with the complete clinical profile of the patient helps place cavitary and spatial bleeding (and effusions) into clinical relevance as to the degree of their contribu- tion to the “leak in the tank” or patient volume loss. Hyperkalemia In part, the Global FAST approach helps trigger hyper- kalemia as a major rule‐out or rule‐in for shock, CPA and need for CPR by the finding of an enlarged urinary bladder, dilated ureters, and even prepubic abdominal urethral dilation using the AFAST target organ approach. During AFAST, the kidneys are inter- rogated routinely at the SR, HR, and 5th bonus views. Fluid‐associated urinary tract conditions such as retro- peritoneal effusion and kidney‐related soft tissue abnormalities resulting from urinary tract obstruction (distended urinary bladder, dilated ureters, renal pelvic dilation, hydronephrosis) and acute renal failure can thus readily be detected with minimal training and have been documented in the veterinary literature (Hall et al. 2015; Nevins et al. 2015; Reineke et al. 2017) (see Chapter 11). Often this information is acquired prior to any blood testing when Global FAST is applied as an extension of the physical examination, as advo- cated by the author (Lisciandro and Armenise 2014). Furthermore, ascites and retroperitoneal effusion are rapidly detected. Ascites, when present, should be assigned an abdominal fluid score (AFS) with positive and negative AFAST views also recorded (see Chapter 7 and Appendices). The free fluid should be sampled when safely accessible for fluid analysis and cytology. This Global FAST approach provides evidence‐based information and expedites diagnosis when minutes count (Table 37.2). See Chapters 6, 7, 10, 11, and 39 and also Figure 39.15. As an aside, urinary obstructed dogs and cats develop ascites that is consistent with a uroabdomen. However, the uroabdomen is medically treated. In a recent feline study, ~60% of obstructed cats were positive for pericystic fluid (analogous to the AFAST CC view) and ~35% were positive for retroperitoneal effusion (Nevins et al. 2015). Importantly, the clinical course for the great majority of these cats (and assume the same for dogs) is unaltered from standard care of unblocking with placement of an indwelling urinary collection system along with resuscitation followed by supportive and symptomatic care. The ascites and retroperitoneal effusion will commonly resolve in time as the patient recovers (Nevins et al. 2015). The author proposes that the cause for the effusions lies in inflammation and backpressure of urine against the urinary bladder wall and renal capsule over alternative speculation (Cooper et al. 2010; Gerken et al. 2019). The AFAST‐applied fluid scoring system not only provides an objective semiquantification of the volume but also specifies positive and negative AFAST views, and, as logic would dictate, the origin of the effusion (Lisciandro et al. 2009, 2019a; Lisciandro 2011, 2014a, 2016b; Hnatusko et al. 2019; Gerken et al. 2019). The abdominal fluid scoring system (score and locations) provides distinct advan- tages over the subjective terms trivial, mild, moderate, and severe (Cooper et al. 2010; Gerken et al. 2019). Assigning an AFS provides a means to monitor these cats including on daily patient rounds and recheck evaluations. From author experience, expect the free fluid (medically treated uroabdomen) to nearly or completely resolve within 48 hours post unblocking in cases in which the patient is successfully resusci- tated and its azotemia is resolving. Hypocontractility – Dilated Cardiomyopathy The TFAST echo views are screening tests for left‐ sided and right‐sided strain/failure/overload and generalized systolic cardiac dysfunction. Thus, TFAST rapidly screens for dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM),

737 POCUS: GLOBAL FAST – RAPIDLY DETECTING TREATABLE FORMS OF SHOCK, ALS, AND CPR low fractional shortening (FS%). From the right TFAST PCS view and its left ventricular short‐axis “mushroom view,” poor contractility is often readily apparent to even the most novice, properly trained sonographer (Figure 37.5; see also Figure 37.3). Of course, there are exceptions to the rule and an asystolic heart or a patient with PEA or marked arrhythmias may have an indeterminate TFAST cardiac assessment. However, the Global FAST approach incorporating TFAST echo views carries diagnostic potential to detect DCM over physical exam, blood and urine testing, vital signs and radiography, and by suspect- ing DCM, appropriate therapy and a much different resuscitation strategy takes place. In other words, the capturing of a DCM case helps better keep alive (manage using inotropes and arterial afterload reducers) for the gold standard test of a complete detailed echocardiogram that is generally not imme- diately available when minutes count during triage (see Table 37.2). Normal FS% ranges from 25–45% in dogs and 30–50% in cats (see Chapter 20). Chapters 17, 18, and 21 provide greater detail. Hypertension – Pulmonary Hypertension The TFAST echo views are screening tests for left‐ sided and right‐sided strain/failure/overload and generalized systolic cardiac dysfunction (FS%). Thus, TFAST rapidly screens for pulmonary hypertension (PHT), which is generally easy to appreciate with minimal training and missed by thoracic radiog- raphy because of its nonspecific radiographic fea- tures (Kellihan and Stepien 2010; Kellihan et al. 2015). From the right TFAST pericardial view, the right ventricular (RV) to left ventricular (LV) ratio is used to assess for right ventricular dilation. An enlarged RV:LV , in which the RV is almost the same size as the LV , supports types of right‐sided failure including PHT. Integrating information is a key part of the Global FAST approach. Thus, the additional finding at the left ventricular short‐axis “mushroom view” of flattening of the interventricular septum and observing a dis- tended or FAT CVC with hepatic venous distension, referred to as the “tree trunk sign” (Lisciandro 2014a,b, T able 37 .2. 740 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER The Ts Covered by Global FAST T ension Pneumothorax The rapid detection of pneumothorax (PTX) is possible using the Global FAST approach in both spontaneously and mechanically ventilated patients. Imaging strategies have improved for “lung sliding” through the incorporation of the TFAST and Vet BLUE “tricks of the trade.” These include the “one‐eyed gator sign” by placing rib in the middle of the screen to scatter echoes, changing the angle of insonation to ricochet the echoes off the reflective aerated lung surface, or performing both sonographic maneuvers simultaneously. These sonographic manipulations are explained and illustrated in more detail in Chapters 17, 18, 22, and 23. In intubated patients, controlled positive pressure ventilation helps easily rule PTX in and out because the respirophasic timing for observing “lung sliding” is controlled. Lastly, use of the “lung point” concept not only further supports the accurate diagnosis of PTX but also semiquanti - tates the degree of PTX as well as serving as a tracking tool, the TFAST PTX 1/3s Rule (Lisciandro et al. 2008; Figure 37 .7 . Tension pneumothorax and using the “lung point” and TFAST PTX 1/3s Rule for semiquantitating degree of pneumothorax. The use of the “lung point” and the TFAST PTX 1/3s Rule with the patient in sternal or standing helps differen- tiate trivial from moderate and severe PTX. The author calls the difference in positioning of lateral to sternal‐standing the “parking garage – skyscraper effect” that is obvious in being able to categorize PTX with more levels. Moreover, in lateral recum- bency, especially with positive pressure ventilation, the free air gets pushed into unnatural regions and has been referred to as a “double lung point.” Be aware of the phenomenon if your patient must be in lateral recumbency and avoid the confounder by moving your patient into sternal‐standing when possible. T rauma – Hemorrhage Hemorrhage (and other effusions) may be rapidly screened for using the Global FAST approach with four cavities or spaces plus lung (Lisciandro et al. 2009; Lisciandro 2011, 2012, 2014a,b,c; Lisciandro and Armenise 2014; Lisciandro 2016a; McMurray et al. 2016). These four areas are the peritoneal cavity, retro- peritoneal space, pleural cavity, pericardial sac plus lung. Importantly, the volume of hemorrhage that can be maximally present varies with each of these locations, as large blood volumes are possible within the peritoneal and pleural cavities and retroperitoneal space but only much smaller blood volumes are gener- ally possible in the less forgiving pericardial sac (affects cardiac output) and lung (affects ventilation). The accumulation within these two locations leads to cardiac and ventilatory failure detected much sooner as secondary events in contrast to the other three locations in which much larger volumes are generally necessary for overt clinical signs. However, the Vet BLUE B‐line scoring system provides a severity score (numbers of B‐lines and their distribution) and serves as a monitoring tool. Furthermore, the AFAST‐applied fluid scoring system can semiquantitate the volume and expected degree of anticipated anemia through the small‐volume versus large‐volume bleeder concept (see Chapter 7) (Figure 37.8; see also Figures 7.2, 7.3, 7.4, 7.5, and 7.8 and for cats Figures 39.24, 39.25, and 39.26). The use of the AFAST‐applied fluid scoring system helps with decision making regarding need for blood transfusion and exploratory surgery dependent on the clinical profile of the patient (Table 37.3). See Chapters 6, 7, 22, and 23 for more detailed information. Thromboembolism – Pulmonary Thromboembolism The detection of thromboembolism in small animals (quadrupeds) is different than in people (bipeds) for two major reasons. The first, deep venous thrombosis (DVT) readily detectable using POCUS in people, has not been described to our knowledge in the canine and feline hindleg(s), and it is unknown if there is indeed any clinical relevance in small animals (see Chapter 25). Thus, within this category, pulmonary thromboembolism (PTE) appears to be the major player in veterinary medicine, although other major veins have been reported to have thrombi (see Chapter 25). The second reason is the ability to detect PTE, which is dependent on whether it may be imaged directly, such as in the pulmonary arteries in the vicinity of their bifurcation, or its effects seen indirectly during Global FAST, such as right ventricular enlargement from acute pulmonary hypertension or the periphery of lung and the “wedge sign” of Vet BLUE (Figures 37.9 and 37.10) (Lisciandro 2013). The gold standard test for PTE is contrast pulmonary angiography using computed tomography (CTPA) along with specialized equipment for contrast injection (Goggs et al. 2014). However, this modality carries risks, including patient movement to radiology, intravenous contrast agents, chemical restraint and often endotra- cheal intubation for full breath studies (Goggs et al. 2014). Furthermore, CTPA is limited to larger PTE and may miss smaller PTE in the lung periphery that would be potentially detected using lung ultrasound. Alternatively, the Global FAST approach may be used for both direct and indirect evidence of PTE directly by visualization of the PTE within the pulmonary artery(ies) or indirectly by acute cor pulmo- nale and an enlarged right ventricle during TFAST (see Chapters 17–21) and the “wedge sign” in upper lung fields, Caudodorsal and Perihilar regions during Vet BLUE (Mathis et al. 2005; Mastruzzo et al. 2008; Lisciandro 2013; Lee et al. 2015) (see Chapters 22 and 23, Figures 23.2 and 23.19). T amponade – Pericardial Effusion The TFAST sonographic diagnosis for PCE is gener - ally easier for most sonographers than determining the presence of cardiac tamponade. The accurate TFAST diagnosis of PCE is described in Chapter 17 (Figure 37.11) (Lisciandro 2014b, 2016a). The determi- nation of cardiac tamponade can be an intimidating proposition for the noncardiologist sonographer. Most specifically, the diagnosis of cardiac tamponade is the imaging of diastolic collapse of the right atrium and ventricle. However, supportive evidence for tam- ponade often includes larger volume pericardial effu- sions (>0.5–1.0 cm), a distended CVC and hepatic veins (FAT CVC and tree trunk sign), along with a patient history of acute collapse and weakness (Figure 37.12). In people, a fluid‐responsive CVC rules out cardiac tamponade because by definition, cardiac tamponade is obstructive shock and thus the CVC would be a FAT with little change in height dur - ing phases of respiration. In people with a fluid‐ responsive CVC with PCE, the attending clinician is to look elsewhere (do a Global FAST‐like approach, i.e., FAST and RUSH) for the cause of acute weakness and collapse because the CVC does not support cardiac tamponade (Himelman et al. 1988; Candotti and Arntfield 2015; Tchernodrinski and Arntfield 2015). Importantly, radiography is an unreliable test (Guglielmini et al. 2012; Côté et al. 2013). The DH view is a rapid way to rule PCE in and out, and make a case for cardiac tamponade (see Figures 17.13, 18.18, and 37.11). The DH view advantageously images through the acoustic window of the liver and gallbladder, avoiding interference from lung that is often problematic via transthoracic TFAST and POCUS heart views (Lisciandro 2014a,b, 2016a, 2019a). Furthermore, if CPR is being performed, the DH view may be performed without interrupting thoracic compressions. The DH view utilizes the strategy of imaging toward the muscular apex of the heart. The “racetrack sign” represents the rounding of PCE around the muscular apex of the heart where there are no heart chambers to confound the sonographer and less interference of lung (air) using the acoustic window provided by the liver and gallbladder (see Figures 7.13, 18.17, 18.18, and Chapter 18) (Lisciandro 2014a,b, 2016a, 2019a). At this level there are no atria. The finding of PCE causing obstructive shock that has lead to CPA and the need for CPR is an immediate indication for lifesaving emergent pericardiocentesis (Boller and Fletcher 2012; Callaway et al. 2012; Link et al. 2015; Soar et al. 2015). Moreover, open‐chest CPR and pericardotomy may be indicated depending on the patient subset (Neumar et al. 2010; Callaway et al. 2012; Link et al. 2015; Soar et al. 2015; Henry et al. 2018). If open‐chest CPR takes place, the attending vet- erinarian must be prepared to surgically address a rup- tured cardiac chamber (Sandanaga et al. 1990; Witt et al. 2000; Witt and Mayhew 2011; Neilsen et al. 2005; Morges et al. 2011; Ployart et al. 2013). 749 POCUS: GLOBAL FAST – RAPIDLY DETECTING TREATABLE FORMS OF SHOCK, ALS, AND CPR congestive heart failure, including pulmonary hyper - tension, and dogs that fit the profile of hemorrhagic gastroenteritis syndrome (HGE) (see Tables 37.2 and 7.5) (Lisciandro 2014a,b, 2016a, 2019a; Vientós‐Plotts et al. 2019). The use of the Global FAST approach in these cases prevents satisfaction of search error because the gallbladder halo sign is not pathogno- monic, and differentiating the “anaphylactic gallbladder” from the “cardiac gallbladder” is imperative in the triage setting. The differentiation between “anaphylactic gallbladder and “cardiac gallbladder” can be accomplished at the DH view by characterizing the CVC and its associated hepatic veins. In canine anaphylaxis, the CVC is flat with a small maximum height and little dynamic change in its height over several respiratory cycles, versus right‐sided heart failure, including PCE and DCM, in which the CVC is FAT with increased maximum height and little dynamic change in height over several respiratory cycles (see Tables 7.6 and 36.11). The Global FAST approach is very important for avoiding satisfaction of search error by including imaging of the abdomen, AFAST, and thorax, TFAST and Vet BLUE, including the pleural cavity, pericardial sac, heart, and lung. Thus, the Global FAST approach should be considered standard of care by providing an unbiased standardized set of imaging data points. Comparison of Global FAST and the RUSH Examination Global FAST provides more information in small ani- mals than the RUSH (Rapid Ultrasound in Shock) pro- tocol by having a fluid scoring system that predicts the degree of anemia and semiquantitates volume, a “lung point” and the TFAST PTX 1/3s Rule for degree of PTX (sternal or standing position), a urinary bladder estimation formula that over time can estimate urine output, and more lung via Vet BLUE with its six lung ultrasound signs, its B‐line scoring system, and its lung contusion severity score (Perera et al. 2010; Lisciandro 2011, 2014c; Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2016, 2017; Ward et al. 2017; Lisciandro and Fosgate 2017; Dicker et al. 2019) (see Table 36.1). Global FAST and RUSH have a similar general premise to use clinically relevant life- saving ultrasound information that is readily available in the abdomen, retroperitoneal space and thorax, and in RUSH for cardiac conditions including the aorta and indirect signs of PTE by searching for DVT (compres- sion technique on legs), conditions unique to people, in addition to both formats’ use for patient volume assessment (Perera et al. 2010). The RUSH protocol may be used as a primary or secondary survey and helps guide resuscitative efforts and similarly address the Hs and Ts of CPR, ideally before CPA occurs and CPR is needed. In the San Antonio area, trauma surgeons and emergency physicians are trained to combine FAST and RUSH, which better approximates the Global FAST approach. In other words, the mindset is one of integrating information. And the sonographer during FAST is right there imaging heart, lung, vena cava, and hepatic veins (with the addition of aorta and deep venous thrombosis in people). So why not pay more attention with a standardized cerebral integrative Global FAST approach rather than just “flashing”? Global FAST has the following features lacking in FAST‐RUSH approach: • an AFAST‐applied abdominal fluid scoring system that predicts the degree of anticipated anemia • an AFAST target organ approach for obvious soft tissue abnormalities • an AFAST cysto‐colic view urinary bladder volume estimation formula for noninvasive urine output estimation • the “lung point” and TFAST PTX 1/3s Rule for assessing the severity of pneumothorax and tracking its course • Vet BLUE for a more comprehensive lung evalua- tion (see Table 36.1). The major difference between RUSH and Global FAST is the evaluation of the aorta (and for DVT) because people have a higher prevalence of aortic aneurysm and dissection that would be missed during FAST without this add‐on ultrasound assessment. Global FAST for Rapidly Detecting Treatable Forms of Shock By dividing the cardiovascular‐respiratory systems into the RUSH exam categories of the “pump” (TFAST echocardiography), the “tank” (the CVC and hepatic veins, and TFAST and AFAST for effusions), and the “pipes” (TFAST and AFAST for effusions and Vet BLUE for PTE and other lung pathology), types of shock may be distinguished. The different types of shock and their features regarding the “pump,” “tank,” and “pipes” are summarized in Table 37.4.

750 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Final Comments on the Global FAST Approach The Global FAST approach provides a baseline of an unbiased set of 15 data imaging points of the abdomen and thorax. Its 15 acoustic windows (views) have exact clarity in relation to their image acquisition and their objectives through the use of goal‐directed templates. Importantly, the Global FAST approach avoids selective imaging and satisfaction error. Thus, Global FAST should be performed in all patients followed by targeted POCUS exams to avoid such error. Lastly, the compo- nents of Global FAST have been studied more than any other FAST or POCUS exams in veterinary medicine, with over 16 clinical studies (Lisciandro et al. 2008, 2009, 2014, 2015, 2017, 2018, 2019a,b; Lisciandro and Fosgate 2017, 2018; Kulhavy and Lisciandro 2015, 2018; Lisciandro 2012, 2013, 2016a,b, 2019a; McMurray et al. 2016; Ward et al. 2017, 2018a,b, 2019; Yarto and Lisciandro 2017; Dicker et al. 2019; Hnatusko et al. 2019).
