751 POCUS: GLOBAL FAST – RAPIDLY DETECTING TREATABLE FORMS OF SHOCK, ALS, AND CPR (see Figures 37.1 and 37.2), which averages ~20–25 seconds per view. Think about the Global FAST exam- ination and its acoustic windows. The five AFAST views have a standardized probe maneuver of fan, rock cranially, and return to the starting point of that view. Vet BLUE is the repetition of the same method- ology for six and arguably eight of its transthoracic windows. The Global FAST examination may be in reality reduced to 4–5 different probe maneuvers. The author’s point is the true simplicity of performing the Global FAST approach with our current improved and evolving methodology. The author recommends setting your machine for a minimum of 6‐second cine clips prospectively and performing each of the 15 views initially as a “pilot,” followed by repeating and recording the same view so it is interrogated twice. Global FAST images, unless unrecognizable, generally require no labeling as each of its acoustic windows is distinct. When the AFAST order and its target organ approach are per - formed according to protocol (see Chapters 6 and 7), labeling is not required unless the view is unrecog- nizable. TFAST and its echo views are undeniable from the left pericardial to the right pericardial site views because the orientation of the heart is so inherently different dependent on left versus right side. Lastly, Vet BLUE poses the most identification problems which are easily overcome by performing the protocol moving from Caudodorsal to Perihilar to Middle and then finishing at the Cranial lung region view and marking each as follows: the Caudodorsal lung region view by its caudodorsal transition zone, which will be from the right of the screen, while including abdominal structures; the Perihilar lung region with no defining features; the Middle lung region by briefly including the heart in the image; and the Cranial lung region with its cranial transition zone, which will from the left of the screen, while including soft tissue neck. Furthermore, performing the AFAST, TFAST and Vet BLUE exami- nations in the same order (following protocol) every time maintains consistency. Global FAST and Goal‐Directed Templates The sonographer must record their findings for an effective Global FAST ultrasound program (see Figure 36.25A,B). The Global FAST template should be blended with the AFAST, TFAST, and Vet BLUE in the order that you typically perform the examination. Two Global FAST goal‐directed template versions are probably best, one with the patient standing and one for when the patient presents in lateral recum- bency. The methodology and order are explained in the beginning sections of this chapter and Chapter 36. The entire examination may be performed in standing‐sternal, making lateral unnecessary unless the patient is AFAST positive for free fluid, or right lateral positioning would provide better TFAST echo views, imaging of the caudal vena cava, or other suspect abnormalities requiring additional scanning planes. Global FAST for Advanced Life Support and Patient Management Global FAST is used as a tool to direct resuscitation and screen for complications. See Chapter 36 for life- saving surveillance to maximize a favorable outcome in the patient in shock, that has experienced CPA, and those that have ROSC. Pearls and Pitfalls, The Final Say • Global FAST and its 15 defined acoustic windows have exact clarity and thus provide a standardized unbiased set of imaging data points of the abdomen and thorax, including heart and lung. • Global FAST is the most published, clinically vali- dated approach in the peer‐reviewed veterinary literature for each of its components – AFAST, TFAST, and Vet BLUE. • Global FAST takes approximately 6–7 minutes (~25 seconds per acoustic window) for the experi- enced properly trained sonographer and may be performed in standing/sternal or lateral recum- bency or combinations thereof. • Global FAST is an effective means to evaluate for the AHA Hs and Ts of CPR for rapid detection of treatable forms of shock, impending CPA, ALS and during CPR. • As dictated by clinical course, POCUS examina- tions may be added as adjunctive POCUS evalua- tions, such as ocular, musculoskeletal, abdominal organs, heart and vascular.

Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 Introduction The FAST‐ABCDE protocol was first developed in human medicine to identify, manage, and treat the most common injuries in traumatized patients (Neri et al. 2007) and has been recently adapted to veterinary patients (Armenise et al. 2019). The intent of the human protocol was to provide credentials through specific training programs after the achievement of accepted standards of knowledge in diagnostic ultrasonography (Neri et al. 2007). FAST‐ABCDE consists of a trans- versal approach to problems and solutions with three different levels of ultrasonography practice, general, comprehensive and expert, consistent with the mul- tiple goal‐directed, multisystem, time‐dependent vision of critical care professionals (Neri et al. 2007). Ultrasound skills expected for the general level are known alphabetically as: • A – airway (airway – patency and ventilation; trachea – displacement, lesion, hematomas, tumors; esophagus – endotracheal tube displacement, pran- dial status) • B – breathing (lung – absence of ventilation, pneu- mothorax [PTX], subcutaneous emphysema, pleural effusion, alveolar‐interstitial syndrome, lung con- solidation, diaphragmatic lesions) • C – circulation (cardiac/hemodynamic assessment – asystole, pulseless electrical activity [PEA] vs pseudo‐PEA, cardiac tamponade, severe left ven- tricular [LV] dysfunction, acute cor pulmonale, biventricular dysfunction, cardiac tumors, eval- uation of inferior vena cava [IVC]; pericardial effusion; abdominal effusion; retroperitoneal space abnormalities; placenta abnormalities; central deep vein thrombosis; aorta abdominal and proximal arch aneurysm) • D – disability (optic nerve sheath diameter [ONSD] enlargement, neonatal/infant hemorrhage, pupil evaluations, cerebral midline shift, cervical spine displacement) • E – exposure (full access to all areas, preventing the misdiagnosis of life‐threatening ABCDE lesions and emerging conditions) (Neri et al. 2007). Additionally, some ultrasound‐guided procedures are included, such as evaluation of endotracheal intubation, tracheostomy, thoracentesis, pericardio- centesis, peripheral and central vascular puncture, venous cutdown, nasogastric tube insertion, and urinary catheterization (Neri et al. 2007). The entire curriculum described may be adapted to the canine and feline critically ill patient, to provide a full ultrasonographic evaluation in time‐dependent scenarios with the final objective of more accurately and expediently diagnosing life‐threatening injuries, thus potentially improving critical diagnosis and treatment processes. The veterinary FAST‐ABCDE (VetFAST‐ABCDE) shows a higher accuracy compared to conventional radiology for the diagnosis of trauma lesions (Armenise et al. 2019), similar to prospective AFAST and TFAST studies (Lisciandro et al. 2008, 2009). VetFAST‐ABCDE consists of serial exams often com- pleted in <10 minutes, similar to findings in human applications (Neri et al. 2007). After mastering the skills needed for the lungs, heart and abdominal views, add‐on evaluations of the eye and upper airway should be learned. VetFAST‐ABCDE, although more technically chal- lenging, incorporates the evaluation of the upper airways, a variant of lung and heart scans, and the evaluation of the ONSD as a marker for intracranial hypertension. 758 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER What POCUS: VetFAST‐ABCDE Can Do • Rapidly detect several of the Ts of cardiopulmonary arrest (CPA) including Tension PTX, Tamponade (pericardial effusion), Trauma (bleeding in large spaces such as pleural, peritoneal, retroperitoneal), and possibly Thromboembolism (lung) and Throm- bosis (heart [myocardial infarction and its sequelae of ventricular fibrillation]). • Rapidly assist in differentiating shock syndromes (hypovolemic, cardiogenic, distributive, obstructive and hypoxic). • Rapidly assist in diagnosis through the triggering of interventional guided‐ultrasound procedures (see Chapters 43 and 44). • Determine the return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) by direct visualization of synchronized heart contractions. • Differentiate between ROSC and PEA. • Confirm whether “pseudo” or “true” asystole is present as shown in humans with flat line ECG tracings who have coordinated heart movements with POCUS heart scans. • Assist in resuscitation by detecting the presence or loss of ROSC, the patient’s volume status and con- tractility (left ventricular short‐axis “mushroom” view and long‐axis views), left‐sided heart status (presence of B‐lines), and right‐sided volume status (FAST dia- phragmatico‐hepatic [DH] view, CVC responsiveness and size, and degree of hepatic venous distension). • Potentially assist in resuscitation by detecting the presence of intracranial hypertension through a measurement of the ONSD. • Monitor for complications of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) such as PTX, pulmonary edema or lung contusions, bleeding into any major spaces, hypovolemia, the development of intracranial hypertension, and others. • May be able to indirectly characterize interstitial edema (B‐lines) as blood (lung contusions) versus forms of pulmonary edema by correlating lung ultrasound findings with the patient’s clinical profile. What POCUS: VetFAST‐ABCDE Cannot Do • Cannot detect several of the Hs of CPA including electrolyte, blood glucose, body (or core) tempera- ture disturbances, and hypoxemia. • Cannot replace blood pressure, electrocardiographic and central venous pressure monitoring. • Cannot replace arterial venous blood gas and other respiratory monitoring. • Cannot characterize effusions based on echogenicity. • Cannot replace appropriate ultrasound training for some of the advanced imaging tasks in the VetFAST‐ABCDE platform. Indications In the emergency and critical care scenarios, using a problem‐based, multidisciplinary approach during resuscitation efforts (shock, advanced life support [ALS], and CPR). 759 POCUS: VETFAST-ABCDE Objectives VetFAST‐ABCDE is used in critical scenarios including shock states, during, before and after CPR and ALS. • Assess upper airway for injury. • Assess laryngeal function. • Assess for pneumothorax. • Assess for pleural and pericardial effusion. • Assess cardiac function. • Assess for abdominal effusion. • Assess eye injury. • Assess for intracranial hypertension via ONSD. • Monitor for developing injuries and complications during and post resuscitation. Ultrasound Settings, Probe Preferences, and Patient Positioning A multifrequency curvilinear (microconvex) probe (5–8 MHz) is used for the entire VetFAST‐ABCDE exam, allowing adequate evaluation of both superficial and deep structures over a wide range of patient sizes in dogs and cats. However, a phased‐array (sector) probe is preferred to better evaluate cardiac perfor - mance and a linear probe is preferred over a curvi- linear probe for superficial structures such as ONSD evaluation, airway, and thoracic views. Patient positioning is adapted to how the patient presents, thus minimizing the stress of respiratory com- promised patients by allowing sternal recumbency, which is preferred by the author. Lateral recumbency is acceptable, and after evaluation of the presented side, the patient is repositioned onto the opposite side to complete the exam. The author prefers to clip the hair to reduce artifacts. Solutions of 70% isopropyl alcohol should not be used if skin wounds are present or electrical defibrillation is anticipated, since alcohol poses a burn hazard to the patient and fire/explosion hazard to the hospital environment. Alternatively, the author uses acoustic coupling gel or saline solution. How to do the POCUS: VetFAST‐ABCDE Exam Airway (A) Ultrasound airway assessment begins with a rapid transverse scan of the larynx and the trachea, then proceeding distally to the thoracic inlet. The larynx normally appears sonographically as a hypoechoic structure behind the thyroid cartilages (Figure 38.1A,B). In contrast, the trachea appears as a hypoechoic curve surrounding a hyperechoic space followed by air reverberation artifact noted by several A‐lines due to the presence of free air (Figure 38.1C,D). Endotracheal placement may also be confirmed using ultrasound as follows: directly by looking for the presence of a hyper- echoic linear artifact below the normal tracheal appear- ance (Chou et al. 2013) or by visualizing an improperly esophageally placed endotracheal tube next to the tra- chea, referred to as the “double tract sign” (Figure 38.2); or indirectly looking for the presence of “lung sliding” (Weaver et al. 2006; Zechner and Breitkreutz 2011). The latter has been shown to be faster and equally or more reliable than chest auscultation and capnography for confirming endotracheal intubation in people (Pfeiffer et al. 2012). The complete upper airway evaluation in the author’s experience is performed in <1.5 minutes, providing important information regarding the presence or absence of normal regional anatomy (mus- cles, veins and arteries, thyroid) and the integrity of upper airway structures. The upper airway evaluation also helps in the diagnosis of laryngeal paralysis by observing for laryngeal motion during respiration and the diagnosis of tracheal collapse by direct visual estimates and comparison between the diameter of the first and most distally accessible cervical tracheal rings during the phases of respiration (Rudorf et al. 2001; Eom et al. 2008) (Figure 38.3). Breathing (B) Thoracic evaluation consists of a scan of both hemitho- races by surveying the thorax in the upper, middle, and lower thirds between the fourth and ninth inter - costal spaces (Figure 38.4). The “B” exam is performed as a continuum along intercostal spaces cranially to caudally and dorsally to ventrally. The “B” lung ultra- sound carries the potential to characterize different types of lung injury, including pneumothorax (A‐lines with no lung sliding), pulmonary contusions (B‐lines), forms of pulmonary edema, although B‐lines are non- specific and must be placed into clinical context; and lung consolidation, also placed into clinical context to discriminate between severe lung contusions and bronchopneumonia or other forms of lung consolida- tion (see Chapters 22 and 23). The “B” scan evaluates the thorax in upper, middle, and lower thirds so when PTX is present, it may deter- mine the location of the “lung point” and thus assess the degree of PTX as partial based on where the “lung

The “lung point” is the physical location along the thorax where aerated lung reop - poses the thoracic wall, most commonly determined by finding the resumption of “lung sliding” (Figure 38.6A–C) or ultrasound lung rockets also called B‐ lines (Figure 38.6D). The lung pulse, however, is a third lung ultrasound finding, defined as collapsed lung directly against the thoracic wall gliding rhyth - mically with each heart beat (Volpicelli et al. 2012). The VetFAST‐ABCDE breathing evaluation in the author’s experience usually requires <3–4 minutes (Armenise et al. 2019). 762 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER spaces at the dorsal/middle part of the thorax (Cambournac et al. 2018). The general rule in human resuscitation is that fluid resuscitation continues as long as the IVC diameter shows responsiveness during fluid challenges by dis - tending (larger diameter) and contracting (smaller diameter) with pre‐ and postfluid boluses, respectively, or until resuscitation endpoints have been met. However, when the IVC becomes distended, losing this dynamic change, patient preload has been maxi - mized (Moretti and Pizzi 2010; Machare‐Delgado et al. 2011). More detailed information may be found in Chapters 26, 36, and 37. A veterinary study similarly evaluated the respon - siveness of CVC diameter during fluid challenges, finding that the CVC at the level of the diaphragm, a different location than VetFAST‐ABCDE but the same used for Global FAST, became distended with volume overload. The CVC and associated hepatic veins reflected a high central venous pressure in their exper- imentally resuscitated dogs (Nelson et al. 2010). Furthermore, the same study sonographically detected gallbladder wall edema (“halo sign”) and pancreatic edema with volume overload (Nelson et al. 2010) (Figure 38.8). In dogs, the CVC diameter (CVC d) and aortic (Ao) ratio (CVC d:Ao) independent of patient size have been shown to be a third way in which to guide fluid resuscitation (Cambournac et al. 2018) (Figure 38.9) (see Chapter 26). Disability (D) Disability consists of measuring the ONSD for intra - cranial hypertension assessment. Safe eye prepara - tion is mandated with the use of an aqueous‐based ultrasound gel labeled for eye use to prevent serious corneal injury (see Chapter 27). The ONSD is mea - sured 3 mm behind the globe, using an electronic caliper and an axis perpendicular to the optic nerve (Figure 38.10). For consistent results, the ONSD technique should be standardized by scanning in the same manner. The author evaluates the left eye with a transverse view through the ventral eyelid with the marker of the probe on the right side, thus visualizing the optic nerve on the right of the screen with the probe marker on the left of the screen (see Figure 38.10). 764 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER as it leaves the posterior eye and appears as an isoechoic line bordered by a hypoechoic line, both laterally and medially (Figure 38.10B). Alternately, the ONSD scan may be performed by placing the probe directly on the cornea with the use of acoustic coupling gel or other medium approved as safe for ophthalmic use. The optic nerve is an extension of the central nervous system (CNS) because of the intraorbital subarachnoid space that surrounds it. Thus, it is subjected to the same pressure changes as the intra - cranial compartment (Geeraerts et al. 2007). The ONSD may be used as an ultrasonographically visible marker for the detection of increased intracra - nial pressure (ICP) by measurements of its diameter and increases in its width. Conversely, decreases in the measurements would support a decreasing ICP . In patients with pathologically elevated ICP (intra - cranial hypertension), perineural cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is displaced into the intraorbital sheath, enlarging the animal’s ONSD. In dogs, a correlation between increased ICP and increased ONSD has been demonstrated in experimentally induced increased ICP (Ilie et al. 2015). Figures 38.6. 765 POCUS: VETFAST-ABCDE In dogs, normal ONSD measured 3 mm from the eye’s posterior wall is ≤2.7 mm, and ≥3.0 mm is considered abnormal (Armenise et al. 2012) (Figure 38.10C). In patients with abnormally measured ONSD and clinical signs related to intra - cranial hypertension, management to decrease ICP is urgently warranted and importantly, response to therapy should be monitored by serial ONSD measurements. The use of the ONSD is especially helpful in heavily sedated or anesthetized veteri - nary patients unable to have accurate mentation assessment. Figure 38.7 . 766 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Recently, a similar method was proposed for scanning from the upper eyelid, fanning the probe dorsally and ventrally to optimize the ONSD evaluation (Smith et al. 2018). Although a comparison between ultra - sound and MRI was not performed, there seems to exist a correlation between age, breed, body weight, and ONSD measurements in normal patients so further studies are necessary to better use ultrasound as a non- invasive method to monitor ICP in dogs and cats (Smith et al. 2018). In summary, ocular ultrasound has been shown to be superior in some trauma‐related conditions when compared to computed tomography (Ritchie et al. 2012). Exposure (E) Serial VetFAST‐ABCDE evaluations are clinically help- ful because serial FAST exams have been shown to increase sensitivity by detecting occult or missed potentially life‐threatening injuries and conditions on initial scans (Blackbourne et al. 2004; Ollerton et al. 2006). Moreover, serial exams may be used to detect complications and for monitoring response to therapy. Serial VetFAST‐ABCDE examinations should be per - formed in all stable patients four hours post admission, as recommended by the American College of Emergency Physicians (www.acep.org) and as fre - quently as every 15–30 minutes in unstable patients. Clinical Significance and Implications of Abnormal VetFAST‐ABCDE Exam Findings The VetFAST‐ABCDE format represents an important clinical tool for the nonradiologist emergency physi - cian, trauma surgeon, intensivist, anesthesiologist, and other pertinent specialties. The protocol is used to assess the “3 Ts” (T 3), standing for trauma, triage and tracking, to expediently diagnose and better manage life‐threatening injuries otherwise occult or speculated based on traditional means without ultrasound and advanced imaging. Airway (A) Confirmation of endotracheal tube (ET) placement may be made in two ways: directly by the “double trachea sign” or indirectly by looking for bilateral “lung sliding” with positive pressure ventilation (see Chapters 17 and 18). 768 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER improperly placed ET tubes may be recognized by observing the “double trachea sign” in which two hyperechoic (bright white) curved structures (the trachea and the misplaced esophageally located ET tube) are side by side (see Figure 38.2C). Otherwise, the indirect method should be performed after all ET intubation, to rule out improper esophageal intubation and unwanted single bronchi intubation. Upper airway obstruction is suspected from the loss of normal A‐lines extending beyond the tracheal rings, because of echogenic material displacing air in the near‐field. Soft tissue may echogenically reflect more benign signs such as significant intratracheal secretions or the more concerning mass. In either case, secretions versus masses are indistinguishable without a more formal ultrasound study, additional imaging, or direct visual examination (by sight or fiberoptically). Laryngeal paralysis may be diagnosed through monolateral or bilateral absence or asymmetry of movement with the respiratory cycle of the arytenoid cartilages, although no studies exist, to the author’s knowledge, regarding the learning and accuracy of this skill. Figure 38.10. Probe positioning and orientation for optic nerve imaging for optic nerve sheath diameter measurements. Horizontally oriented image of a normal canine left eye as shown in (A). The transducer was placed on the ventral eyelid with the probe marker to the right. The optic nerve (located on the right of the image) is visualized as an isoechoic linear structure surrounded by two hyperechoic lines which represent the intraorbital subarachnoid space unlabeled and labeled in (B) and (C), respectively. Discrimination between extraocular muscles (located on the left of the image) and the optic nerve, which can look similar, may be made using color flow Doppler, since the optic nerve has blood vessels on either side. While mastering identification of the optic nerve, it is recommended that the exam be performed in the same manner for each evaluation.

769 POCUS: VETFAST-ABCDE Tracheal rupture can be detected through recog - nized deviations, step signs, from the expected curved or linear continuity of the trachea throughout its cervical course (Figure 38.11). Regional hematomas/masses may be detected by the presence of echogenic irregularities to adjacent soft tissues and their displacement of the larynx, trachea, veins or arteries. Foreign bodies within the cervical esophageal lumen can be responsible for airway obstruction and respiratory distress (Figure 38.12). Jugular veins and carotid artery abnormalities may be detected by the presence of thrombi or aneurisms. Breathing (B) VetFast‐ABCDE consists in ~18 intercostal spaces per each hemithorax (~6 in each – the upper, middle and lower thirds), compared to TFAST (two pulmonary acoustic windows per hemithorax) and Vet BLUE (12 pulmonary acoustic per hemithorax plus the FAST diaphragmatico‐ hepatic [DH] view), dividing the thoracic scan field differ- ently. The formats use the same “wet lung” versus “dry lung” concept and the use of the “lung point.” Circulation (C) Valvular function may be evaluated for obvious mitral and tricuspid abnormalities, looking for any degenerative proliferation and insufficiency. Right‐ sided and left‐sided conditions and volume status problems are similarly screened for as with Global FAST (see Chapters 36 and 37). Disability (D) Ocular sonography is used to screen for any obvious ocular trauma or pathology (retinal detachment, lens luxation, intraocular abnormalities within the eye and periocular) and to measure ONSD (Figure 38.13). Canine ONSD >3 mm according to one study suggests intracranial hypertension (ICH) and the finding placed within clinical context potentially triggers (ICH) therapy (Armenise et al. 2019). Moreover, ONSD may also be used serially to monitor response to therapy. ONSD has not been evaluated in cats and the full clinical utility of ONSD in dogs for ICH requires continued study. The reader is referred to Chapter 27 for greater detail on safely performing ocular ultra - sound and examples of eye pathology. Fractures and herniation may also be sonographi - cally detected at triage, when either radiography is not readily available or the patient cannot be transported. Figure 38.11. Tracheal injury. Tracheal rupture, laceration or other injury is recognized by observing disruption of the normal continuity of the trachea’s near‐field (bright white line) border, a step sign. Here in transverse with a microconvex probe, the trachea’s normal linear continuity is not visualized because of tracheal rupture and its associated deviations and shadowing from maligned cartilaginous tracheal rings. Figure 38.12. Longitudinal scan of the esophagus. In the caudal part of the espohagus, an irregular hyperechoic structure (thin arrow) is seen with an associated hypoechoic structure (bone foreign body) (thick arrows). Pearl: Small‐volume effusions may be missed on initial scanning or may not be present despite significant injury, and thus serial exams are impera- tive to increase the sensitivity of VetFAST‐ABCDE, the “E” aspect of VetFAST‐ABCDE being similar to the premise of Global FAST.

770 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Ultrasound has been shown to have good sensitivity and specificity for certain fracture types including skull, ribs, and long bones (see Chapter 35). Exposure (E) Serial VetFAST‐ABCDE exams increase the probability of initially detecting significant injury and pathology and over time provide a means to detect potentially life‐threatening conditions and complications beyond traditional laboratory testing, radiographic imaging and physical examination. In stable veterinary patients, a serial exam should be performed four hours post admission as recommended with Global FAST, and as often as every 15–30 minutes in unstable and critical patients. VetFAST‐ABCDE addresses this rule‐out list rapidly, including the Ts – Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade (cardiac), Thrombo- embolism and the veterinary additions of Toxin and Trauma, and the Hs of Hypotension, Hypocontractility, and Hypertension (see Chapter 36 and Table 38.2). These Hs and Ts are screened for using both VetFAST‐ ABCDE and Global FAST (see Chapter 36). Interestingly, these rapidly identifiable Hs and Ts as causes of CPA are not addressed in current veterinary CPR guidelines (Boller and Fletcher2012), and neither is the use of POCUS, Global FAST, and VetFAST‐ABCDE, for not only for rapid diagnosis but likewise for patient monitoring. The use of POCUS exams such as VetFAST‐ ABCDE and Global FAST has tremendous potential to improve survival by detecting treatable conditions and better directing resources when minutes count. The POCUS strategy is becoming part of advanced trauma life support (ATLS) in human medicine in North America and Europe (Callaway et al. 2015; Soar et al. 2015). Although the utility of POCUS has not been standardized, it may be used as an adjunct to standard patient evaluation (Callaway et al. 2015; Soar et al. 2015). Additional detail is given in Chapters 36 and 37. VetFAST‐ABCDE has the added facets of evaluating ET placement, upper airway evaluation, and ocular evaluation including eye injury and increased ONSD. Abnormal findings in each part of the exam in differ - ent shock presentations are summarized in Table 38.2. Pearls and Pitfalls, The Final Say The VetFAST‐ABCDE is a more recent format that is similar to Global FAST with the most notable exceptions of upper airway, cardiac, ocular, and musculoskeletal evaluations. The VetFAST‐ABCDE format may be used in trauma and nontrauma conditions to manage, diagnose, treat, and serially monitor to optimize veterinary critical care. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 777 Introduction The anatomy of the dog and cat has important differ - ences, requiring a thorough understanding for accu- rate sonographic image interpretation and clinical integration. With the widespread use of point‐of‐care ultrasound (POCUS) by nonradiologists and noncardi- ologists brought on through the development of stan- dardized FAST ultrasound exams, screening evaluations of the abdomen (AFAST), thorax (TFAST), heart (TFAST), and lung (Vet BLUE) have become commonplace – the Global FAST approach (Lisciandro et al. 2008, 2009, 2015, 2017; Lisciandro 2011, 2012, 2014a–d, 2016; Boysen and Lisciandro 2013; Ward et al. 2017, 2018a,b). This chapter will describe the pertinent sonographic abdominal, thoracic, pulmonary, and cardiac differences between felines and canines. What POCUS: Feline Differences – Abdomen and Thorax Can Do • Clarify major abdominal differences between felines and canines. • Clarify major thoracic differences between felines and canines. • Clarify Global FAST differences – AFAST and its fluid scoring system, TFAST, and Vet BLUE. What POCUS: Feline Differences – Abdomen and Thorax Cannot Do • Account for individual variations in the abdomen. • Account for individual variations in the thorax. • Replace a complete detailed diagnostic abdominal ultrasound. • Replace complete detailed diagnostic echo cardio- graphy. • Replace consultation with a radiologist. • Replace clinical judgment. Indications Sonographers should know these important feline differences if they are performing POCUS examina- tions and Global FAST in cats. Objectives Know the major abdominal and thoracic sonographic differences between felines and canines. The feline abdomen and feline thorax sections will con- trast differences between cats and dogs that are most clin- ically relevant for POCUS, AFAST, TFAST, and Vet BLUE examinations. 778 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Feline Abdomen Complete detailed abdominal ultrasound and many of the POCUS abdominal examinations are performed in dorsal recumbency. In contrast, the AFAST is performed in either lateral recumbency or in standing or sternal, and not in dorsal recumbency. The sonographer should always consider differences in positioning and the associated scanning planes for best interpreting what is imaged within each respective acoustic window. For example, the thigh is rarely ever in view when imaging the urinary bladder with a patient in dorsal recum - bency; however, during AFAST at its cysto‐colic (CC) view, the thigh is almost always in view through the far‐field in either lateral recumbency when imaging the urinary bladder. AFAST in Cats Briefly, image acquisition of the five acoustic windows of AFAST is the same regardless of patient positioning. The AFAST order and its image acquisition using its target organ approach are independent of positioning and performed in the same order at every examination to avoid satisfaction of search error and incomplete examinations (Figure 39.1). The target organs are fanned through in both directions in longitudinal planes and then the probe is rocked cranially before being returned to your starting point for one final look. Sites are mostly named by the target organs you will image at each AFAST view rather than external sites, with the exception of the hepato‐renal (HR) and spleno‐renal (SR) umbilical views (Lisciandro et al. 2009, 2015; Lisciandro 2011, 2012, 2014a; Boysen and Lisciandro 2013; McMurray et al. 2016). The AFAST probe maneuver mantra of “fan, rock cranially, and return to your starting point” is applied to all five AFAST acoustic windows (see Chapters 6 and 7 for more detail) (Lisciandro 2011, 2012, 2014a; Lisciandro et al. 2015). Transverse orientation may be used but can be initially confusing to many nonradiologist veteri - narians and should be considered an “add‐on” skill to be developed once the initial AFAST format is mastered. 779 POCUS: FELINE DIFFERENCES – ABDOMEN AND THORAX within the liver parenchyma in both dogs and cats are the hepatic veins and the intrahepatic portal vasculature, the gallbladder and its associated biliary system, and the porta hilus. The nearby falciform fat in cats may be robust and a confounder during hepatic imaging. The falciform fat is described in more detail below. The determination of normal versus abnormal liver echogenicity differs between dogs and cats. In dogs, hepatic echogenicity is determined by comparing the echogenicity of liver next to spleen; however, in cats comparisons are made between the liver and adjacent falciform fat. The canine liver is hypoechoic to the spleen (darker) and the feline liver is hyperechoic (brighter) to isoechoic (same) to the falciform fat (d’Anjou 2008b; Nyland et al. 2015c). In order to accu- rately compare echogenicity in different windows (dual comparison), the parameters of gain, depth, and transducer frequency must be equal so that the comparison of echogenicity is objective. Using echo- genicity alone to determine if pathology is present is unreliable since the echogenicity of an organ is dependent on factors intrinsic and extrinsic to its com- position, such as angle of insonation, and hence anisot- ropy, acoustic impedance, position of the focal point, and transducer technology, such as compound or harmonic imaging. The echogenicity of images without harmonics tends to be slightly more echogenic and with a coarser echotexture (Figure 39.2). Differences in Falciform Fat The differentiation of falciform fat from liver parenchyma can be difficult if the appropriate depth is not adjusted. The heterogeneous appearance of fat with multiple small hyperechoic (white) lines can be similar to that of the portal veins seen in the normal liver parenchyma. This seems to be a major concern in cats where the falciform fat pad can be robust even in thin body conditions. The echogenicity of falciform fat is usually hypoechoic (darker) to the liver and is some instances isoechoic (same as) to liver (see Figure 39.2). Differences in Hepatic Venous System The hepatic veins in both dogs and cats are anechoic (black) tubular structures that drain into the caudal vena cava (CVC) near the middorsal portion of the diaphragm. The hepatic veins have anechoic incon- spicuous walls unless the ultrasound beam is perpen- dicular to the vein (angle of insonation being 90°) where faint hyperechoic (white), thin walls are noted due to its particular specular properties. The portal veins, on the other hand, will depict hyperechoic (white) walls regardless of the angle of insonation and may look like equal signs (=) (see also Figure 8.10A). This appearance is due to the fatty content of the portal triad and also to the echogenicity generated by the bile duct and the hepatic artery (d’Anjou 2008b; Nyland et al. 2015c). If there is a question over whether or not the vessel of interest is a portal or hepatic vein, the use of color flow Doppler will make this difference clear. The hepatic veins will be depicted in blue with flow away from the transducer (probe) and towards the CVC, and the portal veins depicted in red with flow towards the transducer (probe), away from the porta hepatis, and towards the periphery of the liver parenchyma (Figure 39.3). Differences in Gallbladder Shape and Lumen The shape of the feline gallbladder is more variable than in canines. A bilobed gallbladder is a common normal variant found in cats that is possible but uncommon in dogs (see also Figure 8.4). The orienta- tion of the long axis of the gallbladder also varies in the cat where it is uniquely parallel to the ribs and perpen- dicular to the sternum or obliquely angled with respect to the sternum (Carlisle 1977). In cats, there are two common and one uncommon presentations of a bilobed gallbladder. The most common feline variant has a longitudinal septum dividing the fundus of the gallbladder into two fundi- ces internally, each fusing to form a single cystic duct. This variant often is not appreciated grossly during laparotomy and generally only detected sonographi- cally. The second common feline bilobed variant occurs when there are actually two different lumens, each forming a fundus, but fused at the neck of the gall- bladder. The third variant and the rarest is the presence of a duplex gallbladder with two independent cystic ducts (Moentk and Biller 1993). Differences in Gallbladder Common Bile Duct In cats with a full gallbladder, the bile duct may be looped or tortuous as it approaches the porta hepatis, which may be falsely interpreted as extrabiliary obstruction or a cystic mass. The rule of thumb when interpreting the degree of distension of a tortuous common bile duct is that a bile duct diameter of >5 mm supports extrabiliary tract obstruction and a diameter of <4 mm would be considered within normal limits (Figure 39.4) (d’Anjou 2008b). Differences in Gallbladder Sludge Historically, the presence of a small amount of echo- genic sludge has been considered a normal finding in

780 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER dogs. Recently, the “normal” amount of canine gall - bladder sludge has been suggested to be at least partly false based on the difference in ejection fraction bet - ween dogs with anechoic bile and those having sludge, and those having sludge with a hyperechoic appear - ance along with distal acoustic shadowing and those with a mucocele. This recent finding suggests that the presence of sludge in the canine gallbladder may cause a certain degree of biliary stasis and possibly be indic - ative of early biliary disease. Rather than qualifying the finding as “normal,” the presence of biliary sludge likely warrants close monitoring and assessment of hepatobiliary function, such as repeating the ultra - sound exam in 3–4 weeks and then periodically there - after (Tsukagoshi et al. 2012). Feline bile should be homogeneously anechoic (black). The presence of even a small amount of echo - genic sludge is always considered abnormal in cats. FAST Diaphragmatico‐Hepatic (DH) View Differences in Heart and Gallbladder next to the Diaphragm In dogs, the canine heart will routinely image in the long axis along the diaphragmatic interface, the gall - bladder along the diaphragm’s caudal surface, and the beating heart along the cranial diaphragmatic surface, referred to as the “cardiac bump” (see Chapters 6, 7, 17, 18, and Figures 6.11 and 17.27). The cardiac orienta- tion consistently has the left ventricle (LV) and the left atrium (LA) immediately against or in close proximity to the diaphragm that is sonographically viewable in many dogs (see Figure 6.11). In cats, however, cardiac imaging along the diaphragm is much less reliable because of more inter- posing aerated lung. Thus, a very faint ultrasono - graphic impression of the feline beating heart may or may not be present. One of the reasons for this incon - sistency may be appreciated radiographically with the increased space of aerated lung in between the normal heart and the diaphragm that is more dramatic in cats than dogs (Figure 39.5). In contrast to dogs, the feline gallbladder variably lies against the caudal aspect of the diaphragm because anatomically the feline gall - bladder lies further caudally and further to the right of midline. 784 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Differences in Gallbladder Wall Edema – Halo Sign Gallbladder wall edema in cats is not a marker for ana- phylaxis, as in dogs, because shock organs are different (Quantz et al. 2009; Lisciandro 2014a, 2016b). In canines, the shock organ, where the highest concentration of mast cells reside, is the liver and gastrointestinal tract whereas in cats (and humans) the shock organ is the lung. However, gallbladder wall edema in cats does serve as a marker for right‐sided CHF, right‐sided volume over- load, and the presence of pericardial effusion, similar to that of dogs, although sensitivity and specificity are unknown (Lisciandro 2014a,b, 2019) (Figure 39.6). Thus, when gallbladder wall edema is detected in cats, pericardial effusion and right‐sided CHF (primary or secondary to volume overload) should be ruled out using TFAST and then other causes considered (see Table 7.5). Combining gallbladder wall edema with CVC and hepatic venous characterization integrates clinical information to more accurately interpret the cause for the finding of gallbladder wall edema. In other words, a cat with gallbladder wall edema and a FAT CVC along with hepatic venous distension has convincing evidence without an echo view that pericardial effu- sion or right‐sided failure likely is occurring. By know- ing this information, adjustments may be made to better treat and stabilize for gold standard testing (complete echocardiography) when the cat is more stable or when a more detailed ultrasound study is T able 39.1. On the other hand, in cats with cardiac disease, it is important to consider that the sonographi- cally detected gallbladder wall edema is likely related to right‐sided heart failure, and may not be a comor - bidity of cholecystitis or other causes (see Table 7.5). Spleen Differences in Splenic Vessels, Echogenicity, Size, and Location The canine spleen is divided into two main regions: the dorsal extremity (head) and the ventral extremity (body and tail). The dorsal extremity is most often located along the 11th to 12th dorsal intercostal spaces and will move to some extent according to the size of the stomach. The body of the canine spleen will generally be close enough to the left kidney that it is often readily seen at the AFAST SR view using its dorsolateral acoustic window caudal to the last rib where the costal arch meets the hypaxial muscles. The ventral extremity is seen along the left to midventral abdominal wall and in the presence of splenomegaly, seen cranial to a full urinary bladder. The canine spleen is more echogenic (brighter) than the liver parenchyma, but this is not true in cats, where the splenic and hepatic echogenicity are equal (isoechoic) (Figure 39.7). Finally, the splenic veins may be surrounded by fat in the dog whereas this occurs uncommonly in the cat (Nyland and Mattoon 2015c). In the cat, the spleen is consistently much smaller than the dog and its maximal width should be less than 1 cm (<10 mm) (Reese et al. 2013). 787 POCUS: F ELINE D IFFERENCES – A BDOMEN AND T HORAX feline spleen is not an important reservoir of blood as in the dog. The position of the spleen in very large and obese cats is more dorsal and commonly missed by novice sonographers at the AFAST SR view. The normal feline spleen has an echogenic and homoge - neous appearance nearly equal to that of the liver, markedly different from the canine spleen which is hyperechoic (brighter) to the canine liver. Also, the spleen does not commonly abut the left kidney as in the dog. The splenic veins are not as conspicuous in cats, especially when using curvilinear (microconvex) transducers at medium frequencies. The conspicuity of splenic vessels at the splenic hilus has improved with the linear transducer using newer technology such as cross‐beam B‐mode images, where multiple scan lines are sent from multiple directions instead of the tradi - tional B‐mode where the scan lines follow a consecu - tive and sequential order (Figure 39.8). Even though splenomegaly can be nonspecific for both dogs and cats in differentiating malignant from benign disease, anecdotally and based on the authors’ experience, feline splenomegaly is more commonly associated with malignancies and infectious causes rather than extramedullary hematopoiesis (EMH) or hyperplasia. EMH causes none to mild enlargement, although statistically based studies are needed to con - firm this information. It is important to mention that with new transducer technology, splenic echotexture becomes slightly more heterogeneous in both dogs and cats since newer high‐ frequency transducers are more likely to depict small centers of hyperplasia (Figure 39.9). As a result, there is a learning curve for proper splenic interpretation. Kidney Differences in Renal Size, Echogenicity, and Location Renal Size There is no standardized method to determine normal renal size in dogs because of the great range of canine size, so renal size is subjectively assessed. A canine kidney length to aorta ratio is described, but the range is rather broad and thus unreliable. The measurement of canine kidneys is best done radiographically using the dorsal ventral view. Basic renal anatomy and the methodology for measuring its dimension of length, height, and width are easily learned (Figure 39.10). The normal range of feline kidney dimensions includes length from 3 to 4.5 cm, width from 2.2 to 2.8 cm, and height from 1.9 to 2.5 cm (see Figure 39.10) (Nickel et al. 1973; Walter et al. 1987; d’Anjou 2008a). The comparison of echogenicity between the spleen and the cortex of the left kidney is similar (isoechoic) and a normal finding in cats (Figure 39.12). 791 POCUS: F ELINE D IFFERENCES – A BDOMEN AND T HORAX Location As a rule of thumb, the appropriate depth should be to have approximately 75% of the field of view filled with the organ of interest unless performing AFAST. Regarding renal imaging of cats and small thinner dogs placed in lateral recumbency, both the left and right kidneys are often viewed together with greater depth settings. Care should be taken to ensure that the correct kidney is identified and labeled accurately, and know that rarely would this be a result of a mirror image artifact. The right kidney may be discriminated from the left by its position within the renal fossa of the liver in dogs. In other words, the canine right kidney is cupped by the liver, and the canine left kidney is not. However, in cats, both kidneys are located away from the liver and sometimes more difficult to identify as one being the left or right kidney. AFAST Spleno‐Renal and Hepato‐Renal Views Differences in Spleen next to the Left Kidney Both the canine and feline spleen are attached to the greater curvature of the stomach by their short gastric vessels, making the head of the canine and feline spleen reliably in close proximity to its left kidney. The spleen is thus imaged consistently in both species at the AFAST SR view by rocking the probe cranially under the rib cage unless gas‐filled bowel is interposed (ultrasound does not transmit through air). Thus, both the feline and canine spleen are expected to be seen at the SR view and the feline right kidney is often imaged through the same SR view acoustic window (Figure 39.13). Conversely, the right kidney is viewed analogously from the HR view. Differences in Imaging the Left and Right Kidneys Both kidneys are commonly imaged in cats via the SR view in right lateral or standing or sternal (or analo - gously the HR view in left lateral) rendering the AFAST HR5th bonus view (when in right lateral recumbency) unnecessary in most feline cases (see Figures 6.21, 6.34, and 39.1). Thus, the cat’s left and right retroperitoneal spaces and kidneys are confidently interrogated through the SR view when in right lateral recumbency, and the HR view when in left lateral recumbency. The feline kidney will often sonographically appear differ- ent in echogenicity and detail than in dogs and the feline right kidney is not as intimately associated within a fossa of the right liver because of interposing fat (described in the preceding paragraphs). Imaging Feline Ureters The feline as a species is more prone to ureteral calculi that will partially or completely obstruct urine flow from the renal pelvis to the trigone of the urinary bladder. During AFAST and its target organ approach, renal pelvic dilation and degrees of hydronephro - sis are usually obvious because the conditions are fluid‐associated changes and for some sonographers Figure 39.13. 792 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER ureteral dilation may also be recognized as an AFAST abnormality (Figure 39.14). Importantly, these ultra - sound‐detected changes are missed by physical exam- ination, blood and urine testing, and radiography. Color flow Doppler may be used to determine if the fluid‐filled structure is a vessel (obvious pulsatile flow) versus ureteral distension (absent pulsatile flow). The use of AFAST is a good screening test for soft tissue conditions of the kidneys and associated structures, since most are fluid associated, and carries the poten - tial to trigger more advanced imaging. Urinary Bladder, Urine, Urethra, and Reproductive Structures Differences in Urinary Bladder, Urethra, and Reproductive Structures Artifacts There are several artifacts that may mimic pathology when evaluating the urinary bladder, including side‐ lobe that can mimic wall thickening, nearby small cystic structures, or pseudo sludge, and slice‐thickness artifact that creates images of false sediment. These artifacts can be reduced by adjusting gain (generally decreasing) and focal zone, and using tissue harmonic imaging (THI). Urethra The cat’s urethra is more abdominal in location and much longer than dogs and is thus often readily imaged in cats with a full urinary bladder (Figure 39.15) (d’Anjou 2008a; Nyland et al. 2015a). Prostate The prostatic urethra can be seen in most dogs, but especially in small‐breed dogs, the prostate seems to be directly abutting the neck of the urinary bladder. Having a patient with a full urinary bladder is always helpful for prostatic evaluation, especially in neutered dogs, since the plethoric bladder will pull the prostate cranially from the pelvic inlet. Usually, determination of canine prostatic size using ultrasound is subjective. A more reliable determina - tion is via the use of a lateral radiograph. On a lateral radiograph, the height of the normal prostate should not exceed 70% of the height measured from the sacral promontory to the pubis. An objective determination of prostatic size by length (L), depth (height) (D), and width (W) measurements is straightforward with the use of electronic cursors. The basic equation used to determine prostate volume (V) is an ellipsoid model (V = 0.524 × L × W × H) (Nyland and Mattoon 2015b). The male cat’s prostate is rarely seen sonographi - cally due to the rarity of prostatic disease in the feline and the fact that most cats in general practice are neu - tered. The normal prostate of intact male cats has been described as being small and oval with hyperechoic prostatic parenchyma. Ovaries The ovaries are superficial, round to oval, homoge - neous in echogenicity, and located caudal and ventral to the caudal pole of each kidney (Figure 39.16). The size of the ovaries in dogs is more homogeneous and independent of weight compared to cats. One study showed an average canine ovarian size of 1.7 × 0.7 × 0.5 cm. The cat’s ovaries are much smaller, and both canine and feline ovaries are best imaged with linear transducers, unless the patient is very large (Nyland and Mattoon 2015d). Uterus The nongravid uterus is tubular, homogeneous in echotexture, with a lumen that is not readily seen and is differentiated from small intestine by lack of peristalsis and intraluminal gas, and absence of the layered appearance characteristics (Nyland and Mattoon 2015d). Uterine width varies from 3 to 5 mm in cats and 5 to 10 mm in dogs. If the uterine horn is superficial enough, and a linear transducer is used, the layers of the uterus are more evident, as in Figure 39.17. Further details regarding pathology of reproductive organs are beyond the scope of this chapter (see Section III). Differences in Urine Canine urine should be homogeneously anechoic. If internal echoes are noted, the presence of active sediment should be suspected and urinalysis is necessary to characterize the type of sediment. Regarding cats, the ability of the feline to concentrate urine is greater than the dog. As a result, cat urine is more commonly seen as partially echogenic, which could be a normal variation (floating sediment), and is not uncommonly due to floating fat droplets (Figure 39.18). AFAST Cysto‐Colic View Differences between Cats and Dogs The AFAST CC view is similar in both cats and dogs with no major differences other than those stated in the preceding paragraphs regarding the feline urethra and urine composition. Estimating Urinary Bladder Volume When urinary bladder volume estimation is war - ranted, the formula is length × height × width (cm) × 0.625 = estimated urinary bladder volume (mL) (Lisciandro and Fosgate 2017) (Figure 39.19). If volume is calculated over time then urine output may be estimated noninvasively. The way in which to test the formula and become comfortable with its strengths and weaknesses is to perform your AFAST CC view urinary bladder measurements and then compare to the volume aspirated when placing urinary catheters. 795 POCUS: F ELINE D IFFERENCES – A BDOMEN AND T HORAX Gastrointestinal T ract Differences in Stomach In cats, the position of the stomach is quite different from that of the dog. Whereas the dog’s antrum and pylorus are right‐sided structures, in the cat they are located near midline. This can be better appreciated in radiographic ventrodorsal views of the abdomen, especially in cats with a normal amount of gas. This difference is very important for sonographers who will find it easier to locate the pyloric duodenal junction (PDJ) and duodenum along the midsagittal plane (Figure 39.20). The gastric submucosal layer in the cat can accumulate fat, and this intramural fat will appear distinctly hyperechoic in obese cats. It is important to recognize this difference from dogs and avoid misdi - agnosis as an intramural abnormality. This layer of fat can be seen sonographically, radiographically, and on computed tomography (Heng et al. 2005). Differences in Pancreas The pancreas is one of those organs that can be difficult for the novice sonographer to identify. In order to find the pancreas, the ultrasonographer must rely on regional anatomy. The pancreas of both dogs and cats is usually medial to slightly dorsomedial to the descending duo- denum. In the past, the pancreas was not as clearly seen as today with newer transducer technologies. The pan- creas is isoechoic (same as) to slightly hypoechoic (darker) to the surrounding mesenteric fat. It is also located ven- tral to the prehepatic portal vein and this region of the pancreas corresponds to the pancreatic body. The right pancreatic lobe is larger than the left lobe in the dog and in the cat this is the opposite, the larger left pancreatic lobe predominates over the smaller right lobe. Figure 39.18. 796 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER In dogs, the size of the pancreas varies from 4 mm to 10 mm (Nyland and Mattoon 2015a). A landmark that is used by the author (DR) for both dogs and cats is to find the cranial pole of the left adrenal gland and the most caudal aspect of the left pancreatic lobe will be abutting it. The splenic vein also can be followed dor - sally to the junction of the cranial mesenteric vein just before forming the prehepatic portal vein. The left pancreatic lobe will be ventral to this confluence of tributary veins. The pancreatic duct is difficult to visu- alize and it can be up to 1 mm diameter in normalcy. In cats, the pancreas should be less than 1 cm (Nyland and Mattoon 2015a). The feline left pancreatic lobe can be found in a sagittal to sagittal oblique plane, caudal to the fundus of the stomach, dorsal to the spleen and cranial to the cranial pole of the left kidney, and is larger than the right pancreatic lobe (Figure 39.21). A landmark that is used by the author (DR) for both dogs and cats is to find the cranial pole of the left adrenal gland and the most caudal aspect of the left pancreatic lobe will be abutting it. The splenic vein also can be followed dorsally to the junction of the cranial mesenteric vein just before forming the prehepatic portal vein. The left pancreatic lobe will be ventral to this confluence of veins. The pancreatic duct diameter increases with age. The pancreatic duct can be up to 6 mm (Hecht et al. 2006). Differences in Small Intestine The small intestine in the cat and dog has five distinct layers (Figure 39.22). Extending from the outer surface, the serosa, muscularis, submucosa, mucosa, and lumen make up the ultrasonographic layering. In the cat, the wall thickness is more homogeneous relative to weight compared to the dog where weight‐based intervals are applied to dogs. Figure 39.20. Feline stomach and pyloric duodenal junction. 797 POCUS: F ELINE D IFFERENCES – A BDOMEN AND T HORAX The jejunum of the cat normally measures <2.5 mm and the duodenum and ileum up to 3 mm (Newell et al.1999; Goggin et al. 2000; Winter et al. 2014; di Donato et al. 2014). The muscularis layer (m) and the mucosal layers are the hypoechoic (dark) layers. The author uses the mnemonic M&M, as in chocolate, to remind us that both these layers are hypoechoic. Intestinal layering is as follows from superficial to deep (see also Chapter 11). • Serosal – hyperechoic (white) • Muscularis – anechoic (black) • Submucosal – hyperechoic (white) • Mucosal (thickest) – anechoic (black) • Mucosal‐luminal interface – hyperechoic (white) Differences in Ileocolic Junction In cats, the ileocolic junction region is easy to identify due to its unique appearance having a thicker and hyperechoic submucosa than small and large intestine. The ileum just prior to entering the colon in the transverse plane appears as a small, empty stomach or the classic “wagon wheel” appearance (Figure 39.23). In the author’s experience (DR), the long‐axis plane of the ileum can be confused with the duodenum by novice ultrasonographers for two possible reasons: because it is located medial to the right kidney in the right cranial abdomen, and because it is slightly thicker than other small bowel segments. In dogs, the colon and cecum are typically gas filled. Thus, it is difficult to routinely see the canine ileoceco- colic junction with the exception of an empty colon or a fluid‐filled junction. Differences in Large Intestine There are really no major differences between the colon of the dog and cat. The wall of the colon is thin and with faintly distinct layers, often best imaged using a high‐frequency transducer (probe). AFAST Hepato‐Renal and Spleno‐Renal Umbilical View Differences in Spleen and Small Intestine At the AFAST umbilical views (HRU and SRU), small intestine is commonly seen, but the spleen is variably seen at the level of the umbilicus and less reliably than in dogs. A midabdominal sweep may be necessary to locate the spleen. In most cases, a POCUS spleen exam is recommended following AFAST. Differences bet - ween the feline and canine spleen are described in more detail in the preceding paragraphs. As in the dog, when imaging in the transverse plane at the level of the umbilicus, the liver and stomach should not be in view in normalcy. Small intestine will be imaged at the HRU view (right lateral recumbency, and the analogous SRU view when in left lateral recumbency). Use of the AFS in Bleeding Felines The AFS system semiquantitates the volume and in bleeding cats allows rapidly categorization as a small‐volume bleeder (AFS 1 and 2, AFS <3) versus a large‐volume bleeder (AFS 3 and 4, AFS ≥3) on initial and serial exams (Figure 39.26). Thus, importantly, there is no need to use anticoagulant when harvesting this blood, giving the attending cli - nician the option for autotransfusion with autolo - gous blood in dogs and cats (Higgs et al. 2015; Robinson et al. 2016; Cole and Humm 2019). For autotransfusion, a blood filter is required to prevent thromboembolic complications from any small or occult clots within the harvested blood. Feline Thorax – TFAST and Vet BLUE TFAST has become the staple for quick assessment of the heart, with three major echo views, the presence of pleural and pericardial effusion, and volume status view with the FAST DH view. The three TFAST echo views are performed at the right TFAST pericardial view and include the left ventricular short‐axis view (LVSA, also called the mushroom view), the short‐axis left atrial to aortic ratio (LA:Ao, called the “Mercedes‐ Benz view”), and the long‐axis four‐chamber view (LA4CV) for the right ventricular to left ventricular ratio (RV:LV) (Figure 39.27) (see also Figures 17.25, 17.26). It is important to understand that left‐sided congestive heart failure results in pulmonary edema and right‐sided congestive heart failure in hepatic con- gestion. Thus, “Global FAST nonecho fallback views”, Vet BLUE and the FAST DH view help minimize feline risk when echo views and/or radiographs cannot be safely performed (Lisciandro 2011, 2014a–d, 2019; Boysen and Lisciandro 2013; Lisciandro et al. 2016, 2017, 2018; Ward et al. 2017, 2018a,b). Safe Positioning for Felines The saying that “death begins in radiology” in human medicine rings very true for the hemodynamically fragile and respiratory distressed feline. The axiom in human medicine is never send a patient to radiology without a good physical examination and an EFAST exam (analogous to our Global FAST approach). If you can place a stethoscope on your feline patient, you can place an ultrasound probe and most cats that are focusing on breathing will allow their forelegs to be placed on a roll of paper towels or a towel. Safer Acoustic Coupling Medium for Felines The use of minimal isopropyl alcohol to wet and part the hair followed by alcohol‐based hand sanitizer is a good option because the hand sanitizer lacks the nox - ious fumes, especially when cats are placed in oxygen cages, and is less noxious from the cold feeling when applied to skin (Figure 39.29). Moreover, minimal application of isopropyl alcohol is less likely to lower your patient’s body temperature from its evaporative properties. Assessing Chamber Size (L VSA) In cats, the heart is more challenging to image due to its small size and rounded shape compared to dogs. The cardiac planes are within a tight acoustic window and acquiring standard echo views differs by millimeters, so hand motion is much more subtle. Furthermore, the heart rate is generally much faster than dogs and hence evaluating the chambers, size, and ratios can be chal - lenging without the use of cine loops. In other words, freeze and roll the cine ball to best evaluate the heart in most cats; in fact, in real time, judging cardiac chamber size and filling, the so‐called “eyeball method,” is more prone to error in cats. In contrast, most dogs, unless tachycardic, may be accurately evaluated in real time using the “eyeball method.” Left Atrial to Aortic Ratio on Short Axis When ruling out left‐sided CHF, the ratio of diameters between the left atrium and aorta (LA:Ao) is measured or assessed visually by the “eyeball method” and most commonly in short axis (see Figure 39.27). The normal LA:Ao in cats should be <1.6:1 (versus <1.3:1 in dogs). Most often, the noncardiologist is looking for obvious increases in the LA:Ao (>2:1) in both cats and dogs. This measurement may be done using M‐mode or B‐mode. An increased LA:Ao and a positive Vet BLUE exam of ≥2 Volpicelli Strong Positive sites bilaterally in each hemithorax increase the probability for left‐sided Figure 39.27 . Vet BLUE alone without the LA:Ao has the same high sensitivity and specificity for left‐sided congestive heart failure as radiography and also serves as a rapid test to rule out left‐sided CHF (Lisciandro et al. 2016, 2017, 2018; Ward et al. 2017, 2018b). See Chapters 22 and 23 and Figures 23.14, 23.17, and 36.17. The reader should note that lung ultrasound, Vet BLUE, is the “Global FAST nonecho fallback view” when the TFAST echo view (quick peek LA:Ao) cannot be adequately imaged, especially in unstable, hemody- namically fragile, distressed cats. “Absent B‐lines in All (Vet BLUE) Views” (ABAV) rules out left‐sided CHF in cats with high sensitivity (96%) (Lisciandro et al. 2016) (Figure 39.30). Left Ventricular Short‐axis View for Volume Status and Contractility The left ventricular short‐axis “mushroom view” for volume and contractility, fractional shortening percentage (FS%), is useful in cats, with some important differences from dogs (see Figures 17.25, 17.26, and 39.30). The view is often less reliable when judging in real time for the aforementioned reasons of the faster heart rate of felines making the left ventricular look thick and volume look deficient, and commonly results in assuming hypertrophic cardiomyopathy when in fact the cat is volume contracted (and empirical diuretic therapy potentially harmful). Pressing the freeze button and rolling the cine ball is the best way to estimate volume and contractility. Using Vet BLUE findings will give additional information regarding the presence or absence of alveolar‐interstitial edema, and the degree by numbers of positive sites along with actual numbers of B‐lines (Vet BLUE B‐line scoring system; see Figures 23.14, 23.17, and 36.17). The “Global FAST nonecho fallback view” for volume status is the FAST DH view and the character- ization of the CVC and its associated hepatic veins. Hepatic veins should not be evident in normalcy when cats are imaged in lateral or standing/sternal posi - tioning. The CVC is characterized as being flat with poor volume (hypovolemic CVC), FAT with too much volume (fluid‐intolerant CVC due to high CVP) and right‐sided heart failure/overload, or with a bounce (fluid‐responsive CVC) (see Figures 7.12 and 39.30 and Table 7.6) (see Chapters 6, 7, 17–21, 26, 36, and 37). The reader should note that the characterization of the CVC and its associated hepatic veins are the “Global FAST nonecho fallback views” when the TFAST echo view (LVSA) cannot be adequately imaged, especially in unstable, hemodynamically fragile, distressed cats. Right Ventricular to Left Ventricular Ratio (RV:L V) on Long‐axis Four‐Chamber View With the feline heart being more rounded, and right‐ sided heart disease less common than in dogs and cats having higher heart rates, the right ventricular to left ventricular ratio (RV:LV) is more difficult to assess in real time (see Figure 39.27). Freeze and roll the cine ball to get a better idea of unremarkable versus abnormal. The “Global FAST nonecho fallback view” for right‐ sided CHF is characterizing the CVC and hepatic veins (see previous paragraph, Figure 7.12 and Table 7.6). The RV:LV is observed on the long‐axis four‐chamber view (see Figure 39.30). The reader should note that the characterization of the CVC and its associated hepatic veins are the “Global FAST nonecho fallback views” when the TFAST echo view (LA4CV) cannot be adequately imaged, especially in unstable, hemodynamically fragile, distressed cats (see Figure 7.12 and Table 7.6). 806 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Differences in Echo Assessment The major difference between cats and dogs pri- marily lies in image acquisition. The small size of the feline heart, its rapid rate, coupled with how tight the acoustic windows are for the various short‐ and long‐axis views require very small hand movements. The “eyeball method” or gestalt approach, generally effective in dogs during real‐time B‐mode imaging, is more error prone in the majority of cats due to their more rapid heart rate and difficulty of holding the view of interest. The sonographer will need to learn how to freeze and roll the cine ball to accu- rately evaluate the feline heart and understand the use of “Global FAST nonecho fallback views” for the left and right heart for better clinical integration of information. Differences in the Sonographic Diagnosis and Causes of Pericardial Effusion The accurate diagnosis of pericardial effusion in cats is similar to that in dogs (Lisciandro 2016). The tenets for accurately detecting pericardial effusion are as follows. • See the heart in its entirety using the bright pericar- dium in the far‐field as a landmark. • One view is no view. • Image toward the muscular apex of the heart using the FAST DH view and the TFAST right PCS view, thus minimizing mistaking the heart for free fluid (Lisciandro 2014a,b, 2016). • Only the long‐axis four‐chamber view is an accept- able single view by knowing that the anatomy of the pericardium and the pericardial sac extends from one atrium around the muscular apex of the heart to the other atrium while identifying all four chambers, thus preventing mistaking a heart chamber for pericardial (or pleural) effusion (Lisciandro z2014a,b, 2016). The most common cause of pericardial effusion in cats (~75%) is congestive heart failure, much different than in dogs (Davidson et al. 2008; Hall et al. 2007). In fact, in a recent feline study, pericardial effusion was 100% specific for feline CHF in cats enrolled at two different veterinary colleges (North Carolina State and Iowa State) (Ward et al. 2018a). In contrast to dogs, the feline heart is less reliably imaged via the FAST DH view, but when clinically relevant pericardial effusion is present, it will likely be observed via the FAST DH view. See Chapters 6, 7, 17–21 for more detail. The accurate diagnosis of pleural effusion in cats is similar to that in dogs. The tenets for accurately detecting pleural effusion are as follows (Lisciandro 2014b, 2016). • See the heart in its entirety using the bright pericar- dium in the far‐field as a landmark. • One view is no view – combine views. • Image toward the muscular apex of the heart, FAST DH view, and TFAST right PCS view, minimizing mistaking the heart for free fluid as done for peri- cardial effusion. • Perform the TFAST slide by recognizing the heart and then sliding caudally toward the diaphragm, followed by cranially toward the cervical region to observe for free fluid away from the heart. • Only the long‐axis four‐chamber view is an accept- able single view by knowing that the anatomy of the pericardium and the pericardial sac extends from one atrium around the muscular apex of the heart to the other atrium while identifying all four chambers, thus preventing mistaking a heart chamber for pericardial (or pleural) effusion. See Chapters 6, 7, 17–21 for more detail. Pearl: The single most important TFAST echo view is the LA:Ao in short axis. If that is too risky, per - form a Vet BLUE for two reasons: (1) left‐sided CHF is rapidly ruled out in cats with absent B‐ lines all Vet BLUE views (ABAV), and (2) left‐sided CHF is highly probable in cats with strong positive views (>3 or infinite B‐lines) at two or more Vet BLUE views bilaterally (Ward et al. 2017). Don’t jeopardize your feline patient trying to get the echo view(s) or a radiograph, but rather use the above strategy for an evidence‐based working diagnosis, treat for CHF (or conversely asthma) and give the feline patient more time to stabilize (Ward et al. 2018b). Pearl: Felines with pleural effusion and lung edema detected during TFAST and Vet BLUE, respectively, that have concurrent pericardial effu- sion of any degree very likely have CHF as their cause of distress (Ward et al. 2018a). Don’t jeopar - dize your feline patient trying to get the echo view(s) or a radiograph, but rather use the above strategy for an evidence‐based working diagnosis, treat for CHF (or conversely asthma) and give them time to stabilize.

807 POCUS: F ELINE D IFFERENCES – A BDOMEN AND T HORAX Differences in Detecting “Lung Sliding” and Pneumothorax during TFAST (Figure 39.31) Regardless of the species, rapid shallow breathing is problematic for the detection of pneumothorax (PTX). For cats, mild sedation such as butorphanol, that may be given subcutaneously and is less likely to con - tribute to panting, is very helpful to slow the respiratory pattern through the alleviation of anxiety. Probe maneuvers that enhance “lung sliding” are placing the rib head in the center of the screen to scatter echoes (“one‐eyed gator sign”), and fanning the probe from a 90° angle of insonation to a 75° angle to oblique the echoes (Lisciandro 2014b,c). In the author’s experience (GL), spontaneously breathing cats with PTX have too much thoracic wall movement for M‐mode to be effective (slowing the frame speed down is an important tip). The “lung point” should be sought in any suspect PTX feline and the TFAST PTX 1/3s Rule used for monitoring and decision making (Figure 39.32). See Chapters 17, 18, 22, and 23 for greater detail (Lisciandro et al. 2008; Lisciandro 2011; Boysen and Lisciandro 2013). Differences in Vet BLUE Imaging of the lung is similar in cats and dogs. Expect all Vet BLUE views to be dry, “lung sliding” with A‐ lines, with uncommon B‐lines in both adult and juvenile cats in normalcy (Lisciandro et al. 2017, 2018) (Figure 39.33). Moreover, the absence of B‐lines during Vet BLUE (ABAV) in respiratory distressed cats (and dogs) effectively rules out left‐sided CHF, sparing the patient the risk of restraint for an echocardiogram or thoracic radiography until they are more stable (Lisciandro et al. 2016, 2017; Ward et al. 2017). See Chapters 22 and 23 for greater detail. Differences in Applications of the Vet BLUE B‐line Scoring System Use of the Volpicelli Strong Positive Model, meaning that only a score of >3 or infinite B‐lines is a “positive,” works better for CHF in cats than dogs (see Figures 23.14, 23.17, and 36.17). In cats, Vet BLUE had the same sensitivity (87%) and specificity (89%) as thoracic radiography (Ward et al. 2017). However, regional disease as well as other “wet lung phe - nomena” must also be considered. In Texas, where one of the authors resides, fungal pneumonia caused by histoplasmosis has an overall Vet BLUE wet pattern (many B‐lines) similar to that expected for feline CHF. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 815 Introduction Point‐of‐care ultrasound (POCUS) of small mammal patients can provide important clinical information. The indications and principles in exotic companion mammals are similar to dogs and cats; however, this chapter will discuss more unique exotic companion mammal conditions that may be detected through POCUS. With advances in ultrasound technology, image quality has improved and its cost is more eco- nomical, making ultrasound an option for many exotic companion mammal patients. POCUS and FAST ultrasound of exotic companion mammals, as with dogs and cats, can help direct resuscitation strat- egies and diagnostic testing decisions and thus assist in emergency management during initial triage of these patients. What POCUS: Exotic Companion Mammals Can Do • Diagnose free fluid in the abdomen. • Allow for ultrasound‐guided cystocentesis. • Allow for the detection of urinary bladder abnormalities. • Diagnose pleural effusion and guide thoracocentesis. • Diagnose pericardial effusion and guide pericardiocentesis. • Identify obvious abdominal masses and organomegaly. • Identify obvious cardiac chamber enlargement. What POCUS: Exotic Companion Mammals Cannot Do • Cannot ultrasonographically characterize free fluid, which requires sample acquisition and fluid analysis. • Cannot replace proper training and experience. Indications • Anorexia. • Anemia. • Acute abdomen. • Suspicion of ascites, pleural effusion, or pericardial effusion. • Further investigation of urinary tract abnormalities, such as hematuria, dysuria, stranguria, urine stain- ing of the perineum, or history of cystolithiasis. • Palpable abdominal mass or space‐occupying lesion in the abdomen. • Presence of vaginal discharge. • Pregnancy diagnosis. • Heart murmur, abnormal auscultation, or arrhythmias. • Respiratory distress. Objectives • Recognize basic abnormalities including obvious effusions and masses of the peritoneal and pleural cavities, retroperitoneal space, pericar - dial sac, and lung.
