816 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER • Understand some unique differences between exotic companion mammals and dogs and cats. • Understand the limitations of POCUS and FAST ultrasound in exotic companion mammals. Anatomy Gastrointestinal T racts The anatomy of exotic companion mammals is gener - ally similar to domestic carnivores with some important exceptions. Exotic companion mammal herbivores, par- ticularly rabbits and hystricomorph rodents (i.e., guinea pigs, chinchillas), have a unique gastrointestinal system. Herbivorous hindgut fermenters have gastrointestinal tracts that are much larger than exotic companion carni- vores, and when distended with gas as a result of ileus, these can hamper ultrasound imaging (ultrasound does not transmit through air). Moreover, their stomach is typically larger and never empty of ingesta in normalcy (solids, fluids, air). Furthermore, these herbivores also possess a large cecum, mainly located in the right abdomen in rabbits and in the central to left abdomen in guinea pigs. Unlike carnivores, rabbits have a gastroin- testinal‐associated lymphoid organ at their ileocecal junction, called the sacculus rotundus, which is some - times visible and should not be confused with a mass. Occasionally, the blind end of their cecum is also visual- ized on ultrasound as thickened, finger‐like projections, referred to as the vermiform appendix. It should be noted that ferrets do not have a cecum. Spleen Rabbits have a very small spleen that is sometimes not visualized on a complete detailed abdominal ultrasound examination. Conversely, ferrets have a very large spleen that is easily detected on POCUS and AFAST ultrasound. Reproductive Male guinea pigs have large paired seminal vesicles or vesicular glands that can be mistaken ultrasonographi- cally for uterine horns. Patient Positioning and Probe Selection Hair is generally not shaved but rather parted for max- imal probe‐to‐skin contact with the use of 70% isopropyl alcohol and acoustic coupling gel. Keep in mind the size of the patient and amount of 70% isopropyl alcohol and acoustic coupling gel used because hypothermia can occur quickly, especially in unstable and critical patients. Clinical status should always be evaluated prior to any handling, degrees of restraint, and diagnostics being undertaken. Dyspneic or highly distressed exotic companion mammals often benefit from some degree of sedation and/or anes - thesia prior to performing diagnostics, and supportive care principles should be implemented, such as flow‐ by oxygen. It is also important to have technical support from someone who is comfortable with exotic companion mammal restraint to decrease risk of injury to the patient, handler, and attending veterinarian. Positioning may range from the traditional dorsal recumbency in acceptably stable patients, as in Figure 40.1, to lateral recumbency and even standing (see Chapters 6, 7, 17, 18, 22, 23, 36, and 37). Figure 40.1. Dorsal recumbency positioning in a ferret. Positioning of a ferret ( Mustela putorius furo) for ultrasound examination of the abdomen. The ferret is sedated and receiving flow‐by oxygen for the procedure. Note that the Global FAST approach is now being used in standing position for all three of its components, which may prove helpful in exotic companion mammals by lessening degrees of chemical restraint.

817 POCUS: Ex OTIC C OMPANION M AMMALS A curvilinear (microconvex) or linear transducer (probe) with a range of 5–10 MHz is often acceptable for larger patients such as rabbits and ferrets. However, a 7.5–8 MHz transducer (probe) for smaller patients is generally more useful. Higher frequency transducers (probes) provide better spatial resolution but will have less depth penetration in the patient (Fischetti 2012). Imaging the Normal Exotic Companion Mammal Guidelines for POCUS and FAST ultrasound examina- tions, as well as complete detailed abdominal ultra - sound and complete echocardiography, are generally analogous to those of the dog and cat with similar indi- cations. However, the ferret gastrointestinal ultra - sound examination often provides more diagnostic information and better image quality than the gas‐ filled abdomens of herbivorous rabbit and rodent patients (Fischetti 2012). POCUS‐Detected Conditions FAST ultrasound examinations are highly sensitive and specific for effusions and should be considered as good imaging modalities to rule in and rule out free fluid. On the other hand, soft tissue conditions are more user dependent and should be considered more as a rule‐in test, triggering confirmatory imaging and testing. The different exotic companion mammals and con - ditions that may be potentially recognized using POCUS and the Global FAST approach (AFAST, TFAST, and Vet BLUE) are described. Ferrets Urinary Urolithiasis has become less common in ferrets due to improvements in husbandry and diet. However, urolith- iasis should be considered in the differential diagnosis for any ferret that presents with stranguria and urinary tract signs (Pollock 2012). POCUS would be useful in rapidly ruling in cystolithiasis and soft tissue abnormal- ities of the urinary bladder as a cause of the ferret’s pre- senting signs (Figure 40.2). A cystocentesis with ultrasound guidance can easily be performed in ferrets, providing a safer option over blind cystocentesis. Another important differential for stranguria in the ferret is prostatic cysts, which often develop in association with adrenocortical disease. On POCUS, prostatic cysts often contain hypoechoic to anechoic (black) fluid. (Pollock, 2012) (Figure 40.3). Enlarged or irregular adrenal glands may also be detected or sus - pected via POCUS (Figure 40.4). Gastrointestinal and Hepatobiliary Gastrointestinal foreign bodies in ferrets are typically not radiodense and thus are less obvious. Additionally, there may not be obvious radiographic signs of mechanical ileus compared to other domestic carni - vores. Thus, ultrasonographic confirmation is often required prior to surgery and has been shown to be a more reliable test in dogs, when performed by skilled sonographers (Sharma et al. 2011). Indirect evidence of an obstruction and evidence of peritonitis may be rec - ognized by general AFAST principles and the finding of distended loops of small intestine as well as plica - tion may be noted (see Chapters 6, 7, and 12). Spleen Splenomegaly is a very common clinical finding in most North American ferrets older than 1 year of age (Figure 40.5) (Morrisey and Draus 2012). Several conditions result in splenomegaly in ferrets, including extramedullary hematopoiesis (EMH) most com - monly, as well as neoplasia (mainly lymphoma), hypersplenism, and splenic congestion. Typically, the EMH spleen has a uniform echogenicity compared to neoplasia, where the parenchyma appears mottled, similar to the “Swiss cheese” appearance in dogs (Morrisey and Draus 2012) (see Chapter 9). Other con- ditions such as splenic torsion, splenic abscesses, and splenic ruptures are possible but quite rare (Morrisey and Draus 2012). Pancreas A common ferret presentation is hypoglycemia due to pancreatic beta‐islet cell tumors (Antinoff and Williams 2012). However, abdominal ultrasound has low sensitivity in detecting islet cell tumors, often due to the microscopic size the most of these tumors (Rosenthal and Wyre 2012). If sonographically detectable, these pancreatic beta‐islet cell tumors are only recognized as small nodule(s) by skilled sonographers. Neoplasia Ferrets with lymphoma commonly present with a mediastinal mass, thoracic lymphadenopathy, and/or pleural effusion, as well as enlargement of the spleen, liver, or kidneys (Antinoff and Williams 2012) (Figure 40.6). In these cases, POCUS or TFAST can be useful for diagnosis of pleural effusion, followed by ultrasound‐guided thoracocentesis for sample acquisi- tion and cytological evaluation. Moreover, ultrasound‐ guided aspiration of enlarged lymph node(s) is a common way of diagnosing lymphoma in ferrets (Figure 40.7). Figure 40.5. Splenomegaly in a ferret. 820 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Other Cavitary effusion, especially of the thorax, is relatively common in ferrets due to a variety of underlying causes, including cardiac disease. TFAST with basic echocardiography views can be helpful for expediting diagnosis through the finding of an enlarged left atrial to aortic ratio (LA:Ao) and alveolar‐interstitial edema. Normal echocardiography measurements have been published in ferrets and the LA:Ao should be <1:1.3 (Vastenburg et al. 2004). TFAST provides a more thor - ough initial diagnostic evaluation in these cases over physical exam and auscultation alone when radiog - raphy and a complete echocardiogram are too risky or not immediately available (Figure 40.8; see also Figures 36.6 and 36.7) (see Chapters 17, 18–22, 23, 36 and 37). Rabbits Urinary Rabbits have a unique calcium metabolism and as a result appear to have a high prevalence of urolithiasis when combined with other genetic and husbandry‐related factors (Klaphake 2012). Rabbits have unregulated intestinal absorption of dietary calcium, which is excreted massively through the urine. Therefore, urinary “sludge” or slightly hyper - echoic (bright) urine is a common finding in rabbits with high dietary calcium. Ultrasound can be useful to both detect discrete calculi in the urinary bladder and aid in collection of a urine sample via cystocen - tesis (Figure 40.9) (Klaphake and Paul‐Murphy 2012). Cystocentesis in rabbits may be more challenging than other species because their bladder wall is somewhat flaccid and as a result the needle often indents the wall of the bladder without entering. Additionally, nonsedated rabbits may abruptly react to needle insertions, posing greater patient risk for iatrogenic urinary bladder trauma. Gastrointestinal and Hepatobiliary Liver lobe torsion is not an uncommon problem in rabbits. Diagnosis of liver lobe torsion is best left to a skilled sonographer because the condition is surgically treated in a rabbit that may not be stable. A complete, detailed abdominal ultra - sound is typically the most sensitive test for diagnosing liver lobe torsion, which often requires an emergent lobectomy (Graham et al. 2014). In young rabbits, hepatic coccidiosis is seen, and results in a very heterogeneous hyperechogenic (bright) liver parenchyma with hyperechogenic (bright) bile ducts and a hyperechogenic (bright white) gallbladder wall (Cam et al. 2008). Reproductive Uterine adenocarcinoma is a common disease in intact female rabbits over the age of 4 years (Klaphake and Paul‐Murphy 2012). Ultrasound imaging can assist in a diagnosis when a caudal abdominal soft tissue mass or uterine enlargement is palpable on physical examina - tion (Figure 40.11) (Klaphake and Paul‐Murphy 2012). In advanced stages of disease, enlarged abdominal lymph nodes, peritoneal and organ metastasis, or free abdominal fluid and combinations thereof may be detected. These masses are also frequently calcified (Kunzel et al. 2015). The Global FAST approach is a good way to rapidly stage the rabbit by surveying the remaining abdomen (AFAST), thorax (TFAST) and Vet BLUE (lung) (see Chapters 36 and 37 and Figure 36.20). Reproductive Another common presentation for guinea pigs is the presence of ovarian cysts in the female (Hawkins and Bishop 2012). Affected animals may or may not have associated clinical signs, but when present, are best diagnosed with the use of ultrasound (Hawkins and Bishop 2012). Ovarian cysts can be visualized sono - graphically dorsal to the kidney and contiguous with the ovary (Figure 40.13) (Beregi et al. 1999). The cysts are fluid filled and anechoic (black) with acoustic enhancement, allowing them to be easily distin - guished from a mass (Beregi et al. 1999). Color flow Doppler may also be used for differentiation because cysts have no intracystic blood flow versus a mass. These cysts can be quite large, and an ultrasound‐ guided method may be used to drain large cysts, although recurrence of cystic fluid is common with this method of treatment. Chinchillas Reproductive Pet chinchillas may present with pyometra and often have palpable uterine enlargement on physical examination (Mans and Donnelly 2012). Abdominal ultrasound is the preferred imaging technique for diagnosis of pyometra, with the uterus being fluid distended by various degrees of echogenicity from anechoic (black) to hyperechoic (bright) fluid (Figure 40.14). Hamsters Gastrointestinal and Hepatobiliary Hepatic cystic disease is not an uncommon finding in hamsters (Brown and Donnelly 2012). The cysts are often diagnosed initially on palpation and veri - fied with ultrasonography. They can be of multiple sizes and shapes (Figure 40.15; see also Figures 8.5, 8.6, and 8.9). Hedgehogs Reproductive Various lesions of the uterus are common in African hedgehogs. Some of the most common uterine dis - eases include neoplasia, including adenosarcoma, endometrial stromal sarcomas, adenoleiomyosarcoma, and adenoleiomyoma (Mikaelian et al. 2004). Other common lesions include endometrial polyps, pyome - tra, and metritis (Figure 40.16) (Mikaelian et al. 2004; Ivy and Carpenter 2012). Neoplasia Neoplasia is very common in African hedgehogs and a wide variety of both discrete tumors and dis - seminated neoplasms have been reported (Ivy and Carpenter 2012). An AFAST with its target organ approach or specific POCUS abdominal examina - tions can be useful to investigate the presence of a mass in a hedgehog. Use of the Global FAST approach for staging localized versus disseminated disease is a rapid add‐on or initial approach (see Chapters 36 and 37). Figure 40.13. Guinea pig ovarian cyst . Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 829 Introduction The use of ultrasound has been applied to marine mammals because of the limitations of radiography that require transport and risk. Although not an exhaustive list of contributors to the body of imaging‐ related work in the field of marine mammals, much of the available literature has come from pioneering groups affiliated with the Navy Marine Mammal Program (NMMP); the National Marine Mammal Foundation; Sea World; Ocean Park (Hong Kong); the Brookfield Zoo, and Dolphin Quest. These institutions and affiliated experts have contributed substantially to the body of work and knowledge regarding the diagnostic imaging evaluations of marine mammals, including dolphins. The NMMP publications have included comparative computed tomography (CT) thoracic imaging to lung ultrasound using two differ - ent methods (Smith et al. 2012; Ivančic ́ et al. 2014). They concluded that lung ultrasound was an effective means of cetacean pulmonary evaluation (Smith et al. 2012). The group also provided a full‐body ultrasound approach of routine health assessment (of undisclosed frequency, e.g., annual versus semi‐annual) for evalua- tion of the mixed population of dolphins within their collection (Smith et al. 2012). Dr Enrique Yarto, MVZ, of Mexico City, and I (GL) met several years ago. We spoke about wildlife and zoo medicine, his area of special interest and expertise. Naturally, the subject of Global FAST came up as an extension of the physical exam for both wellness status assessment and preliminary minimally invasive illness evaluation in bottlenose dolphins (Tursiops truncatus). Dr Yarto, familiar with several dolphin collections in Mexico, felt there was a need for advancing routine ultrasound use, especially because of the truncated time constraints typically inherent in sonographic evaluation of the cetacean species. In his experience, the use of ultrasound was primarily restricted to repro- ductive evaluation and pregnancy checks. Numerous other marine mammal veterinarians across the various facilities use abdominal and thoracic ultrasound routinely for overall health assessments as in small animals. An abbreviated point‐of‐care ultra- sound for the species is not described. Likely, most marine mammal veterinarians would like to increase their ultrasound proficiency and the translation of the Global FAST methodology offers an opportunity to do so in a standardized manner. Thus, we completed a prospective pilot study evaluating the Global FAST approach performed on a small population of 20 clini- cally normal bottlenose dolphins (Tursiops truncatus) (Yarto and Lisciandro 2017, unpublished data). A major objective included assessing proficiency at image acquisition of the target organs of the abdomen (AFAST) and thorax including heart and lung (TFAST, Vet BLUE). We also compared a second lung ultrasound meth- odology, referred to as the zig‐zag continuum approach, similar to one of the lung ultrasound examinations previously described (Smith et al. 2012), to our modi- fied Vet BLUE protocol for dolphins (Yarto and Lisciandro 2017, unpublished data) (see Figure 41.23). Our preliminary findings show that Global FAST is effective in capturing its target organs and is easily learned. Similar to adult dogs, cats, puppies, and kit- tens over 6 weeks of age, “dry lung” artifacts, “lung sliding” and A‐lines, predominate in dolphins as well POCUS: Marine Mammals Gregory R. 830 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER (Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2017, 2018; Yarto and Lisciandro 2017, unpublished data). The use of Global FAST pro- vides an unbiased set of data imaging points that may be recorded as part of general health screening and compared to future studies. Moreover, Global FAST provides a standardized and more abbreviated (shorter time duration) option for ultrasound image acquisition than traditional examinations from which images may be stored and forwarded to offsite telemedicine ser - vices, carrying the potential to improve marine mammal care. What POCUS: Marine Mammals Can Do • Establish a Global FAST examination protocol with clear objectives of the abdomen and thorax including heart and lung. • Provide a semi‐annual to annual imaging assessment tool that can be recorded and compared to future serial health assessments with the poten- tial for early detection of disease states and detri- mental medical conditions. • Provide a relatively noninvasive safe point‐of‐care imaging modality with minimal patient risk for recheck assessment during treatment of abdom- inal, thoracic, cardiac, and lung conditions. • Create a rapid screening test for general health status that also provides a standardized set of imaging data points for clinically abnormal dol- phins with the potential to “see” the problem list, and thus help dictate the diagnostic work‐up and need for additional imaging procedures. • Create a screening test for traumatic injury involving the abdominal and thoracic cavities, historically difficult to detect by physical examina- tion alone (Dennison and Saviano 2018). • Provide a standardized ultrasound examination format that may be forwarded to offsite telemedi- cine and specialty consulting services. What POCUS: Marine Mammals Cannot Do • Cannot replace proper ultrasound training and expert knowledge of dolphin anatomy. • Cannot replace a complete detailed abdominal ultrasound, complete detailed transthoracic or transesophageal echocardiogram, and noncardiac thoracic ultrasound examinations by a board‐ certified veterinary radiologist or marine mammal veterinarian with a high level of experience in medical care and ultrasonography. Indications Serves as an extension of the physical exam for clini- cally normal and abnormal marine mammals for abdominal and thoracic conditions including the heart and lung for not only the detection of effusion(s) but also obvious target organ abnormalities within the abdomen and thorax. Objectives • To understand basic anatomy of the dolphin (Figure 41.1). • To provide a systematic, easy‐to‐perform, stan- dardized and repeatable ultrasound examination that is achievable for the nonradiologist marine mammal veterinarian. • To screen the abdominal cavity for the presence of peritoneal effusion and any obvious parenchymal lesions of abdominal target organs using AFAST and its five acoustic windows. • To screen for pleural and pericardial effusion, for obvious cardiac problems, and volume status using TFAST, its echo views and volume status approach. • To screen for pulmonary edema and other lung conditions using the nine transthoracic acoustic windows of Vet BLUE. • To perform a standardized Global FAST with acceptable image acquisition for radiologist review. • To understand that lateral positioning of dolphins is an option for Global FAST. • To understand that avoiding (nonspontaneous) patient breath holding likely improves lung ultra- sound evaluation and is likely safer for the patient. Equipment, Probe Type, and Settings • Macroconvex probe of 2–5 MHz with up to 35 cm depth. • Abdominal presets may be used for the entire Global FAST examination. • No acoustic coupling gel needed if done in the water. • Ultrasound machine. ◦ Portable. ◦ Laptop format. ◦ Durable. ◦ Machine – can withstand rough handling and transport.

It is possible that some dolphins may react negatively to the harmonic sound waves arising from the probe. Most likely, this is due to a lack of conditioning to this specific acoustic stimulus as marine mammals are highly dependent on their acoustic sensory systems. It is also possible that the design of some concrete tank enclosures may enhance harmonic propagation. 834 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER nearby? The distance from the machine to the sonogra- pher must also be considered since the probe’s connection to the machine is also a limiting factor. The closer the machine is to the water, the more risk for damage to the machine if water is splashed. Only bat - tery‐powered ultrasound machines will be safe in the water environment since electric cords pose the serious risk of electrocution. The actual environment and weather must be consid- ered too. Is there a holding tank or will the event take place in an open water scenario with docks? Will the dolphin be scanned from a dock? If so, how elevated is the dock? Or will the sonographer be in the water with the dolphin? The authors have found that some dol - phins might be uncomfortable with ultrasound initially and conditioning to the harmonics of the ultrasound probe is ideal. This may particularly be important when scanning wild dolphin populations where training the dolphins to be comfortable with diagnostic procedures and conditioning them to undergo sonography may not be possible. In the authors’ opinion, conditioning is one of the most important factors for imaging success. The dolphin trainer plays an integral role in the suc- cess of the sonographic assessment and communication is imperative. The sonographer must know where the trainer will be positioned and be familiar with the individual dolphin’s personality. The trainer works in tandem to signal the sonographer as to when the ultrasound examination may be started and stopped or interrupted for any number of reasons, including dolphin breathing or allowing for a scan break including a brief swim or reward, and evaluating for signs of dolphin distress (Figure 41.4). Patient Positioning, Restraint, and Breathing Sonographic evaluation of the dolphin in dorsal recum- bency has been described but dorsal recumbency inherently presents some position‐induced problems: uncomfortable/unsustainable positioning dependent on breath holding necessitating interruption of the ultrasound examination for breathing, and dorsal recumbency could be risky for the cardiovascular or respiratory‐compromised dolphin (Figure 41.5). Spontaneous breathing is recommended for the fol - lowing reasons: breath holding results in pulmonary overinflation which can obscure the heart, breath holding may be stressful and risky for those with respiratory disease or that are hemodynamically fragile, and dolphin breaks are less frequent (see Figure 41.5). Despite performing Global FAST using lateral positioning as in small animals, many dolphins will still breath hold naturally. Distressed dolphins may also whistle or vocalize. When noticed (and ideally prior to its occurrence), the dolphin should be given a break from scanning. The sonographer can hold the pectoral fin to help keep the dolphin stable and still for scanning as well as for making small adjustments in the dolphin’s position (with the help of the trainer). Signs of Dolphin Stress So how does the stressed dolphin behave? Typically, the distressed dolphin may vocalize with a high pitch or frequent whistle or exhibit arch bending of the head and tail ventrally or laterally in the water (see Figure 41.4). Dolphin Restraint and the T rainer Many dolphins have been trained to participate in their own healthcare assessment and working with the dolphin trainers helps establish clear training objec - tives to expedite ultrasound imaging. The Global FAST Examination AFAST The acoustic windows of AFAST are named according to their target organs, similar to small animals but with some modifications (Figures 41.6 and 41.7). The target organ named AFAST views help the sonographer remember the objectives for image acquisition at each AFAST view, and remind the sonographer of the relevant anatomy. The main objective for the sonographer is to quickly identify the target organs and capture them on cine clip images for review. Over time, the sonographer will gain proficiency in interpreting basic ultrasound find - ings and clinically integrating the information to direct diagnostic and therapeutic care, including additional or follow‐up imaging and diagnostic procedures. With standardization of the AFAST acoustic windows, devi- ations from what is sonographically expected will help the sonographer begin to recognize abnormalities (Table 41.1). Probe maneuvers are repetitive in their hand motion, similar to AFAST in small animals, with fanning, rocking and returning to the starting point primarily in a longitudinal scanning plane. Transverse plane (rotating the probe) is an add‐on skill once the sonog - rapher has become comfortable with the anatomy of each AFAST acoustic window. The five AFAST acoustic windows have been modi- fied from small animals (Lisciandro et al. 2009) and are summarized in Table 41.1. They are named as follows. • Diaphragmatico‐hepatic (DH) view • Spleno‐renal (SR) view • Hepato‐renal (HR) view • Cysto‐colic reproductive (CCR) view • Umbilical (U) view Figure 41.5. AFAST view or acoustic window Target organs External landmarks Differs from dogs and cats Diaphragmatico‐hepatic view – right lateral Liver, heart, caudal vena cava, dorsocaudal lung field along the diaphragm Ventral midline immediately caudal to the xiphoid as in dogs and cats The normal caudal vena cava and hepatic veins are large, distended and without dynamic changes with the cardiac and respiratory cycles compared to small animals and thus mimic what would be considered volume overload in small animals Measurements for the marginal lymph node have been established as 5 × 2 × 2 cm in adults (Cowan and Smith 1999; Saviano 2013; Martony et al. 2017; Dennison and Saviano 2018) Spleno‐renal view – right lateral Hepato‐renal view – left lateral Left kidney, spleen Vertical line drawn from the caudal border of the dorsal fin ventrally to where it intersects with the hypaxial muscles The kidneys are similar grossly in margination to bovine kidney due to hundreds of ~1 cm units called renules. The kidneys are quite large. Often, the ureter can be seen along the midcaudal aspect of the kidney. The spleen is similar to the bovine species as it is small (fist‐ like) and difficult to locate, but best imaged in this view from the right with the dolphin in left lateral recumbency. The stomach surrounds the spleen and digestive contents in the gastric complex can obscure evaluation. The ovaries may be identified caudomedial to the kidneys. In sexually immature females they are round and hypoechoic. The vagina is not routinely imaged. 838 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Diaphragmatico‐Hepatic View The DH view target organs include the liver, diaphragm, caudal vena cava, heart, and lung along its pulmonary– diaphragmatic interface (Figures 41.8, 41.9, and 41.10). • Place the probe immediately caudal to the xiphoid and direct the scan plane far cranially so that you can see simultaneously into the abdomen and thorax. The depth is usually between 20–30 cm for an adult. The probe is fanned through the liver in both lateral directions in the longitudinal plane. • The (parietal and visceral) pleuroparenchymal junction is imaged through a relatively thick por - tion of blubber, typically 2–3 cm, depending on health status or seasonal changes of the individual. • The probe is then rocked further cranially to find the “cardiac bump” created by the beating heart against the diaphragm (see Figures 41.8 and 41.9). • The left and right marginal lymph nodes are found by fanning laterally along the cardiac apex from the midline and along the diaphragm (Figure 41.11; see also Figure 41.10). • The pleural space and deep window into lung are observed for pleural and pericardial effusion, and lung lesions along the pulmonary–diaphragmatic interface, respectively. • The caudal vena cava (CVC) is readily appreciated while fanning along the diaphragm. Questions Asked at the DH View • Is there free fluid in the abdominal cavity? In the author’s experience, dolphins can have small to moderate volumes of peritoneal effusion in nor - malcy (Dr Eric Jensen, personal communication). • What does the liver look like? Obvious masses or loss of homogeneous echogenicity? • What does the marginal lymph node look like? And its size? • What do the CVC and its associated hepatic veins look like? • Is there fluid in the pericardial sac? In the author’s experience, a small volume of pericardial effusion (<2–3 mm) can be present in otherwise apparently healthy individuals. • Is there fluid in the pleural cavity? • Are there any abnormalities along the pulmonary– diaphragmatic interface? • Are any artifacts being mistaken for pathology? Comments The dolphin species does not have a gallbladder. The CVC traverses the diaphragm and then courses along the dorsal aspect of the liver and can be confused with free fluid. Interestingly, the hepatic venous system demonstrates prominent distension and branching in clinically normal dolphins, in contrast to dogs, cats and people, in which it would reflect an abnormally high central venous pressure (see Figures 36.8, 41.8F, and 41.9). Although the CVC is used as a marker of volume status in dogs and cats and the analogous inferior vena cava in people, the CVC in dolphins is impressively distended in the normal state (referred to as FAT; see Chapters 36 and 37). Moreover, the dolphin CVC lacks dynamic changes through the cardiac and respiratory cycles; however, most dolphins are breath holding during ultrasound examination, which likely contributes to their unique difference (Fahlman et al. 2015, 2019; Sklansky et al. 2006). The gastric complex gas and contents often obscure evaluation of the spleen. 839 POCUS: M ARINE M AMMALS Though the CVC is typically large (distended) in the normal state in dolphins, we are unsure whether or not any dynamic CVC changes occur with cardiovascular pathology or changes in volume status as occur in small animals and people (see Figure 41.9) (Nelson 2010; Ferrada et al. 2012a,b). For example, pericardial effusion, cardiac tamponade, and right‐sided congestive heart failure in small animals result in a distended CVC with hepatic venous distension. Conversely, profound hypovolemia results in a small flat CVC (Ferrada et al. 2012a,b). Dolphin CVC hemodynamic alterations would be an area of future study but in the author’s experience, there seems to be very little dis - tensibility change during the cardiac cycle and manipulating the respiratory cycle to discourage breath holding (encourage spontaneous breathing) may not be possible (Yarto and Lisciandro 2017, unpub- lished data). 843 POCUS: M ARINE M AMMALS However, the spleen may be imaged from the HR, SR (from left lateral recumbency) and Umbilical views, with SR view from left recumbency presenting the best acoustic window for visualization (see Figure 41.16). The expected target organs are the respective kidney, associated reproductive organs, spleen, and liver in small animals. In the dolphin, the respective kidneys and reproductive tract can be imaged at the SR and HR views. The spleen is a small organ not likely associated with extramedullary hematopoiesis in this species, and uncommonly associated with disease states such as lymphoma, trauma and splenic necrosis in association with Brucella sp. (Bossart et al. 1997; Cowan and Smith 1999; Jauniaux et al. 2010). • Place the probe directly ventral to the caudal border of the dorsal fin. The hypaxial muscles may be thought of as the dorsal border of the abdominal body wall. Move the probe ventrally on the body wall, continuing to use the caudal border of the dorsal fin as your landmark until the multireniculated (mul- tilobed) kidney is encountered (see Figure 41.13). • On the left side, the left kidney should be fanned through in both directions longitudinally then rocked cranially for a view into the abdominal cavity (and in time the add‐on skill of transverse orientation). • On the right side, the right kidney should be fanned through in both directions longitudinally then rocked cranially for a view into the abdominal cavity (and in time the add‐on skill of transverse orientation). • The probe may also be directed ventrocaudal to the kidneys for reproductive organ imaging (see Figure 41.14). Figure 41.13. The spleno‐renal and hepato‐renal views. In (A) and (B) the external starting probe position is shown and in (C) and (D) the left and right kidney are shown. Sliding ventrally from the starting points brings the kidneys into view. Although subtle, the kidney is typically found just below the palpable hypaxial line ventral to slightly caudoventral to the middorsal fin. At this location, the probe is slid immediately along the hypaxial line while fanning until the kidney comes into view. The dolphin kidney can initially be difficult to recognize because its echo architecture is so dissimilar to dogs and cats. AFAST‐Applied Fluid Scoring System The AFAST‐applied abdominal fluid scoring system may be calculated for peritoneal effusion, providing an objective number for recording in medical records and for tracking static, resolving or worsening ascites. The abdominal fluid score (AFS) ranges from 0 (nega- tive all AFAST views) to 4 (positive all four AFAST views) in small animals (see Chapters 6 and 7) (Lisciandro et al. 2009). In dolphins, scoring of 1–5 may be more appropriate. Thus, an AFS of 1 is positive at any single view. An AFS of 2 is positive at any two views. An AFS of 3 and 4 is positive at any three or four views, respectively. A maximum AFS of 5 is positive at all five views. The terms trivial, mild, moderate, and severe in addition to the AFS may also be helpful for better semiquantifying ascites (Lisciandro et al. 2009, 2019; Lisciandro 2011). Regardless, the presence of mild anechoic peritoneal effusion can vary from one day to another and may be of little clinical relevance. TFAST In small animals TFAST examination includes left and right pericardial site (PCS) views, left and right chest tube site (CTS) views, and the singly applied DH view (Lisciandro et al. 2008; Lisciandro 2016; McMurray et al. 2016). When applied to dolphins, the CTS views are eliminated and replaced by the Vet BLUE views when evaluated. The DH view is in fact part of AFAST, TFAST, and Vet BLUE. For pneumo- thorax (PTX), the highest point over the pleural cavity, analogous to the CTS view, would be imaged dependent on the dolphin’s position (where free air in the pleural cavity would rise). In small animals, PCS views are used for pleural and pericardial effu- sion, any adjacent masses, and any obvious chamber enlargement, wall thickening or other abnormalities, including intracardiac masses. These transthoracic views seem to be more limited in the dolphin for cardiac evaluation because of their thoracic confor - mation and marked air interference from lung limiting the acoustic window. Dilated cardiomyopathy and right‐sided congestive heart failure has been described (Lutmerding et al. 2015). TFAST echo views are similar to those in small animals; however, the dolphin heart is very glo- boid in shape and much more difficult to image sonographically because of the barrel‐shaped, somewhat bulldog‐like conformation of the thoracic cavity (Sklansky et al. 2006). Further, air interfer - ence from breath holding can obscure cardiac assessment (Sklansky et al. 2006; Chetboul et al. 2012). During inspiration, dolphins aerate up to 95% of their lung capacity, which is significantly more than in terrestrial mammals, posing another challenging factor for TFAST evaluation (Fahlman et al. 2015). • Find the heart, as in dogs and cats, by palpating with your nonprobe hand for the apical beat. Yes, despite their size, you can generally palpate their apical beat! • Place the probe at the maximum intensity of the apical beat. • Use the pectoral fin for stabilization of the probe and to prevent dolphin drifting. • Theoretically, right parasternal short‐axis views are performed for volume and contractility (fractional shortening, FS%). • The right parasternal short‐axis view for the left atrium:aorta ratio (LA:Ao) is performed to screen for left‐sided problems (specifically left atrial enlargement). • The “TFAST slide” as described in Chapters 17 and 18 may be applied to the dolphin by caudally sliding the probe into the “cardiac‐diaphragmatic pouch” and then cranially into the “cardiac‐cervical pouch” (see Figures 17.17 and 17.18). • During the “TFAST slide” the probe may also be rotated to an orientation parallel to the ribs for an intercostal view detecting smaller volume pleural effusions that may not be obvious in perpendicular orientation (to the long axis of the ribs). It takes repetition and practice to achieve proficiency in the TFAST echo views. Transesophageal echocardi- ography (TEE), when available, is the gold standard for cardiac evaluation in this species and has clear advantages over transthoracic echocardiography because it provides a better acoustic window. Specifically, TEE avoids the acoustic gas artifacts caused by surrounding lung interference (Sklansky et al. 2006). TEE is generally well tolerated by dolphins as a trained medical behavior, but is beyond the scope of this chapter (Sklansky et al. 2006). Questions Asked at TFAST • Is there any pleural effusion? • Is there any pericardial effusion? • Are cardiac chamber ratios unremarkable or abnormal? • Are there soft tissue masses in any cardiac chambers? • Are there soft tissue masses in the pericardium or pleural cavity? • Are any artifacts being mistaken for pathology? Although B‐lines are nonspecific and represent various forms of alveolar‐interstitial edema, their absence rules out left‐sided congestive heart failure (CHF) with high sensitivity in dogs, cats, and people (Lichtenstein et al. 2009; Lichtenstein and Karakitsos 2012; Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2016, 2017; Ward et al. 2017, Vezzosi et al. 2017). The “Global FAST nonecho fallback view” for right‐ sided CHF is the FAST DH view, CVC, and hepatic venous characterization. By definition, right‐sided CHF requires distension of CVC (FAT) and hepatic veins (hepatic venous congestion), referred to as the “tree trunk sign” (Lisciandro et al. 2014) (see Figure 36.8). Our preliminary findings are that the right‐sided CHF “Global FAST nonecho fallback view” is likely unreliable in dolphins because the CVC is generally distended with little to no change in its dimensions (or collapsibility) during the cardiac and respiratory cycles (Yarto and Lisciandro 2017, unpublished data). Finding abnormalities during TFAST cardiac imaging can direct the need for more advanced imaging, including TEE and CT. Vet BLUE Lung Orientation: The “Gator Sign” Vet BLUE is a regional lung ultrasound examination applied bilaterally with nine acoustic windows per hemithorax typically obtained at a depth of 11–13 cm. The Vet BLUE also includes the nontransthoracic DH view as a deeper window into lung along the pulmonary–diaphragmatic interface (see Figures 22.11, 22.12, 22.14, and 41.9). At each acoustic window, three intercostal spaces are evaluated with the probe positioned perpendicular to the long axis of the ribs to establish the “gator sign” as in small animals (Figure 41.18) (Lisciandro et al. 2014). The pulmonary–pleural interface (PPI) is identified by its linear hyperechoic appearance (Figures 41.18, 41.19, 41.20). Basic lung ultrasound signs are easily learned and include A‐lines, “lung sliding,” B‐lines and then signs of varying degrees of consolidation – shred sign, tissue sign, nodule sign and wedge sign (see Figures 22.2 and 23.2–23.13). These artifacts, the six Vet BLUE lung ultrasound signs, plus signs of pneu- mothorax, as well as optimization of lung ultrasound imaging techniques, are detailed in Chapter 17, including the section Tricks of the Trade, and integration of Vet BLUE lung ultrasound signs in Chapters 22 and 23. Artifacts and Vet BLUE Lung Ultrasound Signs A‐lines A‐lines are equidistant horizontal lines that extend from, and are parallel to, the PPI in the absence of pleural space disease in the presence of normal aerated lung at its surface. “Lung sliding” (glide sign or glid- ing), the to and fro motion of lung with phases of respiration, distinguishes dry lung from pneumo- thorax in which “lung sliding” is absent. “A” stands for “air” is a good way to remember A‐lines. The author refers to the finding of A‐lines with “lung sliding” as “dry lung” or normal lung without pathology. “Lung sliding” will not be apparent when the patient is apneic (or breath holding). When scanning dolphins, breath holding is common and “lung sliding” may not be apparent for long periods of time during apnea. “Lung sliding” can be appreciated best when a rib is isolated at the center of the field of view, referred to as the “one‐eyed gator sign” (see Figure 22.8). “Lung sliding” may also be appreciated when visualization and assessment are coordinated with prompted dolphin breath taking commanded by the trainer (see Figures 17.12 and 41.18). B‐lines These are vertical lines that swing like a pendulum with inspiration and expiration that do not fade through the far‐field while obliterating A‐lines. B‐lines have also been called ultrasound lung rockets (Lisciandro et al. 2014). B‐lines most often represent forms of alveolar‐interstitial edema but are nonspecific and thus when observed are referred to as alveolar‐ interstitial syndrome (AIS) (Lichtenstein et al. 1997; Volpicelli et al. 2006; Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2017; Ward et al. 2017, 2018). Less commonly, they represent fibrosis along the lung surface including senescent lung in people (Shyamsundar et al. 2013). The B‐line is created most often by fluid next to air on the outer surface of lung and the strong difference in acoustic impedance causes the artifact (Lichtenstein et al. 1997; Volpicelli et al. 2006). The author refers to the finding of B‐lines as “wet lung” and numbers of B‐lines are counted for a score using the Vet BLUE B‐line scor- ing system (see Chapters 22 and 23). Briefly, the largest number over a single intercostal space representative of each Vet BLUE view is scored as 0 (negative), 1, 2, 3, >3, and infinity (when confluent and blended over the entire intercostal space) (see Figures 23.26, 36.17). In a recent study Vet BLUE detected alveolar‐interstitial edema more frequently than three‐view thoracic radi- ography in dogs and cats (Ward et al. 2018).

854 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Performing Vet BLUE Step by Step Vet BLUE is performed similarly as in dogs and cats (and any other mammals) but there are nine acoustic windows per hemithorax (versus four in dogs and cats) (see Chapters 22 and 23, (Figures 41.6D,E, 41.7D,E, and 41.23) (Yarto and Lisciandro 2017, unpublished data). • The caudodorsal transition zone (CdTZ) is located in the region directly dorsal to the xiphoid (see Figures 41.6D,E and 41.7D,E). The probe is placed perpendicular to the long axis of the ribs to identify the orientation for all lung ultrasound, called the “gator sign” (see Figure 41.18). This is the transition zone of the pleural and peritoneal cavities and is definitively identified by finding the “curtain sign” (see Chapter 17), where a linear distally oriented dirty shadow arises from left to right of the screen during a spontaneous breath and casts a dirty shadow over abdominal structures (see Figures 22.10 and 41.20) (Neelis et al. 2015). The other approach is to slide caudally and identify abdom- inal structures. From the abdominal structures, slide cranial until the “curtain sign” and the hyperechoic PPI or “lung line” are identified. Placing the probe too dorsal will reveal a pennate‐like muscle pattern deep to the blubber with lack of a “lung line.” • From the CdTZ, slide 2–3 spaces cranial and this is Vet BLUE point 1. • Evaluate point 1’s intercostal space and then slide an intercostal space caudal, being aware you are moving toward the CdTZ. Survey that space by moving from the longitudinal to transverse orien- tation (rotating 90° and then returning to the “gator sign”) before returning to point 1, then slide a space cranially, completing the evaluation of three inter - costal spaces at point 1. This methodology is iden- tically repeated at each transthoracic Vet BLUE view (see Figures 41.19. 41.20 and 41.23). • The other eight Vet BLUE views are found by dividing the dolphin thorax into upper, middle, and lower thirds which are then divided into three points of evaluation horizontally across the regions (see Figures 41.6D,E and 41.7D,E). • Slide cranially to point 2 in the upper third thoracic region then repeat sliding one intercostal space caudal and one cranial from your starting point 2 and within each intercostal space rotate 90° into the transverse plane and the return to the “gator sign” orientation. • At point 3, you are moving toward the scapula; being a flat bone, it will have a hyperechcoic line similar to the PPI. Thus, it is important to pay attention as you slide the probe to point 3 and that your PPI line is continuous with that of point 2. Being careful to follow the PPI will avoid mistaking the scapular margin for lung tissue. Three inter - costal spaces are again interrogated for lung ultra- sound artifacts and signs. • Points 4 and 7 in the middle third of the thorax are again in transition zones, referred to as pleural– peritoneal transition zones, and care must be taken not to mistake abdominal structures for lung pathology by repeating the same methodology as for point 1. • Points 6 and 9 in the lower third of the thorax will be at the cranial borders of the thorax and as for point 3, care must be taken to ensure that bone is not mistaken for the PPI at point 6, and point 9 is under the pectoral fin (ventrally). • Count numbers of B‐lines at all Vet BLUE views and note comet‐tails (small, triangular, echogenic reverberation artifacts arising from the PPI but fail- ing to extend through the far‐field as a B‐line would). Comet‐tail artifacts are not B‐lines and should not generally be quantified by convention. See Chapters 22 and 23. • The rule of thumb is that if you cannot clearly define the “gator sign” then you cannot be sure you are in fact imaging lung. The pectoral fin will need to be slightly extended to get a good image of the cranial lung region. It is not uncommon to have comet‐tail artifacts and B‐lines at the most ventral views bilaterally, thus these extremities of lung, where lung is thin, need to be interpreted cautiously. Pitfalls – Probe Positioning and Orientation Longitudinal or Perpendicular to Ribs The “gator sign” orientation must be acquired with the probe held consistently perpendicular to the long axis of the ribs, what some sonographers would describe as a longitudinal orientation (parallel to the long axis [spine] of the patient’s body) (see Figures 17.12, 41.18, and 41.19) (Lisciandro et al. 2014). Without clearly establishing the “gator sign” orientation, the PPI or “lung line” cannot be accurately located (Figures 41.21 and 41.22). There are two ways to describe the PPI. The first is where lung is directly juxtaposed to the inter - costal space, preferred by the author and referred to as the “lung line.” The second description is where parietal

855 POCUS: M ARINE M AMMALS and visceral pleura are directly juxtaposed; however, in disease states, such as pleural effusion, there is often separation of the two pleura so the “lung line” is a better descriptor (see Figures 17.8, 17.9, and 17.12). T ransverse or Parallel to Ribs Some lung sonographers will advocate rotating the probe so that it is parallel to the long axis of the ribs, or in transverse orientation to the patient’s long axis, and we have used this technique in the dolphin Vet BLUE examination. The dorsocaudal margin of the scapula, subcutaneous emphysema, and even air in the stomach (in small ani- mals), and fascial planes below the blubber can be easily mistaken for the lung surface. Comments The zig‐zag continuum (ZZC) is shown in Figure 41.23 along with comparison to Vet BLUE. The ZZC was evaluated in our study by recording 60‐second clips of each hemithorax with similar ultrasound settings and depth proportions as Vet BLUE. We found that although effective as a screening test for obvious lung ultrasound artifacts and lung signs, the ZZC was prob- lematic for the following reasons. • The caudal, dorsal, ventral, and cranial borders of the pleural cavity must be known to avoid con - fusing border structures with lung pathology. Figure 41.22. B‐lines and comet‐tail artifacts. B‐lines are vertical hyperechoic streaks that swing like a pendulum during phases of respiration. Moreover, they do not fade and they obliterate A‐lines. B‐lines have also been called “ultrasound lung rockets” because of their streaky hyperechoic appearance from the “lung line” through the far‐field. In breath holding, B‐lines may be more difficult to recognize and count (score). Comet‐tail artifacts are short and do not extend through the far‐field. In images (A–D) you can see the difference between B‐lines and comet‐tail artifacts; however, B‐lines may be dampened by breath‐holding dolphins as in (B). B‐lines and comet‐tail artifacts are routinely seen at Vet BLUE points 7, 8, and 9 likely due to the least aerated character of the lung tissue in these locations because of some degree of atelectasis as the lungs in this location generally have less air volume and possibly greater compressibility. 858 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER • If the dolphin moved or needed a break, where do you restart the ZZC examination? • Where were the lesions for recording purposes and for comparison on follow‐up (serial) evaluations? The advantage of the ZZC is that it may be a more comprehensive lung screening test. However, compar- ative studies are needed for further investigation of the efficacy of these techniques in identifying lung disease and providing a general lung overview. Vet BLUE likely provides nearly similar amounts of lung cov- erage and representation as the ZZC, with the distinct advantage of being able to record location of lung ultrasound findings for monitoring. Likely both for - mats would be included in a pulmonary assessment. Most Efficient Ways to Perform Global FAST The Global FAST views are efficiently performed in the following manner, beginning with the easiest, quickest views and moving to the most time‐consuming, chal- lenging, and least reliable TFAST echo views, starting with the dolphin in right lateral positioning (Yarto and Lisciandro 2017, unpublished data). • AFAST: DH to SR to CCR and then the umbilical view. • Vet BLUE left views: points 1–9. • TFAST: left PCS view for the left apical view and TFAST slide for pleural effusion followed by the right PCS view for short‐ and long‐axis views and the TFAST slide for pleural effusion. Position change from right lateral to left lateral. • Vet BLUE right views: points 1–9. • AFAST final HR view. If starting in left lateral recumbency, analogously perform the blended AFAST‐Vet BLUE TFAST and the right PCS view may be attempted when the dolphin is moved to right lateral if unsuccessful in left lateral. Findings should be documented on Goal‐Directed Templates (Figure 41.24). Other POCUS – Venipuncture, Thyroids, Testicles, Eyes, and Fetus POCUS can be used for venous puncture of the superficial caudal peduncular vein. This provides access for blood letting or phlebotomies, especially in cases of hemosiderosis. Placement of the animal in dorsal recumbency for sonographic purposes is time limited because the animal has to be turned frequently and repositioned for normal respiration (Kyung‐Yeon et al. 2013). The use of ultrasound for thyroid and testicular evaluation has been described (Brook 1997; Brook et al. 1991, 2000, 2019; Kot et al. 2012). Ocular ultrasound would follow similar principles to other species and is an effective imaging tool especially since the eye is a fluid‐filled structure (Cartee et al. 1995; Brook et al. 2001; Dennison and Saviano 2018). Finally, fetal struc- tures have been described in normalcy and in abnormal conditions not included in this chapter (Brook 1994; Brook et al. 2007; Jensen 1999; Stone et al. 1999; Sklansky et al. 2010). Global FAST Goal‐Directed Template Data must be recorded for it to be valuable. Moreover, the goal‐directed template keeps the sonographer on task and objectives are clear to anyone looking over the report. Soft tissue abnormalities may be placed in the “Comments” section (see Figure 41.24). Pearls and Pitfalls, The Final Say There is little widely accessible information regarding ultrasound use in marine mammals. This chapter serves as a standardized beginning from which sonog- raphers can start building ultrasound skills and create global profiles as an extension of their physical exam for dolphins and other marine mammals. Much is unknown but in time, with more ultrasound use, con- clusions may be better drawn on improving POCUS use in this fascinating species as well as other marine mammals. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 863 Introduction Ultrasound of the coelom is an important diagnostic tool in avian and reptile medicine (Fitzgerald and Beaufrère 2016). Point‐of‐care ultrasound (POCUS) can provide important and timely diagnostic information. Moreover, ultrasonography is a primary diagnostic imaging tool for the detection of soft tissue abnormalities including neoplasia, abscesses, and fluid (Schumacher and Toal 2001). Ultrasound has practical applications for the common presenta- tion of coelomic distension, assisting in distinguish- ing between ascites, organomegaly, and an intracoelomic mass (Doneley 2016). Ultrasound can also be useful for differentiating between cystic and solid masses on the skin (Schumacher and Toal 2001). Additionally, POCUS can be useful for sex determi- nation and evaluation of reproductive activity dependent on sexual cycle (females with follicular development) and actual sex. The male reproductive tract is commonly obscured by air sacs in birds, making sex determination more challenging since ultrasound does not transmit through air (Schumacher and Toal 2001). With advances in ultrasound technology, image quality with smaller sized devices has improved tre- mendously, making ultrasound a practical everyday imaging option for both birds and reptiles (Hochleithner and Holland 2014). As in exotic companion mammals, a brief POCUS and Global FAST approach as part of the physical exam can help “see” the problem list and thus better direct diagnostic efforts and more accu- rately assist in emergency management of sauropsid (avian and reptilian) patients. This chapter first addresses general POCUS princi- ples in birds followed by reptiles. Avian What POCUS Birds Can Do • Identify obvious cardiac abnormalities including chamber dilation, cardiomegaly, and pericardial effusion (Fitzgerald and Beaufrère 2016), • Identify ascites (Fitzgerald and Beaufrère 2016). • Identify organomegaly, • Identify a mass, • Recognize ocular abnormalities. What POCUS Birds Cannot Do Organ visualization in the avian patient is limited due to the presence of their air sac system and the inability of ultrasound waves to penetrate the gas‐filled air sacs (Helmer 2006). • Cannot reliably image dorsally positioned organs such as the reproductive system and kidneys because of air sacs. • Cannot reliably screen for reproductive disease because of air sacs, the dependency on reproduc- tive stage, and the predominantly left‐sided ovipa- rous system in females. • Cannot image for respiratory disease as in mam- malian lungs. • Cannot reliably gain a view into the coelom in many smaller species because of the small acoustic window. 864 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER • Cannot reliably achieve a view of the heart, espe - cially in smaller species because of the small acoustic window. Indications • Suspicion of coelomic effusion based on physical examination and/or radiographic findings. • Palpation of a coelomic mass on physical examina- tion and/or radiographic findings. • Coelomic distension with or without accompa - nying dyspnea. • Suspicion of cardiomegaly based on radiographic findings. • Ocular abnormalities or lack of vision undifferenti- ated via direct eye examination. Objectives • Recognize the acoustic windows in birds. • Diagnose coelomic effusion. • Diagnose obvious coelomic organ abnormalities, including abdominal and cardiac. • Diagnose pericardial effusion. • Recognize basic pathology in birds involving their coelom and heart. • Recognize the limitations of avian ultrasonography and their unique differences among different avian species and from mammals. Anatomy Lungs and Air Sacs Avian anatomy differs markedly from mammalian with important consequences ultrasonographically (Figure 42.1). Of significant note, the respiratory system is inaccessible. The lower respiratory tract is composed of dorsally positioned and relatively incom- pressible lungs where the site of gas exchange is the parabronchial tissue and air capillaries and not alveoli, as in mammals. 865 POCUS: BIRDS AND REPTILES birds is located throughout the entire body and between organs with a multitude of air sac diverticula. The avian lung‐air sac system drastically reduces the acoustic windows for ultrasonographic examination of their coelom to a single median soft tissue window just caudal to the sternum. In addition, birds seldom have pleural effusion and the pleural cavities are not acces- sible to ultrasonographic examination, reducing the usefulness of TFAST‐like examinations. Furthermore, the avian coelom is divided into many subcavities, numbering seven in most birds, and divided by various septa that become apparent on ultrasonographic examination when cavitary effusions are present. Additionally, most organs have different ultrasonographic appearances in different species of birds and from mammals. For instance, the liver pri- marily has two lobes with a gallbladder in cockatoos and raptors, but not in parrots and pigeons. The stomach is divided into a glandular stomach (proven- triculus) and a muscular stomach (ventriculus). The kidneys have three lobes that are typically not accessible by ultrasound when normal. Most female birds have only the left reproductive system and are oviparous. A basic knowledge of ultrasonographic anatomy, even for POCUS and Global FAST‐like exam- inations, is essential for accurate avian ultrasono- graphic interpretation. Coelomic In addition, the anatomy, organ topography, and dis- eases vary among bird species because of their great biodiversity. For instance, sonographic examination of the coelom is relatively easy in chickens because the keel is much smaller and fenestrated compared to other avian species, providing a large acoustic window for ascites and organ changes to be detected. Moreover, chickens commonly present for coelomic distension caused by ascites and diseases of the reproductive system. On the other side of the spectrum, ultrasono- graphic examination is very difficult in passerines due to their small size and large keel, resulting in a very small acoustic window for imaging the coelom and its organs. Patient Positioning and Probe Selection Feathers are parted for maximal probe‐to‐skin contact with the use of combinations of 70% isopropyl alcohol, alcohol‐based hand sanitizer, and acoustic coupling gel. Keep in mind the size of the patient and amount of 70% isopropyl alcohol and acoustic coupling gel used because hypothermia can occur quickly, especially in unstable and critical patients. Clinical status should always be evaluated prior to any handling, degrees of restraint, and diagnostics being undertaken. Dyspneic or highly distressed birds often benefit from sedation and/or anesthesia prior to performing diagnostics and supportive care principles should be implemented, such as flow‐by oxygen (Figure 42.2). It is also impor - tant to have technical support from someone who is comfortable with avian restraint to decrease risk of injury to the patient, handler, and attending veteri- narian. Positioning may range from the traditional dorsal recumbency in acceptably stable patients to lat- eral recumbency and even standing, as for the bird in Figure 42.2. Patients with coelomic distension, a common indica- tion for POCUS or AFAST‐like exam, often present with accompanying dyspnea. The stability of the patient should always be evaluated prior to any handling or diagnostics being undertaken, and the patient should always be stabilized as much as pos- sible prior to restraint. A 7.5–18 MHz transducer (probe) that has a small contact area (pediatric transducer) is preferred (Doneley 2016). The most common “acoustic win- dows” or views used for birds include: • Ventromedian coelom, just caudal to the sternum (Doneley 2016) (see Figures 42.1 and 42.2). • right lateral approach, just behind the last rib in some species such as pigeons and chickens and those with ascites (Doneley 2016). Imaging the Normal Coelom Begin the POCUS coelomic exam with the bird in an upright position. • Find the location of the ventromedial coelomic acoustic window. • Part the feathers and expose areas with apterylae (featherless tracts) and judiciously apply a small amount of 70% isopropyl alcohol, alcohol‐based hand sanitizer, and/or ultrasound coupling gel. Keep in mind the size of the patient and amount of coupling medium used, as hypothermia can occur quickly. Alcohol‐based hand sanitizer is less nox- ious and less cooling than isopropyl alcohol, and wipes off more readily than acoustic coupling gel. • Place the ultrasound probe in a longitudinal fashion on the ventral coelom. • From the ventromedial coelomic approach, image the liver, ventriculus, active gonads, and heart (Helmer 2006; Doneley 2016) (see Figure 42.2). The

866 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER ventromedian coelomic acoustic window is vari - able and limited in smaller birds. • Spleen, normal kidneys, and inactive gonads are often difficult or impossible to identify (Krautwald‐ Junghanns et al. 1991); however, the potential for recognition of obvious coelomic abnormalities and masses exists. Conditions of the Coelom Ascites The presence of fluid in the coelom is easily recogniz - able to the most novice sonographer because of its anechoic and triangular appearance along with struc - tures often wafting within the effusion (Figure 42.3). Positioning the bird upright allows free fluid to pocket in the gravity‐dependent ventral coelomic regions and is much less stressful, especially in birds with compro- mised breathing. Exceptions include effusions that are compartmentalized to the hepatoperitoneal cavities. POCUS also assists in the collection of effusions for analysis (coelomocentesis) (see also Chapters 43 and 44). Following scanning of the coelom for fluid, the probe should be directed more cranial from the ventro- median approach to evaluate the liver and heart and for pericardial effusion (see Figures 42.1, 42.17, and 42.18). 867 POCUS: B IRDS AND R EPTILES Organomegaly and Masses Hepatomegaly is most commonly diagnosed with the use of conventional radiographs, with evidence of the liver extending beyond the sternum caudally and beyond the acetabula laterally (Krautwald‐Junghanns et al. 1991). POCUS may be used to verify the radio - graphic finding of an enlarged liver using the ventro - median coelomic acoustic window. A normal‐sized avian liver ultrasonographically should have a characteristic coarse, homogeneous echotexture similar to a mammalian liver (Krautwald‐Junghanns et al. 1991) (see Figure 42.6). Large coelomic masses or granulomas may be iden - tified quickly during POCUS. Masses and granulomas are typically of complex echogenicity, and appear very different from the sonographic appearance of a normal liver (Figure 42.4). Color flow Doppler is useful to demonstrate blood flow patterns that are helpful in differentiating a vascularized mass or a tumor from hypovascularized structures such as granulomas, ectopic uncalcified eggs, and oviductal impactions (see also Chapters 34 and 35). Reproductive Ultrasonographic visualization of the gonads is only possible in sexually active female birds (Krautwald‐ Junghanns 2008). Active ovaries are characterized by the presence of follicles of different sizes representing various stages of development. An active oviduct is distinguishable due to the presence of eggs and the lack of contractility when differentiating from intestines, Figure 42.3. Ascites and coelomocentesis in a chicken. (A) The POCUS exam is used to identify free coelomic fluid. (B) Ceolomocentesis in shown on a chicken (Gallus gallus domesticus) and performed with ultrasound guidance. Coelomocentesis requires a butterfly catheter and syringe set up for sample collection. For larger volume removal, the use of a three‐way stop- cock can be beneficial. Pearl: Often the sonographer cannot accurately differentiate many of the organs within the coelom; however, identification of free fluid is relatively easy and ultrasound can be used to help guide coe - lomocentesis and avoid complications of inadver - tent puncture of nearby structures. Figure 42.4. Cystic enlarged liver in a sun conure (Aratinga solstitialis). This bird presented with coelomic distension and on POCUS exam, marked abnormalities were detected in the liver, including cystic changes and hepatomegaly. The image shows a clear deviation from the expected normalcy of a homogeneous echogenicity to the liver capturing the abnormal sonographic finding for continued work‐up and imaging.

868 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER which demonstrate contractility (Krautwald‐Junghanns 2008). Cysts, neoplasia, salpingitis, and laminated eggs can be recognized with ultrasound (Figure 42.5). Reproductive in Chickens Coelomic disease is a very common presenting com - plaint in pet chickens and most often reproductive in origin in the female. Ultrasound can be an extremely useful tool in assisting with diagnosis of common asso- ciated reproductive diseases such as free coelomic fluid (ascites), carcinomatosis, and forms of peritonitis (see Figures 42.3 and 42.5). Radiography in these same patients tends to lack coelomic detail and may be of limited use (Gingerich and Shaw 2014). Furthermore, ultrasound is the diagnostic tool of choice to help dif - ferentiate soft tissue opacities within the chicken coelom (Krautwald‐Junghanns 2017). Egg yolk perito- nitis is suspected by the presence of free fluid of het - erogeneous echogenicity, with or without laminated eggs (Krautwald‐Junghanns 2017). Definitive diag - nosis can be obtained using ultrasound‐guided fluid sampling and cytological evaluation. Concurrent sal - pingitis is suspected when the oviduct walls appear to be thickened (Helmer 2006). Oviductal impaction is also quite common and may take up the entire coelom. Figure 42.5. 869 POCUS: B IRDS AND R EPTILES Oviductal impaction is easily identified through a POCUS or AFAST‐like examination. The use of color flow Doppler helps differentiate a mass (positive blood flow) from cysts, abscesses, and granulomas (negative blood flow). Multiple small masses with or without ascites are typical of viral‐induced neoplasia of chickens, such as avian leukosis virus and Marek’s disease or carcinomatosis associated with ovarian adenocarcinoma. Cardiac Abnormalities Often there is suspicion of cardiac disease based on physical examination findings, radiographs, or both. Detection of cardiomegaly on radiographs should prompt the clinician to perform a POCUS heart pending complete echocardiography. The heart is usually visualized cranial to the liver via the ventromedian coelomic acoustic window (see also anatomy Figure 42.1) (Helmer 2006). Cardiac chamber dilation and pericardial effusion can be diagnosed by a properly trained novice sonogra - pher, although can be difficult in small patients with a small acoustic window (see Figure 42.2). Among the pathological conditions diagnosed, the most common abnormalities are pericardial effusion (Figure 42.6) and right ventricular dilation, both usually due to right‐sided congestive heart failure (Krautwald‐Junghanns 2017). 870 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Ocular Conditions Being a fluid‐filled structure, the eye is amenable to ultrasound and often overlooked. Special protective requirements are necessary for the acoustic coupling medium to prevent eye injury (see also Chapter 27) (Figure 42.7). In terms of rehabilitating wild birds that require vision for survival, POCUS of the eye could prove helpful as a screening test for the more novice sonographer. 871 POCUS: BIRDS AND REPTILES recognize basic ocular abnormalities such as lens luxations, retinal detachments, and intraocular hemor- rhage as well as other intraocular abnormalities not apparent or questionable on direct examination. Moreover, images may be sent remotely to a veterinary ophthalmologist. Reptile Successful application of ultrasonography in reptiles requires a good basic understanding of normal anatomy (Schumacher and Toal 2001). Reptile anatomy is heterogeneous among the different groups and some of these anatomical variations will be listed here. Organ structure is typically simple with a two‐lobed liver and a gallbladder that is uniquely caudal to the liver in snakes; a three‐chambered reptilian heart; and usually a simple thoracoabdominal cavity. In some rep- tiles, the coelomic cavity is subdivided by septa, much like in birds. Specifically, tegus (group of lizard species) have a posthepatic septum located in the middle of the coelom (Figures 42.8, 42.9, and 42.10), monitor lizards and chelonians have a postpulmonary septum sepa- rating the pleural cavities from the rest of the coelom, and crocodilians have similar subdivisions to birds. The clinical relevance of these septa is the compartmentali- zation of free coelomic fluid, which can be anatomically useful when fluid is sonographically detected in more specific compartments. Lastly, some reptiles such as chameleons, skinks, and snakes have air sacs like birds, which consequently interfere with POCUS since ultra- sound does not transmit through air. The kidneys of some lizards are relatively caudal and retroperitoneal and thus located between the base of the tail and ventral to the cranial acetabular area. Not all reptiles have a urinary bladder. While snakes and crocodilians do not, chelonians (turtles and tor - toises) and many lizards have a urinary bladder (Figure 42.11). Most reptile species are oviparous, but a few are viviparous such as boas, viperids, and some chameleons and skinks. Lizards have two large fat pads on the ventral coelom and rarely have any other foci of intracoelomic fat. The heart of most reptiles is in a cranial location at the level of the thoracic girdle (except in monitor lizards where it is more caudal) and thus echocardiography is not as easily accessed as in mammals (see Figures 42.8, 42.9, and 42.10). What POCUS Reptiles Can Do • Diagnose ascites. • Identify organomegaly (especially in snakes). • Identify cystolithiasis and urolithiasis. • Identify a mass or an abscess. • Identify reproductive tract abnormalities. • Identify reproductive stage in viviparous species. • Sex squamates (types of lizards and snakes). • Detect eye abnormalities. What POCUS Reptiles Cannot Do • Cannot determine the type of free fluid. • Cannot reliably detect diffuse parenchymal conditions. • Cannot reliably detect lung and air sac pathology. • Sexing is dependent on reproductive cycle, and is therefore not always possible. • Account for wide species variation in anatomy. • Cannot diagnose many specific cardiac abnormalities. Indications • Suspicion of coelomic effusion based on physical examination or radiographic findings. • Palpation of a coelomic mass on physical examination. • Coelomic distension with or without accompa- nying dyspnea. • Suspicion of reproductive tract abnormalities based on history and physical examination findings. • Sexing in squamates. Objectives • Recognize basic abnormalities that can be detected on ultrasound in reptile patients. • Understand the wide anatomical diversity of reptiles. • Understand the limitations of POCUS. Defining Species Squamates are the largest order of reptiles, which includes snakes, lizards, and worm lizards. Chelonians includes turtles, terrapins, and tortoises. Patient Positioning and Probe Selection The stability of the patient should always be evaluated prior to undertaking any handling or diagnostics. Most stable reptiles can be imaged with the use of manual restraint alone (Schumacher and Toal 2001), but forms of chemical restraint may be useful dependent on patient temperament and for more complete detailed

874 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER A single transducer (probe) recommendation does not exist for reptiles due to the many different anatom- ical variations and body sizes encountered (Hochleithner and Holland 2014); however, some generalizations may be made. For smaller snakes and lizards, the use of a linear transducer (probe) is recom- mended (Hochleithner and Holland 2014). For chelo - nians (turtles and tortoises), a sector, also called phased array, transducer (probe) or curvilinear (microconvex) transducer (probe) with a small footprint is more use - ful due to their small acoustic windows located cranial and caudal to the thoracic limbs, and cranial to the pelvic limbs (prefemoral fossa) (see Figures 42.8, 42.9, and 42.10) (Hochleithner and Holland 2014). The frequency of the transducer (probe) selected is size dependent with higher frequency transducers for superior spatial resolution and detail but limited to shallow depths; therefore, these probes are recom - mended for smaller patients (Hochleithner and Holland 2014) (Table 42.2). Imaging the Normal Coelom Begin the POCUS coelomic exam according to the species and its most accessible acoustic windows (see Figures 42.9 and 42.10). • Place the probe in a longitudinal orientation on the ventral coelom of snakes and lizards. • Place the probe cranial and caudal to the thoracic limbs and cranial to the pelvic limbs when imaging chelonians (turtles and tortoises). 875 POCUS: B IRDS AND R EPTILES • The patient’s scales can make imaging difficult, so to improve image quality use appropriate amounts and combinations of isopropyl alcohol, and acoustic coupling gel, working between the scales (Schumacher and Toal 2001). Alternatively, performing POCUS with the patient in a water bath can provide good imaging (Schumacher and Toal 2001), as is done with marine mammals, fish, and some amphibian species (see Chapter 41). • Dependent on the acoustic window and area of interest, the probe is then moved cranially, cau - dally, and laterally, adhering to the rule of thumb of one probe maneuver at a time. • In hard‐shelled chelonians (turtles and tortoises), there are only three accessible acoustic windows. In soft‐shelled chelonians, scanning through the plastron (ventral part of the shell) may be possible (Hochleithner and Holland 2014). These three acoustic windows are described below (see Figure 42.8) ◦ The first acoustic window is located cranial to the forelimb beside the neck and allows for evalua- tion of the heart and liver. ◦ The second acoustic window is located in the axil- lary region caudal to the forelimb and allows for evaluation of the heart and liver. ◦ The third acoustic window is located in the inguinal region, referred to as the prefemoral fossa (cranial to the pelvic limb) and allows for evaluation of the intestines, urogenital tract, and bladder (Hochleithner and Holland 2014).
