876 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Conditions of the Coelom Distension Enlargement of the coelom, due to a mass or fluid, and reproductive monitoring are the most common indica- tions for POCUS and more complete ultrasound exam- inations in reptiles. With any coelomic distension, POCUS may be implemented to help determine obvious causes, such as ascites, cystic or solid tumor, granuloma/abscess, and herniation (Hochleithner and Holland 2014). Ascites The presence of free fluid in the coelom is easily recogniz- able to the sonographer with minimal training because of its anechoic (black) triangulated appearance and wafting of intracoelomic structures, very different from coelomic imaging in the absence of ascites (see Figure 42.3). Organomegaly and Masses Suspected enlargement of organs and intracoelomic masses may be possible to detect ultrasonographically with minimal training, or at least recognize as different from expected normalcy. POCUS is especially useful in snakes where swellings along the body are common and related to a variety of coelomic organs. For example, gastrointestinal impaction, mainly due to ingestion of sand and substrate but also prey items, may be noticed in some lizards and snakes. On POCUS, such gastroin- testinal impactions are imaged as heterogeneous echo- genicity without vascularization on color flow Doppler (no flow) and strong shadowing, often triggering the need for radiography or computed tomography. Hepatic lipidosis is also exceedingly common in a number of pet reptiles, especially bearded dragons (Pogona vitticeps). The liver is typically diffusely hyper- echoic (bright) (Hernandez‐Divers and Cooper 2001) (see Figure 42.16). Kidney and Urinary Bladder Cystolithiasis and urolithiasis may also be suspected during POCUS, especially in higher risk species, such as the desert lizards (uromastyx, chuckwalla) and large tortoises. The same sonographic principles that are applied to mammalian species also apply to reptiles, with visualization of a hyperechoic near‐field with clean acoustic shadowing (see Chapters 10, 11, and 40) (Figures 42.12 and 42.13). However, the reptilian kidney is much less accessible than mammalian kid - neys due to the aforementioned differences in anatomy. Reproductive and Sexing Ultrasound can be useful for determining the sex in some reptile species. The male hemipenes can be visu- alized in some species and are in fact calcified in nor - malcy in some monitor lizards (Figure 42.14) (Bucy et al. 2015). Additionally, seeing ovarian follicles is diagnostic for sexing the reptile as a female. Conversely, inactive female ovaries and male gonads are difficult to identify (Schumacher and Toal 2001) (Figure 42.15). Reproductive Conditions Often reptiles present with various types of reproduc - tive disease. The use of POCUS can help identify the presence of reproductive abnormalities. As previ - ously mentioned, inactive female ovaries and male gonads are difficult to identify (Schumacher and Toal 2001); however, female reptiles commonly present with pre‐ or postovulatory stasis, which can be diag - nosed ultrasonographically. Preovulatory follicles are hypoechoic (dark) compared to the more developed hyperechoic (bright) calcified shell of postovulatory Pearl: It may not be possible to accurately distin - guish many of the organs within the coelom; how - ever, sonographic identification of ascites is relatively easy. 878 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER follicles (Schumacher and Toal 2001). Preovulatory stasis may be differentiated from normal ovarian follicles. As the follicles remain unovulated, the echo - genicity changes to a heterogeneous pattern with the surface of the follicles no longer smooth and well demarcated as is seen with normal follicles. Additionally, anechoic (black) fluid may be present around the follicles during stasis with the presence of echogenic free‐floating particles indicative of inflam - mation. Lastly, and of note, ovarian follicles may be confused or difficult to differentiate from intestines and thus, peristalsis is helpful to distinguish ovarian follicles from the intestinal tract. Peristalsis is signifi - cantly affected by the species examined, diet, temper - ature, and many other factors, and should be a consideration when performing an ultrasound in reptiles. Many female reptiles have large follicles that are not necessarily associated with reproductive disease (see Figure 42.15). Postovulatory stasis can also be differen- tiated from normal eggs by visualizing an irregular surface of the egg (versus expected normal smooth appearance) (see Figure 42.15) (Hochleithner and Holland 2014). 879 POCUS: B IRDS AND R EPTILES Liver The liver of reptile species other than chelonians (tur - tles and tortoises) is relatively simple to locate and image, and should be evaluated for size and the presence of parenchymal changes (Schumacher and Toal 2001). The sonographic expectation of the rep - tilian liver is one of homogeneous echogenicity; thus, the presence of masses (neoplasia, cysts, and abscesses) is often readily identified (Schumacher and Toal 2001) (Figure 42.16). A hyperechoic (bright) liver may be associated with hepatic lipidosis, which is common in a number of pet reptiles, especially bearded dragons (Hernandez‐Divers and Cooper 2001). Cardiac Abnormalities and Aneurysms Echocardiography is challenging in reptiles due to dif- ferences in anatomy from mammals, as well as a lack of available reference data (Schumacher and Toal 2001). Mild valvular regurgitation may be normal in many reptilian species; however, basic cardiac abnor - malities may still be recognized, including obvious cardiac chamber enlargement and pericardial effusion, of which bearded dragons have a more frequent occur- rence than other reptiles (Figures 42.17 and 42.18). Vascular lesions and abnormalities are also possible. The caudal vena cava may be visualized subxiphoid as in dogs and cats and associated with the liver in sim - ilar imaging planes as the heart (see Figures 42.17 and 42.18). Several cases of aneurysms arising from the internal carotid or aorta have been reported in bearded dragons (Barten et al. 2006; Sweet et al. 2009; Finnburgh and Eshar 2018). Affected lizards usually present with a large fluctuant or firm swelling on the dorsolateral aspect of the neck (Barten et al. 2006). POCUS in these cases would be useful to demonstrate the presence of fluid within the mass along with acoustic enhance - ment through the far‐field with variable blood flow on color flow Doppler. 880 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Ocular Conditions Being a fluid‐filled structure, the eye is readily ame - nable to ultrasound and often overlooked. Special requirements are necessary for a safe corneal acoustic coupling medium to prevent iatrogenic eye injury (see also Chapter 27). Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 885 Introduction Ultrasound‐guided interventional techniques are gen- erally classified as indirect, free‐hand and mechanical‐ guided. With the indirect method, ultrasound is used to determine the location and depth of the target (usually fluid), and a needle trajectory is imagined but real‐time ultrasound visualization of the needle during the procedure is not used. The indirect method is com- monly used for pericardiocentesis, thoracocentesis, and abdominocentesis in veterinary patients. With free‐hand ultrasound‐guided centesis, the loca- tion and depth of the target are determined and real‐ time ultrasound is used to visualize and help guide the needle tip into the desired target. The free‐hand method is often preferred because it is less expensive (doesn’t use commercially available needle guides) and allows greater flexibility in angling the needle and changing its location while entering cavities or tissues by using real‐time ultrasound visualization for more precise aspiration or centesis (del Cura et al. 2010). In other words, this flexibility allows the attending clini- cian to move the needle/needle tip through different planes relative to the ultrasound beam, in contrast to the mechanical‐guided ultrasound method. With the mechanical ultrasound‐guided system, a rigid ultrasound probe attachment is used to help guide the needle/needle tip into the target, be it a cavity or tissue, using real‐time visualization. The attachment typically contains a slot for the needle, which fixes the needle track to the angle of the slot. The fixed path of the device ensures that the needle remains in the plane of the ultrasound beam and thus facilitates real‐time ultrasound visualization of the needle/ needle tip. On the other hand, the fixed path of the attachment has the disadvantage of limiting the number of needle/needle tip entry angles that may be utilized (del Cura et al. 2010). Pericardiocentesis Introduction Pericardiocentesis is the aspiration of fluid from the pericardial space and is often performed for therapeutic and/or diagnostic purposes. 886 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER bodies). In cardiovascularly stable cases of pericardial effusion without cardiac tamponade, emergent peri- cardiocentesis may be delayed until a thorough evalu- ation of the underlying cause is undertaken. Given pericardial effusion may occur secondary to coagu- lopathies, the patient’s coagulation status or a toxin‐ induced coagulopathy (e.g., warfarin) should be considered prior to performing pericardiocentesis. When coagulopathy is present and pericardiocentesis is deemed necessary, the coagulopathy should ideally be corrected with rapid fresh frozen plasma (FFP) administration prior to performing pericardiocentesis (e.g., 8–10 mL/kg over 5–10 minutes, or at a slower rate dictated by the patient’s cardiovascular status). If patients are agonal, life‐saving pericardiocentesis is recommended prior to or concurrent with FFP transfusion. Ultrasound‐guided versus Blind Pericardiocentesis In veterinary medicine, pericardiocentesis is often per- formed blindly at the 5th–7th intercostal space, or using indirect ultrasound guidance. With indirect guidance, ultrasound is used to identify the preferred intercostal space, which is typically the deepest pericardial fluid pocket in the absence of surrounding vital structures (e.g., lung and heart), but the actual needle is not fol- lowed in real time. Another option is to use free‐hand ultrasound‐guided pericardiocentesis whereby the needle is tracked using real‐time ultrasound guidance as it enters the pericardial space. There are several studies in humans demonstrating reduced complications with free‐hand ultrasound‐ guided pericardiocentesis compared to blind tech- niques (Callahan et al. 1985;Clarke and Cosgrove 1987; Taavitsainen et al. 1991; Tsang et al. 2002). Reported complications include ventricular or atrial penetration, coronary artery laceration, pneumo- thorax (PTX), dysrhythmias and inadvertent penetra- tion of the diaphragm and abdominal organs (Clarke and Cosgrove 1987). Given anatomical differences in veterinary patients compared to humans, it is unknown if ultrasound‐guided pericardiocentesis would result in fewer complications, although there are preliminary studies to suggest this may be the case in dogs (Celona et al. 2017). In cases of small‐ volume effusion causing tamponade, or compart- mentalized fluid, free‐hand ultrasound‐guided pericardiocentesis may be particularly helpful. By direct visualization of structures and fluid, ultra- sound‐guided techniques should prove safer than blind techniques. Indications for Pericardiocentesis Pericardiocentesis is indicated to remove fluid from the pericardial space, both for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes, and is the life‐saving treatment of choice when cardiac tamponade is present. Scanning T echnique for Pericardiocentesis • Clip hair. • Apply acoustic coupling gel or alcohol. • Place the ultrasound probe between the fourth and fifth ribs on the right side of the patient at the level of the costochondral junction or alternately at the location of the strongest palpable heartbeat if the heart can be easily palpated. • Move the ultrasound probe cranial and caudal 1–2 rib spaces and ventrally and dorsally 2–3 inches until the widest accumulation of pericardial fluid has been identified. Limit the survey to only several seconds in unstable patients. • Dependent on patient stability, measure or approxi- mate the distance from the skin to the pericardium and the greatest width (cm) of the pericardial effusion. • Visualize the needle pericardiocentesis angle and trajectory path that allows safest penetration into the pericardial space (Figure 43.2A), which is usu- ally over the site where the effusion is closest to the thoracic wall, thus minimizing lung trauma. Pearl: Leaving a small volume of pericardial effu- sion provides an acoustic window and helps with the detection of pericardial or heart‐based masses if complete echocardiography is to be subsequently scheduled (Scansen 2011). However, in cardiovascu- larly unstable patients, pericardiocentesis must take precedence over complete echocardiography and sufficient pericardial fluid must be aspirated to ensure the patient is cardiovascularly stable. Pearl: Be familiar with the centimeter (cm) scale on your ultrasound machine, which is typically located on the right side of the screen, to rapidly approxi- mate these measurements (Figure 43.1). Pearl: Measurement of the pericardial effusion width prior to pericardiocentesis helps guide decisions regarding the depth the catheter needs to be inserted to enter the pericardial space and the distance between the pericardium and the heart.

If peri- cardial effusion recurs, placement of an indwelling small‐bore chest tube into the pericardial space allows recurrent pericardial effusion to be removed serially without the need to continually repeat the pericardiocentesis procedure (Figure 43.3). 888 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Procedure for Performing Pericardiocentesis The pericardial space has historically been approached from the right side for anatomical reasons, including the minimization of left coronary artery laceration and lung trauma (cardiac notch). The procedure, however, may be successfully performed from the left side, although conversely, the left coronary artery (major heart artery) is more vulnerable and there is more lung (no window through the cardiac notch). The difference in right‐ versus left‐sided approaches is a more impor- tant consideration in smaller effusions, with a right‐ sided approach considered safer. • Place an intravenous (IV) catheter in case compli - cations develop that may require IV volume expan- sion or the emergent control of arrhythmias using injectable medications. • The patient may be given light sedation if needed. Opioids are generally safest because they are car - diovascularly sparing and may be reversed with naloxone. • Connect the patient to an ECG continuous monitor as ventricular arrhythmias may occur if the catheter or stylet contacts the heart during the procedure. • For right‐sided pericardiocentesis, the patient is placed in sternal or left lateral recumbency. • The procedure should be performed aseptically using sterile technique and sterile gloves. • Clip hair and aseptically prep the skin on the right side of the thorax from the third to seventh inter - costal spaces, extending 3–4 inches ventrally and dorsally from the costochondral junction. • Confirm the pericardiocentesis site using ultra - sound. This is typically the widest accumulation of fluid located near the fifth intercostal space at the costochondral junction. However, the optimal loca- tion may vary depending on the volume and where the widest accumulation of pericardial fluid exists (see Figure 43.2). • Attach a 14–16 gauge, 2–6 inch over‐the‐needle catheter, depending on the size of patient, to an extension set, three‐way stopcock, and 6, 12, 20, 35 or 60 cc syringe, dependent on patient size. Some clinicians prefer to use a smaller syringe (i.e., 10 cc) for the initial aspiration, which they set aside so that a sample of the pericardial effusion has been saved (see below for sample collection). • One or two additional side‐holes may be cut in larger bore catheters to improve drainage of the pericardial space. Care must be taken to preserve the integrity of the catheter, ensuring that the tip does not break off and remain within the pericar - dial sac. Figure 43.3. Free‐hand ultrasound‐guided probe orienta- tion for pericardiocentesis. Place the ultrasound probe parallel to the ribs 1–3 cm below the determined pericardial site at an angle of approximately 60° to the skin. The cath - eter‐to‐skin angle is approximately 60° which creates a cath- eter‐to‐probe angle of approximately 60°. Pearl: Preparing a pericardiocentesis kit in a large, clear bag along with the written list of inventory on a card saves invaluable time when emergent peri - cardiocentesis is needed and keeps the kit stocked. Pearl: Some clinicians prefer to place the patient in right lateral recumbency on an echocardiography table and perform the procedure from the underside of the patient through the table’s cut‐out window because gravity assists in moving the heart, pericar- dium, and pericardial fluid closer to the thoracic wall while displacing the lung to either side of the heart. Pearl: It is recommended to stagger and not to exceed 50% of the circumference of the catheter when making additional side‐holes. Often, creating side‐holes is not necessary.

Using the angle determined by ultrasound (see Figure 43.2B), penetrate the skin and subcuta- neous tissue with the catheter and stylet at the same angle. 3. Apply gentle negative pressure to the syringe when the stylet and catheter have been advanced into the subcutaneous tissues. 4. Continue to advance the catheter and stylet along the imaginary needle–pericardiocentesis trajectory path until fluid is noted within the hub of the stylet and extension tubing. 5. Continue to step 7. Free‐hand Ultrasound‐guided Pericardiocentesis 1. Slide the ultrasound probe 1–3 cm below the perceived site where the stylet and catheter will be advanced through the skin and subcutaneous tissues. 2. Fan the probe such that it will be at a 60–90° angle to the imaginary needle–pericardiocentesis trajec- tory path. 3. Following the predetermined skin site and imaginary needle–pericardiocentesis trajectory path, advance the stylet and catheter through the skin into the subcutaneous tissues. The ultrasound probe should be at a 60–90° angle to the catheter and stylet (see Figure 43.3). The catheter and tip of the stylet should be visible within the subcuta- neous tissues. 4. Apply gentle negative pressure to the syringe when the stylet and catheter have been advanced into the subcutaneous tissues. 5. Use real‐time ultrasound guidance to advance both the stylet and catheter through the tissues until the catheter tip is seen to enter the pericardial space. Be sure to keep the stylet and catheter in plane with the ultrasound probe. 6. Continue to step 7. Completing Both the Indirect and Free‐ hand Ultrasound‐guided Pericardiocentesis T echniques 7. As the tip of the stylet enters the pericardial sac, fluid should be observed in the hub of the stylet and extension set. Pericardial fluid is typically dark red similar to venous blood. 8. Once the stylet has penetrated the pericardial space, advance the stylet and catheter another 2–4 mm to ensure the catheter, in addition to the Pearl: Making a stab incision through the skin helps prevent burring of the catheter and facilitates easier advancement of the catheter and stylet through the skin surface, subsequently allowing better catheter control. Pearl: The stylet and catheter should be passed on the cranial side of the rib to avoid nerves and vessels on the caudal aspect of the ribs. Pearl: If the desired imaginary needle–pericardio- centesis trajectory path is more perpendicular to the skin, the ultrasound probe‐to‐skin angle can be decreased, but image quality may diminish with decreased probe‐to‐skin contact. Advance the catheter off the sharp stylet and into the pericardial space. It is not always necessary to completely advance the catheter into the pericar - dial sac; however, it should be at least advanced a few centimeters to ensure that it is well seated within the pericardial sac along with all of the catheter’s side‐holes, if present. 10. Once the catheter is seated within the pericardial sac, disconnect the extension set from the stylet, remove the stylet from the catheter, and reconnect the extension set to the catheter. 11. Drain fluid from the pericardial sac into an appro- priate receptacle (i.e., kidney bowl) using the three‐way stopcock and syringe. 12. Aseptically collect samples of the fluid into red (plain) and lavender (EDTA) topped tubes for further analysis. An additional red top tube sample should be collected to observe for clot formation because hemorrhagic pericardial effu- sions should typically not clot. If clotting is observed then fresh blood contamination should be suspected and the complication of aspiration of one of the cardiac chambers (most likely the right atrium) or coronary artery laceration may have occurred. Postpericardiocentesis Use of Ultrasound for T racking (Monitoring) • Following the procedure, reevaluate the pericar - dial sac ultrasonographically to be sure cardiac tamponade has resolved and note the presence and quantity of any residual pericardial fluid by caliper measurement (or approximated by using the scale on the right‐hand side of the ultrasound screen) of the greatest width (cm). • Repeat the ultrasound evaluation in 12–24 hours (or sooner as clinical course dictates) to look for reaccumulation of pericardial fluid. Remeasuring the width (cm) of pericardial effusion is helpful in determining if fluid is reaccumulating in the peri- cardial space. • If there are concerns for recurrence of pericardial effusion, a small‐bore chest tube can be guided into the pericardial space using a guidewire Seldinger technique; a guidewire is passed through the 14–16 gauge pericardiocentesis catheter to enter the pericardial space prior to removal of the catheter. The small‐bore chest tube is then passed into the pericardial space along the guidewire in a manner similar to placement of a small‐bore Seldinger technique chest tube. Subsequently, intermittent aspirations can be performed as clinically indi- cated, usually every 4–6 hours, until the fluid return over a 24‐hour period has decreased to less than 25 mL and follow‐up two‐dimensional echo- cardiographic assessment is satisfactory (Tsang et al. 2002) (Figure 43.4). Pearls and Pitfalls regarding Ultrasound‐ guided Pericardiocentesis • Ultrasound‐guided pericardiocentesis allows the operator to visualize the catheter tip as it traverses the pleural space, thus avoiding confusion of pleural with pericardial fluid when both are pre- sent (see Figure 43.2A). • In patients with cardiac tamponade without respiratory distress, pericardiocentesis should take priority over evacuation of pleural fluid; the assistant should be instructed to release negative pressure on the syringe until the tip of the stylet is visualized within the pericardial space, at which point negative pressure is applied. Pearl: If sustained ventricular arrhythmias should occur during pericardial catheter advancement, retract the catheter slightly. If this fails to resolve the arrhythmia, administer a bolus (2 mg/kg) of lido- caine intravenously. Most ventricular arrhythmias are intermittent and self‐limiting. Pearl: Immediately filling and serially observing a red top tube filled with aspirated fluid helps ensure inadvertent puncture of a cardiac chamber has not occurred (pericardial effusion should not clot). Pearl: Leaving a small volume of pericardial effu- sion provides an acoustic window if complete echo- cardiography in search of a mass (neoplasia, foreign body, etc.) is to be performed subsequently. Pearl: Some patients have concurrent pleural effu- sion present, which typically appears straw‐colored and is often encountered as the catheter and stylet pass through the pleural space prior to entering the pericardial sac.

Thoracocentesis Introduction Thoracocentesis is a minimally invasive diagnostic or therapeutic procedure used to remove fluid or air from the pleural space. In the emergent veterinary patient with life‐threatening pleural effusion or PTX, the objective is to remove pleural fluid/air and stabi- lize the patient as quickly as possible. Blind thoraco- centesis is usually the method of choice in these circumstances. In the more stable patient, ultrasound has the advantage of identifying the optimal puncture site, improving success rates, and, most importantly, mini- mizing the complications of the procedure (Nicolaou et al. 2007). Studies in human medicine have shown higher success rates for pleural effusions when using ultrasound‐guided compared to blind thoracocentesis, and that following failed blind thoracocentesis attempts, ultrasound‐guided thoracocentesis was suc- cessful in 88% of these patients (Weingardt et al. 1994). Complication rates with blind thoracocentesis in humans with pleural effusion vary from 20% to 50% and include PTX, inadvertent placement of the needle into the abdominal cavity across the diaphragm or into consolidated lung, or misplacement of the needle above fluid accumulations (Dewitz and Frazee 2003; Jones et al. 2003). Although complications are still pos- sible with ultrasound guidance, rates in humans are reported to be lower when compared to blind tech- niques (Jones et al. 2003). For example, the incidence of postthoracocentesis PTX in humans with pleural effu- sion is reported to be 1.3–2.5% versus 4–30% for ultra- sound‐guided and blind techniques, respectively (Jones et al. 2003). Despite the value of ultrasound in detecting PTX, given ultrasound does not image through air, there is little benefit in performing ultrasound‐guided over blind thoracocentesis in cases of PTX (free air in pleural space). However, the glide sign, referred to as lung sliding in human medicine, should be assessed before and following thoracocentesis as the loss of a previously visible glide sign following thoracocente- sis indicates iatrogenic PTX. In human medicine, the finding of a glide sign following thoracocentesis for PTX obviates the need for chest radiography to rule out PTX. Pleural effusion must be differentiated from peri- cardial fluid and cardiac chambers as well as other intrathoracic structures including masses and intraab- dominal structures in case of occult diaphragmatic herniation. Indications for Thoracocentesis • To provide a therapeutic benefit whenever pleural effusion (fluid in the pleural space) or PTX (air in the pleural space) are present and causing respiratory compromise or distress. • For diagnostic purposes to characterize pleural effusion. Contraindications to Thoracocentesis • An uncooperative patient, although this can typically be managed with sedation/anesthesia. • Severe coagulopathy, although this can typically be managed with blood products prior to thoracocentesis. • A pleural effusion considered too small to be safely aspirated. Potential Complications of Thoracocentesis • Pain (easily controlled with local blocks and systemic analgesia). • Pneumothorax (probably more common with chronic long‐standing pleural effusion). • Reexpansion pulmonary edema (rare). • Inadvertent lung, heart, liver or splenic puncture. • Hemothorax from laceration of intercostal or other vessels (avoidable by performing centesis at the cranial rib margin). • Infection (rare if aseptic technique is used). • Subcutaneous emphysema (rare). • A sheared‐off catheter in the pleural space (ensure any added drainage holes are <50% of the catheter width and they occur on alternating staggered sides of the catheter if added). • Subcutaneous hematoma (rare). Pearl: Use multiple views including at least a single pericardial view and the diaphragmatico‐hepatic (DH) view of FAST to help distinguish pleural effu- sion from pericardial effusion and cardiac chambers (see Chapters 17–21).

893 POCUS: ABDOMINOCENTESIS, THORACOCENTESIS, AND PERICARDIOCENTESIS Scanning for Pleural Effusion to Perform Thoracocentesis The optimal puncture site is located by identifying the largest pocket of fluid superficial to the lung, and scanning throughout a full respiratory cycle. Scanning through a full respiratory cycle is recommended as structures such as the lung and/or diaphragm may enter and leave the ultrasonographic field of view dur- ing different phases of respiration. In addition to lung, other vital structures such as the heart and great ves- sels may lie in proximity to focal fluid accumulations, which can be avoided by direct visualization using ultrasound. 1. The ultrasound probe is placed on either side of the thorax, perpendicular to the ribs, and moved cranially and caudally over several intercostal spaces in the lower third of the thorax. 2. Following identification of the intercostal space containing the deepest fluid pocket, the ultrasound probe is then moved dorsally and ventrally at this site to further clarify the deepest fluid pocket. 3. Once this site has been identified, the ultrasound probe can once again be moved cranially and cau- dally to reconfirm the deepest fluid pocket and identify the presence of any obvious adjacent structures that should be avoided (heart, great ves- sels, lung, diaphragm, liver). 4. A measurement of the depth of the fluid pocket should be made or easily approximated using the centimeter scale to the right of the ultrasound screen to help guide the length of needle or cath- eter insertion to safely use for thoracocentesis. 5. The width of the pleural fluid may vary during the respiratory cycle and should be assessed with ultrasound to minimize complications and maxi- mize success. Materials Checklist for Thoracocentesis • Clippers and antimicrobial scrub. • An 18–22 gauge 1–2 inch butterfly needle, IV cath- eter or hypodermic needle. • Intravenous extension set if using an IV catheter or hypodermic needle. • Three‐way stopcock. • 10–60 mL syringe dependent on patient size and the amount of pleural effusion present. • Receptacle for fluid collection (i.e., kidney bowl). • Ultrasound machine and appropriate ultrasound probes. • Sterile culturettes. • Lidocaine for a local anesthetic block if elected. • Sedation if needed. Procedure for Performing Thoracocentesis • Thoracocentesis should be performed using aseptic technique. • Any existing coagulopathies should ideally be corrected prior to performing the procedure unless the patient is in overt respiratory distress in which case urgent life‐saving thoracocentesis should be performed. • Some sedation is generally beneficial to calm the patient, decrease the need for restraint, and lessen the work of breathing in respiratory compromised patients. • A local anesthetic block using lidocaine may be given but is not usually necessary. If a local anesthetic is used, the skin, subcutaneous tissue, rib periosteum, intercostal muscles, and parietal pleura should be Pearl: The depth of the fluid pocket will help deter- mine the chance of success because smaller fluid accumulations are more difficult to access. Pearl: Freeze the image to take an accurate caliper measurement (cm) from the skin surface to the desired location within the pleural fluid accumulation or approximate using the centimeter scale on the right side of the ultrasound screen. Pearl: Preparing a thoracocentesis kit in a large, clear bag along with the written list of inventory on a card saves invaluable time when emergent thora- cocentesis is needed and keeps the kit stocked. Pearl: In cases of hemothorax, blood may be collected and autotransfused back to the patient using in‐line filters or blood administration lines. Pearl: Changing the ultrasound probe angle during the respiratory cycle and moving the needle tip away from aerated lung will help minimize lung puncture when pleural fluid depths change during the respiratory cycle (Lichtenstein et al. 1999).

A 20–22 gauge needle attached to an IV extension set, three‐way stopcock, and syringe is placed dorsal to the ultrasound probe at an angle of about 30° to the skin, bevel towards the ultrasound probe, starting about 1 cm dorsal to the probe. 2. The needle should be inserted just caudal and dorsal to the center point of the ultrasound probe to avoid the nerves and vessels that run caudal to the ribs (Figure 43.6B). The orientation marker on the ultrasound probe is directed cranially. 3. As the needle is advanced through the skin, the needle tip will be visualized within the subcuta - neous tissues. 4. An assistant can apply gentle negative pressure to the syringe at this time. As the needle is slowly advanced, the ultrasound probe is slid ventrally to follow the needle to the level of the parietal pleura. More specifically, using the dominant hand, the needle is slowly advanced through the subcuta - neous tissues until the tip appears as a white dot on the ultrasound image. As soon as the tip of the needle is identified, advancement of the needle should be halted and held motionless. Using the nondominant hand, the ultrasound probe is then slowly moved ventrally off the needle tip until the tip is no longer visible within the ultrasound image. At this point, the probe is held stationary and the needle is again slowly advanced until the tip becomes visible in the ultrasound image. Once the tip is visualized, advancement of the needle is again halted and the procedure repeated until the tip of the needle can be seen advancing into the pleural space. 5. Once the needle tip is visible within the pleural space (see Figure 43.6A), fluid will be noted in the hub of the needle and IV extension set. Parallel Probe Placement Thoracocentesis 1. When the ultrasound probe is placed parallel to the ribs (Figure 43.7A), care should be taken to avoid inserting the needle at the caudal rib mar - gins as the nerves and vessels are located here. The needle should enter the center to caudal third of the intercostal space. 2. Ultrasonographically identify the widest fluid pocket (see above), which will be the site where the needle is inserted. 3. A 20–22 gauge hypodermic needle attached to an IV extension set, three‐way stopcock, and syringe should enter the thorax at this site. The angle at which the needle enters the thorax will depend on the length of the needle relative to the width of the skin, subcutaneous tissues, and underlying mus - cles. A needle angle of 30–45° relative to the thoracic cage is often used but a 90° angle may be required in cases where the depth required to reach the pleural space is close to the length of the needle used. 4. Once the ideal centesis site is identified, orientate the ultrasound probe such that the orientation marker is directed dorsally and the probe is located just ventral to the site where the needle will be inserted. 5. The needle should enter the thorax 0.5 cm dorsal to the ultrasound probe with the bevel of the needle orientated towards the ultrasound probe (see Figure 43.7A). A lower needle angle will keep the needle more perpendicular to the ultrasound probe, increasing visualization of the needle/ needle tip as it traverses the subcutaneous tissues and enters the pleural space, although the distance travelled by the needle to enter the pleural space will be longer (see Figure 43.7B). Alternatively, the tail of the ultrasound probe may be angled ven - trally to orientate the probe more perpendicularly to the needle trajectory. 6. Once the needle/needle tip is seen to enter the subcutaneous space in real time, an assistant may apply gentle negative pressure while the needle Figure 43.7 . The tip of the needle will typically indent the parietal pleura before piercing it and entering the pleural cavity. 7. As the needle tip is seen entering the pleural effu- sion, fluid should simultaneously enter the needle hub and extension set with the exception of vis- cous exudates. Now the needle should be angled ventrally towards the sternum so that it is lying against the thoracic wall with its bevel facing towards the pleural effusion and away from the thoracic wall. 8. In cases of a therapeutic thoracocentesis, aspira- tion of the pleural space should continue until neg- ative pressure is established, as the patient allows. Once fluid is obtained, samples should be collected into red (plain) and lavender (EDTA) topped tubes for diagnostic analysis. If a hemothorax (HTX) is sus- pected, a sample should be placed within a second red (plain) topped tube and checked after several minutes for clotting since most true noniatrogenic HTX will not clot. The sample should also be analyzed and the packed cell volume (PCV) compared to peripheral PCV for more definitive diagnosis of HTX. Clotting often indicates accidental aspiration of a vessel or a cardiac chamber. Postthoracocentesis Use of Ultrasound for T racking (Monitoring) Ultrasound should be used post thoracocentesis for monitoring recurrence of the pleural effusion and any complications, including HTX and PTX. Measuring the widest aspect with the calipers or by approximation using the scale on the right‐hand side of the screen pro- vides more accurate assessments, especially if multiple veterinarians are involved in case management. As a general rule of thumb, stable postthoracocentesis cases should have TFAST and Vet Blue performed at least once fours hours post procedure (sooner if questionable or unstable) and then serially with time intervals deter- mined by the patient’s clinical course and the suspected condition (see Chapters 17, 18, 22, 23, 36, and 37). Abdominocentesis Introduction Peritoneal effusion, also referred to as ascites, is always abnormal in mature dogs and cats; however, juvenile kittens and puppies may have small‐volume effusions that are purely anechoic and considered normal (see Chapters 6, 7, and Section III). The process of aspi- rating or acquiring fluid from the peritoneal cavity is termed abdominocentesis. In general, veterinary patients with undifferentiated ascites should have their effusion characterized if acquisition may be safely performed at the attending veterinarian’s discretion. Although the complication rate with conventional blind abdominocentesis is low (0.9%) in humans, with hematoma formation being the most common compli- cation, the morbidity associated with complications can be significant (Runyon 1986; Dewitz and Frazee 2003). False‐positive results have been reported with accidental aspiration of abdominal organs such as the spleen or bowel, while false‐negative results may be reported in cases where fluid is compartmentalized, present in small volumes, or the needle is entrapped within omentum or other intraabdominal organs (Bjorling et al. 1983; Crowe 1984; Walters 2003). The frequency of false‐positive and ‐negative results can be reduced with real‐time ultrasound‐guided abdomi- nocentesis; the trajectory path of the needle can be visualized throughout the procedure, allowing other abdominal organs to be visualized and avoided (Bard et al. 1986). Furthermore, ultrasound‐guided abdomi- nocentesis has a higher success rate when compared to blind abdominocentesis (Boysen et al. 2004; Lisciandro et al. 2009). This is especially true when there are small volumes of peritoneal fluid and when peritoneal fluid is compartmentalized (Nazeer et al. 2005; Patel et al. 2012). Indications for Abdominocentesis • Characterization of ascites for diagnostic information. • Characterization of ascites as being septic or sterile, with the former typically considered as life‐threat- ening and an indication for emergent exploratory laparotomy. Pearl: The diagnosis of HTX is made by a nonclot- ting sample with its PCV comparable to the peripheral PCV of the patient; it is very easy to visu- ally overestimate the PCV by looking at a hemorrhagic sample – always spin the fluid and mea- sure the PCV. Pearl: The use of ultrasound has been shown to be superior to chest auscultation and chest radiog- raphy in humans for pleural effusion, PTX, and many lung conditions (see Chapters 17, 18, 22, 23, 36, and 37).

898 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER • Therapeutic relief of symptoms such as respiratory compromise or distress or discomfort from large‐ volume ascites. Scanning T echnique for Abdominocentesis • The abdomen is quickly scanned, typically using the AFAST technique (see Chapter 6) to identify and localize fluid accumulations. • In cases of suspected peritonitis based on physical examination and history, where a rapid AFAST scan is negative, additional emergency POCUS may be indicated (see Chapters 9 and 12). Using additional POCUS exams may help find otherwise occult small amounts of focal or localized ascites and any obvious intraabdominal abnormalities related to the effusion, such as hemoabdomen and splenic mass on POCUS spleen, peritonitis and mucocele on POCUS liver and gallbladder or peri- pancreatic fluid and pancreatic abnormalities on POCUS gastrointestinal and pancreas. Materials Checklist for Abdominocentesis • 20–22 gauge 1–2 inch hypodermic needles. • Clippers for long‐haired patients. • Antimicrobial scrub and solution. • Red (plain) and lavender (EDTA) topped tubes for sterile fluid collection. • Sterile culturettes. • 3 or 6 mL syringes. • Ultrasound machine and appropriate ultrasound probe. Procedure to Perform Abdominocentesis The following is a general overview regarding posi- tioning, site preparation, and approximating needle length. • Abdominocentesis may be performed with the animal in left or right lateral recumbency, dorsal recumbency or standing, depending on patient comfort and clinician preference. • Abdominocentesis should be performed using aseptic technique. • Free‐hand ultrasound‐guided abdominocentesis is typically preferred because it allows greater flexi- bility in choosing access sites and is not limited to a single plane. • The abdomen should be rapidly scanned to iden- tify the largest pocket of fluid, to ascertain the loca- tion of other abdominal organs in proximity to the fluid, and to help determine the possible cause of the abdominal fluid. • The depth of the subcutaneous tissues and perito- neal fluid can be measured using the ultrasound machine’s calipers or by approximating using the centimeter scale to the right of the screen to help ascertain the length of needle required, potentially improving patient safety. • Once the largest fluid pocket has been identified, the abdominocentesis can be performed in longitudinal or transverse views. The procedure for performing ultrasound‐guided abdominocentesis is as follows. 1. Verify the location of the probe marker as it should be directed toward the head of the patient or to its right for longitudinal and transverse views, respec- tively, thus helping with orientation of the ultra- sound probe relative to the needle. 2. For abdominocentesis in the longitudinal view, place the probe at a 60° angle to the skin with the ultrasound probe marker directed cranially (Figure 43.8). 3. Connect an 18–22 gauge hypodermic needle to a syringe. 4. Keeping the needle in plane to the ultrasound probe, angle the needle 30–50° to the skin and 1 cm from the side of the ultrasound probe with the probe marker (see Figure 43.8). 5. Point the bevel of the needle towards the ultra- sound probe. Using real‐time ultrasound‐guided assistance, the tip of the needle can be visualized as it passes through the subcutaneous tissues and into the peritoneal cavity. Pearl: AFAST should be performed after resuscita- tion and rehydration. As serial exams increase the sensitivity of FAST, repeat exams should generally be performed at least once four hours post admission in stable patients (sooner as clinical course dictates), and considered out to 12–24 hours. Pearl: If the needle is not visible ultrasonographi- cally, the probe should be moved slightly to either side of the needle to try and visualize it. Rapid movement of the needle by advancing and retract- ing it a couple of millimeters may also help localize the needle as this will typically result in tissue movement in proximity to the needle.

Look for the tip of the needle as it often can be seen indenting the peritoneal lining before it enters the peritoneal cavity. 7. Track the trajectory of the needle tip until it is lying within the peritoneal fluid to be aspirated (Figure 43.9). 8. Once the tip of the needle is confirmed to be in the desired location, gentle pressure should be applied to the syringe. The presence of fluid in the needle hub and syringe helps confirm proper location of the needle tip. 9. Release negative pressure on the syringe before withdrawing the needle from the peritoneal cavity. 10. Collect sterile samples of peritoneal fluid into sterile red (plain) and lavender (EDTA) topped tubes. Modified Ultrasound‐guided Diagnostic Peritoneal Lavage Ultrasound‐guided versus Blind Diagnostic Peritoneal Lavage Diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL) has been advocated in cases of blunt and penetrating abdominal trauma, acute abdominal pain, and cases of suspected peritonitis when abdominocentesis has resulted in a negative tap (Walters 2003). Ultrasound has essentially replaced the need for DPL in most trauma patients. In humans, ultra- sound has a similar sensitivity and specificity to DPL for diagnosing intraabdominal injury, but is less invasive, associated with fewer complications, and allows for col- lection of undiluted fluid samples via ultrasound‐guided abdominocentesis even when the quantity of peritoneal fluid is very small (Tso et al. 1992; Singh et al. 1997). However, ultrasound‐guided abdominocentesis may not be feasible in clinical situations where peritoneal fluid is present in very small quantities, is walled off, or is located in proximity to vital organs. In these situations, DPL may still prove diagnostically useful. Unfortunately, complications and failure to obtain a fluid samples are common in veterinary and human patients undergoing traditional DPL. For these reasons, the author prefers to use a modified ultrasound ‐guided Pearl: The tip of the needle appears as a hyperechoic (bright) structure either as a dot or line with or without ring‐down artifact (see Figures 43.6A, 43.7B). Pearl: Alternately, the needle may be left open without an attached syringe and fluid acquired through capillary and gravitational flow. Figure 43.8. Free‐hand ultrasound‐guided abdominocen- tesis. The probe is positioned at an angle of 60° to the skin. Keeping the needle in plane to the ultrasound probe, angle the needle 30–60° to the skin (60–90° to the probe) 1–3 cm from the notched side of the probe. Figure 43.9. Furthermore, MUG‐DPL may reduce the complication rate while increasing the success rate of obtaining a fluid sample compared to blind traditional DPL techniques. Indications for MUG‐DPL The MUG‐DPL technique is reserved for use in patients with acute abdominal pain or peritonitis with only small quantities of peritoneal fluid that cannot be aspi- rated by direct ultrasound‐guided abdominocentesis, are unlikely to have advanced imaging, and samples of the fluid are urgently needed (and cannot wait for serial ultrasound exams). In these patients, the quantity of peritoneal fluid is too small to tap or is located in proximity to vital organs that preclude direct ultrasound‐guided abdom- inocentesis. By adding additional sterile fluid to the peritoneal cavity, it may be possible to identify and characterize small amounts of preexisting peritoneal fluid or inflammation. Scanning T echnique for MUG‐DPL See scanning technique for abdominocentesis (this chapter) and Chapter 12. Ultrasonographic Findings Findings are similar to abdominocentesis findings, although the quantity of fluid will be very small and/or localized to an area that is not easily accessible by direct ultrasound‐guided abdominocentesis (Figure 43.10). Materials Checklist for MUG‐DPL • Ultrasound machine and probes. • Sterile, warmed 0.9 % saline. • Intravenous fluid administration set. • 16–22 gauge 1–4 inch over‐the‐needle catheters. • Clippers. • Antimicrobial scrub and solution. • 3–6 mL syringes. • Red (plain) and lavender (EDTA) topped tubes. • Culturettes • #11 scalpel blade • Lidocaine for local anesthetic block if needed. Procedure to Perform MUG‐DPL The following is a general overview regarding posi - tioning, site preparation, chemical restraint and local anesthesia, and approximating needle length. • Aseptic technique should be used and coagulopa - thies should be ruled out or corrected prior to performing MUG‐DPL. • Sedation and/or local anesthetic blocks may be used to calm the patient, although it is not usually necessary unless large‐bore catheters are used. • The patient can be placed in left or right lateral or dorsal recumbency depending on patient comfort and clinician preference. • Ultrasonography is used to localize small pockets of free abdominal fluid or areas of suspect focal peritonitis (see Chapter 12 on findings of focal peri- tonitis) that cannot be aspirated using ultrasound‐ guided techniques. Pearl: Serial AFAST examinations after resuscitation and rehydration will often detect larger and more accessible fluid pockets in cases of initially ultra - sound‐occult peritonitis. Pitfall: MUG‐DPL and traditional DPL will con - found serial imaging because of the introduction of free fluid and possibly free air and should be delayed if the patient is stable and computed tomog- raphy (CT) or other imaging modalities are required. Figure 43.10. Indications for MUG‐DPL. Small quantity of fluid ( arrow) adjacent to plicated small intestine (PSI) and the renal cortex (RC) that is inaccessible to ultrasound‐ guided abdominocentesis due to the small quantity and its location.

The skin is clipped and aseptically prepped over the site where peritoneal fluid was noted with ultrasound. 2. Using a similar technique to performing abdomi - nocentesis, free‐hand ultrasound guidance is used to pass an over‐the‐needle catheter (16–20 gauge, 1–4 inch depending on the size of the patient and location of peritoneal fluid) and stylet into the peritoneal cavity towards the identified focal fluid accumulation, taking care to avoid abdominal organs (Figure 43.11A). 3. Additional side‐holes may be made in the catheter although care should be taken not to damage the integrity of the catheter because it may break off, leaving the tip in the abdominal cavity. 4. A small stab incision can be made into the skin of the abdomen using a #11 scalpel blade, but is not usually necessary unless a 16 gauge catheter or larger is used. Pearl: If 1–3 side‐holes are added, it is recommended to stagger the holes and not to exceed 50% of the circumference of the catheter. Figure 43.11. MUG‐DPL procedure. In this diagram, the probe is positioned at 90° to the skin and the catheter and stylet are placed at approximately 30° to the skin. (B) The catheter is advanced off the stylet and directed towards the identified focal fluid accumulation. (C) Final placement of the catheter prior to fluid administration.

902 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER 5. Once the stylet and catheter tip are within the abdominal cavity, the catheter can be advanced off the stylet and directed as close to the area of interest as possible using real‐time ultrasound guidance (Figure 43.11B). In some instances, it may be easier to reach the area of interest if the stylet is carefully advanced with the catheter. 6. Once the tip of the catheter is at the desired loca - tion, an IV extension set connected to a bag of warmed 0.9% saline solution is attached to the catheter (Figure 43.11C). 7. Approximately 3–5 mL/kg of sterile saline is allowed to flow through the catheter via gravity (Figure 43.12). 8. If the infusate does not appear to reach the area of interest (no swirling of fluid or increase in size of the fluid pocket), or the size of the desired fluid pocket remains inaccessible via ultrasound‐ guided abdominocentesis, additional 3–5 mL/kg saline aliquots (up to 20 mL/kg) may be adminis- tered through the catheter via gravity until it becomes possible to obtain a sample of abdom - inal fluid that is continuous with the area of interest. 9. Monitor the patient for respiratory distress or dis- comfort when using larger quantities of sterile saline. Discontinue the infusion of fluid if dis - comfort or respiratory distress is noted. 10. If the fluid pocket is continuous between the area of interest and the catheter tip, as determined by real‐time ultrasound, a sample can be directly aspirated via the catheter. 11. Alternately, the infusion catheter is removed and a sample of fluid is directly aspirated from the area of interest using real‐time ultrasound‐ guided abdominocentesis (see Ultrasound‐guided Abdominocentesis) (see Figure 43.13). A 20–22 gauge, 1.5–2 inch hypodermic needle connected to a 3–6 mL syringe may be used. If the fluid is deeper than 2 inches, a spinal needle or the stylet from an intravenous catheter may be used with caution. Pearl: The area of interest within the abdominal cavity can be monitored with real‐time ultrasound as the sterile saline enters the abdomen to see if the infusate is reaching the site of interest. Pearl: To prevent excessive dilution and thus obtain a more representative sample of the site in question, the author often aspirates a sample of fluid from as close to the site of interest as possible using a separate needle and real‐time ultrasound‐ guidance (see Abdominocentesis Procedure above and Figure 43.13). Following the mixing of the infused fluid with preexisting free abdominal fluid or inflammation, ultrasonography is repeated and the opportunity to aspirate any visible fluid pockets (particularly those closest to the site of interest) with real‐ time ultrasound‐guidance may be taken (see Figure 43.13). Fluid should be collected into red (plain) and lavender (EDTA) topped tubes and culturette for appropriate analysis. Pearls and Pitfalls, The Final Say With the evolving use of ultrasound among non - radiologist physicians and veterinarians, the demand for newer technologies to improve the success of ultrasound‐guided techniques has increased. Some final comments regarding ultrasound‐guided tech - niques and improving needle visibility are briefly discussed here. Factors Involving Needle Visualization Needle visualization is dependent on the complex interaction between the needle, the tissue type, and the degree of reflection of the ultrasound beam (McGahan 1986). The closer the echogenicity of the tissue is to the needle, the more difficult the needle is to visualize. Because fluid is anechoic, it provides a good contrast to the echogenicity of the needle, which often allows the needle or needle tip to be more readily visible within fluid‐filled structures or spaces (McGahan 1986). Needle Size In general, larger needles are easier to visualize ultra - sonographically than smaller ones (Chapman et al. 2006). To improve visualization, several companies have created ultrasound needles that are scored or marked to provide a more intense reflection of ultrasound waves back to the probe, thus improving visualization of the needle (Figure 43.14). Needle Bevel Pointing the bevel of the needle up towards the ultra - sound beam has been reported to improve needle tip visualization by creating two echogenic foci at the needle tip as opposed to one (Bondestam 1992). The needle tip tends to be easier to visualize because it has an irregular surface as a result of the bevel being machine cut (Chapman et al. 2006). Moreover, the bevel is reported to be even more visually enhanced when the needle tip is within fluid. Needle Angle The angle of the needle relative to the ultrasound beam also affects the ability to see the needle and its tip dur- ing ultrasound‐guided centesis (Bradley 2001). Ultrasound waves reflected back from the needle or its tip will result in greater visibility of the needle during real‐time imaging. The greatest number of ultrasound waves reflected back to the ultrasound probe occur when the needle is placed perpendicular to the probe. Unfortunately, most fluid‐filled structures (with the exception of superficial vessels or lesions) are located too deeply to allow the needle to be passed in this manner. Experimentally, when aspirating deeper struc- tures, the optimal needle/probe angle has been dem - onstrated to be 55–60° degrees (a needle–skin angle of 30° if the probe is perpendicular to the skin) with a dis- tance between the needle insertion and probe of 2–3 cm (Bradley 2001). Needle Movement Quick short 2–4 mm jabs of the needle facilitate visual- ization, as does rocking the ultrasound probe surface towards the needle. However, the benefit of rocking the probe will be lost if the skin–probe interface contact is diminished. Pearl: If infusate does not appear to have reached the area of interest as determined by real‐time ultra- sound despite the maximum administration of 20 mL/kg, remove the catheter and reposition the patient by gently rolling from side to side. If necessary, reposition by standing or walking the patient while concurrently massaging and balloting the abdomen to help additionally redistribute the infused fluid. Figure 43.14. Diagram of a notched needle to improve visualization. Several companies have created ultrasound needles that are scored or marked so that they will reflect more ultrasound waves back to the probe, improving visual- ization of the needle and accuracy of its placement.

904 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Paying Attention to Needle and Probe Looking at the ultrasound probe as well as the needle while performing free‐hand ultrasound‐guided proce- dures is helpful. For example, the needle should lie in the same plane as the ultrasound beam when using the longitudinal technique. To improve longitudinal visu- alization, the probe should be slowly moved above and below the longitudinal axis of the needle. As pre- viously mentioned, it is helpful to also rapidly advance and withdraw the needle 2–4 mm as this creates visible movement of tissues adjacent to the needle. The probe angle can then be adjusted to attempt to maximize visualization at the site of tissue movement. Software Assistance Finally, several companies have developed software (e.g., Sonix GPS, British Columbia, www.ultrasonix. com) that allows sensors within the ultrasound probe to track sensors placed within needles. These tracking systems allow predetermined trajectory tracks to be visualized on the screen and trace the needle outline as it is advanced through tissues, making exact location of the needle tip and needle much easier to see. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 907 Introduction In order to feel comfortable performing an ultrasound‐guided procedure, this chapter will discuss basic principles and artifacts that the sonog- rapher should be aware of and specific transducer (probe) and needle positioning techniques to achieve the best results possible. There are many benefits associated with ultrasound‐guided tech- niques, including improved target accuracy while minimizing complications using real‐time moni- toring when compared to blinded techniques (see also Chapters 24, 30–33, and 43). Ultrasound‐guided procedures often provide a relatively quick way to obtain a diagnosis and at the same time avoid complications such as hemorrhage, pneumothorax, cardiac puncture, infection, etc. Furthermore, the use of color flow Doppler is important to avoid sampling masses of vascular origin or inadvertently puncturing large vessels or the heart, within the lesion itself or adjacent to it. The use of ultrasound‐guided procedures improves accuracy, is relatively quick in most instances, point‐of‐ care without radiation exposure to the sonographer and procedure‐associated healthcare worker(s), and patient, and is generally safe in experienced hands. The focus for this chapter is to describe the ultrasound‐ guided approach for peripheral lesions. What POCUS: Ultrasound‐Guided Lung and Thoracic Sampling Can Do • Facilitates the accurate sampling through visuali- zation of the target of superficially located lesions involving the thoracic wall, mediastinum, pleural cavity, and lung. • Acquires samples for histopathology and cytology and for culture and sensitivity. • Expedites the diagnosis of different pneumonias, interstitial disease, and other forms of lower airway disease. • May identify complications post sampling including pneumothorax, bleeding, pleural effu- sion, and congestive heart failure. What POCUS: Ultrasound‐Guided Lung and Thoracic Sampling Cannot Do • Sample lesions that are not superficial or are sur - rounded by air, making the lesions not ultrasono- graphically visible • Replace proper training. This maneuver may be successful if the distance between the targeted lesion to the lung sur - face is less than 0.5 cm. Indications • Pneumonic processes that are ultrasonographically visible and accessible for sampling, thus directly targeted. • Pneumonic processes nondiagnostic by bronchoal- veolar lavage (BAL), endotracheal wash (ETW), and transtracheal wash (TTW). • Sampling of small animals that are critically ill and hemodynamically fragile that pose excessive risk for a general anesthetic procedure, such as thora- cotomy, thoracoscopy, and advanced imaging such as computed tomography (CT) and magnetic reso- nance imaging (MRI). • Imaging pulmonary lesions undiagnosed or unrec- ognized via other procedures because lung ultra- sound is extremely sensitive for lung surface pathology. Objectives The objective is to obtain representative samples from thoracic and lung pathology in a safe and quick manner while avoiding complications and reducing the time and cost to get a diagnosis with other modalities of thoracic‐related and lung pathology. Performing Ultrasound‐ Guided Lung and Thoracic Sampling Holding the Probe Usually when doing a diagnostic ultrasound examina- tion, the probe is held with the dominant hand; how- ever, when performing ultrasound‐guided procedures the nondominant hand is best used for holding the probe, while the dominant hand will be performing the procedure. Probe Orientation and Maneuvers It is important to hold the probe firmly while doing the procedure without using excessive pressure that will not only fatigue your hand but also bother the patient, especially if only light sedation is used. The probe has a visible marker that will keep you properly oriented and also indicate the location relative to the probe where the needle is observed and guided. The probe can be maneuvered in four main ways: rotation, sliding, fanning, and rocking (see Chapter 4). These probe maneuvers will help you image the region of interest for nearby critical structures (fanning) and to center the target in the middle of the image (rocking) while creating a mental representation of the target in three dimensions. Knowledge of the regional anatomy is essential to optimize a successful ultrasound‐guided procedure while minimizing complications and the reader is referred to a veterinary anatomy textbook and atlas. Relevant Artifacts There are a few ultrasound artifacts of which the sonographer must be aware to accurately perform an ultrasound‐guided procedure, and the reader is referred to Chapter 3 for more detail and illustrative examples. Distal Acoustic Enhancement This artifact occurs when the ultrasound beam encounters a fluid‐filled structure or a structure that contains a homogeneous population of cells with a specific tissue component that will not attenuate the beam. The fluid‐filled structure will appear anechoic or hypoechoic (darker) with a distal area of unattenu- ated beam that will appear hyperechoic (brighter) when compared to the surrounding tissue of attenu- ated ultrasound beam. Reflection This artifact creates generally a clean shadow beyond the reflector (needle) through the distal field of the image. The artifact is used to locate the metallic needle but will also be caused by bone and cartilage (ribs, sternum), and air (lung) because ultrasound does not transmit through these reflectors either. Reverberation This artifact occurs generally at the tip of the metallic needle (metallic reflector) or from adjacent structures like lung (air reflector) where the ultrasound beam reflects or bounces back to a second reflective surface several times before returning to the transducer (probe). As a result, multiple hyperechoic (bright white) lines are created that are evenly spaced beyond or deep into the reflector(s), referred to as ring‐down

909 POCUS: ULTRASOUND‐GUIDED LUNG AND THORACIC SAMPLING artifact or A‐lines (air reverberation artifact). Air‐filled lung, gas‐filled gastrointestinal tract, and the metallic needle tip most commonly create examples of rever - beration artifact. Edge Shadowing This artifact is a type of refraction that occurs along curved structures. When the ultrasound beam strikes the near‐field edge of a curved structure such as the heart, end-on vessels or lymph nodes (intraabdominal examples include kidneys, stomach, gallbladder, and urinary bladder), the ultrasound beam redirects off the edge of the lesion, creating an anechoic shadow (black) that continues from the edge of the curved structure linearly through the far‐field. Mirror Artifact Most commonly, the artifact is seen in the liver– diaphragm–aerated lung interface due to the curved shape of the diaphragm or the soft tissue–air interface of liver and lung with liver and gallbladder being mir- rored, and in the far‐field of the heart-lung interface with the heart being mirrored. As a result, a false rep- resentation or mirroring of the near‐field structure will appear on the other side or past the reflector. The classic example involves the thorax and the liver– diaphragm–aerated lung interface in which the liver and gallbladder are mirrored on the thoracic side of or cranial to the diaphragm. Optimizing Image Quality Optimizing image, using the “big four” features of focal zone, gain, frequency, and depth, should not be underestimated. Having a good image helps you better see the target and the ultrasound‐guided needle, mak- ing for a safer procedure. First, position the focal zone (focus cursor and best to use a single focus cursor) across from the region of interest, and adjust the gain to best image the needle and target and its adjacent structures by first manipulating the time gain compensation (TGC) knobs, often featured on the right side of the machine as sliders, and then the overall gain knob. If the image is not acceptable, then next assess frequency. For instance, if the image is too dark, you may want to decrease your frequency to improve pen- etration. Frequency may be changed independently or through the machine’s presets. Lastly, pay attention to depth and your centimeter scale for approximating distance and size(s) or structures. See Chapter 4 for more information on optimizing the image. Optimizing Imaging and T racking the Needle: In‐Plane and Out‐of‐Plane There are two major ways of directing the needle using ultrasound guidance. The in‐plane technique is most commonly used by the author. When using the in‐ plane technique, the needle and ultrasound beam are oriented in the same plane during the procedure from the needle insertion to its target. Careful orientation of the needle tip is important because if the angle of the needle with respect to the angle of the ultrasound beam is not ideal, the tip of the needle will be difficult to identify or not be seen. Optimizing the image must take into account the shape of the target and the angle of the needle to the ultrasound beam, which should be as close to perpendicular as possible. When using a linear probe with its rectangular shape, a shallow angle of about 20° with respect to the skin is required, whereas with a microconvex (curvilinear) probe, the needle angle often must approximate a 45° angle to create an ultrasound beam 90° to the needle (Figure 44.1). See subsequent comments in this chapter on probe types. Two Methods of Ultrasound Guidance: Free‐hand and Using Probe Guides Patient Preparation and Planning Thoracic radiographs are equally as important as the preparation and planning of the sampling procedure. Thoracic radiography not only will help choose the appropriate acoustic window for ultrasound imaging and the best target approach, but also help determine if the mass is close enough to the thoracic wall for ultra- sound imaging, and what other structures are nearby, complementing your ultrasound imaging (Figure 44.2). Skin Preparation The area to be sampled needs to be clipped and prepared aseptically. The supplies generally needed are shown in Figure 44.3. The need for sedation will depend on several factors and relies on clinical judgment: • the area to be sampled • the patient’s demeanor • the inherent risk of the procedure and what is being sampled

The use of coupling gel is not necessary and should be avoided to prevent contamination of the sample. Following aseptic technique of the skin, a small amount of 70% isopropyl alcohol is often sufficient for transient acoustic coupling of the probe. Probe Hygiene The probe should be cleaned before the procedure according to manufacturer guidelines. If a core biopsy is to be taken, sterile technique including the probe is required to minimize infection. This may be done via two options: covering the probe with sterile gloves (see Chapter 24 for illustrative example) or use of commer - cially available sterile probe covers. Acoustic coupling gel (option 1) is needed between the probe and the glove‐probe cover for transmission of ultrasound and optimization of image quality. Needle Selection General considerations include the type and size of the targeted lesion(s). For instance, with small (<2 cm) cystic lesions, solid masses, vascularized lesions, or when lymphoma is suspected, fine needle aspiration (FNA) or needle biopsy is often adequate and safest Figure 44.1. The smaller needle gauges are often adequate for cyst aspiration and larger needle gauges for abscesses and solid lesions (20–22 gauge). Tissue core Tru‐Cut biopsies generally include larger gauge needles (14– 18 gauge). The use of larger gauge needles during core and Tru‐Cut biopsies has been associated with an increased risk of complications such as hemor - rhage (Haaga et al. 1983; Bigge et al. 2001). In the case of other thoracic sampling, ultrasound‐guided tech - niques are used to sample pleural and pericardial fluid and lung, mediastinal and thoracic wall lesions that are superficial with an appropriate acoustic window of visualization, generally utilizing 20–22 gauge sizes. The length of the needle necessary to acquire the ultrasound‐guided sample must also be considered in addition to gauge. Either hypodermic needles or spinal needles are commonly used. The necessary needle length is best determined by the centimeter scale on the ultrasound image, or by taking measurements off thoracic radiographs, or both. Additionally, the author attaches an extension tube to the needle to have more control during ultrasound guidance of the needle and prefers using the free‐hand technique, especially if the target is smaller than 1.5 cm. Probe attachments that serve as needle and biopsy guides are commercially available. Probe guides are used more often by the author for ultrasound guidance to less superficial targets and while using spring‐ loaded Tru‐Cut biopsy devices for masses >2.5 cm, keeping in mind that sampling complications are much higher (Parker et al. 1989). Probe Selection For thoracic sampling, the author uses either a linear or microconvex (curvilinear) probe. The benefit of using a microconvex array is the ability to fit the probe head or its footprint in between the ribs. Chemical Restraint and Local Anesthetics The use of local anesthetic is variable. The author gen- erally prefers local anesthesia if several ultrasound‐ guided samples are anticipated. The delivery of local anesthesia can be more painful than the procedure itself; however, adding a 1:10 volume mixture of sodium bicarbonate can mitigate the acidity and stinging effect of lidocaine. An intravenous catheter is generally warranted for most patients and especially if a core Tru‐Cut biopsy is undertaken, for two reasons: to deliver chemical restraint, and to deliver emergency drugs if necessary. In more difficult and risky cases, the use of a short‐acting general inhalant anesthetic may be an appropriate choice (see Figure 44.3). Commonly used drugs often considered solely or in safe combinations include ketamine hydrochloride, diazepam, dexmedetomidine, butorphanol, and intra- venous propofol. Choosing the optimal protocol will depend on clinician preference and underlying med- ical conditions. The use of drugs that promote panting or splenomegaly should be avoided (if the target is abdominal). For tissue biopsies and some deep fine needle and needle biopsy procedures or fine needle and needle biopsy of lesions in critical areas, including lung lobe aspirates, the use of short‐acting sedatives and anesthetic should be considered to minimize pain, patient movement, and panting. Panting is especially problematic from an imaging standpoint, since ultra- sound does not transmit through air, and from a safety standpoint, when sampling lung. Lowering the Risk of Hemorrhage and Pneumothorax The author considers four major parameters in assess- ing patient risk of bleeding: • the target being sampled being superficial versus deep • the needle size and type of sampling technique, such as fine needle aspiration (smaller gauge needle) beomg less risky than core or Tru‐Cut biopsy (larger gauge needles) • the coagulation profile of the patient • the patient’s respiratory and cardiovascular status. The risk of postprocedure bleeding increases if the activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) and/or prothrombin time (PT) are increased and the platelet count is low (<50 000) (Bigge et al. 2001). Excessively elevated globulin levels should also be considered because of their effect on platelet function, which can be assessed point‐of‐care through buccal mucosal bleeding time (BMBT) assessment. Clinical judgment, patient history and profile, and risk–benefit assessment must always be considered. In summary, fine needle aspirates of intrathoracic structures would be considered a low risk if the target is superficial, has low vascularity, and a smaller gauge needle is used (22–25 gauge) along with a good acoustic window of visualization and a stable, still, patient with an unremarkable coagulation profile. On the other hand, a target close to the heart, major vessels, and lung poses more risk and so does a fractious or moving patient and a limited acoustic window. Postprocedural point‐of‐care monitoring using a TFAST‐Vet BLUE approach for detecting hemorrhage, developing effu- sions, and pneumothorax and the lung point is recom- mended for intrathoracic procedures. The TFAST‐Vet BLUE approach should be performed immediately fol- lowing the procedure and repeated again minimally four hours post procedure (sooner if status is question- able) (see Chapters 17, 18, 22, and 23). Lesion Identification Usually, peripheral lung lesions have a mostly homoge- neous to heterogeneous hypoechogenicity (darker) with hyperechoic reverberant foci extending past the lesion. The reverberant foci or horizontal A‐lines com- monly represent trapped air within the parenchyma or peripheral smaller airways. On many occasions, lung is consolidated having interstitial‐alveolar edema with air within airways, the equivalent of finding air bron- chograms on thoracic radiographs, and referred to as the shred sign (Figure 44.4). On other occasions, air - ways have luminal fluid and hyperechoic (bright white) walls indicating the presence of “fluid bronchograms” from consolidated lung tissue, resembling liver tissue, referred to sonographically as “hepatization of lung” when there is no air within the consolidation that has fluid bronchograms (Figure 44.5). This finding is referred to as the tissue sign (see Chapters 22 and 23 for more detailed information regarding lung ultrasound). Shape of Lesions The dynamics of the peripheral, intrathoracic lesion can help to differentiate pulmonary from thoracic wall or pleural lesions (Figure 44.6). The pulmonary lesion

The extrapleural lesion will bulge into the pleural cavity from the parietal side of the thoracic wall, creating an extrapleural sign characterized by a well‐ demarcated, convex contour with tapering cranial and caudal edges. Lesion Size Lesion size is also important. Smaller lesions (<1.5 cm) that are peripheral are more challenging to sample due to motion during respiration, and hence increase the risk for the development of postsampling pneumo - thorax (PTX). Also, the presence of underlying intersti- tial disease and bullae increases the risk for PTX. Sedation can be used with caution if the target is small to decrease panting as much as possible. In the author’s practice, a set of thoracic radiographs are always included post FNA to document that the patient is free of PTX. Although more difficult to document PTX, ultrasound is likely a more sensitive test and a “lung point” strategy may be used to not only assess degree of PTX but also track worsening, static or resolving PTX (see Chapters 17 and 18). Ultrasound is also very sensitive and specific for pleural effusion. Slide Preparation for Sample Submission Microscope slides should be clean and wiped with a soft tissue. There are two popular slide preparation techniques: the squash technique and the smear tech - nique, just as if you were making a blood smear (Figure 44.7). Special Echogenic Enhanced Needles When performing ultrasound‐guided interventions, visualization of the needle is important for accurate target sampling and needle tip positioning. We must remember that regular needles are only well visual - ized when the ultrasound beam hits the needle close to 90° (angle of insonation); thus, the lower this angle of insonation, the less visualization of the needle occurs. Coated needles that enhance ultrasound visualization (echogenic coatings) are commercially available and very helpful for successful ultrasound‐ guided procedures (Figure 44.8). The special echo - genic coating may be a polyethersulfone and contain specially designed microbubbles. These microbubbles within the coating can be different sizes, ranging from 10 to 17 mm. Other types of echogenic needles have dimpled echogenic tips. The ideal needle would have the entire needle visible rather than only its tip, espe - cially for small targets (<1.5 cm) that are adjacent to critical structures, where visualization of only the tip could increase the risk for bleeding or traumatizing adjacent more normal tissue.
