916 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Ultrasound‐Guided Biopsies The need for Tru‐Cut biopsy is typically dictated by larger lesions (>3 cm). The Tru‐Cut biopsy procedure inherently poses a higher risk than when using FNA and needle biopsy sampling techniques because of larger versus smaller needles (and spring‐loaded devices). The use of spring‐loaded biopsy guns is preferred over manual devices. The Bard ® Magnum ® reusable core biopsy instrument and MEDCORE automatic reusable biopsy guns are examples of these commercially avail- able devices. When using spring‐loaded guidance, ensuring that the needle does not travel beyond the limits of the lesion is imperative for patient safety. As in any ultrasound‐guided procedure, the sampling should always avoid aerated tissue and large intralesional and extralesional vascular structures to prevent pneumo - thorax and hemorrhage. Generally, the risk of pneumo- thorax is low and self‐limiting; however, close monitoring of respiratory rate and type of breathing pattern, and use of the TFAST‐Vet BLUE approach are warranted. Building Skills on Phantoms Practicing on phantoms before attempting ultrasound‐ guided procedures on your patient is important for the success of this skill. Several types of phantoms have been used historically in human medicine for the purpose of practicing ultrasound‐guided procedures, including water‐based, agar/gelatin‐based, Blue PhantomTM (Sarasota, FL), and meat phantoms. A good phantom has the following features: • provides echogenicity similar to real tissue • readily available • inexpensive • can be reused • provides tactile feedback • will hold the needle in place • does not generate needle tracks • is not a potential health hazard (see chicken breast models, Chapter 24). Blue Phantoms TM are commercially available but are prohibitively expensive for most institutions. The author recommends the use of phantoms made out of a mixture of gelatin and psyllium while using fluid‐ filled Penrose drains or linear balloons to function as a blood vessel(s) and grapes and cubed cheese as solid targets. Recipes for home‐made phantoms are readily available on the internet. Pearls and Pitfalls, The Final Say The skill of performing ultrasound‐guided procedures is a challenge for all sonographers to take on since ultrasound can identify free fluid and parenychymal lesions, although sampling is necessary for definitive diagnosis. Pitfalls – Most Common Errors • Not using the color flow Doppler feature to assess the vascularity of the targeted tissue or around the targeted tissue of interest can generate unnecessary patient risk for puncturing or lacerating large ves - sels or a heart chamber in the path of the needle. • Losing awareness of the location of the ultrasound probe marker and needle orientation, and thus Figure 44.8. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 921 Introduction With the widespread use of ultrasound by nonradi- ologist veterinarians, it is important for the general practitioner, emergency clinician, or nonradiologist veterinarian to develop a structured ultrasound program for their practice or institution. This chapter tackles some of these issues through our own experi- ences over the past 15 years, with the author serving as an assistant and chief medical director for most of that time, and having a spouse being involved in specialty consulting and working as an internist at a referral practice. The chapter will go over several tenets that are imperative for maximizing success for ultrasound skill proficiency as well as profit and generating income from this traditionally expensive technology that is becoming much more affordable. What POCUS: Setting Up Successful POCUS and FAST Ultrasound Programs Can Do • Establish V‐POCUS and Global FAST examinations with clear objectives. • Maximize learning by detecting ultrasound strengths and weaknesses. • Make use of the ultrasound machine accessible on multiple fronts from actual physical placement within the practice, to fee structure and coding, to replacement policies. • Create accountability. • Create quality control and performance measurement. • Generate income by creating value to both the positive and negative examination. What POCUS: Setting Up Successful POCUS and FAST Ultrasound Programs Cannot Do • Cannot replace proper training. • Cannot replace a disciplined, standardized approach. Indications Any practice or institution using POCUS and Global FAST as part of patient care. POCUS: Setting Up Successful POCUS and FAST Ultrasound Programs Gregory R. Lisciandro CHAPTER FOURTY-FIVE

922 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Objectives • To maximize success in your practice or institu- tion’s POCUS and Global FAST programs for profi- ciency and profit. • For the reader to appreciate the following tenets for such success. ◦ Proper training. ◦ Accessibility physically and financially. ◦ Communicating value to clients. ◦ Goal‐directed templates. ◦ Quality control. ◦ Celebrating your victories. Proper Training Standardized Methodology There is no replacement for proper training and repeti- tion through a systematic, standardized methodology. By applying POCUS and Global FAST in a systematic, standardized way, you will become proficient similar to how your skills developed during perfection of your physical exam. Where Should I Learn Ultrasound? Good question. There are veterinary ultrasound com- panies that have been traditionally dedicated to ultra- sound training and likely more that have made recent commitments to ultrasound education. Check with the ultrasound company from which you purchased your equipment. However, you should consider their ultra- sound training model and what fits your practice’s needs. At the time of writing, many companies begin with a basic complete abdominal ultrasound exami- nation, basic echocardiography, or focused organ approaches. However, the case could be made that the nonradiologist veterinarian should learn the Global FAST approach as the initial format. However, a lack of clarity exists in terms of using FAST as a simple binary test of whether fluid is present or absent in the abdomen and thorax, also referred to as a “flash exam.” We encourage a format somewhere in between the complete abdominal and echocardiography study and the “flash exam” by learning AFAST and applying a fluid score and its target organ approach; TFAST and being able to recognize pleural and pericardial effu- sion, three major echo views, pneumothorax, lung pathology and volume status assessment through integration of the aforementioned; and Vet BLUE and its six lung ultrasound signs. The combination of these three FAST formats is referred to as Global FAST. A similar paradigm shift in ultrasound training is occur - ring in human medicine. Accessibility Accessible Machine Your ultrasound machine must be placed in or in very close proximity to the area where all the action takes place in your practice or institution. The machine ide- ally should be turned on, booted up, and ready to go. Alternatively, have an ultrasound machine that may be readily moved to the patient with either a laptop format or a console on a stand with wheels. At the time of writing, hand‐held ultrasound machines are now so portable the attending healthcare provide can carry the device with them to the patient. What you want to avoid is (1) having your ultra- sound machine stored in a closet down the hall in its original box that requires the box to be opened, the machine unpackaged and then transported to the area where it is to be used (followed, after its use, by being repackaged in its box, transported down the hall, and placed in the closet), or (2) placement of your machine in an inconvenient area of your practice, requiring extra effort to move the machine to the patient (in other words, having the machine in a “back area”). Inconvenience of physical accessibility contributes to lack of use of your ultrasound machine. Accessible Fees The fee structure must be simple. • Coding. • Keep the initial fee general. ◦ POCUS is a standard fee independent of the examination (or minimally varied). ◦ Global FAST is a standard fee independent of how many of its components are performed. • Include the serial exam. • Bundle fees. Over time, when your staff and clientele understand the importance of your ultrasound program, then fees can be modified and tailored to the practice and how its use of ultrasound has evolved. Coding Using codes that are easy to remember will help to ensure that the imaging is charged every time. Some

923 POCUS: SETTING UP SUCCESSFUL POCUS AND FAST ULTRASOUND PROGRAMS electronic records now link the data or findings entry to the fee structure, saving time and freeing up resources since coding and entering fees take staff time that could be better spent on patient care. In any event, keep your coding system simple and minimal. Keeping the Initial Fee General POCUS or Global FAST should be considered the same fee no matter what examination is performed. If you institute Global FAST for all patients as an extension of the physical exam, you strive for all its components every time – AFAST with a fluid score, TFAST, and Vet BLUE. If for some reason a component is not performed, the Global FAST fee is the same, and the data or findings entry states “indeterminate” or “not assessed.” These entries should not be consid- ered abject. We are well aware that patient risk if ques- tionably stable or critical and staff safety enter the picture, limiting examination time. Patient body condition may also alter image quality; for example, a very obese patient may be difficult to image because of attenuation of the ultrasound beam through adipose tissue, a patient may be excessively large, exceeding the depth limits of your machine, subcutaneous air may be present, reflecting the ultrasound beam since ultrasound does not transmit through air, or a painful patient may preclude completing all the indicated acoustic windows. The argument could be made that possibly a POCUS of a soft tissue swelling during MSK evaluation should be a different fee from imaging the eye or brain; however, the hospital director should decide at least initially whether keeping the fee struc- ture simple will contribute to more use and changing the hospital paradigm by encouraging habitual POCUS and Global FAST use through simple fee structures. The author suggests making Global FAST standard of care for all cases, with the POCUS exami- nations being an add‐on. Bundling Fees Bundle the Global FAST examination into triage exam- inations, rounds of hospitalized cases, preanesthetic testing, pre‐ and postprocedure evaluations, geriatric annual screening, and likely you may think of other “bundles” depending on the character of your prac- tice. POCUS exams could be bundled depending on the patient subset. For example, eye problems could be bundled into the ocular work‐up of a POCUS eye exam, and lameness into a POCUS MSK. However, the danger is that the eye problem could be fungal related, and a Global FAST examination would potentially detect pulmonary fungal granulomas that would otherwise be missed or delayed in their detection until disease is more advanced. The musculoskeletal problem could have other evidence‐based information or comorbidities missed with Global FAST as part of the physical examination. Similar concerns regarding targeted and focused exams have been recently raised in human medicine (Narasimhan 2016). Bundle Global FAST into All Triaged Examinations Many clients will approve all that you think is necessary to ensure optimal care and expedite a diagnosis. A crit- ical initial fee that includes physical examination, an intravenous catheter and the first liter of intravenous fluids, quick assessment blood testing, and Global FAST is a strategy that has been useful in our practices. Global FAST truly saves lives through expediting an evidence‐based problem list and better directing resus- citation and diagnostic testing. Bundle Global FAST into Patient Rounds for All Hospitalized Cases Some practices make the fee so economical that the client does not require an explanation and it is accepted as standard of care within that institution. The push to do so with this strategy positively contributes to chang- ing the practice culture, to use Global FAST as part of the physical exam. Bundle Global FAST into Your Preanesthetic Evaluation The idea came from a colleague, Dr Bruce Silverman, who has a special interest in veterinary ophthalmol- ogy. Dr Silverman is skilled in performing cataract and other ocular procedures. Several years ago dur - ing a Global FAST course I was teaching, I was curious as to why Dr Silverman would be learning Global FAST. His answer was intriguing. I paraphrase with his permission: “I am already doing ocular ultra- sound. Most of my patients are geriatric, are diabetic, and may have significant occult comorbidities unde- tected by blood and urine testing and radiography if performed. I am going to perform Global FAST as part of their preanesthetic evaluation before I do my eye procedures.” We adopted the Silverman strategy a few months later, and more recently this type of global approach preanesthetically is being proposed in human medicine.

924 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Bundle Global FAST into Pre‐ and Postprocedural Evaluation Pre‐ and postprocedural Global FAST uses screens for potentially life‐threatening complications including bleeding, septic effusions, pneumothorax, aspiration pneumonia, pulmonary thromboembolism, and heart failure, to name a few examples. A board‐certified radi- ologist raised his hand at one of my lectures a few years ago and stated that all practitioners should be using Global FAST on exit exams on same‐day percu- taneous procedures. We agree. A serial Global FAST should be standard postprocedural evaluation, having shown its superiority to physical exam, lab testing, and radiography for most complications. Bundle Global FAST into Geriatric Annual Assessment In addition to a good physical exam, blood and urine testing, add Global FAST as a free fluid and soft tissue screening test of the abdomen, thorax, heart, and lung. Bundle Fees with Complete Studies Global FAST + Complete Echocardiography Make the fee similar to the others and explain to the client and referring veterinarian briefly and succinctly why both are indicated. You ordered complete echocardiog- raphy for your patient and waited on the radiographs due to cost of care. You feel like the complete echocardi- ography is adequate as your starting test and it is per - formed and rules out heart disease. However, the case had a splenic mass and an abdominal fluid score of 1–2, being a small‐volume bleed. The liver was unremarkable and the lung surface had no nodule sign on Vet BLUE. You ordered the wrong test. Or this same patient had no significant heart disease causing its signs, but during Global FAST there are obvious lung nodules. You may have sent the patient home with the answer that no heart disease existed and instructed the client that we will begin with conservative therapy and continue the work‐ up if the patient fails outpatient care. Or, the patient does have left‐sided heart disease, and pre‐echo you already know if the lung is wet or dry and any other Vet BLUE signs are present (left‐sided congestive heart failure), what the caudal vena cava and its associated hepatic veins look like, if ascites is present (right‐sided congestive heart failure), and if there are any comorbidities in the abdominal cavity before complete echocardiography. Global FAST + Complete Abdominal Ultrasound Make the fee similar to the others and explain to the client and referring veterinarian briefly and succinctly why both are indicated. As an example, an older dog was referred to me at a referral practice as the first‐line evaluation. The dog was critical but stable. The signal- ment (older large‐breed dog), physical exam, blood work, and radiographs prompted suspicion of an abdominal effusion and midabdominal mass. I could have passed on the Global FAST, but it is part of every physical exam. I explained to the owner that our next test after my evaluation would be a complete abdominal ultrasound by a board‐certified radiologist. However, they would not look at the heart or lung surface and I would like to screen the abdominal cavity now, look for any obvious problems and confirm or refute the sus- pected abdominal effusion on the referral radiographs by “seeing” if fluid is present rather than suspecting. Moreover, if free fluid was present and safely accessible, I needed to sample and test it. “If your dog has a can- cerous condition with disseminated disease, I am also screening for you before the expense of the complete study. There are two ultrasound examinations but the evaluations are different (as explained).” The owner agreed. The dog had an AFAST with an abdominal fluid score of 4 (large‐volume bleed/effu- sion), and no obvious masses or AFAST target organ conditions. TFAST showed no pleural or pericardial effusion, no pneumothorax, and unremarkable cardiac chambers, and Vet BLUE showed a normal “lung line” at all views. The fluid was sampled and tested in house with a packed cell volume (PCV) and total solids (TS) and brief cytology. The dog unexpectedly had a modi- fied transudate, not the presumed hemoabdomen for which it was referred. I explained to the owner that the fluid was not a bleed but secondary to a splenic, hepatic or cardiac problem that required the complete study, that as far as I could tell, the condition was not wide- spread and I saw no evidence of cancer either localized or disseminated. The radiologist arrived and now my requirement was “The dog has a modified transudate, I need you to find for me why and what is the source.” The case ended up being liver lobe torsion. The dog had a benign process that was surgical and success- fully treated. The radiologist expediently provided me, the patient, and the client with a much better service. Global FAST did not replace the radiologist and with my training I would not have been able to make their diagnosis. Replacements and Loaners Your ultrasound machine will hopefully become part of nearly every patient evaluation in your practice. When the machine malfunctions, you need a replacement or loaner within 24–48 hours; this point

925 POCUS: SETTING UP SUCCESSFUL POCUS AND FAST ULTRASOUND PROGRAMS cannot be overemphasized. Make sure within your sales agreement that a replacement or loaner is provided within 24–48 hours. The frustration of waiting for completion of a repair over several weeks places you in the uncomfortable position of guessing or using less sensitive means to make decisions on inpatient and outpatient care, medical versus surgical conditions, with the daunting potential of sending your valued patient home not knowing if you missed a potentially catastrophic condition. Moreover, a poten- tially catastrophic condition that would have been easily detected using Global FAST. Communicating Value to Clients The Spiel The spiel is imperative and will vary depending on patient subset and objectives of the POCUS and Global FAST examination. We advocate that Global FAST be part of every ultrasound study as the patient dictates because Global FAST provides an overall imaging patient picture and is part of your physical exam. The mindset is Global FAST first and POCUS as add‐on ultrasound imaging. Example 1 – T rauma and T riage “I am going to perform a FAST ultrasound examination on your pet, which includes a four‐point scan of the abdomen looking for free fluid that could be from bleeding, infection or another cause. I will also be looking through major abdominal organs for any obvious pathology. I am not a radiologist or a cardiolo- gist but I am trained to recognize many basic abnor - malities of the liver, gallbladder, kidneys, urinary bladder, and spleen, and I will also look at the heart and lung surface and for any fluid around the lungs and in the heart sac. If there is free fluid that is safely accessible, may I have permission to use a needle about the same size as needles we use to vaccinate to sample that fluid? Ultrasound cannot tell what type of fluid is present without sampling. Your pet will not be shaved, and will have half the examination performed lying on their side and the other half standing (and many times the entire Global FAST standing). I will be back in about 15–20 minutes to let you know what I find. If you were triaged locally here in San Antonio, Texas, and went to the nearby medical center, the attending physician is likely going to perform a similar ultra- sound evaluation on you because we know it is a very good screening test for major problems otherwise delayed or missed.” Example 2 – Preanesthetic T esting “I would like to perform a Global FAST on your pet before sedation/anesthesia to make sure that there are no obvious problems in their abdomen, heart, or along their lung surface. I am not a radiologist or cardiolo- gist, but am trained to detect basic conditions in the abdomen, to look at basic views of the heart, and the lung surface. The examination, called a Global FAST, will be performed without shaving and with your pet on its side and then standing (or many times the entire Global FAST standing). It will take me about 15–20 minutes to perform and I will let you know my findings at that time.” Example 3 – Hospitalized Cases “We are performing Global FAST ultrasound as part of our physical exam on all hospitalized patients to better direct fluid therapy and potentially detect complica- tions earlier within the abdomen and thorax, including your pet’s heart and lung. By using this approach, we can often better detect internal bleeding, infection, vascular and heart problems, and aspiration pneu- monia as well as other conditions, generally much sooner than without ultrasound.” Example 4 – Pre and Post Procedure “We are performing Global FAST ultrasound in patients having invasive procedures to better direct fluid therapy and potentially detect complications ear- lier by screening the abdomen and thorax, including your pet’s heart and lung. By using this approach, we can often better detect internal bleeding, infection, vascular and heart problems, and aspiration pneu- monia as well as other conditions, generally much sooner than without ultrasound.” Example 5 – Geriatric Annual Evaluation “We are making Global FAST ultrasound part of our annual geriatric profile because we know it is a good complement to our physical exam. On the physical exam, I can see the eyes, ears, oral cavity, and skin coat, but I cannot see internally. By using Global FAST, I can see within the abdomen and thorax conditions that may not be apparent on physical exam, blood and urine testing, and even radiography because X‐ray is

926 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER limited to outlines and silhouettes.” This spiel is used courtesy of Dr Mark Thompson, Dipl. ABVP , Brevard Animal Hospital, North Carolina. Example 6 – POCUS of a targeted‐organ POCUS eye – “We are using a point‐of‐care eye exam to screen for any displacement of the lens, any intraoc- ular or periorbital masses, and retinal detachments.” POCUS MSK – “We are going to apply ultrasound to the swelling to screen for any sign of infection, tumor, herniation, or foreign body.” The POCUS spiel will be dependent on the targeted organ and the clinical questions being answered. Addendums to the Spiel • The use of Global FAST provides me with a soft tissue scan of the abdomen, heart, and lung. • If you had trauma (or in nontrauma had weakness, low blood pressure) and you went to the medical center here in San Antonio, Texas, the attending physician is similarly going to use ultrasound to better assess you. • The ultrasound probe is the new stethoscope. By using lung ultrasound, I can better screen for con- ditions requiring additional imaging, and better interpret my thoracic radiographs. You will soon see physicians using a similar approach. • Radiography shows me outlines and silhouettes, whereas ultrasound shows me free fluid and soft tissue abnormalities. • I am not a radiologist or cardiologist but have been trained to screen for problems otherwise missed or delayed by looking with ultrasound through the abdomen and thorax, including the heart and lung. Explaining Y our Findings Don’t Undervalue a Negative Global FAST “I did not see any signs of bleeding or infection in the abdominal cavity, thoracic cavity or heart sac. There were no obvious masses or organ conditions seen in the abdomen. Basic heart chamber ratios appeared normal. The lung surface was normal. I feel much better that we screened for any obvious conditions that could be potentially catastrophic.” Don’t Fear a Positive Global FAST or POCUS Examination You only have to recognize that something looks abnormal, which triggers more advanced imaging and gold standard testing. No matter what we do, no clini- cian is correct 100% of the time, and explaining that something appears suspect that requires x, y, and z for confirmation is better patient care than not looking. Sage advice – “You will miss more by not looking than not knowing.” Use of Goal‐Directed Templates The importance of goal‐directed templates cannot be overemphasized. • Goal‐directed templates establish clear objectives for your Global FAST and POCUS examinations. • They will differ between practices and depending on what clinical questions are to be answered. • They will evolve over time depending on skill set and types of cases seen at your practice. • Goal‐directed templates are best recorded follow- ing the order of the examination. • Goal‐directed templates allow measurement and evaluation of your program’s performance, helping to develop diagnostic algorithms for different patient subsets within your practice. Establish Clear Objectives Goal‐directed templates should convey the Global FAST and POCUS examination goals to you, your practice, your colleagues, and your clients. Examples are shown in Figures 45.1, 45.2, 45.3, and 45.4. See also Appendix I. Qualifiers for Y our T emplates AFAST The AFAST ultrasound examination is a screening test for the detection of free fluid and some types of organ pathology and conditions to better direct resuscitation and diagnostic testing. The AFAST examination is not intended to replace a complete abdominal ultrasound. TFAST The TFAST ultrasound examination is a screening test for the detection of free fluid around the lungs and within the heart sac, collapsed lung lobe(s), and some types of lung and heart pathology, to better direct resuscitation and diagnostic testing. The TFAST exam- ination is not intended to replace complete echocardi- ography and thoracic radiography.

927 POCUS: S ETTING U P SUCCESSFUL POCUS AND FAST U LTRASOUND P ROGRAMS Vet BLUE The Vet BLUE ultrasound examination is a screening test for different types of lung pathology, including congestive heart failure, pneumonia, hemorrhage, lung contusions, and pulmonary thromboembolism, to better direct resuscitation and diagnostic testing. Vet BLUE can also detect nodules and different forms of lung consolidation. It is not meant to replace thoracic radiography. Global FAST Global FAST ultrasound examination is a screening test for different types of abdominal, thoracic, heart, and lung pathology to better direct resuscitation and diagnostic testing. Global FAST is not meant to replace radiography, complete abdominal ultrasound, and complete echocardiography. POCUS of X, Y, or Z These would be dictated by the system being exam - ined and the clinical questions being answered. POCUS eye will differ from POCUS MSK that will differ from a POCUS avian examination. Y ou Must Record Y our Findings If you don’t record patient data, you cannot measure performance, and if you can’t measure performance, you cannot properly evaluate your proficiency. By using goal‐directed templates, skills can be evalu - ated, training can be improved to better maximize suc- cess, and deficiencies and strengths in your program recognized. Moreover, without recording the findings of your Global FAST and POCUS examinations, patient information is lost, likened to performing a physical examination without recording your findings. The recording of findings for the patient’s medical record must be logical and convenient. Reduce staff time by having a standard template within the medical record which limits free typing entries, or a hard copy template that is convenient by checking off boxes with limited need for writing in findings. Moreover, with a standard- ized entry system that mimics the order of image acquisi- tion, findings are more readily remembered and entered. Figure 45.1. Goal‐directed template for AFAST. 930 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Recording and Archiving Images See Quality Control section below. Quality Control • Training individuals in house and offsite and encouraging professional staff to make Global FAST and, over time, POCUS specific for the character of the practice a core skill. • Establishing a consensus within your practice for what the ultrasound program should be. Typically this evolves over time as skills are gained. • Saving images for case review. • Periodically reviewing the overall content of your ultrasound program and making adjustments accordingly. • Establishing a Global FAST and POCUS director or point person to oversee your program. • Communication with colleagues regarding your Global FAST and POCUS program, if your practice is a secondary or referral practice, and with clients so they are aware of your additional training and acumen in assessing their pets. Establishing a Program Director or Point Person It is imperative for one individual within your practice to be specifically responsible for the implementation of the program. • Should be properly trained through relative ultra- sound courses with understanding not only of basic ultrasound principles but also of its limitations. • Should be an effective communicator and motivator. • Should be able to implement quality control with authority. Establishing a Consensus Involve everyone who undertakes image acquisition, image interpretation, and other related in‐house ser - vices in periodically (at least biannually) reviewing your Global FAST and POCUS program. Set out to dis- cuss, determine or revise your program’s objectives and goals, which will include reviewing your goal‐ directed templates for additions, subtractions, and revisions. These periodical reviews will also serve to assess strengths, weaknesses, need for additional training, and strategies to improve your program. Ensuring Quality Control and Periodical Reviews Ideally, the program director or point person should institute a multitiered approach with each ultrasonog- rapher, including (1) being trained with lectures and hands‐on time, followed by (2) a minimum number of proctored exams (suggest 12–25), and then (3) periodic reviews of cases thereafter. Periodic case reviews (suggest monthly at staff meetings) and overall program assessment (suggest bian- nually) are also imperative to ensure quality control in image acquisition and image interpretation through case discussions. As discussed within this chapter, the use of standardized goal‐directed templates and saving of ultra- sound images on all cases (routine and interesting) help pinpoint deficiencies and assist with training and reviews. Saving Images Why Save Images? Saving ultrasound images is important for three major reasons: 1) archives your patient’s Global FAST and POCUS study, allows you to review studies to learn from them, and allows you to show great Global FAST and POCUS cases to your staff. Ideally, video clips are preferable over still images because more information is generally gained. However, the decision is complex and dependent on the resources and character of the practice as well as other factors unique to the practice and veterinary medicine regulations. What Time Frame and How Long Should I Make the Video Clips? We suggest as a starting point recording a six‐second clip that is prospective; thus when you start the recording you know what image is being captured. In some instances, you may need to get two six‐second clips at a view for various reasons. However, by including target organs and transition zones in your recordings, labeling is generally not needed unless the view is so abnormal that labeling is needed for clarity. Unlabeled or mini- mally labeled video clips present a more obvious repre- sentation during review than a still image. Labeling Images When the studies are performed in a standardized pro- tocol‐driven manner, images do not need to be labeled. For example, if my study is an AFAST then I record the study from the DH to the SR to the CC to the HRU

931 POCUS: SETTING UP SUCCESSFUL POCUS AND FAST ULTRASOUND PROGRAMS view. If the AFAST target organ approach is used, the DH is apparent because the diaphragm, liver, gall- bladder, “cardiac bump,” and caudal vena cava are all in view. The SR view is evidenced by the left kidney and spleen, and so forth. When needed because of abnormalities or the captured video clip is not obvious, then label. Cardiac images are also obvious if the image acquired is acceptable. For Vet BLUE, the author always performs left to right and catches transition zone on the Caudodorsal view, the heart on the Middle view, and the thoracic inlet on the Cranial view. The Ph view lacks anything other than lung. Reviewing Images Learning from stored images is extremely helpful, from looking through Global FAST views and focusing on a single artifact to see how that artifact is portrayed by your ultrasound machine, to reviewing Global FAST views after complete studies, to comparing to other imaging modalities for recognizing the strengths and limitations of your approach. Saved images may also be presented to your staff, showing them how important implementation of Global FAST and POCUS was for care in specific patients, catching conditions otherwise missed, and ultimately streamlining and expediting care and saving lives. The use of this strategy carries the poten- tial to build pride in patient care and push the staff to adopt this paradigm and culture change. Training Techniques In addition to scanning on live volunteers, training may be performed on cadavers and phantoms that are commercially available as well as hand made. For example, the chicken breast model is very realistic for training to place central line intravenous catheters (see Figures 24.12, 24.13, and 24.14 and Chapter 24). Moreover, many hand‐made phantom models have been described and some are listed in the Further Reading section of this chapter. There are several com- panies that provide ultrasound training, including the author’s company FASTVet.com that provides both hands‐on and online Global FAST and POCUS training. Pearls and Pitfalls, The Final Say You can have all the information and be able to pro- duce the best image acquisition possible, but if you cannot communicate that to the client, if you are unable to assign fair and affordable financial value to Global FAST and POCUS, if you are unable to record findings, if you are unable to review proficiency and identify the skill level of the practice, your Global FAST and POCUS program will likely fall short. Conversely, if you can make Global FAST and POCUS a new para- digm change in your practice, you will find a new rewarding dimension of patient care that provides renewed confidence in your practice of veterinary medicine. 944 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER DCM: dilated cardiomyopathy DPL: diagnostic peritoneal lavage ECG: electrocardiography FS: fractional shortening GI: gastrointestinal GIT: gastrointestinal tract HCM: hypertrophic cardiomyopathy IVS: interventricular septum LAT: left atrial tear LVFW: left ventricular free wall MUG‐DPL: modified ultrasound‐guided diagnostic peritoneal lavage MVD: mitral valve disease NCPE: noncardiogenic pulmonary edema PA: pulmonary artery PEA: pulseless electrical activity PHT: pulmonary hypertension PTE: pulmonary thromboembolism ROSC: return of spontaneous circulation RVFW: right ventricular free wall T3: trauma, triage, and tracking (monitoring) applications of AFAST and TFAST TXR: thoracic radiographic ZZC: zig‐zag continuum Terminology and Glossary 1 view is no view: Axiom from human medicine to combine views to make an accurate ultrasono- graphic assessment. 2nd episode of anaphylaxis: Describes the inflammatory products that are released into circulation following anaphylaxis contributing to complications including the acquired coagulopathy. 4‐quadrant approach: Lung ultrasound examination in which the thorax is divided into four quadrants and then scanned cranial to caudal to cranial. Abdominal fluid scoring system: The use of AFAST and numbers of positive views to assign an abdom- inal fluid score for ascites. Acoustic enhancement artifact: Occurs with fluid‐ filled structures from which through the far‐field beyond the scanning plane the structures are artifac- tually hyperechoic (brighter). AFAST‐TFAST 48‐hour rule: Expect cavitary bleeding to resolve or nearly resolve within 48 hours once bleeding stops. A‐lines: Equidistant parallel lines that originate from a strong air–ultrasound interface representing air reverberation artifacts most commonly from normal aerated lung, pneumothorax, pneumoperitoneum, air‐filled gastrointestinal tract and also through the far‐field from the caudal vena cava at the FAST dia- phragmatico‐hepatic (DH) view. AFAST®: Abdominal FAST protocol that is made up of targetorgan views rather than external locations as follows: diaphragmatico‐hepatic view (DH), spleno‐renal view (SR), cysto‐ colic view (CC), and hepato‐renal umbilical view (HR). Alveolar‐interstitial syndrome (AIS): The presence of B‐lines most commonly represents a variety of forms of alveolar‐interstitial edema and thus is referred to as a syndrome. Anaphylactic gallbladder: The presence of gall- bladder intramural edema caused by anaphylaxis in dogs. B‐lines: Synonymous with ultrasound lung rockets (ULRs) that most commonly represent alveolar‐inter- stitial edema at the lung surface. By definition, these are hyperechoic vertical artifacts that originate off the lung surface and extend through the far‐ field,obliterating A‐lines while swinging like a pen- dulum in synchrony with inspiration and expiration. Bar code sign: Term applied to the visual of pneumo- thorax during M‐mode that is synonymous with the stratosphere sign. Batman: Right TFAST pericardial short‐axis descriptor of the heart at the level just ventral to the “mushroom view” and dorsal to the bull’s eye. Bounce: Term created by the author (GL) to describe the effect of the caudal vena cava when it has the normal dynamic changes in its height at the dia- phragmatico‐hepatic (DH) view. Boysen maneuver: Term created by the author that describes the rotation of the probe parallel to the ribs in the cardiac‐diaphragmatic pouch for the detection of pleural effusion. Bregmatic fontanelle: Term used for the anterior fontanelle that is the largest fontanelle, open at birth, and closes with age (remains open in some dogs). It is located on the top of the skull at the junction of the sagittal, coronal, and frontal sutures. Bull’s eye: Right TFAST pericardial short‐axis descriptor of the heart at the most ventral level to the sternum representing the muscular apex of the heart. Bull’s eye sign: The effect created at the right peri- cardial view when pericardial effusion is present around the muscular apex of the heart. C‐line: Line that is created by consolidated lung dur- ing lung ultrasound. Nomenclature is not univer - sally accepted. Cardiac bump: The effect created by the muscular apex of the heart (and the left ventricle) immediately

945 ABBREVIATIONS, TERMINOLOGy AND GLOSSAR y against the diaphragm that indents the diaphragm with each heart beat. Cardiac‐cervical pouch: The most gravity‐dependent region in the pleural cavity immediately cranial to the heart, best imaged in the standing patient. Cardiac‐diaphragmatic pouch: The most gravity‐ dependent region in the pleural cavity between the heart and the diaphragm, best imaged in the standing patient. Cardiac gallbladder: The presence of gallbladder intramural edema caused by pericardial effusion and right‐sided heart failure including dilated car - diomyopathy in dogs. Caudodorsal transition zone: The region of the interface of the pleural and peritoneal cavity identi- fied by the presence of the curtain sign. Clean shadowing: Shadowing that is created most often by bone and stone (calculi) that completely reflects the scanning plane, creating an anechoic shadow through the far‐field. Comet‐tail artifact: The term used for partial hyper - echoic lines that originate off the pulmonary–pleural interface and “lung Line” that do not extend through the far‐field. Complete detailed abdominal ultrasound: The term used for a complete abdominal ultrasound examination. Complete detailed echocardiography: The term used for a complete echocardiogram examination. Curtain sign: The term used when a linear border is created along the dirty shadowing created by lung moving to and fro over pleural effusion or abdom- inal structures at the transition zone of pleural and peritoneal cavities. Dirty shadowing: Shadowing that is created most often by air‐filled structures that partially reflects the scanning plane through the far‐field, limiting accurate imaging beyond the reflective structure. Double lung point: Term created in human medi- cine that describes the presence of two lung points most commonly seen when people (adults, children, and neonates) with pneumothorax are placed in supine positioning. Dry lung: The presence of A‐lines and lung sliding. E‐line: Line that is created by subcutaneous emphy- sema during lung ultrasound. Nomenclature is not universally accepted. Edge shadowing artifact: Created off curved soft tissue surfaces in which an anechoic line extends off the curved surface through the far‐field. Eyeball method: Gestalt approach in which assessment is made of the heart and vena cava in which measure- ments are not performed – similar to eyeballing. Eyeballing: Term use for the gestalt approach in which assessment is made of the heart and vena cava in which measurements are not per - formed – similar to eyeball method. False shred sign: Created by the stomach, its wall, rugal folds, and ingesta that appear like consolidated lung. False tissue sign: Created by the liver that appears like consolidated lung. False B‐lines: Created by the stomach and its ingesta that appear like alveolar‐interstitial edema. FAT: Term applied to the characterization of the dis- tended caudal vena cava that represents an abnor - mally high central venous pressure. Flash exam: Term applied to the general sweeping of the abdomen, thorax, and lung in which there is oth- erwise no defined acoustic window(s) in attempt to answer a single binary question of fluid positive or fluid negative (AFAST, TFAST) or B‐lines positive or B‐line negative (Vet BLUE). Flat: Term applied to the characterization of the hypovolemic caudal vena cava that represents severe volume depletion. Fishmouth: Right TFAST pericardial short‐axis descriptor of the heart at the level just ventral to the Mercedes‐Benz view and just above the windshield wipers where the mitral valves form an annulus. Focused ultrasound exams: Term used for a targeted ultrasound examination. Gator sign: The intercostal orientation for all lung ultrasound in which the probe is placed perpen- dicular to the long axis of the ribs, creating the image of a partially submerged alligator peering over the water at the sonographer, with the eyes as the ribs and the bridge of the nose as the inter - costal space. Global FAST®: The term used when AFAST, TFAST, and Vet BLUE are combined as a single ultrasound examination. Global FAST® approach: The application of Global FAST to stage patients for localized versus dissemi- nated disease and for assessing volume status dependent on the subset of patient. Globoid heart: Descriptor of the generalized enlarge- ment of heart that often accompanies chronic peri- cardial effusion. Hammerhead view: Term applied to the left TFAST pericardial short‐axis view and its most ventral level that includes the left and right ventricles. Helper hand: Nonprobe hand that is used for palpa- tion of external landmarks and the apical beat, and for moving skin and stabilizing the patient to opti- mize image quality.

946 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Hepatization: Term describing the discontinuity of the expected linear continuity of the “lung line” along the intercostal space that represents complete lung consolidation without aeration – synonymous with the tissue sign. Kiwi fruit sign: Term used to describe the appear - ance of a gallbladder mucocele. Knuckling the probe: Term used for wrapping your probe hand around the top of the probe, providing a buttress or cushion against the thoracic wall when patients are in right lateral recumbency to acquire the right pericardial TFAST echo views. Line (lung) nomenclature: A terminology system incorporating alphabetically created descriptive lines that include A‐lines and B‐lines as well as others that are not universally accepted for various lung ultrasound findings. Linear transducer: Linear probe used for superior detail of smaller structures. The probe is also limited by depth and frequency. Long‐axis (cardiac) line: The scanning plane that is used for long‐axis views of the heart from the right TFAST pericardial site view. Lung line: Term used to describe the location of the lung surface most accurately in the presence of pleural space disease. Lung point: The location where the lung recontacts the thoracic wall, the transition zone of pneumo- thorax and reopposition of lung against the thoracic wall, as evidenced by any presence of lung immedi- ately against the thoracic wall, most commonly by lung sliding and B‐lines; however, the lung pulse and other Vet BLUE lung ultrasound signs also determine where the lung point is located. Lung pulse: Term for when lung sliding or B‐lines are not in synchrony with inspiration and expiration but rather with each heart beat due to severely atel- ectatic or consolidated lun. Lung sliding: The “to and fro” motion of the lung sliding in synchrony immediately adjacent to the intercostal space during inspiration and expira- tion – replaces the veterinary term “glide sign.” Macroconvex transducer: Used for examining the abdomen and thorax including heart and lung. Allows for deep imaging but limited by its large footprint (probe head). Mediastinum testis: The linear hyperechoic land- mark centered within the parenchyma of the tes- ticle – synonymous with the term rete testis. Microconvex transducer: Most durable and com- monly used probe in small animal veterinary medi- cine because it can image the abdomen, thorax including heart and lung, as well as musculoskel- etal, ocular and smaller parts. Limited by depth and midrange frequency. Mirror image artifact: The duplication, partial and complete, of structures in the near‐field immediately adjacent to a strong air interface. Most commonly occurs at the diaphragm but also can be seen at the cysto‐colic view and the body wall and the heart off the pericardium in the far‐field. MUG‐DPL: Modified ultrasound‐guided diagnostic peritoneal lavage. Mushroom: Right TFAST pericardial short‐axis descriptor of the heart at the level where the chordae tendinae are attached to the left ventricular papillary muscles just ventral the mitral valves. Nodule sign: Term created by the author that describes lung nodules along the pulmonary surface most commonly observed as a homogeneous relatively anechoic (or of low echogenicity) round to oval region at the lung surface with a hyperechoic border along its far side often associated with pseudo B‐lines extending through the far‐field. Nonecho fallback views: Term applied by the author to describe the strategy to rule out left‐ and right‐ sided congestive heart failure without echocardio- gram views. Nonecho fallback view for left‐sided failure/volume overload: Vet BLUE is used to assess for left‐sided congestive heart failure with absent B‐lines ruling out left‐sided congestive heart failure. Nonecho fallback view for right‐sided failure/ volume overload: The FAST diaphragmatico‐ hepatic (DH) view is used to assess for right‐sided congestive heart failure with the absence of a dis- tended (FAT) caudal vena cava and hepatic veins, the tree trunk sign, ruling out right‐sided congestive heart failure. One‐eyed gator sign: A strategy developed by the author to enhance the observation of lung sliding by placing the rib in the center of the screen causing the echoes to scatter off reflective bone and then strike the lung line obliquely. Parking garage effect: The poor ability to categorize the degree of pneumothorax in dogs and cats in lat- eral recumbency because of the small difference in height of the thorax. Parking garage–skyscraper concept: The improved ability to categorize the degree of pneumothorax in dogs and cats in standing or sternal recumbency because of the much greater difference in height bet- ween the ventral and dorsal extremities of the pleural cavity when compared to lateral recumbency. Phased‐array transducer: Also called a sector trans- ducer. This probe’s greatest strength is for cardiac

947 ABBREVIATIONS, TERMINOLOGy AND GLOSSAR y imaging because of its small focal point that can send echoes in between ribs for superior echocardi- ography over other transducers. Probe may also be used for abdominal and lung imaging but our pre- liminary studies have shown it is likely not accurate for counting B‐lines. Pouch: Term that refers to the most gravity‐ dependent region in the abdomen and thorax where free fluid would accumulate. Power slide: Term coined in human medicine for the documentation of lung sliding in people using power Doppler. Pneumothorax (PTX): A‐lines in the absence of lung sliding define pneumothorax. Probe hand: The hand holding the probe. Pleural–peritoneal transition zone: Another term describing more generally the transition zone of the pleural and peritoneal cavities identified by the “curtain sign.” Pseudo‐asystole: Term used in human medicine to describe asystole refuted by echocardiogram by finding coordinated cardiac movement. Pseudo B‐line: Term used to describe B‐lines associ- ated with the gastric lumen and nodules. Pulmonary–diaphragmatic interface: Term used to described the immediate proximity of lung against the diaphragm in the absence of pleural space disease. Pseudo‐gastric B‐lines: Term used to describe B‐ lines created by fluid and air within the gastric lumen. Pulmonary–pleural line: The location where lung is immediately against the intercostal space where the normal “to and fro” motion of lung sliding is observed along the thoracic wall – synonymous with pulmonary–pleural interface. Pulmonary–pleural interface: The location where lung is immediately against the intercostal space where the normal “to and fro” motion of lung sliding is observed along the thoracic wall. Pseudo‐PEA (pulseless electrical activity): Term used in human medicine to describe pulseless electrical activity refuted by echocardiogram by finding coordinated cardiac movement. Racetrack sign: Term applied to the finding of peri- cardial effusion rounding the muscular apex of the heart at the diaphragmatico‐hepatic (DH) view. Rain sign: Term applied to the visual of B‐lines dur- ing M‐mode. Rete testis: The linear hyperechoic landmark cen- tered within the parenchyma of the testicle – synon- ymous with the term mediastinum testis. Reverberation artifact: Most commonly created by air and equidistant parallel lines that continue beyond the first encountered reflective surface referred to as A‐lines with lung but can be seen with other air‐filled structures. Reverse sliding sign: Term applied to the effect of A‐lines sliding opposite that of lung sliding at the caudal transition zone of pleural and peritoneal cav- ities described in dogs, with suspect validity. Rough pericardiocentesis: Term used to describe opening the pericardial sac during pericardiocente- sis to create a temporary pericardial window (should not be performed in patients with ruptured cardiac chambers). Satisfaction of search error: Describes the situation in which a reporting radiologist fails to continue to search for subsequent abnormalities after identi- fying an initial one. Seashore sign: Term applied to the visual of A‐lines and lung sliding in M‐mode. Seldinger technique: A catheter insertion method- ology that generally involves a step‐wise progres- sion of an over‐the‐needle temporary catheter, followed by a guidewire, followed by a dilator, and then the final catheter. Side‐lobe artifact: Fluid‐associated artifact that can make fluid‐filled lumens and structures, most com- monly the gallbladder, urinary bladder, large ves- sels and eye, appear to contain sediment or luminal debris. Shimmy line: Term created by the author that describes the Z‐line. Short‐axis (cardiac) line: The scanning plane that is used for short‐axis views of the heart from the right TFAST pericardial site view. Skyscraper effect: The improved ability to catego- rize the degree of pneumothorax in dogs and cats in standing or sternal recumbency because of the much greater difference in height between the ventral and dorsal extremities of the pleural cavity when com- pared to lateral recumbency. Slice‐thickness artifact: Fluid‐associated artifact that can make fluid‐filled lumens and structures, most commonly the gallbladder, urinary bladder, large vessels and eye, appear to contain sediment or luminal debris or have false rents in their wall. Smiley face view: Term applied to the left TFAST pericardial short‐axis view that includes the left and right ventricles and right atrium and auricle imme- diately dorsal to the hammerhead view. Step sign: Term that describes the deviation from the expected linear continuity of bone when fractured, lung with pathology such as consolidation, and lung that is displaced by thoracic wall trauma or pleural space disease.

948 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Stratosphere sign: Term applied to the visualizing of pneumothorax during M‐mode that is synonymous with the stratosphere sign. TFAST®: Thoracic FAST protocol that includes bilat- erally the left and right chest tube sites, left and right pericardial sites, and a single diaphragmatico‐ hepatic (DH) view. TFAST PTX 1/3s Rule: Term developed by the author to assess the degree of pneumothorax as well as serving as a monitoring tool for tracking static, resolving, and worsening pneumothorax. TFAST slide: Term used to described sliding the probe into the cardiac‐diaphragmatic pouch and cardiac‐cervical pouch. Tree trunk sign: Term used by the author to describe hepatic venous distension. True asystole: Term used in human medicine to describe asystole confirmed by echocardiogram. True PEA (pulseless electrical activity): Term used in human medicine to describe pulseless electrical activity confirmed by echocardiogram. Twinkle artifact: Term used to describe the use of color flow Doppler for the detection of small miner- alizations (<5 mm) within the kidney that create a twinkle effect of colored pixels. Ultrasound lung rockets: Synonymous with B‐lines. Urinary bladder estimation formula: Length × height × width measured in centimeters × 0.625 = volume estimation in milliliters. Urine output: Urine produced over time divided by body weight. Vet BLUE ®: Lung ultrasound protocol that is a regional pattern‐based approach that includes the transthoracic acoustic windows of the caudodorsal, perihilar, middle, and cranial lung regions and the diaphragmatico‐hepatic (DH) view. Vet BLUE B‐line lung contusion system: The counting of maximum numbers of B‐lines associated with each Vet BLUE acoustic window combined with numbers of positive Vet BLUE acoustic views. Vet BLUE lung ultrasound signs: There are six described Vet BLUE lung ultrasound signs: dry lung, B‐lines (wet lung), shred sign, tissue sign, nodule sign and wedge sign. Vet BLUE B‐line scoring system: The counting of maximum numbers of B‐lines associated with each Vet BLUE acoustic window. Wagon wheel: Ultrasonographic appearance of the ileocecal‐colic junction in the cat. Wedge sign: Term created by the author describing a triangulated shred sign in caudodorsal and perihilar lung regions that supports the presence of pulmonary thromboembolism. Shred sign: Term created by the author describing the fractal discontinuity of the expected linear conti- nuity of the lung line along the intercostal space that represents an air bronchogram. Tissue sign: Term created by the author describing the discontinuity of the expected linear conti- nuity of the lung line along the intercostal space that represents complete lung consolidation without aeration – synonymous with hepatiza- tion of lung. Wet lung: The presence of B‐lines (ultrasound lung rockets) that most commonly represent forms of alveolar‐interstitial edema. Windshield wiper: Right TFAST pericardial short‐ axis descriptor of the heart where the mitral valves are apparent just dorsal to the “mushroom view.” Z‐line: Term for a lung ultrasound artifact that is not universally accepted that describes a vertical artifact that does not extend through the far‐field, fades and has no synchrony with phases of respiration created by fascial planes of muscle in the near‐field in the presence of dry lung. Zig‐zag continuum approach: A lung ultrasound examination in which the patient’s thorax is scanned by moving dorsally and ventrally through inter - costal sapces.

It does provide some quick references including normal values, rules of thumb, and some charts and formulas. References may be found in the individual chapters as well as greater detail. AFAST® • Free fluid is abnormal in adult dogs and cats; how- ever, puppies and kittens can have small quantities of anechoic free fluid in normalcy with anechoic stripes and pockets of <3 mm in width and maximum dimensions, respectively, and generally no more than one or two positive AFAST views. The dia- phragmatico‐hepatic view is the most common positive view with anechoic stripes of maximum width <3 mm along the diaphragm and similar anechoic stripes of <3 mm may be found in sedated adult dogs and cats (Lisciandro et al. 2015, 2019). • The abdominal fluid score (AFS) ranges from 0 (negative) to a maximum of 4 (positive all four AFAST sites). The AFS has been modified to include 0, 1/2, and 1 for scoring at each AFAST view dependent on the size of the fluid pocket with the same small‐volume bleeder versus large‐volume bleeder concept originally described. • Small‐volume bleeders, defined as dogs with an AFS <3, are unlikely to become anemic from their intraabdominal bleed. • In a small‐volume bleeder that is anemic there are four major causes: preexisting anemia, bleeding somewhere else, hemodilution, and lab error. • Large‐volume bleeders, defined as an AFS of ≥3, predictably become anemic from their intraabdom- inal bleed, and approximately 20–25% of dogs will become severely anemic, requiring blood transfusion(s) (Lisciandro et al. 2009). • Large‐volume bleeder hit‐by‐car dogs often need blood transfusion(s) but uncommonly exploratory laparotomy for control of their intraabdominal hemorrhage because bleeding often stops with medical management without surgery (Boysen et al. 2004; Lisciandro et al. 2009). • Free intraabdominal fluid in hit‐by‐car trauma is reported in the veterinary literature to be hemoab- domen and uroabdomen at a frequency of ~98% to 2–3% of the time, respectively (Boysen et al. 2004; Simpson et al. 2009). • The AFAST‐applied abdominal fluid scoring system is applied similarly in cats, however, cats don’t sur- vive large volume bleeds as dogs (Lisciandro 2012). • Packed cell volumes (PCV) as low as 3–5% from blood contamination can appear to be grossly bloody and mistaken for a cavitary bleed; thus, samples should always be spun (PCV) and mea- sured for accurate patient assessment. • Once bleeding stops, expect significant resorption of blood within 48 hours with minimal to resolved abdominal fluid scores, referred to as the AFAST‐ TFAST 48‐hour rule. • Large‐volume bleeder postinterventional cases (postoperative laparotomy, laparoscopy, percuta- neous biopsy procedures, etc.) that are noncoagulo- pathic may or may not need blood transfusion(s) depending on their current clinical status and degree of compensation. However, these cases Quick References of Normal V alues and Rules of Thumb APPENDIX III

950 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER nearly always require exploratory surgery to defini- tively control their intraabdominal bleeding, and delaying surgery on a large‐volume bleeder com- monly leads to more morbidity, complications, and expense because of progressive anemia. • The large‐volume bleeder versus small‐volume bleeder concept applied to nontraumatic, noncoag- ulopathic cases (e.g., ruptured splenic mass) helps direct decision making regarding surgery ahead of overt decompensation in acute bleeds, i.e., large‐ volume bleeders even without anemia should be promptly explored and likely will need blood transfusion (autotransfusion is an option when a blood donor is not readily available and uncontam- inated blood can be cleanly harvested). • Small‐volume bleeders without anemia may be seri- ally monitored and medically managed as long as they remain small‐volume bleeders. • In small‐volume bleeders that have significant anemia, a chronic process leading to anemia should be considered such as self‐limiting intermittent low‐grade bleeds or bone marrow disease. • The large‐volume bleeder versus small‐volume bleeder concept applied to nontraumatic, coag- ulopathic cases, i.e., ruptured splenic mass, helps direct decision making regarding the need for blood transfusion(s) since compensated large‐volume bleeders predictably become anemic in time. • Pericardial and pleural effusion in the majority of cases can be diagnosed via the AFAST DH view. In one study, approximately 85% of clinically relevant pericardial effusion (and cardiac tamponade) was reportedly detected via the DH View (Lisciandro 2016a). Always look into the thorax when performing the DH view. • The most common cause for pericardial effusion is neoplasia followed by idiopathic in the dog and is heart failure in cats (75%) (Stafford Johnson et al. 2004; Hall et al. 2007; McDonald et al. 2007). However, the presence of ascites (modified transudate) in dogs, that are also echo negative for a cardiac related mass, has a reported median survival of 605 days (versus 45 days without ascites). • The gallbladder “halo sign” serves as a marker for canine anaphylaxis (Quantz et al. 2009; Lisciandro 2016; Lisciandro and Lisciandro 2019), referred to as an “anaphylactic gallbladder” by the author. The finding, however, is not pathognomonic and in acutely collapsed and weak dogs pericardial effusion and right‐sided heart failure, including dilated cardiomyopathy, should be ruled out, with the gallbladder wall edema in these cases referred to as a “cardiac gallbladder” by the author (Lisciandro 2019). • Always rule out pericardial effusion/cardiac tamponade when observing gallbladder wall edema by looking past the diaphragm for the “racetrack sign” and, in the absence of pericardial effusion, the right TFAST pericardial site views for dilated cardiomyopathy and right‐sided heart enlargement (increased RV:LV). Although rare, cats may also develop the “cardiac gallbladder” (Lisciandro 2019). • Sonographic striation representing gallbladder wall edema can occur in dogs with normal or equivocal abnormal gallbladder wall thickness (Quantz et al. 2009: Lisciandro and Lisciandro 2019). • Integrating characterization of the caudal vena cava (CVC) can rapidly distinguish an “anaphylactic gallbladder” from a “cardiac gallbladder” through the finding of a flat, small CVC, versus a FAT dis- tended CVC, respectively. • Ascites (modified transudate) with an echo‐nega- tive study for a cardiac‐related mass carries a better prognosis in cases of canine pericardial effusion with a reported median survival time of 605 days (versus 45 days without ascites) (Stafford Johnson et al. 2007). • The urinary bladder volume may be estimated using the formula Length × Height × Width (cm) × 0.625 which provides an estimate in milliliters (Lisciandro and Fosgate 2017). Over time, the for - mula may be used serially to estimate urine output non‐invasively. • Normal residual urine after voiding in the dog is 0.2 mL/kg (Atalan et al. 1999). • Both kidneys are often reliably imaged through the SR view in cats and some dogs. • AFAST is superior to radiographic serosal detail in two major ways: it can both detect the presence or absence of free intraabdominal fluid and also semi- quantitate its volume over radiographic assessment that is unreliable (Lisciandro et al. 2009). • AFAST carries the potential to detect soft tissue abnormalities missed radiographically.

POCUS Liver and Gallbladder • Liver assessment is subjective. Edges of the liver lobes should be sharply pointed. Rounded margins of liver lobes and hepatic extension (especially the left lobes) beyond the costal arch suggest enlarge- ment. Abdominal radiography is more reliable for the determination of hepatomegaly. • Target lesions: single target lesions have a high pre- dictive value for malignancy. When multiple target lesions are seen, the positive predictive value of malignancy increases from 74% to 81% (Cuccovillo and Lamb 2002). • Normal echogenicity rule of thumb: the spleen (S) is more echogenic (hyperechoic) than the liver (Li) which is the same or slightly more echogenic (brighter) than the cortex of the kidney (Ck), remembered by the mnemonic “SLiCk.” For the feline, hepatic echogenicity is often compared to the adjacent falciform fat and the feline liver should be isoechoic to slightly hyperechoic (brighter) to the falciform fat. The feline liver, spleen, and cortex of the kidney are isoechoic to one another. • Gallbladder wall thickness is normally <1 mm in cats and <3 mm in dogs (Spaulding 1993; Hittmair et al. 2001; Quantz et al. 2009). • Sonographic striation representing gallbladder wall edema can occur in dogs with normal or equivocal abnormal gallbladder wall thickness. • Gallbladder luminal content is generally homoge- neous anechoic bile although degrees of gallbladder sludge may be considered as clinically irrelevant or may indicate cholestasis based on the patient’s clinical profile (Tsukagoshi et al. 2012). • The gallbladder, being fluid filled, is subject to several artifacts including side‐lobe, edge shadowing, and acoustic enhancement in the far‐field; and the liver and gallbladder, being adjacent to the strong soft tissue–air interface between the diaphragm and the aerated lung, are subject to mirror image artifact. • In cats, tortuosity of the bile duct can be a normal variation and a bile duct greater than 4 mm is con- sidered to be consistent with extrahepatic biliary obstruction (d’Anjou 2008). POCUS Spleen • Spleen size is subjective. A spleen that extends to a small or medium‐sized urinary bladder is consid- ered enlarged. • Sonographic recognizing features of the spleen are its hyperechoic capsule and that its blood supply splits the capsule, unlike the liver.

954 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER • A folded spleen in a cat is always abnormal and indicates splenomegaly (Hecht 2008). • Normal cat spleen thickness is <10 mm (Reese et al. 2012). • Benign nodular hyperplasia usually consists of nodules that are of homogeneous echotexture, being either hypoechoic or hyperechoic. • Splenic masses that deform the capsule of the spleen should always be considered a serious find- ing until proven otherwise. • Splenic lymphoma has been characterized as a “Swiss cheese appearance” with increased echo- genicity (brighter) in contrast to a splenic torsion that looks similar; however, the spleen has decreased echogenicity (darker). • The “whale tail” appearance of the splenic vein that enters and then splits toward the head and tail of the spleen is a landmark for both dogs (more prominent) and cats. • Target lesions: single target lesions have a high pre- dictive value for malignancy. When multiple target lesions are seen, the positive predictive value of malignancy increases from 74% to 81% (Cuccovillo and Lamb 2002). • Normal echogenicity rule of thumb: the spleen (S) is more echogenic (hyperechoic) than the liver (Li) which is the same or slightly more echogenic (brighter) than the cortex of the kidney (Ck), remembered by the mnemonic “SLiCk.” For the feline, hepatic echogenicity is often compared to the adjacent falciform fat and the feline liver should be isoechoic to slightly hyperechoic (brighter) to the falciform fat. The feline liver, spleen, and cortex of the kidney are isoechoic to one another. POCUS kidney • Normal kidney size for cats is generally considered to be 3.0–4.4 cm in length depending on the refer - ence (Nickel et al. 1973; Walter et al. 1987). • Normal kidney size in dogs is variable and depends on the size of the dog so assessment is generally subjective. Therefore, assessment of symmetry and size between the two kidneys is particularly important in dogs (d’Anjou 2008). • Normal renal pelvis size (height in mm). Variability in both species. General rule of thumb is to consider abnormal if ≥3 mm cats and ≥4 mm dogs (normals: cat 1.5–2 mm with maximum of 2.8 mm; dogs 2–3 mm with a maximum of 3.8 mm) (d’Anjou et al. 2011). • Perirenal fluid is not uncommon in cases of urinary obstruction and acute renal failure. • Perirenal fluid and ascites have been reported to occur in feline urinary urethral obstruction that resolves in the great majority of cases without sur - gical intervention (and in dogs too, author experi- ence) (Nevins et al. 2015). • Normal echogenicity rule of thumb: the spleen (S) is more echogenic (hyperechoic) than the liver (Li) which is the same or slightly more echogenic (brighter) than the cortex of the kidney (Ck), remembered by the mnemonic “SLiCk.” For the feline, hepatic echogenicity is often compared to the adjacent falciform fat and the feline liver should be isoechoic to slightly hyperechoic (brighter) to the falciform fat. The feline liver, spleen, and cortex of the kidney are isoechoic to one another. POCUS Urinary Bladder • The thickness of the urinary bladder wall varies depending on the degree of distension. • Normal range for urinary bladder wall thickness in cats is 1.3–1.7 mm (Finn‐Bodner et al. 1995; Nevins et al. 2015). • Normal range for urinary bladder wall thickness in dogs is from 1.4 mm in moderately distended blad- ders to 2.3 mm in minimally distended bladders (Geisse et al. 1997). However, wall thickness in dogs has been reported to increase with body size, with heavier dogs having increased thickness by up to 1 mm or a maximum normal thickness of ≤3 mm (Geisse et al. 1997). • The use of color flow Doppler potentially differen- tiates a thrombus (and artifact) from bladder masses by documenting whether pulsatile blood flow is present. • Voiding urohydropulsion (VUH) guidelines are as follows (Defarges et al. 2013). ◦ Female dogs (>2–kg) can typically void stones <3–4 mm.* ◦ Female cats may be able to void stones <3 mm.* ◦ Male dogs weighing 5–10 kg may be able to void stones <2–3 mm and male dogs >10 kg stones <3 mm.* ◦ Male cats: VUH is not recommended. *The ease of passing a 9 French urinary catheter correlates with the successful voiding of 3 mm stones. • The urinary bladder, being fluid filled, is subject to several artifacts including side‐lobe, slice‐thick- ness, edge shadowing, and acoustic enhancement in the far‐field. Turning down the gain is a quick trick to eliminate slice‐thickness and side‐lobe arti- facts that mimic sediment.

955 QUICk REFERENCES OF NORMAL V ALUES AND RULES OF THUMB POCUS Gastrointestinal and Pancreas Gastrointestinal • Normal stomach wall thickness: dogs 3–5 mm (higher in some giant breeds); cats 2 mm interrugal (up to 4.4 mm if rugal fold is measured) (Nyland et al. 2002; Nyland and Mattoon 2015b). Measure from the hyperechoic outer serosal margin to the inner hyperechoic mucosoluminal surface. • In dogs, the descending duodenal wall is thicker than other small intestinal segments and can nor - mally measure up to 5 mm in large breed dogs (Newell et al. 1999). Measure from the hyperechoic outer serosal margin to the inner hyperechoic mucosoluminal surface. • Small bowel wall measurements other than the duo- denum of greater than 4 mm in dogs and 2.5 mm in cats would generally be considered as abnormally thickened (Newell et al. 1999). Measure from the hyperechoic outer serosal margin to the inner hyperechoic mucosoluminal surface. • Use the mnemonic “the sun is bright and it’s dark at midnight” to remember that layers starting with an “s” like the sun are bright (submucosa and serosa are hyperechoic [bright]), while layers starting with an “m” like midnight are dark (mucosa and muscular layer are hypoechoic [dark]) on the ultrasound image). • Direct evidence of gastrointestinal foreign bodies. The majority of ultrasonographically detectable gastrointestinal foreign bodies typically involve a well‐defined hyperechoic, hyperreflective acoustic interface with strong distal acoustic shadowing (Tidwell and Penninck 1992; Garcia et al. 2011). • Linear foreign bodies: plication vs corrugation. The finding of bowel plication is strongly suggestive of a linear foreign body and should prompt careful evaluation of the intestine (longitudinal and transverse images) at sites where plication is seen (Tidwell and Penninck 1992; Garcia et al. 2011). Intestinal corrugation has also been associated with linear foreign bodies (Tidwell and Penninck 1992) but is less specific than plication. • In differentiating “corrugated” from “plicated” bowel, overall direction of the intestine tends to appear straight with corrugated bowel (medical causes – enteritis/pancreatitis) in contrast to bunched or weaved with plicated bowel (surgical causes – linear foreign body). • Indirect evidence of obstruction, such as a severely dilated jejunum with luminal dilation measuring greater than 1.5 cm, may highlight the need for a more extensive and complete abdominal ultrasonographic evaluation, abdominal radiographs or exploratory surgery. Measure from serosal to serosal surface. • Determine the number of contractions per minute by recording the number of contractions over a three‐minute period and average to get the number of contractions per minute (Penninck et al. 1989). • The mean number of peristaltic contractions of the stomach and proximal duodenum is 4–5 contrac- tions per minute (Penninck et al. 1989). • The mean number of peristaltic contractions of the small intestine (jejunum) averages 1–3 contractions per minute (Penninck et al. 1989). • The large bowel (colon) normally has no peristalsis. • A generalized decrease in gastrointestinal motility is reported in small animals with functional and chronic mechanical ileus, whereas a generalized increase in motility is most commonly reported in cases of acute mechanical obstruction (Penninck 2008a). However, because of considerable overlap in motility, motility alone does not indicate the need for surgery (Sharma et al. 2011; Garcia et al. 2011). Pancreas • The right pancreatic limb is generally easiest to image in dogs and is the more common lobe affected by pancreatitis (Hecht and Henry 2007; Nyland et al. 2002; Penninck 2008b). • The left pancreatic limb is generally easiest to image in cats. • Identification of the pancreas can be challenging for the novice sonographer because the pancreas is isoechoic to adjacent tissues. As a result, its identification commonly relies on the observance of its duct and vasculature. • Historically, it has been thought that a normal pan- creas is generally not seen; however, the normal pan- creas is in fact frequently imaged with high‐frequency transducers and newer machines. • Pancreatitis is particularly common when corruga- tion of the duodenum is noted (Moon et al. 2003). • Even in cases of severe acute pancreatitis, the sen- sitivity of ultrasound may only be 68% (Hess et al. 1998). Note that variability exists in litters where a fetus may be severely distressed and another normal. • M‐mode provides a more accurate heart rate of the fetus; however, the “eyeball method” may also be used. • Normal ultrasonographic layering of the small bowel in the fetus may be used as a guideline for full‐term maturation of puppies and kittens (Mattoon and Nyland 2002). • In anestrus, there is no uterine luminal fluid in nor- malcy; however, in estrus there may be a thin echo- genic stripe also considered as a normal finding (Mattoon and Nyland 2002; Verstegen et al. 2008). • Abdominal radiography is the most accurate way of determining the number of puppies or kittens in the litter (Davidson and Baker 2009). Avoid telling clients numbers in the litter using ultrasound because of its inaccuracy.
