TFAST® • A‐lines with “lung sliding” rules out pneumo- thorax (PTX) and supports “dry lung” at the lung periphery (Lisciandro et al. 2008). • B‐lines immediately rule out PTX at that specific location on the thoracic wall and support “wet lung” at the lung periphery. • “Wet lung” in trauma cases are lung contusions until proven otherwise (Lisciandro 2011; Dicker et al. 2019). • A‐lines without “lung sliding” with a “lung point” diagnose PTX (Lisciandro et al. 2008). • The “lung pulse” is another finding in PTX in which “lung sliding” is in synchrony with the heartbeats rather than phases of respiration due to severely atelectatic or consolidated lung. • Arguably, the best view for evaluating pleural and pericardial spaces is the diaphragmatico‐hepatic (DH) view because of less air interference via the acoustic window of the liver and gallbladder (Reissig et al. 2011; Lisciandro 2016). • The DH view is likely close to 100% sensitive and 100% specific in dogs with clinically relevant peri- cardial effusion via observation of the “racetrack sign” and is a good test in cats (Lisciandro 2014a,b, 2016). • The TFAST right‐sided cardiac markers include (1) the right ventricular to left ventricular ratio (RV:LV), (2) characterization of the caudal vena cava and hepatic veins, and (3) characterization of the gallbladder wall. The pulmonary artery to aortic ratio (PA:Ao) may also be used on right para- sternal short‐axis views. In right‐sided failure, the following changes would be expected: an increased

957 QUICk REFERENCES OF NORMAL V ALUES AND RULES OF THUMB RV:LV , a FAT distended caudal vena cava and hepatic venous distension (“tree trunk sign”), and gallbladder wall edema (“cardiac gallbladder”) as well as a PA:Ao >1:1. • The TFAST “mushroom view” is used to assess volume status and contractility in both dogs and cats. A fractional shortening (FS%) of <20% is diag- nostic of poor systolic function and dilated cardiomyopathy. • The right TFAST pericardial site view and the LA:Ao on short axis screen for left‐sided heart strain/over- load/failure and is obviously abnormal when the left atrium is twice the size of the aorta (LA:Ao >2:1). The “Global FAST nonecho fallback strategy” is the characterization of lung on Vet BLUE. • The right TFAST pericardial site view and the RV:LV on long axis screen for right‐sided strain/ overload/failure and is obviously abnormal when the right ventricle is nearly the same size as the left ventricle (RV:LV ~1:1). The “Global FAST nonecho fallback strategy” is characterization of the caudal vena cava and hepatic veins at the FAST DH view. • TFAST is used to screen for volume status via char- acterization of the caudal vena cava and its associ- ated hepatic veins (combined with the short‐axis left ventricular “mushroom view”) expecting that nei- ther would be distended unless right heart strain/ overload/failure is present (Nelson et al. 2010). • Ascites (modified transudate) with an echo‐ negative study for a cardiac‐related mass carries a better prognosis in canine pericardial effusion (Stafford Johnson et al. 2004). • Heart failure is the most common cause of pericar- dial effusion in cats (Hall et al. 2007; Ward et al. 2018). • Neoplasia and idiopathic are the most common causes of pericardial effusion in dogs (Stafford Johnson et al. 2004; Shaw and Rush 2007; MacDonald et al. 2009). Vet BLUE® • A‐lines with “lung sliding” referred to as “dry lung” (Lisciandro 2011; Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2017). • B‐lines, synonymous with ultrasound lung rockets, are referred to as “wet lung,” representing most commonly forms of alveolar‐interstitial edema that must be placed into clinical context and a regional pattern‐based approach as with Vet BLUE (Lisciandro 2011, 2012; Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2017). • The “step sign” and its subsets including the “shred sign,” “tissue sign,” nodule sign,” and “wedge sign” represent forms of lung consolidation and infiltration (Lisciandro et al. 2009; Lichtenstein 2010; Lisciandro 2011, 2014; Hecht and Penninck 2015; Ward et al. 2017, 2019; Dicker et al. 2019). • In normalcy, adult dogs and cats and puppies and kittens >6 weeks of age uncommonly have B‐lines on Vet BLUE with no more than a single B‐line spo- radically at one and much less commonly two Vet Blue views (Lisciandro et al. 2018). • B‐lines in Caudodorsal and Perihilar lung regions or a widespread presence most commonly repre- sent forms of cardiogenic pulmonary edema from left‐sided congestive heart failure in acute respiratory distress; and integration of TFAST echo findings and Global FAST nonecho fallback views are key (Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2017; Ward et al. 2017). • B‐lines in Caudodorsal and Perihilar lung regions symmetrically support noncardiogenic pulmonary edema when placed into clinical context; and integration of TFAST echo findings and Global FAST nonecho fallback views are key. • B‐lines and “shred signs” in ventral gravity‐ dependent Middle and Cranial lung regions support bacterial and aspiration pneumonia in acute respiratory distress. • “Wedge sign” in Caudodorsal and Perihilar lung regions supports the presence of pulmonary throm- boembolism (Lisciandro 2013, unpublished data). • B‐lines are counted as 1, 2, 3, considered weak pos- itives, and >3 when more than 3 but still recog- nized as individual B‐lines, and ∞ (infinity) when lines are confluent over an entire intercostal space, as strong positives (Ward et al. 2017). • Numbers of B‐lines correlate with the degree of alveolar‐interstitial edema on computed tomog- raphy (CT) in human lung and likely the same holds true for small animals (Volpicelli et al. 2006). • “Absence of B‐lines All (Vet BLUE) Views” effec- tively rules out left‐sided congestive heart failure in dogs and cats with ~96% sensitivity (Lisciandro et al. 2016). • B‐lines in trauma patients represent lung contu- sions until proven otherwise (Soldati et al. 2006; Lisciandro 2011; Dicker et al. 2019). • Expect no B‐lines at all Vet BLUE views as a general rule in adult dogs and cats and puppies and kittens >6 weeks of age (Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2017, 2018). • The more B‐lines, the more alveolar‐interstitial edema, and conversely lower scores represent less alveolar‐interstitial edema. Thus, the strategy may be used to guide loop diuretic administration in left‐sided congestive heart failure, monitor and guide therapy for other forms of lung edema, and score the severity of lung contusions (Lisciandro

POCUS Heart • In normalcy, the left ventricle (LV) should be 3–4 times larger than the right ventricle (RV) in the right parasternal four‐chamber view (3:1). • Cats and left ventricular hypertrophy: feline inter - ventricular septum (IVS) and left ventricular free wall (LVFW) thickness in diastole should be approximately 3–4 mm. LV wall thickness in dias- tole ≥6 mm is diagnostic for left ventricular hypertrophy. • Pseudohypertrophy in cats: extreme hypovolemia causing “pseudohypertrophy” of the left ventricle can be misinterpreted as hypertrophic cardiomy- opathy in the cat. • If the RV is the same size as the LV , then severe right ventricular enlargement can be diagnosed (and its various rule‐outs considered). • In normalcy, the left and right atria are approxi- mately the same size or 1:1 with a neutral (nonde- viated) interatrial septum. • In normalcy, the left atrium (LA) and aorta (Ao) in the short‐axis right parasternal view should be nearly the same size (1:1). • If the left atrium is more than 1.3 times the size of the aorta in dogs and 1.6 times in cats (LA:Ao >1.3:1 dogs, LA:Ao >1.6:1 cats) then the left atrium is enlarged, suggesting left‐sided heart disease (Rishniw and Erb 2000; Abbott and Maclean 2006). • Normal fractional shortening (FS%): in general, normal FS% is 28–45% in the dog and 30–50% in the cat. • Abnormal fractional shortening: a FS% below 20% is suggestive of severe myocardial systolic failure and a FS% above 55% would be considered hyper- dynamic LV function • Causes of pericardial effusion in dogs and cats: neoplasia and idiopathic pericardial effusion are most common causes of PCE in dogs. Heart failure is the most common cause in cats. • Left parasternal cranial view: allows for optimal visualization of the right heart, including the right auricle and tricuspid valve, and is the best view to visualize a small right auricular mass in a dog with pericardial effusion and cardiac tamponade. 963 QUICk REFERENCES OF NORMAL V ALUES AND RULES OF THUMB VetFAST‐ABCDE Exam • Used to confirm endotracheal placement by direct visualization of the cranial cervical region. • Used to survey cervical injury and abnormalities including tracheal lacerations and laryngeal dysfunction. • Optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD) measured 3 mm from the posterior eye should be ≤3 mm in dogs. Normal for cats is unknown. Values >3 mm may correlate with intracranial hypertension (Armenise 2012; Armenise et al. 2019). POCUS Marine Mammals • Breath holding (apnea) limits observation of “lung sliding” until the dolphin takes a breath. • Arching (and vocalizing) is a sign of distress in dol- phins during ultrasound examination. • Water environments make it mandatory to have battery‐powered ultrasound units to prevent electrocution. • Water environments make it mandatory to have screen covers or goggles for viewing the ultra- sound image. • Dolphins have small‐volume ascites in normalcy. Expect a positive AFAST for many dolphins that must be placed into clinical context, fluid scored and recorded, and the examination repeated. • The dolphin kidney is bovine‐like and multirenicu- lated (multilobulated), looking very different from the sonographic character of a canine or feline kidney. • TFAST echo views are more challenging due to breath holding and the barrel‐chested conformation of the dolphin. Transesophageal echocardiography provides much better studies (Chetboul et al. 2012; Sklansky et al. 2006; Sklansky et al. 2010). • The caudal vena cava and hepatic veins in dolphins are robust (hugely distended) in normalcy and appear like right‐sided volume overload in other species. • The “gator sign” orientation for lung is the same as for all other mammalian species. • Vet BLUE differs in dolphins having nine acoustic windows bilaterally on each hemithorax and lung is interrogated in longitudinal and transverse planes by gently rotating the probe from the starting “gator sign” position to 90° and returning to the “gator sign.” • Expect “dry lung” artifacts to predominate in dol- phins, as expected in other mammalian lung (Yarto and Lisciandro 2017, unpublished data). • The Vet BLUE B‐line scoring system and visual lung language are applied to dolphins the same as in small animals (Yarto and Lisciandro 2017, unpublished data; Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2017, 2018; Ward et al. 2017, 2019). • The marginal lymph nodes are markers for pulmonary disease in dolphins and should be imaged on every Global FAST (Smith et al. 2012). • The marginal lymph nodes have published expected normal measurement (Martony et al. 2017).
